  1. Calcium (Oxalate & Phosphate).
  2. Phosphate.
  3. Uric Acid (10% of gout patients).
  4. Rare Types:
    • Cystine (cystinuria, a transport defect).
    • Xanthine (xanthine oxidase deficiency).
    • 2,8-Dihydroxyadenine (APRT enzyme deficiency).

Treatment

  • Increase fluid intake to dilute urine.
  • Potassium citrate & thiazide diuretics (to prevent calcium stones).
  • Alkalinization of urine (to prevent uric acid stones).

Renal Acidosis

Uraemic Acidosis

  • Occurs in acute & chronic renal failure due to reduced H⁺ excretion.
  • High anion gap metabolic acidosis due to phosphate & sulfate retention.
  • Develops when GFR < 20 mL/min.
  • Associated with hyperkalemia.

Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)

  • Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with normal or slightly decreased GFR.
  • Urine pH often inappropriately high despite systemic acidosis.

Types of RTA

  1. Type 1 (Distal RTA)
    • Defective H⁺ secretion in the distal tubule.
    • Urine pH > 5.5, hypokalemia, nephrocalcinosis, rickets.
    • Can be genetic or acquired (e.g., heavy metal toxicity).
  2. Type 2 (Proximal RTA)
    • Defective bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
    • Hypokalemia, renal bicarbonate wasting, Fanconi syndrome.
    • Can be genetic (e.g., cystinosis) or acquired (toxins).
  3. Type 4 RTA
    • Due to mineralocorticoid deficiency or resistance.
    • Associated with hyperkalemia.

Rare Inherited Renal Tubular Disorders

Liddle’s Syndrome (Pseudohyperaldosteronism)

  • Hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Low renin & aldosterone.
  • Due to excess Na⁺ reabsorption (ENaC channel defect).

Pseudohypoaldosteronism Type 1 (PHA1)

  • Failure to thrive, hyponatremia, salt wasting, hyperkalemia.
  • Elevated renin & aldosterone.
  • Genetic mutation in ENaC channels.

Bartter’s Syndrome

  • Features: Failure to thrive (FTT), polyuria, nephrocalcinosis, short stature, mental retardation.
  • Electrolyte Imbalance: Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, renal salt wasting, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypercalciuria.
  • Cause: Sporadic or autosomal recessive (AR) mutation.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Overactivation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and hyperplasia of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
    • Increased production of prostaglandin E2 in the kidney.
    • Defects in epithelial cells of the medullary thick ascending limb (mTAL) of the nephron.
  • Key Mutations:
    1. NKCC2 (Na-K-Cl cotransporter): Impaired NaCl reabsorption → salt wasting, diuresis, kaliuresis, hypercalciuria.
    2. ROMK1 (K+ channel): Prevents normal Na-K exchange, leading to metabolic alkalosis and hypovolaemia.
    3. CLCKB (Basolateral Cl- channel): Causes further impairment of sodium and chloride handling.

Gitelman’s Syndrome

  • Features: Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria, and hypomagnesaemia.
  • Inheritance: Sporadic or autosomal recessive (AR).
  • Presentation: Late childhood or early adulthood.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Defect in the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter (NCCT) in the distal convoluted tubule.
    • Similar effects to chronic thiazide diuretic use.
    • Heterozygotes may develop hypokalaemic alkalosis if given loop or thiazide diuretics.

Dent’s Disease (X-linked Hypercalciuric Nephrolithiasis)

  • Features: Hypercalciuria, low-molecular-weight proteinuria, nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis, renal failure.
  • Associated Conditions: Fanconi syndrome-like tubulopathy, rickets.
  • Cause: Mutation in CLC5 (voltage-gated chloride channel).
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Impaired chloride transport may disrupt proximal tubule reabsorption.
    • Carrier females may show mild proteinuria and hypercalciuria.
  • Treatment: Renal transplant is effective in advanced disease.

Tests to Assess Gastric Function

1. Fractional Test Meal (FTM)

  • Procedure:
    1. Ryle’s tube inserted to aspirate fasting stomach contents.
    2. A test meal (e.g., rice, black coffee) is given.
    3. Gastric contents are collected every 15 min for 2 hours.
    4. Analysis of free and total acidity.
  • Use: Rarely used today.

2. Pentagastrin Stimulation Test

  • Purpose: Measures gastric acid secretion in response to pentagastrin (a gastrin analogue).
  • Procedure:
    1. Fasting gastric contents aspirated (residual juice).
    2. Gastric juice collected for 1 hour (basal acid output - BAO).
    3. Pentagastrin (5 µg/kg) administered.
    4. Gastric juice collected every 15 min for 1 hour (maximal acid output - MAO).
    5. Acidity measured by titration with NaOH.
  • Normal Values:
    • BAO: 4–10 mmol/hr
    • MAO: 20–50 mmol/hr

3. Augmented Histamine Test Meal

  • Purpose: Stimulates maximal gastric acid secretion.
  • Procedure:
    1. Basal secretion collected for 1 hour.
    2. Histamine injected subcutaneously.
    3. Gastric contents aspirated at 15 min intervals for 1 hour.
    4. Acid content measured.

4. Insulin Test Meal (Hollander’s Test)

  • Purpose: Assesses completeness of vagotomy (used in peptic ulcer surgery).
  • Procedure:
    1. Insulin (0.1 U/kg IV) administered.
    2. Hypoglycemia induces gastric acid secretion via vagal stimulation.
    3. No increase in acid secretion → successful vagotomy.
  • Risk: Hypoglycemia can be dangerous.

5. Tubeless Gastric Analysis

  • Principle:
    • Uses cation exchange resin that binds H⁺ ions in the stomach.
    • Excreted in urine → Indirect measure of gastric acidity.
  • Use: Screening test, less invasive.

Abnormalities of Gastric Function

Increased Gastric Acid Secretion

  • Causes:
    • Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumor)
    • Chronic duodenal ulcer
    • Gastric cell hyperplasia
    • Excessive histamine production

Decreased Gastric Acid Secretion

  • Causes:
    • Gastritis
    • Gastric carcinoma
    • Pernicious anemia (loss of parietal cells, low intrinsic factor)

Title: Inhibitors of Transcription
Content:
Inhibitors of Transcription

Transcription inhibitors are compounds that interfere with RNA synthesis by targeting RNA polymerase. Some of these inhibitors are used as antibiotics, while others are natural toxins.

1. Rifamycin (Rifampin) – Inhibitor of Prokaryotic Transcription

  • Produced by: Amycolatopsis rifamycinica (a bacterial species).
  • Targets: Prokaryotic RNA polymerase.
  • Mechanism of Action:
    • Binds to the β-subunit of RNA polymerase.
    • Prevents elongation of the mRNA strand.
    • Inhibits transcription initiation.
  • Clinical Use:
    • Used to treat Mycobacterium tuberculosis (causes tuberculosis).
    • Effective against other bacterial infections.

2. α-Amanitin – Inhibitor of Eukaryotic Transcription

  • Produced by: Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom).
  • Targets: Eukaryotic RNA polymerase II.
  • Mechanism of Action:
    • Strongly inhibits RNA polymerase II, which is responsible for synthesizing mRNA.
    • Moderate effect on RNA polymerase III (tRNA synthesis).
    • No effect on RNA polymerase I (rRNA synthesis).
  • Effects:
    • Leads to severe hepatotoxicity (liver damage).
    • Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and eventually organ failure.

Differences Between Transcription in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

Post-Transcriptional Modifications in Eukaryotic mRNA

  1. 5’ Capping:
    • Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap at the 5’ end.
    • Protects mRNA from degradation and helps in ribosome binding.
  2. Polyadenylation:
    • Addition of a poly-A tail at the 3’ end (about 200 adenine residues).
    • Helps in stability and nuclear export of mRNA.
  3. Splicing:
    • Removal of introns (non-coding sequences).
    • Exons (coding regions) are joined together to form mature mRNA.

Summary

  • Rifamycin inhibits prokaryotic transcription by binding to RNA polymerase β-subunit.
  • α-Amanitin inhibits eukaryotic transcription by targeting RNA polymerase II.
  • Key differences exist between transcription in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, including location, mRNA processing, regulation, and termination.
  • Eukaryotic mRNA requires post-transcriptional modifications before translation.

Translation: Protein Biosynthesis

Translation is the second step in gene expression, following transcription. It is the process by which ribosomes synthesize proteins using mRNA as a template.

1. Location of Translation

  • Prokaryotes: Occurs in free ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
  • Eukaryotes: Ribosomes can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER), where protein processing occurs.

2. Stages of Translation

Protein synthesis occurs in three major steps:

(A) Initiation

  • The goal is to bring together the mRNA, tRNA carrying the first amino acid, and the ribosomal subunits.
  • The mRNA contains a sequence of codons (triplets of nucleotides) that dictate which amino acids will be incorporated into the protein.
  • tRNA molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome.
  • The ribosome assembles, with:
    • The small ribosomal subunit binding to the mRNA.
    • The large ribosomal subunit joining later to complete the ribosome.

(B) Elongation

  • The ribosome moves along the mRNA, reading codons and adding amino acids in the correct sequence.
  • Each new amino acid is added to the growing protein chain by peptide bond formation.
  • Three key sites in the ribosome:
    • A (Aminoacyl) Site – Binds incoming tRNA carrying an amino acid.
    • P (Peptidyl) Site – Holds tRNA with the growing polypeptide chain.
    • E (Exit) Site – Where empty tRNA exits after donating its amino acid.

(C) Termination

  • Occurs when the ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) on the mRNA.
  • A release factor binds to the ribosome, causing it to disassemble, and the newly formed protein is released.

3. Role of tRNA in Translation

  • tRNA (Transfer RNA) molecules bring amino acids from the cytoplasm to the ribosome.
  • tRNA has a unique cloverleaf structure with 73-93 nucleotides.
  • Four distinct regions (lobes) are present:
    1. Anticodon Loop – Contains a sequence complementary to the mRNA codon to ensure correct amino acid pairing.
    2. Amino Acid Attachment Site – Located at the 3' end, where the correct amino acid binds.

4. Summary of Key Concepts

  • Translation is the process of protein synthesis from mRNA.
  • Takes place in the ribosomes in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
  • Involves three stages: Initiation, Elongation, and Termination.
  • tRNA molecules play a crucial role by bringing amino acids to the ribosome and matching codons with their anticodons.

Aminoacylation of tRNA (tRNA Charging)

1. Attachment of Amino Acids to tRNA

  • Each tRNA molecule must be attached to its corresponding amino acid to participate in protein synthesis.
  • This attachment process is catalyzed by an enzyme called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
  • There are 20 standard amino acids involved in protein synthesis.
  • Each amino acid has a specific synthetase enzyme that facilitates its attachment to tRNA.

2. Naming of Aminoacyl-tRNA Synthetase

  • The naming of synthetase enzymes is based on the amino acid they attach:
    • Example: The enzyme that attaches leucine to tRNA is called leucyl-tRNA synthetase.
    • Example: The enzyme that attaches glycine to tRNA is called glycyl-tRNA synthetase.

3. Types of tRNA Molecules

  • When an amino acid is correctly attached to its tRNA, the resulting molecule is called acylated tRNA or charged tRNA.
  • If a tRNA molecule lacks an amino acid (e.g., before aminoacylation), it is called uncharged tRNA.
  • If a tRNA molecule is mistakenly attached to the wrong amino acid, it is referred to as mischarged tRNA.

4. tRNA and Codon-Anticodon Interactions

  • Despite having only 20 amino acids, cells possess around 45 different tRNA molecules.
  • Messenger RNA (mRNA) contains 61 codons that specify amino acids.
  • The 45 different tRNA molecules must recognize 61 codons on mRNA, which is possible due to the "wobble hypothesis".

5. The Wobble Hypothesis

  • Each tRNA molecule carries an anticodon, which pairs with a codon on the mRNA.
  • The third base of the codon (the "wobble position") can pair with more than one nucleotide, allowing fewer tRNA molecules to recognize multiple codons.
  • Example: At the wobble position, uracil (U) on the tRNA anticodon can pair with adenine (A) or guanine (G) in the mRNA codon.

6. Role of Modified Nucleotides

  • Some tRNA anticodons contain modified bases, such as inosine (I), which can pair with uracil (U), adenine (A), or cytosine (C) on mRNA codons.
  • These modifications further increase the flexibility of codon-anticodon pairing.

7. Errors in tRNA Charging (Mischarged tRNA)

  • If a tRNA is mischarged (attached to the wrong amino acid), it must be corrected before translation.
  • Cells have proofreading mechanisms that prevent errors:
    • Hydrolytic editing removes incorrectly attached amino acids from the tRNA.
    • If mischarged tRNA is not corrected, the incorrect amino acid could be incorporated into the protein, leading to malfunction.
  • If codon-anticodon binding does not match, translation is halted, preventing errors in protein synthesis.

Steps in Transcription and Translation

1. Transcription Overview

Transcription is the process of converting DNA into mRNA, which occurs in three main stages:

  1. Initiation
  2. Elongation
  3. Termination

Steps in Translation

Translation is the process by which ribosomes read mRNA sequences and build proteins. It has three stages:

A. Initiation (Starting Translation)

The goal of initiation is to bring together:

  • mRNA
  • tRNA carrying the first amino acid
  • Two ribosomal subunits (small and large)

Steps in Initiation

  1. Binding of the Small Ribosomal Subunit to mRNA
    • In prokaryotes, mRNA binds to the small ribosomal subunit at a unique sequence called the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.
    • In eukaryotes, the ribosome recognizes the 5' cap at the beginning of mRNA. Without this cap, mRNA cannot bind to the ribosome.
  2. Binding of the Initiator tRNA
    • A special initiator tRNA binds to the start codon (AUG) on the mRNA.
    • In prokaryotes, this tRNA carries N-formylmethionine (fMet).
    • In eukaryotes, this tRNA carries methionine (Met).
  3. Recruitment of the Large Ribosomal Subunit
    • Initiation factors (special proteins) help bring the large ribosomal subunit to interact with the small ribosomal subunit.
    • The initiator tRNA occupies the P-site of the ribosome.
    • Once everything is in place, initiation is complete.

B. Elongation (Building the Protein)

During elongation, amino acids are added one by one to the growing protein. This process follows a continuous three-step cycle:

1. Codon Recognition

  • A charged tRNA (a tRNA carrying an amino acid) enters the A-site of the ribosome.
  • This tRNA has an anticodon complementary to the codon on the mRNA at the A-site.
  • The next tRNA, carrying an amino acid, enters the A-site of the ribosome.
  • This requires elongation factors, which help tRNA recognize and match the mRNA codon.
  • Base pairing occurs between the mRNA codon in the A-site and the corresponding tRNA anticodon.

2. Peptide Bond Formation

  • The ribosome has an enzyme-like rRNA (Peptidyl transferase) that catalyzes the formation of a peptide bond.
  • This bond links the amino acid in the P-site to the new amino acid in the A-site.
  • The growing polypeptide chain is transferred to the tRNA in the A-site.

3. Translocation (Shifting the Ribosome)

  • The ribosome moves along the mRNA to the next codon.
  • This movement shifts:
    • The tRNA in the P-site moves to the E-site, where it is ejected (it no longer carries an amino acid).
    • The tRNA in the A-site moves to the P-site, carrying the growing polypeptide chain.
    • A new tRNA enters the A-site, bringing the next amino acid.
  • This process requires energy from one GTP molecule.

This three-step cycle (Codon Recognition → Peptide Bond Formation → Translocation) repeats continuously until a stop codon is reached.

What Happens to tRNA in the E-Site?

  • The tRNA in the E-site has already transferred its amino acid to the growing chain and is now uncharged (without an amino acid).
  • It exits the ribosome and goes back to the cytoplasm to be recharged with another amino acid.

C. Termination (Ending Translation)

  1. When a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) reaches the A-site, translation stops.
  2. A release factor binds to the stop codon.
  3. The ribosome disassembles, and the completed polypeptide is released.

Summary of Key Points

  • Initiation: Small ribosomal subunit binds mRNA → Initiator tRNA binds AUG → Large subunit joins.
  • Elongation: Codon recognition → Peptide bond formation → Translocation.
  • Termination: Stop codon is recognized → Polypeptide is released → Ribosome disassembles.

Termination of Translation

Translation ends when a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) reaches the A-site of the ribosome. Unlike regular codons, stop codons do not have a corresponding tRNA. Instead, a release factor (RF) binds to the stop codon.

Steps in Termination

  1. A stop codon enters the A-site of the ribosome.
  2. A release factor binds to the stop codon instead of tRNA.
  3. The release factor triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the tRNA in the P-site.
  4. The newly synthesized polypeptide is released.
  5. The tRNA exits the ribosome.
  6. The ribosomal subunits disassemble, making the ribosome ready for a new round of translation.

1. What Happens When a Stop Codon Appears?

  • The ribosome moves along the mRNA, reading codons and matching them with tRNAs carrying amino acids.
  • At some point, a stop codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) reaches the A-site.
  • Stop codons do not have a matching tRNA—no tRNA can bind to them.

2. What Binds to the Stop Codon Instead?

  • Instead of a tRNA, a release factor (RF) enters the A-site.
    • In prokaryotes: RF-1 (for UAA, UAG) or RF-2 (for UAA, UGA).
    • In eukaryotes: eRF binds to any stop codon.

3. What Does the Release Factor Do?

  • The release factor causes hydrolysis of the bond between the last tRNA (in the P-site) and the polypeptide chain.
  • This releases the completed polypeptide from the ribosome.

4. What Happens to the Ribosome?

  • Another protein, Ribosome Recycling Factor (RRF), helps disassemble the ribosome.
  • The ribosome separates into its large and small subunits.
  • These subunits are now free to start translation again on another mRNA.

Why Doesn't Another tRNA Keep Coming?

  • Once the stop codon is reached, no new tRNA can enter the A-site because there is no matching anticodon.
  • The release factor stops the process and ensures everything is properly released.

How Are Amino Acids Attached to the Right Codons?

  • Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid that matches its anticodon.
  • This specificity is ensured by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, enzymes that attach the correct amino acid to the correct tRNA before translation starts.

Post-Translational Modifications (PTMs)

Once a protein is synthesized, it is not fully functional. Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic proteins undergo post-translational modifications to become active and functional.

Types of Post-Translational Modifications

1. Phosphorylation

  • Definition: Addition of a phosphate group to specific amino acids.
  • Target Amino Acids: Serine, Threonine, Tyrosine (all contain hydroxyl groups).
  • Function: Regulates protein activity (e.g., in signal transduction).
  • Example: Glycolysis - Activation of Glucose
    • The enzyme hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to form glucose-6-phosphate (G6P).
    • This traps glucose inside the cell and makes it available for further metabolism.

2. Glycosylation

  • Definition: Addition of sugar molecules to proteins.
  • Target Amino Acids: Asparagine (N-linked glycosylation), Serine, Threonine (O-linked glycosylation).
  • Function: Helps in protein folding, stability, and cell signaling.
  • Example: Glycoproteins like antibodies.

3. Acylation

  • Definition: Addition of an acyl group (fatty acid-like) to a protein.
  • Target Amino Acids: Asparagine, Lysine, Glutamine (contain nitrogen in their side chains).
  • Function: Regulates membrane attachment and signaling.
  • Example: Lipoproteins, including high-density lipoprotein (HDL).

4. Alkylation

  • Definition: Addition of an alkyl group (e.g., methyl) to proteins.
  • Target Amino Acids: Lysine, Arginine (contain nitrogen atoms in their side chains).
  • Function: Affects gene regulation and chromatin structure.
  • Example: Histone methylation, which controls DNA accessibility.

5. Hydroxylation

  • Definition: Addition of a hydroxyl (-OH) group to proteins.
  • Target Amino Acids: Proline, Lysine.
  • Function: Strengthens structural proteins.
  • Example: Collagen, which provides tensile strength to skin, bones, and muscles.

Polyribosomes in Prokaryotes

  • In prokaryotes, multiple ribosomes attach to a single mRNA molecule to synthesize multiple proteins at the same time.
  • This structure is called a polyribosome (polysome).
  • Translation in prokaryotes is fast, with ribosomes taking less than a minute to synthesize a polypeptide.

Summary

  • Termination occurs when a stop codon is reached, triggering polypeptide release and ribosome disassembly.
  • Post-translational modifications make proteins functional.
  • Key PTMs include:
    • Phosphorylation (Ser, Thr, Tyr) – regulates activity.
    • Glycosylation (Asn, Ser, Thr) – helps folding and stability.
    • Acylation (Asn, Lys, Gln) – membrane attachment.
    • Alkylation (Lys, Arg) – gene regulation.
    • Hydroxylation (Pro, Lys) – strengthens structural proteins like collagen.
  • Prokaryotes use polyribosomes to rapidly translate proteins.

Title: Inhibitors of Translation
Content:
Inhibitors of Translation

Translation inhibitors are mostly antibiotics that target bacterial ribosomes. Since bacteria rely heavily on protein synthesis, these drugs disrupt translation and prevent bacterial growth.

Differences Between Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Ribosomes

  • Prokaryotic ribosomes: 70S, composed of 30S (small subunit) and 50S (large subunit).
  • Eukaryotic ribosomes: 80S, composed of 40S (small subunit) and 60S (large subunit).

Most antibiotics target the differences between bacterial (prokaryotic) and human (eukaryotic) ribosomes to avoid harming human cells.

Differences Between Translation in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes

Categories of Translation Inhibitors (Antibiotics)

1. Aminoglycosides

  • Mechanism:
    • Bind to both 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits.
    • Block codon recognition, preventing translation.
    • Cause misreading of mRNA, leading to defective proteins.
  • Examples:
    • Streptomycin, Gentamicin, Kanamycin.
  • Toxicity & Side Effects:
    • Ototoxicity (hearing loss) – damages the ear.
    • Nephrotoxicity (kidney damage) – inhibits prostaglandins (vasodilators).
    • Vestibular damage – causes dizziness.
  • Resistance Mechanisms:
    • Ribosomal mutations preventing drug binding.
    • Enzymatic modification of the drug (phosphorylation).
    • Efflux pumps remove the drug from bacteria.

2. Tetracyclines

  • Mechanism:
    • Bind to 30S ribosomal subunit.
    • Block tRNA binding to mRNA, preventing elongation.
  • Examples:
    • Doxycycline, Oxytetracycline, Chlorotetracycline.
  • Toxicity & Side Effects:
    • Photosensitivity – avoid sun exposure.
    • Teeth discoloration – should not be given to children.
    • Gastrointestinal distress.
  • Resistance Mechanisms:
    • Efflux pumps remove the drug from bacterial cells.
    • Mutations in ribosomal binding sites.
    • Plasmid-coded resistance genes.

3. Macrolides

  • Mechanism:
    • Bind to 50S ribosomal subunit.
    • Prevent mRNA movement between the A-site and P-site, stopping elongation.
  • Examples:
    • Erythromycin, Clarithromycin, Azithromycin.
  • Toxicity & Side Effects:
    • Gastrointestinal (GIT) disturbances.
    • Metallic taste.
  • Resistance Mechanisms:
    • Methylation of 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing drug binding.
    • Efflux pumps remove the drug from the cell (plasmid-mediated).

4. Chloramphenicol

  • Mechanism:
    • Binds to 50S ribosomal subunit.
    • Inhibits peptide bond formation, stopping protein synthesis.
  • Toxicity & Side Effects:
    • Bone marrow suppression – can lead to aplastic anemia.
    • Mitochondrial damage – causes toxicity in human cells.
  • Resistance Mechanisms:
    • Bacteria produce enzymes that modify chloramphenicol, preventing its action.

Short-Answer Questions and Answers

1. Discuss in detail the mechanisms, actions, toxicity, and effects of translation-inhibiting drugs.

Answer:

  • Aminoglycosides bind both ribosomal subunits, interfere with codon recognition, and cause misreading of mRNA. They are bactericidal but cause renal and ear toxicity.
  • Tetracyclines bind to 30S, block tRNA attachment, and prevent elongation. They cause teeth discoloration and photosensitivity.
  • Macrolides bind 50S, block mRNA movement, and prevent elongation. They cause GIT issues and metallic taste.
  • Chloramphenicol binds 50S, blocks peptide bond formation, but has high toxicity (anemia, mitochondrial damage).
