SECTION B - SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (30 MARKS)

Question 1: Explain the astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling in the brain (6 marks)

Answer: Astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling, also known as the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, describes the metabolic partnership between these two cell types in the brain:

Mechanism:

  • Astrocytes preferentially take up glucose from blood capillaries via GLUT1 transporters
  • Glucose undergoes glycolysis in astrocytes, producing lactate even in the presence of adequate oxygen
  • Lactate is released from astrocytes via monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1)
  • Neurons take up lactate through MCT2 transporters
  • Neurons convert lactate to pyruvate via lactate dehydrogenase
  • Pyruvate enters neuronal mitochondria for oxidative metabolism via the TCA cycle

Significance:

  • This coupling allows efficient energy supply to neurons during periods of high synaptic activity
  • Astrocytes serve as glucose sensors and metabolic buffers
  • The system provides rapid energy substrate delivery to active neurons
  • It explains why brain glucose consumption exceeds what would be expected from direct neuronal uptake alone

Question 2: How does insulin release affect metabolism in liver and skeletal muscle tissues? (8 marks)

Answer:

Effects on Liver Metabolism:

Carbohydrate Metabolism:

  • Activates glycogen synthase (through dephosphorylation) promoting glycogen synthesis
  • Inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, reducing glycogen breakdown
  • Inhibits gluconeogenesis by suppressing key enzymes (PEPCK, G6Pase)
  • Promotes glycolysis by activating key regulatory enzymes

Lipid Metabolism:

  • Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, promoting fatty acid synthesis
  • Increases malonyl-CoA production, inhibiting fatty acid oxidation
  • Promotes triglyceride synthesis and VLDL formation
  • Inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase, reducing lipolysis

Effects on Skeletal Muscle Metabolism:

Glucose Utilization:

  • Stimulates GLUT4 translocation to cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake
  • Activates glycogen synthase, promoting muscle glycogen storage
  • Enhances glycolysis for immediate energy needs
  • Improves glucose tolerance and reduces blood glucose levels

Protein Metabolism:

  • Stimulates amino acid uptake into muscle cells
  • Promotes protein synthesis through mTOR pathway activation
  • Inhibits protein degradation, creating positive nitrogen balance
  • Enhances muscle growth and repair processes

Overall Integration:

  • Shifts metabolism from catabolic (fasting) to anabolic (fed) state
  • Coordinates substrate storage across tissues
  • Maintains glucose homeostasis by promoting glucose utilization and storage

Question 3: Elucidate the differences between how the body deals with moderate amounts of alcohol versus excess alcohol (8 marks)

Answer:

Moderate Alcohol Consumption:

Primary Pathway - Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH):

  • Ethanol → Acetaldehyde (via ADH in liver cytoplasm)
  • Acetaldehyde → Acetate (via aldehyde dehydrogenase in mitochondria)
  • Rate-limited by NAD+ availability (zero-order kinetics)
  • Typical elimination rate: 7-10g/hour
  • Produces moderate amounts of NADH

Metabolic Effects:

  • Mild inhibition of gluconeogenesis due to altered NAD+/NADH ratio
  • Minimal impact on fatty acid oxidation
  • No significant ketone body formation
  • Normal lactate/pyruvate ratio maintained relatively well

Excess Alcohol Consumption:

Secondary Pathway Activation - MEOS:

  • Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (CYP2E1) is induced
  • Located in liver endoplasmic reticulum
  • Consumes NADPH and generates ROS (reactive oxygen species)
  • Can handle higher alcohol concentrations

Severe Metabolic Consequences:

  • Massive NADH production overwhelms NAD+ regeneration
  • Severe inhibition of gluconeogenesis → hypoglycemia risk
  • Blocked fatty acid oxidation → fatty acid accumulation
  • Enhanced lipogenesis → fatty liver development
  • Lactate accumulation → lactic acidosis
  • Ketone body formation from impaired metabolism
  • Acetaldehyde accumulation → toxic effects

Pathological Effects:

  • Oxidative stress from ROS production
  • Hepatocellular damage and inflammation
  • Disrupted cellular energy charge
  • Impaired protein synthesis
  • Risk of alcoholic ketoacidosis

Question 4: How does lipid metabolism contribute to ketoacidosis? (8 marks)

Answer:

Initiation of Ketoacidosis:

Hormonal Triggers:

  • Insulin deficiency (diabetes) or glucagon excess
  • Increased epinephrine and cortisol during stress
  • Enhanced lipolysis in adipose tissue
  • Massive free fatty acid release into circulation

Hepatic Fatty Acid Metabolism:

Enhanced β-Oxidation:

  • Free fatty acids taken up by liver
  • Converted to fatty acyl-CoA by acyl-CoA synthetase
  • Transported into mitochondria via carnitine shuttle
  • Undergoes rapid β-oxidation producing acetyl-CoA

Overwhelming of TCA Cycle:

  • Acetyl-CoA production exceeds TCA cycle capacity
  • Oxaloacetate depletion due to gluconeogenesis
  • Unable to condense all acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate
  • Excess acetyl-CoA diverted to ketogenesis

Ketone Body Formation:

Biochemical Pathway:

  • Two acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA (via thiolase)
  • Acetoacetyl-CoA + Acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (via HMG-CoA synthase)
  • HMG-CoA → Acetoacetate (via HMG-CoA lyase)
  • Acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate (via β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase)
  • Spontaneous decarboxylation → Acetone

Development of Acidosis:

Acid Production:

  • Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are strong organic acids
  • Dissociate completely at physiological pH
  • Release H+ ions into circulation
  • Overwhelm blood buffering systems (bicarbonate, phosphate)

Compensatory Mechanisms Overwhelmed:

  • Respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) inadequate
  • Renal H+ excretion capacity exceeded
  • Progressive metabolic acidosis develops
  • Can lead to coma and death if untreated

Clinical Consequences:

  • Blood pH drops below 7.35
  • Anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • Dehydration from osmotic diuresis
  • Electrolyte imbalances (K+, Na+, Cl-)

SECTION C - LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (40 MARKS)

Question 1: Methanol Poisoning Case Study

a) Explain the metabolism of methanol and the mechanism of its toxicity (15 marks)

Methanol Metabolism:

Phase 1 - Initial Oxidation:

  • Methanol (CH₃OH) enters hepatocytes
  • Oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) to formaldehyde (HCHO)
  • Same enzyme that metabolizes ethanol but with lower affinity for methanol
  • Rate-limiting step in methanol toxicity

Phase 2 - Toxic Metabolite Formation:

  • Formaldehyde rapidly oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase
  • Converted to formic acid (HCOOH) - the primary toxic metabolite
  • Formic acid accumulates because its elimination is slow
  • Half-life of formic acid is 20 hours vs. 2-3 hours for formaldehyde

Phase 3 - Formic Acid Elimination:

  • Formic acid oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O via folate-dependent pathway
  • Requires tetrahydrofolate and 10-formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase
  • Process is easily saturated, leading to accumulation

Mechanisms of Toxicity:

Metabolic Acidosis:

  • Formic acid is a strong organic acid (pKa = 3.8)
  • Dissociates completely at physiological pH
  • Produces severe anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • Overwhelms blood buffering systems

Cellular Toxicity:

  • Formic acid inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV)
  • Blocks electron transport chain at final step
  • Prevents oxygen utilization despite adequate oxygen delivery
  • Creates "histotoxic hypoxia" condition

Tissue-Specific Effects:

  • Retinal toxicity: Rod and cone cell death, optic nerve damage
  • CNS toxicity: Basal ganglia necrosis, particularly putamen
  • Systemic effects: Multi-organ dysfunction from cellular hypoxia

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Initial CNS depression (similar to ethanol intoxication)
  • Latent period (6-30 hours) as methanol is metabolized
  • Severe acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation
  • Visual disturbances progressing to blindness
  • Altered mental status, seizures, coma

b) Explain the rationale behind treatment of methanol poisoning with ethanol (5 marks)

Competitive Inhibition Mechanism:

  • Ethanol and methanol compete for the same enzyme (alcohol dehydrogenase)
  • Ethanol has 10-20 times higher affinity for ADH than methanol
  • Administration of ethanol preferentially occupies ADH active sites
  • Prevents methanol conversion to toxic formaldehyde and formic acid

Therapeutic Strategy:

  • Maintain blood ethanol levels at 100-150 mg/dL
  • Allows time for methanol elimination through lungs and kidneys
  • Methanol eliminated unchanged via these routes (20-25%)
  • Prevents further toxic metabolite formation

Clinical Implementation:

  • IV ethanol infusion or oral administration
  • Monitor both ethanol and methanol blood levels
  • Continue until methanol levels drop to safe range (<20 mg/dL)
  • May require dialysis in severe cases to remove both methanol and metabolites

Additional Benefits:

  • Buys time for supportive care measures
  • Allows correction of acidosis with bicarbonate
  • Prevents irreversible organ damage
  • Modern alternative: fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) - specific ADH inhibitor

Question 2: Temperature regulation in infants with regard to adipose tissue (20 marks)

Answer:

Introduction to Neonatal Thermoregulation: Newborn infants face significant thermoregulatory challenges due to their high surface area-to-volume ratio, thin skin, limited subcutaneous fat, and immature nervous system. Unlike adults, infants cannot shiver effectively, making them dependent on specialized metabolic mechanisms for heat production.

Brown Adipose Tissue (BAT) - The Primary Thermogenic Organ:

Anatomical Distribution:

  • Located primarily in interscapular, axillary, and perirenal regions
  • Surrounds major blood vessels and organs (heart, kidneys, adrenals)
  • Comprises 2-5% of total body weight in healthy newborns
  • Rich vascularization with sympathetic innervation

Cellular Characteristics:

  • Multilocular adipocytes (multiple small lipid droplets)
  • High mitochondrial density (giving brown color)
  • Abundant cytochrome c oxidase
  • Expression of uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1/thermogenin)

Mechanism of Non-Shivering Thermogenesis:

Neural Activation:

  • Cold exposure detected by peripheral thermoreceptors
  • Signal transmitted to hypothalamic thermoregulatory center
  • Sympathetic nervous system activation
  • Norepinephrine release at BAT sympathetic terminals

Biochemical Cascade:

  • Norepinephrine binds β3-adrenergic receptors on brown adipocytes
  • Activates adenylyl cyclase → increased cAMP levels
  • Protein kinase A activation
  • Phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
  • Lipolysis of stored triglycerides

Mitochondrial Heat Production:

  • Free fatty acids activate UCP1 in inner mitochondrial membrane
  • UCP1 allows protons to bypass ATP synthase
  • Energy normally used for ATP synthesis is released as heat
  • Process called "uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation"
  • Can increase metabolic rate by 100-200%

Metabolic Integration:

Substrate Utilization:

  • Primary reliance on stored triglycerides in BAT
  • Glucose uptake increased to support thermogenesis
  • Fatty acid oxidation provides both fuel and UCP1 activation
  • Oxygen consumption dramatically increased

Hormonal Regulation:

  • Thyroid hormones (T3, T4) essential for UCP1 expression
  • Cortisol modulates thermogenic response
  • Insulin affects glucose uptake in BAT
  • Growth hormone influences BAT development

Clinical Significance:

Risk Factors for Hypothermia:

  • Premature infants have less BAT
  • Small for gestational age infants
  • Hypoglycemia impairs thermogenesis
  • Hypoxia reduces thermogenic capacity

Assessment and Monitoring:

  • Core temperature maintenance (36.5-37.5°C)
  • Monitoring for signs of cold stress
  • Oxygen consumption as indicator of thermogenic stress
  • Blood glucose monitoring during cold exposure

Therapeutic Interventions:

  • Maintaining neutral thermal environment
  • Appropriate clothing and swaddling
  • Incubator temperature control
  • Skin-to-skin contact (kangaroo care)
  • Nutritional support to maintain energy stores

Developmental Changes:

  • BAT activity highest in first weeks of life
  • Gradual decrease as shivering capacity develops
  • Transition to adult-type thermoregulation by 6 months
  • Environmental temperature control remains critical during this period

Pathological Conditions:

  • Hypothyroidism impairs BAT function
  • Sepsis can overwhelm thermogenic capacity
  • Malnutrition reduces substrate availability
  • Drug effects (anesthetics) can impair thermoregulation

Question 3: The three principles of fuel utilization during exercise (20 marks)

Answer:

PRINCIPLE 1: EXERCISE INTENSITY DETERMINES FUEL SELECTION

Low-Intensity Exercise (25-65% VO₂ max):

Fat as Primary Fuel:

  • Adequate oxygen availability for aerobic metabolism
  • Fatty acids mobilized from adipose tissue via hormone-sensitive lipase
  • Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA for TCA cycle
  • High ATP yield (129 ATP per palmitate molecule)
  • Sustained energy supply for prolonged activities

Metabolic Characteristics:

  • Low respiratory exchange ratio (RER = 0.70-0.85)
  • Enhanced fat oxidation enzymes (CPT-1, HAD)
  • Increased mitochondrial biogenesis with training
  • Sparing of limited carbohydrate stores

Moderate-Intensity Exercise (65-85% VO₂ max):

Mixed Fuel Utilization:

  • Combination of fat and carbohydrate oxidation
  • Crossover point where carbohydrate becomes dominant
  • Muscle glycogen and blood glucose contribute significantly
  • Maintained aerobic metabolism with some anaerobic contribution

High-Intensity Exercise (>85% VO₂ max):

Carbohydrate Dominance:

  • Rapid ATP demand exceeds fat oxidation capacity
  • Muscle glycogen becomes primary fuel source
  • Anaerobic glycolysis activated (lactate production)
  • RER approaches 1.0 (pure carbohydrate metabolism)
  • Limited duration due to substrate depletion and acidosis

PRINCIPLE 2: EXERCISE DURATION AFFECTS SUBSTRATE DEPLETION AND UTILIZATION

Immediate Energy (0-10 seconds):

Phosphocreatine System:

  • Creatine kinase rapidly regenerates ATP
  • No oxygen requirement (alactic)
  • Limited by phosphocreatine stores (~3-5 times ATP levels)
  • Power output can exceed 1000 watts in trained athletes

Short-Term Energy (10 seconds - 2 minutes):

Anaerobic Glycolysis:

  • Muscle glycogen breakdown without oxygen
  • Rapid ATP production (3 ATP per glucose from glycogen)
  • Lactate accumulation and pH decrease
  • Performance limited by acidosis and enzyme inhibition

Medium-Term Energy (2 minutes - 30 minutes):

Aerobic Glycolysis and Fat Oxidation:

  • Transition to oxidative metabolism
  • Muscle glycogen remains primary carbohydrate source
  • Increasing contribution from fat oxidation
  • Blood glucose maintains brain function
  • Liver glycogenolysis supports blood glucose

Long-Term Energy (>30 minutes):

Progressive Substrate Shifts:

  • Muscle glycogen depletion after 60-90 minutes
  • Increased reliance on blood glucose and fat
  • Hepatic glucose production becomes critical
  • Fat oxidation contribution increases progressively
  • Potential for gluconeogenesis from amino acids

"Hitting the Wall" Phenomenon:

  • Occurs when liver and muscle glycogen stores depleted
  • Blood glucose falls, affecting brain and muscle function
  • Performance dramatically decreases
  • Can be delayed by carbohydrate feeding during exercise

PRINCIPLE 3: TRAINING STATUS MODIFIES FUEL UTILIZATION PATTERNS

Metabolic Adaptations in Trained Athletes:

Enhanced Fat Oxidation Capacity:

  • Increased mitochondrial density (mitochondrial biogenesis)
  • Higher concentrations of oxidative enzymes
  • Improved capillarization of muscle fibers
  • Enhanced mobilization and transport of fatty acids
  • Greater intramuscular triglyceride stores

Improved Carbohydrate Utilization:

  • Increased muscle glycogen storage capacity
  • Enhanced glucose transporters (GLUT4)
  • Improved insulin sensitivity
  • Better lactate clearance and buffering capacity
  • Enhanced gluconeogenesis during prolonged exercise

Fiber Type Influences:

Type I (Slow-Twitch) Fibers:

  • High oxidative capacity
  • Abundant mitochondria and oxidative enzymes
  • Preferential fat utilization
  • Fatigue-resistant
  • Dominant in endurance athletes

Type IIa (Fast-Twitch Oxidative) Fibers:

  • Moderate oxidative and glycolytic capacity
  • Adaptable to training stimulus
  • Can utilize both fat and carbohydrate efficiently
  • Important for sustained power output

Type IIx (Fast-Twitch Glycolytic) Fibers:

  • High glycolytic capacity
  • Limited oxidative capacity
  • Preferential carbohydrate utilization
  • Rapid fatigue
  • Dominant in power/sprint athletes

Training-Induced Adaptations:

Endurance Training Effects:

  • Shifts crossover point to higher exercise intensities
  • Increases fat oxidation at submaximal intensities
  • Spares carbohydrate stores
  • Improves exercise economy and efficiency
  • Enhances lactate threshold

High-Intensity Training Effects:

  • Improves anaerobic power and capacity
  • Enhances lactate buffering and clearance
  • Increases muscle glycogen utilization
  • Improves neuromuscular coordination
  • Maintains high power output longer

Nutritional Strategies Based on Fuel Utilization:

Pre-Exercise Nutrition:

  • Carbohydrate loading for events >90 minutes
  • Fat adaptation strategies for ultra-endurance
  • Timing of meals to optimize substrate availability
  • Avoiding reactive hypoglycemia

During Exercise Nutrition:

  • Carbohydrate feeding for events >60 minutes
  • 30-60g carbohydrate per hour for moderate duration
  • Up to 90g/hour for events >2.5 hours (multiple transporters)
  • Maintaining blood glucose and sparing muscle glycogen

Post-Exercise Nutrition:

  • Rapid glycogen resynthesis within 2-hour window
  • Protein intake for muscle protein synthesis
  • Replenishing intramuscular triglyceride stores
  • Optimizing recovery for subsequent training

Clinical Applications:

Metabolic Diseases:

  • Diabetes management during exercise
  • Glycogen storage diseases
  • Fatty acid oxidation disorders
  • McArdle's disease (muscle phosphorylase deficiency)

Performance Optimization:

  • Periodization of training and nutrition
  • Altitude training adaptations
  • Heat acclimatization effects on metabolism
  • Age-related changes in fuel utilization

Integration of the Three Principles:

The three principles work synergistically to optimize energy production during exercise:

  1. Intensity-Duration Interaction: High-intensity exercise of short duration relies on stored phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis, while low-intensity, long-duration exercise progressively shifts toward fat oxidation.
  2. Training-Intensity Relationship: Well-trained athletes can maintain higher intensities while still utilizing significant amounts of fat, effectively shifting their crossover point rightward.
  3. Duration-Training Interaction: Trained athletes have enhanced capacity for both carbohydrate storage and fat oxidation, allowing them to sustain exercise longer at any given intensity.

Practical Applications:

  • Exercise prescription based on metabolic demands
  • Nutrition periodization aligned with training phases
  • Performance testing and monitoring
  • Rehabilitation considerations for different populations
  • Understanding individual metabolic responses

This comprehensive understanding of fuel utilization principles allows for evidence-based approaches to training, nutrition, and performance optimization across various exercise modalities and populations.

Question 1

Smooth muscles are confined to the following tissues, except:

  • A. Uterus
  • B. Arteries
  • C. Heart
  • D. Veins
  • E. GIT system

Answer: C. Heart

Explanation: The heart contains cardiac muscle, which is striated and involuntary, not smooth muscle. Smooth muscle is found in the uterus, blood vessels (arteries and veins), and the gastrointestinal tract.

Question 2

The following are components of the reticulo-endothelial system, except:

  • A. The spleen
  • B. The pancreas
  • C. The liver
  • D. The bone marrow
  • E. The blood

Answer: B. The pancreas

Explanation: The reticuloendothelial system includes organs involved in immune function and phagocytosis: spleen, liver, bone marrow, and circulating blood cells. The pancreas is primarily an endocrine and exocrine gland, not part of the reticuloendothelial system.

Question 3

The following statements are true regarding cerebral metabolism, except:

  • A. Brain receives a constant supply of glucose through the blood stream and cannot store glycogen
  • B. Ketone and glucose can both be fuel molecules for the brain
  • C. Ketone bodies and lactate are important substrates for energy and synthesis of lipids and amino acids
  • D. The brain cells adapt quickly and utilize ketone bodies in the event of starvation
  • E. Normally, glucose is the sole preferred fuel of the brain

Answer: D. The brain cells adapt quickly and utilize ketone bodies in the event of starvation

Explanation: Brain adaptation to ketone bodies takes several days to weeks, not quickly. The brain normally uses glucose but can adapt to use ketones during prolonged starvation or metabolic states like ketosis.

Question 4

Erythrocyte Production:

  • A. Is inhibited by anemia due to blood loss
  • B. Production is impaired at high altitude
  • C. Production is stimulated by erythropoietin
  • D. Are produced by the bone marrow of almost every bone in the body during the first 5 years of life
  • E. Are not produced in the fetal liver

Answer: C. Production is stimulated by erythropoietin

Explanation: Erythropoietin, produced by the kidneys, stimulates red blood cell production in response to hypoxia. Blood loss actually stimulates (not inhibits) erythropoiesis, and high altitude also stimulates production due to lower oxygen levels.

Question 5

Bile salts:

  • A. Are converted to secondary bile salts in the liver
  • B. Inhibit fat digestion
  • C. Inhibit intestinal motility
  • D. Help digestion of proteins
  • E. Stimulate bile secretion from the liver

Answer: E. Stimulate bile secretion from the liver

Explanation: Bile salts facilitate fat digestion and absorption. Secondary bile salts are formed in the intestine by bacterial action, not in the liver. They enhance, not inhibit, fat digestion.

Question 6

Individuals at risk of developing fatal Rh incompatibility are:

  • A. Any Rh+ fetus
  • B. Second Rh- fetus of Rh+ mother
  • C. Second Rh+ fetus of Rh- mother
  • D. Rh- mother
  • E. Rh- father

Answer: C. Second Rh+ fetus of Rh- mother

Explanation: Rh incompatibility occurs when an Rh- mother carries an Rh+ fetus. The second pregnancy is at risk because the mother was sensitized during the first pregnancy and developed antibodies against Rh+ blood.

Question 7

The following are functions of the liver, except:

  • E. Detoxification of xenobiotics

Answer: D. Synthesis of immunoglobulins

Explanation: Immunoglobulins (antibodies) are synthesized by plasma cells, not the liver. The liver performs all other listed functions: bile secretion, glycogen storage, clotting factor synthesis, and detoxification.

Question 8

In the vitreous humor glucose is converted to sorbitol by the enzyme:

  • C. Aldose reductase
  • D. Aldose dehydrogenase

Explanation: Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol in the polyol pathway. This is particularly important in diabetic complications where excess glucose leads to sorbitol accumulation in tissues like the eye.

Substances which are inactivated and excreted by the liver include the following except:

Explanation: Amino acids are not typically "inactivated" by the liver; they are metabolized for energy or used in protein synthesis. The liver does inactivate and excrete drugs, steroid hormones, enzymes, and bilirubin.

Explanation: About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the enterohepatic circulation. Bile is synthesized in the liver, not the gallbladder.

Question 36: Evaluate the use of proteins as markers for cancer diagnosis (4 Marks)

Answer:

Proteins serve as valuable tumor markers for cancer diagnosis through several mechanisms:

Tumor-Specific Proteins:

  • Cancer cells often produce abnormal proteins not found in healthy cells
  • Examples include PSA (prostate-specific antigen) for prostate cancer and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) for liver cancer
  • These proteins can be detected in blood, providing non-invasive diagnostic tools

Elevated Normal Proteins:

  • Some cancers cause overproduction of normally present proteins
  • CA-125 for ovarian cancer and CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) for colorectal cancer
  • Elevated levels indicate possible malignancy requiring further investigation

Enzyme Markers:

  • Cancer cells may release specific enzymes into circulation
  • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) isoenzymes can indicate tissue-specific cancers
  • Acid phosphatase elevation may suggest prostate cancer metastasis

Limitations:

  • Protein markers are often not specific to one cancer type
  • False positives can occur in benign conditions
  • Early-stage cancers may not produce detectable levels
  • Combined with imaging and biopsy for definitive diagnosis

Question 37: Explain the significance of laboratory tests to a medical practitioner (4 Marks)

Answer:

Laboratory tests are fundamental tools in medical practice with multiple critical applications:

Diagnostic Confirmation:

  • Biochemical tests confirm clinical suspicions with measurable data
  • Enzyme levels, hormone concentrations, and metabolite analysis provide objective evidence
  • Essential for distinguishing between conditions with similar symptoms

Disease Monitoring:

  • Track disease progression and treatment effectiveness
  • Blood glucose monitoring in diabetes management
  • Liver function tests during hepatotoxic drug therapy
  • Tumor markers for cancer recurrence surveillance

Preventive Medicine:

  • Early detection of disease through screening programs
  • Cholesterol levels for cardiovascular risk assessment
  • Hemoglobin A1c for diabetes screening
  • Identify risk factors before clinical symptoms appear

Treatment Guidance:

  • Determine appropriate therapeutic interventions
  • Drug level monitoring for optimal dosing
  • Therapeutic drug monitoring prevents toxicity
  • Guides decisions on medication adjustments and treatment duration

Question 38: How can a medical doctor detect errors in laboratory results (3 Marks)

Answer:

Medical doctors can identify laboratory errors through systematic evaluation:

Clinical Correlation:

  • Compare results with patient's clinical presentation and symptoms
  • Abnormal values that don't match the clinical picture suggest potential errors
  • Consider if results explain the patient's condition adequately

Reference Range Analysis:

  • Evaluate results against established normal ranges for the patient's age, sex, and condition
  • Critical values that seem implausible require verification
  • Consider physiological impossibilities (e.g., glucose levels incompatible with consciousness)

Trend Analysis:

  • Compare current results with previous laboratory values
  • Sudden dramatic changes without clinical explanation warrant investigation
  • Serial measurements should show logical progression with treatment

Quality Control Indicators:

  • Review sample collection details and timing
  • Check for hemolysis, lipemia, or other pre-analytical factors
  • Verify proper sample handling and storage conditions
  • Request repeat testing when values are inconsistent with clinical judgment

Question 39: Explain the clinical significance of determining blood lipid profiles (2 Marks)

Answer:

Blood lipid profiles provide crucial information for cardiovascular health assessment:

Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:

  • Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglyceride levels predict atherosclerotic disease risk
  • High LDL cholesterol promotes arterial plaque formation
  • Low HDL cholesterol reduces protective mechanisms against atherosclerosis
  • Elevated triglycerides contribute to cardiovascular disease, especially with diabetes

Treatment Monitoring:

  • Guides lipid-lowering therapy decisions and effectiveness
  • Monitors response to statins, fibrates, and other lipid medications
  • Helps achieve target levels for optimal cardiovascular protection
  • Assesses lifestyle modification success in conjunction with pharmaceutical interventions

Question 40: Explain the biochemical basis of methanol poisoning (3 Marks)

Answer:

Methanol poisoning involves toxic metabolite formation through alcohol dehydrogenase pathway:

Metabolic Pathway:

  • Methanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde
  • Formaldehyde is further oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to formic acid
  • Formic acid accumulates and causes systemic toxicity

Toxic Effects:

  • Formic acid inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondrial electron transport
  • This disrupts cellular respiration and ATP production
  • Metabolic acidosis develops due to lactate accumulation and formic acid
  • Optic nerve damage occurs due to selective vulnerability to formic acid

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Initial CNS depression similar to ethanol intoxication
  • Delayed onset of metabolic acidosis (12-24 hours)
  • Visual disturbances and potential permanent blindness
  • Treatment involves ethanol or fomepizole to compete with alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation

Question 41: Outline THREE factors contributing to muscle endurance adaptation during exercise (3 Marks)

Answer:

Mitochondrial Adaptations:

  • Increased mitochondrial number and size in muscle fibers
  • Enhanced oxidative enzyme activity for improved aerobic metabolism
  • Better oxygen utilization efficiency for sustained energy production

Cardiovascular Improvements:

  • Increased capillary density in muscle tissue
  • Enhanced cardiac output and stroke volume
  • Improved oxygen delivery and waste product removal from working muscles

Metabolic Efficiency:

  • Enhanced fat oxidation capacity, sparing muscle glycogen
  • Improved lactate buffering and clearance mechanisms
  • Increased muscle glycogen storage capacity for sustained energy availability

Question 42: Explain THREE distinct enzymatic pathways for ethanol metabolism (3 Marks)

Answer:

Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) Pathway:

  • Primary pathway occurring in liver cytoplasm
  • Ethanol + NAD+ → Acetaldehyde + NADH + H+
  • Acetaldehyde is oxidized to acetate by aldehyde dehydrogenase
  • Acetate is converted to acetyl-CoA for energy production

Microsomal Ethanol-Oxidizing System (MEOS):

  • Involves cytochrome P450 2E1 (CYP2E1) in liver microsomes
  • Ethanol + NADPH + H+ + O2 → Acetaldehyde + NADP+ + 2H2O
  • Becomes more important at high ethanol concentrations
  • Contributes to ethanol tolerance and drug interactions

Catalase Pathway:

  • Minor pathway using catalase enzyme
  • Ethanol + H2O2 → Acetaldehyde + 2H2O
  • Requires hydrogen peroxide as cofactor
  • Contributes minimally to overall ethanol metabolism under normal conditions

Question 43: Explain the role of Cori cycle in maintenance of blood sugar levels (3 Marks)

Answer:

The Cori cycle maintains glucose homeostasis through lactate recycling between muscle and liver:

Muscle Metabolism:

  • During intense exercise, muscle uses glucose anaerobically
  • Glycolysis produces lactate as an end product
  • Lactate is released into circulation to prevent intracellular acidosis

Hepatic Gluconeogenesis:

  • Liver takes up circulating lactate from muscle
  • Lactate is converted back to glucose through gluconeogenesis
  • This process requires ATP energy investment by the liver

Glucose Recycling:

  • Newly formed glucose is released back into circulation
  • Maintains blood glucose levels during periods of high muscle glucose consumption
  • Provides continuous glucose supply for brain and other glucose-dependent tissues
  • Particularly important during exercise when muscle glucose uptake is high

SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS [40 MARKS]

Answer TWO questions from this section

Question 44: Describe thermogenesis and regulation of non-shivering thermogenesis

(20 Marks)

A. Definition of Thermogenesis

  • Thermogenesis is the production of heat by metabolic processes to maintain body temperature.
  • It helps preserve homeostasis, especially during cold stress.

B. Types of Thermogenesis

  1. Shivering Thermogenesis
    • Involuntary, rhythmic muscle contractions.
    • Generates heat via increased ATP hydrolysis in skeletal muscle.
  2. Non-Shivering Thermogenesis (NST)
    • Occurs without muscle activity.
    • Mainly occurs in brown adipose tissue (BAT).
    • Prominent in neonates and cold-exposed adults.
    • Mediated by mitochondrial uncoupling via UCP1 (thermogenin).

C. Process of Non-Shivering Thermogenesis

  1. Cold Detection by Thermoreceptors
    • Thermoreceptors in the skin detect cold.
    • Signal transmitted via sensory neurons to the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center (preoptic area).
  2. Hypothalamic Activation of Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS)
    • Hypothalamus activates sympathetic efferent fibers.
    • Nerve endings in BAT release norepinephrine (NE).
  3. Adrenergic Activation in Brown Adipose Tissue
    • NE binds to β3-adrenergic receptors on brown adipocytes.
    • Activates adenylate cyclase → ↑ cAMP → activates Protein Kinase A (PKA).
  4. Stimulation of Lipolysis
    • PKA activates hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL).
    • Triglycerides in BAT are broken down into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol.
    • FFAs are used as fuel and also activate UCP1.
  5. Mitochondrial β-Oxidation of Fatty Acids
    • FFAs undergo β-oxidation in mitochondria.
    • Produces acetyl-CoA, NADH, FADH₂ → feeds TCA cycle and electron transport chain (ETC).
  6. Uncoupling via UCP1 (Thermogenin)
    • UCP1 is a proton channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
    • It allows protons to re-enter the mitochondrial matrix without generating ATP.
    • Energy from proton gradient is released as heat.

D. Regulation of Non-Shivering Thermogenesis

  1. Norepinephrine (SNS Mediator)
    • Primary stimulator via β3-receptors in BAT.
    • Triggers entire cascade from lipolysis to UCP1 activation.
  2. Thyroid Hormones (T3 & T4)
    • Increase basal metabolic rate.
    • Upregulate UCP1 gene expression.
    • T3 potentiates NE action by enhancing β-receptor sensitivity.
  3. Insulin
    • Promotes glucose uptake into brown adipocytes.
    • Provides substrate for oxidation and thermogenesis.
  4. Leptin
    • Secreted by white adipose tissue.
    • Acts on hypothalamus to stimulate sympathetic output.
    • Enhances BAT activation.
  5. Cortisol (Glucocorticoids)
    • Suppress NST at high levels.
    • Inhibit UCP1 transcription during chronic stress.

E. Clinical Importance

  • Neonates rely exclusively on NST due to:
    • High surface area to volume ratio.
    • Immature muscle coordination.
    • Abundant brown adipose tissue in interscapular region, neck, kidneys.
  • NST dysfunction leads to:
    • Neonatal hypothermia.
    • Increased risk of cold stress-related morbidity.
  • Research into BAT activation has implications for:
    • Obesity management.
    • Metabolic syndrome therapy.

Question 45: Describe in detail specific tissue enzymes of clinical importance

(20 Marks)

A. Concept of Tissue-Specific Enzymes

  • Tissue enzymes are concentrated in specific organs.
  • Leakage into blood signals tissue injury or pathology.
  • Serve as biochemical markers for diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring.

B. Examples of Key Tissue-Specific Enzymes

  1. Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
    • Found in hepatocytes (cytosol).
    • High specificity for liver damage (e.g., hepatitis, toxic injury).
    • Normal range: ~7–56 U/L.
  2. Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
    • Present in liver, cardiac and skeletal muscles.
    • Increased in MI, liver injury, muscular dystrophies.
    • ALT/AST ratio helps differentiate liver vs muscle injury.
  3. Creatine Kinase (CK/CPK)
    • Three isoenzymes:
      • CK-MM (muscle), CK-MB (cardiac), CK-BB (brain).
    • CK-MB elevated within 3–6 hrs post myocardial infarction.
    • CK-MM rises in muscle trauma, rhabdomyolysis.
  4. Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
    • Five isoenzymes (LDH1–5):
      • LDH1 – heart, RBCs.
      • LDH5 – liver, muscle.
    • LDH1/LDH2 flip indicates MI.
    • Elevated in hemolysis, cancer, liver diseases.
  5. Amylase
    • Secreted by pancreas and salivary glands.
    • Elevated in acute pancreatitis, salivary gland infections.
    • Rises within hours of attack.
  6. Lipase
    • More specific than amylase for pancreatic damage.
    • Remains elevated longer than amylase.
  7. Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
    • Found in liver, bone, placenta.
    • Raised in obstructive jaundice, bone growth (rickets), metastases.
    • Differentiated using isoenzyme studies.
  8. Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
    • Highly sensitive for hepatobiliary injury.
    • Elevated in alcoholism, biliary obstruction.
    • Raised ALP + GGT → hepatic origin.
  9. Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA)
    • Produced by prostatic epithelial cells.
    • Elevated in prostate cancer, BPH, or inflammation.
    • Used in screening and monitoring.

C. Clinical Applications

  • Diagnosis: Confirm tissue-specific damage (e.g., ALT in hepatitis).
  • Monitoring: Track disease progression or response to therapy.
  • Screening: PSA for prostate cancer, ALP for bone turnover.
  • Differential Diagnosis: CK-MB vs troponin in cardiac injury; ALT vs AST in liver diseases.

Question 46a: Describe tests that can be used to assess gastric functions

(10 Marks)

  1. Gastric Acid Secretion Test
    • Measures basal and stimulated gastric HCl output.
    • Pentagastrin used as stimulant.
    • Used in diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome or hypochlorhydria.
  2. Serum Gastrin Assay
    • Evaluates gastrin hormone levels.
    • Elevated in gastrinoma, atrophic gastritis, Pernicious anemia.
  3. Tubeless Gastric Analysis
    • Uses resin dye that changes color in acidic pH.
    • Indicates presence of gastric acid without endoscopy.
  4. Urea Breath Test
    • Detects Helicobacter pylori infection.
    • Patient ingests labeled urea; H. pylori produces urease → labeled CO₂ exhaled.
  5. Pepsinogen I and II
    • Proenzymes of pepsin.
    • Low levels may indicate mucosal atrophy or gastric carcinoma risk.
  6. Endoscopy with Biopsy
    • Direct visualization of mucosa.
    • Biopsy enables diagnosis of gastritis, ulcers, neoplasia.

Question 46b: Discuss briefly any FOUR intermediates acting as metabolic junctions

(10 Marks)

  1. Acetyl-CoA
    • Central to carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism.
    • Formed from pyruvate, fatty acids, and some amino acids.
    • Entry point into TCA cycle, fatty acid synthesis, ketogenesis.
  2. Pyruvate
    • Final product of glycolysis.
    • Can be converted to:
      • Acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle
      • Lactate (anaerobic)
      • Oxaloacetate (gluconeogenesis)
      • Alanine (via transamination)
  3. Ribulose-5-Phosphate
    • Intermediate in pentose phosphate pathway.
    • Source of ribose sugars for nucleotides.
    • Linked with generation of NADPH.
  4. NADPH
    • Key reducing agent in biosynthetic reactions.
    • Required for:
      • Fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis
      • Detoxification (cytochrome P450)
      • Regeneration of reduced glutathione

Title: Mount Kenya University – Medical Biochemistry II (MBMB 2200) -2
Content:
End of Year Examination for Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery
Date:.....can't say😂 | Time: 2 Hours
Unit Title: Medical Biochemistry II
Paper A (MBMB ...😂)
Section B: LAQs & SAQs

  • Understanding Disease Mechanisms: Integrated metabolism helps a doctor understand how metabolic pathways interact in different tissues, aiding in the recognition of systemic metabolic disorders like diabetes mellitus, obesity, and metabolic syndrome.
  • Clinical Decision Making: Enables better interpretation of laboratory results (e.g., glucose levels, lipid profiles) in the context of the body's overall metabolic state.
  • Pharmacological Insights: Understanding metabolic interrelationships helps doctors predict drug interactions and metabolic side effects, especially in diseases like liver failure or renal impairment.
  • Nutritional Management: Supports dietary planning in patients with chronic illnesses (e.g., advising low-carbohydrate diets in insulin resistance).
  • Emergency Care: Assists in acute cases such as diabetic ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis, where quick understanding of metabolic pathways is crucial.
  • Thermogenic Properties: Brown and beige fat have high mitochondrial density and express uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which dissipates energy as heat. This helps in increasing energy expenditure.
  • Weight Reduction: Activation of brown/beige fat promotes lipolysis and fat oxidation, leading to reduction in adipose tissue and body weight.
  • Improved Glucose Tolerance: These tissues increase glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity, thus improving glycemic control in diabetic patients.
  • Target for Therapy: Research is ongoing to identify drugs (like β3-adrenergic agonists or cold exposure mimetics) that stimulate brown/beige fat activity.
  • Metabolic Health: Enhances lipid clearance from blood, reducing risk of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular diseases linked to obesity and diabetes.
  • Integrated metabolism refers to the coordination of biochemical pathways across multiple organs and tissues to meet the energy and biosynthetic demands of the body.
  • Key metabolic organs include the liver, muscle, adipose tissue, brain, and kidneys.
  • Hormones such as insulin, glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, and growth hormone play vital roles in maintaining metabolic balance.
  • During feeding, anabolic pathways are activated (e.g., glycogenesis, lipogenesis), while in fasting, catabolic pathways (e.g., glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis) dominate.
  • Integration ensures efficient substrate allocation, energy conservation, and homeostasis, adapting to physiological states like rest, exercise, stress, or illness.
  • Serum enzyme levels serve as markers of hepatocellular injury or cholestasis.
  • Alanine aminotransferase (ALT): Highly specific to liver; elevation indicates hepatocyte injury.
  • Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): Less specific; also found in muscle and heart; ratio of AST/ALT may help differentiate alcoholic vs non-alcoholic liver disease.
  • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP): Elevated in bile duct obstruction and cholestatic liver diseases.
  • Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT): Supports cholestatic diagnosis and alcohol-induced damage.
  • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): Less specific but can suggest hepatocellular necrosis.
  • Monitoring enzyme trends over time helps assess disease severity, progression, and treatment response.
  • Correct Collection Technique: Use of sterile containers, avoiding hemolysis and contamination.
  • Labeling: Accurate patient identifiers, date and time of collection are essential.
  • Preservation: Certain tests (e.g., blood gases, hormones) require refrigeration or immediate analysis.
  • Transport: Samples must be sent promptly to the lab to prevent degradation or clotting.
  • Pre-analytical Variations: Diet, timing, and patient posture can affect results; clinicians must understand these.
  • Documentation: Proper record-keeping ensures traceability and supports legal and diagnostic accuracy.
  1. Blood Glucose: Evaluates carbohydrate metabolism; used in diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes mellitus.
  2. Serum Creatinine: Indicates kidney function; elevated levels suggest impaired glomerular filtration.
  3. Serum Bilirubin: Detects liver function or hemolysis; distinguishes between direct and indirect causes of jaundice.
  4. Serum Electrolytes (Na+, K+): Monitor hydration status, renal function, and heart rhythm stability.
  • The Van den Bergh test measures serum bilirubin using diazotized sulfanilic acid.
  • Direct (Conjugated) bilirubin: Reacts immediately (within 30 seconds) = direct positive reaction.
  • Indirect (Unconjugated) bilirubin: Requires alcohol as a solubilizer = indirect positive reaction.
  • Mixed reaction: Suggests hepatocellular jaundice.
  • Clinical Interpretation:
    • Direct positive: Obstructive jaundice (post-hepatic).
    • Indirect positive: Hemolytic jaundice (pre-hepatic).
    • Mixed reaction: Hepatitis or intrahepatic obstruction.

1. Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT):

  • ALT is mainly found in the liver and is a key marker of hepatocellular injury.
  • It rises significantly in viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver damage, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
  • Its specificity to the liver makes it useful for monitoring disease progression and treatment response.

2. Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST):

  • Present in liver, heart, skeletal muscle, and kidneys.
  • Elevated in myocardial infarction (MI), acute liver diseases, and muscle trauma.
  • When combined with ALT, the AST/ALT ratio helps differentiate alcoholic liver disease (>2) from viral hepatitis (<1).

3. Amylase:

  • Produced by pancreas and salivary glands.
  • Serum levels rise in acute pancreatitis, mumps, and salivary gland inflammation.
  • Levels increase within hours of pancreatic injury and are useful for early diagnosis.

4. Creatine Kinase (CK):

  • Exists in three isoforms: CK-MB (heart), CK-MM (skeletal muscle), and CK-BB (brain).
  • CK-MB rises in myocardial infarction and is used to confirm cardiac muscle damage.
  • CK-MM increases in muscular dystrophies and trauma; CK is also used to monitor statin toxicity.

5. Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP):

  • When elevated, it is often assessed alongside gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) to confirm hepatic origin.
  • Found in liver (biliary tract), bones, placenta, and intestines.
  • Raised in bile duct obstruction, bone diseases like rickets, and during pregnancy.

1. Pyruvate:

  • Formed from glycolysis.
  • Can be converted into acetyl-CoA (aerobic conditions), lactate (anaerobic), or oxaloacetate (gluconeogenesis).
  • Also a precursor for alanine in amino acid metabolism.
  • Thus, it links carbohydrate, lipid, and protein pathways.

2. Acetyl-CoA:

  • Produced from pyruvate, fatty acid β-oxidation, and amino acid catabolism.
  • Enters the TCA cycle for ATP production, forms ketone bodies during starvation, and serves as a precursor for cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis.
  • A major hub connecting energy production and biosynthetic processes.

3. Glucose-6-Phosphate (G6P):

  • A key intermediate of glycolysis.
  • Enters glycogenesis for storage, the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) for NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate, or continues through glycolysis for energy.
  • Connects glucose metabolism to anabolic and antioxidant pathways.

4. Oxaloacetate:

  • TCA cycle intermediate that combines with acetyl-CoA to form citrate.
  • Also a precursor for gluconeogenesis and transamination reactions.
  • Can convert to aspartate or malate, playing a key role in amino acid metabolism and the malate-aspartate shuttle.

Cori Cycle (Lactic Acid Cycle):

  • Demonstrates cooperation between skeletal muscle and liver.
  • During anaerobic exercise, muscles convert glucose to lactate (via glycolysis).
  • Lactate is transported via blood to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose by gluconeogenesis.
  • This glucose is then returned to the muscles for energy production.
  • The cycle prevents lactic acid accumulation and supports glucose homeostasis, especially during fasting or intense exercise.

1. Age:

  • Children and elderly have different metabolic rates and enzyme activity.
  • For example, ALP is naturally higher in children due to bone growth.

2. Sex/Gender:

  • Hormonal differences influence biochemical values.
  • Males usually have higher hemoglobin, creatinine, and ALT levels than females.

3. Diet and Fasting Status:

  • Recent food intake alters glucose, lipid, and insulin levels.
  • Fasting samples are preferred for accurate interpretation.

4. Physical Activity:

  • Strenuous exercise temporarily increases CK, AST, and lactate levels.
  • Can mimic pathological findings if not considered during interpretation.

5. Time of Day (Circadian Rhythm):

  • Some parameters vary by time.
  • Cortisol is highest in the morning; growth hormone peaks during sleep.
  • Hence, sample timing is standardized for accurate comparisons.

Title: Integrated Tissue Metabolism -LAQs and SAQs
Content:
a. Xenobiotic
A xenobiotic is any chemical substance that is foreign to a biological system, including drugs, pollutants, and food additives.

b. Hyperplasia
Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ, leading to its enlargement, often in response to a stimulus.

c. Tetany
Tetany is a condition characterized by involuntary muscle cramps or spasms, typically due to hypocalcemia (low blood calcium levels).

d. Fast-twitch fibers
Fast-twitch fibers are skeletal muscle fibers that contract quickly and powerfully but fatigue rapidly. They rely primarily on anaerobic metabolism.

e. Caul
A caul is a membrane, part of the amniotic sac, that may cover a newborn's head or face at birth. It is rare and usually harmless.

Mononuclear agranulocytes are white blood cells with a single, non-lobed nucleus and no visible cytoplasmic granules. The two main types are:

a. Lymphocytes

  • Types: B cells, T cells, and Natural Killer (NK) cells.
  • Roles:
    • B cells produce antibodies for humoral immunity.
    • T cells mediate cellular immunity (e.g., cytotoxic and helper functions).
    • NK cells destroy virus-infected and tumor cells without prior sensitization.

b. Monocytes

  • Role:
    • Circulate in the blood and migrate to tissues where they differentiate into macrophages or dendritic cells.
    • Macrophages perform phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and cytokine secretion.
    • Dendritic cells act as antigen-presenting cells to initiate immune responses.

Together, mononuclear agranulocytes play crucial roles in adaptive and innate immunity, inflammation, and tissue repair.

(2 marks each)

  1. Vascular Spasm
    Immediate vasoconstriction of injured blood vessels to reduce blood loss.
  2. Platelet Plug Formation
    Platelets adhere to exposed collagen, become activated, release chemical signals, and aggregate to form a temporary plug.
  3. Coagulation (Blood Clotting)
    A cascade of clotting factors activates the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, stabilizing the plug into a solid clot.

(3 marks each)

Neuro-glial metabolic coupling refers to the metabolic interaction between neurons and astrocytes, ensuring energy supply during neuronal activity.

  • Glucose uptake: Astrocytes take up glucose from the blood.
  • Lactate production: Astrocytes metabolize glucose to lactate via glycolysis.
  • Lactate shuttle: Lactate is released and taken up by neurons as a preferred energy source during activation.
  • Regulation: This supports neurotransmission and prevents excitotoxicity through neurotransmitter clearance (e.g., glutamate uptake by astrocytes).
  1. To convert lipophilic xenobiotics into hydrophilic forms for easier excretion.
  2. To detoxify potentially harmful substances.
  3. To sometimes activate prodrugs into their active pharmacological forms.

Non-shivering Thermogenesis (8 Marks)

  1. Thermoreceptor Activation:
    Cold exposure triggers thermoreceptors in the skin, sending signals to the hypothalamus to initiate heat production.
  2. Sympathetic Nervous System Activation:
    The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is activated and releases norepinephrine into brown adipose tissue (BAT).
  3. Norepinephrine Effect:
    Norepinephrine binds to β3-adrenergic receptors on BAT cells, activating adenylate cyclase and increasing cAMP levels.
  4. Hormone-Sensitive Lipase Activation:
    cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA), which stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase, leading to lipolysis in BAT.
  5. Fatty Acid Release:
    Lipolysis breaks down triglycerides (TAGs) into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol, which are released into the bloodstream.
  6. Fatty Acid Transport:
    FFAs are transported into the mitochondria of BAT for oxidation.
  7. Beta-Oxidation:
    In the mitochondria, FFAs undergo beta-oxidation, producing acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle.
  8. Electron Transport Chain (ETC):
    The citric acid cycle generates high-energy electrons, which fuel the electron transport chain (ETC), creating a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  9. Uncoupling by UCP1:
    Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1) in BAT uncouples the proton gradient, allowing energy to be released as heat instead of ATP, a process known as non-shivering thermogenesis.
  1. Fuel Substrate Shifting:
    • Low-intensity exercise: Muscles primarily use fatty acids as they are abundant and provide long-lasting energy.
    • High-intensity exercise: The body switches to glycogen, which provides a faster ATP supply for rapid energy production.
  2. Oxygen Availability:
    • Aerobic exercise: Sufficient oxygen allows muscles to use fatty acids and glucose for ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation.
    • Anaerobic exercise: When oxygen is limited, muscles rely on glycogen which is converted into lactate through anaerobic glycolysis.
  3. Energy Efficiency:
    • Fatty acids generate more ATP per molecule but are slower to metabolize, making them suitable for sustained, lower-intensity exercise.
    • Glycogen, while limited in storage, provides a faster ATP supply, making it ideal for high-intensity, short-duration exercise.
  1. Hormonal Regulation:
    • Insulin promotes lipogenesis, leading to fat storage in adipocytes.
    • Cortisol and catecholamines (e.g., epinephrine) activate lipolysis, promoting the breakdown of fat for energy.
  2. Dietary Factors:
    • High carbohydrate intake increases insulin levels, which stimulates fat storage in adipose tissue.
    • Fatty acids from dietary fats are stored directly in adipose tissue, influencing the type of fat (saturated or unsaturated) stored.
  3. Physical Activity:
    • Exercise, especially aerobic activities, increases lipid oxidation by enhancing mitochondrial function and improving the enzyme activity involved in fat metabolism.
  4. Genetic Factors:
    • Genetic predisposition determines how much fat is stored, the type of fat (visceral or subcutaneous), and the efficiency of lipid metabolism.
  5. Environmental/Lifestyle Factors:
    • Factors such as sleep, stress, and a sedentary lifestyle can disturb hormonal regulation, leading to increased fat storage and metabolic disorders like obesity.
  1. Passive Diffusion:
    • Lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and steroid hormones can diffuse directly across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) due to their ability to pass through the lipid-rich membrane.
  2. Facilitated Diffusion:
    • Larger, hydrophilic molecules like glucose and amino acids require specific transporters (e.g., GLUT1 for glucose, LAT1 for amino acids) to move across the BBB. This process doesn’t require energy but depends on the concentration gradient.
  3. Active Transport:
    • Active transport mechanisms, using ATP-powered pumps, actively transport essential ions (e.g., Na+, K+) and molecules like dopamine and neurotransmitters into or out of the brain. This maintains ion balance and proper brain function.
  4. Endocytosis:
    • Certain large molecules, such as insulin and some proteins, are transported into the brain via receptor-mediated endocytosis. These molecules bind to specific receptors on the BBB endothelial cells, triggering internalization and transcytosis across the barrier.
  5. Efflux Transport:
    • P-glycoprotein and other efflux pumps actively remove unwanted or harmful substances (e.g., toxins, drugs) from the brain into the bloodstream, protecting the brain from harmful compounds. This process requires energy and helps maintain the integrity of the BBB.
  1. Glycolysis
    • Control Point: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
    • This enzyme is regulated by ATP (inhibits) and AMP (activates), controlling the rate of glucose metabolism.
  2. Gluconeogenesis
    • Control Point: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
    • This enzyme is inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, regulating the synthesis of glucose.
  3. Citric Acid Cycle
    • Control Point: Isocitrate dehydrogenase
    • Activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH, controlling the pace of the Krebs cycle.
  4. Fatty Acid Synthesis
    • Control Point: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
    • Activated by insulin and inhibited by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and glucagon.
  5. Fatty Acid Oxidation
    • Control Point: Carnitine acyltransferase I
    • This enzyme controls the transport of fatty acids into the mitochondria for β-oxidation, regulated by malonyl-CoA.
  6. Glycogen Metabolism
    • Control Point: Glycogen synthase and Glycogen phosphorylase
    • Glycogen synthase is activated by insulin and inhibited by glucagon. Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by glucagon and inhibited by insulin.
  1. Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH)
    • Produced in the hypothalamus, it initiates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, triggering cortisol release from the adrenal glands.
  2. Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS)
    • Activated by stress, it releases norepinephrine and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and blood flow to muscles.
  3. Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)
    • Released from the pituitary gland, it stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol, which plays a central role in stress adaptation.
  4. Cortisol
    • A steroid hormone that enhances glucose production, suppresses inflammation, and affects metabolism during stress, contributing to the "fight or flight" response.
  5. Vasopressin (Antidiuretic Hormone, ADH)
    • Released from the posterior pituitary, it helps conserve water and increases blood volume, enhancing blood pressure during stress.
  6. Cytokines
    • Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1, TNF-α) are released during stress, contributing to inflammation and the acute stress response.
  1. Liver
    • Glycogen Breakdown: During fasting, glycogenolysis occurs to release glucose into the bloodstream to maintain blood glucose levels.
    • Gluconeogenesis: The liver increases glucose production from non-carbohydrate sources (e.g., lactate, glycerol, and amino acids).
    • Fatty Acid Oxidation: Increased breakdown of fatty acids into ketones to provide an alternative energy source for tissues like the brain.
    • Ketogenesis: The liver produces ketone bodies from fatty acids, which become a primary energy source during prolonged fasting.
  2. Adipose Tissue
    • Lipolysis: Adipose tissue breaks down stored triglycerides into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. The FFAs are used for energy production by other tissues, and glycerol is used in gluconeogenesis by the liver.
    • Increased Fat Mobilization: The body relies more on fatty acids for energy during fasting, reducing reliance on glucose.
  1. Cardiovascular System
    • Increased risk of hypertension, atherosclerosis, and coronary artery disease due to excess fat and associated inflammation.
    • Higher likelihood of heart failure and stroke from increased blood pressure and clot formation.
  2. Endocrine System
    • Insulin resistance leading to type 2 diabetes due to impaired insulin action in tissues.
    • Altered levels of adipokines (e.g., leptin, adiponectin) can disturb metabolic regulation.
  3. Respiratory System
    • Obesity contributes to sleep apnea, restrictive lung disease, and impaired lung function due to fat deposition around the chest and abdomen.
  4. Liver
    • Development of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which can progress to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and cirrhosis.
  5. Musculoskeletal System
    • Increased mechanical stress on joints, particularly in the knees and hips, leading to osteoarthritis and chronic pain.
  6. Reproductive System
    • Obesity can cause hormonal imbalances, leading to infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) in women, and reduced testosterone levels in men.
  7. Immune System
    • Chronic low-grade inflammation, which increases the risk of autoimmune diseases, infections, and cancer.
  8. Gastrointestinal System
    • Increased risk of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and gallstones due to altered bile metabolism and excess abdominal fat.
  1. Muscles
    • Glucose Uptake: Insulin stimulates glucose transporter (GLUT4) translocation to the cell membrane, promoting glucose uptake for energy and glycogen storage.
    • Protein Synthesis: Insulin enhances amino acid uptake and stimulates protein synthesis, promoting muscle growth and repair.
  2. Adipocytes (Fat Cells)
    • Lipogenesis: Insulin promotes the conversion of glucose into fat by activating lipogenic enzymes and inhibiting lipolysis (fat breakdown).
    • Fat Storage: Insulin enhances the storage of triglycerides by promoting the uptake of fatty acids into adipocytes.
  3. Liver
    • Glycogen Synthesis: Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis by activating glycogen synthase and inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase, which reduces glucose release from the liver.
    • Inhibition of Gluconeogenesis: Insulin inhibits gluconeogenesis, the production of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources, thereby reducing glucose output from the liver.
    • Fat Storage: Insulin promotes fat storage by stimulating lipogenesis and inhibiting fatty acid oxidation.
  1. Increased mitochondrial density: Endurance training stimulates the production of more mitochondria in muscle cells, enhancing aerobic ATP production.
  2. Enhanced capillary density: Increased capillarization improves oxygen and nutrient delivery to working muscles.
  3. Upregulation of oxidative enzymes: Enzymes involved in aerobic metabolism (e.g., citrate synthase, succinate dehydrogenase) increase, improving oxidative capacity.
  4. Elevated myoglobin content: Higher myoglobin levels in muscle improve oxygen storage and transport within muscle fibers.
  • Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) pathway:
    • Converts ethanol to acetaldehyde in the cytosol of liver cells.
    • Uses NAD⁺ as a coenzyme, producing NADH.
  • Aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) pathway:
    • Converts toxic acetaldehyde into acetate in mitochondria.
    • Also uses NAD⁺, producing additional NADH.
  • Microsomal Ethanol-Oxidizing System (MEOS):
    • Involves cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2E1 in the endoplasmic reticulum.
    • Becomes significant with chronic alcohol intake; generates reactive oxygen species (ROS).
  • Catalase pathway:
    • Catalase in peroxisomes oxidizes ethanol using hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂).
    • Minor role under normal conditions, but can contribute in the brain or under oxidative stress.
  • Cori Cycle:
    • Occurs between muscle and liver.
    • During anaerobic exercise, muscles convert glucose to lactate.
    • Lactate is transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis.
    • The newly formed glucose returns to the muscle, maintaining blood glucose levels.
  • Glucose-Alanine Cycle:
    • Involves transamination of pyruvate to form alanine in muscle.
    • Alanine is transported to the liver, where it is converted back to pyruvate and then to glucose.
    • The cycle helps remove nitrogen from muscle while maintaining glucose supply to tissues.
  • Purpose: Converts lipophilic drugs into hydrophilic metabolites for easier excretion.
  • Phase I reactions: Include oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis—often introduce reactive or polar groups (e.g., hydroxylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes).
  • Phase II reactions: Conjugation with glucuronic acid, sulfate, or glutathione to increase water solubility.
  • Detoxification: Reduces toxicity and inactivates active drugs or toxins.
  • Excretion: Metabolites are excreted mainly via kidneys (urine) or bile (feces), thus clearing drugs from the body effectively.
  1. Increased mitochondrial biogenesis – Enhances oxidative phosphorylation capacity.
  2. Enhanced capillary density – Improves oxygen and nutrient delivery to muscles.
  3. Upregulation of oxidative enzymes – Boosts efficiency of aerobic metabolism.
  4. Improved fatty acid oxidation – Shifts fuel usage from glucose to lipids, sparing glycogen.
  1. Alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) – Converts ethanol to acetaldehyde in the cytosol.
  2. Aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) – Oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetate in mitochondria.
  3. Microsomal ethanol-oxidizing system (MEOS) – Utilizes cytochrome P450 2E1 to metabolize ethanol, especially during chronic intake.
  4. Catalase pathway – Uses hydrogen peroxide in peroxisomes to oxidize ethanol (minor role).
  • Cori Cycle: Lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in muscles is transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis. This glucose is then returned to muscles, maintaining blood glucose levels during intense exercise.
  • Glucose-Alanine Cycle: In muscle, amino acids are catabolized and their nitrogen is transferred to pyruvate to form alanine. Alanine travels to the liver, where it's converted back to pyruvate (for gluconeogenesis) and urea (for nitrogen excretion). This supports glucose regeneration and nitrogen disposal.
  • Biotransformation: Converts lipophilic drugs into hydrophilic metabolites for easier excretion.
  • Phase I reactions: Introduce or expose functional groups via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis (e.g., by cytochrome P450 enzymes).
  • Phase II reactions: Conjugate metabolites with polar groups (e.g., glucuronidation, sulfation), enhancing water solubility.
  • Inactivation of drugs: Metabolism reduces drug activity or toxicity before elimination.
  • Facilitated excretion: Metabolites are removed via urine or bile, preventing drug accumulation and toxicity.

(12 Marks – 2 marks per pathway)

  1. Glycolysis
    • Key control point: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
    • Regulated by: ATP (inhibits), AMP (activates), citrate (inhibits), and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (activates)
  2. Gluconeogenesis
    • Key control point: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase
    • Regulated by: Inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
  3. Glycogen synthesis and breakdown
    • Glycogenesis control: Glycogen synthase (activated by insulin and G6P)
    • Glycogenolysis control: Glycogen phosphorylase (activated by glucagon and epinephrine, inhibited by ATP and G6P)
  4. Fatty acid synthesis
    • Key control point: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC)
    • Regulated by: Activated by citrate and insulin; inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA and AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)
  5. Beta-oxidation of fatty acids
    • Key control point: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I)
    • Regulated by: Inhibited by malonyl-CoA (to prevent simultaneous synthesis and oxidation of fatty acids)
  6. Cholesterol synthesis
    • Key control point: HMG-CoA reductase
    • Regulated by: Inhibited by cholesterol and statins; activated by insulin

(10 Marks – 5 marks for liver, 5 marks for adipose tissue)

Liver:

  1. Glycogenolysis becomes the immediate source of glucose during early fasting.
  2. Gluconeogenesis increases to maintain blood glucose (using lactate, glycerol, alanine).
  3. Fatty acid oxidation rises to provide ATP and acetyl-CoA for gluconeogenesis.
  4. Ketogenesis begins after prolonged fasting, forming ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA.
  5. Inhibition of glycolysis and lipogenesis due to low insulin levels.

Adipose tissue:

  1. Lipolysis increases, breaking down triacylglycerols into glycerol and free fatty acids.
  2. Decreased glucose uptake, as insulin levels drop and GLUT4 expression reduces.
  3. Glycerol released from lipolysis is sent to the liver for gluconeogenesis.
  4. Fatty acids are used as energy by muscle and liver or converted into ketone bodies.
  5. Hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) becomes activated due to low insulin/high catecholamines.

(10 Marks – at least 5 systems with 2 effects each)

  1. Cardiovascular System
    • Increases risk of hypertension
    • Promotes atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease
  2. Endocrine System
    • Leads to insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes
    • Causes hormonal imbalance (e.g., polycystic ovarian syndrome)
  3. Respiratory System
    • Contributes to obstructive sleep apnea
    • Reduces lung volume and increases breathing effort
  4. Musculoskeletal System
    • Increases stress on joints, leading to osteoarthritis
    • Impairs mobility and posture
  5. Gastrointestinal and Liver
    • Increases risk of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
    • Associated with gallstone formation

(8 Marks – 2 marks for each process, across tissues)

Glucose uptake

  • Muscle & Adipose Tissue: Insulin stimulates GLUT4 translocation to the membrane, increasing glucose uptake.
  • Liver: Insulin indirectly increases uptake by promoting glucokinase activity and glucose utilization.

Glycogen synthesis

  • Muscle & Liver: Insulin activates glycogen synthase, enhancing glycogen formation from glucose.

Fatty acid synthesis

  • Liver: Insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, promoting de novo lipogenesis.
  • Adipose Tissue: Increases glucose uptake, providing glycerol-3-phosphate for triglyceride synthesis.

Protein synthesis

  • Muscle: Insulin stimulates amino acid uptake and promotes translation and transcription, enhancing protein synthesis.
  • Liver: Supports synthesis of structural and plasma proteins by enhancing mRNA translation.

Glucose uptake, Glycogen synthesis, Fatty acid synthesis, Protein synthesis
(8 Marks – 2 marks per process)

1. Glucose Uptake

  • Muscle and Adipose Tissue:
    Insulin stimulates the translocation of GLUT4 transporters to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake from the blood.
  • Liver:
    Insulin enhances glucose uptake indirectly by activating glucokinase, which phosphorylates glucose, maintaining a gradient for continuous uptake.

2. Glycogen Synthesis

  • Muscle and Liver:
    Insulin activates glycogen synthase, promoting conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage.
    It also inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, reducing glycogen breakdown.

3. Fatty Acid Synthesis

  • Liver:
    Insulin promotes de novo lipogenesis by activating acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase.
  • Adipose Tissue:
    Insulin increases glucose uptake, supplying glycerol-3-phosphate for triacylglycerol synthesis and inhibits lipolysis by deactivating hormone-sensitive lipase.

4. Protein Synthesis

  • Muscle:
    Insulin enhances amino acid uptake and activates translation initiation factors, promoting protein synthesis.
  • Liver:
    Stimulates synthesis of plasma proteins and structural proteins by enhancing transcription and translation.
