Title: Principles of Medical Microbiology and Parasitology LAQs & SAQs
Content:
• Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX): First-line prophylaxis for both PCP and toxoplasmic encephalitis, especially when CD4 count <200 cells/μL or <100 cells/μL with positive Toxoplasma IgG.
  • Alternative agents: Dapsone, atovaquone, or aerosolized pentamidine may be used in TMP-SMX-intolerant patients.
  • CD4 Monitoring: Regular CD4+ T-cell count assessment to guide initiation and discontinuation of prophylaxis.
  • ART initiation: Early antiretroviral therapy helps restore immunity and prevent opportunistic infections.
  • Adherence counseling: Ensures compliance with prophylactic regimens and ART.
  • Leucovorin (folinic acid) supplementation: To prevent bone marrow suppression from pyrimethamine.
  • Regular hematologic monitoring: Monitor CBC for neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia.
  • Renal function monitoring: Sulfadiazine can cause crystalluria or renal toxicity.
  • Hydration: Ensure adequate fluid intake to prevent renal complications.
  • Allergy surveillance: Watch for hypersensitivity reactions or rash, especially from sulfonamides.
  • Cutaneous lesions: Ulcerated or nodular skin lesions at the site of sandfly bite, often painless.
  • Regional lymphadenopathy: Enlargement of nearby lymph nodes.
  • Disfiguring scars: Chronic or healing lesions may result in visible scarring.
  • Secondary bacterial infection: May complicate ulcerated lesions.
  • Systemic symptoms (in some cases): Low-grade fever and malaise, depending on the species and immune status.
  • Bactericidal effect occurs when an antibiotic kills bacteria directly. This is typically seen:
    • At higher drug concentrations.
    • In rapidly dividing bacterial populations.
    • In infections where immune clearance is inadequate (e.g., endocarditis, meningitis, neutropenia).
  • Bacteriostatic effect inhibits bacterial growth and replication without killing, relying on the host immune system to eliminate the organism.
  • Effect depends on the drug, dose, organism, and host immunity.
    For example, chloramphenicol may be bacteriostatic for some organisms and bactericidal for others.
  • Avoid in immunocompromised patients: These patients may require bactericidal agents due to reduced immune clearance.
  • Avoid combination with bactericidal drugs: Some combinations (e.g., bactericidal + bacteriostatic) can lead to antagonism and reduced efficacy.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Prions are misfolded proteins (PrP^Sc) that induce conformational changes in normal cellular prion proteins (PrP^C) to the abnormal form.
    • PrP^Sc accumulates in neural tissue, forming amyloid plaques.
    • This accumulation leads to neuronal death, spongiform degeneration, and progressive neurodegeneration.
    • There is no immune response or inflammation due to the host-derived nature of prions.
  • Human prion diseases:
    1. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) – the most common prion disease, often sporadic.
    2. Variant CJD – associated with consumption of BSE (mad cow disease)-infected beef.
A. Life Cycle (Illustration-friendly — include with diagram if submitting)

.

Click to see Life Cycle
  1. Mosquito stage (Definitive host)
    • Female Anopheles mosquito inoculates sporozoites during a blood meal.
  2. Human liver stage (Pre-erythrocytic)
    • Sporozoites enter hepatocytes → multiply asexually → form schizonts → release merozoites into bloodstream.
  3. Human blood stage (Erythrocytic cycle)
    • Merozoites invade RBCs → mature into trophozoites → form schizonts → rupture RBCs, releasing more merozoites.
    • Some trophozoites form gametocytes (sexual forms).
  4. Back to mosquito (sexual cycle)
    • Mosquito ingests gametocytes → gamete fusion → zygote → ookinete → oocyst → sporozoites → cycle continues.

Illustration tip: Use a circular flow chart with human and mosquito phases clearly labeled.

B. Pathogenesis
  • RBC Destruction → Hemolytic anemia, jaundice.
  • Cytoadherence → P. falciparum causes infected RBCs to adhere to endothelium (via PfEMP1) → microvascular obstruction, cerebral malaria, placental malaria.
  • Immune response → Fever, chills, cytokine release.
  • Sequestration → In spleen/liver; can lead to organomegaly and immune evasion.
C. Treatment
  1. Uncomplicated malaria:
    • Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs): e.g., artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine.
  2. Severe malaria:
    • IV artesunate (preferred), followed by oral ACT.
  3. Supportive care:
    • Manage hypoglycemia, anemia, renal failure, cerebral edema.

Note: Chloroquine is ineffective due to resistance.

D. Control and Prevention
  • Vector control: Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs), indoor residual spraying (IRS).
  • Chemoprophylaxis: E.g., atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline (travelers).
  • Surveillance: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), microscopy.
  • Vaccination: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) approved for children in endemic regions.
  • Public education: Elimination of breeding sites, early diagnosis.
A. Molecular Diagnostics
  • PCR and RT-PCR: High sensitivity/specificity for Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, Leishmania, Trypanosoma.
  • Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP): Field-friendly alternative to PCR.
B. Immunodiagnostics
  • ELISA: Detection of parasite antigens or antibodies (e.g., Entamoeba histolytica, Toxoplasma gondii).
  • Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs):
    • E.g., Plasmodium falciparum HRP2 detection.
    • Cryptosporidium antigen tests in stool.
C. Point-of-care testing (POCT)
  • Handheld or dipstick tests with visual results.
    • E.g., Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas) lateral flow assays.
D. Imaging and Serology
  • MRI/CT: Neurocysticercosis, toxoplasmosis.
  • Western blot: Confirmatory for T. gondii, T. solium, Leishmania.
E. AI and Digital Microscopy
  • Image recognition tools to automate parasite detection in blood films or stool samples.
F. Metagenomics and NGS
  • Next-generation sequencing for rare or mixed infections (e.g., intestinal protozoa).
G. Biosensor and Nanotech
  • Experimental tools for real-time detection using parasite-derived DNA/proteins.

(a)

1. Reverse Transcriptase (RT)
  • Converts viral ssRNA into dsDNA.
  • Has RNA-dependent DNA polymerase and RNase H activity.
  • Critical for forming a DNA provirus from HIV RNA.
  • Error-prone → high mutation rate → rapid resistance development.
2. Integrase
  • Facilitates integration of viral DNA into host genome.
  • Steps:
    1. Viral DNA is processed by integrase.
    2. Integrase binds host DNA.
    3. Catalyzes insertion of proviral DNA.
  • Allows viral genome to become part of host DNA → persistent infection.
Mechanism of Action of Zidovudine (ZDV/AZT)

(10 Marks)

  • Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI).
  • Structural analogue of thymidine.
  • Enters host cells → phosphorylated to active triphosphate form.
  • Competitively inhibits reverse transcriptase.
  • Incorporates into viral DNA chain → terminates elongation (lacks 3’-OH group).
Effect on Integrase
  • No direct effect on integrase.
  • Indirect impact: By blocking DNA synthesis, ZDV prevents substrate formation for integration.
Clinical Relevance
  • One of the first ARVs developed.
  • Used in combination therapy (HAART).
  • Prevents mother-to-child transmission effectively.
  • Side effects: Anemia, neutropenia, lactic acidosis (rare).

a) Psychrophile
Organisms that thrive in extremely cold environments, typically at temperatures below 15°C.
Example: Pseudomonas fluorescens found in Arctic soils.

b) Peritrichous
Bacteria that have flagella uniformly distributed over the entire cell surface.
Example: Escherichia coli.

c) Koch’s Postulates
A set of four criteria used to establish a causative relationship between a microbe and a disease:

  1. The microorganism must be found in all organisms suffering from the disease.
  2. It must be isolated and grown in pure culture.
  3. The cultured microbe should cause disease when introduced into a healthy organism.
  4. The same microbe must be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host.

d) Thermodimorphism
The ability of certain fungi to exist in two morphological forms depending on temperature: mold at lower temperatures (25°C) and yeast at body temperature (37°C).
Example: Histoplasma capsulatum.

e) Microaerophile
Microorganisms that require oxygen for growth but at lower concentrations than those in the atmosphere (typically 2–10% O₂).
Example: Helicobacter pylori.

a) Endospores
Highly resistant, dormant structures formed by certain bacteria (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) during nutrient deprivation. They allow bacteria to survive extreme heat, desiccation, chemicals, and radiation.

b) Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) Layer of Gram-Negative Bacteria
LPS contains Lipid A, which acts as an endotoxin. When released during cell lysis, it can trigger septic shock, fever, and inflammation.

c) Plasmid
Small, circular DNA molecules separate from chromosomal DNA. Plasmids often carry genes for antibiotic resistance and virulence, and can be transferred via conjugation.

d) Capsule
A gelatinous outer layer that protects bacteria from phagocytosis by host immune cells. Enhances virulence.
Example: Capsule of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

e) Fimbriae and Pili
Fimbriae help bacteria adhere to host tissues, aiding colonization. Pili (especially sex pili) are involved in genetic exchange through conjugation.

  • Dry heat sterilizes by oxidizing cellular components and denaturing microbial proteins.
  • It requires higher temperatures and longer exposure times than moist heat (e.g., 160°C for 2 hours or 180°C for 1 hour).
  • Effective for moisture-sensitive materials such as powders, oils, and petroleum-based products.
  • Suitable for metal instruments, glassware, and sharp tools as it does not cause corrosion.
  • Used in hot air ovens for sterilizing syringes, forceps, and lab glassware.

a) Light Microscopy:

  • Uses visible light to illuminate the specimen.
  • Magnification is up to 1,000–1,500×.
  • Lower resolution (~200 nm); suitable for observing living or stained organisms.
  • Types include bright field, dark field, phase contrast, and fluorescence.
  • Commonly used in clinical labs for quick diagnostics.

b) Electron Microscopy:

  • Uses a beam of electrons for imaging.
  • Magnification can reach up to 500,000×.
  • Very high resolution (up to 0.2 nm); useful for observing ultrastructure of cells and viruses.
  • Types include transmission (TEM) and scanning (SEM).
  • Requires fixed, dehydrated, and metal-coated specimens.

a) Roles of Pili (2 marks):

  1. Adherence to host cells – helps bacteria attach to epithelial surfaces.
  2. Genetic exchange – sex pili facilitate conjugation, transferring resistance genes.

b) Morphological Forms of Fungi (1 mark):

  1. Yeast – unicellular, reproduce by budding (e.g., Candida albicans).
  2. Mold – multicellular, form hyphae and spores (e.g., Aspergillus).

c) Steps in Peptidoglycan Biosynthesis (2 marks):

  1. Synthesis of precursors – N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM) with peptide chains are formed in the cytoplasm.
  2. Transport – precursors are carried across the membrane by bactoprenol.
  3. Polymerization – transglycosylation links sugar chains; transpeptidation forms cross-links between peptide chains for strength.
  1. Eukaryotic organisms – have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  2. Heterotrophic nutrition – absorb nutrients from organic matter, often as saprophytes or parasites.
  3. Cell wall contains chitin – provides structural rigidity and protection.
  4. Reproduce by spores – either sexually or asexually, depending on species.
  5. Can exist as unicellular (yeasts) or multicellular (molds) – with dimorphic species able to switch forms depending on environment.

Note: Deuteromycota (Fungi Imperfecti) is a classification used for fungi whose sexual stages have not been observed.

i) Morphology (4 Marks)
  • Ancylostoma duodenale is a hookworm with a curved anterior end resembling a hook.
  • Adult male measures about 8–11 mm, and the female is about 10–13 mm long.
  • The buccal capsule contains two pairs of ventral teeth used for attachment to the intestinal mucosa.
  • The posterior end of the male has a copulatory bursa, while the female has a pointed tail.
ii) Pathophysiology (5 Marks)
  • Infection begins when filariform larvae penetrate the skin, migrate via blood to lungs, then to the pharynx, are swallowed, and reach the small intestine.
  • In the intestine, they attach to the mucosa and suck blood, causing mechanical damage and blood loss.
  • Chronic blood loss leads to iron-deficiency anemia and hypoproteinemia.
  • Tissue invasion during larval migration can cause pneumonitis and eosinophilia.
  • The parasite also induces a chronic inflammatory response, impairing nutrient absorption and contributing to growth retardation in children.
iii) Signs and Symptoms (4 Marks)
  • Localized pruritic rash (“ground itch”) at the site of skin penetration.
  • Cough and wheezing during pulmonary migration phase.
  • Abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and anorexia during intestinal phase.
  • Pallor, fatigue, and weakness due to chronic iron-deficiency anemia.
iv) Diagnosis (3 Marks)
  • Microscopic examination of stool for characteristic oval eggs with thin shells.
  • Concentration techniques (e.g., formalin-ether) may increase sensitivity.
  • Complete blood count may show eosinophilia and microcytic hypochromic anemia.
v) Treatment (Drug of choice) (4 Marks)
  • Albendazole 400 mg orally as a single dose is the drug of choice.
  • Alternative: Mebendazole 100 mg twice daily for 3 days.
  • Iron supplementation and nutritional support are important in managing anemia.
  • Good hygiene and wearing shoes help prevent reinfection.
i) Etiology (2 Marks)
  • Schistosomiasis is caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma.
  • Key species affecting humans include:
    • S. haematobium (urinary),
    • S. mansoni (intestinal),
    • S. japonicum (intestinal).
ii) Pathogenesis (5 Marks)
  • Cercariae penetrate human skin and transform into schistosomula, migrating through lungs to the liver.
  • In the liver, they mature into adult worms and migrate to venous plexuses (e.g., mesenteric or pelvic veins).
  • Eggs produced by adults elicit intense granulomatous inflammation as they lodge in tissues.

  • Inside the snail, they develop into sporocysts and release cercariae into the water.

iv) Diagnosis (3 Marks)

Definition:
  • Chemical agents used to destroy or inhibit microorganisms on non-living surfaces.
  • Important in infection control, hospital hygiene, and public health.
Classification Based on Level:
  • High-level disinfectants:
    • Kill all microbes including spores.
    • E.g., Glutaraldehyde, Peracetic acid.
  • Intermediate-level disinfectants:
    • Kill bacteria, most viruses, and fungi, but not spores.
    • E.g., Alcohols (70%), Iodophors.
  • Low-level disinfectants:
    • Kill vegetative bacteria and some viruses.
    • E.g., Quaternary ammonium compounds.
Common Types and Actions:
  1. Alcohols (Ethanol, Isopropanol):
    • Denature proteins and dissolve lipids.
    • Used on skin, thermometers.
  2. Chlorine compounds (e.g., Sodium hypochlorite):
    • Oxidize cellular components.
    • Used for surfaces, blood spills.
  3. Aldehydes (e.g., Glutaraldehyde):
    • Crosslink proteins and DNA.
    • Used in high-level disinfection of surgical instruments.
  4. Phenolics:
    • Disrupt cell walls and membranes.
    • Used in environmental cleaning.
  5. Hydrogen peroxide:
    • Produces free radicals that damage cell components.
    • Effective for surfaces and instruments.
  6. Quaternary ammonium compounds:
    • Disrupt membrane permeability.
    • Used for non-critical surfaces.
Applications in Disease Prevention:
  • Hospital disinfection: Operating theatres, instruments.
  • Community settings: Water treatment, surface disinfection.
  • Sterilization of critical items: Endoscopes, surgical tools.
  • Prevention of nosocomial infections.
Advantages:
  • Rapid action.
  • Broad-spectrum activity.
  • Easy to apply and cost-effective.
Limitations:
  • Inactivation by organic matter.
  • Toxicity (some agents).
  • Limited sporicidal activity (for many).
Overview:
  • Cell wall inhibitors target peptidoglycan synthesis, weakening bacterial cell walls and causing cell lysis.
  • Effective only on actively growing bacteria.
  • Mostly bactericidal.
Major Classes of Cell Wall Inhibitors:
  1. Beta-lactams:
    • Include Penicillins, Cephalosporins, Carbapenems, Monobactams.
    • Mechanism: Bind to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibit transpeptidation → prevent cross-linking of peptidoglycan.
    • Examples:
      • Penicillin G – gram-positive infections.
      • Ceftriaxone – broad-spectrum cephalosporin.
      • Imipenem – broad spectrum, β-lactamase resistant.
  2. Glycopeptides:
    • e.g., Vancomycin, Teicoplanin.
    • Mechanism: Bind to D-Ala-D-Ala terminals → inhibit polymerization and cross-linking.
    • Effective against gram-positive bacteria (e.g., MRSA).
    • Reserved for resistant infections.
  3. Fosfomycin:
    • Inhibits early peptidoglycan precursor synthesis.
    • Used in urinary tract infections.
  4. Bacitracin:
    • Blocks transport of peptidoglycan precursors across membrane.
    • Topical use only.
Clinical Relevance:
  • First-line agents in respiratory infections, skin infections, meningitis, septicemia, UTI, etc.
  • Beta-lactam antibiotics are commonly prescribed due to broad-spectrum activity and safety.
  • Glycopeptides used when resistance (e.g., MRSA) is suspected.
Resistance Mechanisms:
  • Beta-lactamase production (e.g., by Staph aureus).
  • Altered PBPs (e.g., MRSA).
  • Efflux pumps and reduced permeability in gram-negatives.
Combination Therapy:
  • Use of beta-lactam + beta-lactamase inhibitors (e.g., Amoxicillin + Clavulanic acid) to overcome resistance.
A. Interferons (IFNs)
  • Type I IFNs (IFN-α, IFN-β):

B. AZT (Zidovudine / ZDV / Azidothymidine):
  • Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI).
  • Mechanism:
    • Mimics thymidine → incorporated into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase.
    • Causes chain termination → halts viral DNA synthesis.
  • Used in HIV treatment and prevention of mother-to-child transmission.
  • Reduces viral load, slows disease progression.

  • Stimulate strong immune response, including:

    • Humoral immunity (B cells → antibodies).
  • Mimic natural infection → formation of memory cells.
  • Provide long-lasting protection.
  • Can induce herd immunity by reducing virus transmission.
  • Example: Measles vaccine protects by inducing high antibody titers and T-cell response.

A. Pathogenesis of Severe Malaria (8 marks)
  1. Causative Agent
    • Most commonly Plasmodium falciparum.
  2. Cytoadherence and Sequestration
    • Infected RBCs adhere to endothelium via PfEMP1, causing microvascular obstruction and tissue hypoxia (e.g., cerebral malaria).
  3. RBC Destruction and Anemia
    • Hemolysis of infected and non-infected RBCs leads to severe anemia and hemoglobinuria ("blackwater fever").
  4. Immune Activation and Cytokine Storm
    • TNF-α, IL-1 release contributes to fever, inflammation, and endothelial damage.
  5. Metabolic Derangements
    • Hypoglycemia, acidosis, hyperlactatemia, and renal failure due to parasite metabolism and host response.
  6. Cerebral Malaria
    • Neurological symptoms due to sequestration in cerebral microvasculature (confusion, seizures, coma).
B. Treatment of Severe Malaria (7 marks)
  1. Antimalarial Therapy (Parenteral)
    • Artesunate IV (preferred): 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hrs, then daily.
    • Quinine dihydrochloride IV if artesunate unavailable.
  2. Follow-up Oral Therapy
    • Complete course with ACT (artemisinin-based combination therapy) once oral therapy is tolerated.
  3. Supportive Treatment
    • IV fluids, correction of hypoglycemia, antipyretics, anticonvulsants (for seizures), dialysis if needed.
  4. Monitoring
    • Frequent monitoring of parasitemia, renal function, blood glucose, and neurological status.

A. Introduction to Viral Receptors (3 marks)
  • Viral receptors are specific molecules (usually glycoproteins or glycolipids) on host cell surfaces that viruses bind to in order to gain entry into cells.
  • The nature and distribution of these receptors determine host specificity, tissue tropism, and transmission dynamics, all of which influence whether an infection remains localized or escalates into an epidemic/pandemic.
B. Roles of Viral Receptors in Epidemic and Pandemic Infections (10 marks)
  1. Host Range Expansion
    • Mutation or recombination in viruses can allow binding to receptors of new species, facilitating zoonotic spillover (e.g., SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2 via ACE2).
    • This jump can spark new outbreaks in immunologically naïve populations.
  2. Tissue Tropism and Severity
    • Receptors like DC-SIGN or CD4 guide viruses to specific tissues (e.g., HIV to T-helper cells), affecting disease progression and clinical outcome.
    • Severe outcomes can increase viral shedding and community transmission.
  3. Viral Fitness and Transmission
    • High-affinity binding (e.g., HA of influenza virus to sialic acid) increases viral entry efficiency and replication, contributing to higher viral loads and greater transmission potential.
  4. Genetic Variation in Host Populations
    • Polymorphisms in receptors (e.g., CCR5-Δ32 mutation confers HIV resistance) influence susceptibility, shaping outbreak dynamics and geographic spread.
  5. Antigenic Shift and Receptor Usage Change
    • Influenza A virus can acquire genes from animal strains via reassortment, changing receptor preferences (e.g., from α-2,3-linked to α-2,6-linked sialic acids), promoting human-to-human transmission.
  6. Immune Evasion
    • Some viruses bind to complement receptors or use decoy receptors to modulate immune detection, allowing wider spread before containment.
C. Conclusion (2 marks)
  • Viral receptors play a central role in determining transmission patterns, host adaptation, and outbreak severity.
  • Understanding receptor biology is crucial for predicting epidemics, vaccine design, and antiviral drug development.
A. Introduction (2 marks)
  • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) results from genetic and biochemical adaptations in bacteria that allow them to survive drug exposure.
  • Resistance can arise via mutation or horizontal gene transfer, and involves various biochemical mechanisms.
B. Key Biochemical Mechanisms of Drug Resistance (12 marks)
  1. Enzymatic Drug Inactivation
    • Bacteria produce enzymes that chemically modify or degrade antibiotics.
      • Example: β-lactamases hydrolyze β-lactam rings of penicillins and cephalosporins.
      • Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyltransferases, adenyltransferases).
  2. Target Modification
    • Mutations or enzymatic alterations of antibiotic targets reduce drug binding.
      • Example: Altered PBPs (penicillin-binding proteins) in MRSA.
      • Methylation of 23S rRNA in macrolide resistance (via erm genes).
  3. Reduced Permeability
    • Decreased expression or mutation of porins reduces drug entry, especially in Gram-negative bacteria.
      • Example: Pseudomonas aeruginosa limiting carbapenem uptake.
  4. Efflux Pumps
    • Active expulsion of antibiotics via efflux proteins lowers intracellular drug concentration.
      • Example: Tet(A) efflux pump for tetracycline resistance.
  5. Bypass of Metabolic Pathways
    • Alternative enzymes or pathways reduce dependence on the drug-inhibited target.
      • Example: Resistance to sulfonamides via a plasmid-encoded dihydropteroate synthase with lower affinity for the drug.
  6. Biofilm Formation
    • Biofilms protect bacteria from antibiotics and host defenses.
      • Reduced drug penetration, altered pH, and presence of dormant cells contribute to resistance.
  7. Quorum Sensing and Persistence
    • Communication via quorum sensing can trigger resistance gene expression or induce a persister state.
C. Conclusion (1 mark)
  • These biochemical adaptations reflect the plasticity of bacterial physiology under selective pressure, and pose a major challenge to effective antimicrobial therapy.
a) Etiology (2 marks)
  • Paragonimiasis is caused by lung flukes of the genus Paragonimus.
  • The most common species affecting humans is Paragonimus westermani, found mainly in East Asia. Other species (e.g., P. africanus, P. mexicanus) occur in other regions.
b) Transmission and Control (3 marks)
  • Transmission: Humans acquire infection by consuming undercooked or raw freshwater crabs or crayfish harboring metacercariae.
  • Control Measures:
    • Proper cooking of freshwater crustaceans.
    • Health education on food safety practices.
    • Control of intermediate hosts (snails and crustaceans).
    • Improved sanitation to prevent contamination of water bodies with human feces and sputum.
c) Pathogenesis (3 marks)
  • Metacercariae excyst in the duodenum, penetrate the intestinal wall, and migrate through the peritoneum, diaphragm, and pleura to reach the lungs.
  • In the lungs, the flukes form cysts, causing granulomatous inflammation, fibrosis, and cavitation.
  • Chronic infection results in cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, and sometimes secondary bacterial infection.
  • Ectopic paragonimiasis may affect the brain or skin, leading to seizures or subcutaneous nodules.
d) Diagnosis (4 marks)
  • Microscopy: Detection of characteristic golden-brown, operculated eggs in sputum or stool.
  • Serological Tests: ELISA and other antibody tests are useful, especially in light or ectopic infections.
  • Imaging: Chest X-ray or CT may show coin lesions, cysts, or pleural effusion.
  • Differential Diagnosis: Must distinguish from tuberculosis, lung cancer, and fungal infections.
e) Treatment (3 marks)
  • Praziquantel: 25 mg/kg orally three times daily for 2–3 days (drug of choice).

  • Supportive Therapy: Analgesics, bronchodilators, and antibiotics if secondary bacterial infection occurs.
a) Etiology (2 marks)

40 mg/kg for S. haematobium and S. mansoni.

  • Bacterial external structures include capsules, flagella, fimbriae (pili), S-layers, and outer membrane components.
  • These structures play critical roles in adherence, immune evasion, motility, and colonization, which are central to bacterial pathogenicity.
A. Introduction (2 marks)
  1. Capsule (Glycocalyx)
    • Composed of polysaccharides or polypeptides.
    • Functions:
      • Anti-phagocytic: Inhibits engulfment by neutrophils and macrophages (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae).
      • Immune evasion: Masks surface antigens from immune recognition.
      • Adhesion: Facilitates binding to epithelial cells and biofilm formation.
      • Serotyping basis: Different capsular types are linked to virulence.
  2. Fimbriae and Pili
    • Hair-like projections primarily composed of pilin protein.
    • Functions:
      • Adhesion to host tissues: Crucial for initial colonization (e.g., uropathogenic E. coli in urinary tract infections).
      • Biofilm formation: Helps bacteria adhere to surfaces and to each other.
      • Type IV pili: Involved in twitching motility and uptake of DNA (transformation).
  3. Flagella
    • Long, whip-like structures enabling motility.
    • Functions:
      • Motility toward favorable environments (chemotaxis).
      • Invasion and dissemination in host tissues.
      • Flagellin (flagellar protein) can act as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP), triggering immune responses.
  4. Outer Membrane (in Gram-negative bacteria)
    • Contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS) with lipid A as the endotoxin.
    • Functions:
      • Endotoxic shock: Lipid A induces cytokine storm and septic shock.
      • Barrier function: Protects against antibiotics and host defenses.
      • O-antigen: Contributes to antigenic variation and immune evasion.
  5. S-layers and Surface Proteins
    • Crystalline arrays of protein or glycoprotein.
    • Functions:
      • Resistance to complement-mediated lysis.
      • Adherence to surfaces and host cells.
      • May help in avoiding immune detection.
  6. Biofilm Matrix (Exopolysaccharides)
    • Bacteria in biofilms are encased in self-produced matrix.
    • Functions:
      • Antibiotic resistance.
      • Persistence in host tissues and medical devices.
      • Protection from immune cells.
A. Introduction (2 marks)
  • Obligate aerobic bacteria require oxygen for growth and energy production.
  • They rely on aerobic respiration, where oxygen acts as the terminal electron acceptor in the electron transport chain (ETC).
B. Energy Acquisition in Obligate Aerobes (12 marks)
  1. Substrate Uptake and Catabolism
    • Organic compounds (e.g., glucose, amino acids) are taken up and catabolized for energy.
    • Glucose is metabolized via:
      • Glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway)
      • Pentose phosphate pathway
      • Entner-Doudoroff pathway (in some species)
  2. Conversion to Pyruvate
    • Glycolysis yields:
      • 2 ATP
      • 2 NADH
      • 2 Pyruvate
    • Pyruvate enters pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, converting it to acetyl-CoA.
  3. Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle (TCA/Krebs Cycle)
    • Acetyl-CoA is oxidized in the TCA cycle:
      • Produces NADH, FADH₂, and GTP/ATP.
      • Supplies high-energy electrons to the ETC.
  4. Electron Transport Chain (ETC)
    • Located in the cytoplasmic membrane of prokaryotes.
    • NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the ETC.
    • Electrons are transferred through complexes (I-IV) to oxygen, which is reduced to water.
  5. Proton Motive Force and ATP Generation
    • ETC activity pumps protons across the membrane, creating a proton gradient.
    • Protons flow back via ATP synthase, generating ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
  6. Oxygen as Final Electron Acceptor
    • Essential for:
      • Maintaining ETC activity.
      • Preventing accumulation of reduced cofactors.
    • Without oxygen, ETC halts, and the bacterium cannot survive.

This process supports rapid growth and high energy yield (~38 ATP/glucose).

Obligate aerobes derive energy efficiently via aerobic respiration, using oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor.

Laboratory Diagnosis:

  • Stool microscopy is the primary method: identification of characteristic Taenia eggs (spherical, with a thick radially striated shell) or gravid proglottids in feces.
  • Gross examination: Proglottids may be seen in stool or on underwear; T. saginata proglottids are motile and longer than wide.
  • Serology and molecular methods (e.g., PCR) can differentiate between T. saginata and T. solium in specialized settings.

Treatment:

  • Praziquantel (single oral dose of 5–10 mg/kg) is the drug of choice, inducing paralysis and detachment of the worm.
  • Niclosamide is an alternative where available.
  • Supportive advice includes improved sanitation, meat inspection, and thorough cooking of beef to prevent reinfection.

Pathogenesis:

  • Caused primarily by Plasmodium falciparum, which infects erythrocytes.
  • Infected red cells express PfEMP1, leading to cytoadherence to endothelial cells and microvascular obstruction, particularly in the brain, kidneys, and lungs.
  • Results in cerebral malaria, renal failure, metabolic acidosis, severe anemia, and hypoglycemia.
  • Inflammatory cytokines contribute to systemic complications.

Treatment:

  • Intravenous artesunate is the first-line treatment for all ages and pregnancy.
  • Intravenous quinine is used where artesunate is unavailable.
  • Supportive management includes glucose correction, antipyretics, fluid management, blood transfusion, and monitoring for complications.

Life Cycle Stages:

  • Infection begins when a tsetse fly bites a human and injects metacyclic trypomastigotes into the blood.
  • These multiply extracellularly as bloodstream trypomastigotes, spreading to lymph nodes and CNS in late-stage disease.
  • The fly ingests the parasites during a blood meal, which transform into procyclic trypomastigotes in the midgut, then into epimastigotes, and finally into infective metacyclic forms in the salivary glands.

Treatment:

  • Stage I (early/haemolymphatic stage): Pentamidine.
  • Stage II (CNS involvement): Eflornithine or NECT (Nifurtimox-Eflornithine Combination Therapy).
  • Early diagnosis is critical to prevent irreversible neurological damage.
  • Viral receptors are specific host cell surface molecules (proteins, glycoproteins) that facilitate viral entry.
  • A virus’s ability to bind receptors determines host range, tissue tropism, and infectivity.
  • Mutations in viral surface proteins (e.g., glycoproteins or spikes) can enhance binding affinity to human receptors, promoting cross-species transmission.
  • Example: SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2 receptors in the respiratory tract, facilitating human-to-human transmission and contributing to the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • Widespread receptor expression, high replication rate, and absence of immunity in populations contribute to epidemic or pandemic spread.
  • Enzymatic degradation of antibiotics: e.g., β-lactamases hydrolyze β-lactam antibiotics like penicillins and cephalosporins.
  • Target modification: Mutations in ribosomal subunits (e.g., 23S rRNA) or DNA gyrase reduce binding affinity of antibiotics like macrolides and fluoroquinolones.
  • Efflux pumps: Actively expel antibiotics out of the cell, reducing intracellular concentration.
  • Reduced permeability: Changes in outer membrane porins decrease antibiotic entry, especially in gram-negative bacteria.
  • Metabolic bypass: Acquisition of alternative enzymes or pathways that are not inhibited by the drug, e.g., altered dihydropteroate synthase confers sulfonamide resistance.

Etiology:

  • Paragonimiasis is caused by trematodes (lung flukes) of the genus Paragonimus, most commonly Paragonimus westermani in Asia, and Paragonimus africanus in parts of Africa.

b) Transmission and Control:

  • Humans acquire infection by ingesting undercooked or raw freshwater crustaceans (crabs/crayfish) harboring metacercariae.
  • Control measures include:
    • Public health education on safe cooking practices
    • Control of intermediate hosts
    • Improved sanitation to prevent egg contamination of freshwater bodies.

c) Pathogenesis:

  • After ingestion, metacercariae excyst in the duodenum, penetrate the intestinal wall, migrate through the peritoneum and diaphragm to reach the lungs, where they mature.
  • Adult flukes form encysted cavities in the lungs, causing inflammation, fibrosis, and cavitation.
  • Ectopic migration to brain or skin may occur, especially in heavy infections.

d) Diagnosis:

  • Sputum or stool microscopy: Identification of characteristic operculated eggs.
  • Chest X-ray/CT scan: Cavitary or nodular lesions resembling tuberculosis.
  • Serological tests: ELISA and other antibody detection methods.
  • History of raw crustacean consumption is key.

e) Treatment:

  • Praziquantel: 25 mg/kg orally, three times daily for 2–3 days.
  • Alternative: Triclabendazole (in regions where available).
  • Surgical drainage may be necessary in complicated pulmonary or cerebral cases.

Etiology:

  • Bilharzia, or schistosomiasis, is caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma.
  • Major human species include S. haematobium, S. mansoni, and S. japonicum.

b) Transmission and Control:

  • Transmission occurs when cercariae released by freshwater snails penetrate human skin during contact with infested water.
  • Control strategies include:
    • Mass drug administration (MDA) with praziquantel
    • Snail control (e.g., molluscicides)
    • Provision of safe water and sanitation
    • Health education.

c) Pathogenesis:

  • Adult worms live in venous plexuses and release eggs that induce granulomatous inflammation.
  • S. haematobium targets urinary tract → hematuria, fibrosis, squamous cell carcinoma risk.
  • S. mansoni and S. japonicum affect the intestines and liver → hepatosplenic schistosomiasis, portal hypertension.

d) Diagnosis:

  • Microscopy of urine (S. haematobium) or stool (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) for characteristic eggs.
  • Serological tests: Useful in low-endemic or early infections.
  • Ultrasound: Liver fibrosis and urinary tract involvement.
  • Hematuria dipstick: Useful screening tool.

e) Treatment:

  • Praziquantel: 40–60 mg/kg orally in a single or divided dose.
  • Repeat doses may be required in heavy infections.
  • Preventive chemotherapy in endemic areas is effective in reducing morbidity.

Bacteria possess several external structures that enhance virulence and contribute to their ability to invade, survive, and cause disease in host tissues:

  1. Capsule:
    • Composed of polysaccharides or polypeptides.
    • Prevents phagocytosis by immune cells (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae).
    • Aids in adherence and biofilm formation.
  2. Fimbriae and Pili:
    • Short, hair-like structures that mediate attachment to host cells, a critical step in colonization (e.g., E. coli fimbriae in UTI).
    • Sex pili facilitate horizontal gene transfer via conjugation, which may spread antibiotic resistance.
  3. Flagella:
    • Long, whip-like appendages used for motility, helping bacteria to reach optimal niches.
    • Flagellar components may act as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), triggering immune responses.
  4. Outer Membrane (Gram-negative bacteria):
    • Contains lipopolysaccharide (LPS): LPS acts as an endotoxin, causing fever, shock, and immune activation.
    • Acts as a permeability barrier to some antibiotics and host defense molecules.
  5. Slime Layer / Biofilm Formation:
    • Loosely attached extracellular matrix that enables biofilm development, which protects bacteria from antibiotics and immune responses (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa in CF patients).
  6. S-layers and Surface Proteins:
    • Protein arrays that help evade complement activation and promote host-cell adhesion.

Overall, these external structures are key in immune evasion, adhesion, invasion, antibiotic resistance, and persistence, making them central to bacterial pathogenicity.

Obligate aerobic bacteria rely on aerobic respiration to generate energy, as they require oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor.

  1. Substrate Utilization:
    • Organic compounds (e.g., glucose, amino acids, fatty acids) are used as carbon and energy sources.
    • Glucose enters the glycolytic pathway (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) to form pyruvate.
  2. Krebs Cycle (TCA Cycle):
    • Pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, which enters the TCA cycle, producing NADH and FADH₂.
    • These electron carriers transfer high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain (ETC).
  3. Electron Transport Chain (ETC):
    • Located in the cytoplasmic membrane, ETC consists of a series of protein complexes.
    • Electrons are passed along the chain, and oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor, forming water.
  4. ATP Generation:
    • The ETC generates a proton motive force (PMF) across the membrane.
    • ATP synthase uses the PMF to convert ADP to ATP via oxidative phosphorylation.
  5. Energy Yield:
    • Complete oxidation of one glucose molecule yields up to 38 ATP molecules.
    • This high energy yield supports active growth and metabolism.

Failure to access oxygen or disruptions in the ETC are lethal to obligate aerobes, as they lack alternative anaerobic pathways (e.g., fermentation).

Question 1

Which one of the following is an intracellular parasite?
A. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense
B. Trichomonas vaginalis
C. Entamoeba histolytica
D. Leishmania donovani
E. All of the above
Answer: D. Leishmania donovani

Question 2

Parasites can be classified based on their hosts. Which one of the following statements classifies a Mesoparasite?
A. A parasite which is occasionally found in both intermediate and definitive host
B. A parasite which entirely lives in an intermediate host
C. A parasite which entirely lives in a definitive host
D. A parasite which partly lives in and on a host
E. None of the above
Answer: D. A parasite which partly lives in and on a host

Question 3

Single-celled parasites utilize various physiological modes to take in molecules. Which one of the following is adopted for intake of a molecule for mutualism existence within the parasite?
A. Endocytosis
B. Active transport
C. Pinocytosis
D. Exocytosis
E. None of the above
Answer: A. Endocytosis

Question 4

The following are genetic-based conditions which can lead to resistance against malaria infection EXCEPT?
A. Sickle cell trait
B. Thalassemia
C. Presence of Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
D. Absence of Duffy antigens
E. None of the above
Answer: C. Presence of Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase

Question 5

In which form does Fasciola hepatica get into the human host?
A. Eggs
B. Cercariae
C. Trophozoites
D. Metacercariae
E. Larvae
Answer: D. Metacercariae

Question 6

Malaria infection is characterized by paroxysms. What is the interval of these paroxysms in a Plasmodium vivax infection?
A. 24 hours
B. 96 hours
C. 48 hours
D. 72 hours
E. 12 hours
Answer: C. 48 hours

Question 7

Which of the following parasites can be diagnosed by cerebrospinal fluid biopsy?
A. Giardia lamblia
B. Ascaris lumbricoides
C. Trichinella spiralis
D. Taenia solium
E. All of the above
Answer: D. Taenia solium

Question 8

Trichomonas vaginalis is characterized by how many flagella?
A. Five
B. Four
C. Three
D. Two
E. Six
Answer: A. Five

Question 9

Which of the following is NOT true about bacterial flagella?
A. Most of their length consists of a hollow, rigid protein tube.
B. They are constructed largely of a single protein called flagellin.
C. They spin like wheels, either clockwise or counterclockwise.
D. They use cytoplasmic ATP as their primary energy source.
E. None of the above
Answer: D. They use cytoplasmic ATP as their primary energy source.

Question 10

What is the purpose of bacterial endospores?
A. Allow the bacterium to make hundreds of "seeds" to spread on the wind.
B. Help the bacterium differentiate into faster-growing stages.
C. Allow the bacterium to survive the absence of oxygen.
D. Allow the bacterium to survive extended periods of heat or dryness.
E. All of the above
Answer: D. Allow the bacterium to survive extended periods of heat or dryness.

Question 11

Cells containing many nuclei are called:
A. Coenocyte
B. Hyphae
C. Mycelium
D. Sporophore
E. None of the above
Answer: A. Coenocyte

Question 12

The group or mass of hyphae is:
A. Coenocyte
B. Hyphae
C. Mycelium
D. Sporophore
E. B and C
Answer: E. B and C

Question 13

The spores produced inside the sporangia are:
A. Conidia
B. Endospore
C. Zoospore
D. Sporangiospores
E. Microspores
Answer: D. Sporangiospores

Question 14

The spores produced at the tip of hyphae outside the sporangia are:
A. Conidia
B. Endospore
C. Zoospore
D. Oidia
E. Sporangiospores
Answer: A. Conidia

Question 15

In some fungi, the hyphae break up into individual cells. These cells behave as spores and are called:
A. Blastospores
B. Endospore
C. Zoospore
D. Arthrospores
E. Conidiaspores
Answer: D. Arthrospores

Question 16

The most crucial step in infection of a host cell by a virus is:
A. Adsorption
B. Attachment
C. Penetration
D. Replication
E. Release
Answer: C. Penetration

Question 17

The viral nucleocapsid is the combination of:
A. Genome and capsid
B. Capsid and spikes
C. Envelope and capsid
D. Capsomere and genome
E. Genome and spikes
Answer: A. Genome and capsid

Question 18

In the absence of cytopathic effects (CPE), how would one demonstrate that a permissive cell is infected by a virus?
A. By Immunofluorescence Test (IFT)
B. By plaque test
C. By cell counting
D. By hemagglutination assay
E. None of the above
Answer: A. By Immunofluorescence Test (IFT)

Question 19

What is a phage?
A. Bacterium that infects viruses
B. A virus that infects bacteria
C. A bacterium that infects animal cells
D. An arbovirus
E. Virus-transformed cell
Answer: B. A virus that infects bacteria

Question 20

Prevention of viral diseases is best achieved by:
A. Antibiotics
B. Use of condoms
C. Vaccination
D. Antiviral drugs
E. All of the above
Answer: C. Vaccination

Question 21

A chemical component that is found in all viruses is:
A. Protein-coated nucleic acid
B. Lipid
C. DNA
D. RNA
E. All of the above
Answer: A. Protein-coated nucleic acid

Question 22

Interferons are:
A. Synthesized by the virus when infecting a cell
B. Synthesized by the host cell when infected by a virus
C. Synthesized by defective particles during infection
D. Synthesized by subviral agents in the cell during infection
E. A and B
Answer: B. Synthesized by the host cell when infected by a virus

Question 23

During what stage of the viral life cycle is the nucleic acid packed inside the capsid?
A. Penetration
B. Late protein synthesis (capsid)
C. Early protein synthesis
D. Assembly
E. At the time of uncoating
Answer: D. Assembly

Question 24

Which of the following is true of lysogenic viral infection?
A. Viral nucleic acid exists free, and no new viruses are produced.
B. Viral nucleic acid is associated with host nucleic acid, and no new viruses are produced.
C. Viral nucleic acid is associated with host nucleic acid, and new viruses are produced.
D. Viral nucleic acid is free, and new viruses are produced.
E. Viral nucleic acid exists as an episome.
Answer: B. Viral nucleic acid is associated with host nucleic acid, and no new viruses are produced.

Question 25

Which types of viruses contain reverse transcriptase?
A. Herpes viruses
B. Adenoviruses
C. Influenza viruses
D. Retroviruses
E. All single-stranded RNA viruses
Answer: D. Retroviruses

Question 26

A phage that exhibits both lytic and lysogenic life cycles is called:
A. Prophage
B. Provirus
C. Virulent
D. Temperate
E. Plaque
Answer: D. Temperate

Question 27

In which type of virus is the production of double-stranded DNA from RNA a necessary intermediate in the life cycle?
A. Influenza virus
B. Polio virus
C. Herpes virus
D. Retrovirus
E. T-even phage
Answer: D. Retrovirus

Question 28

The significance of the plasma membrane is that:
A. It selectively allows some molecules to pass into the organism.
B. It prevents movement of molecules out of the organism.
C. It is the site of protein synthesis.
D. B and C
E. All of the above
Answer: A. It selectively allows some molecules to pass into the organism.

Question 29

Commonly encountered bacteria are roughly spherical. The microbiological term describing this shape is:
A. Coccus
B. Coccobacillus
C. Pleomorphic
D. None of the above
E. Coccus and sometimes coccobacillus
Answer: A. Coccus

Question 30

Another common bacterial shape is that of a rod, often called:
A. Coccus
B. Bacillus
C. Pleomorphic
D. Vibrio
E. None of the above
Answer: B. Bacillus

Question 31

In bacterial cells, ribosomes are packed into the cytoplasmic matrix and also loosely attached to the plasma membrane. What is the function of ribosomes?
A. Site of energy production
B. Site of protein synthesis
C. Site of genetic reproduction
D. Both A and B
E. None of the above
Answer: B. Site of protein synthesis

Question 32

What is a plasmid?
A. Self-replicating segment of double-stranded DNA
B. Self-replicating segment of single-stranded RNA
C. A bacterial chromosome
D. All of the above
E. None of the above
Answer: A. Self-replicating segment of double-stranded DNA

Question 33

Plasmids are important to the genetics of many bacteria because:
A. They are inherited from one generation to the next.
B. They may carry genes that give their host a selective advantage.
C. They can render bacteria drug-resistant.
D. All of the above.
E. They facilitate lysogeny.
Answer: D. All of the above.

Question 34

Some bacteria are considered pleomorphic. This means:
A. They are shaped like bent rods.
B. They have a corkscrew shape.
C. They do not have just one shape.
D. They are restricted to one biotope.
E. They are not either bacilli or cocci.
Answer: C. They do not have just one shape.

Question 35

The 70S prokaryotic ribosomes consist of:
A. Two 40S subunits.
B. A 50S and a 30S subunit.
C. A 40S and a 30S subunit.
D. A 50S and a 20S subunit.
E. A 20S and a 60S subunit.
Answer: B. A 50S and a 30S subunit.

Question 36

Gram-positive cells:
A) Have thick, homogeneous cell walls.
B) Have large amounts of teichoic acids.
C) Have large molecular chitins.
D) Do not have an outer membrane.
E) All of the above are true.
Answer: E) All of the above are true.

Question 37

The outer membrane of Gram-negative cells is more permeable than the plasma membrane because:
A) LPS is larger than most membrane phospholipids.
B) Lipoproteins stretch the outer membrane.
C) Porin proteins establish holes in the outer membrane.
D) The core polysaccharide spans the lipid bilayer.
E) None of the above.
Answer: C) Porin proteins establish holes in the outer membrane.

Question 38

The most important role of the prokaryotic cell wall is to:
A) Maintain the shape of the cell.
B) Protect the cell from osmotic pressures.
C) Prevent ions from diffusing away from the cell.
D) Block the effects of antibiotics like penicillin.
E) All of the above.
Answer: B) Protect the cell from osmotic pressures.

Question 39

Which of the following is NOT true about capsules and slime layers?
A) They consist of secreted material lying outside of the bacterial cell wall.
B) They can prevent desiccation of bacterial cells.
C) They are required for bacteria to grow normally in culture.
D) They help bacteria resist phagocytosis by macrophages.
E) None of the above.
Answer: C) They are required for bacteria to grow normally in culture.

Question 40

Fimbriae:
A) Attach bacteria to various surfaces.
B) Cause bacteria to move through fluids.
C) Sense changes in nutrient concentration.
D) Are pathways for the secretion of exoenzymes.
E) C and D.
Answer: A) Attach bacteria to various surfaces.

Question 41

A bacillus bacterium with a single flagellum at each end is described as:
A) Monotrichous
B) Amphitrichous
C) Lophotrichous
D) Peritrichous
E) All of the above
Answer: B) Amphitrichous

Question 42

Bacterial capsules are useful for:
A) Attachment to surfaces.
B) Protection against macrophages.
C) Production of toxins.
D) Motility.
E) Reproduction.
Answer: B) Protection against macrophages.

Question 43

Which of the following is a true pathogen?
A) Candida
B) Sporothrix
C) Mucor
D) Aspergillus
E) None
Answer: B) Sporothrix

Question 44

Bacterial capsules are best demonstrated by:
A) Methylene blue stain.
B) Gram stain.
C) Negative staining.
D) Impregnation technique.
E) None of the above.
Answer: C) Negative staining.

Question 45

In a light microscope, what function does the condenser serve?
A) Focuses the light rays on the sample.
B) Magnifies the light rays after their passage through the sample.
C) Focuses the light rays into the observer’s eyes.
D) Increases the light intensity.
E) Reduces glare.
Answer: A) Focuses the light rays on the sample.

Question 46

One of the diseases below is not caused by bacteria:
A) Leprosy
B) Plague
C) Rabies
D) Tetanus
E) Meningitis
Answer: C) Rabies

Question 47

The presence of D-amino acids in the crosslinks of the peptidoglycan layer is most likely because:
A) Most peptidases can only cleave L-amino acids.
B) D-amino acids fit the structural constraints of the cell wall better than L-amino acids.
C) Most L-amino acids have already been used for protein synthesis.
D) D-amino acids are easier to crosslink in the absence of ribosomes.
E) They promote synthesis of much-needed essential amino acids.
Answer: A) Most peptidases can only cleave L-amino acids.

Question 48

Gram-positive cells:
A) Have thick, homogeneous cell walls.
B) Have large amounts of teichoic acids.
C) Have large molecular chitins.
D) Do not have an outer membrane.
E) All of the above.
Answer: E) All of the above.

Question 49

Which of the following is not a characteristic of fungi?
A) Can be unicellular or multicellular.
B) Have cell walls made of chitin.
C) Are photosynthetic.
D) Can produce antibiotics.
E) Can be infected by viruses.
Answer: C) Are photosynthetic.

Question 50

The spores produced by fungi at the tip of hyphae outside the sporangia are called:
A) Conidia
B) Endospores
C) Zoospores
D) Oidia
E) Sporangiospores
Answer: A) Conidia

28. Each of the following statements concerning Ascaris lumbricoides is correct EXCEPT:

Title: ANATOMY LAQs and SAQs
Content:
Fetal circulation is designed to bypass the non-functioning fetal lungs and ensure preferential delivery of oxygen-rich blood to the developing brain and heart.

  • Oxygenated blood from the placenta is delivered to the fetus through the umbilical vein.
  • Approximately 50% of this blood bypasses the liver via the ductus venosus, entering the inferior vena cava (IVC), while the remainder perfuses the hepatic sinusoids.
  • The IVC carries this mixed but relatively oxygen-rich blood to the right atrium.
  • From the right atrium, blood follows two main routes:
    1. Majority of oxygenated blood is shunted through the foramen ovale (interatrial opening) into the left atrium, bypassing pulmonary circulation. From there, it flows to the left ventricle, and is pumped into the ascending aorta, supplying the heart, brain, and upper body.
    2. Deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and is pumped into the pulmonary trunk.
      • Due to high pulmonary vascular resistance, most of this blood is diverted through the ductus arteriosus into the descending aorta, bypassing the lungs.
  • Blood from the descending aorta supplies the lower body, and deoxygenated blood is returned to the placenta via the paired umbilical arteries, which arise from the internal iliac arteries.

Key adaptations: Foramen ovale, ductus venosus, ductus arteriosus
Clinical relevance: These shunts must close at birth to transition to adult circulation.

There are three key shunts in fetal circulation, each ensuring efficient distribution of oxygenated blood while bypassing non-functional fetal organs like the lungs and liver.

  1. Ductus venosus
    • Embryological origin: Derived from the vitelline venous system.
    • Function: Shunts oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic circulation.
    • Fate: Closes shortly after birth and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
  2. Foramen ovale
    • Embryological origin: Formed between the septum primum and septum secundum in the interatrial septum.
    • Function: Allows blood to bypass the non-ventilated lungs by shunting blood from the right atrium to the left atrium.
    • Fate: Functionally closes at birth due to reversal of atrial pressure; anatomically forms the fossa ovalis.
  3. Ductus arteriosus
    • Embryological origin: Derived from the left sixth aortic arch.
    • Function: Connects the pulmonary trunk to the descending aorta, bypassing the lungs.
    • Fate: Closes in response to increased oxygen tension and decreased prostaglandins, becoming the ligamentum arteriosum.
(i) Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
  • Components:
    1. Pulmonary stenosis
    2. Overriding aorta
    3. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
    4. Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Embryological basis:
    • Caused by anterior and superior displacement of the infundibular (conotruncal) septum, derived from neural crest cells.
    • This leads to unequal division of the truncus arteriosus, favoring the aortic outflow over the pulmonary, and malalignment of the interventricular septum.
(ii) Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)
  • Embryological basis:
    • The ductus arteriosus, derived from the left sixth aortic arch, fails to close postnatally.
    • Persistence is often related to prematurity or conditions associated with low oxygen tension (e.g., respiratory distress).
  • Clinical consequence:
    • Causes a left-to-right shunt, leading to pulmonary overcirculation and heart failure if untreated.

Lung development involves both structural maturation and functional readiness for gas exchange, divided into five overlapping stages:

  1. Embryonic stage (4–7 weeks)
    • Origin: Lung bud (respiratory diverticulum) arises from the ventral foregut endoderm.
    • Bud bifurcates into primary bronchial buds, which invade the splanchnic mesoderm.
  2. Pseudoglandular stage (5–17 weeks)
    • Branching continues to form terminal bronchioles.
    • Histologically resembles an exocrine gland.
    • No gas exchange is possible.
  3. Canalicular stage (16–25 weeks)
    • Terminal bronchioles give rise to respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
    • Vascularization increases, and the epithelium starts to thin.
    • Type I pneumocytes begin forming.
  4. Saccular stage (24–38 weeks)
    • Formation of terminal sacs (primitive alveoli).
    • Type II pneumocytes differentiate and start secreting surfactant, crucial for alveolar stability post-birth.
  5. Alveolar stage (36 weeks to 8 years postnatally)
    • Mature alveoli form via septation of terminal sacs.
    • Gas exchange becomes efficient, and lung capacity expands after birth.

Clinical note: Premature infants born before surfactant production (~24–28 weeks) are at risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS).

Oogenesis is the process by which female gametes (ova) are formed from primordial germ cells (PGCs), beginning during fetal life and continuing until menopause.

Stages of oogenesis:
  1. Primordial germ cells (PGCs) migrate to the gonadal ridge (~4th week of embryogenesis).
  2. They differentiate into oogonia via mitosis (~5th–6th week).
    • Peak number (~6–7 million) is reached by mid-gestation (around 20 weeks).
  3. Oogonia enter meiosis I and become primary oocytes, arrested in prophase I (diplotene stage) until puberty.
    • Each is surrounded by flattened follicular cells, forming primordial follicles.
  4. At puberty, under FSH stimulation, some follicles resume meiosis I during each menstrual cycle.
    • Completion of meiosis I yields a secondary oocyte and a first polar body.
  5. The secondary oocyte immediately begins meiosis II, but is arrested at metaphase II until fertilization.
  6. Upon fertilization, meiosis II is completed, producing the ovum and a second polar body.
Key features:
  • Oogenesis is a discontinuous process, with long arrest periods.
  • Only 400–500 oocytes are ovulated during a woman’s reproductive life.
  • Aging affects oocyte quality, increasing the risk of meiotic nondisjunction (e.g., trisomies).

Placental abnormalities can be classified based on structural development and implantation site.

A. Structural abnormalities:
  1. Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS):
    • Accreta: Villi attach directly to myometrium (defective decidua basalis).
    • Increta: Villi invade the myometrium.
    • Percreta: Villi penetrate through to the serosa or adjacent organs (e.g., bladder).
    • Cause: Often associated with previous C-sections or endometrial damage.
  2. Circumvallate placenta:
    • The chorionic plate is smaller than the basal plate, leading to a rolled, thickened edge.
    • May be associated with bleeding, preterm labor, and fetal growth restriction.
  3. Succenturiate lobe:
    • An accessory placental lobe, increasing the risk of retained placental tissue postpartum.
B. Positional abnormalities:
  1. Placenta previa:
    • Implantation over or near the internal cervical os.
    • Presents with painless vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy.
    • Types: Total, partial, marginal.
  2. Placenta abruptio:
    • Premature separation of a normally implanted placenta.
    • Associated with painful bleeding and fetal distress.

The placenta forms from both embryonic and maternal tissues, beginning in the second week of development.

Fetal (embryonic) contribution:
  • From the trophoblast:
    • Cytotrophoblast: Inner cellular layer; proliferative.
    • Syncytiotrophoblast: Outer multinucleated layer; invades endometrium and forms lacunae.
  • Extraembryonic mesoderm invades and forms the chorionic villi.
Developmental stages:
  1. Primary villi (Day 13): Core of cytotrophoblast covered by syncytiotrophoblast.
  2. Secondary villi (Day 16): Extraembryonic mesoderm invades primary villi.
  3. Tertiary villi (~Day 21): Capillaries develop within mesodermal core.

These villi become vascularized, allowing maternal–fetal exchange.

Maternal contribution:
  • From the decidua basalis of the endometrium.
  • Forms the maternal side of the placenta with intervillous spaces filled with maternal blood.
Mature placenta:
  • By the end of the first trimester, villi on the chorion frondosum (fetal side) persist.
  • The decidua basalis fuses with it, forming the full discoid placenta.

Functions: Exchange of gases, nutrients, waste; endocrine function (e.g., hCG, progesterone); immunological barrier.

The urinary bladder receives both autonomic and somatic innervation:

Somatic innervation: From the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), supplying the external urethral sphincter, allowing voluntary control of urination.

Parasympathetic innervation: From pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4). These fibers stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and relaxation of the internal urethral sphincter to facilitate micturition.

Sympathetic innervation: From the hypogastric plexus (T11–L2). These fibers promote relaxation of the detrusor muscle and contraction of the internal sphincter, aiding bladder filling.

  • Anatomical components:
    1. Kidneys – filter blood to form urine.
    2. Ureters – transport urine from kidneys to bladder.
    3. Urinary bladder – stores urine.
    4. Urethra – conducts urine to the exterior.
  • Functional components:
    1. Filtration – occurs in the glomeruli of nephrons.
    2. Reabsorption and secretion – primarily in the renal tubules.
    3. Urine storage and excretion – via the bladder and urethra.
  1. Glomerular filtration:
    • Blood pressure forces plasma through the glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s capsule, forming the filtrate.
    • Large molecules (e.g., proteins) are retained in the blood.
  2. Tubular reabsorption:
    • Essential substances like glucose, amino acids, and water are reabsorbed from the renal tubule into the peritubular capillaries.
    • Most reabsorption occurs in the proximal convoluted tubule.
  3. Tubular secretion:
    • Active transport of substances (e.g., H⁺, K⁺, drugs) from peritubular capillaries into the tubular fluid.
    • Helps maintain acid-base balance and eliminate waste.
  1. Cortical nephrons – Located mostly in the renal cortex; have short loops of Henle.
  2. Juxtamedullary nephrons – Located near the cortex-medulla junction; have long loops of Henle that extend deep into the medulla and are crucial for urine concentration
  1. Hypospadias – Urethral opening on the ventral side of the penis.
  2. Epispadias – Urethral opening on the dorsal side of the penis.
  3. Micropenis – Abnormally small penis.
  4. Clitoromegaly – Enlarged clitoris, possibly due to androgen exposure.
  5. Ambiguous genitalia – Indistinct or atypical development of external genitalia, often associated with disorders of sex development (DSDs).
  1. Bicornuate uterus – Partial failure of Müllerian duct fusion resulting in two uterine horns.
  2. Septate uterus – Incomplete resorption of the uterine septum.
  3. Unicornuate uterus – Development of only one Müllerian duct.
  4. Uterus didelphys – Complete failure of fusion of the Müllerian ducts; results in two uteri and two cervices.
  5. Aplastic uterus (Müllerian agenesis) – Complete absence or underdevelopment of the uterus.

Urethral anomalies:

  1. Hypospadias – Urethral opening on ventral penis surface.
  2. Epispadias – Urethral opening on dorsal penis surface.
  3. Urethral stricture – Narrowing of urethra.
  4. Urethral duplication – Two urethral canals.
  5. Persistent cloaca (in females) – Common opening for urinary, genital, and GI tracts.

Urinary bladder anomalies:

  1. Exstrophy of the bladder – Ventral wall defect exposing bladder mucosa.
  2. Urachal anomalies – e.g., patent urachus causing urine leakage at the umbilicus.
  3. Bladder agenesis – Absence of the bladder (rare).
  4. Duplicated bladder – Two bladder cavities.
  5. Diverticulum of the bladder – Outpouching of the bladder wall.

Each nephron consists of the following parts:

  1. Renal corpuscle – Composed of:
    • Glomerulus (capillary tuft)
    • Bowman’s capsule (parietal and visceral layers)
  2. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) – Reabsorption of water, ions, glucose.
  3. Loop of Henle – Descending and ascending limbs for urine concentration.
  4. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) – Selective reabsorption and secretion.
  5. Collecting duct – Receives urine from multiple nephrons; concentrates and conveys urine to the renal pelvis.
  1. Hepatocytes → secrete bile into
  2. Bile canaliculi → drain into

  4. Interlobular bile ducts → unite to form
  5. Left and right hepatic ducts → join to form
  6. Common hepatic duct → joins
  7. Cystic duct (from gallbladder) → to form
  8. Common bile duct → empties into
  9. Duodenum (via the hepatopancreatic ampulla of Vater, regulated by the sphincter of Oddi)

  2. Through the interventricular foramina (of Monro) →
  3. Into the third ventricle (in diencephalon) →
  4. Through the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) →
  5. Into the fourth ventricle (between pons and cerebellum) →
  6. CSF exits via:

The male sexual response cycle involves four main phases, regulated by autonomic and somatic nerves:

  1. Erection (Parasympathetic, S2–S4):
    • Initiated by tactile, visual, or psychological stimuli.
    • Parasympathetic nerves from pelvic splanchnic nerves cause vasodilation of penile arteries.
    • Helicine arteries in the corpora cavernosa dilate, increasing blood flow.
    • Ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles compress veins → blood retention → erection.
  2. Emission (Sympathetic, T12–L2):
    • Movement of sperm and glandular secretions into urethra.
    • Involves contraction of vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate.
    • Controlled by sympathetic fibers via the hypogastric plexus.
  3. Ejaculation (Somatic reflex via pudendal nerve):
    • Rhythmic contractions of pelvic floor muscles (bulbospongiosus).
    • External urethral sphincter relaxes; semen expelled.
  4. Resolution (Sympathetic):
    • Vasoconstriction of penile arteries.
    • Detumescence due to decreased blood inflow and increased venous drainage.

Similar to the male, but with female-specific features:

  1. Excitement Phase (Parasympathetic, S2–S4):
    • Clitoral erection via vasodilation of deep arteries.
    • Vaginal lubrication by transudation and Bartholin gland secretions.
    • Engorgement of labia and vaginal wall.
    • Uterus elevates and elongation of the vaginal canal occurs.
  2. Plateau Phase:
    • Further vasocongestion of clitoris, vagina, and breasts.
    • Tent effect: upper vagina expands to form a tent-like structure.
  3. Orgasm (Somatic via pudendal nerve; Sympathetic reflex):
    • Rhythmic contractions of pelvic muscles, uterus, and vaginal walls.
    • Accompanied by a surge in sympathetic output.
  4. Resolution:
    • Return of pelvic organs to pre-arousal state.
    • Generally lacks a refractory period, allowing for multiple orgasms.
  1. Omphalocele – Herniation of abdominal contents into the base of the umbilical cord, covered by a membrane.
  2. Gastroschisis – Herniation of intestines through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall (usually to the right of the umbilicus) without a membrane covering.
  3. Meckel’s diverticulum – A persistent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct forming a small pouch in the ileum.
  4. Imperforate anus – Failure of the anal membrane to perforate, resulting in a blind-ending rectum.
  5. Malrotation of the gut – Abnormal rotation and fixation of the intestines during development, increasing the risk of volvulus.

Scrotum consists of several layers (superficial to deep):

  1. Skin – Thin and pigmented with sweat glands.
  2. Dartos muscle and fascia – Smooth muscle for temperature regulation.
  3. External spermatic fascia – Derived from the external oblique aponeurosis.
  4. Cremaster muscle and fascia – From the internal oblique muscle.
  5. Internal spermatic fascia – From the transversalis fascia.
  6. Tunica vaginalis – Serous membrane covering testis (parietal and visceral layers).

Testis is organized into:

  • Tunica albuginea – Thick fibrous capsule surrounding the testis.
  • Lobules (250–300) – Each contains 1–4 seminiferous tubules (site of spermatogenesis).
  • Rete testis – Network of tubules in the mediastinum testis.
  • Efferent ductules – Connect rete testis to the epididymis.

The male urethra is divided into 3 parts, each with distinct histology:

  1. Prostatic urethra:
    • Lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium).
    • Surrounded by the prostate gland; receives openings of prostatic ducts, ejaculatory ducts, and prostatic utricle.
  2. Membranous urethra:
    • Lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
    • Surrounded by external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle).
    • Narrowest and least distensible part.
  3. Spongy (penile) urethra:
    • Lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium, becomes stratified squamous distally.
    • Surrounded by corpus spongiosum.
    • Contains mucous glands (of Littre).

The pancreas has both exocrine and endocrine components:

  1. Exocrine pancreas (majority):
    • Composed of serous acini (pyramidal cells with zymogen granules).
    • Secretes digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases).
    • Intercalated ducts → intralobular ducts → interlobular ducts → main pancreatic duct.
  2. Endocrine pancreas (Islets of Langerhans):
    • Lightly stained clusters scattered among acini.
    • Contains:
      • Alpha cells – secrete glucagon
      • Beta cells – secrete insulin
      • Delta cells – secrete somatostatin
      • PP cells – secrete pancreatic polypeptide

Origin: From the internal carotid artery.
Course: Enters the lateral (Sylvian) fissure and divides into superior and inferior branches.

Functional distribution:

  1. Lateral cerebral cortex:
    • Motor cortex (precentral gyrus): Upper limb and face.
    • Sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus): Upper limb and face.
    • Broca’s area (dominant hemisphere): Motor speech.
    • Wernicke’s area (posterior part of superior temporal gyrus): Language comprehension.
    • Auditory cortex (superior temporal gyrus).
    • Frontal eye fields.
  2. Deep branches (Lenticulostriate arteries):
    • Supply basal ganglia, internal capsule (especially posterior limb) → motor fibers.

Clinical relevance:

  • MCA stroke → contralateral hemiparesis (face/arm), aphasia (if dominant hemisphere), hemineglect (non-dominant).

Parts (from medial to lateral):

  1. Intramural (interstitial) – within uterine wall.
  2. Isthmus – narrow and straight.
  3. Ampulla – widest part, site of fertilization.
  4. Infundibulum – funnel-shaped with fimbriae.

Wall layers:

  • Mucosa: Highly folded; lined by ciliated columnar and secretory cells.
  • Muscularis: Inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers.
  • Serosa: Peritoneal covering (mesosalpinx part of broad ligament).

Blood supply:

  • Arterial:
    • Uterine artery (from internal iliac)
    • Ovarian artery (from abdominal aorta)
  • Venous:
    • Follows arteries into uterine and ovarian veins.

Below the arcuate line (found approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis), the rectus sheath is organized as follows:

Anterior wall:
  • Formed by the aponeuroses of all three abdominal muscles:
    • External oblique
    • Internal oblique
    • Transversus abdominis
      → These aponeuroses pass entirely anterior to the rectus abdominis.
Posterior wall:
  • Absent below the arcuate line.
  • Rectus abdominis lies directly on the transversalis fascia.
Clinical relevance:
  • The absence of a posterior sheath makes this region prone to herniation and vulnerable during abdominal surgeries.

Anomalies of the Urethra:

  1. Hypospadias – Abnormal opening of the urethra on the underside of the penis.
  2. Epispadias – Urethral opening is located on the dorsal aspect of the penis.
  3. Urethral atresia – Complete absence or closure of the urethra.
  4. Posterior urethral valves – Obstructive congenital folds in the posterior urethra (males).
  5. Urethral duplication – Presence of two urethral channels.

Anomalies of the Urinary Bladder:

  1. Bladder exstrophy – The anterior bladder wall and abdominal wall fail to close, exposing the bladder mucosa.
  2. Patent urachus – Failure of the urachus to close, resulting in urine leakage from the umbilicus.
  3. Urachal cyst or sinus – Partial closure of the urachus, leading to fluid-filled remnants.
  4. Bladder agenesis – Complete absence of the bladder (very rare).
  5. Duplication of the bladder – Presence of two bladders due to incomplete embryological fusion.

The elbow joint is a synovial hinge joint, involving 3 bones and several stabilizing structures:

Bones involved:
  1. Humerus – Trochlea and capitulum
  2. Ulna – Trochlear notch, olecranon, coronoid process
  3. Radius – Head articulates with capitulum and radial notch of ulna
Articulations:
  • Humeroulnar (main hinge movement)
  • Humeroradial
  • Proximal radioulnar (for supination/pronation)
Stability factors:
  1. Bony congruence – Deep trochlear notch of the ulna provides a strong fit for the trochlea.
  2. Joint capsule – Encloses the joint; reinforced by ligaments.
  3. Ligaments:
    • Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament
    • Radial (lateral) collateral ligament
    • Annular ligament – stabilizes the radial head against the ulna.
  4. Muscles crossing the joint – Especially brachialis, triceps, biceps brachii, and supinator.
  5. Negative intra-articular pressure – Adds passive stability.

A nephron is the functional unit of the kidney and consists of:

  1. Renal corpuscle:
    • Glomerulus – A tuft of capillaries where filtration occurs.
    • Bowman’s capsule – Surrounds the glomerulus and collects filtrate.
  2. Renal tubule:
    • Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) – Reabsorption of water, ions, and nutrients.
    • Loop of Henle
      • Descending limb – Permeable to water.
      • Ascending limb – Permeable to salts but not water.
    • Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) – Further reabsorption and secretion.
    • Collecting duct – Receives filtrate from several nephrons, helps concentrate urine.

Each nephron is associated with a rich capillary network (peritubular capillaries and vasa recta).

Metabolism of Vitamin D:

  1. Synthesis begins in the skin where UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (Vitamin D₃).
  2. In the liver, cholecalciferol is hydroxylated to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol).
  3. In the kidney, specifically the proximal tubules, 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted by 1α-hydroxylase to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), the active form.

Role of the Kidney:

  • Performs the final activation step in Vitamin D metabolism.
  • Regulates enzyme activity (1α-hydroxylase) under the control of PTH, calcium, and phosphate levels.
  • Maintains calcium-phosphate balance and bone health via active Vitamin D.
State the role of active Vitamin D in calcium homeostasis (5 marks)

Active Vitamin D (Calcitriol):

  1. Enhances intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
  2. Promotes renal reabsorption of calcium in the distal tubules.
  3. Stimulates osteoclast activity indirectly to release calcium from bone stores (when needed).
  4. Suppresses parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion through negative feedback.
  5. Maintains serum calcium levels, supporting bone mineralization, nerve transmission, and muscle contraction.

The male sexual response cycle consists of four main phases: Erection, Emission, Ejaculation, and Resolution. The anatomical basis for each phase involves neural, vascular, and muscular structures:

  1. Erection (Parasympathetic Response)
    • Mediated by pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).
    • Parasympathetic stimulation causes vasodilation of the helicine arteries within the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum.
    • Nitric oxide (NO) is released, increasing cGMP, relaxing smooth muscle and allowing blood engorgement.
    • The tunica albuginea compresses venous outflow, maintaining erection.
  2. Emission (Sympathetic Response)
    • Controlled by sympathetic fibers (T11–L2).
    • Contraction of the smooth muscles of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate propels semen into the prostatic urethra.
    • The internal urethral sphincter contracts to prevent retrograde ejaculation into the bladder.
  3. Ejaculation (Somatic and Sympathetic Response)
    • Coordinated by somatic nerves (pudendal nerve, S2–S4) and sympathetic nerves.
    • Rhythmic contractions of the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus muscles expel semen from the urethra.
    • The external urethral sphincter remains relaxed during ejaculation.
  4. Resolution
    • Sympathetic tone returns, causing vasoconstriction of penile arteries.
    • Blood drains from erectile tissue, and the penis becomes flaccid.

The female sexual response cycle consists of four phases: Excitement, Plateau, Orgasm, and Resolution. It involves autonomic (parasympathetic and sympathetic) and somatic innervation, as well as vascular and muscular responses.

  1. Excitement Phase (Parasympathetic – S2–S4)
    • Vasocongestion of clitoris, labia, and vaginal walls via pelvic splanchnic nerves.
    • Erection of clitoris due to increased blood flow in corpora cavernosa.
    • Lubrication of the vagina occurs via transudate from vaginal walls and secretion from Bartholin’s glands.
    • Enlargement of breasts and nipples due to vasodilation.
  2. Plateau Phase
    • Increased blood flow and muscle tension.
    • Expansion of the vaginal canal, elevation of the uterus (tenting effect).
    • Inner vagina expands, outer third becomes engorged (orgasmic platform).
  3. Orgasm (Sympathetic + Somatic)
    • Involuntary rhythmic contractions of the pelvic floor muscles, uterus, and vaginal walls.
    • Mediated by sympathetic nerves (T11–L2) and somatic pudendal nerve (S2–S4).
    • No ejaculation, but strong muscular contractions assist sperm movement.
  4. Resolution
    • Gradual return to baseline vascular and muscular tone.
    • Longer refractory period compared to males.
