SECTION B

Cholinomimetic drugs mimic the action of acetylcholine and can be direct-acting (bind receptors) or indirect-acting (inhibit acetylcholinesterase).

Examples and Effects:

  1. Pilocarpine (Direct-acting muscarinic agonist):
    • Increases salivation and sweating
    • Induces miosis (pupil constriction)
    • Lowers intraocular pressure in glaucoma
  2. Neostigmine (Indirect-acting cholinesterase inhibitor):
    • Enhances neuromuscular transmission in myasthenia gravis
    • Increases GI motility and bladder contraction
    • Reverses non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockade

Significance:

  • Mechanism: Inhibit reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) at synaptic clefts, increasing serotonin availability.
  • Clinical Use: First-line treatment for depression, anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD.
  • Examples: Fluoxetine, Sertraline, Paroxetine, Escitalopram.

Definition:
The GABA shunt is a closed-loop metabolic pathway that converts glutamate into GABA and recycles GABA into metabolites for energy and neurotransmitter balance.

Key Steps:

  1. Glutamate → GABA:
    • Enzyme: Glutamate decarboxylase (GAD)
    • Cofactor: Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6)
  2. GABA → Succinic semialdehyde:
    • Enzyme: GABA transaminase (GABA-T)
    • Transfers amino group to α-ketoglutarate
  3. Succinic semialdehyde → Succinate:
    • Enzyme: Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase
    • Enters the TCA cycle

Significance:

  • Maintains GABA levels, the chief inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS
  • Regulates neuronal excitability
  • Connects neurotransmitter metabolism with energy production
Dopamine Degradation Pathways (15 Marks)

Overview: Dopamine is a catecholamine neurotransmitter synthesized from L-DOPA and degraded primarily via monoamine oxidase (MAO) and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). The pathways occur in the presynaptic neuron, glial cells, and extracellular space.

I. Main Enzymes Involved:
  1. MAO (Monoamine Oxidase)
    • Location: Mitochondria of neurons and glia
    • Type: Two isoforms – MAO-A and MAO-B
  2. COMT (Catechol-O-methyltransferase)
    • Location: Cytoplasm of glial cells, liver, kidney, postsynaptic neurons
II. Degradation Pathways:
Pathway 1 (Intraneuronal – MAO first):
  1. Dopamine → DOPAC (3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid)
    • Enzyme: MAO-B
    • Intermediate: Dopamine aldehyde
  2. DOPAC → HVA (homovanillic acid)
    • Enzyme: COMT
Pathway 2 (Extraneuronal – COMT first):
  1. Dopamine → 3-Methoxytyramine (3-MT)
    • Enzyme: COMT
  2. 3-MT → HVA
    • Enzyme: MAO-B
Final Excretion Product:
  • Homovanillic Acid (HVA)
    • Excreted in urine; useful in clinical diagnostics (e.g., neuroblastoma, Parkinson’s disease monitoring)
  1. Regulates GI Motility:
    • Coordinates peristalsis and segmental contractions.
  2. Controls Secretion:
    • Modulates mucus, enzyme, and hormone secretion from glands.
  3. Maintains Mucosal Integrity:
    • Involved in epithelial cell turnover and barrier protection.
  4. Regulates Blood Flow:
    • Controls vasodilation/constriction in gut vasculature.
  5. Sensory Integration:
    • Detects stretch, pH, and nutrient content, triggering reflexes independently of CNS.

1. Resting Membrane Potential (RMP):

  • Maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase and K⁺ leak channels (~ -70 mV)

2. Depolarization:

  • Trigger: Stimulus raises membrane potential above threshold (~ -55 mV)
  • Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open:
    → Na⁺ influx
    → Membrane potential becomes more positive (~+30 mV)

3. Peak and Inactivation:

  • Na⁺ channels inactivate after peak depolarization
  • Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open:
    → K⁺ efflux
    → Initiates repolarization

4. Repolarization and Hyperpolarization:

  • Outflow of K⁺ returns membrane potential toward RMP
  • K⁺ channels remain open longer → hyperpolarization (~ -80 mV)

5. Refractory Periods:

  • Absolute Refractory: Na⁺ channels inactivated – no new AP possible
  • Relative Refractory: Stronger stimulus needed to generate new AP

Overview: Steroid hormones are metabolized primarily in the liver and excreted via urine and bile.

1. Liver Metabolism:

  • Phase I Reactions:
    • Involves oxidation, reduction, and hydroxylation reactions (mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes).
    • Increases water solubility and introduces functional groups for conjugation.
  • Phase II Reactions (Conjugation):
    • Glucuronidation (via UDP-glucuronosyltransferase).
    • Sulfation (via sulfotransferase).
    • These conjugates are hydrophilic and ready for excretion.

2. Excretion Pathways:

  • Urinary Excretion:
    • Majority of conjugated steroid metabolites (e.g., pregnanediol, tetrahydrocortisol) are excreted in urine.
    • Measurement used for hormonal assessments (e.g., 17-ketosteroids).
  • Biliary Excretion:
    • Some conjugates are excreted in bile → enter intestine → partly deconjugated by gut bacteria → may undergo enterohepatic circulation.

3. Clinical Significance:

  • Impaired liver function affects hormone clearance → hormonal imbalance.
  • Enzyme deficiencies (e.g., in glucuronidation) can lead to altered excretion profiles.

1. Osmotic Opening of Tight Junctions:

  • Hyperosmotic agents (e.g., mannitol) shrink endothelial cells → temporarily open tight junctions.
  • Allows passive diffusion of drugs.
  • Used in treating brain tumors.

2. Receptor-Mediated Transcytosis:

  • Conjugate drugs to ligands (e.g., transferrin, insulin) that bind endothelial receptors.
  • The complex undergoes endocytosis and is transported across the BBB.
  • Allows selective and controlled delivery.

3. Nanocarrier and Liposome Systems:

  • Drugs encapsulated in nanoparticles or liposomes with surface modifications.
  • Surface ligands facilitate receptor-mediated uptake.
  • Enhances drug stability and targeting.

4. Inhibition of Efflux Transporters (e.g., P-glycoprotein):

  • Co-administer P-gp inhibitors (e.g., verapamil) to prevent drug efflux from brain back to blood.
  • Enhances brain accumulation of therapeutic agents.
  • Important in CNS cancer and epilepsy treatment.

1. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the myenteric ganglia of the

fibers.

Title: Molecular Biology,Molecular Genetics &  Microbial-Biochemistry MCQs
Content:
SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQs) (35 MARKS)

Answer ALL questions.

Question 1

The larvae of the following helminths enter the human body by penetrating the intact skin:
A. Ancylostoma duodenale and Strongyloides stercoralis ✅
B. Trypanosoma brucei gambiense
C. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense
D. Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium species
E. Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis

Answer: A (Ancylostoma duodenale and Strongyloides stercoralis)

Question 2

Which two protozoa may infect the human fetus transplacentally?
A. Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium species ✅
B. Giardia lamblia and Trichomonas vaginalis
C. Ancylostoma duodenale and Strongyloides stercoralis
D. Trypanosoma brucei gambiense
E. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense

Answer: A (Toxoplasma gondii and Plasmodium species)

Question 3

In aerobic respiration, the terminal electron acceptor is:
A. Oxygen ✅
B. Nitrogen
C. Hydrogen
D. Nitrate
E. a and b

Answer: A (Oxygen)

Question 4

Which of the following are NOT examples of a terminal electron acceptor in anaerobic respiration?
A. Nitrate
B. Hydrogen sulfide
C. Iron hydroxide
D. H₂ ✅
E. Sulfate

Answer: D (H₂)

Question 5

When acetate is the sole source of carbon for some microorganisms, the cycle used is called:
A. Pentose phosphate pathway
B. Glycolytic pathway
C. Glyoxylate pathway ✅
D. Oxaloacetate pathway
E. Both C and D

Answer: C (Glyoxylate pathway)

Question 6

Most of the energy in aerobic respiration of glucose is captured by:
A. Substrate-level phosphorylation
B. Electron transport of electrons from NADH ✅
C. Long-chain fatty acid oxidation
D. The enzyme formic-hydrogen lyase
E. Both C and D

Answer: B (Electron transport of electrons from NADH)

Question 7

The role of bacteriochlorophyll in anoxygenic photosynthesis:
A. Reduce ferredoxin directly
B. Reduce NADP directly
C. Use light energy to energize an electron ✅
D. Transfer electrons to an intermediate in the sulfide oxidation pathway
E. A and B

Answer: C (Use light energy to energize an electron)

Question 8

Entner-Doudoroff pathway is NOT found in:
A. Aerobic prokaryotes
B. Anaerobic prokaryotes
C. Both (a) and (b)
D. Eukaryotes ✅
E. Atypical viral agents

Answer: D (Eukaryotes)

Question 9

Which process could result in the net movement of a substance into a cell if the substance is more concentrated in the cell than in the surroundings?
A. Active transport ✅
B. Diffusion
C. Osmosis
D. Facilitated diffusion
E. None of the above

Answer: A (Active transport)

Question 10

Which is NOT a function of the plasma membrane? The plasma membrane:
A. Has receptors for chemical messages
B. Plays a role in signal transduction
C. Is involved in self-recognition
D. Is the control center of the cell ✅
E. Forms a selective barrier around the cell

Answer: D (Is the control center of the cell)

Question 11

The following substance is used in Gram staining:
A. Iodine
B. Crystal violet ✅
C. Alcohol
D. Safranin
E. Congo red

Answer: B (Crystal violet)

This disinfecting agent does NOT act on microbial membrane structures:
A. Cationic detergents (e.g., quaternary ammonium compounds)
B. Phenol compounds (e.g., cresol, hexachlorophene)
C. Chlorhexidine
D. Alcohols (ethanol, isopropanol) ✅
E. None of the above

Answer: D (Alcohols)

Question 13

The name of the compound shown (pyrimidine base) is:

CLICK TO VIEW


A. Uracil
B. Thymine
C. Cytosine ✅
D. Adenine
E. Guanine

Answer: C (Cytosine)

Question 14

What makes the Watson and Crick model of DNA most plausible?
A. It explains DNA structure
B. It explains the base ratios in DNA
C. It explains how DNA can be packaged in the cell
D. It explains DNA structure and its replication ✅
E. It won a Nobel prize

Answer: D (It explains DNA structure and its replication)

Question 15

A chromosomal aberration where a chromosome arm is lost and replaced by an exact mirror image is called:
A. Duplication
B. Translocation
C. Isochromosome ✅
D. Inversion

Answer: C (Isochromosome)

The base sequence of the DNA template strand is GATCTAC. What is the RNA product?
A. CTAGATG
B. GTAGATC
C. GAUCUAC ✅
D. GUAGUAC
E. CUAGAUG

Answer: C (GAUCUAC)

Question 17

A mutation where a changed base introduces a stop codon is:
A. Nonsense mutation ✅
B. Missense mutation
C. Silent mutation
D. Deletion mutation
E. None of the above

Answer: A (Nonsense mutation)

Question 18

What is a tandem repeat?

GOOD LUCK

  • Gene structure:
    Eukaryotic genes are composed of exons (coding sequences) and introns (non-coding sequences), with introns being removed during RNA splicing.
  • Promoter region:
    Upstream of the coding sequence lies a promoter containing specific sequences (e.g., the TATA box) essential for the initiation of transcription by RNA polymerase II.
  • Regulatory elements:
    Eukaryotic genes are also controlled by enhancers, silencers, and insulators, which regulate the level, timing, and tissue-specific expression of genes.
  • Chromatin packaging:
    DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, enabling compaction into chromatin; gene accessibility depends on the degree of chromatin condensation (euchromatin vs. heterochromatin).
  • Post-transcriptional modification:
    After transcription, primary RNA undergoes capping, polyadenylation, and splicing to form mature mRNA before translation.

  • Ingestion of oocysts:
    Consuming food or water contaminated with mature oocysts from cat feces.
  • Ingestion of tissue cysts:
    Eating undercooked or raw meat containing tissue cysts (especially from pigs, sheep, or goats).
  • Congenital transmission:
    Vertical transmission from an infected mother to her fetus across the placenta during pregnancy.

  • Mutation:
    Spontaneous changes in DNA introduce new alleles into a population, altering genotype frequencies.
  • Natural selection:
    Differential survival and reproduction favor certain genotypes over others, leading to changes in allele frequencies.
  • Genetic drift:
    Random fluctuations in allele frequencies, especially in small populations, can lead to loss or fixation of alleles.
  • Gene flow (migration):
    Movement of individuals between populations introduces new genetic material, affecting allele frequencies.
  • Non-random mating:
    Mating preferences (such as assortative or disassortative mating) can alter genotype distributions by increasing homozygosity or heterozygosity.

  • Denaturation (94–98°C):
    Double-stranded DNA is heated to separate into two single strands.
  • Annealing (50–65°C):
    Short DNA primers bind (anneal) to complementary sequences on the single-stranded templates.
  • Extension (72°C):
    Taq DNA polymerase synthesizes new DNA strands by adding nucleotides to the primers.

  • Importance:
    Taq DNA polymerase is thermostable, meaning it remains active at the high temperatures used in PCR, allowing continuous DNA synthesis without denaturation of the enzyme.
  • Source:
    It is derived from Thermus aquaticus, a thermophilic bacterium found in hot springs.

  1. Mediating virus entry:
    Virus receptors on host cells enable attachment and entry of viruses, initiating infection.
  2. Tropism determination:
    The type and distribution of receptors determine the host range and tissue specificity of the virus (e.g., HIV uses CD4 receptors found on T-helper cells).
  3. Disease pathogenesis:
    Viral binding to specific receptors can influence disease severity and clinical manifestations.
  4. Therapeutic targets:
    Virus-receptor interactions are targeted in drug development (e.g., receptor blockers to prevent viral entry).

1. Initiation
  • Chromatin remodeling opens DNA (via HATs and remodeling complexes).
  • Core promoter: Usually has a TATA box (~25 bp upstream).
  • Pre-Initiation Complex (PIC):
    • TFIID binds TATA (TBP subunit).
    • TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIF (brings RNA Pol II), TFIIE, and TFIIH assemble.
  • TFIIH:
    • Helicase: Unwinds DNA.
    • Kinase: Phosphorylates RNA Pol II CTD → activates transcription.
  • Promoter clearance: RNA polymerase II escapes the promoter and starts RNA synthesis.
2. Elongation
  • RNA polymerase II synthesizes RNA 5’ → 3’, reading DNA 3’ → 5’.
  • Uses ribonucleotide triphosphates (NTPs).
  • Co-transcriptional processing:
    • 5’ Capping (7-methylguanosine).
    • Splicing (introns removed, exons joined).
    • Elongation factors help polymerase move efficiently.
3. Termination
  • Polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA) triggers termination.
  • Cleavage of RNA transcript downstream.
  • Poly-A tail (~200 As) added at 3’ end.
  • RNA polymerase II disengages from DNA.
4. Post-Transcriptional Modifications
  • 5’ cap: Protects RNA, aids translation.
  • Splicing: Removes introns; can allow alternative splicing.
  • Poly-A tail: Stabilizes RNA, helps export from nucleus.

Protein Translation (8 Marks)

Definition:
Translation is the process of protein synthesis where the ribosome reads the mRNA codon sequence and assembles amino acids into a polypeptide chain.

Stages of Translation

🔵 1. Initiation

  • mRNA binds to the small ribosomal subunit.
  • Initiator tRNA (carrying methionine) binds to the start codon (AUG).
  • Large ribosomal subunit joins → functional ribosome formed.

🔵 2. Elongation

  • Ribosome reads mRNA one codon at a time.
  • tRNA delivers correct amino acids based on codon-anticodon matching.
  • Peptide bonds form between amino acids.
  • Ribosome shifts (translocates) along the mRNA.

🔵 3. Termination

  • Ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA).
  • Release factors bind → polypeptide chain is released.
  • Ribosomal subunits dissociate.
Role of tRNA
  • tRNA molecules bring amino acids to ribosome.
  • Each tRNA has:
    • Anticodon loop (binds mRNA codon).
    • Amino acid attachment at 3′ end.
Location
  • Prokaryotes: Cytoplasm (free ribosomes).
  • Eukaryotes: Cytoplasm and rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER).
Summary Line:

Translation = mRNA is decoded by ribosomes → tRNA delivers amino acids → polypeptide chain forms.

Key Points:
  • Each organism carries two alleles for each gene (one from each parent).
  • During gamete formation (meiosis), these two alleles separate (segregate).
  • Each gamete receives only one allele for each gene.
  • Fertilization restores the pair of alleles (one from each parent).
  • Segregation is random — either allele is equally likely to go into any gamete.
  • Explains the 3:1 ratio seen in monohybrid crosses (dominant to recessive traits).
Example:
  • A pea plant with genotype Tt (tall) will produce gametes:
    • 50% with T (tall allele).
    • 50% with t (short allele).
Summary Line for Quick Memory:

In Mendel’s Principle of Segregation, alleles separate during gamete formation, ensuring each gamete carries only one allele for each trait.

Development of a Live-Attenuated Vaccine:

  1. Isolate the Pathogen: Obtain the virus or bacterium causing the disease.
  2. Attenuation: Weaken the pathogen through culturing in non-human cells or genetic modification to reduce virulence.
  3. Safety Testing: Test in animals to ensure no disease is caused but immunity is stimulated.
  4. Immune Response: The weakened pathogen stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells.
  5. Production: Grow the pathogen in large quantities, purify, and prepare the vaccine.
  6. Clinical Trials: Conduct phased human trials for safety, efficacy, and optimal dosing.
  7. Approval: Regulatory bodies approve the vaccine after successful trials.
  8. Examples: MMR, Yellow Fever, Polio (oral).

Summary: Live-attenuated vaccines are made by weakening a pathogen to stimulate immunity without causing disease.

Mechanism Underlying the Immune Protective Ability of Live-Attenuated Vaccines:
  1. Mimics Natural Infection: The weakened pathogen in the vaccine replicates in the body, mimicking a natural infection without causing disease.
  2. Activation of Innate Immune Response: Upon entry, the immune system detects the pathogen using pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on immune cells like macrophages and dendritic cells, triggering an innate immune response.
  3. Adaptive Immune Response:
    • Humoral Immunity: B cells are activated, produce antibodies specific to the pathogen, and provide protection against future infections.
    • Cell-Mediated Immunity: T cells (both helper and cytotoxic) are activated to recognize and destroy infected cells.
  4. Memory Formation: The immune system creates memory B cells and T cells, which "remember" the pathogen and respond more rapidly and effectively if exposed again in the future.
  5. Long-Term Immunity: Because the vaccine contains a weakened but replicating form of the pathogen, it provides long-lasting immunity, often for years or even life.

Summary: Live-attenuated vaccines stimulate both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, leading to the creation of memory cells, which provide long-term protection against future infections.

Here are four key areas where chromosomal studies are important in laboratory diagnostics:

  1. Genetic Disorders Diagnosis: Chromosomal studies help diagnose genetic conditions like Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45,X), and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) through karyotyping or FISH.
  2. Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis: Chromosomal abnormalities, such as translocations (e.g., Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myelogenous leukemia), are critical for diagnosing cancers and determining prognosis.
  3. Prenatal Screening: Chromosomal analysis (e.g., amniocentesis or CVS) is used to detect chromosomal abnormalities in a fetus, such as trisomies or other congenital disorders.
  4. Infertility and Miscarriage Investigation: Chromosomal studies can identify structural or numerical chromosomal abnormalities in couples with recurrent miscarriages or unexplained infertility, guiding appropriate management.

These areas are vital for diagnosing and managing various genetic and health conditions.

Explain, using illustrations, how DNA replicates in a semi-conservative manner. (2 marks)
Explanation: During DNA replication, each of the two strands of the DNA double helix serves as a template for the formation of a new complementary strand. After replication, each daughter DNA molecule consists of one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand. This is called semi-conservative replication because each new DNA molecule conserves one of the original strands.
Illustration:
The DNA double helix unwinds.
Each original strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand.
The result is two DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand.

  1. DNA polymerase: Adds complementary nucleotides to the growing DNA strand during replication. It also has proofreading abilities to correct errors.
  2. DNA ligase: Seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds, ensuring the integrity of the newly synthesized DNA strand.
  3. DNA helicase: Unwinds the DNA double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs, creating single-stranded templates for replication.

Transcription is the process by which an RNA molecule is synthesized from a DNA template. RNA polymerase binds to a specific region of DNA called the promoter, unwinds the DNA, and synthesizes a complementary RNA strand. This RNA strand is a copy of the coding sequence of the gene, which will later be translated into a protein.

List and explain the function of the three major RNA molecules present in the cell. (3 marks)

  1. mRNA (messenger RNA): Carries the genetic information from DNA in the nucleus to the ribosome, where it is used as a template for protein synthesis.
  2. tRNA (transfer RNA): Delivers specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation, matching its anticodon with the codon on the mRNA.
  3. rRNA (ribosomal RNA): Forms the structural and functional components of the ribosome, catalyzing the assembly of amino acids into protein chains during translation.

Post-translational modification primarily occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and the Golgi apparatus.


The Minimal Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of an antibiotic that inhibits visible bacterial growth. The following methods can be used to determine MIC:

  1. Broth Dilution Method:
    • Prepare a series of test tubes with varying concentrations of the antibiotic in a broth medium.
    • Inoculate each tube with a standard amount of the bacterial isolate.
    • After incubation, observe the lowest concentration where no visible bacterial growth is present. This is the MIC.
  2. Agar Dilution Method:
    • Prepare agar plates with different concentrations of the antibiotic.
    • Inoculate the plate with the bacterial isolate.
    • After incubation, examine the lowest concentration that prevents bacterial growth. This is the MIC.
  3. E-test (Gradient Method):
    • A strip containing a gradient of the antibiotic is placed on an agar plate inoculated with the bacterial isolate.
    • After incubation, the MIC is determined by reading the point where the growth inhibition intersects the strip.


Acyclovir is selectively toxic to cells infected by alpha-herpesviruses due to its activation mechanism and viral specificity:

  1. Viral Thymidine Kinase Activation:
    • Acyclovir is a nucleoside analogue. It requires phosphorylation by the viral enzyme thymidine kinase, which is produced by the herpesvirus.
    • Once phosphorylated, acyclovir becomes acyclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA replication.
  2. Selective Incorporation into Viral DNA:
    • Acyclovir triphosphate competes with the natural nucleoside, guanosine, for incorporation into the viral DNA.
    • Once incorporated into the DNA, it causes chain termination, preventing further DNA replication.
  3. Minimal Host Cell Activity:
    • Human cells do not possess significant thymidine kinase activity, so acyclovir is not activated in uninfected cells. This ensures that acyclovir primarily targets infected cells, making it selectively toxic to herpesvirus-infected cells.

Development of Multidrug Resistance in Bacteria (10 marks)

  1. Spontaneous Mutations:
    • Mutations in bacterial DNA can occur naturally during replication. These mutations may confer resistance to one or more antibiotics by altering the target sites or enzymes involved in drug metabolism.
    • For example, mutations in the gene encoding the target of the antibiotic can lead to reduced drug binding or drug inactivation, rendering the antibiotic ineffective.
  2. Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT):
    • Conjugation: Bacteria can transfer resistance genes through direct contact, especially via plasmids, between bacterial cells. This can spread resistance quickly within a population.
    • Transformation: Bacteria can uptake naked DNA from their environment that contains resistance genes, incorporating it into their genome.
    • Transduction: Bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) can transfer resistance genes between bacterial species during infection.
  3. Selective Pressure from Overuse/Misuse of Antibiotics:
    • Overprescription or incorrect use of antibiotics creates a selective pressure that favors the survival of bacteria with mutations or resistance genes.
    • Bacteria resistant to one antibiotic survive and reproduce, passing on their resistance. When multiple antibiotics are used inappropriately, this can lead to the development of resistance to multiple drugs.
  4. Efflux Pumps and Enzyme Production:
    • Some bacteria develop efflux pumps that actively expel antibiotics from the cell, reducing the drug concentration inside the bacterium to sub-lethal levels.
    • Bacteria can also produce enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamases) that degrade antibiotics before they can exert their effect, leading to resistance.
  5. Biofilm Formation:
    • Many bacteria form biofilms on surfaces, which protect them from antibiotic penetration and immune system attacks. Biofilms act as a physical barrier, reducing the effectiveness of antibiotics and contributing to chronic infections that are difficult to treat.
  6. Cross-Resistance:
    • Some bacteria develop resistance to one class of antibiotics, and this can result in cross-resistance to other structurally or functionally similar antibiotics. This can occur due to the shared mechanisms of resistance, such as efflux pumps or mutations in common bacterial targets.
  7. Fitness Cost and Compensatory Mechanisms:
    • Some MDR strains may initially have a fitness cost associated with resistance. However, through compensatory mutations, bacteria may adapt to maintain resistance without incurring a significant fitness disadvantage, allowing them to thrive in antibiotic-treated environments.

In Drosophila melanogaster, dosage compensation occurs through X-chromosome doubling in males to balance gene expression between males and females. In males (XY), the single X chromosome is hyperactivated, meaning it transcribes genes at a higher rate than the two X chromosomes in females (XX).

The three major DNA conformations are A-DNA, B-DNA, and Z-DNA:

1. B-DNA (Biological DNA)

  • Structure: Right-handed helix, 10 base pairs (bp) per turn.
  • Helix Diameter: ~2 nm.
  • Base Tilt: Nearly perpendicular to helix axis.
  • Environment: Forms under high hydration (physiological conditions).
  • Importance: Most common form in living cells; Watson-Crick model is based on B-DNA.

2. A-DNA

  • Structure: Right-handed helix, 11 bp per turn.
  • Helix Diameter: ~2.6 nm (wider and shorter than B-DNA).
  • Base Tilt: Bases are tilted away from the helix axis (~20°).
  • Environment: Forms under dehydrated conditions (low humidity).
  • Importance: Often found in double-stranded RNA, DNA-RNA hybrids.

3. Z-DNA

  • Structure: Left-handed helix, 12 bp per turn.
  • Helix Diameter: ~1.8 nm (narrow and elongated).
  • Base Tilt: Zig-zag backbone conformation (hence "Z"-DNA).
  • Environment: Forms in regions rich in alternating purine-pyrimidine (e.g., GC repeats), and under high salt or negative supercoiling.
  • Importance: May play a role in gene regulation and chromatin remodeling.

Introduction to PCR

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a technique used to amplify specific segments of DNA. It was developed by Kary Mullis in 1983 and involves repeated cycles of DNA denaturation, primer annealing, and DNA extension using a heat-stable enzyme called Taq polymerase. This process produces millions of copies of a DNA segment, enabling the analysis of very small amounts of DNA.

Key Steps in PCR
  1. Denaturation: DNA is heated to 94-98°C, separating the double strands.
  2. Annealing: The temperature is lowered to 50-65°C, allowing primers to bind to the target DNA.
  3. Extension: The temperature is raised to 72°C, where Taq polymerase synthesizes the complementary strand.
Applications of PCR in Pharmaceutical and Medical Studies
  1. Genetic Disease Diagnosis
    • PCR can identify mutations in genes (e.g., BRCA1 for breast cancer), enabling early diagnosis of genetic disorders.
    • Used for newborn screening to detect genetic conditions such as cystic fibrosis.
  2. Pathogen Detection
    • PCR is essential for detecting viruses (e.g., HIV, SARS-CoV-2), bacteria (TB, E. coli), and fungi from clinical samples.
    • Allows early detection of infections even with low amounts of pathogen DNA.
  3. Pharmacogenomics
    • PCR can detect genetic variations that affect drug metabolism (e.g., CYP450 gene variants) and predict patient responses to medications, enabling personalized treatment plans.
  4. Cancer Diagnosis and Monitoring
    • PCR detects mutations in cancer-related genes (p53, EGFR), aiding in early cancer detection and monitoring treatment progress.
    • Used in detecting minimal residual disease (MRD) in leukemia patients.
  5. Viral Load Quantification
    • In HIV and Hepatitis infections, PCR quantifies viral load, guiding therapy decisions and monitoring treatment effectiveness.
  6. Vaccine Development
    • PCR ensures the presence of desired genetic sequences in vaccine candidates, ensuring safety and efficacy.
    • Can detect viral or bacterial sequences to confirm the absence of contaminants.
  7. Forensic Medicine
    • PCR is used for DNA profiling in paternity testing, criminal investigations, and disaster victim identification by analyzing biological samples.
  8. Gene Therapy and Genetic Engineering
    • PCR verifies the successful incorporation of therapeutic genes in gene therapy and gene editing projects like CRISPR.
    • Ensures genetic modifications are accurate and safe.
Conclusion

PCR is a powerful tool with widespread applications in medical diagnostics, pharmaceutical research, genetic studies, and therapeutic development. Its ability to amplify small DNA samples enables significant advancements in disease detection, personalized medicine, and molecular biology.

b) Synthesis of Peptidoglycan
Introduction
  • Peptidoglycan is a rigid, mesh-like polymer forming the bacterial cell wall.
  • It provides mechanical strength and protects against osmotic lysis.
  • It is made of repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), cross-linked by short peptide chains.
1. Synthesis in the Cytoplasm
  • UDP-NAG is synthesized from glucose.
  • UDP-NAG is converted into UDP-NAM by the addition of a lactyl group.
  • A pentapeptide chain (commonly containing L-alanine, D-glutamic acid, meso-diaminopimelic acid [or L-lysine], and two D-alanines) is sequentially attached to UDP-NAM.
2. Attachment to Membrane Carrier (Bactoprenol)
  • UDP-NAM-pentapeptide is linked to bactoprenol phosphate (a lipid carrier) in the membrane, forming Lipid I.
  • UDP-NAG then adds to Lipid I, forming Lipid II (NAM-pentapeptide + NAG).
3. Transport Across the Cytoplasmic Membrane
  • Bactoprenol carries the Lipid II complex across the membrane to the outer side (periplasmic side in Gram-negative bacteria).
4. Polymerization (Transglycosylation)
  • Transglycosylase enzymes catalyze the linking of the NAG of the new unit to the NAM of the existing chain via β-1,4-glycosidic bonds.
  • This extends the glycan strands (the sugar backbone).
5. Cross-Linking (Transpeptidation)
  • Transpeptidase enzymes (also called Penicillin-Binding Proteins, PBPs) form peptide bonds between the peptide chains attached to NAM residues.
  • This cross-linking provides strength and rigidity to the wall.
  • Example: Bond between the third amino acid (often diaminopimelic acid or lysine) and the fourth D-alanine of another chain, releasing one D-alanine (energy source).
Clinical Relevance
  • β-lactam antibiotics (e.g., penicillin) inhibit transpeptidases, preventing cross-linking and weakening the cell wall, leading to bacterial lysis.
  • Vancomycin binds to D-Ala-D-Ala residues, inhibiting both transglycosylation and transpeptidation.

  2. Anaerobic Respiration: In the absence of oxygen, uses alternative electron acceptors (e.g., nitrate, sulfate) to produce ATP.
  3. Fermentation: When oxygen is absent, breaks down organic compounds (e.g., glucose) into simpler molecules like lactic acid or ethanol to produce ATP.
  4. Organic and Inorganic Compounds: Can metabolize a variety of organic substrates (e.g., sugars, lipids) and some inorganic compounds (e.g., hydrogen, sulfur) for energy.

Title: Prefrontal Association Areas
Content:
Functions of the Parieto-Occipitotemporal Cortex in the Nondominant Hemisphere
  • Damage to Wernicke’s Area in the Dominant Hemisphere:
    • Loss of intellectual functions associated with language and verbal symbolism.
    • Inability to:
      • Read.
      • Perform mathematical operations.
      • Solve logical problems.
    • These deficits illustrate the dominant hemisphere’s specialization for language-based intellectual functions.
  • Functions Retained by the Nondominant Hemisphere:
    • Despite language-related deficits, many interpretative capabilities remain intact due to activity in the nondominant hemisphere.
    • Psychological studies suggest the nondominant hemisphere is crucial for:
      • Understanding and interpreting music.
      • Interpreting nonverbal visual experiences, especially:
        • Visual patterns.
        • Spatial relationships (understanding where objects and oneself are positioned in space).
      • Recognizing body language (gestures, facial expressions).
      • Interpreting intonations (emotional tones in voices).
      • Processing somatic (bodily) experiences, especially related to:
        • Limb coordination.
        • Hand use.
  • Summary:
    • The term "dominant" hemisphere refers mostly to language and logic.
    • The "nondominant" hemisphere could be considered dominant for other forms of intelligence, such as:
      • Artistic abilities.
      • Emotional and spatial understanding.
      • Nonverbal communication.
Higher Intellectual Functions of the Prefrontal Association Areas
  • Historical View:
    • The prefrontal cortex has long been considered the seat of "higher intellect," especially because of its large size in humans compared to monkeys.
  • Modern Understanding:
    • Destruction of Wernicke’s area (language comprehension) and the angular gyrus causes far greater intellectual decline than destruction of the prefrontal areas.
    • However, the prefrontal cortex has important, though less easily definable, intellectual functions.
Insights from Prefrontal Lobotomy Patients

(A lobotomy involved cutting the connections between the prefrontal cortex and the rest of the brain.)

Mental changes observed:

  1. Loss of ability to solve complex problems.
  2. Inability to perform sequential tasks to achieve complex goals.
  3. Difficulty learning multiple parallel tasks simultaneously.
  4. Decreased aggressiveness and ambition.
  5. Inappropriate social behavior, including:
    • Loss of morals.
    • Lack of reticence regarding sex and excretion.
  6. Preservation of speech and language comprehension, but:
    • Inability to maintain long, coherent trains of thought.
    • Rapid and extreme mood changes (e.g., shifting from sweetness to rage).
  7. Preservation of motor functions, but actions often became purposeless.
Functions of Specific Prefrontal Areas
  1. Ventral Prefrontal Cortex (part of the Limbic Association Cortex):
    • Related to behavioral control.
    • Damage leads to:
      • Decreased aggressiveness.
      • Inappropriate social responses.
  2. Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex (true Prefrontal Association Area):
    • Responsible for:
      • Sequencing thoughts towards goals.
      • Maintaining logical, sustained thinking over time.
      • Filtering distractions and maintaining focus.
    • Damage results in:
      • Short attention span.
      • Easily distracted thought processes.
      • Inability to complete complex tasks.
Key Prefrontal Functions Explained
1. Inability to Progress Toward Goals and Sequential Thinking
  • The prefrontal cortex organizes information from different parts of the brain.
  • It allows for deep analytical thinking needed to:
    • Solve problems.
    • Plan and act toward achieving complex goals.
  • Without it:
    • Thinking becomes disorganized.
    • Focus on a single theme or purpose cannot be sustained.
2. Elaboration of Thought and Higher Intellectual Functions
  • Elaboration of thought: Ability to expand thoughts by integrating multiple pieces of information.
  • Prefrontal cortex enables:
    • Abstract reasoning.
    • Deep analysis beyond surface facts.
3. Working Memory Concept
  • Working memory: The ability to hold and manipulate multiple bits of information temporarily.
  • Functions of working memory include:
    • Remembering sequences and steps.
    • Linking sensory information for decision-making.
    • Planning multi-step actions.
  • Specific areas within the prefrontal cortex specialize in:
    • Storing shapes and forms (visual working memory).
    • Storing movements (motor working memory).
4. Advanced Cognitive Abilities Enabled by Prefrontal Cortex
  • Prognostication: Predicting future outcomes based on current actions.
  • Planning for the future.
  • Delaying actions to allow better decisions after careful analysis.
  • Considering consequences before performing actions.
  • Solving complex problems, including:
    • Mathematical.
    • Legal.
    • Philosophical.
  • Integrating diverse information for tasks such as diagnosing rare diseases.
  • Moral reasoning and self-control: Acting in accordance with moral and social norms.

  1. Gastrin is a peptide hormone secreted by G cells in the antrum of the stomach.
  2. Stimulated by peptides/amino acids, stomach distension, and vagal stimulation (via GRP).
  3. Increases gastric motility by enhancing contractions of the gastric smooth muscle.
  4. Promotes gastric emptying by increasing the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, relaxing the pyloric sphincter, and stimulating antral contractions.
  5. Indirectly stimulates motility of the small intestine via increased gastrin-mediated secretions.
  6. Enhances peristaltic movements, thus aiding in mixing and propulsion of gastric contents.
  7. Excess gastrin (e.g., in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) can lead to hyper-motility and diarrhea.
Inhibition of Pancreatic Autodigestion
  • Pancreatic enzymes are synthesized and secreted as inactive zymogens (e.g., trypsinogen).
  • Trypsinogen is activated only in the duodenum by enterokinase (enteropeptidase).
  • The pancreas also secretes trypsin inhibitor (e.g., SPINK1) to prevent premature trypsin activation.
  • Compartmentalization of enzymes in zymogen granules within acinar cells prevents cytoplasmic exposure.
  • The ductal cells secrete bicarbonate, flushing enzymes into the duodenum and diluting them.
  • Any prematurely activated trypsin is rapidly inactivated by autolysis or inhibitors.
  • Disruption of these safety mechanisms (e.g., in pancreatitis) leads to autodigestion.
Process of Digestion of Fats
  • Begins in the mouth (lingual lipase) and stomach (gastric lipase) – minor role.
  • Major digestion occurs in the small intestine, especially duodenum and jejunum.
  • Emulsification by bile salts increases surface area for enzyme action.
  • Pancreatic lipase (with colipase) hydrolyzes triglycerides into monoglycerides and free fatty acids.
  • These products form micelles with bile salts for transport to the intestinal brush border.
  • Absorbed into enterocytes, where triglycerides are re-esterified.
  • Packaged into chylomicrons and transported via lacteals into lymphatics.
Physiology Behind Satiety After a Heavy Meal
  • Stomach distension activates mechanoreceptors that signal the hypothalamus (satiety center) via vagal afferents.
  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released from the duodenum in response to fats and proteins, slowing gastric emptying and promoting satiety.
  • Insulin and GLP-1 rise postprandially and act on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to inhibit hunger.
  • Leptin (from adipose tissue) exerts longer-term satiety effects but contributes postprandially.
  • PYY from the ileum/colon also contributes to delayed gastric emptying and reduced appetite.
  • Serotonin (from enterochromaffin cells) contributes to early satiety by modulating enteric and central pathways.
  • Integration of neural and hormonal signals leads to inhibition of the lateral hypothalamic (hunger) center and activation of the ventromedial nucleus (satiety center).
Effects of Thyroid Hormones on the Cardiovascular System
  • Increased heart rate (positive chronotropic effect): Thyroid hormones enhance the sensitivity of the heart to catecholamines, increasing heart rate.
  • Increased cardiac output: Both heart rate and stroke volume are elevated, leading to an increase in cardiac output.
  • Increased myocardial contractility (positive inotropic effect): Thyroid hormones increase the force of myocardial contraction.
  • Peripheral vasodilation: Thyroid hormones cause vasodilation in peripheral vessels, lowering systemic vascular resistance.
  • Increased blood volume: Thyroid hormones increase sodium and water retention by the kidneys, contributing to increased blood volume.
  • Arrhythmias: Hyperthyroidism can lead to arrhythmias, including atrial fibrillation, due to increased myocardial excitability.
  • Enhanced oxygen consumption: Increased metabolic rate from thyroid hormones raises myocardial oxygen demand.
Physiological Functions of the Pancreatic Hormone Glucagon
  • Increases blood glucose levels: Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis in the liver, converting stored glycogen to glucose.
  • Promotes gluconeogenesis: Stimulates the liver to produce glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (e.g., amino acids).
  • Stimulates lipolysis: Glucagon activates the breakdown of stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol.
  • Increases ketogenesis: In periods of fasting, glucagon stimulates the liver to convert fatty acids to ketone bodies.
  • Inhibits insulin secretion: Glucagon reduces insulin secretion to prevent hypoglycemia during fasting.
  • Enhances protein catabolism: Glucagon increases the breakdown of proteins to provide amino acids for gluconeogenesis.
  • Supports muscle energy needs: Although it has limited direct action on muscle, glucagon increases available glucose and fatty acids for energy.
Countercurrent Multiplier System in the Kidneys

(Short notes with diagram)

DIAGRAM
  • Descending limb: Permeable to water, but not solutes; water is reabsorbed into the surrounding hypertonic medulla, concentrating the tubular fluid.
  • Ascending limb: Impermeable to water, actively transports Na+, K+, and Cl- out into the interstitium, diluting the tubular fluid. This creates a countercurrent multiplier effect that generates an osmotic gradient.
  • Vasa recta: Blood vessels that run parallel to the loop of Henle; they preserve the osmotic gradient by allowing water and solutes to exchange without disrupting the medullary concentration gradient.
  • Urea recycling: Urea contributes to the medullary osmotic gradient, further enhancing water reabsorption and concentrating urine.

Diagram Explanation:

  • Descending Limb: Water moves out.
  • Ascending Limb: NaCl is pumped out.
  • Vasa Recta: Blood flow maintains osmotic gradient.
  • Urea: Contributes to the concentration of urine in the medulla.
Hormones Secreted During Pregnancy
  1. Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG):
    • Produced by the placenta.
    • Supports the corpus luteum to maintain progesterone production in early pregnancy.
    • Basis for pregnancy tests.
  2. Progesterone:
    • Produced by the corpus luteum and later the placenta.
    • Maintains the uterine lining and suppresses uterine contractions.
    • Essential for pregnancy maintenance.
  3. Estrogen (Estradiol):
    • Secreted initially by the corpus luteum, later by the placenta.
    • Stimulates uterine growth and prepares mammary glands for lactation.
    • Promotes vascularization of the endometrium.
  4. Human Placental Lactogen (hPL):
    • Secreted by the placenta.
    • Modulates maternal metabolism to increase glucose availability for the fetus.
    • Promotes insulin resistance to ensure fetal nutrition.
  5. Relaxin:
    • Secreted by the corpus luteum and placenta.
    • Relaxes pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix for childbirth.
    • Inhibits uterine contractions in early pregnancy.
  6. Prolactin:
    • Secreted by the anterior pituitary and placenta.
    • Stimulates mammary gland development for lactation.
    • Levels rise progressively during pregnancy.
  7. Cortisol:
    • Secreted by the adrenal glands.
    • Regulates metabolism and helps in fetal maturation (especially lung development).
    • Increases blood glucose to meet maternal and fetal needs.
  8. Oxytocin:
    • Secreted by the posterior pituitary near labor.
    • Stimulates uterine contractions during labor.
    • Promotes milk ejection during breastfeeding.
Phases of the Male Sexual Response

The male sexual response can be divided into four main phases:

  1. Excitement Phase:
    • The excitement phase is initiated by sexual stimuli, such as visual, tactile, or psychological stimuli.
    • It leads to the erection of the penis, due to increased blood flow through the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum.
    • Increased heart rate and blood pressure are observed as part of the body's physiological response to sexual arousal.
    • Testicular enlargement and scrotal elevation also occur.
  2. Plateau Phase:
    • The plateau phase is the period of sexual tension just before orgasm.
    • Erection is maintained, and further vasocongestion occurs in the genital area.
    • Prostatic secretion and pre-ejaculatory fluid may be released.
    • There is heightened muscle tension, increased respiration, and heart rate as the body prepares for orgasm.
  3. Orgasm (Climax) Phase:
    • The orgasm phase is marked by ejaculation, which involves the rhythmic contraction of the pelvic muscles, prostate, and seminal vesicles.
    • Release of semen occurs through the urethra.
    • Muscle contractions and intense pleasure characterize this phase, which is mediated by the autonomic nervous system.
    • Sympathetic activation leads to ejaculation, while dopaminergic systems are involved in the experience of pleasure.
  4. Resolution Phase:
    • The resolution phase follows orgasm and involves the return of the body to its normal state.
    • Erection subsides, and blood flow to the penis decreases.
    • Heart rate and blood pressure normalize.
    • There is typically a refractory period during which the male is not responsive to sexual stimuli.
Associative Learning (with Examples)

Associative learning is a process by which an individual learns to associate two stimuli or a behavior with its consequences. It can be classified into classical conditioning and operant conditioning.

  1. Classical Conditioning (Pavlovian Conditioning):
    • Definition: Involves learning to associate a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus to produce a conditioned response.
    • Example: Ivan Pavlov’s experiment with dogs. The sound of a bell (neutral stimulus) was paired with the presentation of food (unconditioned stimulus), leading to the dogs salivating (conditioned response) upon hearing the bell alone.
  2. Operant Conditioning (Instrumental Conditioning):
    • Definition: Involves learning that a behavior will lead to a particular consequence (either reinforcement or punishment).
    • Example: B.F. Skinner’s experiment with rats. A rat in a box learns to press a lever (behavior) to receive food (reinforcer). If the rat presses the lever but receives an electric shock (punishment), it will stop the behavior.
    • Positive reinforcement: Giving a reward to increase the behavior (e.g., praising a child for cleaning their room).
    • Negative reinforcement: Removing an unpleasant stimulus to increase the behavior (e.g., turning off a loud noise when a rat presses a lever).

Applications: Associative learning plays a key role in everyday life, such as in advertising (associating positive emotions with products) and phobias (associating a neutral stimulus with fear).

Components and Functions of the Blood–Brain Barrier

The blood–brain barrier (BBB) is a selective permeability barrier that separates the circulating blood from the brain and extracellular fluid in the central nervous system (CNS).

  1. Components of the BBB:
    • Endothelial Cells: The blood vessels in the brain have tightly joined endothelial cells, which form a continuous layer, preventing most substances from passing freely between blood and the brain.
    • Tight Junctions: These are special proteins that connect adjacent endothelial cells tightly, restricting the passage of large molecules and pathogens.
    • Astrocyte End-feet: Astrocytes, a type of glial cell, extend their processes (end-feet) around blood vessels and help maintain the integrity of the BBB.
    • Pericytes: These cells wrap around endothelial cells and help regulate the development and function of the BBB.
    • Basement Membrane: A thin layer of extracellular matrix that supports the endothelial cells and contributes to the structural integrity of the BBB.
  2. Functions of the BBB:
    • Protects the brain from harmful substances: The BBB prevents toxins, pathogens, and large, hydrophilic molecules from entering the brain.
    • Maintains homeostasis: It regulates the ionic composition of the brain extracellular fluid, maintaining the electrochemical environment for neurons.
    • Prevents fluctuations in neurotransmitter levels: The BBB regulates the entry of neurotransmitters, ions, and other substances that could disrupt neuronal function.
    • Selective nutrient transport: The BBB allows for the controlled transport of essential nutrients, such as glucose, amino acids, and oxygen, to the brain.
    • Limit drug delivery: The BBB limits the passage of certain medications, which poses challenges in treating CNS diseases.
Basal Ganglia Pathway Affected in Parkinson's Disease

Parkinson’s disease primarily affects the dopaminergic pathways within the basal ganglia, leading to motor dysfunction.

  1. Basal Ganglia Components:
    • The basal ganglia consists of several nuclei, including the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and the substantia nigra.
    • The dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra project to the striatum, and their activity is crucial for controlling voluntary movement.
  2. Pathophysiology in Parkinson's Disease:
    • Degeneration of Dopaminergic Neurons: In Parkinson’s disease, there is progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to a dopamine deficiency in the striatum.
    • This imbalance affects the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia, which are involved in initiating and regulating movement:
      • Direct pathway (facilitates movement): Normally, dopamine from the substantia nigra excites the direct pathway, allowing smooth and voluntary movement. Loss of dopamine reduces this excitation, leading to hypokinesia (decreased movement).
      • Indirect pathway (inhibits movement): The loss of dopamine also leads to increased activity in the indirect pathway, which further inhibits movement, causing rigidity and bradykinesia (slowness of movement).
    • Clinical Manifestations: The result is the hallmark symptoms of Parkinson's disease, including tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability.
a. Secretion and Function of Growth Hormone (GH)

1. Secretion of Growth Hormone (GH):

  • Produced by: Secreted by the anterior pituitary gland (specifically by somatotroph cells).
  • Regulation:
    • Stimulated by: Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) from the hypothalamus.
    • Inhibited by: Somatostatin (GHIH), also from the hypothalamus.
    • Circadian Rhythm: GH secretion follows a pulsatile pattern, peaking during sleep (especially in the early stages).
    • Feedback Mechanism: Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) from the liver negatively feeds back to inhibit GH secretion.

2. Function of Growth Hormone (GH):

  • Promotes Growth:
    • Stimulates linear bone growth in children and adolescents through IGF-1, particularly acting on the growth plates (epiphyseal plates).
  • Metabolic Effects:
    • Increases protein synthesis: GH promotes the growth of muscle mass by stimulating amino acid uptake and protein synthesis.
    • Fat Mobilization: Stimulates lipolysis, increasing the breakdown of fats and free fatty acid release, leading to a decrease in body fat.
    • Carbohydrate Metabolism: GH has an anti-insulin effect, reducing glucose uptake and promoting hyperglycemia (which can lead to insulin resistance over time).
  • Influence on Bone and Cartilage:
    • GH promotes the production of cartilage and bone tissue by stimulating the chondrocytes and osteoblasts, promoting bone remodeling and growth.
  • Tissue Regeneration:
    • Stimulates the repair and regeneration of tissues, especially after injury, by enhancing the cellular division and protein synthesis.

The adrenal glands are located on top of the kidneys and consist of two main parts: the adrenal cortex (outer part) and the adrenal medulla (inner part). They secrete a variety of hormones involved in stress response, metabolism, and fluid balance.

1. Hormones Secreted by the Adrenal Cortex:

a. Mineralocorticoids (Mainly Aldosterone):

  • Secretion: Released from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex.
  • Function:
    • Regulates salt and water balance.
    • Increases sodium retention and potassium excretion in the kidneys.
    • Helps to maintain blood pressure by increasing blood volume.

b. Glucocorticoids (Mainly Cortisol):

  • Secretion: Released from the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.
  • Function:
    • Stress Response: Cortisol is the “stress hormone,” increasing in response to physical or emotional stress.
    • Metabolic Effects: Increases glucose synthesis (gluconeogenesis) in the liver, increases fat breakdown, and mobilizes amino acids from muscles.
    • Anti-inflammatory: Cortisol has potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects.

c. Sex Hormones (Mainly Androgens, e.g., DHEA):

  • Secretion: Released from the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex.
  • Function:
    • Contributes to secondary sexual characteristics in both males and females.
    • In females, adrenal androgens serve as a precursor for estrogen.
    • Has a minor role in male testosterone production, especially after puberty.
2. Hormones Secreted by the Adrenal Medulla:

a. Catecholamines (Mainly Epinephrine (Adrenaline) and Norepinephrine (Noradrenaline)):

  • Secretion: Released from the adrenal medulla, which is regulated by sympathetic nervous system activity.
  • Function:
    • Fight or Flight Response: These hormones prepare the body for immediate action during stress by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate.
    • Vasoconstriction: Norepinephrine causes vasoconstriction to increase blood flow to vital organs (heart, brain).
    • Energy Mobilization: Epinephrine increases the breakdown of glycogen to glucose (glycogenolysis) and enhances lipolysis for rapid energy use.

a. Draw and Explain the Stages of the Menstrual Cycle (10 Marks)
Diagram:

Day 1 5 14 28
|--------|------|------------|
↓ Menses | Follicular | Luteal → (If no fertilization: menstruation)
Ovulation (Day 14)

A typical 28-day menstrual cycle (You can draw a simple four-phase diagram showing hormone levels, ovary changes, and endometrial changes).

Stages:
  1. Menstrual Phase (Day 1–5):
    • Shedding of the functional layer of the endometrium due to a drop in estrogen and progesterone.
    • Associated with menstrual bleeding (~3–5 days).
    • Marks Day 1 of the cycle.
  2. Follicular (Proliferative) Phase (Day 6–13):
    • Controlled by FSH from the anterior pituitary.
    • FSH stimulates maturation of ovarian follicles.
    • Estrogen is secreted by the developing follicles.
    • Estrogen causes regrowth (proliferation) of the endometrium.
  3. Ovulation (Day 14):
    • Triggered by a surge in LH (Luteinizing Hormone).
    • The mature (Graafian) follicle ruptures, releasing the ovum.
    • This is the most fertile period.
  4. Luteal (Secretory) Phase (Day 15–28):
    • Corpus luteum forms from the ruptured follicle.
    • Secretes progesterone (mainly) and some estrogen.
    • Progesterone prepares the endometrium for implantation (increases secretions, vascularity).
    • If fertilization does not occur, corpus luteum degenerates → ↓ progesterone → menstruation restarts.
b. Roles of Sertoli Cells in the Male Reproductive System (5 Marks)
  1. Support Spermatogenesis:
    • Provide nutrients and structural support to developing sperm cells.
  2. Blood-Testis Barrier:
    • Form tight junctions that create a specialized environment protecting germ cells from autoimmune attack.
  3. Secretion of Androgen-Binding Protein (ABP):
    • Concentrates testosterone in the seminiferous tubules, essential for spermatogenesis.
  4. Phagocytosis:
    • Engulf and remove residual cytoplasm and defective germ cells.
  5. Hormonal Regulation:
    • Secrete inhibin, which provides negative feedback on FSH secretion from the pituitary.
c. Short Notes on the Fertilization of the Ovum (5 Marks)
  1. Site of Fertilization:
    • Occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.
  2. Sperm Capacitation:
    • Biochemical changes in the female tract make sperm capable of fertilizing the egg.
  3. Acrosome Reaction:
    • Sperm releases enzymes (e.g., hyaluronidase) to penetrate the zona pellucida of the ovum.
  4. Fusion of Gametes:
    • One sperm fuses with the ovum’s plasma membrane → triggers cortical reaction to block polyspermy.
  5. Zygote Formation:
    • The sperm and ovum nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote (46 chromosomes).
    • The zygote begins cleavage divisions and moves toward the uterus for implantation.
a. Renal Mechanisms That Regulate Blood Pressure When Blood Pressure Decreases (10 Marks)

When blood pressure drops, the kidneys help restore it via the following mechanisms:

1. Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)
  • ↓ BP → ↓ renal perfusion → stimulates juxtaglomerular cells to release renin.
  • Renin converts angiotensinogen (from liver) → angiotensin I.
  • Angiotensin I → angiotensin II (via ACE in lungs).

Effects of Angiotensin II:

  • Vasoconstriction → increases total peripheral resistance → raises BP.
  • Stimulates aldosterone from adrenal cortex → ↑ Na⁺ & water reabsorption → ↑ blood volume.
  • Stimulates ADH → ↑ water retention in collecting ducts.
2. Sympathetic Nervous System Activation
  • Baroreceptors detect low BP → activate sympathetic output.
  • Vasoconstriction of renal arterioles → conserves fluid.
  • Stimulates renin release and increases cardiac output.
3. Decreased GFR and Enhanced Na⁺/Water Reabsorption
  • ↓ BP → afferent arteriole constriction → ↓ GFR.
  • Allows more time for Na⁺ and water reabsorption in proximal tubule.
4. Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) Secretion
  • Angiotensin II & hypothalamus stimulate ADH release.
  • Increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts → ↑ blood volume.
5. Reduced Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP)
  • Low BP → reduced atrial stretch → ↓ ANP release.
  • Less Na⁺ excretion → promotes fluid retention.

Summary: The kidneys raise BP by increasing vasoconstriction, Na⁺/water reabsorption, and blood volume, primarily via RAAS, ADH, and sympathetic activation.

b. Short Notes on the Vestibular Apparatus and Maintenance of Equilibrium (10 Marks)
1. Location and Components
  • Located in the inner ear (labyrinth).
  • Composed of:
    • Semicircular canals (3): detect angular (rotational) acceleration.
    • Utricle and saccule: detect linear acceleration and head position (gravity).
    • All filled with endolymph and lined by hair cells (sensory receptors).
2. Semicircular Canals
  • Each canal has an ampulla with a crista ampullaris (contains hair cells).
  • Rotational movement → endolymph lags behind → bends cupula → stimulates hair cells → impulses sent via vestibular nerve.
3. Utricle and Saccule
  • Contain maculae with otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals).
  • Detect linear movements (forward-backward, up-down).
  • Changes in head position shift otoliths → deflect hair cells → trigger action potentials.
4. Vestibular Nerve Pathway
  • Hair cells synapse with vestibular branch of CN VIII (vestibulocochlear).
  • Signals sent to vestibular nuclei (brainstem) and cerebellum for processing.
5. Role in Equilibrium
  • Maintains static equilibrium (upright posture at rest) and dynamic equilibrium (during movement).
  • Coordinates with visual and proprioceptive input to maintain balance and spatial orientation.
  • Sends reflex signals to eye muscles (vestibulo-ocular reflex) and postural muscles.
