Title: TRACTS
Content:
Notes on Ascending Tracts
1. Dorsal White Column (Posterior Column Pathway)
a. Fasciculus Gracilis
  • Location:
    • Found in the dorsal (posterior) column of the spinal cord.
    • Medially positioned, adjacent to the midline of the spinal cord.
  • Function:
    • Carries sensory information related to:
      • Fine touch (discriminative touch).
      • Vibration sense.
      • Proprioception (awareness of body position) specifically from the lower limbs and inferior trunk.
  • Origin:
    • Sensory receptors located in the lower limbs and lower trunk (below T6 vertebral level).
    • Primary neurons enter the spinal cord via the dorsal root ganglia.
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons ascend ipsilaterally (same side) within the fasciculus gracilis.
    2. Synapse occurs in the nucleus gracilis located in the medulla oblongata.
    3. Second-order neurons cross (decussate) at the medial lemniscus in the medulla and continue to ascend to the thalamus.
    4. Synapse occurs in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
    5. Third-order neurons project to the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions affecting the fasciculus gracilis result in ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception below the level of the lesion.
b. Fasciculus Cuneatus
  • Location:
    • Found in the dorsal (posterior) column of the spinal cord.
    • Lateral to the fasciculus gracilis.
  • Function:
    • Transmits sensory information related to:
      • Fine touch.
      • Vibration sense.
      • Proprioception from the upper limbs, upper trunk, and neck (above T6 vertebral level).
  • Origin:
    • Sensory receptors in the upper limbs, upper trunk, and neck.
    • Primary neurons enter the spinal cord via the dorsal root ganglia.
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons ascend ipsilaterally within the fasciculus cuneatus.
    2. Synapse occurs in the nucleus cuneatus located in the medulla oblongata.
    3. Second-order neurons decussate at the medial lemniscus in the medulla and ascend to the thalamus.
    4. Synapse occurs in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
    5. Third-order neurons project to the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions affecting the fasciculus cuneatus result in ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception above the T6 level.
2. Spinocerebellar Tracts

The spinocerebellar tracts are responsible for transmitting unconscious proprioceptive information to the cerebellum. This information is used for maintaining posture, balance, and coordination.

a. Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract
  • Location:
    • Found in the lateral white column of the spinal cord.
  • Function:
    • Conveys unconscious proprioceptive information from the lower limbs and trunk to the cerebellum.
    • Assists in maintaining balance and coordinating movement.
  • Origin:
    • Arises from sensory receptors in muscles, tendons, and joints (proprioceptors).
    • First-order neurons terminate in Clarke’s nucleus (nucleus dorsalis) in the thoracic spinal cord (T1-L2).
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons from peripheral receptors enter the spinal cord and synapse in Clarke's nucleus.
    2. Second-order neurons ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
    3. Fibers terminate in the cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions cause ipsilateral loss of proprioception, leading to uncoordinated movements and balance disturbances.
b. Ventral Spinocerebellar Tract
  • Location:
    • Found in the lateral white column of the spinal cord.
  • Function:
    • Transmits unconscious proprioceptive information related to whole limb movements and posture.
  • Origin:
    • Arises from spinal interneurons in the lumbar and sacral segments.
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons synapse with interneurons in the spinal gray matter.
    2. Second-order neurons cross (decussate) in the spinal cord and ascend contralaterally in the ventral spinocerebellar tract.
    3. Fibers re-cross (double decussation) in the cerebellum and terminate in the cerebellar cortex via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions result in partial loss of proprioception, affecting coordination.
3. Spinothalamic Tracts

The spinothalamic tracts transmit pain, temperature, crude touch, and pressure sensations to the brain.

a. Lateral Spinothalamic Tract
  • Location:
    • Found in the lateral white column.
  • Function:
    • Conveys sensations of pain and temperature.
  • Origin:
    • Peripheral nociceptors and thermoreceptors.
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons synapse in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.
    2. Second-order neurons cross to the opposite side of the spinal cord (anterior white commissure) and ascend in the lateral spinothalamic tract.
    3. Synapse occurs in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
    4. Third-order neurons project to the somatosensory cortex.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions cause contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion level.
b. Ventral Spinothalamic Tract
  • Location:
    • Found in the anterior white column.
  • Function:
    • Transmits sensations of crude touch and pressure.
  • Origin:
    • Mechanoreceptors in the skin.
  • Pathway:
    1. First-order neurons synapse in the dorsal horn.
    2. Second-order neurons cross to the opposite side and ascend in the ventral spinothalamic tract.
    3. Synapse occurs in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
    4. Third-order neurons project to the somatosensory cortex.
  • Clinical Significance:
    • Lesions result in contralateral loss of crude touch and pressure sensation.

Key Points

  • Somatotopic Organization: Ascending tracts maintain a spatial organization representing different body regions.
  • Ipsilateral vs. Contralateral:
    • Proprioceptive tracts like the dorsal spinocerebellar are ipsilateral.
    • Pain and temperature tracts like the lateral spinothalamic are contralateral.
  • Double Decussation: The ventral spinocerebellar tract crosses twice, ensuring ipsilateral representation.
🔽 Descending Pyramidal Tracts: Corticospinal)
✅ Overview
  • The corticospinal tract is responsible for voluntary motor control of the body (trunk + limbs).
  • Divided into:
    • Lateral corticospinal tract (90% of fibers) – decussates at medulla
    • Ventral (anterior) corticospinal tract (10%) – remains mostly ipsilateral
🧠 1. Origin of Corticospinal Tracts
  • Arise from:
    • Primary motor cortex (Area 4) – precentral gyrus
    • Premotor cortex (Area 6)
    • Supplementary motor area
    • Somatosensory cortex (Areas 3,1,2) – for modulation
🧠 2. Course Through Brain Structures (Detailed)
A. Corona Radiata
  • Fibers descend through fan-like projection fibers of the corona radiata.
B. Internal Capsule – ✨ HIGH YIELD!
  • Posterior limb of the internal capsule
  • Somatotopic arrangement (from anterior to posterior):
    • Face (most anterior)
    • Arm
    • Trunk
    • Leg (most posterior)

🔺 Lesions here can cause pure motor strokes (commonly middle cerebral artery territory).

C. Crus Cerebri (Cerebral Peduncles) – Midbrain
  • Located in the middle 2/3 of the basis pedunculi (crus cerebri)
  • Somatotopic arrangement (medial to lateral):
    • Face
    • Arm
    • Leg

🔺 Weber’s syndrome involves these regions → contralateral hemiparesis + ipsilateral CN III palsy.

D. Basis Pontis (Pons)
  • Fibers get dispersed into pontine nuclei and then regroup.
  • Decussation has not yet occurred.
E. Pyramids – Medulla Oblongata
  • Corticospinal fibers regroup in medullary pyramids.
  • Pyramidal decussation:
    • ~90% decussate → enter lateral corticospinal tract
    • ~10% remain ipsilateral → form anterior corticospinal tract
🧠 3. Spinal Cord Pathways
A. Lateral Corticospinal Tract
  • Location: Lateral white column
  • Function: Fine, skilled voluntary movement of distal limbs.
  • Fibers synapse in anterior horn (lamina IX) with lower motor neurons.
B. Anterior (Ventral) Corticospinal Tract
  • Location: Anterior white column
  • Function: Control of axial/proximal muscles (neck, shoulder, trunk)
  • Most fibers decussate at spinal cord level via ventral white commissure.
🧠 4. Somatotopy in Spinal Cord
  • Lateral corticospinal tract:
    • Cervical fibers: medial
    • Lumbar/sacral fibers: lateral

🔺 Injury to lateral cord (e.g., Brown-Séquard syndrome) affects ipsilateral motor function below lesion.

🩺 Clinical Correlates (Targeted for Exams)
🚨 Summary Table – Important Locations & Fractions
🧠 EXTRAPYRAMIDAL TRACTS

The extrapyramidal system is responsible for the modulation and regulation of involuntary motor activity (e.g. posture, tone, balance). These tracts originate from subcortical nuclei in the brainstem and do not pass through the pyramids of the medulla.

🚨 Key Tracts:
  • Rubrospinal tract
  • Reticulospinal tracts (medial & lateral)
  • Vestibulospinal tracts (medial & lateral)
  • Tectospinal tract
  • (Olivospinal tract – vestigial, often omitted)
1. RUBROSPINAL TRACT
  • Origin: Red nucleus (magnocellular part), midbrain tegmentum
  • Decussation: Ventral tegmental decussation in midbrain, just after origin
  • Course:
    • Fibers descend contralaterally through:
      • Lateral funiculus of the spinal cord (just anterior to lateral corticospinal tract)
  • Internal capsule passage:
    • Rubrospinal tract does not traverse the internal capsule directly — inputs from motor cortex reach red nucleus via corticorubral fibers in the posterior limb of internal capsule (upper 1/3)
  • Cerebral crus: Fibers pass through the middle 1/3 of crus cerebri as part of the corticorubral projection
  • Termination: Cervical spinal cord (especially upper limb flexors)
  • Function:
    • Facilitates flexor muscle tone
    • Inhibits extensor tone
    • Important in upper limb posturing and fine motor control
  • Clinical correlation:
    • Lesions → Decerebrate vs. decorticate postures
    • May compensate for corticospinal injury
2. VESTIBULOSPINAL TRACTS
a. Lateral Vestibulospinal Tract
  • Origin: Lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters' nucleus) in pons
  • Course:
    • Descends ipsilaterally through:
      • Ventromedial brainstem
      • Anterior funiculus of the spinal cord
  • Internal capsule: Does not pass through internal capsule
  • Termination: Interneurons and motor neurons of all spinal levels
  • Function:
    • Facilitates extensor muscles for posture & balance
    • Inhibits flexors
  • Clinical relevance: Lesions → imbalance, ataxia
b. Medial Vestibulospinal Tract
  • Origin: Medial vestibular nucleus
  • Decussation: Partial, in the brainstem
  • Course:
    • Descends bilaterally via medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)
    • Restricted to cervical and upper thoracic levels
  • Function:
    • Stabilizes head and neck position during body movements
    • Coordinates head-eye reflexes
3. RETICULOSPINAL TRACTS
a. Medial Reticulospinal Tract (Pontine)
  • Origin: Pontine reticular formation
  • Course:
    • Descends ipsilaterally in anterior funiculus
  • Internal capsule: Receives input via corticoreticular fibers in posterior limb of internal capsule (upper 1/3)
  • Cerebral crus: Middle 1/3 as part of corticoreticular fibers
  • Function:
    • Facilitates extensor muscle tone
    • Enhances voluntary and reflex postural adjustments
b. Lateral Reticulospinal Tract (Medullary)
  • Origin: Medullary reticular formation
  • Course:
    • Descends bilaterally (predominantly ipsilateral) in lateral funiculus
  • Function:
    • Inhibits extensors, facilitates flexors
    • Suppresses spinal reflexes to allow smooth voluntary movement
4. TECTOSPINAL TRACT
  • Origin: Superior colliculus (midbrain tectum)
  • Decussation: Dorsal tegmental decussation (midbrain)
  • Course:
    • Descends contralaterally in anterior funiculus
    • Travels medially, closely associated with MLF
  • Termination: Cervical spinal cord
  • Function:
    • Coordinates head and neck movements in response to visual/auditory stimuli (startle reflex)
  • Clinical relevance:
    • Lesions impair orientation to stimuli
✳️ INTERNAL CAPSULE INVOLVEMENT – Summary
🔎 FUNCTIONAL CLASSIFICATION SUMMARY
💡 EXAM POINTS TO REMEMBER:
  1. Rubrospinal: Red nucleus → ventral tegmental decussation → lateral funiculus → UL flexors
  2. Lateral vestibulospinal: Lateral vestibular nucleus → ipsilateral anterior funiculus → extensors
  3. Reticulospinal: Pontine = facilitates extensors; Medullary = facilitates flexors
  4. Tectospinal: Superior colliculus → dorsal decussation → cervical spinal cord → head reflexes
  5. Vestibulospinal and tectospinal: No direct cortical input
  6. Somatotopy preserved in lateral and anterior funiculi
  7. Lesions cause postural imbalance, spasticity, or loss of reflexive movements

    A. Plerocercoid
    B. Procercoid
    C. Cysticercus bovis
    D. Cysticercus cellulosae
    E. Cercariae
    Answer: D. Cysticercus cellulosae
  7. In which muscles are hexacanth filtered out in the intermediate hosts?
    A. Smooth muscles
    B. Striated muscles
    C. Cardiac muscles
    D. All of the above
    Answer: B. Striated muscles
  8. Which part of the human body is not inhabited by the larvae in cysticercosis?
    A. Brain
    B. Liver
    C. Lung
    D. Kidney
    E. None of the above
    Answer: B. Liver
  9. Which of the following parasites cause sparganosis?
    A. Ancylostoma braziliense
    B. Taenia saginata
    C. Strongyloides stercoralis
    D. Toxocara canis
    E. Spirometra theileri
    Answer: E. Spirometra theileri
  10. Which parasite is best diagnosed using lymphatic fluid?
    A. Ascaris lumbricoides
    B. Wuchereria bancrofti
    C. Enterobium vermicularis
    D. Taenia multiceps
    E. All of the above
    Answer: B. Wuchereria bancrofti
  11. Which of the following tapeworm infections will require prescription with clonazepam? (Select all)
    A. Broad tapeworm
    B. Pork tapeworm
    C. Beef tapeworm
    D. Dwarf tapeworm
    E. All of the above
    Answer: B. Pork tapeworm
  12. Which parasite results into micropthalmia condition?
    A. Diphyllobothrium latum
    B. Toxoplasma gondii
    C. Strongyloides stercoralis
    D. Toxocara canis
    E. Enterobium vermicularis
    Answer: D. Toxocara canis
  13. Which of the following medication is given after a light breakfast?
    A. Niclosamide
    B. Praziquantel
    C. Metriphonate
    D. Albendazole
    E. All of the above
    Answer: B. Praziquantel
  14. Albendazole mode of action include interference with?
    A. ATP production
    B. Glucose uptake
    C. Water absorption
    D. Membrane permeability
    E. RNA synthesis
    Answer: B. Glucose uptake
  15. Which of the following medication is contraindicated in thrombocytopenia taenia infected patients?
    A. Niclosamide
    B. Praziquantel
    C. Metriphonate
    D. Albendazole
    E. All of the above
    Answer: B. Praziquantel
  16. Swimmer's itch is produced by?
    A. Necator americanus
    B. Schistosoma haematobium
    C. Enterobium vermicularis
    D. Diphyllobothrium latum
    E. All of the above
    Answer: B. Schistosoma haematobium
  17. Which one is associated with nocturnal pruritis ani?
    A. Necator americanus
    B. Enterobium vermicularis
    C. Ascaris lumbricoides
    D. Diphyllobothrium latum
    E. None of the above
    Answer: B. Enterobium vermicularis
  18. Which of the following is ciliated?
    A. Rediae
    B. Cercariae
    C. Coracidium
    D. Filariform
    E. Microfilariae
    Answer: C. Coracidium
  19. National Institute of Health (NIH) tape technique is used for diagnosis of?
    A. Ancylostoma braziliense
    B. Enterobium vermicularis
    C. Strongyloides stercoralis
    D. Toxocara canis
    E. Diphyllobothrium latum
    Answer: B. Enterobium vermicularis
  20. Which of the following is a false tapeworm?
    A. Ancylostoma braziliense
    B. Enterobium vermicularis
    C. Strongyloides stercoralis
    D. Toxocara canis
    E. Diphyllobothrium latum
    Answer: E. Diphyllobothrium latum
  21. Which parasite can cause erosion of bones?
    A. Ascaris lumbricoides
    B. Echinococcus granulosus
    C. Gnathostoma spinigerum
    D. Taenia multiceps
    E. All of the above
    Answer: E. All of the above
  22. Prolonged coughing and chest pains can be associated with?
    A. Echinostoma ilocanum
    B. Paragonimus westermanii
    C. Fasciolopsis buski
    D. Clonorchis sinensis
    E. Schistosoma haematobium
    Answer: B. Paragonimus westermanii
  23. Bothriocephalus anaemia is due to:
    A. Ancylostoma braziliense
    B. Taenia saginata
    C. Strongyloides stercoralis
    D. Toxocara canis
    E. Diphyllobothrium latum
    Answer: E. Diphyllobothrium latum
  24. Which of the following medication is given based on age in treatment of broad tapeworm?
    A. Niclosamide
    B. Praziquantel
    C. Metriphonate
    D. Albendazole
    E. All of the above
    Answer: A. Niclosamide
  25. Squamous carcinoma of the bladder is associated with which stage?
    A. Adult
    B. Egg
    C. Cercarial
    D. Metacercaria
    E. All of the above
    Answer: C. Cercarial
  26. Which of the following parasites is associated with achlorhydria?
    A. Amoeba species
    B. Trichomonas species
    C. Giardia species
    D. Leishmania species
    Answer: C. Giardia species
  27. Metronidazole parasite site of target is?
    A. RNA
    B. DNA
    C. Ribosomes
    D. Cytoskeleton
    Answer: B. DNA
  28. Which of the following parasites is associated with pyosalpingitis?
    A. Amoeba species
    B. Trichomonas species
    C. Giardia species
    D. Leishmania species
    Answer: B. Trichomonas species
  29. Which of the following biomolecules helps in the survival of both Leishmania and Plasmodium parasites?
    A. Lpg
    B. Gpi
    C. Gp63
    D. G6pd
    E. All of the above
    Answer: E. All of the above
  30. Which of the following medication is administered IV?
    A. Artesunate
    B. Pentamidine
    C. Arthemeter
    D. Emetine
    E. Paromomycin
    Answer: A. Artesunate

31. Which of the following medicines is antagonist to folic acid?
A. Sulfadiazine
B. Pentamidine
C. Arthemeter
D. Fansidar
E. Paromomycin
Answer: D. Fansidar
(Fansidar is a combination of sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine—both folate antagonists.)

32. Which drug targets the A site of the ribosomes?
A. Pyrimethamine
B. Pentamidine
C. Benzimidazoles
D. Miltefosine
E. Paromomycin
Answer: E. Paromomycin
(Paromomycin binds to the A site of the 30S ribosomal subunit, disrupting protein synthesis.)

33. Which drug targets the dihydropteroate synthase?
A. Pyrimethamine
B. Sulfadoxine
C. Benzimidazoles
D. Miltefosine
E. Paromomycin
Answer: B. Sulfadoxine
(Sulfadoxine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase in folate synthesis pathway.)

34. Which drug targets the dihydrofolate reductase?
A. Pyrimethamine
B. Sulfadiazine
C. Benzimidazoles
D. Nifurtimox
E. Sulfadoxine
Answer: A. Pyrimethamine
(Pyrimethamine is a selective inhibitor of protozoan dihydrofolate reductase.)

35. Which drug targets the vicynyl sulfhydryl groups of pyruvate kinase?
A. Pyrimethamine
B. Sulfadiazine
C. Meglumine antimonate
D. Melarsoprol
E. Sulfadoxine
Answer: D. Melarsoprol
(Melarsoprol reacts with vicinal thiol groups of enzymes like pyruvate kinase, disrupting parasite metabolism.)

36. Which drug targets the ornithine decarboxylase?
A. Eflornithine
B. Sulfadiazine
Answer: A. Eflornithine
(Eflornithine irreversibly inhibits ornithine decarboxylase, crucial in polyamine synthesis in trypanosomes.)

37. Mucoid stools are associated with?
A. Schistosoma japonicum
B. Giardia lamblia
C. Schistosoma mansoni
D. Entamoeba histolytica
E. Fasciola hepatica
Answer: D. Entamoeba histolytica
(Causes amoebic dysentery with bloody, mucoid stools.)

38. Each of the following statements concerning Malaria is correct except:
A. The female anopheles mosquito is the vector
B. The principal site of gametocyte formation is the human gastrointestinal tract
C. Release of merozoites from red blood cells causes fever and chills
D. Early infection, sporozoites enter hepatocytes
E. None of the above
Answer: B. The principal site of gametocyte formation is the human gastrointestinal tract
(Gametocytes form in red blood cells, not the GI tract.)

39. Which of the following lesions progress to ulcerate?
A. Nodular lesions
B. Diffuse cutaneous
C. Erythematous patches
D. Depigmented macules
E. All of the above
Answer: A. Nodular lesions
(Nodular lesions, such as those in cutaneous leishmaniasis, can ulcerate.)

40. Which of the following causes both visceral and cutaneous leishmaniasis?
A. L. donovani
B. L. infantum
C. L. chagasi
D. L. braziliensis
E. L. aethiopica
Answer: E. L. aethiopica
(L. aethiopica is primarily cutaneous but can rarely cause visceral symptoms.)

41. Which one of the following causes espundia?
A. L. tropica
B. L. infantum
C. L. chagasi
D. L. braziliensis
E. L. aethiopica
Answer: D. L. braziliensis
(L. braziliensis causes mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, also known as espundia.)

42. Which one of the following causes chiclero's ulcers?
A. L. mexicana
B. L. infantum
C. L. chagasi
D. L. braziliensis
E. L. major
Answer: A. L. mexicana
(Chiclero’s ulcer is caused by L. mexicana, typically affecting the ear.)

43. Which of the following lesions do not respond to chemotherapy?
A. Oriental sores
B. Delhi boil
C. Zoonotic rural
D. Diffuse cutaneous
E. Leishmaniasis recidivans
Answer: E. Leishmaniasis recidivans
(Leishmaniasis recidivans is a chronic form that responds poorly to treatment.)

44. How many dose(s) is/are recommended for RTS, S/AS01?
A. 1
B. 2
C. 3
D. 4
E. 6
Answer: D. 4
(The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is given in 4 doses.)

45. Quinine medication can be best combined with _____ in pregnancy malaria.
A. Tetracycline
Answer: [Incomplete options]
(Tetracycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. Quinine is best combined with clindamycin in pregnant women.)
Correct answer: Clindamycin (Please update the option list)

46. Which of the following asymptomatic infections should not be treated?
A. Amoebiasis
B. Giardiasis
C. Trichomoniasis
D. Trypanosomiasis
Answer: D. Trypanosomiasis
(Due to its severity and progression, trypanosomiasis is treated even if asymptomatic. However, asymptomatic giardiasis may not be treated in endemic areas.)
Correct answer (based on standard protocols): A. Amoebiasis is typically treated
Best Answer: B. Giardiasis, in endemic cases
(Please confirm local guidelines for clarity)

47. Which of the following medications should NOT be given to 1st trimester of pregnancy?
A. Furazolidone
B. Paromomycin
C. Tinidazole
D. Iodoquinol
Answer: C. Tinidazole
(Tinidazole is contraindicated in the first trimester due to potential teratogenic effects.)

48. Which of the following exists only as a trophozoite?
A. E. histolytica
B. T. hominis
C. G. intestinalis
D. None of the above
Answer: B. T. hominis
(Trichomonas hominis exists only in the trophozoite form.)

49. Which of the following medication should NOT be given to children <1 month old?
A. Furazolidone
B. Paromomycin
C. Tinidazole
D. Nitazoxanide
Answer: D. Nitazoxanide
(Nitazoxanide is not recommended for infants under 1 year, particularly under 1 month.)

50. Which of the following drugs targets the A site of parasite ribosome?
A. Furazolidone
B. Paromomycin
C. Tinidazole
D. Diloxanide furoate
Answer: B. Paromomycin
(It binds to the A site of the 30S ribosomal subunit, disrupting protein synthesis in parasites.)

1. Katayama fever is due to which infection?
Answer: Acute schistosomiasis (commonly caused by Schistosoma japonicum or S. mansoni)

2. Casoni's skin test is best for diagnosis of which condition?
Answer: Hydatid disease (caused by Echinococcus granulosus)

3. Percutaneous thermal ablation uses what devices for treatment of hydatid cyst?
Answer: Radiofrequency probes or microwave ablation devices

4. Which drug can be used to subside epileptic symptoms in neurocysticercosis patients?
Answer: Albendazole (antiparasitic) along with antiepileptic drugs like carbamazepine or phenytoin

5. S. haematobium infects what types of cells of the bladder?
Answer: Transitional epithelial cells (urothelium)

6. Loa loa is transmitted by what vector and causes what disease?
Answer:

  • Vector: Chrysops (deer fly or mango fly)
  • Disease: Loiasis

7. Scotch tape technique is best for diagnosis of which parasite?
Answer: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)

8. Cutaneous larva migrans is a suspicious sign of which infection?
Answer: Ancylostoma braziliense (dog or cat hookworm)

9. Rectal prolapse is a suspicious sign of which infection?
Answer: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm infection)

10. Which nematode resides in muscles of pigs for human consumption?
Answer: Trichinella spiralis

11. Which malaria parasite results into relapse?
Answer: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale
(Due to dormant liver forms called hypnozoites)

12. Prescribe use of artesunate (dosage, route, frequency).
Answer:

  • Dosage: 2.4 mg/kg body weight
  • Route: Intravenous (IV) or intramuscular (IM)
  • Frequency: At 0, 12, and 24 hours, then once daily until oral therapy can be started

13. Which malaria vaccine is currently in the roll out phase?
Answer: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix)

14. What is the probability of the fetus to get toxoplasma infection when mother gets infection in 2nd trimester?
Answer: Approximately 25–30%

15. Which is the drug of choice to reduce toxoplasma encephalitis in immunocompromised patients?
Answer: Pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine (with leucovorin to reduce toxicity)

16. What is the basis of pathogenesis of non-protein synthesis in diphyllobothriasis?
Answer: Vitamin B12 deficiency due to parasite absorption, leading to megaloblastic anemia

17. Prescribe niclosamide in T. saginata infection (dosage, route, frequency).
Answer:

  • Dosage: 2 g single dose (for adults)
  • Route: Oral
  • Frequency: Single dose; may be followed by a mild laxative 1–2 hours later

18. What is the mode of action of albendazole?
Answer:
Albendazole binds to β-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerization, thereby impairing glucose uptake and depleting glycogen stores in parasites.

19. Which of the following is a free-living parasite?
A. Dientamoeba fragilis
B. Iodamoeba butschlii
C. Indolimax nana
D. Naegleria fowleri
E. All of the above
Answer: D. Naegleria fowleri

20. Which of the following drugs have musculo and neurotoxic effects?
A. Melarsoprol
B. Suramin
C. Emetine
D. Amphotericin
E. All of the above
Answer: E. All of the above

21. All asymptomatic patients should be treated EXCEPT in which infection?
A. Giardiasis
B. Entamoebiasis
C. Toxoplasmosis
D. Babesiosis
E. Trypanosomiasis
Answer: C. Toxoplasmosis

22. Chlorination of water DOES NOT help in the control of:
A. Giardiasis
B. Entamoebiasis
C. Cholera
D. Dysentery
E. None of the above
Answer: A. Giardiasis
(Because Giardia cysts are resistant to standard chlorination)

23. How do Giardia parasites evade the host immune system?
A. They have an anti-phagocytic capsule
B. They are obligate intracellular parasites
C. They continuously alter their surface glycoproteins
D. They produce enzymes that digest antibodies
E. All of the above
Answer: C. They continuously alter their surface glycoproteins

24. Each of the following statements concerning kala-azar is correct EXCEPT:
A. Kala-azar is caused by Leishmania donovani
B. Kala-azar occurs primarily in rural Latin America
C. Kala-azar is transmitted by the bite of sandflies
D. Kala-azar can be diagnosed by finding amastigotes in bone marrow
E. None of the above
Answer: B. Kala-azar occurs primarily in rural Latin America
(Correct: It occurs mainly in South Asia, East Africa, and parts of Brazil)

25. Which parasite may produce Winterbottom's sign in man?
A. Ascaris lumbricoides
B. Trypanosoma gambiense
C. Gnathostoma spinigerum
D. Taenia multiceps
E. Fasciola hepatica
Answer: B. Trypanosoma gambiense

26. Write the prescription for:
a) Chagas disease in children → Nifurtimox: 10–15 mg/kg/day orally in 2–3 doses for 60 days
b) Giardiasis in children <5 years old → Metronidazole: 15 mg/kg/day orally in 3 divided doses for 5–7 days
c) EASS stage (late stage African trypanosomiasis) → Eflornithine: 100 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 14 days or in combination with nifurtimox
d) Leishmaniasis → Amphotericin B deoxycholate: 0.75–1 mg/kg/day IV on alternate days for 15–20 doses
(alternatively: Liposomal amphotericin B, or miltefosine in certain cases)

27. Give the mode of action of the following medications:
a) Eflornithine → Irreversible inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase, halting polyamine synthesis
b) Paromomycin → Inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit (aminoglycoside)
c) Meglumine antimonate → Disrupts glycolysis and fatty acid oxidation in the parasite
d) Nifurtimox → Generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) that damage parasite DNA and macromolecules

28. Which of the following parasites results into intestinal bilharzia?
A. Enterobius vermicularis
B. Schistosoma mansoni
C. Schistosoma haematobium
D. Schistosoma japonicum
Answer: B. Schistosoma mansoni

29. Which of the following parasites interferes with Vitamin A utilization in children?
A. E. histolytica
B. T. hominis
C. G. intestinalis
D. None of the above
Answer: C. G. intestinalis

30. Which of the following medication is administered as a slow bolus?
A. Artesunate
B. Pentamidine
C. Arthemeter
D. Emetine
E. Paromomycin
Answer: B. Pentamidine

31. Which of the following medication is given in IPTm (Intermittent Preventive Treatment in infants)?
A. Artesunate
B. Pyrimethamine
C. Arthemeter
D. Fansidar
E. Sulfadoxine
Answer: D. Fansidar
(Fansidar = Sulfadoxine + Pyrimethamine)

32. Which of the following should NOT be prescribed during first trimester of pregnancy?
A. Furazolidone
B. Nitazoxanide
C. Metronidazole
D. Tetracycline
Answer: D. Tetracycline

33. Which of the following medication has myotoxic and cardiotoxic effects?
A. Furazolidone
B. Emetine
C. Metronidazole
D. Tetracycline
Answer: B. Emetine

34. Which of the following medication dosage should be re-administered after 6 weeks?
A. Furazolidone
B. Emetine
C. Metronidazole
D. Tetracycline
Answer: A. Furazolidone

35. Which of the following parasites exhibit Variant Surface Specific Antigens?
A. Amoeba species
B. Trichomonas species
C. Giardia species
D. Leishmania species
Answer: D. Leishmania species

Title: Comprehensive Immunology Quiz
Content:
Section 1: Basic Concepts and Components of the Immune System

1.1 The ____ immune system uses ____ as well as molecules (e.g. complement components). The ____ immune system uses ____ as well as antigen recognition molecules.

a) Adaptive; Phagocytes; Innate; Lymphocytes
b) Adaptive; Lymphocytes; Innate; Phagocytes
c) Innate; Phagocytes; Adaptive; Lymphocytes
d) Innate; Lymphocytes; Adaptive; Phagocytes

Correct Answer: C

1.2 Phagocytic white cells (leukocytes, e.g. macrophages) congregate within ____ when foreign organisms get through a cut in the skin.

a) Microseconds
b) Seconds
c) Minutes
d) Hours
e) Days

Correct Answer: C

1.3 Which of the following mediates an early response to viral infections by the innate immune system?

a) Complement components
b) Vaccines
c) T and B lymphocytes
d) Cytokines
e) Interferons

Correct Answer: E

1.4 Which of the following is a messenger that mediates the connection between the innate and adaptive immune systems?

a) Complement components
b) Vaccines
c) T and B lymphocytes
d) Cytokines
e) Interferons

Correct Answer: D

1.5 Which of the following immune system components would NOT recognize a macromolecule epitope (binding site)?

a) Phagocyte
b) T lymphocyte
c) B lymphocyte
d) Antibody

Correct Answer: A

1.6 Which of the following is a large genomic region or gene family found in most vertebrates, playing an important role in immunity?

a) Antigen-recognition molecules
b) Major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs)
c) Human leukocyte antigens (HLAs)
d) Immunoglobulin
e) Epitopes

Correct Answer: B

1.7 B-cell antigen receptors can interact directly with antigen, whereas T-cell antigen receptors only recognize antigen when it is presented to them on the surface of another cell.

a) True
b) False

Correct Answer: A

1.8 How are B-cell and T-cell antigen receptors distributed?

a) By size (steric hindrance)
b) By molecular weight
c) By activation (clonal)
d) By location in the body
e) Equally (same number of each receptor)

Correct Answer: C

1.9 A medical student acquired hepatitis B through a needle-stick injury. The student had not received their vaccinations for this virus and eventually experienced liver problems. One of the clinical signs of this disease is jaundice, which turns the skin and sclera what color?

a) Black
b) Red
c) White
d) Yellow
e) Blue

Correct Answer: D

1.10 Monoclonal antibodies (mAb) are antibodies with a wide range of clinically important applications, such as pregnancy tests, cancer diagnosis, and cancer treatment. These antibodies are ____ and come from ____ parent cell(s).

a) Dissimilar; Multiple
b) Dissimilar; A single
c) Identical; Multiple
d) Identical; A single

Correct Answer: D

1.11 Adaptive immune system response typically takes how long?

a) Microseconds
b) Seconds
c) Minutes
d) Hours
e) Days

Correct Answer: E

Section 2: Basic Concepts

2.1 Which of the following is NOT true when comparing innate to adaptive immunity?

a) Innate responds quickly and adaptive responds slowly
b) Innate has few pathogen (non-self) recognition mechanisms and adaptive has many
c) Innate has immunologic memory and adaptive does not
d) Innate does not show response improvements over time and adaptive does
e) Innate response is non-specific and adaptive is very specific

Correct Answer: C

2.2 Phagocytes ingest particular matter into cells for degradation. Which of the following is NOT considered a phagocyte?

a) Macrophage
b) Neutrophil
c) Eosinophil
d) Basophil
e) Lymphocyte

Correct Answer: E

2.3.1 Which of the following components of the innate immune system involves recognition molecules such as mannan-binding lectin (MBL) for bacteria with mannose on the surface?

a) Natural killer (NK) cells
b) Complement system
c) Oxygen dependent and independent killing
d) Interferons
e) Acute phase proteins

Correct Answer: B

2.3.2 Which of the following components of the innate immune system involves cytokines produced by macrophages, which are produced during infection?

a) Natural killer (NK) cells
b) Complement system
c) Oxygen dependent and independent killing
d) Interferons
e) Acute phase proteins

Correct Answer: E

2.3.3 Which of the following components of the innate immune system involves the release of histamine?

a) Neutrophil
b) Eosinophil
c) Macrophage
d) Tissue mast cell
e) Natural killer cell

Correct Answer: D

2.4.1 Which of the following components of the adaptive immune system secretes immunoglobulin (Ig)?

a) Activated B cell (plasma cell)
b) CD4+ activated T cell
c) CD8+ cytotoxic T cell (CTL)
d) Resting lymphocytes (B cell, CD4+ T cell, CD8+ T cell)
e) B and C

Correct Answer: A

2.4.2 Which of the following components of the adaptive immune system causes lysis of virally infected cells and the release of cytokines?

a) Activated B cell (plasma cell)
b) CD4+ activated T cell
c) CD8+ cytotoxic T cell (CTL)
d) Resting lymphocytes (B cell, CD4+ T cell, CD8+ T cell)
e) B and C

Correct Answer: C (Note: Original answer key shows E, but C is the correct answer as CD8+ CTL specifically lyse infected cells)

2.4.3 Antigen presenting cells (APCs) include macrophages and dendritic cells, which are found in lymphoid tissues and the ____. These are critical in the uptake and presentation of antigen to T cells.

a) Liver
b) Kidney
c) Skin
d) Brain
e) Gallbladder

Correct Answer: C

2.4.4 Which of the following is NOT a major feature (characteristic) of the adaptive immune system?

a) Specificity
b) Diversity
c) Memory
d) Improvement
e) Speed

Correct Answer: E

2.5 Humoral immunity is mediated by antibodies from ____ and is involved in the elimination of ____ pathogens. Cell mediated immunity is mediated by ____ and is involved in the elimination of ____ pathogens.

a) B lymphocytes; Intracellular; T lymphocytes; Extracellular
b) B lymphocytes; Extracellular; T lymphocytes; Intracellular
c) T lymphocytes; Intracellular; B lymphocytes; Extracellular
d) T lymphocytes; Extracellular; B lymphocytes; Intracellular

Correct Answer: B

2.6 How many doses of the Hepatitis B vaccine (5µg HBsAg in 0.5mL intramuscular) are required to reach a protective level of antibody?

a) One
b) Two
c) Three
d) Four
e) Five

Correct Answer: C

2.7.1 Eosinophils function in:

a) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms, antigen presentation
b) Lysis of some virally infected cells
c) Killing parasites
d) Release of histamine and other mediators
e) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms

Correct Answer: C

2.7.2 Macrophages function in:

a) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms, antigen presentation
b) Lysis of some virally infected cells
c) Killing parasites
d) Release of histamine and other mediators
e) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms

Correct Answer: A

2.7.3 Tissue mast cells function in:

a) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms, antigen presentation
b) Lysis of some virally infected cells
c) Killing parasites
d) Release of histamine and other mediators
e) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms

Correct Answer: D

2.7.4 Natural killer cells function in:

a) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms, antigen presentation
b) Lysis of some virally infected cells
c) Killing parasites
d) Release of histamine and other mediators
e) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms

Correct Answer: B

2.7.5 Neutrophils function in:

a) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms, antigen presentation
b) Lysis of some virally infected cells
c) Killing parasites
d) Release of histamine and other mediators
e) Phagocytosis and bacteriocidal mechanisms

Correct Answer: E

2.7.6 In a resting lymphocyte, B cells and T cells can be distinguished from each other via a simple blood smear.

a) True
b) False

Correct Answer: B

2.7.7 T cells are made in the ____ and complete their differentiation in the ____.

a) Spleen; Thyroid
b) Spleen; Thymus
c) Bone marrow; Thyroid
d) Bone marrow; Thymus
e) Bone marrow; Thalamus

Correct Answer: D

Question 1: Which of the following is NOT true when comparing primary immune response to subsequent (secondary) immune response?

Question 1: Parasitic Worm Immunity

Parasitic worm eggs are resistant to low pH and proteolytic digestion in the stomach. Adult worms living inside the lower gut are protected from many of the components of the immune response. Mast cells respond to worms. What immunoglobulin activates these mast cells, leading to degranulation?

a) IgA
b) IgD
c) IgE
d) IgG
e) IgM

Correct Answer: C) IgE

Explanation: IgE is the primary immunoglobulin involved in allergic reactions and parasitic infections. It binds to high-affinity receptors (FcεRI) on mast cells and basophils. When parasitic antigens cross-link IgE molecules on these cells, it triggers degranulation, releasing histamine and other inflammatory mediators that help combat the parasitic infection.

d) Cytokines/TNF

Correct Answer: B) Histamine

Explanation: Histamine is the primary mediator responsible for increased vascular permeability. It causes vasodilation and increases the leakiness of blood vessels, allowing immune cells and proteins to enter tissues more easily.

Question 2.2

Increase mucus secretion and smooth muscle contraction

a) Trypase & Chemotrypsin
b) Histamine
c) Cytokines/IL-4
d) Cytokines/TNF

Correct Answer: A) Trypase & Chemotrypsin

Explanation: These are proteolytic enzymes stored in mast cell granules. They contribute to tissue remodeling, mucus secretion, and smooth muscle contraction, particularly important in asthmatic responses.

Question 2.3

Enhance diapedesis and stimulate TH2 responses

a) Trypase & Chemotrypsin
b) Histamine
c) Cytokines/IL-4
d) Cytokines/TNF

Correct Answer: D) Cytokines/TNF

Explanation: TNF-α (Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha) enhances diapedesis (movement of immune cells through blood vessel walls) and helps coordinate inflammatory responses, including stimulating TH2 cell responses.

Question 2.4

Activates TH2 and stimulates eosinophil production

a) Trypase & Chemotrypsin
b) Histamine
c) Cytokines/IL-4
d) Cytokines/TNF

Correct Answer: C) Cytokines/IL-4

Explanation: IL-4 is a key cytokine that promotes TH2 differentiation and stimulates eosinophil production and activation. It's crucial in allergic responses and anti-parasitic immunity.

Question 2.5: Arachidonic Acid Metabolites

Mast cell arachidonic acid metabolites include cyclo-oxygenase, which produces prostaglandins that stimulate ____ and increase ____ of smooth muscle in the gut and bronchi. Metabolites also include leukotrienes, which have a ____ effect than prostaglandins.

a) Vasoconstriction; Constriction; Slower
b) Vasoconstriction; Constriction; Faster
c) Vasodilation; Dilation; Slower
d) Vasodilation; Dilation; Faster
e) Vasodilation; Constriction; Slower
f) Vasodilation; Constriction; Faster

Correct Answer: E) Vasodilation; Constriction; Slower

Explanation: Prostaglandins cause vasodilation (increased blood flow) but also cause smooth muscle constriction in airways and gut. Leukotrienes have a slower onset but more prolonged effect compared to prostaglandins and are particularly important in asthma.

Question 2.6: Initial Mast Cell Activation

Which of the following would NOT act initially during mast cell (or basophil) activation?

a) Trypase
b) Chemotrypsin
c) Histamine
d) Prostaglandins
e) Leukotrienes

Correct Answer: E) Leukotrienes

Explanation: Leukotrienes are newly synthesized mediators that require time for production from arachidonic acid metabolism. The other options are either pre-stored in granules (trypase, chemotrypsin, histamine) or rapidly produced (prostaglandins).

Question 3: Eosinophils

Which of the following is NOT true regarding eosinophils?

a) They are specifically recruited to tissues during some types of inflammation
b) Their granules contain particularly toxic substances
c) Their production is stimulated by IL-3 and IL-5
d) They are recruited to parasite infected sites by chemokine eotaxin
e) They are a major acidic and anionic protein

Correct Answer: E) They are a major acidic and anionic protein

Explanation: Eosinophils CONTAIN major basic protein (which is cationic/basic, not acidic and anionic). This protein is toxic to parasites and is stored in their granules. All other statements are correct about eosinophils.

Natural Killer (NK) Cells

Questions 4.1-4.4: NK Cell Functions

Question 4.1

Natural killer (NK) cells are excellent killers of cells infected by some ____. They also have an additional role of stimulating the ____ immune response.

a) Bacteria; Adaptive
b) Viruses; Adaptive
c) Bacteria; Innate
d) Viruses; Innate

Correct Answer: B) Viruses; Adaptive

Explanation: NK cells primarily target virus-infected cells and tumor cells. They bridge innate and adaptive immunity by releasing cytokines that stimulate adaptive immune responses, particularly T cell responses.

Question 4.2

Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is the process by which natural killer cells destroy infected cells, identified by what immunoglobulin on the surface?

a) IgA
b) IgD
c) IgE
d) IgG
e) IgM

Correct Answer: D) IgG

Explanation: NK cells have Fc receptors that bind to IgG antibodies coating target cells. This allows NK cells to recognize and destroy cells that have been marked by IgG antibodies in a process called ADCC.

Question 4.3

Natural killer cells are thought to fill the gap between initial innate response and adaptive immune response. They evolved to detect low levels of MHC caused by the diseases of ____ and ____.

a) Staph bacteria; Strep bacteria
b) Catalase positive bacteria; Helminths (worms)
c) Herpes virus; Tumor cells
d) Influenza virus; Rabies virus
e) Leprosy; Gonorrhea bacteria

Correct Answer: C) Herpes virus; Tumor cells

Explanation: Both herpes viruses and tumor cells often downregulate MHC class I expression to evade CD8+ T cell recognition. NK cells evolved to detect this "missing self" and eliminate these dangerous cells.

Question 4.4

Natural killer cell receptors NKG2/CD94 and killer inhibitory receptors allow for the killing of antibodies in the presence of:

a) MHC class I
b) MHC class II
c) Both MHC class I and II
d) Either MHC class I or II
e) Neither MHC class I nor II

Correct Answer: D) Either MHC class I or II

Explanation: NK cells are inhibited when they detect normal levels of MHC molecules. They become activated to kill when MHC expression is reduced or absent ("missing self" recognition).

Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CTLs)

Questions 5.1-5.3: CTL Killing Mechanisms

Question 5.1

Match the description with the cytotoxic T cell (CTL) killing mechanism: Potent inducer of apoptosis

a) Perforin
b) Granzyme
c) Fas ligand

Correct Answer: C) Fas ligand

Explanation: Fas ligand (FasL) on CTLs binds to Fas receptors on target cells, directly triggering the apoptotic pathway through death receptor signaling.

Question 5.2

Degrade host cell proteins, activate caspase enzyme system

a) Perforin
b) Granzyme
c) Fas ligand

Correct Answer: B) Granzyme

Explanation: Granzymes are serine proteases that cleave cellular proteins and activate caspases, leading to apoptosis once they enter the target cell through perforin pores.

Question 5.3

Forms a pore in the target cell membrane (like MAC)

a) Perforin
b) Granzyme
c) Fas ligand

Correct Answer: A) Perforin

Explanation: Perforin polymerizes to form pores in the target cell membrane, similar to the membrane attack complex (MAC) of complement. These pores allow granzymes to enter the cell.

Chapter 24: Infections and Vaccines

Question 1: Vaccine Classification

Vaccines (natural exposure) is considered active immunotherapy and leads to the development of immunologic memory.

a) True
b) False

Correct Answer: A) True

Explanation: Vaccines expose the immune system to antigens, stimulating active immunity and memory cell formation, providing long-term protection against future infections.

Questions 2.1-2.3: Live Vaccines

Question 2.1

Which of the following is NOT true about live vaccines?

a) They were the first vaccines to be discovered
b) They are currently the least effective vaccines
c) They replicate and thus deliver sustained doses of antigen
d) They deliver antigenic peptides to MHC class I
e) They replicate at the infection site, focusing immune response

Correct Answer: B) They are currently the least effective vaccines

Explanation: Live vaccines are actually among the MOST effective vaccines because they closely mimic natural infection and provide strong, long-lasting immunity.

Question 2.2

Which of the following live vaccines is recommended for children but not adults?

a) Poliovirus
b) Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR)
c) Varicella
d) Meningococcal
e) Influenza

Correct Answer: A) Poliovirus

Explanation: Live oral poliovirus vaccine (OPV) is given to children in some countries but not recommended for adults due to risk of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis.

Question 2.3

Which of the following live vaccines is recommended for adults but not children?

a) Poliovirus
b) Measles, mumps, rubella (MMR)
c) Varicella
d) Meningococcal
e) Influenza

Correct Answer: D) Meningococcal

Explanation: Meningococcal vaccines are typically recommended for adults in high-risk situations (college dormitories, military) rather than routine childhood immunization.

Question 3: Killed Vaccines

Killed vaccines are theoretically much safer than live vaccines, but cannot replicate in hosts and cannot enter intracellular antigen presenting pathways. Which of the following killed vaccines is recommended for children but not adults?

a) Hepatitis A
b) Influenza
c) Inactivated poliovirus

Correct Answer: C) Inactivated poliovirus

Explanation: Inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) is part of routine childhood immunization but not typically given to adults who were vaccinated as children.

Questions 4.1-4.2: Subunit Vaccines

Question 4.1

Subunit vaccines contains components from pathogens, which are inactivated and referred to as ____. These vaccines are generally of low immunogenicity and may need ____ to work effectively.

a) Cytokines; IgE
b) LPS; Live vaccination
c) Capsules; Homeostasis
d) Toxoids; Adjuvants
e) Antigens; B & T cells

Correct Answer: D) Toxoids; Adjuvants

Explanation: Toxoids are inactivated bacterial toxins used in vaccines. Adjuvants are added to enhance immune response since purified antigens alone may not stimulate strong immunity.

Question 4.2

Which of the following subunit vaccines is recommended for children but not adults?

a) Pneumonococcal (PCV)
b) Haemophilus influenzae type B
c) Hepatitis B
d) Diptheria, tetanus, pertussis

Correct Answer: B) Haemophilus influenzae type B

Explanation: Hib vaccine is primarily given to children under 5 years as they are most susceptible to invasive Hib disease. Adults rarely need this vaccine.

Questions 5.1-5.3: Advanced Vaccine Technologies

Question 5.1

DNA vaccines (tested in mice) use the gene for the immunogenic protein and coat it with what element, which is injected into cells and results in antibody production?

a) Tin
b) Zinc
c) Copper
d) Gold
e) Silver
f) Lead

Correct Answer: D) Gold

Explanation: Gene gun technology uses gold particles coated with DNA to deliver genetic material into cells for vaccine purposes.

Question 5.2

Immunostimulatory complexes (ISCOMS) can be used for mucosal vaccines and induce widespread mucosal immunity in the gut and respiratory tract. They are the one way that ____ response can be promoted.

a) B cell
b) Helper T cell
c) Cytotoxic T cell
d) Eosinophil
e) Macrophage

Correct Answer: C) Cytotoxic T cell

Explanation: ISCOMS are particularly effective at promoting cytotoxic T cell responses, which are important for eliminating intracellular pathogens.

Question 5.3

Which of the following is NOT true regarding live viral vectored vaccines?

a) They require strong adjuvants
b) They are economical to produce
c) They can be delivered through needle-free methods
d) They induce a broad and long-lasting immune response
e) They induce both cellular and humoral immunity
f) Adenovirus vectors are a good choice to use for vaccines

Correct Answer: A) They require strong adjuvants

Explanation: Live viral vectored vaccines do NOT require strong adjuvants because the viral vector itself provides natural immune stimulation.

Question 6: Antigenic Variation

Pathogens can evade the immune system through antigenic drift, which is a ____ mutation that leaves existing antibodies ____, and antigenic shift, which is a ____ mutation that leaves existing antibodies ____.

a) Minor; Partially effective; Major; Ineffective
b) Minor; Ineffective; Major; Partially effective
c) Major; Partially effective; Minor; Ineffective
d) Major; Ineffective; Minor; Partially effective

Correct Answer: A) Minor; Partially effective; Major; Ineffective

Explanation: Antigenic drift involves small mutations that reduce but don't eliminate antibody effectiveness. Antigenic shift involves major changes (like reassortment in influenza) that make existing antibodies ineffective.

Chapter 31: Primary Immunodeficiency Diseases

Questions 1.1-1.5: Major Immunodeficiency Syndromes

Question 1.1

Which of the following diseases occurs with the absence of a thymus?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
c) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
d) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
e) Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

Correct Answer: A) DiGeorge's syndrome

Explanation: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by developmental abnormalities affecting the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to absent or underdeveloped thymus and parathyroid glands.

Question 1.2

Which of the following diseases affect neutrophils?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
c) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
d) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
e) Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

Correct Answer: C) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

Explanation: CGD affects neutrophil function, specifically their ability to produce reactive oxygen species needed to kill certain bacteria and fungi.

Question 1.3

Which of the following diseases affects mature T cells?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
c) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
d) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
e) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

Correct Answer: D) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)

Explanation: BLS affects the expression of MHC molecules on mature T cells, preventing proper antigen presentation and T cell function.

Question 1.4

A child presents with a maculopapular rash on the extremities and trunk. Petechiae is found on the trunk and mucous membranes. Lab tests show a Neisseria infection and the physician is concerned about meningococcemia. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) C3 deficiency
b) C5-C9 deficiency
c) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD)
d) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)
e) Selective IgA deficiency

Correct Answer: B) C5-C9 deficiency

Explanation: C5-C9 deficiencies affect the membrane attack complex, making patients particularly susceptible to Neisseria infections (meningococcal and gonococcal).

Question 1.5

A patient in their early 20s presents with recurrent bacterial infections. Lab work shows B cells in the periphery as well as low immunoglobulin levels. History shows immunoglobulin levels have decreased with age. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Myeloperoxidase deficiency
b) DiGeorge's syndrome
c) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
d) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
e) Common variable immunodeficiency

Correct Answer: E) Common variable immunodeficiency

Explanation: CVID typically presents in early adulthood with declining antibody levels over time, despite the presence of B cells. This distinguishes it from X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

Questions 1.6-1.10: Specific Immunodeficiency Disorders

Question 1.6

A child presents with recurrent infections with bacteria, fungi, and viruses. The resident asks the attending physician about IL-2R γ chain mutations, as the patient is a male. The attending physician makes a diagnosis and begins writing orders for bone marrow transplantation and possible gene therapy. Which of the following does the patient have?

a) Ataxia telangiectasia
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Hereditary angioedema
d) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: D) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)

Explanation: X-linked SCID is caused by IL-2Rγ chain mutations, affecting both T and B cell function. The severity requires immediate bone marrow transplantation.

Question 1.7

A young child presents with cervical adenitis and gingivostomatitis. History reveals recurrent pyogenic infections. Tests are done to determine leukocytosis and the presence of cell adhesion molecules. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) C3 deficiency
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD)
d) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)
e) Selective IgA deficiency

Correct Answer: C) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD)

Explanation: LAD patients have defective neutrophil adhesion and migration, leading to recurrent bacterial infections and characteristic gingivostomatitis without pus formation.

Question 1.8

A patient presents in the winter months with swollen lips. The patient says they forgot their lip balm. Uncontrolled activation of the classical complement pathway is responsible for the swelling. Records show the patient has a C1inh deficiency. Which of the following does this patient have?

a) C5-C9 deficiency
b) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
c) Hereditary angioedema
d) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: C) Hereditary angioedema

Explanation: Hereditary angioedema is caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, leading to uncontrolled complement activation and characteristic swelling.

Question 1.9

An infant presents with recurrent bacterial infections and partial albinism. Lab work reveals giant granules and neutropenia. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Chediak-Higashi disorder
c) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)
d) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
e) Myeloperoxidase deficiency

Correct Answer: B) Chediak-Higashi disorder

Explanation: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is characterized by giant granules in neutrophils, partial albinism, and recurrent infections due to defective lysosomal trafficking.

Question 1.10

A male patient presents with severe and recurrent bacterial infections. Lab work confirms the patient is only infected with certain bacteria due to a mutation in a gene for NADPH oxidase. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Chediak-Higashi disorder
c) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
d) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
e) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

Correct Answer: E) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

Explanation: CGD is caused by mutations in NADPH oxidase components, preventing neutrophils from producing reactive oxygen species needed to kill catalase-positive bacteria.

Questions 1.11-1.15: Additional Immunodeficiency Syndromes

Question 1.11

A 6-year-old presents with the appearance of being intoxicated while walking. Ophthalmoscopic findings reveal broken capillaries in the sclera of the eye. Lab work reveals IgA deficiency. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Ataxia telangiectasia
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Hereditary angioedema
d) Myeloperoxidase deficiency
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: A) Ataxia telangiectasia

Explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia presents with cerebellar ataxia (appearing "intoxicated"), telangiectasias (broken capillaries), and immunodeficiency with IgA deficiency.

Question 1.12

A male infant presents with a triad of symptoms including thrombocytopenia, eczema, and immunodeficiency. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Hereditary angioedema
d) Selective IgA deficiency
e) Hyper IgM deficiency

Correct Answer: B) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)

Explanation: WAS is characterized by the classic triad of thrombocytopenia, eczema, and immunodeficiency. It's X-linked, affecting males.

Question 1.13

A young patient presents with severe infections from encapsulated bacteria and collagen vascular disease. Lab work confirms a diagnosis via CH50 and AP50. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
d) Selective IgA deficiency
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: E) C3 deficiency

Explanation: C3 deficiency affects both classical and alternative complement pathways (abnormal CH50 and AP50), leading to susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria and autoimmune disease.

Question 1.14

An infant presents with recurrent infections with Candida and viruses. Cardiac abnormalities result in the patient requiring heart surgery. During surgery, no thymus is found. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) DiGeorge's syndrome
b) Chediak-Higashi disorder
c) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
d) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
e) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

Correct Answer: A) DiGeorge's syndrome

Explanation: DiGeorge syndrome involves absent thymus, cardiac abnormalities, and T cell deficiency leading to viral and fungal infections.

Question 1.15

A patient presents for a follow-up visit after a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The physician suspects a misdiagnosis after finding immune complexes accumulated in the blood, lymph, and tissues. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) C3 deficiency
b) C5-C9 deficiency
c) Early complement deficiency
d) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)
e) Selective IgA deficiency

Correct Answer: C) Early complement deficiency

Explanation: Early complement component deficiencies (C1, C2, C4) impair immune complex clearance, leading to SLE-like autoimmune disease.

Questions 1.16-1.23: Final Immunodeficiency Cases

Question 1.16

A patient presents with complaints of dark urine in the morning that clears up partially during the day. Lab work reveals hemolytic anemia, thrombosis in large vessels, and a deficiency in hematopoiesis. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Selective IgA deficiency
d) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
e) Chediak-Higashi disorder

Correct Answer: D) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)

Explanation: PNH causes complement-mediated hemolysis that's worse at night (dark morning urine), thrombosis, and bone marrow dysfunction.

Question 1.17

A patient presents with symptoms similar to chronic granulomatous disease (CGD). It is found that there is a problem with generation of NADPH. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) C5-C9 deficiency
b) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
c) Myeloperoxidase deficiency
d) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID)
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: B) Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

Explanation: G6PD deficiency affects NADPH production, which is needed for the respiratory burst in neutrophils, causing CGD-like symptoms.

Question 1.18

A patient is being seen for recurrent infections. However, the patient does not seem to think anything special of these infections and there has been no previous diagnosis other than the infections. Lab work reveals abnormalities with hypochlorous acid and H2O2 conversion. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Ataxia telangiectasia
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Hereditary angioedema
d) Myeloperoxidase deficiency
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: D) Myeloperoxidase deficiency

Explanation: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is often asymptomatic or causes mild infections. It affects the conversion of H2O2 to hypochlorous acid in neutrophils.

Question 1.19

A patient presents at age 6-months with pneumonia and difficulty fighting off infections of encapsulated bacteria and enteroviruses. A mutation in Bruton's tyrosine kinase (btk) is suspected. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Myeloperoxidase deficiency
b) DiGeorge's syndrome
c) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
d) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
e) Common variable immunodeficiency

Correct Answer: C) X-linked agammaglobulinemia

Explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia is caused by BTK mutations, leading to absent mature B cells and antibodies, with susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria.

Question 1.20

A male infant presents with decreased levels of IgA, IgG, and IgE. History reveals recurrent bacterial infections and severe diarrhea. A mutation on CD40L (CD154) on T cells is suspected. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
b) C5-C9 deficiency
c) Early complement deficiency
d) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)
e) Selective IgA deficiency

Correct Answer: D) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)

Explanation: Hyper IgM syndrome is caused by CD40L deficiency, preventing class switching from IgM to other antibody isotypes.

Question 1.21

A patient presents at 3-years-old for a follow-up visit. At age 6-months, the patient had a delayed onset of synthesis of an immunoglobulin. At this visit, the mother reports that the recurrent respiratory infections have stopped due to antibiotics and globulin replacement. Which of the following was the most likely for this patient?

a) Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
b) Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
c) Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
d) Selective IgA deficiency
e) C3 deficiency

Correct Answer: A) Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy

Explanation: This condition involves delayed maturation of antibody production but resolves with time and supportive care.

Question 1.22

Which of the following is often asymptomatic to presenting with an increased incidence of respiratory tract infections and is the most common immunodeficiency disease?

a) C3 deficiency
b) C5-C9 deficiency
c) Early complement deficiency
d) Hyper IgM syndrome (HIM)
e) Selective IgA deficiency

Correct Answer: E) Selective IgA deficiency

Explanation: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency (1 in 600 people). Many patients are asymptomatic, while others have increased respiratory and GI tract infections due to lack of secretory IgA at mucosal surfaces.

Question 1.23

A patient presents with symptoms similar to DiGeorge's syndrome. It is determined that the patient's TH cells are unable to develop. Which of the following is the most likely?

a) Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD)
b) Chediak-Higashi disorder
c) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)
d) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS)
e) Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)

Correct Answer: C) Bare lymphocyte syndrome (BLS)

Explanation: Bare lymphocyte syndrome involves defective MHC class II expression, preventing proper T helper cell development and function. This creates symptoms similar to DiGeorge syndrome but through a different mechanism.

Summary of Key Concepts

Immunoglobulin Functions

  • IgE: Parasitic infections, allergic reactions, mast cell activation
  • IgG: ADCC, opsonization, complement activation
  • IgA: Mucosal immunity, secretory antibody

Mast Cell Mediators

  • Pre-stored: Histamine, tryptase, chemotrypsin
  • Newly synthesized: Prostaglandins (fast), leukotrienes (slow)
  • Cytokines: IL-4 (TH2 activation), TNF-α (inflammation)

Cell-Mediated Immunity

  • NK cells: Kill virus-infected and tumor cells, detect "missing self"
  • CTLs: Perforin/granzyme pathway, Fas/FasL pathway

Vaccine Types

  • Live: Most effective, replicate, provide long-lasting immunity
  • Killed: Safer, cannot replicate, may need boosters
  • Subunit: Specific components, require adjuvants

Primary Immunodeficiencies

  • B cell defects: X-linked agammaglobulinemia, CVID, selective IgA deficiency
  • T cell defects: DiGeorge syndrome, SCID, bare lymphocyte syndrome
  • Phagocyte defects: CGD, LAD, Chediak-Higashi
  • Complement defects: Early components (autoimmunity), late components (Neisseria infections)

Clinical Pearls

  1. Recurrent bacterial infections → Think B cell or complement deficiency
  2. Viral/fungal infections → Think T cell deficiency
  3. Catalase-positive bacterial infections → Think CGD
  4. Neisseria infections → Think complement C5-C9 deficiency
  5. Autoimmune disease + infections → Think early complement deficiency

This comprehensive guide covers the major concepts in cellular immunology, vaccines, and primary immunodeficiencies with clinical correlations to help understand the underlying mechanisms and clinical presentations.

Title: Neurochemistry Test – Questions and Answers
Content:
MBMB2234 Neurochemistry Test - Questions and Answers

Question 1

What neurotransmitter is associated with runner's high?

A. GABA
B. Dopamine
C. Endorphins
D. Norepinephrine

Answer: C. Endorphins

Explanation: Endorphins are the body's natural opioids that create feelings of euphoria and pain relief. During intense exercise like running, the body releases endorphins, which bind to opioid receptors and produce the characteristic "runner's high" - a feeling of well-being and reduced pain perception.

Question 2

What neurotransmitter is associated with anxiety disorders?

A. GABA
B. Dopamine
C. Glutamate
D. Acetylcholine
E. Serotonin

Answer: A. GABA

Explanation: GABA (Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Low GABA activity is associated with increased anxiety, as GABA normally helps calm neural activity. Many anti-anxiety medications work by enhancing GABA function.

Question 3

Where do neurons store the genetic information they use to code and build all the proteins required for their functions?

A. In the axon
B. In the endoplasmic reticulum
C. In the nucleus
D. In the synapse
E. In the messenger ribonucleic acids (mRNAs)

Answer: C. In the nucleus

Explanation: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA, which stores all genetic information. This DNA is transcribed into mRNA, which then travels to ribosomes for protein synthesis. The nucleus is the central control center for all cellular functions.

Question 4

Which of the following are major inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs)?

A. Synaptobrevin and glutamate
B. GABA and glycine
C. Glycine and acetylcholine
D. Glycine and norepinephrine
E. Glycine and epinephrine

Answer: B. GABA and glycine

Explanation: GABA is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, while glycine is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord. Both cause hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane, making it less likely to fire an action potential.

Question 5

The effect of tetrodotoxin (puffer fish poison) on axons demonstrates:

A. The role of potassium channels in hyperpolarization
B. The role of sodium channels in depolarization
C. The role of potassium channels in depolarization
D. The role of chloride channels in hyperpolarization
E. The role of sodium channels in hyperpolarization

Answer: B. The role of sodium channels in depolarization

Explanation: Tetrodotoxin specifically blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials from occurring. This demonstrates that sodium influx through these channels is essential for depolarization and action potential generation.

Question 6

What neurotransmitter is associated with mood disorders?

A. Acetylcholine
B. GABA
C. Serotonin
D. Dopamine
E. Norepinephrine

Answer: C. Serotonin

Explanation: Serotonin is strongly associated with mood regulation. Low serotonin levels are linked to depression, anxiety, and other mood disorders. SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) are commonly prescribed antidepressants that increase serotonin availability.

Question 7

Which of the following is not true?

A. The cell membrane is impermeable to large charged protein molecules
B. The semi-permeable membrane keeps sodium ions outside and potassium inside neurons
C. Neuron membranes have sodium/potassium ion pumps that take out potassium ions
D. The summed charges of the unequally distributed ions leave the inside of the membrane at approximately -65 mV relative to the outside of the cell. This is the resting potential

Answer: C. Neuron membranes have sodium/potassium ion pumps that take out potassium ions

Explanation: This statement is incorrect. The sodium-potassium pump actually pumps potassium ions INTO the cell and sodium ions OUT of the cell (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in). This maintains the concentration gradients necessary for the resting potential.

Question 8

What neurotransmitter is associated with insomnia?

A. Dopamine
B. Norepinephrine
C. GABA
D. Glutamate
E. Serotonin

Answer: E. Serotonin

Explanation: Serotonin plays a crucial role in sleep regulation. It's a precursor to melatonin and helps regulate sleep-wake cycles. Imbalances in serotonin can lead to sleep disorders including insomnia.

Question 9

What neurotransmitter is associated with seizures?

A. Serotonin
B. Acetylcholine
C. Glutamate
D. GABA
E. Glutamate

Answer: C. Glutamate

Explanation: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Excessive glutamate activity or insufficient GABA inhibition can lead to seizures, as the brain becomes hyperexcitable with uncontrolled neuronal firing.

Question 10

What is one of the functions of Dopamine?

A. Eating
B. Memory
C. Pleasure
D. Sleeping
E. Arousal

Answer: C. Pleasure

Explanation: Dopamine is central to the brain's reward system and pleasure pathways. It's released in response to rewarding experiences and motivates behavior toward pleasurable activities. This is why dopamine is often called the "feel-good" neurotransmitter.

Question 11

What is one of the functions of Endorphins?

A. Major excitatory neurotransmitter
B. Major inhibitory neurotransmitter
C. Sleeping
D. Emotion centers of the brain
E. Pleasure

Answer: E. Pleasure

Explanation: Endorphins are the body's natural opioids that produce feelings of pleasure and well-being. They're released during exercise, stress, pain, and other activities, binding to opioid receptors to create euphoric feelings and reduce pain perception.

Question 12

What neurotransmitter is associated with Parkinson's disease?

A. Norepinephrine
B. Serotonin
C. Dopamine
D. Endorphins
E. GABA

Answer: C. Dopamine

Explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by the death of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra. This leads to decreased dopamine levels, causing the characteristic motor symptoms like tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia (slowness of movement).

Question 13

What neurotransmitter is associated with Alzheimer's disease?

A. Acetylcholine
B. Serotonin
C. GABA
D. Dopamine
E. Glutamate

Answer: A. Acetylcholine

Explanation: Alzheimer's disease involves significant loss of acetylcholine-producing neurons, particularly affecting memory and cognitive function. Cholinesterase inhibitors, which increase acetylcholine availability, are used as treatments for Alzheimer's.

Question 14

Which of the following best discriminates between small-molecule neurotransmitters and peptide neurotransmitters?

A. Peptide neurotransmitter precursors and their enzymes are axonally transported in vesicles
B. Small-molecule neurotransmitters are stored in large dense-core vesicles
C. Small-molecule neurotransmitters are synthesized in the soma
D. Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized at the synaptic terminals
E. Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized in the nucleus of the neuron

Answer: A. Peptide neurotransmitter precursors and their enzymes are axonally transported in vesicles

Explanation: Peptide neurotransmitters are synthesized in the cell body and transported down the axon in vesicles, while small-molecule neurotransmitters are typically synthesized locally at nerve terminals. This is a key distinguishing feature between these two types of neurotransmitters.

Question 15

Which neurotransmitter is released by the postganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous system?

A. GABA
B. Dopamine
C. Serotonin
D. Norepinephrine

Answer: D. Norepinephrine

Explanation: Most postganglionic sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine (noradrenaline) as their neurotransmitter. This activates adrenergic receptors on target organs, producing the "fight or flight" response characteristic of sympathetic activation.

Question 23

Enkephalins are peptide neurotransmitters that function in the perception of pain. This is because:

A. They interact with specific opioid receptor proteins to produce their effects
B. They are small enough to directly enter post-synaptic membranes
C. They have special membrane channels that let them through the post-synaptic cells
D. They interact with morphine
E. They are found in very high concentrations at nociceptive (pain related) synapses

Answer: A. They interact with specific opioid receptor proteins to produce their effects

Explanation: Enkephalins are endogenous opioid peptides that bind to opioid receptors (mu, delta, and kappa) to reduce pain perception. They work similarly to morphine and other opioid drugs by activating these same receptor systems.

Question 24

What determines the effect of neurotransmitter release on the post-synaptic neurons?

A. The size of the action potential
B. The postsynaptic receptors
C. The neurotransmitter contained in the synaptic vesicles
D. The concentration of calcium ions reached in presynaptic terminals
E. The size of the synaptic vesicles

Answer: B. The postsynaptic receptors

Explanation: The type of postsynaptic receptors determines whether the effect will be excitatory or inhibitory, and the magnitude of the response. The same neurotransmitter can have different effects depending on which receptors are present on the postsynaptic cell.

Question 25

A neuron cannot produce an action potential:

A. During the relative refractory period
B. When there is an inhibitory postsynaptic potential
C. When the voltage-dependent potassium channels are closed
D. During the absolute refractory period
E. Both b and d

Answer: D. During the absolute refractory period

Explanation: During the absolute refractory period, sodium channels are inactivated and cannot be reopened regardless of stimulus strength. This ensures unidirectional propagation of action potentials and limits firing frequency.

Question 26

What would happen to the resting membrane potential of a neuron if sodium (Na+) channels were normally open in the membrane, but everything else was the same?

A. Nothing much would happen, and it would remain at approximately -65 mV
B. It would definitely be less negative than the normal resting potential
C. It would definitely be more negative than the normal resting potential
D. It would lose its polarization and stand at exactly 0 mV
E. None of the above

Answer: B. It would definitely be less negative than the normal resting potential

Explanation: If sodium channels were normally open, sodium would continuously flow into the cell down its concentration gradient, making the inside less negative (more positive) than the normal resting potential of -65 mV.

Question 29

Conduction of action potentials is faster in myelinated axons. This happens mainly because these axons:

A. Avoid sending their action potentials through the nodes of Ranvier
B. Expend (use) less energy
C. Are usually short
D. Make use of faster internodal passive electrical conduction
E. Produce bigger action potentials

Answer: D. Make use of faster internodal passive electrical conduction

Explanation: Myelination allows for saltatory conduction, where the action potential "jumps" from node to node via fast passive electrical conduction through the myelinated segments, rather than having to actively propagate along the entire axon length.

Question 30

Synaptic autoreceptors normally:

A. Increase the number of excitatory postsynaptic potentials at a synapse
B. Reduce neurotransmitter release at a synapse
C. Increase the size of action potentials in the post-synaptic neuron
D. Decrease the size of action potentials in the post-synaptic neuron
E. Increase neurotransmitter release at a synapse

Answer: B. Reduce neurotransmitter release at a synapse

Explanation: Autoreceptors provide negative feedback control. When activated by the neurotransmitter they respond to, they reduce further neurotransmitter release, serving as a self-regulating mechanism to prevent excessive synaptic activity.

Question 31

The process whereby the content of synaptic vesicles is released into the synaptic cleft/gap is called:

A. Exocytosis
B. Endocytosis
C. Phagocytosis
D. Pinocytosis
E. None of the above

Answer: A. Exocytosis

Explanation: Exocytosis is the process by which synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitter contents into the synaptic cleft. This is triggered by calcium influx following action potential arrival.

Question 32

Which channel membrane protein is specifically important in the process of neurotransmitter release?

A. Neurotransmitter receptor sodium channels
