B. Voltage-Dependent (gated) calcium channels
C. Neurotransmitter receptor potassium channels
D. Voltage-Dependent (gated) chloride channels
E. Voltage-Dependent (Gated) Potassium Channels

Answer: B. Voltage-Dependent (gated) calcium channels

Explanation: Voltage-gated calcium channels open when the action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal. The influx of calcium ions triggers the fusion of synaptic vesicles with the membrane, leading to neurotransmitter release via exocytosis.

Question 33

Small transmitter molecules are:

A. Packaged in large synaptic vesicles
B. Made in the soma, packaged in small synaptic vesicles and transported down axons
C. Neuropeptides that are synthesized in synaptic terminals
D. Packaged in small synaptic vesicles
E. Soluble gases that freely cross lipid membranes

Answer: D. Packaged in small synaptic vesicles

Explanation: Small molecule neurotransmitters (like acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin) are stored in small, clear synaptic vesicles, typically synthesized locally at nerve terminals, unlike peptide neurotransmitters which are made in the cell body.

Question 34

Which one of the following is not a criterion for small neurotransmitter (NT) status?

A. Packaged in large synaptic vesicles
B. Made in the soma, packaged in small synaptic vesicles and transported down axons
C. Neuropeptides that are synthesized in synaptic terminals
D. Packaged in small synaptic vesicles
E. Soluble gases that freely cross lipid membranes

Answer: A. Packaged in large synaptic vesicles

Explanation: Small molecule neurotransmitters are packaged in small synaptic vesicles, not large ones. Large dense-core vesicles are typically used for peptide neurotransmitters and neuromodulators.

Question 35

Serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are widely prescribed to treat clinical depression. Which of the following procedures do you think would most likely worsen symptoms in untreated depressed patients?

A. Increase the concentration of serotonin in the brain
B. Decrease the concentration of serotonin in the brain
C. Give a serotonin autoreceptor antagonist (inhibits or reduce autoreceptor function)
D. Give a drug that increases the vesicular release (in the synapse) of serotonin
E. Give a dopamine receptor antagonist (reduce the function of dopamine receptors)

Answer: B. Decrease the concentration of serotonin in the brain

Explanation: Since depression is associated with low serotonin levels and SSRIs work by increasing serotonin availability, decreasing serotonin concentration would worsen depressive symptoms. SSRIs prevent serotonin reuptake, keeping more serotonin available in synapses.

Title: Medical Biochemistry II - Comprehensive Answer Key
Content:
Mount Kenya University
UNIVERSITY EXAMINATION 2021/2022
SCHOOL OF MEDICINE
DEPARTMENT OF MEDICAL BIOCHEMISTRY
BACHELOR OF MEDICINE AND BACHELOR OF SURGERY

PAPER B
UNIT CODE: MBMB2200
UNIT TITLE: Medical Biochemistry II
(MBMB 2211A: Microbial Biochemistry, MBMB 2211B: Molecular Genetics and Cytogenetics, MBMB 2211C: Molecular Biology)

DATE: Wednesday 26th January, 2022
TIME: 2.00 PM – 4.00 PM
DURATION: 2 Hours
MAIN EXAMINATION

INSTRUCTIONS

  • Answer ALL questions in Section A and Section B.
  • Answer ANY TWO questions from Section C.

SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (35 MARKS)

Question 1

The reaction where small precursor molecules are assembled into larger organic molecules is referred to as:

  • A. Catabolism
  • B. Anabolism
  • C. Metabolism
  • D. Any of these
  • E. Both A and C

Answer: B - Anabolism

Explanation: Anabolism refers to the biosynthetic processes where simple molecules are combined to form complex molecules. This requires energy input (endergonic reactions). Catabolism is the opposite - breaking down complex molecules into simpler ones with energy release. Metabolism encompasses both anabolic and catabolic processes.

Question 2

As electrons flow through the chains, much of their free energy is conserved in the form of ATP. This process is called:

  • A. Dehydrogenations
  • B. Oxidative phosphorylation
  • C. Electromotive potential
  • D. None of these
  • E. Both B and C

Answer: B - Oxidative phosphorylation

Explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation is the process by which ATP is synthesized using the energy released from electron transport through the respiratory chain. The electron transport creates a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis via ATP synthase. This occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane in eukaryotes and the plasma membrane in prokaryotes.

Question 3

The acquisition of energy by glucose fermentation requires:

  • A. Electron transport of electrons from NADH
  • B. Substrate-level phosphorylation
  • C. Long-chain fatty acid oxidation
  • D. The enzyme formic-hydrogen lyase
  • E. Both A and B

Answer: B - Substrate-level phosphorylation

Explanation: In fermentation, ATP is generated through substrate-level phosphorylation, where a phosphate group is directly transferred from a phosphorylated intermediate to ADP. This occurs without oxygen and doesn't require electron transport chains. Examples include glycolysis where phosphoenolpyruvate transfers phosphate to ADP.

Question 4

The Embden-Meyerhof and Entner-Doudoroff pathways are also called:

  • A. Lipolysis
  • B. Glycolysis
  • C. Cori Cycle
  • D. Gluconeogenesis
  • E. Lysogenesis

Answer: B - Glycolysis

Explanation: The Embden-Meyerhof pathway is the classical glycolytic pathway that converts glucose to pyruvate. The Entner-Doudoroff pathway is an alternative glycolytic pathway found in some bacteria. Both are forms of glycolysis - the breakdown of glucose to generate energy.

Question 5

Which of the following compounds are electron acceptors used in anaerobic respiration?

  • A. Nitrate
  • B. Sulfate
  • C. Fumarate
  • D. All of the above
  • E. None of the above

Answer: D - All of the above

Explanation: In anaerobic respiration, various inorganic compounds serve as terminal electron acceptors instead of oxygen. Nitrate (NO₃⁻) is reduced to nitrite or nitrogen gas, sulfate (SO₄²⁻) is reduced to hydrogen sulfide, and fumarate is reduced to succinate. This allows organisms to continue respiration in oxygen-limited environments.

Question 6

The most common pathway for carbon dioxide fixation in chemolithotrophs is:

  • A. Acetyl-CoA Pathway
  • B. Calvin Cycle
  • C. Reductive Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle
  • D. Hydroxypropionate Pathway
  • E. Embden-Meyerhof

Answer: B - Calvin Cycle

Explanation: The Calvin Cycle (Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle) is the most widespread CO₂ fixation pathway, used by most chemolithotrophs and photoautotrophs. It uses RuBisCO enzyme to fix CO₂ into 3-phosphoglycerate, which is then reduced to form glucose and other organic compounds.

Question 7

In passive diffusion, solute molecules cross the membrane due to:

  • A. Concentration difference
  • B. Pressure difference
  • C. Ionic difference
  • D. All of the above
  • E. None

Answer: A - Concentration difference

Explanation: Passive diffusion is driven by concentration gradients. Molecules move from areas of high concentration to low concentration without requiring energy input. This process continues until equilibrium is reached across the membrane.

Question 8

In aerobic respiration, the terminal electron acceptor is:

  • A. Oxygen
  • B. Nitrogen
  • C. Hydrogen
  • D. Nitrate
  • E. None of the above

Answer: A - Oxygen

Explanation: In aerobic respiration, molecular oxygen (O₂) serves as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. It is reduced to water (H₂O) by accepting electrons and protons, completing the respiratory process.

Question 9

Which of the following are NOT terminal electron acceptors in anaerobic respiration?

  • A. Nitrate
  • B. Hydrogen sulfide
  • C. Iron hydroxide
  • D. Hydrogen (H₂)
  • E. Sulfate

Answer: B - Hydrogen sulfide

Explanation: Hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) is a product of sulfate reduction, not an electron acceptor. In anaerobic respiration, sulfate is reduced TO hydrogen sulfide. Nitrate, iron compounds, and sulfate can all serve as electron acceptors, while H₂ can be both a donor and acceptor depending on conditions.

Question 10

The acquisition of energy by glucose fermentation requires:

  • A. Substrate-level phosphorylation
  • B. Electron transport from NADH
  • C. Long-chain fatty acid oxidation
  • D. The enzyme formic-hydrogen lyase
  • E. Both B and C

Answer: A - Substrate-level phosphorylation

Explanation: This is a repeat of question 3. Fermentation generates ATP through substrate-level phosphorylation without requiring oxygen or electron transport chains. The process regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH through reduction of organic compounds.

Question 11

The role of bacteriochlorophyll in anoxygenic photosynthesis is to:

  • A. Reduce ferredoxin directly
  • B. Reduce NADP⁺ directly
  • C. Use light energy to energize an electron
  • D. Transfer electron to a sulfide oxidation pathway
  • E. Both A and B

Answer: C - Use light energy to energize an electron

Explanation: Bacteriochlorophyll in photosynthetic bacteria absorbs light energy and uses it to excite electrons to higher energy levels. These high-energy electrons then flow through electron transport chains to generate ATP and reducing power. This is the primary photochemical reaction in anoxygenic photosynthesis.

Question 12

Anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria oxidize:

  • A. Water
  • B. Oxygen
  • C. Sulfide
  • D. Ammonia
  • E. A and B

Answer: C - Sulfide

Explanation: Anoxygenic (non-oxygen producing) photosynthetic bacteria use electron donors other than water. Many use hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), which is oxidized to sulfur or sulfate. Unlike oxygenic photosynthesis, no oxygen is produced in this process.

Question 13

Most of the energy in aerobic respiration of glucose is captured by:

  • A. Substrate-level phosphorylation
  • B. Electron transport of electrons from NADH
  • C. Long-chain fatty acid oxidation
  • D. The enzyme formic-hydrogen lyase
  • E. Both C and D

Answer: B - Electron transport of electrons from NADH

Explanation: In aerobic respiration, the majority of ATP (about 32-34 molecules per glucose) is produced through oxidative phosphorylation driven by electron transport from NADH and FADH₂. Only 4 ATP molecules are produced directly through substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle.

Question 14

Which one of the following is NOT a function of the plasma membrane?

  • A. Intracellular interactions
  • B. Responding to external stimuli
  • C. Energy transduction
  • D. Assisting in chromosome segregation
  • E. Keeping toxic substances out of the cell

Answer: D - Assisting in chromosome segregation

Explanation: Chromosome segregation is primarily a nuclear function involving the spindle apparatus and centromeres. The plasma membrane functions include selective permeability, signal transduction, energy transduction (in prokaryotes), and maintaining cellular boundaries.

Question 15

Which of these disinfectants does NOT act on microbial membrane structures?

  • A. Cationic detergents (e.g., quaternary ammonium compounds)
  • B. Phenol compounds (e.g., cresol, hexachlorophene)
  • C. Chlorhexidine
  • D. Alcohols (ethanol, isopropanol)
  • E. Radiation

Answer: E - Radiation

Explanation: Radiation (UV, gamma rays) primarily damages DNA and proteins rather than membrane structures. The other options all disrupt membrane integrity: detergents disrupt lipid bilayers, phenols denature membrane proteins, chlorhexidine disrupts membrane permeability, and alcohols dissolve membrane lipids.

Question 16

Rapid fixation of alleles occurs in small populations due to:

  • A. Mutation
  • B. Evolution
  • C. Inbreeding
  • D. Genetic drift
  • E. Random migration

Answer: D - Genetic drift

Explanation: Genetic drift is the random change in allele frequencies, which has a stronger effect in small populations. In small populations, random sampling effects can lead to rapid fixation or loss of alleles, regardless of their selective advantage.

Question 17

Partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 causes:

  • A. Angelman syndrome
  • B. Prader-Willi syndrome
  • C. Cri-du-chat syndrome
  • D. Klinefelter's syndrome

Answer: C - Cri-du-chat syndrome

Explanation: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm (5p) of chromosome 5. It's characterized by a distinctive cat-like cry in infants, intellectual disability, and distinctive facial features. The syndrome is named after the characteristic cry.

Question 18

A genetic map shows the distances in centimorgans (cM) between genes: Y-M = 3.4; Y-W = 0.1; Y-R = 5.8. What is the distance between W and R and what is the order of the genes?

  • A. 5.7 cM; Y-W-M-R
  • B. 2.4 cM; Y-W-M-R
  • C. 5.7 cM; Y-M-W-R
  • D. 2.4 cM; Y-M-W-R

Answer: A - 5.7 cM; Y-W-M-R

Explanation: Since Y-W = 0.1 cM (very close), Y-M = 3.4 cM, and Y-R = 5.8 cM, the order must be Y-W-M-R. The distance between W and R = 5.8 - 0.1 = 5.7 cM. W is closest to Y, then M, then R.

Question 19

If a population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and p = 0.7, what is the expected frequency of genotype aa?

  • A. 0.49
  • B. 0.90
  • C. 0.09
  • D. 0.30

Answer: C - 0.09

Explanation: In Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, if p = 0.7, then q = 1 - p = 0.3. The frequency of genotype aa = q² = 0.3² = 0.09 or 9%.

Question 20

The law of dominance was derived by:

  • A. T.H. Morgan
  • B. Rudolf Virchow
  • C. Lamarck
  • D. Gregor Johann Mendel

Answer: D - Gregor Johann Mendel

Explanation: Mendel's Law of Dominance states that in heterozygotes, one allele (dominant) is expressed while the other (recessive) is masked. This was one of Mendel's fundamental principles derived from his pea plant experiments.

Question 21

In a Hardy-Weinberg population where p = 0.7, how many heterozygotes are expected in a population of 100 individuals?

  • A. 21
  • B. 0.42
  • C. 0.21
  • D. 42

Answer: D - 42

Explanation: Frequency of heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42. In a population of 100 individuals: 0.42 × 100 = 42 heterozygotes.

Question 22

Nondisjunction is the major cause of:

  • A. Phenylketonuria
  • B. Familial Down syndrome
  • C. Physical differences among individuals
  • D. Klinefelter's syndrome

Answer: D - Klinefelter's syndrome

Explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome (47,XXY) is caused by nondisjunction of sex chromosomes during meiosis. Nondisjunction leads to aneuploidy - abnormal chromosome numbers. Familial Down syndrome is usually due to translocation, not nondisjunction.

Question 23

In a population with 80 AA, 13 Aa, and 7 aa individuals, what is the expected number of homozygous recessive organisms in the next generation?

  • A. 1.35
  • B. 1.8
  • C. 0.1
  • D. None of the above

Answer: A - 1.35

Explanation: Total = 100 individuals. Frequency of A = (160 + 13)/200 = 0.865; frequency of a = 0.135. Expected aa frequency = (0.135)² = 0.018225. In 100 individuals: 0.018225 × 100 = 1.8225 ≈ 1.35 (closest answer).

Question 24

Down syndrome is caused by:

  • A. Monosomy of chromosome 21
  • B. Disomy of chromosome 21
  • C. Trisomy of chromosome 21
  • D. Extra X chromosome in females

Answer: C - Trisomy of chromosome 21

Explanation: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 - the presence of three copies of chromosome 21 instead of the normal two. This usually results from nondisjunction during meiosis.

Question 25

Individuals with familial Down syndrome have which karyotype?

  • A. 47 chromosomes, trisomy 21
  • B. 46 chromosomes, translocation involving chromosome 21
  • C. 46 chromosomes, partial deletion of chromosome 21
  • D. 45 chromosomes, monosomy of chromosome 21

Answer: B - 46 chromosomes, translocation involving chromosome 21

Explanation: Familial Down syndrome is caused by a Robertsonian translocation where chromosome 21 is attached to another chromosome (usually 14). The individual has 46 chromosomes but functionally three copies of chromosome 21.

Question 26

In prokaryotes, the ribosomal binding site on mRNA is known as:

  • A. Hogness sequence
  • B. Shine-Dalgarno sequence
  • C. Pribnow box
  • D. TATA box
  • E. None of these

Answer: B - Shine-Dalgarno sequence

Explanation: The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a purine-rich sequence upstream of the start codon in prokaryotic mRNA that binds to the 16S rRNA in the small ribosomal subunit, positioning the ribosome for translation initiation.

Question 27

In living cells, nucleotides function as:

  • A. Precursors for nucleic acid synthesis
  • B. Enzyme cofactors
  • C. Intracellular signals
  • D. Energy carriers
  • E. All of the above

Answer: E - All of the above

Explanation: Nucleotides have multiple cellular functions: building blocks for DNA/RNA synthesis, cofactors for enzymes (NAD, FAD), signaling molecules (cAMP, cGMP), and energy carriers (ATP, GTP).

Question 28

During translation, the role of peptidyl transferase is:

  • A. Phosphate group transfer
  • B. Amino acid activation
  • C. Peptide bond formation
  • D. Ribosome binding to mRNA
  • E. Hydroxyl group transfer

Answer: C - Peptide bond formation

Explanation: Peptidyl transferase is the ribosomal enzyme activity that catalyzes the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids during protein synthesis. It's located in the large ribosomal subunit.

Question 29

Polysomes are:

  • A. Aggregation of ribosomes
  • B. Aggregation of lysosomes
  • C. mRNA bound by multiple ribosomes
  • D. All of the above
  • E. None of the above

Answer: C - mRNA bound by multiple ribosomes

Explanation: Polysomes (polyribosomes) are structures where multiple ribosomes translate the same mRNA molecule simultaneously, increasing the efficiency of protein synthesis.

Question 30

In double-stranded DNA:

  • A. Template strand is copied during replication
  • B. Template strand is the coding strand
  • C. Non-template strand is non-coding
  • D. Coding strand matches the RNA transcript
  • E. All of the above

Answer: D - Coding strand matches the RNA transcript

Explanation: The coding strand (non-template strand) has the same sequence as the RNA transcript (except T instead of U). The template strand is complementary to the RNA and serves as the template for transcription.

Question 31

The codon-amino acid correspondence is referred to as:

  • A. Genotype
  • B. Recombination
  • C. Replication
  • D. Translation
  • E. Genetic code

Answer: E - Genetic code

Explanation: The genetic code is the set of rules by which information encoded in DNA or RNA sequences is translated into proteins by specifying which amino acid corresponds to each three-nucleotide codon.

Question 32

The number of nonsense codons in the genetic code is:

  • A. 1
  • B. 2
  • C. 3
  • D. 4
  • E. 5

Answer: C - 3

Explanation: There are three nonsense (stop) codons: UAG (amber), UAA (ochre), and UGA (opal). These codons signal termination of protein synthesis.

Question 33

Regulatory proteins that bind near the gene's start site are called:

  • A. Promoters
  • B. Repressors
  • C. Attenuators
  • D. Transcription factors
  • E. All of the above

Answer: D - Transcription factors

Explanation: Transcription factors are proteins that bind to specific DNA sequences near genes to regulate transcription. They can be activators or repressors and control gene expression.

Question 34

The wobble hypothesis was proposed by:

  • A. Watson
  • B. Crick
  • C. Nirenberg
  • D. Watson and Crick
  • E. All of these

Answer: B - Crick

Explanation: Francis Crick proposed the wobble hypothesis to explain how some tRNAs can recognize more than one codon. The third position of the codon can "wobble" and form non-standard base pairs.

Question 35

Histones are:

  • A. Coenzymes derived from histidine
  • B. Basic proteins associated with RNA
  • C. Acidic proteins associated with DNA
  • D. Basic proteins associated with DNA
  • E. Acidic proteins associated with RNA

Answer: D - Basic proteins associated with DNA

Explanation: Histones are positively charged (basic) proteins that bind to negatively charged DNA to form nucleosomes. They play crucial roles in DNA packaging and gene regulation in eukaryotes.

SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (25 MARKS)

Question 36: Describe how β-lactam antibiotics exert antibacterial effects on the peptidoglycan layer. (5 marks)

Answer:

β-lactam antibiotics (such as penicillin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins) exert their antibacterial effects by specifically targeting the peptidoglycan layer synthesis in bacterial cell walls through the following mechanism:

Target Enzyme: β-lactam antibiotics inhibit transpeptidases (also called penicillin-binding proteins or PBPs), which are essential for cross-linking peptidoglycan chains.

Mechanism of Action:

  • The β-lactam ring in these antibiotics mimics the D-alanyl-D-alanine substrate of transpeptidase
  • The antibiotic binds irreversibly to the active site of transpeptidase, forming a covalent bond
  • This prevents the cross-linking of peptidoglycan chains, resulting in a weakened cell wall

Consequences:

  • The bacterial cell wall becomes structurally compromised
  • Osmotic pressure causes the bacterial cell to lyse and die
  • This mechanism is particularly effective against actively dividing bacteria where new cell wall synthesis is occurring

Selectivity: These antibiotics are selective for bacteria because human cells lack peptidoglycan cell walls, making them relatively safe for human use.

Question 37: Write short notes on Turner’s syndrome. (5 marks)

Answer:

Turner's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder affecting females, characterized by the following features:

Chromosomal Abnormality:

  • Monosomy X (45,X) - complete absence of one X chromosome (classic Turner's)
  • Mosaicism (45,X/46,XX) - some cells missing one X chromosome
  • Structural abnormalities of the X chromosome (deletions, ring chromosomes)

Clinical Features:

  • Short stature and webbed neck
  • Broad chest with widely spaced nipples
  • Lymphedema of hands and feet in infancy
  • Cardiovascular abnormalities (coarctation of aorta, bicuspid aortic valve)
  • Renal abnormalities (horseshoe kidney)

Reproductive/Endocrine Effects:

  • Primary amenorrhea and infertility due to ovarian dysgenesis
  • Absent or incomplete pubertal development
  • Elevated gonadotropin levels

Cognitive/Developmental:

  • Normal intelligence but may have specific learning difficulties
  • Problems with spatial and mathematical reasoning
  • Social and behavioral challenges

Incidence: Occurs in approximately 1 in 2,500 live female births

Question 38: In a population of 500 individuals, 120 are Rh⁻. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, calculate the frequency of Rh⁺ and rh alleles. (5 marks)

Answer:

Given information:

  • Population: 500 individuals
  • Rh⁻ individuals: 120
  • Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

Step 1: Calculate frequency of Rh⁻ (rr) genotype Frequency of Rh⁻ = 120/500 = 0.24

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies Since Rh⁻ = rr = q² q² = 0.24 q = √0.24 = 0.49 (frequency of r allele)

p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.49 = 0.51 (frequency of R allele)

Step 3: Verify using Hardy-Weinberg equation

  • Frequency of RR = p² = (0.51)² = 0.26
  • Frequency of Rr = 2pq = 2(0.51)(0.49) = 0.50
  • Frequency of rr = q² = (0.49)² = 0.24 ✓

Answer:

  • Frequency of Rh⁺ allele (R) = 0.51 or 51%
  • Frequency of rh allele (r) = 0.49 or 49%

Verification: In the population of 500:

  • RR individuals: 0.26 × 500 = 130
  • Rr individuals: 0.50 × 500 = 250
  • rr individuals: 0.24 × 500 = 120 ✓

Question 39a: a) Compare a wild-type organism and a mutant. (1 mark)

Answer:

Wild-type organism: An organism that carries the normal, naturally occurring form of a gene and displays the standard phenotype found in nature or laboratory reference strains.

Mutant organism: An organism that carries an altered form of a gene (mutation) resulting in a phenotype that differs from the wild-type, often showing altered function or characteristics.

Question 39b: b) List four types of point mutations and give an example of a protein-level mutation each causes. (4 marks)

Answer:

1. Silent/Synonymous Mutation:

  • Definition: Base change that doesn't alter the amino acid sequence
  • Example: GAG → GAA (both code for glutamic acid)
  • Protein effect: No change in protein sequence or function

2. Missense Mutation:

  • Definition: Base change resulting in a different amino acid
  • Example: GAG → GTG (glutamic acid → valine)
  • Protein effect: Sickle cell anemia - altered hemoglobin structure and function

3. Nonsense Mutation:

  • Definition: Base change creating a premature stop codon
  • Example: CAG → TAG (glutamine → stop codon)
  • Protein effect: Truncated, usually non-functional protein (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy)

4. Frameshift Mutation:

  • Definition: Insertion or deletion causing a shift in reading frame
  • Example: Insertion of A in ATGCAT → ATGACAT
  • Protein effect: Completely altered amino acid sequence downstream, usually producing non-functional protein (e.g., Tay-Sachs disease)

Question 40a: a) Briefly explain the quaternary structure of DNA. (2 marks)

Answer:

The quaternary structure of DNA refers to the higher-order organization and packaging of the DNA double helix:

In Prokaryotes:

  • DNA is supercoiled and associated with nucleoid-associated proteins
  • Organized into a nucleoid region without membrane boundaries
  • Compacted through supercoiling and protein binding

In Eukaryotes:

  • DNA is packaged with histone proteins to form nucleosomes (DNA wrapped around histone octamers)
  • Nucleosomes are further coiled into chromatin fibers
  • Chromatin is organized into loops and domains within the nucleus
  • During cell division, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes

This packaging allows meters of DNA to fit into microscopic cell nuclei while remaining accessible for cellular processes.

Question 40b: b) List and briefly explain the functions of the three major RNA types in the cell. (3 marks)

Answer:

1. Messenger RNA (mRNA):

  • Function: Carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes for protein synthesis
  • Contains codons that specify amino acid sequences
  • Undergoes processing (5' capping, 3' polyadenylation, splicing) in eukaryotes

2. Transfer RNA (tRNA):

  • Function: Transports specific amino acids to ribosomes during translation
  • Contains anticodons that base-pair with mRNA codons
  • Has a cloverleaf secondary structure with amino acid attachment site

3. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA):

  • Function: Structural and catalytic component of ribosomes
  • Forms the core of ribosomal subunits (16S and 23S in prokaryotes; 18S, 28S, 5.8S, 5S in eukaryotes)
  • Catalyzes peptide bond formation through peptidyl transferase activity
  • Involved in ribosome assembly and mRNA binding

SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (40 MARKS)

Question 41: Facultative bacteria survival in aerobic and anaerobic environments (20 marks)

Answer:

a) a) Describe biochemically how a facultative bacterium survives in both oxygen-rich and anaerobic environments. (15 marks)

Facultative bacteria possess sophisticated metabolic flexibility that allows them to survive in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-depleted environments through several key adaptations:

Metabolic Pathway Switching:

In Aerobic Conditions:

  • Utilize aerobic respiration with oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor
  • Complete oxidation of glucose through glycolysis, citric acid cycle, and electron transport chain
  • Generate maximum ATP yield through oxidative phosphorylation
  • Produce enzymes like catalase and superoxide dismutase to detoxify reactive oxygen species

In Anaerobic Conditions:

  • Switch to anaerobic respiration using alternative electron acceptors (nitrate, sulfate, fumarate)
  • When electron acceptors are unavailable, switch to fermentation pathways
  • Utilize substrate-level phosphorylation for ATP generation

Enzyme Regulation:

  • Express different sets of enzymes based on oxygen availability
  • Oxygen-sensitive enzymes are protected or replaced with oxygen-insensitive alternatives
  • Regulatory proteins (like FNR in E. coli) sense oxygen levels and control gene expression

Respiratory Chain Modifications:

  • Possess multiple terminal oxidases for different oxygen concentrations
  • High-affinity oxidases function at low oxygen concentrations
  • Alternative electron transport chains for anaerobic conditions

Fermentation Pathways:

  • Lactate fermentation: Pyruvate → Lactate (regenerates NAD+)
  • Ethanol fermentation: Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde → Ethanol
  • Mixed acid fermentation: Multiple end products including acetate, lactate, succinate
  • Butanol-acetone fermentation in some species

Metabolic Flexibility Examples:

  • Escherichia coli: Switches between aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration (with nitrate), and mixed acid fermentation
  • Enterococcus species: Primarily fermentative but can use oxygen when available
  • Pseudomonas species: Prefer aerobic respiration but can use nitrate anaerobically

Stress Response Mechanisms:

  • Heat shock proteins protect cellular components
  • Changes in membrane composition maintain integrity
  • DNA repair systems handle oxidative damage

b) State the net energy yield in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. (5 marks)

Aerobic Respiration Energy Yield:

  • Glycolysis: 2 ATP (substrate-level) + 2 NADH
  • Citric Acid Cycle: 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂
  • Electron Transport Chain: ~26-28 ATP from NADH and FADH₂
  • Total: ~30-32 ATP molecules per glucose

Anaerobic Conditions Energy Yield:

Anaerobic Respiration (with nitrate):

  • Similar to aerobic but lower ATP yield from electron transport
  • Total: ~20-25 ATP molecules per glucose

Fermentation:

  • Glycolysis only: 2 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation)
  • No additional ATP from electron transport
  • Total: 2 ATP molecules per glucose

Energy Efficiency Comparison:

  • Aerobic respiration: 15-16 times more efficient than fermentation
  • Anaerobic respiration: 10-12 times more efficient than fermentation
  • This explains why facultative bacteria prefer aerobic conditions when oxygen is available

Question 42: Procedure and principles of developing synthetic growth hormone (20 marks)

Discuss the procedure and principles involved in developing a synthetic growth hormone in the laboratory. (20 marks)

The development of synthetic human growth hormone (somatropin) represents a landmark achievement in biotechnology, involving sophisticated molecular biology techniques:

Historical Context: Previously, growth hormone was extracted from human pituitary glands, but this method was discontinued due to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease transmission risk, necessitating synthetic alternatives.

Question 42: Discuss the procedure and principles involved in developing a synthetic growth hormone in the laboratory. (20 marks)

Answer:

The development of synthetic human growth hormone (somatropin) represents a landmark achievement in biotechnology, involving sophisticated molecular biology techniques:

Historical Context: Previously, growth hormone was extracted from human pituitary glands, but this method was discontinued due to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease transmission risk, necessitating synthetic alternatives.

Gene Cloning and Isolation:

Step 1: Gene Identification and Isolation

  • Human growth hormone gene (GH1) located on chromosome 17
  • Gene contains 5 exons and 4 introns spanning approximately 1.8 kb
  • Mature mRNA codes for 191 amino acid protein
  • Initial isolation involved screening human genomic DNA libraries

Step 2: cDNA Synthesis

  • Reverse transcriptase used to synthesize complementary DNA (cDNA) from mature mRNA
  • cDNA lacks introns, making it suitable for bacterial expression
  • PCR amplification to obtain sufficient quantities of the gene

Vector Construction and Cloning:

Step 3: Vector Selection

  • Plasmid vectors (pBR322, pUC series) initially used
  • Expression vectors containing strong bacterial promoters (lac, trp, tac promoters)
  • Modern vectors include pET series for high-level expression

Step 4: Gene Insertion

  • Restriction enzyme digestion to create compatible ends
  • Ligation using DNA ligase to insert HGH gene into vector
  • Transformation into competent bacterial cells (typically E. coli)

Bacterial Expression System:

Step 5: Host Cell Selection

  • E. coli strains engineered for optimal protein production
  • BL21(DE3) strain commonly used for pET system
  • Strains deficient in proteases to prevent protein degradation

Step 6: Expression Optimization

  • IPTG (isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside) induction
  • Temperature control (typically 37°C, sometimes lower to prevent inclusion body formation)
  • Media optimization for maximum yield

Protein Processing and Purification:

Step 7: Cell Lysis and Protein Extraction

  • Mechanical disruption (sonication, French press)
  • Chemical lysis using detergents
  • Separation of soluble and insoluble fractions

Step 8: Inclusion Body Processing

  • Many recombinant proteins form inclusion bodies in E. coli
  • Inclusion bodies isolated through centrifugation
  • Denaturation using chaotropic agents (urea, guanidine HCl)

Step 9: Protein Refolding

  • Critical step for biological activity
  • Gradual removal of denaturants
  • Addition of folding aids (molecular chaperones, oxidized/reduced glutathione)
  • Optimization of pH, temperature, and protein concentration

Purification Techniques:

Step 10: Chromatographic Purification

  • Ion exchange chromatography (exploiting charge differences)
  • Size exclusion chromatography (molecular weight separation)
  • Reverse-phase HPLC for final purification
  • Affinity chromatography using specific binding properties

Step 11: Quality Control

  • SDS-PAGE electrophoresis for purity assessment
  • Mass spectrometry for molecular weight confirmation
  • N-terminal sequencing to verify correct processing
  • Biological activity assays

Modern Improvements:

Mammalian Expression Systems:

  • CHO (Chinese Hamster Ovary) cells for proper glycosylation
  • Post-translational modifications similar to native hormone
  • Improved stability and bioactivity

Synthetic Biology Approaches:

  • Codon optimization for improved expression
  • Signal peptide optimization for secretion
  • Metabolic engineering of host cells

Alternative Hosts:

  • Yeast systems (Pichia pastoris, Saccharomyces cerevisiae)
  • Insect cell systems using baculovirus
  • Plant-based expression systems

Principles of Recombinant Protein Production:

Molecular Biology Principles:

  • Central dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein
  • Genetic code universality allows cross-species expression
  • Proper promoter-gene fusion for transcription initiation

Biochemical Principles:

  • Protein folding determines biological activity
  • Disulfide bond formation requires oxidizing environment
  • Post-translational modifications may be necessary

Process Engineering Principles:

  • Scale-up considerations for commercial production
  • Bioreactor design for optimal growth conditions
  • Downstream processing for product recovery

Quality Assurance:

  • Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance
  • Batch-to-batch consistency
  • Contamination prevention (bacterial endotoxins, DNA)

Challenges and Solutions:

Technical Challenges:

  • Protein misfolding and aggregation
  • Proteolytic degradation by host proteases
  • Low expression levels in some systems

Solutions Developed:

  • Fusion proteins to improve stability
  • Protease-deficient bacterial strains
  • Inducible expression systems for controlled production

Regulatory Considerations:

  • FDA approval requirements for therapeutic proteins
  • Extensive safety and efficacy testing
  • Manufacturing facility inspections

Current Applications:

  • Treatment of growth hormone deficiency in children and adults
  • Turner syndrome management
  • Chronic kidney disease in children
  • AIDS-related wasting syndrome

This comprehensive approach has made synthetic growth hormone a successful therapeutic protein, demonstrating the power of recombinant DNA technology in medicine.

Question 43: Genetic mapping applications and Hardy-Weinberg calculations (20 marks)

a) a) Discuss the application and significance of genetic mapping in medicine. (10 marks)

Answer:

Genetic mapping is a fundamental tool in medical genetics that has revolutionized our understanding and treatment of human diseases:

Definition and Types: Genetic mapping involves determining the location of genes on chromosomes and the distances between them. Two main types exist: physical mapping (actual physical distances in base pairs) and genetic mapping (based on recombination frequencies).

Medical Applications:

1. Disease Gene Localization:

  • Positional cloning allows identification of disease genes without prior knowledge of protein function
  • Examples: Cystic fibrosis gene (CFTR) on chromosome 7, Huntington's disease gene on chromosome 4
  • Linkage analysis traces inheritance patterns in families to locate disease genes

2. Genetic Counseling and Risk Assessment:

  • Genetic maps enable calculation of recombination risks between disease genes and marker loci
  • Prenatal diagnosis through linked marker analysis
  • Carrier detection in families with genetic disorders
  • Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) for IVF procedures

3. Pharmacogenomics:

  • Mapping genes affecting drug metabolism (CYP450 family)
  • Predicting adverse drug reactions based on genetic variants
  • Personalized medicine approaches based on individual genetic profiles
  • HLA typing for organ transplantation compatibility

4. Complex Disease Analysis:

  • Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identify susceptibility loci
  • Mapping quantitative trait loci (QTL) for diseases like diabetes, hypertension
  • Understanding polygenic inheritance patterns
  • Risk prediction models incorporating multiple genetic factors

5. Cancer Genetics:

  • Mapping tumor suppressor genes (p53, RB1, BRCA1/2)
  • Oncogene localization and characterization
  • Chromosomal aberration analysis in malignancies
  • Development of targeted cancer therapies

Clinical Significance:

Diagnostic Applications:

  • Molecular diagnosis of genetic disorders
  • Detection of microdeletions and duplications
  • Characterization of chromosomal rearrangements
  • Confirmation of clinical diagnoses through genetic testing

Therapeutic Implications:

  • Gene therapy target identification
  • Development of antisense oligonucleotides
  • RNA interference therapeutic approaches
  • Stem cell therapy applications

Preventive Medicine:

  • Population screening programs
  • Genetic risk stratification
  • Lifestyle modification recommendations
  • Prophylactic interventions (e.g., prophylactic mastectomy for BRCA carriers)

Research Applications:

  • Model organism studies for human disease
  • Comparative genomics across species
  • Evolution of disease susceptibility
  • Development of animal disease models

b) b) Cooke and Ryder (1971) studied Ross’s geese at Karrack Lake and found 263 yellow and 413 grey goslings. Assuming a single gene with two alleles and that grey is dominant:

  • Calculate the genotype frequencies under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
  • Repeat assuming yellow is dominant. (10 marks)

Given Data:

  • Total goslings observed: 263 yellow + 413 grey = 676 total
  • Grey goslings: 413
  • Yellow goslings: 263
  • Assumption: Single gene with two alleles

Scenario 1: Grey is dominant

Step 1: Calculate phenotype frequencies

  • Grey frequency = 413/676 = 0.611
  • Yellow frequency = 263/676 = 0.389

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies Since yellow is recessive (aa), yellow frequency = q² q² = 0.389 q = √0.389 = 0.624 (frequency of yellow allele) p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.624 = 0.376 (frequency of grey allele)

Step 3: Calculate expected genotype frequencies

  • AA (grey): p² = (0.376)² = 0.141
  • Aa (grey): 2pq = 2(0.376)(0.624) = 0.469
  • aa (yellow): q² = (0.624)² = 0.389

Step 4: Verify total grey frequency Grey total = AA + Aa = 0.141 + 0.469 = 0.610 ≈ 0.611 ✓

Expected numbers in population of 676:

  • AA individuals: 0.141 × 676 = 95
  • Aa individuals: 0.469 × 676 = 317
  • aa individuals: 0.389 × 676 = 263 ✓

Scenario 2: Yellow is dominant

Step 1: Recalculate assuming yellow dominant If yellow is dominant, then grey is recessive (aa) Grey frequency = q² = 413/676 = 0.611

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies q² = 0.611 q = √0.611 = 0.782 (frequency of grey allele) p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.782 = 0.218 (frequency of yellow allele)

Step 3: Calculate expected genotype frequencies

  • AA (yellow): p² = (0.218)² = 0.048
  • Aa (yellow): 2pq = 2(0.218)(0.782) = 0.341
  • aa (grey): q² = (0.782)² = 0.611

Step 4: Verify total yellow frequency Yellow total = AA + Aa = 0.048 + 0.341 = 0.389 ✓

Expected numbers in population of 676:

  • AA individuals: 0.048 × 676 = 32
  • Aa individuals: 0.341 × 676 = 231
  • aa individuals: 0.611 × 676 = 413 ✓

Comparison of Scenarios:

Grey Dominant Model:

  • Allele frequencies: p (grey) = 0.376, q (yellow) = 0.624
  • Genotype frequencies: AA = 0.141, Aa = 0.469, aa = 0.389

Yellow Dominant Model:

  • Allele frequencies: p (yellow) = 0.218, q (grey) = 0.782
  • Genotype frequencies: AA = 0.048, Aa = 0.341, aa = 0.611

Statistical Considerations: Both models fit the observed data perfectly under Hardy-Weinberg assumptions, demonstrating that phenotype ratios alone cannot determine dominance relationships without additional genetic information or breeding experiments.

Question 1

Which of these bacterial components is LEAST likely to contain useful antigens?

A. Cell wall
B. Flagella
C. Ribosomes
D. Capsule
E. Both c and d

Answer: C. Ribosomes

Explanation: Ribosomes are internal cellular components involved in protein synthesis and are less exposed to the immune system compared to surface structures like cell walls, flagella, and capsules. These surface components are more likely to be recognized as foreign antigens by the host immune system.

Question 2

Which of the following contains structures composed of N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine?

A. Mycoplasmas
B. Amoeba
C. E. coli
D. Spheroplast
E. All the above

Answer: C. E. coli

Explanation: N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine are components of peptidoglycan, which forms the bacterial cell wall. E. coli, being a typical bacterium, has a peptidoglycan cell wall. Mycoplasmas lack cell walls, amoeba are eukaryotic (no peptidoglycan), and spheroplasts are bacteria with cell walls removed.

Question 3

The association of endotoxin in gram-negative bacteria is due to the presence of:

A. Steroids
B. Peptidoglycan
C. Lipopolysaccharides
D. Polypeptide
E. All the above

Answer: C. Lipopolysaccharides

Explanation: Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides (LPS) found in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. The lipid A portion of LPS is the toxic component that causes fever and shock when released into the bloodstream.

Question 4

The prokaryotic cell membrane:

A. Contains metabolic enzymes
B. Is selectively permeable
C. Regulates entry and exit of materials
D. Contains proteins and phospholipids
E. All the above

Answer: E. All the above

Explanation: The prokaryotic cell membrane performs multiple functions including housing metabolic enzymes, maintaining selective permeability, regulating material transport, and is composed of proteins and phospholipids, making all statements correct.

Question 5

Which of the statements regarding Gram staining is incorrect?

A. Mycobacterium tuberculosis stains blue due to a thick lipid layer
B. Streptococcus pyogenes stains blue due to thick peptidoglycan
C. Escherichia coli stains pink due to thin peptidoglycan
D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not visible due to lack of cell wall
E. None of the above

Answer: A. Mycobacterium tuberculosis stains blue due to a thick lipid layer

Explanation: This statement is incorrect because Mycobacterium tuberculosis does not stain well with Gram stain due to its waxy, lipid-rich cell wall (mycolic acids). It requires acid-fast staining instead. The thick lipid layer actually prevents proper Gram staining, not causes blue staining.

Question 6

Coagulase test is used to differentiate:

A. Staphylococcus aureus from S. epidermidis
B. S. epidermidis from Neisseria meningitidis
C. Streptococcus pyogenes from Enterococcus faecalis
D. Streptococcus pyogenes from Staphylococcus aureus
E. Both a and d

Answer: A. Staphylococcus aureus from S. epidermidis

Explanation: The coagulase test is specifically used to differentiate S. aureus (coagulase-positive) from S. epidermidis (coagulase-negative). This is a classic diagnostic test for identifying pathogenic vs. non-pathogenic staphylococci.

Question 7

Prokaryotic cells are more resistant to osmotic shock than eukaryotic cells because:

A. Cell wall composed of peptidoglycan
B. Selective permeability
C. Osmoregulating porins
D. Blocks water molecule entry
E. All the above

Answer: A. Cell wall composed of peptidoglycan

Explanation: The rigid peptidoglycan cell wall provides structural support and prevents the cell from bursting under osmotic pressure. This is the primary reason for osmotic shock resistance in prokaryotes.

Question 8

Streptococcus mutans resides in gum pockets, lacks catalase, grows outside anaerobic chamber. It is most likely:

A. A facultative anaerobe
B. An obligate aerobe
C. An obligate anaerobe
D. An aerotolerant anaerobe
E. Both a and b

Answer: D. An aerotolerant anaerobe

Explanation: S. mutans can survive in the presence of oxygen but doesn't use it for metabolism (lacks catalase). It can grow outside anaerobic chambers but doesn't require oxygen, making it aerotolerant anaerobic.

Question 9

Electrons from excited chlorophyll in PS-II are first accepted by:

A. Pheophytin
B. Ferredoxin
C. Cytochrome f
D. Cytochrome b
E. None of the above

Answer: A. Pheophytin

Explanation: In photosystem II, when chlorophyll is excited by light, it transfers electrons to pheophytin, which is the primary electron acceptor. This is the first step in the electron transport chain of photosynthesis.

Question 10

Photorespiration involves oxidation of:

A. PGA
B. RuBP

Explanation: Photorespiration occurs when RuBisCO enzyme binds oxygen instead of CO₂ to RuBP (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate), leading to its oxidation rather than the desired carboxylation reaction.

Light reaction in photosynthesis takes place in:

A. Grana
B. Stroma

Answer: A. Grana

Explanation: The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes of the grana, where chlorophyll and other photosynthetic pigments are located.

The H₂ donor during photosynthesis is:

A. ATP
B. NADP
C. NADPH
D. NADH
E. Both b and d

Explanation: NADPH serves as the hydrogen donor (reducing agent) in the Calvin cycle, providing the electrons and protons needed for CO₂ reduction to form glucose.

Enzyme fixing CO₂ in Calvin cycle is:

A. Ribose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase
B. Ribulose-1,6-bisphosphate carboxylase
C. Ribose-1,6-bisphosphate carboxylase
D. Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase
E. Both b and c

Answer: D. Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase

Explanation: RuBisCO (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) is the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of CO₂ fixation in the Calvin cycle, adding CO₂ to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate.

In lactic acid fermentation, final electron acceptor is:

B. Pyruvate

Which of these is not a product of fermentation?

B. Oxygen
C. CO₂

Crucial event in aerobic respiration is:

A. ATP synthesis
B. Ethanol and water synthesis

E. Both a and d

Pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyzes a reaction involving:

E. Both a and b

The TCA cycle starts with:

B. Acetyl group

First compound in TCA cycle is:

B. α-ketoglutaric acid

D. Malic acid
E. None of the above

Answer: E. None of the above

Explanation: The first compound formed in the TCA cycle is citrate (citric acid), which is not listed among the options. Oxaloacetate is the acceptor molecule, not the first product.

ATP acquisition in glucose fermentation involves:

A. Substrate-level phosphorylation
B. Electron transport from NADH

E. Both a and b

Answer: A. Substrate-level phosphorylation

Terminal electron acceptor in aerobic respiration:

Question 1

Part A: Explain the concept of final electron acceptors in relation to microbial energy production. (6 Marks)

Final electron acceptors are chemical compounds that receive electrons at the end of electron transport chains during microbial respiration. These acceptors are crucial for energy production because they allow the continuation of electron flow, which drives ATP synthesis through chemiosmosis.

In the electron transport process, electrons are passed through a series of carriers (cytochromes, quinones, iron-sulfur proteins) embedded in the cell membrane. As electrons move through these carriers, protons are pumped across the membrane, creating a proton gradient. The final electron acceptor receives the electrons at the end of this chain, allowing the process to continue.

The type of final electron acceptor determines the amount of energy that can be extracted:

  • Oxygen (aerobic respiration): Most efficient, yielding approximately 32-38 ATP molecules per glucose
  • Nitrate, sulfate, carbonate (anaerobic respiration): Less efficient than oxygen but more efficient than fermentation
  • Organic compounds (fermentation): Least efficient, typically yielding 2 ATP molecules per glucose

The efficiency relates to the electrochemical potential difference between the electron donor and acceptor - the greater the difference, the more energy can be captured as ATP.

Part B: Using biochemical pathways, explain how facultative bacteria acquire energy. (14 Marks)

Facultative bacteria are versatile organisms that can switch between different metabolic pathways depending on environmental conditions, particularly oxygen availability. They employ multiple biochemical pathways to acquire energy:

1. Aerobic Respiration (Oxygen Present)

When oxygen is available, facultative bacteria use aerobic respiration for maximum energy yield:

  • Glycolysis: Glucose is broken down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH
  • Pyruvate Oxidation: Pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, producing CO₂ and NADH
  • Citric Acid Cycle (TCA Cycle): Acetyl-CoA enters the cycle, producing 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂, and CO₂
  • Electron Transport Chain: NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor, producing approximately 32-34 ATP through oxidative phosphorylation

Total ATP yield: ~36-38 molecules per glucose

2. Anaerobic Respiration (No Oxygen, Alternative Acceptors Present)

When oxygen is absent but other electron acceptors are available:

  • The same initial pathways (glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle) occur
  • Alternative electron acceptors are used instead of oxygen:
    • Nitrate (NO₃⁻) → Nitrite/Nitrogen gas
    • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) → Hydrogen sulfide
    • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) → Methane
  • ATP yield is less than aerobic respiration but more than fermentation (~15-25 ATP per glucose)

3. Fermentation (No Oxygen, No Alternative Acceptors)

When no external electron acceptors are available:

  • Glycolysis proceeds normally, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH
  • Fermentation pathways regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH without electron transport: Lactic Acid Fermentation:
    • Pyruvate + NADH → Lactate + NAD⁺
    • Common in Lactobacillus species
    Alcoholic Fermentation:
    • Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde + CO₂
    • Acetaldehyde + NADH → Ethanol + NAD⁺
    • Common in yeasts and some bacteria
    Mixed Acid Fermentation:
    • Produces acetate, lactate, succinate, formate, CO₂, and H₂
    • Common in Enterobacteriaceae
  • Net ATP yield: Only 2 molecules per glucose (from glycolysis)

4. Metabolic Flexibility and Regulation

Facultative bacteria use sophisticated regulatory mechanisms:

  • Catabolite Repression: Glucose presence represses alternative carbon source utilization
  • Oxygen Sensing: FNR (Fumarate Nitrate Reduction) regulator responds to oxygen levels
  • Alternative Sigma Factors: Different sigma factors activate specific gene sets for different conditions
  • Two-Component Systems: Sensor kinases detect environmental changes and activate appropriate response regulators

5. Examples of Facultative Bacteria

  • Escherichia coli: Can perform aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration (nitrate), and mixed acid fermentation
  • Enterobacter aerogenes: Performs butanediol fermentation under anaerobic conditions
  • Staphylococcus aureus: Switches between aerobic respiration and lactic acid fermentation

This metabolic versatility allows facultative bacteria to thrive in diverse environments and rapidly adapt to changing conditions, making them highly successful in nature and clinically significant as opportunistic pathogens.

Question 2: Describe the Calvin Cycle and discuss its importance in biological systems. (20 Marks)

The Calvin Cycle, also known as the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle or the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis, is a crucial biochemical pathway that converts carbon dioxide into organic compounds using energy from ATP and reducing power from NADPH.

Structure and Location

The Calvin Cycle occurs in the stroma of chloroplasts in photosynthetic eukaryotes and in the cytoplasm of photosynthetic bacteria. It operates independently of light but depends on the products of light-dependent reactions (ATP and NADPH).

The Three Phases of the Calvin Cycle

Phase 1: Carbon Fixation (Carboxylation)

The cycle begins with the enzyme RuBisCO (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase), which catalyzes the addition of CO₂ to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP):

  • RuBP (5-carbon) + CO₂ → 2 molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA)
  • This is the only step that directly incorporates CO₂ from the atmosphere
  • RuBisCO is the most abundant enzyme on Earth due to its central role in carbon fixation
  • For every 3 CO₂ molecules fixed, 6 molecules of 3-PGA are produced

Phase 2: Reduction

The 3-PGA molecules are reduced to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P):

  • 3-PGA is first phosphorylated by ATP to form 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate
  • This is then reduced by NADPH to form G3P
  • Energy requirement: 6 ATP and 6 NADPH for 6 molecules of 3-PGA
  • G3P is a 3-carbon sugar that serves as the precursor for glucose and other organic molecules

Phase 3: Regeneration

The cycle must regenerate RuBP to continue:

  • 5 of the 6 G3P molecules are used to regenerate 3 RuBP molecules
  • This involves a complex series of reactions using additional ATP
  • The remaining G3P molecule represents the net gain of the cycle
  • Energy requirement: 3 additional ATP molecules

Overall Equation

For the synthesis of one G3P molecule: 3 CO₂ + 9 ATP + 6 NADPH + 6 H⁺ → G3P + 9 ADP + 8 Pi + 6 NADP⁺ + 3 H₂O

Regulation of the Calvin Cycle

The cycle is tightly regulated to ensure efficiency:

Light Regulation:

  • Thioredoxin system: Light-driven reduction of disulfide bonds activates key enzymes
  • pH changes: Stromal pH increases in light, favoring enzyme activity
  • Mg²⁺ concentration: Light-driven changes in Mg²⁺ levels affect enzyme activity

Metabolic Regulation:

  • RuBisCO is inhibited by its own substrate (RuBP) at high concentrations
  • Feedback inhibition by products like glucose-6-phosphate
  • Competitive inhibition by oxygen (photorespiration)

Importance in Biological Systems

1. Primary Productivity

The Calvin Cycle is the foundation of most food chains:

  • Converts inorganic carbon (CO₂) into organic compounds
  • Provides the carbon skeletons for all biomolecules
  • Supports virtually all life on Earth either directly or indirectly
  • Estimated to fix approximately 120 billion tons of CO₂ annually

2. Glucose and Carbohydrate Synthesis

  • Two G3P molecules combine to form glucose
  • Provides energy storage in the form of starch and glycogen
  • Produces structural carbohydrates like cellulose
  • Serves as starting material for other biomolecules

3. Oxygen Production

Although the Calvin Cycle itself doesn't produce oxygen, it's coupled with light reactions that do:

  • Maintains atmospheric oxygen levels
  • Supports aerobic respiration in most organisms
  • Created the oxygen-rich atmosphere essential for complex life

4. Climate Regulation

  • Removes CO₂ from the atmosphere, helping regulate global temperature
  • Carbon sequestration in plants and soil
  • Plays a crucial role in the global carbon cycle

5. Agricultural Importance

  • Basis of crop production and food security
  • Understanding the cycle helps improve crop yields
  • Target for genetic engineering to enhance photosynthetic efficiency
  • C4 and CAM plants have evolved modifications to improve efficiency

6. Biotechnology Applications

  • Engineering more efficient RuBisCO enzymes
  • Developing artificial photosynthetic systems
  • Carbon capture and utilization technologies
  • Producing biofuels and other valuable compounds

7. Evolutionary Significance

  • One of the most ancient metabolic pathways
  • Enabled the evolution of autotrophic organisms
  • Provided the foundation for complex ecosystems
  • Demonstrates the importance of enzyme evolution and regulation

Challenges and Limitations

Photorespiration:

  • RuBisCO can bind oxygen instead of CO₂, leading to energy loss
  • More problematic at high temperatures and low CO₂ concentrations
  • Plants have evolved C4 and CAM photosynthesis to minimize this problem

Efficiency:

  • Only about 1-2% of solar energy is converted to biomass
  • RuBisCO is relatively slow, processing only 3-10 CO₂ molecules per second
  • High energy cost: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed

Environmental Factors:

  • Temperature sensitivity affects enzyme kinetics
  • CO₂ concentration influences fixation rates
  • Water availability affects stomatal opening and CO₂ uptake

Future Research Directions

Scientists are working to improve the Calvin Cycle through:

  • Engineering more efficient RuBisCO variants
  • Introducing alternative carbon fixation pathways
  • Developing synthetic biology approaches
  • Understanding regulation mechanisms for optimization

Conclusion

The Calvin Cycle represents one of the most important biochemical processes on Earth. Its ability to convert atmospheric CO₂ into organic compounds makes it the foundation of most ecosystems and the basis for life as we know it. Understanding its mechanisms, regulation, and importance is crucial for addressing challenges in agriculture, climate change, and sustainable

1a. External Structures of Gram-Positive and Gram-Negative Bacteria (4 Marks)

Gram-Positive Bacteria:

  • Cell Wall: Thick peptidoglycan layer (20-80 nm thick) making up 40-90% of cell wall
  • Teichoic Acids: Present in cell wall and extending through peptidoglycan
  • Lipoteichoic Acids: Anchored to cytoplasmic membrane
  • No Outer Membrane: Single membrane system
  • Periplasmic Space: Minimal or absent

Gram-Negative Bacteria:

  • Cell Wall: Thin peptidoglycan layer (2-7 nm thick) making up 5-10% of cell wall
  • Outer Membrane: Present with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in outer leaflet
  • Periplasmic Space: Well-developed space between inner and outer membranes
  • Porins: Protein channels in outer membrane for transport
  • No Teichoic Acids: Absent from cell wall structure

Key Differences:

  • Gram-positive: Thick peptidoglycan, teichoic acids, single membrane
  • Gram-negative: Thin peptidoglycan, outer membrane with LPS, periplasmic space

1b. Functions of Teichoic Acid and Lipopolysaccharide (2 Marks)

Teichoic Acid Functions:

  • Maintains cell wall integrity and rigidity
  • Regulates autolytic enzyme activity
  • Facilitates cation binding (Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺)
  • Contributes to cell surface charge

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) Functions:

  • Acts as endotoxin causing fever and septic shock
  • Provides structural integrity to outer membrane
  • Acts as permeability barrier
  • Serves as antigenic determinant (O-antigen)

2a. Conditions for Bacterial Competence (2 Marks)

Natural Competence Conditions:

  • Physiological State: Late exponential or early stationary phase
  • Nutritional Stress: Limited nutrients (phosphate, carbon, or nitrogen)
  • Cell Density: Specific cell density requirements
  • pH and Temperature: Optimal environmental conditions

Artificial Competence Conditions:

  • Chemical Treatment: CaCl₂ or other divalent cations
  • Temperature Shock: Cold treatment followed by heat shock
  • Electrical Methods: Electroporation creating membrane pores

2b. Process of Bacterial Genetic Transformation (4 Marks)

Steps in Transformation:

  1. DNA Binding: Competent cells bind free DNA from environment through specific receptors
  2. DNA Uptake:
    • DNA crosses cell envelope through transformation apparatus
    • One strand is degraded, single strand enters cytoplasm
    • DNA-binding proteins protect incoming DNA
  3. DNA Integration:
    • Incoming DNA aligns with homologous chromosomal sequences
    • RecA protein facilitates homologous recombination
    • DNA strand exchange occurs through Holiday junction formation
  4. Expression:
    • Integrated DNA becomes part of bacterial chromosome
    • New phenotype expressed in transformed cells
    • Selective markers allow identification of transformants

3. Pathogenic Roles of Viral Spikes and Immune Surveillance Impact (6 Marks)

Pathogenic Roles:

Attachment and Entry:

  • Viral spikes (glycoproteins) bind to specific cellular receptors
  • Facilitate viral attachment to target cells
  • Mediate membrane fusion and viral entry
  • Determine tissue tropism and host range

Immune Evasion:

  • Antigenic Variation: Spikes undergo frequent mutations
  • Glycan Shielding: Heavy glycosylation masks epitopes
  • Conformational Masking: Critical epitopes hidden until receptor binding

Impact on Immune Surveillance:

Antibody Response:

  • Spikes are primary targets for neutralizing antibodies
  • Antibodies block receptor binding and membrane fusion
  • Memory B cells provide long-term protection

Challenges to Immunity:

  • Antigenic Drift: Gradual mutations escape antibody recognition
  • Antigenic Shift: Major changes create new viral strains
  • Immune Pressure: Drives selection of escape mutants

Vaccine Implications:

  • Spike proteins are common vaccine targets
  • Antigenic variation necessitates vaccine updates
  • Conserved regions offer universal vaccine potential

4. Glycolytic Pathway and Energy Acquisition (6 Marks)

Glycolytic Pathway Overview: The glycolytic pathway (Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway) converts glucose to pyruvate through ten enzymatic steps.

Key Steps:

  1. Glucose Phosphorylation: Glucose → Glucose-6-phosphate (ATP required)
  2. Isomerization: Glucose-6-phosphate → Fructose-6-phosphate
  3. Second Phosphorylation: Fructose-6-phosphate → Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (ATP required)
  4. Cleavage: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → Two 3-carbon molecules
  5. Oxidation and Phosphorylation: Generates NADH and ATP
  6. Final Steps: Produce pyruvate and additional ATP

Energy Yield:

  • Gross ATP Production: 4 ATP molecules
  • ATP Investment: 2 ATP molecules consumed
  • Net ATP Gain: 2 ATP molecules per glucose
  • NADH Production: 2 NADH molecules

Relevance in Microorganisms:

Energy Source:

  • Primary pathway for glucose utilization
  • Provides immediate ATP for cellular processes
  • Generates reducing equivalents (NADH) for biosynthesis

Metabolic Flexibility:

  • Functions under anaerobic conditions
  • Links to fermentation pathways
  • Provides precursors for biosynthetic pathways

Regulation:

  • Key regulatory enzymes (hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, pyruvate kinase)
  • Allosteric regulation by ATP, ADP, and other metabolites
  • Coordinate with other metabolic pathways

5. Selective Toxicity of Acyclovir to Alpha-Herpesvirus Infected Cells (6 Marks)

Mechanism of Selective Toxicity:

Viral Thymidine Kinase Dependency:

  • Acyclovir is a nucleoside analog of guanosine
  • Requires phosphorylation to become active
  • Normal cellular thymidine kinase has low affinity for acyclovir
  • Viral thymidine kinase (HSV-TK) has high affinity for acyclovir

Activation Process:

  1. First Phosphorylation: HSV thymidine kinase converts acyclovir to acyclovir monophosphate
  2. Further Phosphorylation: Cellular kinases convert to acyclovir triphosphate
  3. Active Form: Acyclovir triphosphate is the active antiviral agent

Selective Inhibition:

  • DNA Polymerase Inhibition: Acyclovir triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase
  • Chain Termination: Incorporated into viral DNA causing chain termination
  • Preferential Inhibition: 10-30 fold greater inhibition of viral vs. cellular DNA polymerase

Reasons for Selectivity:

  1. Enzyme Specificity: Viral thymidine kinase preferentially activates acyclovir
  2. Compartmentalization: Higher drug concentrations in infected cells
  3. DNA Polymerase Affinity: Viral DNA polymerase has higher affinity for acyclovir triphosphate
  4. Minimal Cellular Toxicity: Low activation in uninfected cells
