Question 4 (10 marks)

Describe the motor aspects of speech production, including the roles of different brain structures in phonation and articulation, and discuss how damage to these systems affects speech output.

Answer:

Motor Aspects of Speech Production

Overview of Speech Motor Control: Speech production involves the precise coordination of multiple motor systems to generate intelligible vocal communication. This complex process requires integration of respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory mechanisms under sophisticated neural control.

Phonation Control:

Primary Control Center:

  • Broca's Area and Higher Centers serve as the primary controllers of phonation
  • These areas coordinate the complex process of vocal cord vibration and breath control
  • Integration with respiratory centers ensures adequate airflow for voice production

Phonation Process:

  • Respiratory Control: Coordination of diaphragm and intercostal muscles for controlled exhalation
  • Laryngeal Control: Precise adjustment of vocal cord tension, position, and vibration
  • Resonance Control: Modification of vocal tract shape for voice quality

Articulation Control System:

Multiple Brain Structure Coordination:

1. Cerebellum:

  • Function: Provides precise timing and coordination of speech movements
  • Role: Ensures smooth, coordinated transitions between speech sounds
  • Impact: Fine-tunes motor commands for accurate articulation

2. Basal Ganglia:

  • Function: Controls movement initiation, scaling, and sequencing
  • Role: Regulates automatic aspects of speech motor control
  • Impact: Maintains appropriate speech rate and rhythm

3. Motor Cortex:

  • Function: Generates voluntary motor commands for speech muscles
  • Role: Controls conscious aspects of articulation
  • Impact: Directs specific muscle contractions for speech sound production

4. Pyramidal Tracts:

  • Function: Transmit motor commands from cortex to cranial and spinal motor neurons
  • Role: Provide direct pathway for voluntary speech control
  • Impact: Enable precise, voluntary speech movements

Integrated Motor Speech Network: The coordination between these structures enables:

  • Temporal Precision: Exact timing of muscle contractions
  • Spatial Accuracy: Precise positioning of articulators
  • Sequential Coordination: Smooth transitions between speech sounds
  • Adaptive Control: Real-time adjustments based on auditory feedback

Effects of System Damage:

Cerebellar Damage (Ataxic Dysarthria):

  • Speech Characteristics: Irregular, imprecise, and poorly coordinated articulation
  • Specific Features: Scanning speech, irregular rhythm, imprecise consonants
  • Underlying Problem: Loss of motor coordination and timing

Basal Ganglia Damage (Hypokinetic/Hyperkinetic Dysarthria):

Hypokinetic (Parkinson's Disease):

  • Characteristics: Reduced movement amplitude, monotone voice, rapid speech rate
  • Features: Soft voice, imprecise articulation, reduced facial expression
  • Problem: Difficulty initiating and scaling movements

Hyperkinetic (Huntington's Disease):

  • Characteristics: Involuntary movements affecting speech
  • Features: Irregular rhythm, variable loudness, unpredictable interruptions
  • Problem: Excess involuntary movements disrupting speech

Motor Cortex/Pyramidal Tract Damage (Spastic Dysarthria):

  • Characteristics: Slow, effortful, strained-strangled voice quality
  • Features: Imprecise consonants, harsh voice, reduced speech rate
  • Problem: Spasticity and weakness of speech muscles

Upper vs. Lower Motor Neuron Effects:

Upper Motor Neuron Damage:

  • Result: Spastic dysarthria with hyperactive reflexes
  • Features: Strained voice, slow rate, effortful speech
  • Cause: Loss of cortical inhibition leading to muscle spasticity

Lower Motor Neuron Damage:

  • Result: Flaccid dysarthria with reduced reflexes
  • Features: Breathy voice, weak articulation, nasal speech
  • Cause: Direct muscle weakness due to nerve damage

Phonation-Specific Disorders:

Vocal Cord Paralysis:

  • Unilateral: Breathy voice, reduced loudness, vocal fatigue
  • Bilateral: Severe voice impairment, possible breathing difficulties
  • Cause: Damage to recurrent laryngeal nerve or vagus nerve

Functional Voice Disorders:

  • Characteristics: Voice problems without structural damage
  • Features: Variable voice quality, often stress-related
  • Cause: Inappropriate vocal cord tension or breathing patterns

Clinical Assessment and Management:

Diagnostic Approach:

  • Perceptual Analysis: Listening to speech characteristics
  • Acoustic Analysis: Measuring voice parameters
  • Physiological Testing: Assessing muscle strength and coordination
  • Imaging Studies: Evaluating structural integrity

Treatment Strategies:

  • Speech Therapy: Exercises to improve coordination and strength
  • Medical Management: Treating underlying neurological conditions
  • Surgical Intervention: For structural problems affecting phonation
  • Compensatory Techniques: Alternative communication methods when necessary

Prognosis and Recovery:

  • Plasticity Factors: Age, extent of damage, time since onset
  • Rehabilitation Potential: Varies by underlying cause and location
  • Functional Outcomes: Range from complete recovery to requiring assistive devices

Research and Future Directions:

  • Neuroplasticity Studies: Understanding brain reorganization after injury
  • Technology Integration: Computer-assisted speech therapy
  • Pharmacological Interventions: Medications to enhance recovery
  • Biomarker Development: Predictors of recovery potential

This comprehensive understanding of motor speech control demonstrates the intricate neural networks required for normal speech production and explains the diverse patterns of speech disorders that can result from damage to different components of the system. The complexity of these interactions highlights why speech rehabilitation requires specialized knowledge and individualized treatment approaches.

Title: MBCHB CAT - GENETICS ANSWER KEY
Content:
MBMB2211B - Date: 27/3/2025

SECTION A (30 marks) - MCQs

Question 1

Two pure breeding parents are crossed similar to Mendel's Parental generation. A tall plant is crossed with a short plant. What is the expected outcome for the F1 generation?

A. all short
B. all tall
C. all medium height
D. half tall, half short

Answer: B. all tall

Explanation: When crossing pure breeding tall (TT) with pure breeding short (tt) plants, all F1 offspring will be heterozygous (Tt). Since tall is dominant over short, all F1 plants will express the tall phenotype.

Question 2

If the cross from #1 is continued, what would be the expected outcome in the F2 generation?

A. all short
B. all tall
C. 3 tall, 1 short
D. half tall, half short

Answer: C. 3 tall, 1 short

Explanation: F1 × F1 cross (Tt × Tt) produces: 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt genotypic ratio. Since T is dominant, the phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 short.

Question 3

Which of the following is the BEST definition of inbreeding?

A. mating of individuals who are closely related genetically
B. mating of genetically unrelated individuals
C. mating in which individuals who are alike for particular trait or phenotype mate
D. mating in which individuals who are not genetically alike for particular traits mate

Answer: A. mating of individuals who are closely related genetically

Explanation: Inbreeding specifically refers to reproduction between genetically related individuals, which increases homozygosity and can lead to expression of deleterious recessive alleles.

Question 4

If a plant that has round seeds has a parent that has wrinkled seeds, what is its genotype? (Assume that round is dominant.)

A. RR
B. Rr
C. rr
D. RrWw

Answer: B. Rr

Explanation: Since the plant has round seeds (dominant phenotype) but has a parent with wrinkled seeds (rr), the round-seeded plant must be heterozygous (Rr) to have inherited the recessive allele from the wrinkled parent.

Question 5

Below is a Punnett square showing a cross between two parents. Use this information to respond to the next three questions. P generation: BB x bb Complete dominance: B = black rat b = white rat

Referring to the Punnett square above, which of the following accurately represents the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of the F1 generation?

A. Phenotypic ratio 100% white, genotypic ratio 100% Bb
B. Genotypic ratio 100% black, phenotypic ratio 100% Bb
C. Phenotypic ratio 100% black, genotypic ratio 100% Bb
D. Phenotypic ratio 50% black, 50% white, genotypic ratio 100% Bb

Answer: C. Phenotypic ratio 100% black, genotypic ratio 100% Bb

Explanation: BB × bb cross produces all Bb offspring. Since B (black) is dominant over b (white), all offspring will be black phenotypically but heterozygous (Bb) genotypically.

Question 6

Using the information in the Punnett square above, how would we refer to the parents and the offspring?

A. One parent homozygous, one is heterozygous, the offspring are homozygous
B. One parent is homozygous dominant, one parent is homozygous recessive, the offspring are heterozygous
C. One parent is homozygous dominant, one parent is heterozygous recessive, the offspring are homozygous dominant
D. One parent is heterozygous dominant, one is heterozygous recessive, the offspring are heterozygous dominant

Answer: B. One parent is homozygous dominant, one parent is homozygous recessive, the offspring are heterozygous

Explanation: BB is homozygous dominant, bb is homozygous recessive, and all Bb offspring are heterozygous.

Question 7

If we were to cross the offspring in the Punnett square above (known as the F1 generation), what will be the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of the F2 generation?

A. Phenotypic ratio 3:1; genotypic ratio 1:2:1
B. Phenotypic ratio 1:2:1, genotypic ratio 3:1
C. Phenotypic ratio 3:1, genotypic ratio 3:1
D. Phenotypic ratio 1:2:1, genotypic ratio 1:2:1

Answer: A. Phenotypic ratio 3:1; genotypic ratio 1:2:1

Explanation: F1 × F1 (Bb × Bb) produces: 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb (genotypic ratio 1:2:1). Phenotypically: 3 black : 1 white (ratio 3:1).

Question 8

Recombination frequency of < 0.5 suggests:

A. Linkage
B. No linkage
C. Homozygotes
D. Heterozygotes

Answer: A. Linkage

Explanation: Recombination frequency less than 50% indicates that genes are linked on the same chromosome. Independent assortment would give 50% recombination frequency.

Question 9

Use the information and the Punnett square below to respond to the next three questions: Hemophilia is an X linked recessive disorder

What are the chances that this couple will have a child with hemophilia?

A. 75%
B. 50%
C. 25%
D. 0%

Answer: C. 25%

Explanation: Assuming carrier female (X^H X^h) × normal male (X^H Y): 25% X^H X^H, 25% X^H X^h, 25% X^H Y, 25% X^h Y. Only X^h Y males have hemophilia = 25%.

Question 10

The mother undergoes amniocentesis during her pregnancy, and is told that the child she is carrying is a boy. What are the chances that her son will have hemophilia?

A. 75%
B. 50%
C. 25%
D. 0%

Answer: B. 50%

Explanation: Given the child is male, only male offspring are considered: X^H Y (normal) and X^h Y (hemophiliac) are equally likely, so 50% chance.

Question 11

The mother has a second pregnancy four years later. She is told that her baby will be a girl. What are the chances that her daughter will have hemophilia?

A. 75%
B. 50%
C. 25%
D. 0%

Answer: D. 0%

Explanation: Female offspring are X^H X^H or X^H X^h. Since hemophilia is X-linked recessive and father contributes X^H, no daughters can have hemophilia (they need X^h X^h).

Question 12

The principle that states that alleles separate during gamete formation is the:

A. principle of multiple alleles
B. principle of dominance and recessiveness
C. principle of independent assortment
D. principle of segregation

Answer: D. principle of segregation

Explanation: Mendel's first law (principle of segregation) states that paired alleles separate during gamete formation, with each gamete receiving only one allele.

Question 13

If you crossed two heterozygous plants, how many of the offspring will also be heterozygous?

A. All
B. Half
C. 3/4
D. 1/4

Answer: B. Half

Explanation: Aa × Aa cross produces: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Therefore, 2/4 = 1/2 = 50% are heterozygous.

Question 14

A plant that has purple flowers is crossed with one that has white flowers. The offspring were half white and half purple. What were the genotypes of the parents?

A. Pp × pp
B. Pp × Pp
C. PP × pp
D. PP × WW

Answer: A. Pp × pp

Explanation: 1:1 ratio indicates a testcross between heterozygous (Pp) and homozygous recessive (pp) parents.

Question 15

Cystic fibrosis is:

A. Sex-linked recessive disorder
B. Autosomal dominant disorder
C. Autosomal recessive disorder
D. Sex-linked dominant disorder

Answer: C. Autosomal recessive disorder

Explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7 (autosome) and requires two copies of the defective allele.

Question 16

A dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) will result in what offspring ratio?

A. 4:4:2:2
B. 1:3:1
C. 3:1
D. 9:3:3:1

Answer: D. 9:3:3:1

Explanation: Classic dihybrid cross phenotypic ratio: 9 dominant for both traits : 3 dominant for first, recessive for second : 3 recessive for first, dominant for second : 1 recessive for both.

Question 17

Phenotype refers to an organism's:

A. genetic code
B. physical appearance
C. parents
D. ratio

Answer: B. physical appearance

Explanation: Phenotype is the observable physical or biochemical characteristics of an organism, determined by both genotype and environment.

Question 18

In each case where Mendel crossed true breeding plants as parents, the offspring displayed only one of the two traits seen in the parents. This observation supports which principle of genetics?

A. Segregation
B. independent assortment
C. dominance and recessiveness
D. allele frequency

Answer: C. dominance and recessiveness

Explanation: The observation that F1 offspring show only one parental trait demonstrates that one allele (dominant) masks the expression of another (recessive).

Question 19

A human being has __ autosomes and __ sex chromosomes:

A. 22 pairs, 1 pair
B. 23, 1
C. 2, 2
D. 23, 23

Answer: A. 22 pairs, 1 pair

Explanation: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes total: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).

Question 20

Somatic cells of a human have __ chromosomes and are called:

A. 10, haploid
B. 92, diploid
C. 23, haploid
D. 46, diploid

Answer: D. 46, diploid

Explanation: Human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) and are diploid (2n), meaning they have two copies of each chromosome.

Question 21

A person who receives an extra chromosome could have:

A. Heightened intelligence
B. Red eyes
C. Down Syndrome
D. Polygenic traits

Answer: C. Down Syndrome

Explanation: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 (an extra copy of chromosome 21), making it a classic example of chromosomal abnormality due to extra chromosome.

Question 22

A selection type which works by constantly removing individuals from both ends of a phenotype distribution thus maintaining the same mean over time is:

A. Stabilizing
B. Disruptive
C. Directional
D. None of the above

Answer: A. Stabilizing

Explanation: Stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes and removes extreme variants, maintaining the population mean and reducing variation.

Question 23

Which selection type fits sickle cell anemia?

A. Stabilizing
B. Disruptive
C. Directional
D. None of the above

Answer: A. Stabilizing

Explanation: In malaria-endemic areas, heterozygotes (HbAS) have selective advantage over both homozygotes, representing balancing/stabilizing selection.

Question 24

Which selection type fits CCR5 mutant gene?

A. Stabilizing
B. Disruptive
C. Directional
D. None of the above

Answer: C. Directional

Explanation: CCR5-Δ32 mutation provides HIV resistance, leading to directional selection favoring the mutant allele in populations exposed to HIV.

Question 25

What is an allele?

A. Characteristics of an organism
B. Alternate forms of genes
C. Homologous chromosomes
D. Pair of centrioles

Answer: B. Alternate forms of genes

Explanation: Alleles are different versions of the same gene that occupy the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

Question 26

Given a biallelic system (Aa) 500 people were sampled for a certain disease. One SNP locus was segregating for two alleles ("A" and "a") and three genotypes were found in the following proportions: A/A = 250; A/a = 100; a/a = 150. What is the frequency of the dominant allele?

A. 0.6
B. 0.5
C. 0.7
D. 0.4

Answer: A. 0.6

Explanation:

  • Total individuals = 500
  • A alleles = (250 × 2) + (100 × 1) = 600
  • Total alleles = 500 × 2 = 1000
  • Frequency of A = 600/1000 = 0.6

Question 27

What is the frequency of the recessive allele (from Q26 above)?

A. 0.6
B. 0.5
C. 0.7
D. 0.4

Answer: D. 0.4

Explanation: Since p + q = 1, and p (frequency of A) = 0.6, then q (frequency of a) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4

Question 28

Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from the defect of phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme. 1/3000 Jews descendant carry the deleterious recessive allele. What is the frequency for the dominant allele?

A. 0.982
B. 0.82
C. 0.981
D. 0.81

Answer: A. 0.982

Explanation:

  • q² = 1/3000 ≈ 0.000333
  • q = √0.000333 ≈ 0.018
  • p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.018 = 0.982

Question 29

What is the frequency for the recessive allele (from Q28 above)?

A. 0.018
B. 0.18
C. 0.019
D. 0.19

Answer: A. 0.018

Explanation: As calculated above, q = √(1/3000) ≈ 0.018

Question 30

The following are autosomal dominant disorders EXCEPT:

A. Achondroplasia
B. Osteogenesis imperfecta
C. Marfan's syndrome
D. Tay-Sachs

Answer: D. Tay-Sachs

Explanation: Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive disorder, while the others are autosomal dominant conditions.

SECTION B (70 marks) - Essay Questions

Question 1 (5 marks)

A pea plant is the F1 offspring of a true-breeding plant with purple flowers and a true-breeding plant with white flowers. This plant is crossed with one that has white flowers (recessive). How many of the plants in the next generation will have white flowers? Use letter P for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Define the genotypes

  • True-breeding purple = PP
  • True-breeding white = pp
  • F1 offspring = Pp (purple phenotype)

Step 2: Set up the testcross

  • F1 plant (Pp) × white plant (pp)

Step 3: Perform the cross

    P   p
p   Pp  pp
p   Pp  pp

Step 4: Analyze results

  • Genotypic ratio: 1 Pp : 1 pp
  • Phenotypic ratio: 1 purple : 1 white
  • Answer: 50% (or half) of the plants will have white flowers

Question 2 (5 marks)

In humans, Cystic Fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele on chromosome 7. A person must inherit two of these alleles to have the disease. What are the chances of a child having the disease if both of the parents are heterozygous? Use letter C for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Define the genotypes

  • C = normal allele (dominant)
  • c = cystic fibrosis allele (recessive)
  • Both parents are heterozygous = Cc

Step 2: Set up the cross

  • Cc × Cc

Step 3: Perform the cross using Punnett square

    C   c
C   CC  Cc
c   Cc  cc

Step 4: Analyze results

  • Genotypic ratio: 1 CC : 2 Cc : 1 cc
  • Only cc individuals have cystic fibrosis
  • Answer: 25% (or 1/4) chance of having a child with cystic fibrosis

Question 3 (5 marks)

The ability to curl your tongue up on the sides (T, tongue rolling) is dominant to not being able to roll your tongue. A woman who can roll her tongue marries a man who cannot. Their first child has his father's phenotype. What are the genotypes of the mother, father, and child? Use letter T for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Analyze the given information

  • T = tongue rolling (dominant)
  • t = cannot roll tongue (recessive)
  • Woman can roll tongue = T_ (TT or Tt)
  • Man cannot roll tongue = tt
  • Child cannot roll tongue = tt

Step 2: Determine genotypes using genetic logic

  • Since the child has genotype tt, it must have inherited one t allele from each parent
  • Father is tt (given)
  • Mother must be Tt (not TT, because she passed a t allele to her child)

Step 3: Verify with cross

  • Tt (mother) × tt (father)
    T   t
t   Tt  tt
t   Tt  tt

Answer:

  • Mother: Tt
  • Father: tt
  • Child: tt

Question 4 (10 marks)

Gene A controls fin length in Plecostomus. Short fins are dominant to long fins. Gene B controls fin colour (grey and lemon) grey dominant over lemon. State the alleles and possible gamete combinations. Generate a cross of the same using a Punnett square and predict the phenotype of their progeny. Use letters A and B for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Define alleles

  • A = short fins (dominant)
  • a = long fins (recessive)
  • B = grey fins (dominant)
  • b = lemon fins (recessive)

Step 2: Assuming dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb)

Step 3: Determine possible gametes Each parent (AaBb) can produce: AB, Ab, aB, ab

Step 4: Create Punnett square (4×4)

        AB    Ab    aB    ab
AB    AABB  AABb  AaBB  AaBb
Ab    AABb  AAbb  AaBb  Aabb
aB    AaBB  AaBb  aaBB  aaBb
ab    AaBb  Aabb  aaBb  aabb

Step 5: Determine phenotypes

  • A_B_ = Short fins, Grey color (9/16)
  • A_bb = Short fins, Lemon color (3/16)
  • aaB_ = Long fins, Grey color (3/16)
  • aabb = Long fins, Lemon color (1/16)

Answer:

  • Phenotypic ratio: 9:3:3:1
  • 9 Short Grey : 3 Short Lemon : 3 Long Grey : 1 Long Lemon

Question 5 (5 marks)

In humans, Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a disease where muscles become weaker over time. Those afflicted with this disease usually die in childhood. If a female is a carrier for DMD is married to a healthy male, what percentage of her sons will inherit the disease? What percentage of her daughters will inherit the disease? Use letter D for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Define the inheritance pattern

  • DMD is X-linked recessive
  • D = normal allele
  • d = DMD allele

Step 2: Define genotypes

  • Carrier female = X^D X^d
  • Healthy male = X^D Y

Step 3: Perform the cross

        X^D    Y
X^D   X^D X^D  X^D Y
X^d   X^D X^d  X^d Y

Step 4: Analyze offspring Sons:

  • X^D Y = healthy (50%)
  • X^d Y = DMD affected (50%)

Daughters:

  • X^D X^D = healthy (50%)
  • X^D X^d = carrier (50%)
  • None affected with DMD (0%)

Answer:

  • 50% of sons will inherit DMD
  • 0% of daughters will inherit DMD

Question 6 (5 marks)

If a man is colorblind, what percentage of his sons will be colorblind (assuming mother is not a carrier meaning healthy)? Use letter C for uniformity.

Solution:

Step 1: Define the inheritance pattern

  • Colorblindness is X-linked recessive
  • C = normal vision
  • c = colorblind

Step 2: Define genotypes

  • Colorblind man = X^c Y
  • Healthy woman (not carrier) = X^C X^C

Step 3: Perform the cross

        X^c    Y
X^C   X^C X^c  X^C Y
X^C   X^C X^c  X^C Y

Step 4: Analyze male offspring

  • All sons receive Y from father and X^C from mother
  • All sons have genotype X^C Y (normal vision)

Answer: 0% of sons will be colorblind

Question 7 (5 marks)

If 9% of an African population is born with a severe form of sickle-cell anemia (ss), what percentage of the population will be more resistant to malaria because they are heterozygous (Ss) for the sickle-cell gene?

Solution:

Step 1: Use Hardy-Weinberg principle

  • q² = frequency of ss = 0.09
  • q = √0.09 = 0.3 (frequency of s allele)
  • p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.3 = 0.7 (frequency of S allele)

Step 2: Calculate heterozygote frequency

  • Frequency of Ss = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42

Step 3: Convert to percentage

  • 0.42 × 100 = 42%

Answer: 42% of the population will be heterozygous (Ss) and more resistant to malaria

Question 8 (5 marks)

There are 100 students in a class. Ninety-six did well in the course whereas four blew it totally and received a grade of F. Sorry. In the highly unlikely event that these traits are genetic rather than environmental, if these traits involve dominant and recessive alleles, and if the four (4%) represent the frequency of the homozygous recessive condition, calculate the frequency of the recessive and the dominant allele and the number of heterozygous individuals.

Solution:

Step 1: Apply Hardy-Weinberg principle

  • q² = 4/100 = 0.04 (frequency of homozygous recessive)
  • q = √0.04 = 0.2 (frequency of recessive allele)
  • p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.2 = 0.8 (frequency of dominant allele)

Step 2: Calculate heterozygote frequency

  • 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32

Step 3: Calculate number of heterozygous individuals

  • 0.32 × 100 = 32 students

Answer:

  • Frequency of recessive allele = 0.2 (20%)
  • Frequency of dominant allele = 0.8 (80%)
  • Number of heterozygous individuals = 32 students

Question 9 (5 marks)

The ability to taste PTC is due to a single dominant allele "T". You sampled 215 individuals and determined that 138 could detect the bitter taste of PTC and 77 could not. Calculate the allele and genotypic frequencies.

Solution:

Step 1: Determine phenotype frequencies

  • Cannot taste PTC (tt) = 77/215 = 0.358
  • Can taste PTC (T_) = 138/215 = 0.642

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies

  • q² = 0.358, so q = √0.358 = 0.598 (frequency of t)
  • p = 1 - q = 1 - 0.598 = 0.402 (frequency of T)

Step 3: Calculate genotypic frequencies

  • TT = p² = (0.402)² = 0.162
  • Tt = 2pq = 2 × 0.402 × 0.598 = 0.481
  • tt = q² = (0.598)² = 0.358

Answer:

  • Allele frequencies: T = 0.402 (40.2%), t = 0.598 (59.8%)
  • Genotypic frequencies: TT = 0.162 (16.2%), Tt = 0.481 (48.1%), tt = 0.358 (35.8%)

Question 10 (5 marks)

Discuss a selection model where the heterozygous is selectively advantaged.

Solution:

Balancing Selection (Heterozygote Advantage)

Definition: A form of natural selection that maintains genetic diversity by favoring heterozygotes over both homozygotes.

Mechanism:

  • Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote
  • Both alleles are maintained in the population at intermediate frequencies
  • Results in balanced polymorphism

Classic Example: Sickle Cell Anemia

  • HbA HbA: Normal hemoglobin, susceptible to malaria
  • HbA HbS: Heterozygote, resistant to malaria, normal oxygen transport
  • HbS HbS: Sickle cell disease, severe anemia

Population Genetics:

  • In malaria-endemic areas, heterozygotes have selective advantage
  • Equilibrium allele frequencies maintained by opposing selective forces
  • Frequency depends on relative fitness values

Evolutionary Significance:

  • Maintains genetic variation in populations
  • Provides raw material for future adaptation
  • Demonstrates that "harmful" alleles can persist due to heterozygote advantage

Question 11 (5 marks)

In a population of fish, the colour red is dominant to white. A sample of 300 fish is observed and the following frequencies are noted: 40 RR, 150 Rr and 110 rr. Determine whether the population is inbred or not.

Solution:

Step 1: Calculate observed genotype frequencies

  • RR: 40/300 = 0.133
  • Rr: 150/300 = 0.500
  • rr: 110/300 = 0.367

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies

  • p (R) = (40×2 + 150×1)/(300×2) = 230/600 = 0.383
  • q (r) = (110×2 + 150×1)/(300×2) = 370/600 = 0.617

Step 3: Calculate expected Hardy-Weinberg frequencies

  • Expected RR = p² = (0.383)² = 0.147
  • Expected Rr = 2pq = 2×0.383×0.617 = 0.472
  • Expected rr = q² = (0.617)² = 0.381

Step 4: Compare observed vs expected

  • Observed: RR=0.133, Rr=0.500, rr=0.367
  • Expected: RR=0.147, Rr=0.472, rr=0.381

Step 5: Calculate inbreeding coefficient (F) F = (He - Ho)/He = (0.472 - 0.500)/0.472 = -0.059

Answer: The population shows slight outbreeding (negative F value), not inbreeding. The excess of heterozygotes suggests random mating or slight outbreeding.

Question 12 (10 marks)

In cats, friendliness is determined by a dominant gene F. The recessive genotype produces an unfriendly cat. The genotypes of several cats are determined to be: 40 FF, 60 Ff, and 50 ff. Is this population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

Solution:

Step 1: Calculate observed frequencies

  • Total cats = 40 + 60 + 50 = 150
  • FF: 40/150 = 0.267
  • Ff: 60/150 = 0.400
  • ff: 50/150 = 0.333

Step 2: Calculate allele frequencies

  • p (F) = (40×2 + 60×1)/(150×2) = 140/300 = 0.467
  • q (f) = (50×2 + 60×1)/(150×2) = 160/300 = 0.533

Step 3: Calculate expected Hardy-Weinberg frequencies

  • Expected FF = p² = (0.467)² = 0.218
  • Expected Ff = 2pq = 2×0.467×0.533 = 0.498
  • Expected ff = q² = (0.533)² = 0.284

Step 4: Calculate expected numbers

  • Expected FF = 0.218 × 150 = 32.7
  • Expected Ff = 0.498 × 150 = 74.7
  • Expected ff = 0.284 × 150 = 42.6

Step 5: Perform Chi-square test χ² = Σ(observed - expected)²/expected

χ² = (40-32.7)²/32.7 + (60-74.7)²/74.7 + (50-42.6)²/42.6 χ² = (7.3)²/32.7 + (-14.7)²/74.7 + (7.4)²/42.6 χ² = 53.29/32.7 + 216.09/74.7 + 54.76/42.6 χ² = 1.63 + 2.89 + 1.28 = 5.8

Step 6: Determine degrees of freedom and critical value

  • df = number of genotypes - number of alleles = 3 - 2 = 1
  • Critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84

Step 7: Interpret results Since χ² = 5.8 > 3.84 (critical value), we reject the null hypothesis.

Conclusion: The population is NOT in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p < 0.05).

Analysis of deviations:

  • Deficit of heterozygotes: Observed Ff (60) < Expected Ff (74.7)
  • Excess of homozygotes: Both FF and ff are higher than expected
  • This pattern suggests inbreeding in the population

Possible causes for deviation:

  1. Inbreeding - Most likely cause given the pattern
  2. Population stratification - Subpopulations with different allele frequencies
  3. Assortative mating - Non-random mating patterns
  4. Wahlund effect - Population subdivision

Biological significance: The deficit of heterozygotes and excess of homozygotes indicates that cats in this population are more likely to mate with genetically similar individuals, leading to increased homozygosity and potential expression of recessive traits.

MBCHB CAT - GENETICS ANSWER KEY

MBMB2211B - Date: 15/4/2025

SECTION A - MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (30 marks)

Question 1

In incomplete dominance, when a red flower (RR) is crossed with a white flower (WW), the F1 generation will be:

A. all red
B. all white
C. all pink
D. half red, half white

Answer: C. all pink

Question 7 (5 marks)

A population of wildflowers has the following genotype frequencies for flower color: 250 RR (red), 500 Rr (pink), 250 rr (white). Calculate the allele frequencies and determine if this population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Show all calculations.

Answer:

Step 1: Calculate Total Population Total = 250 + 500 + 250 = 1000 individuals

Step 2: Calculate Observed Genotype Frequencies

  • Frequency of RR = 250/1000 = 0.25
  • Frequency of Rr = 500/1000 = 0.50
  • Frequency of rr = 250/1000 = 0.25

Step 3: Calculate Allele Frequencies

  • Frequency of R allele (p) = (2 × RR + Rr)/(2 × total) p = (2 × 250 + 500)/(2 × 1000) = 1000/2000 = 0.5
  • Frequency of r allele (q) = (2 × rr + Rr)/(2 × total) q = (2 × 250 + 500)/(2 × 1000) = 1000/2000 = 0.5

Verification: p + q = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 ✓

Step 4: Calculate Expected Hardy-Weinberg Frequencies

  • Expected RR frequency = p² = (0.5)² = 0.25
  • Expected Rr frequency = 2pq = 2(0.5)(0.5) = 0.50
  • Expected rr frequency = q² = (0.5)² = 0.25

Step 5: Compare Observed vs Expected

Conclusion: This population IS in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium because observed frequencies match expected frequencies exactly.

Step 2: Calculate Dominant Allele Frequency (p)

  • Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2(0.98)(0.02) = 0.0392

Answer c: Frequency of carriers = 0.0392 or 3.92%

Question 9 (5 marks)

Huntington's disease is an autosomal dominant disorder with delayed onset. If the frequency of the disease allele is 0.0001 in a population, what proportion of the population will eventually develop the disease? What proportion will be carriers?

Answer:

Given:

  • Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant
  • Frequency of disease allele (H) = p = 0.0001
  • Frequency of normal allele (h) = q = 1 - 0.0001 = 0.9999

Step 1: Determine Genotype Frequencies

Using Hardy-Weinberg equation: p² + 2pq + q² = 1

  • HH frequency = p² = (0.0001)² = 0.00000001
  • Hh frequency = 2pq = 2(0.0001)(0.9999) = 0.00019998
  • hh frequency = q² = (0.9999)² = 0.99980001

Step 2: Determine Disease Expression

Since Huntington's is dominant:

  • Affected individuals: HH + Hh = p² + 2pq
  • Unaffected individuals: hh = q²

Step 3: Calculate Proportions

Affected (will develop disease): p² + 2pq = 0.00000001 + 0.00019998 = 0.00019999 ≈ 0.0002 or 0.02%

Note about "carriers": In dominant disorders, there are no true "carriers" in the traditional sense, as anyone with the allele will express the disease. However, if the question refers to heterozygotes:

Heterozygotes (Hh): 2pq = 0.00019998 ≈ 0.0002 or 0.02%

Answers:

  • Proportion developing disease: 0.02% (approximately 1 in 5,000)
  • Proportion of heterozygotes: 0.02% (virtually all affected individuals are heterozygotes due to the low allele frequency)

Question 10 (5 marks)

Explain the concept of genetic anticipation using Huntington's disease as an example. Include in your answer the molecular mechanism and inheritance pattern.

Answer:

Definition of Genetic Anticipation: Genetic anticipation is the phenomenon where a genetic disorder shows earlier onset and/or increased severity in successive generations, particularly when transmitted through certain parent-child combinations.

Huntington's Disease Example:

Inheritance Pattern:

  • Autosomal dominant inheritance
  • Located on chromosome 4
  • Shows anticipation primarily through paternal transmission
  • Affects both males and females equally

Molecular Mechanism:

1. CAG Repeat Expansion:

  • Huntington's disease is caused by expanded CAG trinucleotide repeats in the huntingtin gene (HTT)
  • Normal individuals: 6-35 CAG repeats
  • Affected individuals: 36+ CAG repeats
  • The CAG repeats code for glutamine residues in the huntingtin protein

2. Repeat Instability:

  • CAG repeats are unstable during DNA replication
  • Tendency for expansion increases with repeat number
  • Paternal transmission shows greater instability than maternal transmission
  • Expansions typically occur during spermatogenesis

3. Genotype-Phenotype Correlation:

  • Larger repeat numbers correlate with:
    • Earlier age of onset
    • More severe symptoms
    • Faster disease progression

Clinical Manifestation of Anticipation:

  • Grandparent: onset at age 60, 40 CAG repeats
  • Parent: onset at age 45, 45 CAG repeats
  • Child: onset at age 30, 55 CAG repeats

Molecular Consequences:

  • Expanded polyglutamine tract causes protein misfolding
  • Formation of toxic protein aggregates
  • Neuronal dysfunction and death, particularly in the striatum
  • Progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms

This mechanism explains why genetic counseling is crucial for families with Huntington's disease, as the risk and severity can change between generations.

Question 11 (5 marks)

A researcher studying a quantitative trait in plants finds that the variance in a controlled environment (V_E) is 20, and the total phenotypic variance (V_P) in the natural population is 80. Calculate the heritability (h²) of this trait and explain what this value means for breeding programs.

Answer:

Step 1: Identify the Components of Variance

  • Environmental variance (V_E) = 20
  • Total phenotypic variance (V_P) = 80
  • Genetic variance (V_G) = V_P - V_E = 80 - 20 = 60

Step 2: Calculate Heritability Narrow-sense heritability: h² = V_A / V_P

Assuming all genetic variance is additive (V_G = V_A): h² = V_G / V_P = 60 / 80 = 0.75

Answer: h² = 0.75 or 75%

Step 3: Interpretation for Breeding Programs

Meaning of h² = 0.75:

  • 75% of the phenotypic variation in this population is due to genetic factors
  • 25% of the variation is due to environmental factors
  • This is considered high heritability

Implications for Breeding:

1. Response to Selection:

  • High heritability means good response to selection
  • Selection intensity will be effective in improving the trait
  • Response to selection (R) = h² × Selection differential (S)

2. Breeding Strategy:

  • Individual selection will be highly effective
  • Phenotypic selection can reliably identify genetically superior individuals
  • Fast genetic progress possible over few generations

3. Environmental Control:

  • Less need for extensive environmental controls during selection
  • Field selection may be as effective as controlled environment selection

4. Breeding Program Design:

  • Can use moderate population sizes
  • Shorter testing periods may be sufficient
  • Higher confidence in breeding value predictions

5. Economic Considerations:

  • Cost-effective breeding program
  • Rapid return on investment
  • Lower risk of selection failure

Caution: Heritability is population and environment-specific, so this value applies only to this specific population under these conditions.

Question 12 (10 marks)

In a small island population of birds, a hurricane reduces the population from 1000 to 50 individuals. The allele frequency for beak size changes from p = 0.6 to p = 0.8 after the hurricane. Explain what evolutionary forces are acting on this population and predict the long-term consequences for genetic diversity. Discuss how this relates to conservation genetics.

Answer:

Step 1: Identify the Evolutionary Forces

Primary Force: Genetic Drift (Population Bottleneck)

  • Severe reduction from 1000 to 50 individuals represents a population bottleneck
  • Random sampling effect causes allele frequency change (0.6 → 0.8)
  • Bottleneck effect is a special case of genetic drift

Secondary Forces:

  • Founder effect: If survivors establish new colonies
  • Inbreeding: Increased mating between relatives due to small population size
  • Reduced gene flow: Isolation limits migration

Step 2: Immediate Genetic Consequences

Loss of Genetic Diversity:

  • Allelic diversity: Many rare alleles likely lost during bottleneck
  • Heterozygosity reduction: Expected heterozygosity decreases
  • Population variance: Reduced genetic variation for quantitative traits

Mathematical Analysis:

  • Original He = 2pq = 2(0.6)(0.4) = 0.48
  • Post-bottleneck He = 2pq = 2(0.8)(0.2) = 0.32
  • Loss of heterozygosity = (0.48 - 0.32)/0.48 = 33% reduction

Step 3: Long-term Consequences

Genetic Factors:

  1. Continued genetic drift: Small population size maintains strong drift effects
  2. Inbreeding depression: Increased homozygosity may expose deleterious recessive alleles
  3. Reduced adaptive potential: Limited genetic variation constrains evolutionary response
  4. Fixation of alleles: Random fixation or loss of alleles continues

Population Dynamics:

  • Effective population size (Ne): Remains small, amplifying genetic drift
  • Breeding success: Potential reduction due to inbreeding depression
  • Demographic stochasticity: Random fluctuations in birth/death rates more impactful

Step 4: Recovery Scenarios

Scenario 1: Population Recovery

  • If population grows back to large size quickly:
    • Genetic diversity remains permanently reduced
    • "Genetic bottleneck signature" persists
    • Some heterozygosity may be restored but allelic diversity lost forever

Scenario 2: Continued Small Population

  • Progressive loss of genetic variation
  • Increased inbreeding coefficient (F)
  • Higher extinction risk due to genetic factors

Step 5: Conservation Genetics Implications

Immediate Conservation Actions:

  1. Population Monitoring:
    • Track population size and breeding success
    • Monitor genetic diversity using molecular markers
    • Assess inbreeding levels through pedigree analysis
  2. Genetic Management:
    • Genetic rescue: Introduce individuals from other populations
    • Minimize inbreeding: Manage breeding to maximize genetic diversity
    • Maintain detailed pedigrees: Track relationships to guide breeding decisions
  3. Habitat Management:
    • Ensure sufficient carrying capacity for population growth
    • Reduce environmental stressors that compound genetic problems
    • Create corridors for potential gene flow

Long-term Conservation Strategy:

Population Size Targets:

  • 50/500 rule: Minimum 50 individuals to avoid inbreeding depression short-term
  • Target 500+ individuals for long-term evolutionary potential
  • Current population (50) is at critical threshold

Genetic Rescue Considerations:

  • Source populations: Identify genetically compatible populations
  • Outbreeding depression risk: Assess genetic differentiation before introduction
  • Adaptive differences: Consider local adaptation when selecting source populations

Monitoring Programs:

  • Genetic monitoring: Regular assessment using molecular markers
  • Demographic monitoring: Track population growth and reproductive success
  • Fitness monitoring: Measure survival, reproduction, and health parameters

Step 6: Broader Conservation Principles

Minimum Viable Population (MVP):

  • Current population below most MVP estimates
  • Genetic factors now primary threat to persistence
  • Demographic and environmental stochasticity also increased risks

Conservation Genetics Theory:

  • Effective population size: Ne = 4NmNf/(Nm + Nf) for breeding population
  • Inbreeding coefficient: F increases by 1/(2Ne) per generation
  • Loss of heterozygosity: Progressive decline without gene flow

Management Recommendations:

Immediate (1-2 years):

  • Implement genetic rescue if compatible populations available
  • Establish breeding program to minimize inbreeding
  • Conduct genetic assessment of remaining individuals

Medium-term (5-10 years):

  • Monitor population recovery and genetic diversity
  • Assess need for continued genetic management
  • Evaluate success of conservation interventions

Long-term (>10 years):

  • Maintain genetic monitoring program
  • Plan for habitat expansion to support larger populations
  • Develop protocols for future genetic management

Conclusion: This population faces severe genetic constraints due to the bottleneck event. The 95% population reduction and associated loss of genetic diversity represents a conservation emergency requiring immediate genetic management. Without intervention, the population faces high extinction risk due to combined genetic, demographic, and environmental factors. The case illustrates why maintaining large, connected populations is crucial for species conservation, and demonstrates the central role of population genetics in conservation biology.

The change in allele frequency from 0.6 to 0.8, while appearing minor, represents a significant loss of genetic diversity that will have lasting consequences for this population's evolutionary potential and long-term viability.

The ability of an organism to resist infections by the pathogens is called:

a) Infection
b) Hypersensitivity
c) Immunity
d) Allergy
e) Attenuation

Answer: c) Immunity

Explanation: Immunity is the body's natural defense mechanism against pathogenic microorganisms, toxins, and other harmful substances.

Question 2

Name the group of pattern recognition molecules which functions exclusively as a signaling receptor:

a) CRP
b) Toll-like receptor
c) MBL
d) LPS
e) MMLS

Answer: b) Toll-like receptor

Explanation: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are pattern recognition receptors that recognize PAMPs and function exclusively as signaling receptors.

Question 3

Name the first cells which are recruited at the place of infection:

a) NK cells
b) Basophils
c) Neutrophils
d) Macrophages
e) A and B

Answer: c) Neutrophils

Explanation: Neutrophils are the first immune cells to arrive at the site of infection during acute inflammation.

Question 4

Which of the following antibody gives a primary immune reaction:

a) IgG
b) IgM
c) IgA
d) IgE
e) A and B

Answer: b) IgM

Explanation: IgM is the first antibody produced during a primary immune response and is most effective at complement activation.

Question 5

Which of these is NOT a characteristic feature of adaptive immunity:

a) Immunogenic memory
b) Antigen non-specific
c) Self/non-self recognition
d) Diversity
e) None of the above

Answer: b) Antigen non-specific

Explanation: Adaptive immunity is highly antigen-specific, unlike innate immunity which is non-specific.

Question 6

The major role of the complement system is to work in conjunction with:

a) Antibodies to lyse cells via the C8 and C9 components
b) Antibodies to lyse cells via the perforin molecules
c) Antibodies to opsonize cells
d) The major histocompatibility complex for cell recognition
e) The T-cell receptor for production of lymphokines

Answer: a) Antibodies to lyse cells via the C8 and C9 components

Explanation: The complement system works with antibodies to form the membrane attack complex (MAC) using C5b-C9 components.

Question 7

One principal function of complement is to:

a) Bind antibodies attached to cell surfaces and to lyse these cells
b) Cross-link allergens
c) Inactivate perforins
d) Mediate the release of histamine
e) Phagocytize antigens

Answer: a) Bind antibodies attached to cell surfaces and to lyse these cells

Explanation: The complement system binds to antibodies on target cells and forms MAC to lyse the cells.

Question 8

Complement component C3 is cleaved by:

a) C3bB
b) C3bBb
c) Factor B
d) Factor D
e) Factor H

Answer: b) C3bBb

Explanation: C3bBb is the C3 convertase of the alternative pathway that cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

Question 9

The membrane attack complex in the complement pathway consists of:

a) C3b3b, Bb
b) C5b,6,7,8,9
c) Colicins
d) OH
e) Properdin

Answer: b) C5b,6,7,8,9

Explanation: The membrane attack complex (MAC) is formed by complement components C5b, C6, C7, C8, and C9.

Question 10

Acute inflammation can be initiated by:

a) An increase in vascular permeability
b) C3
c) Influx of neutrophils
d) Lysozyme
e) Mast cell activation

Answer: e) Mast cell activation

Explanation: Mast cell activation releases inflammatory mediators like histamine, which initiate acute inflammation.

Question 11

Clonal selection occurs when antigen is encountered by:

a) Basophils
b) Eosinophils
c) Mast cells
d) Neutrophils
e) T-cell

Answer: e) T-cell

Explanation: Clonal selection is the process where specific T cells that recognize a particular antigen are selected for proliferation.

Question 12

Complement component C3b:

a) Directly injures bacteria
b) Is an anaphylatoxin
c) Is chemotactic
d) Is the inactive form of C3
e) Opsonizes bacteria

Answer: e) Opsonizes bacteria

Explanation: C3b is a major opsonin that coats bacteria, marking them for phagocytosis by immune cells.

Question 13

Naturally acquired active immunity would be most likely acquired through which of the following processes:

a) Vaccination
b) Drinking colostrum
c) Natural birth
d) Infection with disease-causing organism followed by recovery
e) Both A and C

Answer: d) Infection with disease-causing organism followed by recovery

Explanation: Naturally acquired active immunity occurs when the immune system responds to a natural infection.

Question 14

Which of the following convey the longest-lasting immunity to an infectious agent:

a) Naturally acquired passive immunity
b) Artificially acquired passive immunity
c) Naturally acquired active immunity
d) All of these
e) None of these

Answer: c) Naturally acquired active immunity

Explanation: Naturally acquired active immunity provides the longest-lasting protection through memory cell development.

Question 15

Which of the following substances will not stimulate an immune response unless they are bound to a larger molecule:

a) Antigen
b) Virus
c) Hapten
d) Mitogen
e) Antibody

Answer: c) Hapten

Explanation: Haptens are small molecules that become immunogenic only when conjugated to larger carrier molecules.

Question 16

B and T cells are produced by stem cells that are formed in:

a) Bone marrow
b) The liver
c) The circulatory system
d) The spleen
e) The lymph nodes

Answer: a) Bone marrow

Explanation: Hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow give rise to all blood cells, including B and T cell precursors.

Question 17

B cells mature in the....... while T cells mature in the........:

a) Thymus/bone marrow and gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT)
b) Spleen/bone marrow and GALT
c) Bone marrow and GALT/Thymus
d) Liver/Kidneys

Answer: c) Bone marrow and GALT/Thymus

Explanation: B cells mature in bone marrow and GALT, while T cells migrate to and mature in the thymus.

Question 18

Which of the following immune cells/molecules are most effective at destroying intracellular pathogens:

a) T helper cells
b) B cells
c) Antibodies
d) Complement
e) T cytolytic cells

Answer: e) T cytolytic cells

Explanation: T cytolytic cells (CD8+ T cells) are specialized to kill cells infected with intracellular pathogens.

Question 19

A living microbe with reduced virulence that is used for vaccination is considered:

a) A toxoid
b) Dormant
c) Virulent
d) Attenuated
e) Denatured

Answer: d) Attenuated

Explanation: Attenuated microorganisms are live pathogens that have been weakened to stimulate immunity without causing disease.

Question 20

B cells that produce and release large amounts of antibody are called:

a) Memory cells
b) Basophils
c) Plasma cells
d) Killer cells
e) Neutrophils

Answer: c) Plasma cells

Explanation: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells specialized for antibody production.

Question 21

The specificity of an antibody is due to:

a) Its valence
b) The heavy chains
c) The Fc portion of the molecule
d) The variable portion of the heavy and light chain
e) A and B

Answer: d) The variable portion of the heavy and light chain

Explanation: The variable regions of both heavy and light chains form the antigen-binding site, determining antibody specificity.

Question 22

In agglutination reactions, the antigen is a....... in precipitation reactions, the antigen is a......:

a) whole cell/soluble molecule
b) Soluble molecule/whole cell
c) Bacterium/virus
d) Protein/carbohydrates
e) Protein/Antibody

Answer: a) whole cell/soluble molecule

Explanation: Agglutination involves clumping of whole cells, while precipitation involves soluble antigens.

Question 23

B Cells are activated by:

a) Complement
b) Antibody
c) Interferon
d) Memory cells
e) Antigen

Answer: e) Antigen

Explanation: B cells are activated when their surface immunoglobulin receptors bind to specific antigens.

Question 24

Fusion between a plasma cell and a tumor cell creates a:

a) Myeloma
b) Natural killer cell
c) Lymphoblast
d) Lymphoma
e) Hybridoma

Answer: e) Hybridoma

Explanation: Hybridomas are created by fusing plasma cells with tumor cells to produce monoclonal antibodies.

Question 25

Monoclonal antibodies recognize a single:

a) Antigen
b) Bacterium
c) Epitope
d) B cell
e) Virus

Answer: c) Epitope

Explanation: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by identical B cell clones and recognize a single specific epitope.

Question 26

Cell-mediated immunity is carried out by...... while humoral immunity is mainly carried out by......:

a) B cells/T cells
b) Epitopes/Antigens
c) T cells/B cells
d) Antibodies/Antigens
e) Antibodies/Phagocytes

Answer: c) T cells/B cells

Explanation: Cell-mediated immunity involves T cells, while humoral immunity involves B cells producing antibodies.

Question 27

The ability of the immune system to recognize self-antigens versus non-self-antigen is an example of:

a) Specific immunity
b) Tolerance
c) Cell-mediated immunity
d) Antigenic immunity
e) Humoral immunity

Answer: b) Tolerance

Explanation: Immune tolerance allows the immune system to distinguish between self and non-self antigens.

Question 28

Which of the following antibodies would most likely be found in body secretions such as tears, milk, saliva and mucus:

a) IgA
b) IgM
c) IgE
d) IgD
e) IgG

Answer: a) IgA

Explanation: IgA is the predominant antibody in mucosal secretions and provides protection at body surfaces.

Question 29

Which antibody is the first to be released into the blood following an infection:

a) IgD
b) IgG
c) IgA
d) IgE
e) IgM

Answer: e) IgM

Explanation: IgM is the first antibody produced during a primary immune response.

Question 30

Which is NOT true of memory cells:

a) Are part of a secondary response
b) Are part of an anamnestic response
c) They can survive without dividing for many months to many years
d) They produce more IgG than IgM
e) Are natural killer cells

Answer: e) Are natural killer cells

Explanation: Memory cells are long-lived B and T cells that provide rapid response upon re-exposure to antigen, not NK cells.

Question 31

An antigen that over stimulates the immune system by binding non-specifically to MHC on antigen presenting cells is termed a:

a) Non-specific antigen
b) Super antigen
c) Epitope
d) Toxic shock syndrome
e) Super necrotic

Answer: b) Super antigen

Explanation: Superantigens bind directly to MHC class II molecules, causing massive T cell activation.

Question 32

The variable regions in the light chains participate in:

a) Fc receptor binding
b) Epitope binding
c) Affinity of the complement receptors
d) Interaction of the Fab with cytokines
e) None of the above

Answer: b) Epitope binding

Explanation: Variable regions of light chains form part of the antigen-binding site for epitope recognition.

Question 33

Which of the following does not protect body surfaces:

a) Skin
b) Mucus
c) Gastric acid
d) Salivary amylase
e) Gut microflora

Answer: d) Salivary amylase

Question 34

Which of the following immunity is obtained during a lifetime:

b) Active immunity

Answer: d) Both A and B

The variable regions in the light chains participate in:

Which of the following immunity is obtained during a lifetime:

b) Active immunity

Which of the following statements is true about the IgM of humans:

SECTION B: ESSAY QUESTION (10 MARKS)

Question:

Explain how APCs and MHC I and II collaborate to prevent spread of an infection (10 Marks)

Answer:

Antigen Presenting Cells (APCs) and Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) molecules work together in a sophisticated system to prevent the spread of infections through effective immune surveillance and response coordination.

MHC Class I Pathway (Endogenous Antigen Presentation)

MHC Class I molecules are present on all nucleated cells and present intracellular peptides to CD8+ T cells. When cells are infected by intracellular pathogens such as viruses, the pathogen's proteins are degraded by the proteasome in the cytoplasm. The resulting peptides are transported into the endoplasmic reticulum via TAP (Transporter associated with Antigen Processing) proteins, where they bind to newly synthesized MHC Class I molecules. This MHC I-peptide complex is then transported to the cell surface.

CD8+ T cells (cytotoxic T lymphocytes) recognize these foreign peptides presented on MHC Class I molecules through their T cell receptors. Once activated, these cytotoxic T cells release perforin and granzymes, leading to the destruction of infected cells before the pathogen can replicate and spread to neighboring cells.

MHC Class II Pathway (Exogenous Antigen Presentation)

Professional APCs, including dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells, express MHC Class II molecules and specialize in presenting exogenous antigens. These cells capture pathogens or pathogen-derived materials from the extracellular environment through phagocytosis, pinocytosis, or receptor-mediated endocytosis.

The internalized antigens are processed in endosomal/lysosomal compartments where they are degraded by acidic proteases. MHC Class II molecules, synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum and initially associated with the invariant chain, are transported to these compartments. The invariant chain is then cleaved, leaving CLIP (Class II-associated invariant chain peptide), which is subsequently replaced by the processed antigenic peptides through the action of HLA-DM.

The MHC II-peptide complexes are then transported to the cell surface where they are recognized by CD4+ T helper cells. This recognition, along with co-stimulatory signals, leads to T helper cell activation and proliferation.

Collaborative Prevention of Infection Spread

The collaboration between APCs and MHC molecules prevents infection spread through several mechanisms:

1. Early Detection and Response: Dendritic cells act as sentinels in tissues, capturing antigens and migrating to lymph nodes where they present processed antigens to naive T cells, initiating adaptive immune responses before widespread infection occurs.

2. Coordinated Immune Activation: MHC Class II presentation by APCs activates CD4+ T helper cells, which then provide help to CD8+ T cells (through cytokine production) and B cells (for antibody production), creating a coordinated immune response.

3. Memory Formation: The presentation of antigens by APCs leads to the formation of memory T and B cells, providing long-term protection against reinfection.

4. Cross-Presentation: Some dendritic cells can present exogenous antigens on MHC Class I molecules (cross-presentation), allowing for CD8+ T cell responses against pathogens that don't directly infect the dendritic cells.

5. Immune Surveillance: The continuous presentation of self and foreign peptides on MHC molecules allows the immune system to monitor cellular health and detect abnormal or infected cells throughout the body.

This integrated system ensures that infections are detected early, appropriate immune responses are mounted, and immunological memory is established to prevent future infections by the same pathogen.

1. Role of Gastrin in Gastro-intestinal Motility

Question: Write short notes on the role of Gastrin in Gastro-intestinal motility

Answer: Gastrin is a peptide hormone secreted by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum that plays crucial roles in gastrointestinal motility:

Gastric Motility Effects:

  • Stimulates gastric smooth muscle contractions, enhancing gastric mixing and churning
  • Increases antral contractions, promoting gastric emptying
  • Enhances lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone, preventing gastroesophageal reflux

Small Intestinal Effects:

  • Stimulates duodenal and jejunal peristalsis
  • Coordinates migrating motor complexes (MMCs) during fasting periods
  • Promotes segmentation contractions for mixing

Colonic Effects:

  • Stimulates colonic motility and mass movements
  • Enhances ileocecal valve function

Mechanism: Gastrin acts through CCK-B receptors on smooth muscle cells and enteric neurons, activating calcium-dependent pathways that increase contractility and coordinate peristaltic waves throughout the digestive tract.

2. Inhibition of Auto-digestion of the Pancreas

Question: Briefly explain how Auto-digestion of the Pancreas is inhibited

Answer: The pancreas protects itself from auto-digestion through multiple protective mechanisms:

Enzyme Synthesis as Inactive Precursors:

  • Proteolytic enzymes are synthesized as inactive zymogens (trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase)
  • Stored in zymogen granules within acinar cells
  • Activated only after secretion into the duodenum

Protease Inhibitors:

  • Pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor (PSTI) blocks premature trypsin activation
  • Serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1 (SPINK1) provides additional protection
  • α1-antitrypsin in plasma neutralizes any leaked enzymes

Cellular Compartmentalization:

  • Strict separation between synthesis, storage, and secretion compartments
  • Zymogen granules maintain acidic pH preventing activation
  • Regulated exocytosis prevents intracellular enzyme release

Ductal Bicarbonate Secretion:

  • High bicarbonate concentration in pancreatic juice neutralizes any acidic conditions
  • Maintains optimal pH for enzyme stability during transport

Rapid Enzyme Clearance:

  • Efficient drainage through pancreatic duct system
  • Quick transit to duodenum prevents accumulation

3. Process of Fat Digestion

Question: Briefly highlight the process of digestion of fats

Answer: Fat digestion occurs through a coordinated process involving mechanical, chemical, and enzymatic breakdown:

Oral Phase:

  • Minimal digestion occurs
  • Lingual lipase begins triglyceride hydrolysis (10-30% of total)
  • Mechanical breakdown through chewing

Gastric Phase:

  • Gastric lipase continues fat hydrolysis
  • Gastric acid and pepsin help break down fat-protein complexes
  • Gastric churning creates crude emulsification

Intestinal Phase - Emulsification:

  • Bile salts from gallbladder create stable emulsions
  • Reduces fat droplet size from 1mm to 1μm
  • Phospholipids and proteins aid emulsification

Pancreatic Enzyme Action:

  • Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides to monoglycerides and fatty acids
  • Colipase facilitates lipase binding to lipid interface
  • Phospholipase A2 breaks down phospholipids
  • Cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes cholesterol esters

Micelle Formation:

  • Bile salts form mixed micelles with digestion products
  • Facilitates absorption at brush border membrane
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) incorporated into micelles

Absorption:

  • Occurs primarily in jejunum
  • Passive diffusion into enterocytes
  • Reformation into chylomicrons for lymphatic transport

4. Physiology of Satiety Following Heavy Meal

Question: Following a heavy meal, discuss the physiology behind Satiety

Answer: Satiety after a heavy meal involves complex hormonal, neural, and mechanical mechanisms:

Mechanical Factors:

  • Gastric distension activates stretch receptors in stomach wall
  • Vagal afferents signal fullness to brainstem
  • Increased intragastric pressure triggers satiety reflexes

Hormonal Signals:

  • Cholecystokinin (CCK): Released from duodenal I-cells, promotes satiety through vagal pathways
  • Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1): Secreted by L-cells, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite
  • Peptide YY (PYY): Released from ileum and colon, inhibits gastric motility and food intake
  • Leptin: Increases from adipose tissue, provides long-term satiety signaling

Neural Mechanisms:

  • Hypothalamic integration of satiety signals
  • Activation of POMC/CART neurons in arcuate nucleus
  • Inhibition of NPY/AgRP neurons (hunger centers)
  • Brainstem processing of vagal afferent signals

Metabolic Factors:

  • Increased blood glucose and amino acid levels
  • Enhanced insulin sensitivity
  • Metabolic switching from hunger to fed state

Integration:

  • Hypothalamic nuclei integrate peripheral signals
  • Modulation of feeding behavior through higher brain centers
  • Coordination with autonomic nervous system responses

5. Effects of Thyroid Hormone on Cardiovascular System

Question: List the effects of thyroid hormone on the cardiovascular system

Answer: Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) have profound effects on cardiovascular function:

Cardiac Effects:

  • Increased heart rate: Direct chronotropic effect on SA node
  • Increased contractility: Enhanced myocardial contractile force (positive inotropic effect)
  • Increased cardiac output: Result of increased HR and stroke volume
  • Shortened cardiac cycle: Reduced diastolic filling time

Vascular Effects:

  • Decreased peripheral vascular resistance: Vasodilation in peripheral tissues
  • Increased blood volume: Enhanced erythropoiesis and plasma volume
  • Improved endothelial function: Enhanced nitric oxide production
  • Increased coronary blood flow: Meets increased metabolic demands

Blood Pressure Changes:

  • Widened pulse pressure: Increased systolic, decreased diastolic pressure
  • Systolic hypertension: Common in hyperthyroidism
  • Enhanced sensitivity to catecholamines: Increased β-adrenergic receptor expression

Electrophysiological Effects:

  • Shortened action potential duration: Altered ion channel expression
  • Increased conduction velocity: Enhanced AV node conduction
  • Arrhythmia predisposition: Particularly atrial fibrillation

Metabolic Cardiovascular Effects:

  • Increased oxygen consumption: Enhanced cellular metabolism
  • Increased heat production: Cardiovascular adaptation to thermoregulation
  • Enhanced calcium cycling: Improved sarcoplasmic reticulum function

6. Physiological Functions of Pancreatic Hormone Glucagon

Question: Briefly discuss the physiological functions of the Pancreatic Hormone Glucagon

Answer: Glucagon, secreted by alpha cells of pancreatic islets, serves as the primary counter-regulatory hormone to insulin:

Hepatic Effects:

  • Glycogenolysis: Stimulates glycogen breakdown to glucose
  • Gluconeogenesis: Promotes glucose synthesis from amino acids, lactate, and glycerol
  • Ketogenesis: Enhances fatty acid oxidation and ketone body production
  • Inhibits glycogen synthesis: Blocks glycogen synthase activity

Metabolic Functions:

  • Lipolysis: Activates hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue
  • Protein catabolism: Promotes amino acid mobilization for gluconeogenesis
  • Maintains blood glucose: Prevents hypoglycemia during fasting states
  • Metabolic switching: Shifts from glucose utilization to fat oxidation

Regulatory Mechanisms:

  • Insulin antagonism: Opposes insulin's anabolic effects
  • Stress response: Increases during physical and metabolic stress
  • Amino acid sensitivity: Stimulated by protein-rich meals
  • Autonomic regulation: Enhanced by sympathetic nervous system

Clinical Significance:

  • Hypoglycemia treatment: Emergency glucose mobilization
  • Fasting adaptation: Maintains glucose homeostasis
  • Exercise physiology: Supports glucose production during physical activity

Mechanism of Action:

  • Acts through G-protein coupled receptors
  • Activates adenylyl cyclase and increases cAMP
  • Activates protein kinase A pathway
  • Phosphorylates key enzymes in glucose metabolism

7. Countercurrent Multiplier System in Kidneys

Question: With the aid of a diagram write short notes on the Countercurrent Multiplier system in the Kidneys

Answer: The countercurrent multiplier system in the nephron's loop of Henle concentrates urine and conserves water:

Structure:

Mechanism:

  • Descending limb: Permeable to water, impermeable to solutes
  • Ascending limb: Impermeable to water, actively transports Na+, K+, Cl-
  • Countercurrent flow: Opposite directions create concentration gradient

Process:

  1. Active transport in thick ascending limb creates initial concentration difference
  2. Water moves out of descending limb, concentrating tubular fluid
  3. Solutes move out of ascending limb, diluting tubular fluid
  4. Continuous flow multiplies the concentration gradient
  5. Vasa recta maintains the gradient through countercurrent exchange
  6. Result: Ability to produce concentrated urine when needed

Functions:

  • Urine concentration: Enables production of concentrated urine
  • Water conservation: Reduces water loss during dehydration
  • Osmotic gradient: Creates medullary hypertonicity
  • ADH sensitivity: Allows collecting duct to respond to hormonal control

Clinical Importance:

  • Diabetes insipidus: Defective concentration ability
  • Diuretic action: Loop diuretics disrupt the multiplier system
  • Kidney function assessment: Concentrating ability indicates nephron health

8. Hormones Secreted During Pregnancy and Their Roles

Question: In systematic order briefly discuss the hormones secreted during Pregnancy and their roles

Answer: Pregnancy involves complex hormonal changes that support fetal development and maternal adaptation:

First Trimester:

  • Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG):
    • Maintains corpus luteum
    • Prevents menstruation
    • Basis for pregnancy tests
    • Peaks at 8-10 weeks

Throughout Pregnancy:

  • Progesterone:
    • Maintains uterine quiescence
    • Prepares mammary glands
    • Modulates immune system
    • Supports fetal development
  • Estrogen (Estradiol, Estriol):
    • Promotes uterine growth
    • Increases blood volume
    • Prepares breasts for lactation
    • Enhances uteroplacental blood flow

Second/Third Trimester:

  • Human Placental Lactogen (hPL):
    • Maternal glucose homeostasis
    • Promotes mammary gland development
    • Anti-insulin effects
    • Fetal growth promotion
  • Relaxin:
    • Softens cervix and pubic symphysis
    • Inhibits uterine contractions
    • Promotes blood vessel formation
    • Facilitates delivery

Near Term:

  • Prostaglandins:
    • Initiate labor contractions
    • Cervical ripening
    • Membrane rupture
    • Coordinate parturition
  • Oxytocin:
    • Stimulates uterine contractions
    • Facilitates milk ejection
    • Promotes maternal bonding
    • Positive feedback during labor

Maternal Adaptations:

  • Insulin: Increased production, decreased sensitivity
  • Cortisol: Elevated levels, fetal lung maturation
  • Parathyroid hormone: Calcium homeostasis
  • Thyroid hormones: Increased metabolic rate

9. Phases of Male Sexual Response

Question: Write short notes on the phases for Male sexual response

Answer: The male sexual response follows a predictable pattern with distinct physiological phases:

1. Excitement Phase:

  • Duration: Variable, minutes to hours
  • Physiological changes:
    • Penile erection through vascular engorgement
    • Increased heart rate and blood pressure
    • Scrotal thickening and testicular elevation
    • Nipple erection and muscle tension
  • Mechanism: Parasympathetic nervous system activation
  • Neurovascular: Nitric oxide release, smooth muscle relaxation

2. Plateau Phase:

  • Duration: Few minutes to extended period
  • Characteristics:
    • Sustained erection with increased rigidity
    • Glans penis color deepening
    • Cowper's gland secretion (pre-ejaculatory fluid)
    • Further testicular elevation and size increase
  • Physiological: Continued sympathetic and parasympathetic activity
  • Preparation: Body prepares for orgasmic response

3. Orgasmic Phase:

  • Duration: 3-15 seconds
  • Two stages:
    • Emission: Seminal fluid collection in prostatic urethra
    • Ejaculation: Rhythmic contractions expel semen
  • Physiological response:
    • Intense pleasurable sensation
    • Rhythmic contractions of bulbospongiosus muscle
    • Sympathetic nervous system dominance
  • Systemic effects: Peak heart rate, blood pressure, and respiration

4. Resolution Phase:

  • Duration: Minutes to hours
  • Characteristics:
    • Gradual loss of erection (two-stage detumescence)
    • Return of testes to normal size and position
    • Generalized muscle relaxation
    • Refractory period (inability to achieve another erection)
  • Recovery: Parasympathetic activity returns to baseline
  • Age-related: Refractory period lengthens with age

10. Associative Learning with Examples

Question: Giving appropriate examples, write short notes on Associative Learning

Answer: Associative learning involves forming connections between stimuli, responses, or events:

Classical Conditioning (Pavlovian):

  • Definition: Learning association between neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus
  • Example: Pavlov's dogs - bell (neutral) + food (unconditioned) → salivation (conditioned response)
  • Medical example: White coat hypertension - medical setting associated with stress
  • Mechanism: Temporal contiguity between stimuli strengthens neural pathways

Operant Conditioning (Instrumental):

  • Definition: Learning through consequences of behavior
  • Positive reinforcement: Behavior increases due to rewarding consequence
    • Example: Studying hard → good grades → continued studying
  • Negative reinforcement: Behavior increases by removing aversive stimulus
    • Example: Taking pain medication → pain relief → continued medication use
  • Punishment: Behavior decreases due to aversive consequence
    • Example: Speeding → traffic ticket → reduced speeding

Observational Learning:

  • Definition: Learning through observing others' behaviors and consequences
  • Example: Medical students learning procedures by watching experienced doctors
  • Mirror neurons: Specialized cells that fire when observing others' actions
  • Social modeling: Imitation of successful behaviors

Habituation:

  • Definition: Decreased response to repeated harmless stimuli
  • Example: Healthcare workers becoming less startled by medical equipment alarms
  • Mechanism: Synaptic depression in neural pathways
  • Adaptive value: Prevents sensory overload

Sensitization:

  • Definition: Increased response to stimuli after exposure to intense stimulus
  • Example: Hypervigilance to medical symptoms after traumatic diagnosis
  • Mechanism: Enhanced neural responsiveness
  • Clinical relevance: Post-traumatic stress responses

11. Components and Functions of Blood-Brain Barrier

Question: Discuss the components and functions of the Blood brain barrier

Answer: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a selective barrier protecting the central nervous system:

Anatomical Components:

  • Endothelial cells: Specialized brain capillary cells with tight junctions
  • Tight junctions: Occludin, claudin, and ZO proteins prevent paracellular transport
  • Basement membrane: Extracellular matrix supporting endothelial structure
  • Pericytes: Contractile cells regulating capillary diameter and BBB integrity
  • Astrocytes: Glial cells with end-feet processes surrounding capillaries

Molecular Components:

  • Efflux pumps: P-glycoprotein, BCRP remove xenobiotics
  • Transporters: GLUT1 (glucose), LAT1 (amino acids), specific carriers
  • Enzymes: Metabolic barriers degrading potential toxins
  • Receptors: Transferrin receptor, insulin receptor for selective transport

Protective Functions:

  • Selective permeability: Prevents harmful substances entering brain
  • Homeostasis maintenance: Maintains stable brain environment
  • Immune privilege: Limits inflammatory cell infiltration
  • pH regulation: Maintains optimal brain pH

Transport Functions:

  • Glucose transport: Primary energy source for brain
  • Amino acid transport: Essential for neurotransmitter synthesis
  • Lipophilic molecules: Passive diffusion of small, fat-soluble compounds
  • Receptor-mediated transport: Insulin, transferrin, leptin

Regulation:

  • Astrocyte influence: Maintain BBB integrity through growth factors
  • Pericyte control: Regulate tight junction formation
  • Inflammatory modulation: Cytokines can increase permeability
  • Pathological changes: Disruption in stroke, multiple sclerosis, Alzheimer's

Clinical Significance:

  • Drug delivery challenge: Limits CNS drug penetration
  • Disease states: BBB dysfunction in neurological disorders
  • Therapeutic targets: Strategies to enhance or bypass BBB

12. Basal Ganglia Pathway Affected in Parkinson's Disease

Question: Briefly write short notes on Basal Ganglia pathway affected in Parkinson's disease

Answer: Parkinson's disease involves degeneration of dopaminergic pathways in the basal ganglia motor circuit:

Normal Basal Ganglia Circuitry:

  • Direct pathway: Cortex → Striatum → GPi/SNr → Thalamus → Cortex
  • Indirect pathway: Cortex → Striatum → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr → Thalamus → Cortex
  • Dopamine modulation: SNc dopamine facilitates direct, inhibits indirect pathways

Pathological Changes in Parkinson's:

  • Primary lesion: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc)
  • Lewy bodies: Alpha-synuclein protein aggregates in remaining neurons
  • Progressive loss: 50-70% neuronal loss before symptoms appear

Circuit Dysfunction:

  • Reduced dopamine: Decreased D1 receptor activation (direct pathway)
  • Increased D2 inhibition: Enhanced indirect pathway activity
  • Net result: Increased inhibitory output from GPi/SNr to thalamus
  • Thalamic suppression: Reduced thalamocortical drive to motor cortex

Compensatory Changes:

  • Increased STN activity: Hyperactive subthalamic nucleus
  • GPe dysfunction: Altered globus pallidus externa firing patterns
  • Striatal plasticity: Maladaptive changes in striatal neurons
  • Cortical adaptation: Altered cortical motor planning

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Bradykinesia: Slowness of movement initiation and execution
  • Rigidity: Increased muscle tone and resistance to passive movement
  • Tremor: Resting tremor, typically 4-6 Hz
  • Postural instability: Impaired balance and gait disturbances

Therapeutic Implications:

Neuroprotective strategies: Preventing further neuronal loss

Dopamine replacement: L-DOPA, dopamine agonists

Deep brain stimulation: STN or GPi stimulation

Pathway modulation: Targeting specific circuit components

Answer all questions

MEDICAL PHYSIOLOGY EXAM ANSWERS

MBMP 2300 - Section A: Short Answer Questions

Question 1: How does the tubular secretion of H⁺ occur, and how does it achieve HCO₃⁻ reabsorption? (5 Marks)

Answer:

Tubular secretion of H⁺ occurs through two primary mechanisms:

Primary Active Transport:

  • H⁺-ATPase pumps in the apical membrane of intercalated cells actively transport H⁺ into the tubular lumen
  • This process requires ATP and creates an electrochemical gradient

Secondary Active Transport:

  • Na⁺/H⁺ antiporter (exchanger) in proximal tubule cells exchanges intracellular H⁺ for luminal Na⁺
  • Driven by the sodium gradient maintained by basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase

HCO₃⁻ Reabsorption Mechanism:

  • Secreted H⁺ combines with filtered HCO₃⁻ in the lumen to form H₂CO₃
  • Carbonic anhydrase on the brush border converts H₂CO₃ to H₂O and CO₂
  • CO₂ diffuses into the cell and is converted back to HCO₃⁻ by intracellular carbonic anhydrase
  • HCO₃⁻ exits the cell via basolateral Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ cotransporter, achieving net reabsorption

Question 2: Discuss potassium secretion by the nephron. (5 Marks)

Answer:

Location and Mechanism:

  • Primarily occurs in the principal cells of the collecting duct
  • K⁺ enters cells via basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump
  • K⁺ exits into tubular lumen through apical K⁺ channels (ROMK channels)

Regulation:

  1. Aldosterone: Increases K⁺ secretion by:
    • Increasing Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity
    • Increasing apical K⁺ channel expression
    • Enhancing Na⁺ reabsorption, creating favorable electrical gradient
  2. Plasma K⁺ concentration: High K⁺ levels directly stimulate aldosterone release and increase K⁺ secretion
  3. Tubular flow rate: Increased flow enhances K⁺ secretion by maintaining concentration gradients
  4. Acid-base status: Alkalosis promotes K⁺ secretion, while acidosis inhibits it

Clinical Significance:

  • Essential for K⁺ homeostasis and prevention of hyperkalemia
  • Dysregulation can lead to dangerous cardiac arrhythmias

Question 3: A male athlete taking large amounts of an androgenic steroid becomes sterile (unable to produce sperm capable of causing fertilization). Explain. (5 Marks)

Answer:

Mechanism of Steroid-Induced Infertility:

Negative Feedback Suppression:

  • Exogenous androgens suppress hypothalamic GnRH release
  • This leads to decreased pituitary FSH and LH secretion
  • Without adequate LH, Leydig cells reduce endogenous testosterone production
  • Without adequate FSH, Sertoli cells cannot support spermatogenesis

Direct Effects on Spermatogenesis:

  • High concentrations of synthetic androgens may have direct toxic effects on developing sperm cells
  • Altered testosterone/estrogen ratios affect normal sperm maturation
  • Disruption of the blood-testis barrier function

Testicular Atrophy:

  • Prolonged suppression of gonadotropins leads to testicular shrinkage
  • Reduced seminiferous tubule diameter and function
  • Decreased sperm production and quality

Reversibility:

  • Effects are typically reversible but may take 6-12 months after cessation
