Answer: E Explanation: CCK inhibits gastric motility but stimulates small intestinal motility. It doesn't inhibit intestinal motility.

Question 20

The GIT hormones are characterized by all the following except:

  • (A) They are secreted by APUD system and are divided into 2 families on the basis of their structural similarity.
  • (B) They are secreted in response to specific physiological stimuli during digestion.
  • (C) Their effects are abolished by cutting the nervous connections of GIT.
  • (D) They affect areas in GIT that may be far away from the sites of their release.
  • (E) I.V injection of their extracts produces similar effects to those produced by the stimuli that release them.

Answer: C Explanation: GIT hormones work through the bloodstream (endocrine action) and their effects are not abolished by cutting nerve connections, unlike neural control mechanisms.

Question 21

About the GRP, all the followings are true except:

  • (A) It inhibits the intestinal motility (through liberating gastrin).
  • (B) It increases the gastric secretion (through liberating gastrin).
  • (C) It increases the pancreatic secretion (through liberating gastrin).
  • (D) It is found in the hypothalamus (in addition to GIT).
  • (E) It is the neurotransmitter of the vagal nerve endings that terminate on G cells.

Answer: A Explanation: GRP (Gastrin-Releasing Peptide) stimulates gastrin release, which increases gastric and pancreatic secretion. However, gastrin doesn't significantly inhibit intestinal motility.

Question 22

Concerning the gastrin, all the following are true except:

  • (A) It is a polypeptide hormone that is secreted in several chemical forms.
  • (B) It is released from almost the whole GIT mucosa and its secretion is stimulated by vagal stimulation.
  • (C) It has a trophic effect on gastric mucosa and increases the gastric motility.
  • (D) Its release is stimulated by gastric distension and inhibited by presence of excess acid in pyloric antrum.
  • (E) It stimulates insulin secretion from pancreas.
  • (F) It is released only during gastric phase of gastric secretion and increases the secretion of only the oxyntic cells.

Answer: F Explanation: Gastrin is released during multiple phases (cephalic, gastric, and intestinal) and affects both parietal cells (acid) and chief cells (pepsinogen), not just parietal cells.

Question 23

All the followings are correct about gastrin except:

  • (A) It is stimulated by distension of antrum.
  • (B) It is stimulated by insulin-induced hypoglycemia.
  • (C) Its secretion is increased by secretin.

Answer: C Explanation: Secretin inhibits gastrin secretion as part of the negative feedback control of gastric acid secretion when acidic chyme enters the duodenum.

Question 24

A patient with trigeminal lesion would have the greatest difficulty with which of the following?

  • (A) Swallowing.
  • (B) Chewing.
  • (C) Receptive relaxation of the upper esophageal sphincter.
  • (D) Secondary peristalsis in the esophagus.

Answer: B Explanation: The trigeminal nerve (CN V) provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication. Damage would primarily affect chewing ability.

Question 25

Mastication is important because:

  • (A) Minimizes the mechanical damage to the gut mucosa.
  • (B) Allows the salivary enzymes to act for a longer time.
  • (C) Increases the surface area of the food particles.
  • (D) Destroys the protective coating present around some foods.
  • (E) All of the above.

Answer: E Explanation: Mastication serves all these functions: reduces particle size to prevent mucosal damage, increases surface area for enzyme action, allows more time for salivary enzyme activity, and breaks down protective coatings.

Question 26

Mastication:

  • (A) Is entirely a voluntary act.
  • (B) Includes both voluntary and reflex components.
  • (C) Is performed by muscles supplied by 7th (facial) nerve.
  • (D) It is normally initiated by conditioned reflexes.
  • (E) Is important for digestion of carbohydrates only.

Answer: B Explanation: Mastication has both voluntary initiation and reflex components (chewing reflex). The muscles of mastication are supplied by the trigeminal nerve (CN V), not facial nerve.

Question 27

Man is unable to digest dietary:

  • (A) Glycogen.
  • (B) Dextrin.
  • (C) Saccharose.
  • (D) Cellulose.
  • (E) Glucose.

Answer: D Explanation: Humans lack cellulase enzyme and cannot digest cellulose. All other carbohydrates listed can be digested by human enzymes.

Question 28

The salivary amylase:

  • (A) Is also called ptyalin and it is beta amylase.
  • (B) Is the only amylase in GIT.
  • (C) Digests mainly cooked starch.
  • (D) Is activated by either HCl or Ca++.
  • (E) Releases free glucose in the stomach.

Answer: C Explanation: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) is an alpha-amylase that works best on cooked (gelatinized) starch. It's inactivated by stomach acid and doesn't release free glucose directly.

Question 29

About salivary secretion (true or false):

  • (A) At rapid rate of secretion, its Na+ & Cl- concentrations increase while its K+ concentration decreases.
  • (B) It plays a significant role in digestion of lipids.
  • (C) It is best stimulated by sour food.
  • (D) It is entirely under nervous control.

Answer: A, C, D Explanation: At higher flow rates, saliva becomes more isotonic (higher Na+ and Cl-). Sour stimuli are potent salivary stimulants. Salivary secretion is under nervous control. Saliva contains minimal lipase.

Question 30

About salivary secretion (true or false):

  • (A) It is an alkaline hypertonic fluid.
  • (B) Its enzymes come mainly from the parotid and submaxillary glands.
  • (C) It is largely under hormonal control.
  • (D) Its mucus comes mainly from the submaxillary, sublingual and buccal glands.

Answer: B, D Explanation: Saliva is alkaline but hypotonic. Enzymes come from serous glands (parotid and submandibular), while mucus comes from mucous glands (submandibular, sublingual, and minor salivary glands). Control is neural, not hormonal.

Question 31

During the chewing of a bolus of food, but before swallowing, salivary secretion, gastric secretion and pancreatic secretion are stimulated by which of the following?

  • (A) Acetylcholine, gastrin, histamine.
  • (B) Acetylcholine, CCK, nitric oxide.
  • (C) Nitric oxide, VIP, histamine.
  • (D) VIP, gastrin, somatostatin.
  • (E) Nitric oxide, CCK, serotonin.

Answer: A Explanation: During the cephalic phase (before swallowing), acetylcholine stimulates salivary secretion, gastrin stimulates gastric secretion, and histamine (released by vagal stimulation) contributes to gastric acid secretion.

Question 32

The salivary secretion:

  • (A) Is rich in glucose.
  • (B) Is produced by a nervous mechanism only.
  • (C) Digests starch to glucose.
  • (D) Has the largest volume relative to other digestive juices.
  • (E) Is hyperosmotic relative to plasma.

Answer: B Explanation: Salivary secretion is under nervous control (parasympathetic primarily). It's hypotonic, contains minimal glucose, and breaks starch to maltose, not glucose.

Question 33

About salivary glands, which of the following statement is true?

  • (A) Their secretion is mainly under hormonal control.
  • (B) The sympathetic system is the only natural pathway for stimulation of their secretion.
  • (C) Both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves stimulate their secretion.
  • (D) Bradykinin decreases their blood flow rate.
  • (E) Their secretion increases in conditions of dehydration.

Answer: C Explanation: Both sympathetic and parasympathetic stimulation can increase salivary secretion, though parasympathetic is more important for volume and sympathetic for protein content.

Question 34

The saliva (true or false)?

  • (A) Contains no organic substances.
  • (B) Is markedly increased in amount after sympathetic stimulation.
  • (C) Secretion is increased after injection of atropine.
  • (D) Secreted by submandibular glands is about 70% of the total secretion.
  • (E) Volume averages 500 ml daily.

Answer: D Explanation: Submandibular glands produce about 70% of resting saliva. Saliva contains organic substances (enzymes, mucins), atropine decreases secretion, and daily volume is about 1500 ml.

Question 35

Secretion of the saliva increases when (true or false)?

  • (A) Touch receptors in the mouth are stimulated.
  • (B) The mouth is flushed with acid fluid with a pH of about 4.
  • (C) A subject thinks of unappetizing food.
  • (D) Vomiting is imminent.
  • (E) The sympathetic nerve supply is stimulated.

Answer: A, B, D, E Explanation: Mechanical stimulation, acid stimulation, pre-vomiting reflexes, and sympathetic stimulation all increase salivary secretion. Unappetizing food typically doesn't stimulate secretion.

Question 36

The presentation of a bolus of solid food to the mouth:

  • (A) Stimulates taste buds.
  • (B) Is usually followed by mastication.
  • (C) Reflexively stimulates the salivary glands.
  • (D) All are correct.

Answer: D Explanation: Food in the mouth stimulates taste buds, triggers chewing reflexes, and stimulates salivary secretion through multiple pathways.

Question 37

The salivary secretion (true or false)?

  • (A) Has a serous component.
  • (B) Has a mucous component.
  • (C) A and B are correct.
  • (D) It is largely under hormonal control.
  • (E) All are correct.

Answer: C Explanation: Saliva has both serous (watery, enzyme-rich) and mucous (viscous, mucin-rich) components. However, control is neural, not hormonal.

Question 38

Saliva is necessary for (true or false)?

  • (A) Digestion of food.
  • (B) Swallowing of food.
  • (C) Normal speech.
  • (D) Antisepsis in the mouth.
  • (E) Taste sensation.

Answer: C, D, E Explanation: Saliva is essential for speech articulation, oral hygiene (antibacterial action), and taste sensation (dissolves tastants). While it aids digestion and swallowing, it's not absolutely necessary for these functions.

Question 39

The salivary secretion:

  • (A) Is stimulated by most GIT hormones specially gastrin.
  • (B) Is essential for complete digestion of starch.
  • (C) Increases more by sweet than by bitter substances.
  • (D) Markedly increases by parasympathetic stimulation.
  • (E) Contains lower concentration of K+ & HCO3- than those in the plasma.

Answer: D Explanation: Parasympathetic stimulation (especially via the facial and glossopharyngeal nerves) is the primary stimulus for copious salivary secretion.

Question 40

Salivation can become a conditioned reflex. This suggests that:

  • (A) Pleasant taste sensations are not related to the reflex.
  • (B) Only salivatory nuclei in the brainstem need to be excited by taste sensation without participation of suprasegmental influences.
  • (C) The cerebral cortex partially controls salivation.
  • (D) Salivation could be completely interrupted in a decorticate animal whose tongue is mechanically stimulated.

Answer: C Explanation: The ability to form conditioned reflexes indicates higher brain center involvement, particularly cortical control over the salivatory centers.

Question 41

Saliva is characterized by all the following except:

  • (A) Its concentration of K+ is the same as that in plasma.
  • (B) Its Na+ & Cl- concentrations are lower than those in plasma.
  • (C) Its osmotic pressure and pH are lower than their corresponding values in plasma.
  • (D) It exerts antibacterial action.

Answer: A Explanation: Saliva has a higher K+ concentration than plasma (about 7 times higher). The other characteristics are correct.

Question 42

Which of the following statements about salivary secretion is untrue?

  • (A) Saliva contains digestive enzymes.
  • (B) Saliva has important antiseptic action.
  • (C) It is largely under hormonal control.

Answer: C Explanation: Salivary secretion is under neural control, not hormonal control. The autonomic nervous system regulates both volume and composition of saliva.

Question 43

Which of the following statements about salivary secretion is untrue?

  • (A) Saliva has constant composition regardless of the rate of secretion.
  • (B) The submandibular glands secrete about 70% of the total secretion.
  • (C) The buccal phase of salivary secretion is due to unconditioned reflex.

Answer: A Explanation: Salivary composition changes with flow rate - at higher rates, it becomes more isotonic with higher Na+ and Cl- concentrations.

Question 44

Deglutition is associated with (true or false)?

  • (A) Relaxation of upper esophageal sphincter.
  • (B) Temporary apnea.
  • (C) Closure of the glottis.
  • (D) Food entrance into the nasopharynx.

Answer: A, B, C Explanation: During swallowing, the upper esophageal sphincter relaxes, breathing stops temporarily, and the glottis closes. Food should not enter the nasopharynx due to soft palate elevation.

Question 45

The pharyngeal phase of swallowing:

  • (A) Can be voluntarily inhibited.
  • (B) Involves closure of larynx by the vocal cords.
  • (C) Is associated with lowering of the soft palate.
  • (D) Is accompanied by deep inspiration.
  • (E) Is initiated by conditioned reflex.

Answer: B Explanation: The pharyngeal phase involves reflex closure of the larynx by vocal cord approximation. This phase is involuntary and includes soft palate elevation and respiratory inhibition.

Question 46

About Deglutition (Swallowing) (true or false)?

  • (A) It is entirely an involuntary act that is controlled by medullary center.
  • (B) Bilateral vagotomy abolishes the esophageal peristalsis.
  • (C) Damage of the deglutition center abolishes the buccal phase.
  • (D) The peristalsis in the lower part of the esophagus can be initiated by local enteric reflex.

Answer: A, B, D Explanation: Swallowing has voluntary initiation but involuntary pharyngeal and esophageal phases controlled by medullary centers. Vagotomy affects esophageal peristalsis, and local reflexes can initiate secondary peristalsis.

Question 47

The esophageal phase of deglutition:

  • (A) Occurs only as a result of peristalsis originating in the pharynx.
  • (B) Is controlled only by enteric reflex.
  • (C) Is normal (i.e. not changed) after bilateral vagotomy.
  • (D) Is opposed (antagonized) by gravity.
  • (E) Is controlled by vagal nerves.

Answer: E Explanation: The esophageal phase is primarily controlled by vagal nerves, though local reflexes can also initiate secondary peristalsis.

Question 48

Swallowing is a reflex which (true or false)?

  • (A) Has its reflex center in the cervical segments of the spinal cord.
  • (B) Includes inhibition of respiration.
  • (C) Is initiated by voluntary act.
  • (D) Is dependent on intrinsic nerve network in the esophagus.
  • (E) Is more effective with the trunk in the upright posture.

Answer: B, C, D, E Explanation: The swallowing center is in the medulla, not spinal cord. The other statements are correct.

Question 49

The act of swallowing is associated with:

  • (A) Concurrent inhibition of respiration.
  • (B) Opening of the glottis.
  • (C) Movement of food into the nasopharynx.
  • (D) Upper esophageal sphincter constriction when food placed in contact with the anterior pillars of the pharynx.
  • (E) A and B are correct.

Answer: A Explanation: Swallowing involves respiratory inhibition, closure (not opening) of the glottis, and prevention of food entry into the nasopharynx.

Question 50

During which stage of swallowing is respiration inhibited?

  • (A) Voluntary stage.
  • (B) Pharyngeal stage.
  • (C) Esophageal stage.
  • (D) Postprandial stage.

Answer: B Explanation: Respiration is inhibited during the pharyngeal stage of swallowing to prevent aspiration.

Question 51

Deglutition (Swallowing):

  • (A) Is a complicated act requiring the precise coordination of many muscle groups.
  • (B) Is an automatic function of smooth muscle.
  • (C) Is associated with a lowering of hard palate to prevent reflux of food into the nasopharynx.
  • (D) Does not require relaxation of cricopharyngeal muscle.
  • (E) A and C are correct.

Answer: A Explanation: Swallowing requires precise coordination of multiple muscle groups. The soft palate (not hard palate) elevates, and the cricopharyngeal muscle must relax.

Question 52

During a normal swallowing sequence, the smooth muscle which surrounds the gastroesophageal junction:

  • (A) Remains tonically constricted until the bolus arrives at this junction.
  • (B) Relaxes even before the oncoming peristaltic wave has arrived.
  • (C) Constricts further on the passing bolus and allows a gradual esophageal emptying.
  • (D) Is never constricted at all, and has no participation of any kind in the swallowing process.

Answer: B Explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter undergoes receptive relaxation at the initiation of swallowing, before the peristaltic wave arrives.

Question 53

Of the following cranial nerves, one does not participate with motor efferents to the act of swallowing:

  • (A) Trigeminal nerve.
  • (B) Glossopharyngeal nerve.
  • (C) Accessory (11th cranial nerve).
  • (D) Hypoglossal.
  • (E) Intermedius.

Answer: E Explanation: The intermedius nerve is sensory and doesn't provide motor innervation for swallowing muscles.

Question 54

During swallowing, all the following occur except:

  • (A) The palatopharyngeal folds approximate to each other.
  • (B) The larynx moves upwards and is closed by the epiglottis.
  • (C) The pharyngoesophageal sphincter is relaxed.
  • (D) The vocal cords relax and separate from each other.
  • (E) The pharyngeal muscles contract and the soft palate is elevated.

Answer: D Explanation: During swallowing, the vocal cords approximate (come together) to close the glottis and prevent aspiration, they don't relax and separate.

Question 55

About the process of swallowing, all the followings are true except:

  • (A) As a peristaltic wave passes along the esophagus, the cardiac sphincter, stomach wall and duodenum relax.
  • (B) The esophageal musculature below the pharynx contains striated (skeletal) muscles which is entirely under control of vagal nerves.
  • (C) The most sensitive site for initiation of the pharyngeal phase is the tonsillar pillars.
  • (D) Food does not enter the trachea mainly due to approximation of the vocal cords.
  • (E) The voluntary phase includes the period during which food passes through both the buccal cavity and pharynx.

Answer: E Explanation: The voluntary phase only includes movement of food through the buccal cavity to the pharynx. Once food reaches the pharynx, the pharyngeal phase (involuntary) begins.

Question 56

Select a single incorrect answer about swallowing:

  • (A) Reflex apnea occurs during the pharyngeal phase.
  • (B) The buccal phase of swallowing is voluntary.
  • (C) Food is prevented from entering the nose during swallowing by elevation of epiglottis.

Answer: C Explanation: Food is prevented from entering the nose by elevation of the soft palate, not the epiglottis. The epiglottis helps prevent food from entering the larynx.

Question 57

The lower esophageal sphincter (true or false)?

  • (A) Prevents reflux of the gastric content into the esophagus (gastroesophageal reflux).
  • (B) Relaxes in response to the peristaltic waves passing down the esophagus.
  • (C) Is abnormally contracted in achalasia.
  • (D) Is tonically contracted by high doses of gastrin hormone.

Answer: A, B, C, D Explanation: All statements are correct. The LES prevents reflux, undergoes receptive relaxation during swallowing, fails to relax properly in achalasia, and is stimulated to contract by gastrin.

Question 58

Esophageal peristalsis:

  • (A) Is stimulated by acetylcholine.
  • (B) Is initiated by vagal reflexes.
  • (C) Can be caused by distension of the esophagus.
  • (D) All are correct.

Answer: D Explanation: Esophageal peristalsis is stimulated by ACh, initiated by vagal reflexes (primary peristalsis), and can be triggered by local distension (secondary peristalsis).

Question 59

The musculature of the esophagus below the pharynx is:

  • (A) Smooth only.
  • (B) Mainly striated.
  • (C) Incapable of peristalsis in absence of impulses from the swallowing center.
  • (D) Primarily innervated by spinal nerves.
  • (E) Strongly affected by all circulating GIT hormones.

Answer: B Explanation: The upper esophagus contains mainly striated muscle, while the lower third is smooth muscle. The middle third is mixed.

Question 60

Secondary esophageal peristalsis:

  • (A) Is preceded by an oral-pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
  • (B) Involves activation of medullary swallowing centers.
  • (C) Is accompanied by lower esophageal sphincter relaxation.
  • (D) Occurs in both skeletal and smooth muscle portions of the esophagus.
  • (E) Is abolished by vagotomy.

Answer: C Explanation: Secondary peristalsis is a local reflex that doesn't involve the swallowing center or oral-pharyngeal phase. It's accompanied by LES relaxation to allow passage of the bolus.

Question 61

In contrast to secondary esophageal peristalsis, primary esophageal peristalsis is characterized by which of the following statements?

  • (A) It does not involve relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter.
  • (B) It involves only contraction of esophageal smooth muscle.
  • (C) It is not influenced by intrinsic nervous system.
  • (D) It has an oropharyngeal phase.
  • (E) It involves only contraction of esophageal skeletal muscle.

Answer: D Explanation: Primary peristalsis is initiated by swallowing and includes the oropharyngeal phase, unlike secondary peristalsis which is a local reflex.

Question 62

All the following statements about esophagus are true except:

  • (A) UES is a true sphincter.
  • (B) Gastrin increases tone of LES.
  • (C) LES contracts during swallowing.

Answer: C Explanation: The LES relaxes (not contracts) during swallowing to allow passage of the bolus. This is called receptive relaxation.

Question 63

The rate of gastric emptying is delayed by (true or false)?

  • (A) The enterogastric reflex.
  • (B) The gastrin hormone.
  • (C) GIP.
  • (D) A moderate stomach distension.

Answer: A, C Explanation: Enterogastric reflex (triggered by fat, acid, or hypertonic solutions in duodenum) and GIP both delay gastric emptying. Gastrin accelerates emptying, and moderate distension promotes emptying.

Question 64

Vagotomy prevents increased gastric secretion in response to (true or false)?

  • (A) Sight and smell of food.
  • (B) Injection of insulin.
  • (C) Emotional disturbances.
  • (D) Injection of gastrin.

Answer: A, B, C Explanation: Vagotomy prevents cephalic phase stimulation (sight, smell, emotions, insulin-induced hypoglycemia) but doesn't prevent the response to exogenous gastrin, which acts directly on parietal cells.

Question 65

HCl secretion in the stomach:

  • (A) Is a function of peptic cells.
  • (B) Requires no energy.
  • (C) Occurs by passive diffusion of both H+ and Cl- in the gastric lumen.
  • (D) Requires presence of carbonic anhydrase enzyme.

Answer: D Explanation: HCl secretion is performed by parietal cells (not peptic cells), requires significant energy (H+/K+ ATPase), involves active transport, and requires carbonic anhydrase to generate H+ from CO2 and H2O.

Question 66

Gastric emptying:

  • (A) Is normally completed about 9 hours after ingestion of a usual meal.
  • (B) Is slowest if the food is soft and rich in carbohydrates.
  • (C) Is inhibited by excessive acidity in the duodenum.
  • (D) Is accelerated by presence of fat or hypertonic solutions in the duodenum.
  • (E) Is delayed by stomach distension and by vagal stimulation.

Answer: C Explanation: Excessive acidity in the duodenum triggers the enterogastric reflex, which inhibits gastric emptying. Normal emptying takes 3-4 hours, liquids and carbohydrates empty fastest, and fats/hypertonic solutions delay emptying.

Question 67

Acidification of the duodenum will:

  • (A) Decrease pancreatic secretion of bicarbonate.
  • (B) Increase secretion of gastric acid.
  • (C) Decrease gastric emptying.
  • (D) Increase contraction of the gall bladder.
  • (E) Increase contraction of the sphincter of Oddi.

Answer: C Explanation: Duodenal acidification triggers the enterogastric reflex, which decreases gastric emptying. It also stimulates secretin release, which increases pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion.

Digestive System MCQ Questions

Question 68

Oxyntic or parietal cells secrete:

  • a. HCl
  • b. Trypsin
  • c. Zymogen granules
  • d. Pepsinogen
  • e. a & c

Answer: a (HCl)

Explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the stomach primarily secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and intrinsic factor. Trypsin is from pancreas, zymogen granules are from chief cells, and pepsinogen is also from chief cells.

Question 69

The passage of gastric contents to the duodenum may cause (True or False):

  • a. Copious secretion of pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate
  • b. Decreased gastric motility
  • c. Contraction of the gall bladder
  • d. Contraction of the sphincter of Oddi
  • e. Release of Pancreozymin

Answer: a, b, c, e (All except d)

Explanation: Acidic chyme entering duodenum triggers secretin release (causing bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion), enterogastric reflex (decreasing gastric motility), CCK release (causing gallbladder contraction and pancreozymin release). Sphincter of Oddi relaxes, not contracts.

Question 70

Ingesting antacids with and after a meal so that pH doesn't decrease below 6 will cause a greater than normal secretion of:

  • a. Gastrin
  • b. Secretin
  • c. Pancreatic bicarbonate
  • d. CCK
  • e. Somatostatin

Answer: a (Gastrin)

Explanation: Maintaining high gastric pH (>6) prevents the normal inhibition of gastrin secretion that occurs when pH drops below 2. This leads to increased gastrin secretion.

Question 71

The pangs associated with hunger:

  • a. Are decreased at low level of blood sugar
  • b. Are accompanied with feeling of hunger and pain in the pit of the stomach
  • c. Usually appear 3 to 4 hours after fasting begins
  • d. Diminish after 1 to 2 days of starvation
  • e. b & d

Answer: b (Are accompanied with feeling of hunger and pain in the pit of the stomach)

Explanation: Hunger pangs are strong contractions of the empty stomach accompanied by subjective feelings of hunger and epigastric pain.

Question 72

Chronic gastritis is often associated with which of the following:

  • a. Microcytic anemia
  • b. Hyperchlorohydria
  • c. Steatorrhea
  • d. Pernicious anemia

Answer: d (Pernicious anemia)

Explanation: Chronic gastritis can destroy parietal cells, leading to loss of intrinsic factor production, which is essential for vitamin B12 absorption. This results in pernicious anemia.

Question 73

Vitamin B12 absorption:

  • a. Depends on presence of intrinsic factor
  • b. Depends on passive diffusion
  • c. Occurs in the jejunum
  • d. Occurs in the stomach
  • e. a & c

Answer: a (Depends on presence of intrinsic factor)

Explanation: Vitamin B12 absorption requires intrinsic factor (produced by parietal cells) and occurs in the terminal ileum, not jejunum.

Question 74

The secretion of intrinsic factor occurs in:

  • a. Parietal cells of the stomach
  • b. Chief cells of the stomach
  • c. Upper duodenum
  • d. Beta cells of pancreas
  • e. Liver

Answer: a (Parietal cells of the stomach)

Explanation: Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells along with HCl. It's essential for vitamin B12 absorption.

Question 75

Gastric HCl secretion:

  • a. Occurs secondary to active transport of H⁺ by the parietal cells into the lumen of the stomach
  • b. Requires the presence of the carbonic anhydrase enzyme
  • c. In response to hypoglycemia is mediated via the vagus nerves
  • d. Is increased by administration of histamine
  • e. Is inhibited by the secretin hormone and H₂ receptor blockers (e.g., cimetidine)
  • f. All of the above

Answer: f (All of the above)

Explanation: All statements are correct regarding HCl secretion mechanisms and regulation.

Question 76

So-called hunger pangs:

  • a. Are truly due to smooth muscle spasm of the transverse colon
  • b. Are associated with esophageal and pyloric contraction that coexist with an empty relaxed stomach
  • c. Are more common if starvation is associated with hypoglycemia
  • d. May occur in a totally vagotomized patient

Answer: c (Are more common if starvation is associated with hypoglycemia)

Explanation: Hypoglycemia stimulates the vagus nerve, increasing gastric contractions and hunger pangs.

Question 77

Basal acid output is increased with which of the following:

  • a. Acidification of the antrum
  • b. Administration of H₂ receptor antagonist
  • c. Vagotomy
  • d. Alkalinization of the antrum
  • e. Acidification of the duodenum

Answer: d (Alkalinization of the antrum)

Explanation: Alkaline pH in the antrum stimulates gastrin release, which increases acid secretion. Acidification inhibits gastrin release.

Question 78

The cephalic phase of gastric secretion:

  • a. Occurs when food reaches the stomach
  • b. Is not accompanied by release of GRP
  • c. Is controlled by the vagus nerves
  • d. Is not blocked by injection of atropine
  • e. Constitutes about one-half of the gastric juice secreted on eating

Answer: c (Is controlled by the vagus nerves)

Explanation: The cephalic phase occurs before food reaches the stomach and is mediated by vagal stimulation in response to sight, smell, or thought of food.

Question 79

Gastric HCl secretion:

  • a. Is a passive process that occurs in all parts of the stomach
  • b. Is stimulated by somatostatin, cimetidine & pirenzepine
  • c. Is inhibited by histamine, gastrin & acetylcholine
  • d. Plays a significant role in iron absorption

Answer: d (Plays a significant role in iron absorption)

Explanation: HCl converts Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺, facilitating iron absorption. The other options are incorrect - HCl secretion is active, and the mentioned substances have opposite effects.

Question 80

The gastric peristalsis (True or False):

  • a. Depends on the basic electric rhythm (BER)
  • b. Originates at the midpoint of the greater curvature and increases in intensity as it sweeps towards the pylorus
  • c. Is associated with a strong contraction of the antrum at the end of each wave
  • d. Always ejects the contents of the gastric antrum into the duodenum

Answer: a, b, c (All except d)

Explanation: Gastric peristalsis depends on BER, originates from the pacemaker region, and increases in intensity toward the pylorus. However, it doesn't always eject contents - the pyloric sphincter controls emptying.

Question 81

Distension of the stomach:

  • a. Is associated with a decrease in its peristaltic movement
  • b. Leads to reduction of gastric juice secretion
  • c. Decreases the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter
  • d. Causes an acute increase in the intragastric pressure
  • e. Results in an increase in the volume of the stomach with little rise in the intragastric pressure

Answer: e (Results in an increase in the volume of the stomach with little rise in the intragastric pressure)

Explanation: The stomach shows receptive relaxation - it can accommodate large volumes with minimal pressure increase due to its compliance.

Question 82

All of the following statements are untrue except:

  • a. Peptic ulcers can be treated by anticholinesterase drugs
  • b. Gastric secretion in response to hypoglycemia is due to gastrin
  • c. Peptic ulcers tend to heal by removal of the pyloric antrum
  • d. Vomiting occurs more by smooth muscle than by skeletal muscle activity
  • e. Gastric emptying is not affected after bilateral vagotomy

Answer: c (Peptic ulcers tend to heal by removal of the pyloric antrum)

Explanation: Antrectomy removes the gastrin-producing area, reducing acid secretion and helping ulcer healing.

Question 83

Which of the following statements is true?

  • a. The intrinsic factor is secreted by the parietal cells of the gastric mucosa
  • b. The gastric juice can't digest the gastric mucosa because the cell membranes contain a pepsin activator
  • c. The stomach normally absorbs about 30% of the ingested food
  • d. The secretion of the gastric juice is associated with increased H⁺ in the blood
  • e. The gastric juice is essential for the digestion of both fat and protein

Answer: a (The intrinsic factor is secreted by the parietal cells of the gastric mucosa)

Explanation: Parietal cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor. The stomach absorbs very little, and gastric juice is mainly for protein digestion.

Question 84

Under normal conditions, the gastric secretion is:

  • a. Not affected by presence of food in the stomach
  • b. Stimulated by norepinephrine and inhibited by curare
  • c. Increased by distention of the stomach
  • d. Maximal before food ingestion
  • e. Absent after the food has entered into the duodenum

Answer: c (Increased by distention of the stomach)

Explanation: Gastric distention stimulates mechanoreceptors, triggering vagal reflexes that increase gastric secretion (gastric phase).

Question 85

About pepsins:

  • a. There are 5 types of exopeptidase enzymes
  • b. They are secreted by endocytosis as active enzymes
  • c. They are incapable of autoactivation
  • d. Their optimum pH of action is 1.6-3.2
  • e. They don't increase in the cephalic phase of gastric secretions

Answer: d (Their optimum pH of action is 1.6-3.2)

Explanation: Pepsins are endopeptidases that work optimally in the acidic environment of the stomach (pH 1.6-3.2).

Question 86

The stomach is a poor area for absorption primarily because:

  • a. Most foods are swallowed before ptyalin has a chance to break down starch
  • b. pH of the stomach is too high
  • c. The junction between epithelial cells presents wide spaces for fluid/ion movement
  • d. The stomach lacks villous membranes
  • e. b & d

Answer: d (The stomach lacks villous membranes)

Explanation: The stomach lacks villi and microvilli that increase surface area for absorption, making it primarily a storage and digestion organ.

Question 87

Hydrochloric acid secretion:

  • a. Is accomplished by passive diffusion
  • b. Requires the dissociation of water with subsequent exchange of the hydrogen ion for potassium ion
  • c. Requires anaerobic metabolism
  • d. Utilizes protein molecules to neutralize OH⁻ remaining in the secretory cells
  • e. b & d

Answer: b (Requires the dissociation of water with subsequent exchange of the hydrogen ion for potassium ion)

Explanation: HCl secretion involves active transport with H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump exchanging H⁺ for K⁺.

Question 88

A 45-year-old man is found to have a condition in which the parietal cells of his stomach have been destroyed by an autoimmune mechanism. This condition is often associated with which of the following?

  • a. Pernicious anemia
  • b. Gastric ulceration
  • c. Steatorrhea
  • d. Protein deficiency

Answer: a (Pernicious anemia)

Explanation: Destruction of parietal cells leads to loss of intrinsic factor, resulting in vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia.

Question 89

It's believed that in parietal cells of the gastric mucosa (which secrete hydrochloric acid), an active transport system is responsible for the transmembrane passage of:

  • a. Chloride
  • b. Carbon dioxide
  • c. Bicarbonate
  • d. Water

Answer: a (Chloride)

Explanation: Chloride ions are actively transported across the apical membrane to combine with H⁺ to form HCl.

Question 90

Pepsin, secreted by the gastric mucosa:

  • a. Continues to act in the neutral medium of the duodenum
  • b. Is proteolytic on the mucosal surface, in the alkaline medium provided by the mucus secreted by the surface cells of the stomach
  • c. Is synthesized within the chief cells
  • d. Does not increase in concentration in response to the mental stimuli found in the so-called cephalic phase of gastric digestion

Answer: c (Is synthesized within the chief cells)

Explanation: Pepsinogen is synthesized in chief cells and activated to pepsin by HCl. It's inactive in alkaline environments.

Question 91

Acid secretion in ulcer disease can be reduced by which of the following?

  • a. Blockage of secretin secretion
  • b. Blockage of histamine H₂ receptors
  • c. Blockage of action of pepsin
  • d. Treatment with antibiotics

Answer: b (Blockage of histamine H₂ receptors)

Explanation: H₂ receptor blockers (like cimetidine) directly inhibit acid secretion by blocking histamine's stimulatory effect on parietal cells.

Question 92

The normally innervated stomach (True or False):

  • a. Is stimulated to secrete gastric juice when food is chewed, even if it's not swallowed
  • b. Can't secrete HCl when its H₁ histamine receptors are blocked
  • c. The denervated stomach can secrete gastric juice after a meal is ingested
  • d. Empties more quickly than the denervated stomach
  • e. Is stimulated to secrete gastric juice by the hormone secretin

Answer: a, c, d

Explanation: The cephalic phase can be triggered by chewing alone; denervated stomachs can still respond to hormonal stimuli; intact vagal innervation promotes faster emptying.

Question 93

Under normal conditions, the bulk of gastric secretions are produced:

  • a. Before the food is ingested and while the pleasure of its ingestion is anticipated
  • b. While the food stays in the stomach
  • c. After the food has entered the duodenum
  • d. During fasting periods

Answer: b (While the food stays in the stomach)

Explanation: The gastric phase (when food is in the stomach) produces the majority of gastric secretions through mechanical and chemical stimuli.

Question 94

Mucus present on the surface of the mucosa of the stomach, small and large intestine is:

  • a. Resistant to enzymes secreted into the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract
  • b. Alkaline, and thus a poor buffer for alkaline foods
  • c. A non-amphoteric protein
  • d. Easily removed from the surface of the stomach by the gastric secretions during the gastric phase of digestion

Answer: a (Resistant to enzymes secreted into the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract)

Explanation: Mucus forms a protective barrier that resists enzymatic digestion, protecting the underlying mucosa.

Question 95

The enterogastric reflex can be elicited by which of the following?

  • a. Distension of the duodenum
  • b. Acid chyme in the duodenum
  • c. Hyperosmotic chyme in the duodenum
  • d. All of the above

Answer: d (All of the above)

Explanation: The enterogastric reflex is triggered by mechanical (distension), chemical (acid), and osmotic stimuli in the duodenum to slow gastric emptying.

Question 96

The secretion of gastrin by the pyloric antrum ceases:

  • a. When the stomach is distended by a full meal
  • b. When the gastric mucosal contents have a pH of about 2.0
  • c. If histamine is injected
  • d. If the vagi are stimulated

Answer: b (When the gastric mucosal contents have a pH of about 2.0)

Explanation: Low pH (around 2.0) in the antrum inhibits gastrin release through negative feedback to prevent excessive acid production.

Question 97

Gastric peristalsis:

  • a. Originates in the distal half of the stomach
  • b. Is characterized by strong contractions of the antrum at the end of the wave
  • c. Ejects all the contents of the antrum into the duodenum
  • d. Decreases in intensity as it sweeps toward the pylorus
  • e. b & d

Answer: b (Is characterized by strong contractions of the antrum at the end of the wave)

Explanation: Peristaltic waves increase in intensity as they approach the antrum, with strong antral contractions for mixing and grinding.

Question 98

Which of the following substances is released from the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic gastric juice?

  • a. Histamine
  • b. Secretin
  • c. Norepinephrine
  • d. Acetylcholine

Answer: b (Secretin)

Explanation: Secretin is released from duodenal S cells in response to acidic chyme, stimulating bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.

Question 99

The chyme entering the small intestine causes a release of secretin which results in:

  • a. Stimulation of pancreatic fluids which contain no enzymes
  • b. A pancreatic fluid that aids in protection against the development of duodenal ulcers
  • c. A pancreatic secretion whose pH is just right for action of the pancreatic enzymes that are eventually released
  • d. Pancreatic fluid secretion of a large volume containing low chloride but high bicarbonate concentration
  • e. All are correct

Answer: e (All are correct)

Explanation: Secretin stimulates enzyme-poor, bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion that neutralizes acid and creates optimal pH for enzyme function.

Question 100

Which of the following hormones is involved in the initiation of the migrating motor complex?

  • a. Gastrin
  • b. Motilin
  • c. Secretin
  • d. Cholecystokinin
  • e. Enterogastrone

Answer: b (Motilin)

Explanation: Motilin initiates the migrating motor complex (MMC) during fasting, which clears the GI tract of residual material.

Question 101

The main function of the cardiac sphincter of the stomach is to:

  • a. Prevent the reflux of the gastric content to the esophagus
  • b. Facilitate storage of food in the lower part of the esophagus
  • c. Mix the food particles entering the stomach
  • d. Control the rate of food entry into the stomach
  • e. None of the above

Answer: a (Prevent the reflux of the gastric content to the esophagus)

Explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter (cardiac sphincter) primarily prevents gastroesophageal reflux by maintaining a pressure barrier between the stomach and esophagus.

Question 102

Which of the following statements is correct?

  • a. The gastric juice contains pepsins, gelatinase, lipase and α-amylase enzymes
  • b. The only essential constituent of the gastric juice is the intrinsic factor
  • c. The hunger contractions disappear after bilateral vagotomy or damage of the feeding center in the hypothalamus
  • d. HCl is essential for both carbohydrate and fat digestion

Answer: c (The hunger contractions disappear after bilateral vagotomy or damage of the feeding center in the hypothalamus)

Explanation: Hunger contractions are mediated by vagal stimulation and hypothalamic feeding centers. Damage to either eliminates these contractions.

Question 103

Which of the following is the major factor that protects the duodenal mucosa from damage by gastric acid?

  • a. Pancreatic bicarbonate secretions
  • b. The endogenous mucosal barrier of the duodenum
  • c. Duodenal bicarbonate secretion
  • d. Hepatic bicarbonate secretion
  • e. Bicarbonate contained in bile

Answer: a (Pancreatic bicarbonate secretions)

Explanation: Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion (stimulated by secretin) is the primary mechanism neutralizing acidic chyme and protecting the duodenal mucosa.

Question 104

Which of the following substances is released from the duodenal mucosa in response to acidic gastric juice?

  • a. CCK
  • b. Substance P
  • c. Secretin
  • d. GIP

Answer: c (Secretin)

Explanation: Secretin is specifically released from duodenal S cells when pH drops below 4.5, triggering bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.

Question 105

A 42-year-old salesman presents with the chief complaint of intermittent mid-epigastric pain that is relieved by antacids or eating. Gastric analysis reveals that basal and maximal acid output exceed normal values. The gastric hypersecretion can be explained by an increase in the plasma concentration of which of the following?

  • a. Somatostatin
  • b. Histamine
  • c. Gastrin
  • d. Secretin
  • e. Enterogastrone

Answer: c (Gastrin)

Explanation: The clinical picture suggests peptic ulcer disease. Elevated gastrin levels (as in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) cause gastric acid hypersecretion and peptic ulcers.

Question 106

Removal of the stomach can lead to all of the following except:

  • a. Marked digestive disturbances
  • b. Megaloblastic anemia (pernicious anemia)
  • c. A fall in plasma volume after a heavy meal (due to dumping syndrome)
  • d. Diminished Ca²⁺ absorption and weak development of bones

Answer: a (Marked digestive disturbances)

Explanation: Surprisingly, gastrectomy patients can adapt well digestively. The other complications (B12 deficiency, dumping syndrome, calcium malabsorption) are common post-gastrectomy problems.

Question 107

About the cephalic phase of gastric secretion, all the following are true except:

  • a. It occurs before food enters the stomach
  • b. It's inhibited by bilateral vagotomy
  • c. It involves some release of gastrin
  • d. It's due to both conditioned and unconditioned reflexes
  • e. It begins only when food is tasted and accounts for most of the gastric secretion

Answer: e (It begins only when food is tasted and accounts for most of the gastric secretion)

Explanation: The cephalic phase begins with sight, smell, or thought of food (not just taste) and accounts for only about 20% of total gastric secretion, not most.

Question 108

HCl secretion includes all the following processes except:

  • a. Active transport of H⁺ into gastric lumen
  • b. H⁺ is exchanged for K⁺ from the extracellular fluid
  • c. HCO₃⁻ diffuses into the extracellular fluid in exchange for Cl⁻
  • d. It's associated with production of a postprandial alkaline tide

Answer: b (H⁺ is exchanged for K⁺ from the extracellular fluid)

Explanation: H⁺ is exchanged for K⁺ from the gastric lumen, not the extracellular fluid. The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pumps H⁺ out and K⁺ in.

Question 109

The gastric juice has all the following characteristics except:

  • a. It contains an alkaline secretion from the surface epithelium
  • b. Its pH is always less than 3
  • c. It contains the intrinsic factor which is essential for vitamin B₁₂ absorption
  • d. Its antibacterial action is produced by its mucus content
  • e. Its volume averages 2.5 liters/day

Answer: d (Its antibacterial action is produced by its mucus content)

Explanation: The antibacterial action of gastric juice is due to its low pH (HCl), not the mucus content. Mucus provides protection, not antibacterial action.

Question 110

The gastric mucosal barrier is maintained by all the following except:

  • a. The nature of the surface membrane of the gastric mucosal cells and the tight junctions between these cells
  • b. Certain prostaglandins and the alkaline mucus secretion of the stomach
  • c. The mucus gel-like membrane that coats the gastric mucous membrane
  • d. Administration of H₂ receptor blocking drugs (e.g., cimetidine)
  • e. Excessive amounts of bile salts, aspirin or ethanol

Answer: e (Excessive amounts of bile salts, aspirin or ethanol)

Explanation: Bile salts, aspirin, and ethanol actually damage the gastric mucosal barrier rather than maintain it.

Question 111

Which of the following statements is wrong?

  • a. Repeated vomiting leads to dehydration, alkalosis, and K⁺ depletion
  • b. The rate of gastric emptying is affected by the fat content of food
  • c. The enterogastric reflex is a gastro-inhibitory reflex
  • d. The enterogastric reflex depends on vagal impulses as well as local enteric and prevertebral ganglionic reflexes
  • e. The enterogastric reflex is of value in facilitating carbohydrate digestion

Answer: e (The enterogastric reflex is of value in facilitating carbohydrate digestion)

Explanation: The enterogastric reflex slows gastric emptying and doesn't specifically facilitate carbohydrate digestion. It's a protective mechanism.

Question 112

About gastric motility, all the following is true except:

  • a. It's marked in the distal half of the stomach
  • b. It's inhibited in painful conditions
  • c. It increases by vagal stimulation and decreases by sympathetic stimulation
  • d. It decreases by the enterogastric reflex and by the secretin and CCK hormones
  • e. It increases by over-distension of the stomach
  • f. It decreases in response to presence of excess fat in the duodenum

Answer: e (It increases by over-distension of the stomach)

Explanation: Over-distension of the stomach actually inhibits motility through receptive relaxation and reflex inhibition.

Question 113

Gastric secretion is inhibited by all the following except:

  • a. Presence of excess H⁺ in the pyloric antrum
  • b. Presence of excess protein digestive products in the stomach
  • c. Certain emotions e.g., fear and depression
  • d. Certain GIT hormones e.g., secretin, CCK and VIP
  • e. Presence of fat, hypertonic solutions and excess acid in the duodenum
  • f. The enterogastric reflex

Answer: b (Presence of excess protein digestive products in the stomach)

Explanation: Protein digestive products (amino acids, peptides) actually stimulate gastric secretion, particularly gastrin release, rather than inhibit it.

Question 114

Concerning HCl secretion, all the following is true except:

  • a. It's associated with increased pH of the gastric venous blood
  • b. It's stimulated by gastrin, acetylcholine, histamine and norepinephrine
  • c. The energy required is derived from ATP breakdown
  • d. It involves formation of carbonic acid
  • e. There is an active transport of H⁺ from oxyntic cells into the gastric lumen and K⁺ in the opposite direction

Answer: b (It's stimulated by gastrin, acetylcholine, histamine and norepinephrine)

Explanation: Norepinephrine (sympathetic stimulation) actually inhibits gastric acid secretion, not stimulates it.

Question 115

All the following statements are true except:

  • a. VIP stimulates intestinal secretion and inhibits gastric acid secretion
  • b. Diamox (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) increases both gastric HCl formation and the HCO₃⁻ content in the pancreatic juice
  • c. Both gastrin and glucagon are secreted from the pyloric antrum and duodenum
  • d. Gastrin is secreted from almost the whole GIT mucosa
  • e. Glicentin is formed by the intestinal mucosa and has some glucagon activity
  • f. The pancreatic endocrine secretion is stimulated by both GIP and CCK

Answer: b (Diamox (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) increases both gastric HCl formation and the HCO₃⁻ content in the pancreatic juice)

Explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors would decrease both gastric HCl formation and pancreatic bicarbonate content, not increase them.

Question 116

Which of the following statements is wrong?

  • a. The gastric peristalsis includes propulsive, mixing and grinding movements
  • b. The cephalic phase of gastric secretion involves no release of gastrin
  • c. Deficiency of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia
  • d. Large doses of gastrin cause contraction of the pyloric sphincter

Answer: b (The cephalic phase of gastric secretion involves no release of gastrin)

Explanation: The cephalic phase does involve gastrin release through vagal stimulation of G cells in the antrum.

Question 117

The following statements about gastric secretion are correct except:

  • a. Gastric secretion increases when a hungry person thinks about food
  • b. Gastric secretion helps vitamin B₁₂ absorption
  • c. Production of HCl depends on activity of carbonic anhydrase
  • d. Gastric secretion is associated with increased H⁺ concentration in venous blood coming from stomach

Answer: d (Gastric secretion is associated with increased H⁺ concentration in venous blood coming from stomach)

Explanation: During HCl secretion, H⁺ is secreted into the lumen while HCO₃⁻ enters the blood, creating an "alkaline tide" - decreased H⁺ in venous blood.

Question 118

Which of the following statements about gastric secretion is incorrect:

  • a. Gastric acid secretion can be inhibited by somatostatin
  • b. The main phase of gastric secretion is the gastric phase
  • c. Gastric secretion increases in response to the presence of food in mouth after the vagi to stomach have been cut

Answer: c (Gastric secretion increases in response to the presence of food in mouth after the vagi to stomach have been cut)

Explanation: After vagotomy, the cephalic phase (triggered by food in mouth) is eliminated, so gastric secretion wouldn't increase in response to food in the mouth.

Question 119

A 55-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol consumption presents to his local physician with nonspecific complaints of dyspepsia. Examination and diagnostic testing reveal that he has destruction of the gastric glands. This condition would predispose the patient to which of the following?

  • a. Steatorrhea
  • b. Gastric hypomotility
  • c. Gastric ulcer
  • d. Anemia

Answer: d (Anemia)

Explanation: Destruction of gastric glands leads to loss of intrinsic factor production, resulting in vitamin B₁₂ deficiency and pernicious anemia.

Question 120

Which of the following statements about motor function of stomach is untrue?

  • a. The frequency of gastric peristaltic contraction is about 3/min
  • b. Fasting hypoglycemia produces hunger contractions
  • c. The enterogastric reflex stimulates gastric emptying

Answer: c (The enterogastric reflex stimulates gastric emptying)

Explanation: The enterogastric reflex inhibits gastric emptying and motility, not stimulates it. It's a protective mechanism.

Question 121

Which of the following statements about motor function of stomach is untrue?

  • a. Motility of stomach increases when fat enters duodenum
  • b. MMC prevents duodenogastric reflux
  • c. Receptive relaxation of stomach is mediated by purinergic vagal fibers

Answer: a (Motility of stomach increases when fat enters duodenum)

Explanation: Fat in the duodenum decreases gastric motility through CCK release and the enterogastric reflex.

Question 122

Vomiting:

  • a. Occurs only in a denervated stomach
  • b. Occurs by strong contraction of the stomach wall
  • c. May be produced by conditioned reflex
  • d. Occurs only in an empty stomach

Answer: c (May be produced by conditioned reflex)

Explanation: Vomiting can be triggered by conditioned reflexes (psychological stimuli), involves abdominal muscle contraction more than gastric contraction, and can occur with or without food in the stomach.

Question 123

Vomiting:

  • a. Leads to expulsion of gastric contents by violent rhythmic contractions of gut smooth muscle
  • b. Is coordinated by a midbrain vomiting center
  • c. Of green fluid suggests that duodenal contents have regurgitated into the stomach
  • d. May be accompanied by a fall in arterial blood pressure
  • e. May be induced by drugs acting on centers in the medulla

Answer: c, d, e

Explanation: Green vomitus indicates bile (duodenal contents), vomiting can cause hypotension, and emetic drugs act on medullary centers. The vomiting center is in the medulla, not midbrain.

Question 124

The so-called chemoreceptor trigger zone:

  • a. Is synonymous with the vomiting center
  • b. Is located in the cerebral peduncles, ventral to the Aqueduct of Sylvius
  • c. Is sensitive to the action of morphine
  • d. May be destroyed experimentally; the ablation of both chemoreceptor trigger zones abolishes all forms of vomiting

Answer: c (Is sensitive to the action of morphine)

Explanation: The CTZ is sensitive to various drugs including morphine and is located in the area postrema of the medulla, not the cerebral peduncles.

Question 125

As regards the process of vomiting:

  • a. It is controlled by a center in the cerebral cortex
  • b. It always begins with nausea
  • c. Prolonged vomiting usually produces dehydration associated with acidosis
  • d. It's associated with relaxation of the body and fundus of the stomach
  • e. Uremic toxins stimulate the vomiting center directly
  • f. The vomiting center is stimulated by chlorpromazine and inhibited by apomorphine and digitalis

Answer: d (It's associated with relaxation of the body and fundus of the stomach)

Explanation: During vomiting, the stomach body and fundus relax while the antrum contracts. The vomiting center is in the medulla, and prolonged vomiting causes alkalosis, not acidosis.

Question 126

Vomiting:

  • a. Results in dehydration, depletion of body HCO₃⁻, Na⁺ and K⁺ and alkalosis
  • b. Is the forceful expulsion of the contents of the digestive tract through the mouth
  • c. Results in loss of fluid and if prolonged, can result in circulatory collapse and death
  • d. Is a complex reflex act, which is coordinated by a center located in the sacral region of the spinal cord
  • e. a, b & c

Answer: e (a, b & c)

Explanation: Vomiting causes dehydration, electrolyte loss, and alkalosis; it's forceful expulsion of GI contents; and can lead to circulatory collapse. The center is in the medulla, not sacral cord.

Question 127

The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ):

  • a. Is the name given to the vomiting center in the medulla oblongata
  • b. Is not related to the vomiting center
  • c. Initiates vomiting as a result of irritation of the upper part of the GIT
  • d. Is stimulated by impulses discharged from an irritated peritoneum
  • e. Is responsible for the vomiting produced by emetic drugs (e.g., apomorphine)

Answer: e (Is responsible for the vomiting produced by emetic drugs (e.g., apomorphine))

Explanation: The CTZ is separate from but connected to the vomiting center and is specifically responsible for drug-induced vomiting.

Question 128

A pyloric obstruction in an infant which results in a prolonged bout of severe vomiting is likely to cause a primary:

  • a. Metabolic acidosis
  • b. Metabolic alkalosis
  • c. Respiratory acidosis
  • d. Respiratory alkalosis

Answer: b (Metabolic alkalosis)

Explanation: Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric acid (H⁺ and Cl⁻), leading to metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia.

Question 129

An obstruction of the small bowel leading to severe vomiting with a preponderant loss of duodenal contents is likely to cause a primary:

  • a. Metabolic acidosis
  • b. Metabolic alkalosis
  • c. Respiratory acidosis
  • d. Respiratory alkalosis

Answer: a (Metabolic acidosis)

Explanation: Small bowel obstruction causes loss of alkaline pancreatic and biliary secretions, leading to metabolic acidosis.

Question 130

A likely reason why a to-and-fro motion, such as that encountered during airplane flights or in an automobile ride over a bumpy road, tends to cause nausea and vomiting, is because during such motions:

  • a. Much air is swallowed and the stomach becomes distended
  • b. The stomach is more likely to develop reverse peristalsis
  • c. The cerebral cortex can no longer inhibit an intrinsic tendency of the brainstem to cause vomiting
  • d. Vestibular reflexes eventually excite a chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla
  • e. The cerebellum is strongly inhibited

Answer: d (Vestibular reflexes eventually excite a chemoreceptor trigger zone in the medulla)

Explanation: Motion sickness results from vestibular stimulation that activates the CTZ, leading to nausea and vomiting.

Question 131

Select a single incorrect answer about vomiting:

  • a. Vomiting center is in hypothalamus
  • b. The role of stomach is passive in the process of vomiting
  • c. Vomiting may occur as a conditioned reflex

Answer: a (Vomiting center is in hypothalamus)

Explanation: The vomiting center is located in the medulla oblongata, not the hypothalamus.

Question 132

Trypsinogen in pancreatic juice is activated by:

  • a. Alkaline pH
  • b. Enterokinase
  • c. Bile salts

Answer: b (Enterokinase)

Explanation: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) from the duodenal brush border specifically activates trypsinogen to trypsin.

Question 133

Chymotrypsinogen in pancreatic juice is activated by:

  • a. Enterokinase
  • b. Alkaline pH
  • c. Trypsin
  • d. Bile salts

Answer: c (Trypsin)

Explanation: Chymotrypsinogen is activated by trypsin, not enterokinase. This is part of the enzyme cascade.

Question 134

Pancreatic lipase is activated by:

  • a. Gastrin
  • b. Bile salts
  • c. Enterokinase

Answer: b (Bile salts)

Explanation: Pancreatic lipase requires bile salts for activation and optimal function in fat digestion.

Question 135

All of the following statements concerning pancreatic secretion are true except:

  • a. Its pH is about 8
  • b. Has high HCO₃⁻ content
  • c. Its secretion is primarily under neural control
  • d. Contains digestive enzymes

Answer: c (Its secretion is primarily under neural control)

Explanation: Pancreatic secretion is primarily under hormonal control (secretin and CCK), not neural control.

Question 136

The following stimulate pancreatic secretion rich in enzymes and poor in HCO₃⁻ except:

  • a. CCK
  • b. Gastrin
  • c. Secretin
  • d. Vagal stimulation

Answer: c (Secretin)

Explanation: Secretin stimulates enzyme-poor, bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion. CCK, gastrin, and vagal stimulation promote enzyme-rich secretion.

Question 137

Loss of pancreatic secretion produces the following except:

  • a. Maldigestion
  • b. Malabsorption
  • c. Dehydration
  • d. Alkalosis

Answer: d (Alkalosis)

Explanation: Loss of pancreatic secretion would cause acidosis, not alkalosis, due to loss of bicarbonate-rich secretions.

Question 138

Pancreatic amylase is activated by:

  • a. Bile salts
  • b. Trypsin
  • c. Cl⁻ ions
  • d. Enterokinase

Answer: c (Cl⁻ ions)

Explanation: Pancreatic amylase requires chloride ions for activation and optimal enzymatic activity.

Question 139

pH of pancreatic secretion is about:

  • a. 1
  • b. 6.5-7.5
  • c. 8

Answer: c (8)

Explanation: Pancreatic juice has a pH of about 8.1-8.3 due to its high bicarbonate content.

Question 140

The volume of pancreatic secretion per day is about:

  • a. 0.6 L
  • b. 1.5 L
  • c. 3 L

Answer: b (1.5 L)

Explanation: Normal pancreatic secretion is approximately 1.5 liters per day.

Question 141

Pancreatic secretion contains all the following enzymes except:

  • a. Trypsin
  • b. Chymotrypsin
  • c. Lipase
  • d. Amylase
  • e. Nucleotidase

Answer: e (Nucleotidase)

Explanation: Nucleotidase is found in intestinal brush border enzymes, not pancreatic secretion.

Question 142

All the following statements concerning pancreatic secretion are true except:

  • a. Sympathetic stimulation inhibits pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion
  • b. The cephalic phase accounts for about 20% of secretion after meal
  • c. Pancreatic HCO₃⁻ depresses further release of secretin
  • d. Contains enzymes which digest polysaccharides to monosaccharides

Answer: d (Contains enzymes which digest polysaccharides to monosaccharides)

Explanation: Pancreatic amylase digests polysaccharides to oligosaccharides, not monosaccharides. Final digestion to monosaccharides occurs at the brush border.

Question 143

Pancreatic secretion is inhibited by all the following except:

  • a. Somatostatin
  • b. Glucagon
  • c. Acid in the duodenum
  • d. Sympathetic stimulation

Answer: c (Acid in the duodenum)

Explanation: Acid in the duodenum stimulates (not inhibits) pancreatic secretion by releasing secretin. The other factors all inhibit pancreatic secretion.

Digestive System MCQs - Organized Format

144. Pancreatic Secretion

Question: All the following statements about pancreatic secretion are true except:

  • (A) The intestinal phase is the main phase of pancreatic secretion
  • (B) Gastro-pancreatic reflex stimulates pancreatic secretion
  • (C) Failure of both pancreatic and biliary secretions is needed before steatorrhea develops

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Steatorrhea (fatty stools) can develop with failure of either pancreatic OR biliary secretions alone. You don't need both to fail simultaneously. Pancreatic lipase deficiency or bile salt deficiency can each independently cause fat malabsorption.

145. Pancreatic Secretion

Question: All the following are correct statements about pancreatic secretion except:

  • (A) HCO₃⁻ rich fluid is secreted by ductal cells in response to secretin
  • (B) Secretion of enzymes by acinar cells occurs in response to CCK
  • (C) Vagotomy augments secretion of enzymes after meal

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Vagotomy (cutting the vagus nerve) actually reduces enzyme secretion after meals, not augments it. The vagus nerve stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion, so cutting it would decrease this response.

146. Pancreatic Secretion

Question: Select a single incorrect answer about pancreatic secretion:

  • (A) Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase
  • (B) Chymotrypsinogen is activated by trypsin
  • (C) Pancreatic lipase is activated by alkaline pH

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Pancreatic lipase is not activated by alkaline pH. It's activated by colipase and bile salts. The alkaline pH of pancreatic juice provides optimal conditions for enzyme activity but doesn't activate lipase itself.

147. Pancreatic Secretion

Question: The following statements about pancreatic secretion are false except:

  • (A) Pancreatic acini contain trypsin
  • (B) Vagal stimulation produces HCO₃⁻ rich juice
  • (C) The hormone which stimulates enzyme-rich secretion also causes contraction of gall bladder

Answer: (C)

Explanation: CCK (cholecystokinin) both stimulates enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion AND causes gallbladder contraction. This is the only true statement among the options.

148. Liver Functions

Question: All the following are true about liver functions except:

  • (A) Liver cells are the only important site for plasma albumin synthesis
  • (B) Liver cells can store vitamin B₁₂
  • (C) Liver cells inactivate certain hormones by conjugation
  • (D) Essential fatty acids are synthesized in liver

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Essential fatty acids cannot be synthesized by the human body (including the liver) and must be obtained from diet. The liver synthesizes non-essential fatty acids.

149. Liver Functions

Question: All the following statements are correct about liver cells except:

  • (A) They form non-essential amino acids
  • (B) They form hippuric acid by conjugation of benzoate with glycine
  • (C) They form TPP from vitamin B₆

Answer: (C)

Explanation: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) is formed from vitamin B₁ (thiamine), not vitamin B₆. Vitamin B₆ is converted to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP).

150. Liver Functions

Question: Liver performs the following functions except:

  • (A) Hematopoiesis in adults
  • (B) Formation of about half of body lymph
  • (C) Formation of bile salts

Answer: (A)

Explanation: Hematopoiesis in adults occurs primarily in bone marrow, not the liver. The liver is involved in fetal hematopoiesis but not adult hematopoiesis under normal conditions.

151. Liver Functions

Question: Liver functions include all the following except:

  • (A) Excretion of bile
  • (B) Glycogenolysis
  • (C) Glycogenesis
  • (D) Formation of essential amino acids

Answer: (D)

Explanation: The liver cannot synthesize essential amino acids - these must be obtained from dietary sources. The liver can synthesize non-essential amino acids.

152. Bile Secretion

Question: The following statements about bile secretion are correct except:

  • (A) Canalicular secretion represents 75% of bile secretion
  • (B) Ductular secretion represents 75% of bile secretion
  • (C) Bile is secreted by both hepatocytes and cholangiocytes

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Canalicular secretion (from hepatocytes) represents about 75% of bile secretion, while ductular secretion (from cholangiocytes) represents about 25%, not 75%.

153. Bile Secretion

Question: All the following statements about bile secretion are true except:

  • (A) Bile contains cholesterol and fatty acids
  • (B) Hepatic bile has lower specific gravity
  • (C) Gallbladder bile contains less organic constituents than hepatic bile

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Gallbladder bile is concentrated and contains MORE organic constituents than hepatic bile due to water and electrolyte reabsorption in the gallbladder.

154. Gallbladder Bile

Question: Gallbladder bile is characterized by all the following except:

  • (A) It is relatively acidic
  • (B) Darker in color
  • (C) More inorganic constituents
  • (D) Higher specific gravity

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Gallbladder bile has MORE organic constituents (bile salts, cholesterol, bilirubin) due to concentration, not more inorganic constituents.

155. Bile Salts

Question: The following statements about bile salts are correct except:

  • (A) They are 2 types: primary and secondary
  • (B) They are Na⁺ and K⁺ salts of bile acids conjugated with glucuronic acid
  • (C) They are actively reabsorbed from the terminal ileum

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Bile salts are conjugated with glycine or taurine, not glucuronic acid. Glucuronic acid conjugation is used for bilirubin.

156. Bile Salts

Question: All the following are true about bile salts except:

  • (A) 50% of canalicular flow is dependent on bile salts in the enterohepatic circulation
  • (B) The amount of bile salts in stool is about 0.2-0.4g/day
  • (C) The total circulating pool of bile salts is 0.2-0.4g

Answer: (C)

Explanation: The total circulating pool of bile salts is about 2-4g, not 0.2-0.4g. The small amount (0.2-0.4g/day) refers to fecal loss.

157. Choleretics

Question: The following are choleretics except:

  • (A) Bile salts
  • (B) Secretin
  • (C) Acetylcholine
  • (D) Bile pigments

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Bile pigments (like bilirubin) are not choleretics. Choleretics are substances that stimulate bile flow - bile salts, secretin, and acetylcholine all increase bile secretion.

158. pH Comparison

Question: Which of the following has the highest pH:

  • (A) Gastric juice
  • (B) Pancreatic juice
  • (C) Hepatic bile
  • (D) Succus entericus

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Hepatic bile has the highest pH (around 8.0-8.6). Pancreatic juice is also alkaline but slightly lower pH than bile.

159. Bile Constituents

Question: Bile secretion contains the following constituents except:

  • (A) Bile salts
  • (B) Cholesterol
  • (C) Free bilirubin
  • (D) Urobilinogen

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Bile contains conjugated bilirubin (bilirubin glucuronide), not free bilirubin. Free bilirubin is not water-soluble and cannot be excreted in bile.

160. Bile Secretion Stimulation

Question: Bile secretion is stimulated by the following except:

  • (A) Secretin
  • (B) Bile salts
  • (C) Sympathetic stimulation
  • (D) Increased blood flow to liver

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Sympathetic stimulation generally inhibits bile secretion. Parasympathetic stimulation increases bile secretion.

161. Bile Salts and Lipid Absorption

Question: Bile salts promote lipid absorption as a result of all the following except:

  • (A) Emulsifying fat
  • (B) Formation of micelles
  • (C) Activation of pancreatic lipase
  • (D) None of the above

Answer: (D)

Explanation: This is a tricky question. Bile salts DO emulsify fats and form micelles, but they don't directly activate pancreatic lipase. However, the answer is (D) "None of the above" because all the listed mechanisms (A, B, C) are actually ways bile salts help with lipid absorption.

162. Bile Salt Absorption

Question: The following statements about absorption of bile salts are true except:

  • (A) Active transport occurs in the distal ileum
  • (B) Removal of distal ileum reduces their absorption
  • (C) Passive diffusion transports them

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Bile salts are primarily absorbed by active transport in the terminal ileum, not by passive diffusion. This is a specific, energy-requiring process.

163. Gallbladder Emptying

Question: Emptying of gallbladder is stimulated by the following except:

  • (A) Vagal stimulation
  • (B) Sympathetic stimulation
  • (C) CCK

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Sympathetic stimulation inhibits gallbladder emptying. Vagal stimulation and CCK both promote gallbladder contraction and emptying.

164. Gallbladder Functions

Question: The following statements are correct about functions of gallbladder except:

  • (A) The capacity of gallbladder is 20-60 ml
  • (B) Bile can be concentrated in gallbladder up to 12-20 folds
  • (C) Secretion of NaHCO₃ by gallbladder prevents precipitation of calcium

Answer: (C)

Explanation: The gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing water and electrolytes; it doesn't secrete NaHCO₃. The gallbladder's primary function is concentration and storage, not secretion.

165. Bile Pigments

Question: Select the single correct answer about bile pigments:

  • (A) The principal bile pigment is biliverdin
  • (B) Free bilirubin is the conjugated bilirubin
  • (C) Cholebilirubin is the conjugated bilirubin
  • (D) Urobilinogen is converted into bilirubin by action of bacteria

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Cholebilirubin (bilirubin glucuronide) is indeed the conjugated form of bilirubin found in bile. The principal bile pigment is bilirubin (not biliverdin), and free bilirubin is the unconjugated form.

166. Bile Pigments

Question: All the following statements about bile pigments are true except:

  • (A) They are formed from Hb in RBCs
  • (B) In blood bilirubin combines with plasma albumin to form conjugated bilirubin
  • (C) Mostly urobilinogen passes with feces as stercobilinogen

Answer: (B)

Explanation: In blood, bilirubin combines with plasma albumin to form UNCONJUGATED bilirubin complex, not conjugated bilirubin. Conjugation occurs in the liver with glucuronic acid.

167. Gallbladder Contraction

Question: Contraction of gallbladder is described by the following statements except:

  • (A) Occurs in response to CCK
  • (B) It is stimulated mainly by acid chyme in duodenum
  • (C) It is inhibited by atropine

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Gallbladder contraction is stimulated mainly by fat and amino acids in the duodenum (which release CCK), not by acid chyme. Acid chyme primarily stimulates secretin release.

168. Liver Cells

Question: All the following are correct statements about liver cells except:

  • (A) They convert amino acids into glucose
  • (B) They form cholesterol
  • (C) They release glucose when blood glucose tends to decrease
  • (D) They are the only site of synthesis of plasma globulins

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Plasma globulins (immunoglobulins) are synthesized primarily by plasma cells and B lymphocytes, not liver cells. The liver synthesizes albumin and most other plasma proteins, but not immunoglobulins.

169. Bile Salts

Question: The following statements about bile salts are true except:

  • (A) They help digestion and absorption of fat
  • (B) They have choleretic action
  • (C) They are actively absorbed from duodenum

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Bile salts are actively absorbed from the terminal ileum, not the duodenum. This is part of the enterohepatic circulation.

170. Bile Salts

Question: Choose a single incorrect answer about bile salts:

  • (A) Bile salts are secreted as conjugated bile salts by liver
  • (B) They are converted to secondary bile salts by action of intestinal bacteria
  • (C) They help absorption of calcium and iron
  • (D) None of the above

Answer: (D)

Explanation: All statements A, B, and C are actually correct. Bile salts are secreted conjugated, bacteria do convert them to secondary bile salts, and they do help with mineral absorption.

171. Gallbladder Emptying Inhibition

Question: Emptying of gallbladder is inhibited by the following except:

  • (A) Somatostatin
  • (B) Sympathetic stimulation
  • (C) Estrogen
  • (D) Progesterone

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Estrogen doesn't significantly inhibit gallbladder emptying. Somatostatin, sympathetic stimulation, and progesterone all inhibit gallbladder contraction.

172. Succus Entericus

Question: The following statements about succus entericus are true except:

  • (A) It contains digestive enzymes
  • (B) Its secretion depends on the amount of chyme in small intestine
  • (C) It is secreted by intestinal glands
  • (D) It is released mainly by vagal stimulation

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Succus entericus secretion is mainly controlled by local axon reflexes in response to mechanical and chemical stimuli, not primarily by vagal stimulation.

173. Succus Entericus Inhibition

Question: Succus entericus is inhibited by the following except:

  • (A) Adrenaline and noradrenaline
  • (B) Sympathetic stimulation
  • (C) Prostaglandins
  • (D) Endogenous opiates

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Prostaglandins (especially PGE₂) actually stimulate intestinal secretion, they don't inhibit it. They can cause secretory diarrhea.

174. Intestinal Proteolysis

Question: Intestinal proteolysis is caused by the following except:

  • (A) Trypsin
  • (B) Carboxypeptidase
  • (C) Chymotrypsin
  • (D) Pepsin

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Pepsin is a gastric enzyme that works in the acidic environment of the stomach, not in the intestine. Trypsin, carboxypeptidase, and chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes that work in the alkaline intestinal environment.

175. Intestinal Brush Border

Question: The intestinal brush border helps digestion by the following except:

  • (A) Facilitating movements of intestinal content
  • (B) Supplying digestive enzymes and special transport systems
  • (C) Increasing surface area of intestinal mucosa

Answer: (A)

Explanation: The brush border doesn't facilitate movements of intestinal content. Its functions are to increase surface area and provide digestive enzymes/transport systems. Intestinal movements are controlled by smooth muscle.

176. Cholera Toxin

Question: Cholera toxin causes diarrhea by:

  • (A) Activation of calcium-activated Cl⁻ channels in intestinal crypt cells
  • (B) Activation of cAMP-activated Cl⁻ channels
  • (C) Activation of both Ca²⁺ activated and cAMP-activated Cl⁻ channels

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Cholera toxin activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP levels, which then opens cAMP-activated Cl⁻ channels leading to massive chloride and fluid secretion.

177. Succus Entericus Volume

Question: The volume of succus entericus per day is about:

  • (A) 0.6L
  • (B) 2L
  • (C) 3L

Answer: (B)

Explanation: The small intestine secretes approximately 2 liters of succus entericus per day.

178. Succus Entericus Enzymes

Question: Digestion of proteins by succus entericus enzymes includes all the following except:

  • (A) Aminopeptidase
  • (B) Carboxypeptidase
  • (C) Nucleases
  • (D) Dipeptidase

Answer: (C)

Explanation: Nucleases digest nucleic acids (DNA/RNA), not proteins. Aminopeptidase, carboxypeptidase, and dipeptidase are all involved in protein digestion.

179. Lactase

Question: Lactase enzyme splits lactose into:

  • (A) Glucose
  • (B) Glucose and galactose
  • (C) Glucose and fructose

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Glucose and fructose would be the products of sucrase acting on sucrose.

180. Enteric Lipase

Question: Enteric lipase splits neutral fat into:

  • (A) Fatty acids and glycerol
  • (B) Fatty acids, glycerol and monoglycerides
  • (C) Monoglycerides

Answer: (B)

Explanation: Enteric lipase (like pancreatic lipase) splits triglycerides into fatty acids, glycerol, and monoglycerides - not completely into fatty acids and glycerol.

181. Succus Entericus Secretion Mechanism

Question: The main mechanism of succus entericus secretion is:

  • (A) Vagal stimulation
  • (B) CCK
  • (C) Secretin
  • (D) Local axon reflex

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Succus entericus secretion is primarily controlled by local axon reflexes in response to mechanical and chemical stimuli in the intestine.

182. Extracellular Enzyme

Question: The extracellular enzyme in succus entericus is:

  • (A) Dipeptidase
  • (B) Enteric lipase
  • (C) Lactase
  • (D) Enterokinase

Answer: (D)

Explanation: Enterokinase is secreted into the intestinal lumen (extracellular), while most other intestinal enzymes are bound to the brush border membrane.

183. Small Intestine Absorption
