Anatomy Questions and Answers - Comprehensive Study Guide

SECTION B - SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS

1. Describe how the epithelium of the urinary system is adapted to its functions (in the ureter, bladder and male urethra) (10 marks)

URETER (3 marks)

Transitional Epithelium Features:

  • Distensibility: Dome-shaped cells flatten during urine passage (1 mark)
  • Peristalsis support: Smooth epithelial surface allows coordinated muscular contractions (1 mark)
  • Protective barrier: Prevents urine backflow and protects against toxic substances (1 mark)

BLADDER (4 marks)

Transitional Epithelium Adaptations:

  • Maximum distensibility: Cells can stretch from 6 layers (empty) to 3 layers (full) (1 mark)
  • Impermeability: Tight junctions and specialized membrane prevent urine absorption back into blood (1 mark)
  • Umbrella cells: Surface cells with asymmetric unit membrane provide waterproof barrier (1 mark)
  • Regeneration capacity: High mitotic activity replaces damaged cells from acidic urine exposure (1 mark)

MALE URETHRA (3 marks)

Epithelial Variations by Region:

  • Prostatic and membranous urethra: Transitional epithelium continues bladder function (1 mark)
  • Penile urethra: Stratified squamous epithelium resists friction during intercourse (1 mark)
  • Navicular fossa: Stratified squamous with mucus-secreting cells for lubrication (1 mark)

2. State the stages of the male sexual response and the anatomical basis (10 marks)

Sexual Response Stages:

  1. Stimulation (2 marks)
    • Sensory stimulation (tactile receptors)
    • Psychogenic stimulation (cerebral cortex)
  2. Penile Tumescence (1 mark)
    • Arterial dilation and venous compression
  3. Lubrication (1 mark)
    • Bulbourethral glands secretion
  4. Orgasm (2 marks)
    • Emission: Seminal fluid accumulation in urethral bulb
    • Ejaculation: Rhythmic contractions of bulbospongiosus muscle
  5. Penile Detumescence (1 mark)
    • Arterial constriction and venous drainage
  6. Resolution (1 mark)
    • Return to baseline physiological state
  7. Refractory Period (1 mark)
    • Temporary inability to achieve arousal

3. State TEN functional areas of the cerebral cortex (10 marks)

  1. Primary motor area (M1)
  2. Motor speech area (Broca's area)
  3. Sensory speech area (Wernicke's area)
  4. Premotor area
  5. Cognitive area (prefrontal cortex)
  6. Limbic area
  7. Gustatory area
  8. Olfactory area
  9. Primary visual area (V1)
  10. Primary somatosensory area (S1)

Additional areas that could be included:

  • Secondary visual area
  • Tertiary visual area
  • Face recognition area
  • Association cortex
  • Arithmetic area

4. State the organization of the biliary tree, add notes on the structures compressed by a tumor of the head of the pancreas (10 marks)

BILIARY TREE ORGANIZATION (5 marks)

  1. Right hepatic duct: Drains right lobe of liver (1 mark)
  2. Left hepatic duct: Drains left lobe of liver (1 mark)
  3. Common hepatic duct: Union of right and left hepatic ducts (1 mark)
  4. Cystic duct: Connects gallbladder to common hepatic duct (1 mark)
  5. Common bile duct: Formed by union of common hepatic duct and cystic duct (1 mark)

STRUCTURES COMPRESSED BY PANCREATIC HEAD TUMOR (5 marks)

  1. Common bile duct: Causes obstructive jaundice with clay-colored stools (1 mark)
  2. Portal vein: Leads to portal hypertension and ascites (1 mark)
  3. Superior mesenteric artery: Causes mesenteric ischemia (1 mark)
  4. Duodenum: Results in gastric outlet obstruction (1 mark)
  5. Inferior vena cava: Causes lower limb edema and venous congestion (1 mark)

5. Write notes on the following:

a. The site of the major conducting parts of the heart (5 marks)

  • Sinoatrial node: Junction of superior vena cava and right atrium (posteromedial aspect)
  • Atrioventricular node: Triangle of Koch
  • Bundle of His: Interventricular septum
  • Purkinje fibers: Lower 1/3 of ventricles

b. FIVE features of the right atrium of the heart (5 marks)

  1. Fossa ovalis
  2. Limbus of fossa ovalis
  3. Opening of inferior vena cava
  4. Opening of coronary sinus
  5. Crista terminalis

6. Regarding the placenta, state:

a. The two main components (2 marks)

  1. Decidua basalis (maternal component)
  2. Chorion frondosum (fetal component)

b. One abnormality associated with:

  • Excessive invasion into the uterine wall: Placenta percreta
  • Implantation in the lower part of the uterus: Placenta previa

c. List two types of neurulation and indicate what they form (2 marks)

  1. Primary neurulation: Forms neural tube
  2. Secondary neurulation: Forms filum terminale

d. Name two derivatives of the neural crest cells in the abdomen (2 marks)

  1. Adrenal medulla
  2. Sympathetic ganglia

e. Give two possible causes of oligohydramnios (2 marks)

  1. Renal agenesis
  2. Rupture of membranes

7. Regarding the anatomy of swallowing describe the following:

a. The closure mechanisms (4 marks)

  1. Soft palate elevation: Levator veli palatini and palatoglossus muscles raise soft palate to close nasopharynx (1 mark)
  2. Passavant's ridge: Circular muscle contraction in posterior pharyngeal wall creates ridge that meets elevated soft palate (1 mark)
  3. Epiglottic closure: Epiglottis tilts backwards to cover laryngeal inlet during swallowing (1 mark)
  4. Vocal cord adduction: True and false vocal cords close tightly to protect lower respiratory tract (1 mark)

b. The muscles of the tongue involved and their respective role (4 marks)

  1. Genioglossus: Protrudes tongue and moves bolus posteriorly toward pharynx (1 mark)
  2. Intrinsic muscles: Longitudinal, transverse, and vertical fibers shape and mold the food bolus (1 mark)
  3. Palatoglossus: Elevates posterior tongue to push bolus toward oropharyngeal isthmus (1 mark)
  4. Styloglossus and hyoglossus: Retract tongue and assist in bolus propulsion toward esophagus (1 mark)

c. Movements of the hyoid bone and the larynx (2 marks)

  1. Hyoid bone: Geniohyoid and mylohyoid muscles pull hyoid anteriorly and superiorly, opening upper esophageal sphincter (1 mark)
  2. Larynx: Thyrohyoid muscle pulls larynx upward and forward, further protecting airway and facilitating swallowing (1 mark)

8. Describe the carpal tunnel under the following headings:

a. Boundaries (4 marks)

  1. Roof: Flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) spans from medial to lateral carpal bones (1 mark)
  2. Floor: Concave arch formed by carpal bones creating tunnel shape (1 mark)
  3. Medial boundary: Hook of hamate and pisiform bones (1 mark)
  4. Lateral boundary: Scaphoid tubercle and trapezium bones (1 mark)

b. Contents (6 marks)

Tendons (5 marks):

  1. Four flexor digitorum superficialis tendons: Flex proximal interphalangeal joints of fingers (1 mark)
  2. Four flexor digitorum profundus tendons: Flex distal interphalangeal joints of fingers (1 mark)
  3. One flexor pollicis longus tendon: Flexes thumb at interphalangeal joint (1 mark)
  4. Synovial sheaths: Ulnar and radial bursae surround tendons for smooth gliding (1 mark)
  5. Tendon arrangement: Superficialis tendons lie superficial to profundus tendons (1 mark)

Nerve (1 mark): 6. Median nerve: Provides sensation to lateral 3½ fingers and motor to thenar muscles (1 mark)

SECTION C - LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS

1. Describe the parotid gland under the following:

Relations, parts and structures (superficial to deep) that pass through it (10 marks)

Relations (3 marks):

  • Anterior: Ramus of mandible and masseter muscle (1 mark)
  • Posterior: External acoustic meatus and mastoid process (1 mark)
  • Medial: Styloid process and parapharyngeal space (1 mark)

Parts (2 marks):

  • Superficial lobe: Larger portion lateral to facial nerve (1 mark)
  • Deep lobe: Smaller portion medial to facial nerve (1 mark)

Structures passing through (superficial to deep) (5 marks):

  1. External jugular vein: Most superficial structure (1 mark)
  2. Facial nerve (CN VII): Divides gland into superficial and deep lobes (1 mark)
  3. Retromandibular vein: Formed by maxillary and superficial temporal veins (1 mark)
  4. External carotid artery: Gives rise to terminal branches (1 mark)
  5. Parotid duct (Stensen's duct): Emerges from anterior border, crosses masseter (1 mark)

Innervation (5 marks)

  1. Secretomotor (parasympathetic): Glossopharyngeal nerve → lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → gland (2 marks)
  2. Sympathetic: Superior cervical ganglion → plexus around external carotid artery → vasoconstriction (1 mark)
  3. Sensory: Great auricular nerve (C2, C3) → general sensation to gland capsule (1 mark)
  4. Motor: Facial nerve branches → muscles of facial expression (not gland tissue) (1 mark)

Clinical relevance (5 marks)

  1. Parotid tumors: Pleomorphic adenoma most common, risk of facial nerve injury during surgery (1 mark)
  2. Parotitis: Mumps causes painful swelling, Sjögren's syndrome causes dry mouth (1 mark)
  3. Facial nerve paralysis: Surgical trauma during parotidectomy can cause facial asymmetry (1 mark)
  4. Parotid duct stones: Cause pain during eating, palpable along duct course (1 mark)
  5. Frey's syndrome: Gustatory sweating after parotid surgery due to aberrant nerve regeneration (1 mark)

2. Describe the anatomy of vagus nerve:

a. Branches in the neck (3 marks)

  1. Superior laryngeal nerve
    • Internal branch (sensory)
    • External branch (motor to cricothyroid)

b. Course and extents (7 marks)

Course: Medulla oblongata → jugular foramen → carotid sheath → superior mediastinum → posterior mediastinum → esophageal opening of diaphragm → vagal trunks → hollow GIT up to right 2/3 of transverse colon

c. Associated functional components of the brainstem vagal nuclei (10 marks)

  1. Nucleus ambiguous: Special visceral efferent (SVE) - motor to laryngeal muscles
  2. Dorsal vagal nucleus: General visceral efferent (GVE) - parasympathetic to organs
  3. Nucleus of tractus solitarius: Special visceral afferent (SVA) - taste sensation
  4. Spinal nucleus of trigeminal: General somatic afferent (GSA) - sensation from ear
  5. General visceral afferent (GVA): Sensation from organs
  6. Pre-Bötzinger complex: Respiratory rhythm generation

3. Describe the ventricular system:

a. Origin and formation (4 marks)

  • Choroid plexus: Produces CSF
  • Ependymal cells: Line ventricles
  • Tela choroidea: Vascular membrane
  • Ultrafiltration: Mechanism of CSF production

b. Flow and course (8 marks)

CSF Flow Pattern: Lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina (of Monro) → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka (lateral) and Magendie (median) → subarachnoid cisterns → absorption at arachnoid granulations

c. Types of hydrocephalus and their respective anatomical basis (6 marks)

  1. Communicating hydrocephalus:
    • Excessive formation or blockage of drainage
    • CSF can flow between ventricles
  2. Non-communicating hydrocephalus:
    • Blockage of CSF flow within ventricular system
  3. Ex-vacuo hydrocephalus:
    • Increased ventricular size due to reduced brain tissue

d. Anatomical basis of hydranencephaly (2 marks)

  • Cause: Blockage of internal carotid artery
  • Result: No formation of prosencephalon (forebrain)

4. Regarding the lower limb:

i. Innervation of Adductor Magnus muscle (2 marks)

  • Tibial nerve (hamstring portion)
  • Obturator nerve (adductor portion)

ii. About the common peroneal nerve:

Two branches apart from terminal branches (2 marks):

  1. Sural communicating branch
  2. Muscular branch to short head of biceps femoris

Two clinical effects of injury at fibular neck (2 marks):

  1. Foot drop (inability to dorsiflex)
  2. Loss of sensation over dorsum of foot

iii. Two structures that traverse both greater and lesser sciatic foramina (2 marks)

  1. Pudendal nerve
  2. Internal pudendal vessels

iv. Two actions of gluteus minimus muscle (2 marks)

  1. Medial rotation of hip
  2. Abduction of hip

v. Two regions not drained by superficial inguinal nodes (2 marks)

  1. Lateral heel
  2. Calf

vi. Extents of the popliteal artery (2 marks)

  • Proximally: Adductor hiatus
  • Distally: Soleal arch

vii. Two structures in lateral compartment of femoral sheath (2 marks)

  1. Femoral artery
  2. Femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve

viii. Why femoral hernias are more common in females (1 mark)

  • Wider pelvis creates larger femoral canal

ix. Three main components of femoral arterial system (3 marks)

  1. Common femoral artery
  2. Deep femoral artery (profunda femoris)
  3. Superficial femoral artery

5. Regarding the abdomen:

i. Two vertically oriented muscles in anterior abdominal wall (2 marks)

  1. Pyramidalis
  2. Rectus abdominis

ii. Boundaries of triangle of Hesselbach (3 marks)

  1. Inguinal ligament (inferior)
  2. Inferior epigastric artery (lateral)
  3. Rectus sheath (medial)

iii. Three modifications of Scarpa's fascia (3 marks)

  1. Buck's fascia (penis)
  2. Colles' fascia (perineum)
  3. Dartos fascia (scrotum)

iv. Boundaries of epiploic foramen of Winslow (4 marks)

  • Anterior: Hepatoduodenal ligament
  • Posterior: Inferior vena cava
  • Superior: Caudate lobe of liver
  • Inferior: First part of duodenum

v. Anatomical and functional division of the liver (2 marks)

  • Anatomical: Ligamentum teres hepatis
  • Functional: Cantlie's plane

vi. Boundaries of triangle of Calot (3 marks)

  1. Cystic duct
  2. Common hepatic duct
  3. Cystic artery

vii. Vertebral levels of abdominal aorta branches (3 marks)

  • Celiac artery: T12
  • Superior mesenteric artery: L1
  • Inferior mesenteric artery: L3

6. Respiratory System:

a. Three mechanisms of ventilation and their anatomical basis (6 marks)

  1. Bucket handle movement: Lower ribs move upwards and outwards
  2. Pump handle movement: Sternum moves anteriorly
  3. Diaphragm contraction: Primary muscle of inspiration

b. Branching pattern of respiratory tree and lung areas (8 marks)

  1. Trachea → both lungs
  2. Principal bronchi → one lung each
  3. Secondary bronchi → individual lobes
  4. Tertiary bronchi → bronchopulmonary segments
  5. Terminal bronchioles → lobules
  6. Respiratory bronchioles → functional respiratory units

c. Pattern of fetal circulation (6 marks)

Main pathway (90%): Placenta → umbilical vein → ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium → foramen ovale → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → iliac arteries → umbilical arteries → placenta

Secondary pathway (10%): Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → ductus arteriosus → aorta → systemic circulation

ADDITIONAL POSSIBLE QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS

RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

1. Describe the lymphatic drainage of the lungs (10 marks)

Lymphatic Drainage Pattern:

  • Superficial (pleural) lymphatics: Drain to hilar nodes
  • Deep (pulmonary) lymphatics: Follow bronchial tree to hilar nodes
  • Hilar nodes → Mediastinal nodes → Tracheobroncheal nodes → Paratracheal nodes → Thoracic duct (left) or Right lymphatic duct (right)

Clinical Significance:

  • Cancer metastasis pathway
  • Pneumonia spread
  • Tuberculous infection pattern

2. State the blood supply of the lungs (8 marks)

Dual Blood Supply:

  1. Pulmonary circulation (deoxygenated blood):
    • Pulmonary trunk → Right & Left pulmonary arteries
    • Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to left atrium
  2. Bronchial circulation (oxygenated blood):
    • Bronchial arteries from aorta
    • Supply bronchi, bronchioles, and lung tissue
    • Bronchial veins drain to azygos system

3. Describe the surface anatomy and clinical correlations of lung fissures (6 marks)

Fissures:

  • Oblique fissure: T3 spinous process → 6th rib at midclavicular line
  • Horizontal fissure (right lung only): 4th rib → 5th rib at midaxillary line

Clinical Correlations:

  • Percussion boundaries
  • Chest tube insertion sites
  • Surgical approach landmarks

CARDIOVASCULAR SYSTEM

4. Describe the coronary circulation and its clinical significance (12 marks)

Coronary Arteries:

  1. Right coronary artery (RCA):
    • Supplies right ventricle, inferior wall of left ventricle
    • Posterior descending artery
    • Right marginal artery
  2. Left coronary artery:
    • Left anterior descending (LAD): Anterior wall, interventricular septum
    • Left circumflex (LCX): Lateral wall, posterior wall

Coronary Dominance:

  • Right dominant (85%): RCA gives posterior descending artery
  • Left dominant (8%): LCX gives posterior descending artery
  • Co-dominant (7%): Both contribute

Clinical Significance:

  • Myocardial infarction patterns
  • Collateral circulation
  • Surgical revascularization

5. State the layers of the heart wall and their histological features (8 marks)

Heart Wall Layers:

  1. Epicardium (visceral pericardium):
    • Simple squamous epithelium
    • Connective tissue
    • Coronary vessels
  2. Myocardium:
    • Cardiac muscle fibers
    • Intercalated discs
    • Conduction system
  3. Endocardium:
    • Endothelium
    • Subendothelial layer
    • Lines chambers and valves

NERVOUS SYSTEM

6. Describe the blood supply of the brain (Circle of Willis) (10 marks)

Arterial Supply: Anterior circulation:

  • Internal carotid arteries
  • Anterior cerebral arteries
  • Middle cerebral arteries
  • Anterior communicating artery

Posterior circulation:

  • Vertebral arteries
  • Basilar artery
  • Posterior cerebral arteries
  • Posterior communicating arteries

Clinical Significance:

  • Stroke patterns
  • Collateral circulation
  • Aneurysm locations

7. State the cranial nerves and their functional components (12 marks)

Cranial Nerves:

  1. Olfactory (I): SVA - smell
  2. Optic (II): SSA - vision
  3. Oculomotor (III): GSE, GVE - eye movement, pupil
  4. Trochlear (IV): GSE - superior oblique
  5. Trigeminal (V): GSA, SVE - sensation, mastication
  6. Abducens (VI): GSE - lateral rectus
  7. Facial (VII): SVE, GVE, SVA, GSA - facial expression, taste
  8. Vestibulocochlear (VIII): SSA - hearing, balance
  9. Glossopharyngeal (IX): SVE, GVE, GVA, SVA, GSA
  10. Vagus (X): SVE, GVE, GVA, SVA, GSA
  11. Accessory (XI): SVE - sternocleidomastoid, trapezius
  12. Hypoglossal (XII): GSE - tongue muscles

8. Describe the meninges and their clinical significance (10 marks)

Meningeal Layers:

  1. Dura mater:
    • Periosteal layer
    • Meningeal layer
    • Dural venous sinuses
  2. Arachnoid mater:
    • Arachnoid granulations
    • Subarachnoid space (CSF)
  3. Pia mater:
    • Closely adherent to brain
    • Follows sulci and gyri

Clinical Significance:

  • Epidural hematoma
  • Subdural hematoma
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Meningitis

GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM

9. Describe the blood supply of the stomach (8 marks)

Arterial Supply:

  1. Left gastric artery (from celiac trunk)
  2. Right gastric artery (from proper hepatic)
  3. Left gastroepiploic artery (from splenic)
  4. Right gastroepiploic artery (from gastroduodenal)
  5. Short gastric arteries (from splenic)

Venous Drainage:

  • Portal circulation: Left gastric vein → Portal vein
  • Systemic circulation: Short gastric veins → Splenic vein

10. State the parts of the duodenum and their relations (10 marks)

Four Parts:

  1. First part (5cm):
    • Relations: Liver, gallbladder, gastroduodenal artery
    • Common site for peptic ulcers
  2. Second part (7.5cm):
    • Descending part
    • Ampulla of Vater
    • Relations: Pancreatic head, bile duct
  3. Third part (10cm):
    • Horizontal part
    • Relations: IVC, aorta, superior mesenteric vessels
  4. Fourth part (2.5cm):
    • Ascending part
    • Relations: Left psoas, aorta

GENITOURINARY SYSTEM

11. Describe the blood supply of the kidney (8 marks)

Arterial Supply:

  • Renal artery → Segmental arteries → Interlobar arteries → Arcuate arteries → Interlobular arteries → Afferent arterioles → Glomerular capillaries → Efferent arterioles → Peritubular capillaries

Venous Drainage:

  • Follows arterial pattern in reverse
  • Left renal vein: Longer, receives left gonadal and left suprarenal veins
  • Right renal vein: Shorter, drains directly to IVC

12. State the anatomy of the male urethra (10 marks)

Four Parts:

  1. Pre-prostatic/Intramural (1cm):
    • Through bladder wall
    • Lined by transitional epithelium
  2. Prostatic (3cm):
    • Through prostate gland
    • Prostatic utricle
    • Ejaculatory duct openings
  3. Membranous (2cm):
    • Through urogenital diaphragm
    • External urethral sphincter
    • Narrowest part
  4. Penile/Spongy (15cm):
    • Through corpus spongiosum
    • Bulbous and pendulous parts
    • External urethral orifice

MUSCULOSKELETAL SYSTEM

13. Describe the rotator cuff muscles (8 marks)

SITS Muscles:

  1. Supraspinatus:
    • Origin: Supraspinous fossa
    • Insertion: Greater tubercle
    • Action: Abduction (first 15°)
  2. Infraspinatus:
    • Origin: Infraspinous fossa
    • Insertion: Greater tubercle
    • Action: External rotation
  3. Teres minor:
    • Origin: Lateral border of scapula

  4. Subscapularis:
    • Origin: Subscapular fossa
    • Insertion: Lesser tubercle
    • Action: Internal rotation

14. State the compartments of the thigh and their nerve supply (9 marks)

Three Compartments:

  1. Anterior compartment:
    • Muscles: Quadriceps femoris, sartorius
    • Nerve: Femoral nerve
    • Action: Hip flexion, knee extension
  2. Medial compartment:
    • Muscles: Adductor group
    • Nerve: Obturator nerve
    • Action: Hip adduction
  3. Posterior compartment:
    • Muscles: Hamstring group
    • Nerve: Sciatic nerve
    • Action: Hip extension, knee flexion

EMBRYOLOGY

15. Describe the development of the heart (10 marks)

Heart Development:

  1. Week 3: Heart tube formation
  2. Week 4: Cardiac looping
  3. Week 5-8: Septation
    • Atrial septum (septum primum, septum secundum)
    • Ventricular septum
    • Atrioventricular canal division
    • Truncus arteriosus division

Congenital Anomalies:

  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Atrial septal defect
  • Tetralogy of Fallot
  • Transposition of great vessels

16. State the derivatives of the branchial arches (12 marks)

Six Branchial Arches:

  1. First arch:
    • Mandible, maxilla, trigeminal nerve
    • Muscles of mastication
  2. Second arch:
    • Stapes, facial nerve

  3. Third arch:
    • Hyoid bone, glossopharyngeal nerve

  4. Fourth arch:
    • Thyroid cartilage, superior laryngeal nerve
    • Cricothyroid muscle
  5. Fifth arch:
    • Rudimentary in humans
  6. Sixth arch:
    • Laryngeal cartilages, recurrent laryngeal nerve

HISTOLOGY

17. Describe the structure of a typical synovial joint (8 marks)

Synovial Joint Components:

  1. Articular cartilage: Hyaline cartilage
  2. Joint capsule: Fibrous outer layer
  3. Synovial membrane: Inner secretory layer
  4. Synovial fluid: Lubricant and nutrient

Title: Abdomen/Pelvis Anatomy MCQs
Content:
Organized Study Guide

Section 1

Question 1

A midline abdominal incision below the umbilicus passes through all the following EXCEPT:

a) pyramidalis
b) linea alba
c) extraperitoneal fat
d) transversalis fascia
e) Scarpa's fascia

Answer: A - pyramidalis

Explanation: The pyramidalis muscle is not consistently present in all individuals (absent in about 20% of people) and when present, it lies within the rectus sheath but is not always encountered in midline incisions below the umbilicus.

Question 2

The spleen:

a) has a lower pole which normally projects forward to the anterior axillary line
b) lies between the 8th and 10th ribs
c) has a long axis lying in the line of the 9th rib
d) as it enlarges, glides in contact with the anterior abdominal wall in front of the splenic flexure of the colon
e) when palpable on abdominal examination, is identified by being resonant to percussion

Answer: D - as it enlarges, glides in contact with the anterior abdominal wall in front of the splenic flexure of the colon

Explanation: When the spleen enlarges (splenomegaly), it moves anteriorly and inferiorly, coming into contact with the anterior abdominal wall anterior to the splenic flexure of the colon. This is the typical pattern of splenic enlargement.

Question 3

Which is the most common site for the appendix found at appendicectomy?

a) retro-ileal
b) retro-caecal
c) pelvic
d) anterior to terminal ileum
e) below terminal ileum overlying psoas

Answer: B - retro-caecal

Explanation: The retro-caecal position is the most common anatomical position of the appendix, found in approximately 65% of cases. This position places the appendix behind the caecum.

Question 4

The abdominal aorta:

a) passes into the abdomen behind the diaphragm at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra
b) bifurcates at the level of the body of the 2nd lumbar vertebra
c) has a surface marking for its bifurcation as 2cm below and to the right of the umbilicus
d) gives rise to the coeliac artery at the level of the body of the 10th thoracic vertebra
e) has the renal arteries arising at the level of the body of the 1st lumbar vertebra

Answer: D - gives rise to the coeliac artery at the level of the body of the 10th thoracic vertebra

Explanation: The coeliac trunk (first major branch of the abdominal aorta) arises at the level of T12, not T10. The aorta enters the abdomen at T12, bifurcates at L4, and renal arteries arise at L1-L2 level.

Question 5

With regard to the spleen, which is NOT true?

a) in splenomegaly, the splenic flexure of the colon lies superficial to its anterior border
b) its anterior border is notched
c) its medial relations include left kidney, lienorenal ligament, pancreas and lesser sac
d) it lies between the 9th and 11th ribs
e) accessory spleens occur in 10% of people

Answer: A - in splenomegaly, the splenic flexure of the colon lies superficial to its anterior border

Explanation: In splenomegaly, the enlarged spleen moves anteriorly and the splenic flexure of the colon lies deep (posterior) to the spleen, not superficial to it.

Question 6

With regard to the duodenum, which is NOT true?

a) the duodenal cap has plicae circulares which are often evident on x-ray
b) the third part may be compressed by the superior mesenteric artery
c) the second part lies at level of 2nd lumbar vertebra in cadavers
d) the duodenal cap lies upon bile duct, hepatic artery and portal vein
e) the accessory pancreatic duct opens into it proximal to the ampulla of Vater

Answer: A - the duodenal cap has plicae circulares which are often evident on x-ray

Explanation: The duodenal cap (first part of duodenum) is characteristically smooth and lacks plicae circulares (circular folds), which are found in the more distal parts of the duodenum and small intestine.

Question 7

The ejaculatory ducts:

a) are formed by the union of the prostatic ducts and the ducts of the seminal vesicle
b) lie on the superior surface of the bladder
c) open into the membranous urethra
d) contract with parasympathetic stimulation
e) have none of the above properties

Answer: E - have none of the above properties

Explanation: The ejaculatory ducts are formed by the union of the vas deferens and seminal vesicle ducts (not prostatic ducts), they lie within the prostate gland, open into the prostatic urethra (not membranous), and contract with sympathetic (not parasympathetic) stimulation.

Question 8

The ureter passes deep to the:

a) femoral nerve
b) gonadal artery
c) psoas muscle
d) genitofemoral nerve
e) common iliac artery

Answer: B - gonadal artery

Explanation: The ureter passes deep (posterior) to the gonadal vessels (testicular/ovarian artery and vein) as it descends in the retroperitoneum.

Question 9

With respect to the testicle:

a) the tunica albuginea overlies tunica vaginalis
b) the head of the epididymis is attached to the lower pole of the testis
c) the appendix testis (if present) is attached to the upper pole of the testicle
d) testicular and scrotal lymph drainage is the superficial inguinal nodes
e) parasympathetic supply is via the T10 segment of the cord

Answer: C - the appendix testis (if present) is attached to the upper pole of the testicle

Explanation: The appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni) is a small remnant structure attached to the upper pole of the testis near the head of the epididymis.

Question 10

With regard to the spleen, which is NOT true?

a) it is in direct contact with the lesser sac
b) it projects into the greater sac
c) its anterior border is notched
d) it receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply
e) lymph drainage is via retropancreatic channels to the coeliac nodes

Answer: D - it receives both sympathetic and parasympathetic supply

Explanation: The spleen receives only sympathetic innervation from the celiac plexus. It does not receive parasympathetic supply.

Question 11

Regarding abdominal vascular anatomy, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

a) the left renal vein lies under the superior mesenteric artery
b) the appendix is supplied by the ileo colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery
c) the left gastro epiploic artery is a branch of the splenic artery
d) the portal vein lies posterior to the pylorus
e) the duodenum receives no supply from the superior mesenteric artery

Answer: E - the duodenum receives no supply from the superior mesenteric artery

Explanation: The duodenum does receive blood supply from the superior mesenteric artery via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which supplies the third and fourth parts of the duodenum.

Question 12

With regard to the ureter, which is NOT true?

a) it is narrowed at its halfway mark
b) it crosses the genitofemoral nerve under cover of peritoneum
c) the upper part of the right ureter lies behind the duodenum
d) it lies just lateral to the tips of the transverse processes of L3-5
e) it is adherent to the peritoneum of the posterior abdominal wall

Answer: D - it lies just lateral to the tips of the transverse processes of L3-5

Explanation: The ureter lies medial to the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, not lateral to them.

Question 13

With regard to the female pelvis, which is NOT true?

a) the cervix is separated from the rectum by the Pouch of Douglas
b) the cervix is separated from the bladder by the vesicouterine pouch
c) the ureter passes 1-2cm lateral to the cervix
d) the ureter passes under both the broad ligament and the uterine artery
e) lymph drainage from the body of the uterus includes the inguinal nodes

Answer: B - the cervix is separated from the bladder by the vesicouterine pouch

Explanation: The cervix is not separated from the bladder by the vesicouterine pouch. The vesicouterine pouch is between the body of the uterus and the bladder, not between the cervix and bladder.

Question 14

With regard to the duodenum:

a) it is wholly retro-peritoneal
b) it lies wholly inferior to gallbladder
c) the third part overlies the superior mesenteric vessels
d) the second part projects slightly behind the right renal hilus
e) the head of pancreas is wholly contained within its c-shaped loop

Answer: E - the head of pancreas is wholly contained within its c-shaped loop

Explanation: The head of the pancreas is not wholly contained within the duodenal loop. Part of the head extends beyond the duodenal C-loop, and the uncinate process extends posteriorly.

Question 15

The transversalis fascia contributes to which of the following structures on the anterior abdominal wall?

a) superficial inguinal ring
b) deep inguinal ring
c) inguinal ligament
d) sac of an indirect inguinal hernia
e) anterior wall of the inguinal canal

Answer: B - deep inguinal ring

Explanation: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia, so the transversalis fascia forms the margins of the deep inguinal ring.

Question 16

The transpyloric plane of the abdomen (passing through the lower border of L1 vertebra) passes through:

a) the spleen
b) the third part of the duodenum
c) the tail of the pancreas
d) the origin of the superior mesenteric artery
e) the fundus of the gallbladder

Answer: D - the origin of the superior mesenteric artery

Explanation: The transpyloric plane passes through the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta at the level of L1.

Question 17

Afferent pain fibres for the biliary tract:

a) as far as known do not exist; pain sensation relates to inflamed overlying parietal peritoneum
b) run with the vagus nerve to the Nucleus of the Solitary Tract
c) may run with the right phrenic nerve
d) run with spinal nerves to T2-5
e) do not respond to distension of the viscus

Answer: C - may run with the right phrenic nerve

Explanation: Gallbladder pain can be referred to the right shoulder via the right phrenic nerve, indicating that some afferent pain fibers from the biliary tract may run with the phrenic nerve.

Question 18

With regard to the usual vasculature of the abdomen, which is NOT true?

a) the splenic vein mainly drains into the inferior vena cava
b) the portal vein drains nearly all of the gastrointestinal tract and unpaired abdominal glands except liver
c) the left gastroepiploic artery and the short gastric arteries are branches of the splenic artery
d) the right gastric artery is a branch of the hepatic artery
e) the right gastroepiploic artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery

Answer: A - the splenic vein mainly drains into the inferior vena cava

Explanation: The splenic vein drains into the portal vein (joining with the superior mesenteric vein), not directly into the inferior vena cava.

Question 19

Which is NOT related to the kidneys as indicated:

a) the pleura posteriorly
b) the second part of the duodenum, anterior to the right kidney
c) the tail of the pancreas, anterior to the left kidney
d) the peritoneum of the lesser sac, anterior to the left kidney
e) the splenic artery, anterior to the lower pole of the left kidney

Answer: E - the splenic artery, anterior to the lower pole of the left kidney

Explanation: The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas and is not in direct relation to the lower pole of the left kidney.

Question 20

With regard to the kidneys, which is NOT true?

a) the renal nerves are from spinal segment T12-L1
b) at the hilum, the vein is anterior to the artery which is anterior to the ureter
c) in horseshoe kidneys, ureters pass behind the isthmus of the kidney substance
d) percutaneous renal biopsy is via a point 2.5cm below the 12th rib
e) renal fascia helps prevent spread of infection from perinephric abscesses

Answer: C - in horseshoe kidneys, ureters pass behind the isthmus of the kidney substance

Explanation: In horseshoe kidneys, the ureters pass anterior to the isthmus (connecting bridge of kidney tissue), not behind it.

Question 21

With regard to the urethra in the young adult male, which is NOT true?

a) the prostatic urethra is narrower than the membranous urethra
b) it is approximately 20cm long
c) has a short dilated region just proximal to the external urethral meatus
d) it is horizontal in cross-section when empty
e) the bulbous part is part of the spongy urethra

Answer: A - the prostatic urethra is narrower than the membranous urethra

Explanation: The prostatic urethra is actually wider than the membranous urethra. The membranous urethra is the narrowest part of the male urethra.

Question 22

The first part of the duodenum:

a) lies at the level of L2 in the supine body
b) is approximately 10cm long in the adult
c) partially overlies the right crus of the diaphragm and psoas muscle
d) is entirely retroperitoneal
e) receives the common opening of the bile duct on its posteromedial wall

Answer: C - partially overlies the right crus of the diaphragm and psoas muscle

Explanation: The first part of the duodenum (duodenal cap) lies at the level of L1 and posteriorly is related to the right crus of the diaphragm and psoas muscle.

Question 23

Which of the following forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?

a) conjoint tendon
b) internal oblique muscle
c) transversus abdominus muscle
d) lacunar ligament
e) external oblique muscle

Answer: A - conjoint tendon

Explanation: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the conjoint tendon (combined aponeuroses of internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles) medially and the transversalis fascia laterally.

Question 24

Fibres of transversus abdominus arise from which part of the inguinal ligament?

a) medial one third
b) lateral one third
c) lateral two thirds
d) lateral half
e) middle one third

Answer: D - lateral half

Explanation: The transversus abdominis muscle arises from the lateral half of the inguinal ligament, while the internal oblique arises from the lateral two-thirds.

Question 25

A patient presents with a deep stab wound high up in the costovertebral angle beneath the 12th rib on the left side. The most likely internal injury is?

a) laceration of the infra-renal aorta
b) laceration of the right renal vascular pedicle
c) puncture of the 3rd part of the duodenum
d) puncture of the 4th part of the duodenum
e) pneumothorax of the left lung

Answer: E - pneumothorax of the left lung

Explanation: A wound high up in the costovertebral angle beneath the 12th rib is most likely to injure the pleura and lung, causing pneumothorax, as the pleura extends below the 12th rib in this region.

Question 26

Concerning the abdominal aorta and branches:

a) the inferior mesenteric artery arises below the L4 lumbar arteries
b) the superior mesenteric artery arises at the level of L2
c) the renal artery arises below the level of the superior mesenteric artery
d) the suprarenal arteries arise above the coeliac trunk
e) the coeliac trunk is the highest branch of the abdominal aorta

Answer: C - the renal artery arises below the level of the superior mesenteric artery

Explanation: The renal arteries arise at L1-L2 level, which is below the superior mesenteric artery that arises at L1 level.

Question 27

The relations of the THIRD part of the duodenum include:

a) the hilum of the right kidney
b) the attachment of the transverse mesocolon
c) the inferior pole of the right kidney
d) the superior mesenteric vein
e) the portal vein

Answer: D - the superior mesenteric vein

Explanation: The third part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein).

Question 28

All of the following are true regarding the pancreas EXCEPT:

a) the neck and body of the pancreas lie anterior to the first lumbar vertebrae
b) the neck of the pancreas lies over the right and left renal veins at the level of L2 vertebra
c) the splenic artery supplies all of the pancreas
d) parasympathetic vagal fibres stimulate the exocrine secretion from the gland
e) the uncinate process drains via an accessory pancreatic duct into the duodenum

Answer: C - the splenic artery supplies all of the pancreas

Explanation: The splenic artery supplies the body and tail of the pancreas, but the head and uncinate process are supplied by the pancreaticoduodenal arteries from the gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries.

Question 29

The spleen:

a) weighs 15 ounces
b) lies between the 8th and 11th ribs
c) has an identifiable notch on its posterior border
d) is supplied with parasympathetic fibres from coeliac plexus
e) lymphatic drainage is to coeliac nodes

Answer: E - lymphatic drainage is to coeliac nodes

Explanation: The spleen's lymphatic drainage is to the pancreaticosplenic lymph nodes and then to the coeliac nodes.

Question 30

Regarding the kidneys:

a) the right kidney lies at a lower level to the left kidney
b) they lie inferior to the pleura
c) the hilum of the left kidney is separated from the peritoneum by the duodenum
d) the renal fascia encloses the kidney and suprarenal gland within the same sheath
e) the renal pelvis is lined with columnar epithelium

Answer: A - the right kidney lies at a lower level to the left kidney

Explanation: The right kidney lies slightly lower than the left kidney due to the presence of the liver above it.

Question 31

Regarding the ureters, which is INCORRECT?

a) the line of projection of the ureter on a radiograph is medial to the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae and crosses the pelvic brim at the sacroiliac joint
b) they exhibit peristaltic activity when stimulated
c) they are lined by transitional epithelium with a thick muscularis mucosae
d) they are supplied with sympathetic fibres from T11-L2
e) they are crossed superficially by the gonadal vessels

Answer: C - they are lined by transitional epithelium with a thick muscularis mucosae

Explanation: The ureters are lined by transitional epithelium but do not have a muscularis mucosae. They have a muscular wall with inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers.

Question 32

Regarding the inguinal canal:

a) the deep inguinal ring lies 1cm above and at the junction of the lateral third and medial two thirds of the inguinal ligament
b) the deep inguinal ring is formed by an opening in the transversalis fascia
c) an indirect inguinal hernia bulges into the inguinal triangle, posterior to the canal and medial to the inferior epigastric artery
d) contains the spermatic cord that has two fascial layers/coverings and eight contents

Answer: B - the deep inguinal ring is formed by an opening in the transversalis fascia

Explanation: The deep inguinal ring is indeed an opening in the transversalis fascia, located above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.

Question 33

Which structure does not enter the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring?

a) testicular artery
b) vas deferens
c) ilioinguinal nerve
d) genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
e) artery to the vas deferens

Answer: C - ilioinguinal nerve

Explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve does not pass through the deep inguinal ring. It pierces the internal oblique muscle and enters the inguinal canal more superficially.

Question 34

The testis:

a) the epididymis arises from the lower pole of the testis
b) the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis but does not encase the epididymis
c) vas deferens ascends on the anterior surface of the testis
d) the testicular appendix lies on the testis upper pole near the origin of the epididymis

Answer: D - the testicular appendix lies on the testis upper pole near the origin of the epididymis

Explanation: The appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni) is a small vestigial structure located at the upper pole of the testis near the head of the epididymis.

Question 35

The testicular blood supply:

a) is mainly from the ductal artery
b) the right drains directly into the inferior vena cava
c) venous drainage does not have valves
d) a varicocele is more common on the right than the left

Answer: B - the right drains directly into the inferior vena cava

Explanation: The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava, while the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.

Question 36

The transpyloric plane:

a) lies on a line connecting left and right 10th costal cartilages
b) lies at the level of T12
c) lies at the origin of the superior mesenteric artery off the aorta
d) is 2cm below the xiphisternum

Answer: C - lies at the origin of the superior mesenteric artery off the aorta

Explanation: The transpyloric plane passes through the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta at the level of L1.

Question 37

Regarding potential spaces in the abdomen:

a) the entrance to the lesser sac is inferiorly via the transverse mesocolon foramen
b) the right hepatorenal pouch is the lowest lying region of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position (excluding pelvis)
c) the peritoneal cavity is divided into supracolic and infracolic by the epiploic foramen
d) the root of the mesentery of the small intestine is a small 2cm area at the duodenojejunal junction

Answer: B - the right hepatorenal pouch is the lowest lying region of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position (excluding pelvis)

Explanation: The hepatorenal pouch (of Morison) is the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity when supine, making it a common site for fluid collection.

Question 38

The foregut:

a) includes from the abdominal aorta to the end of the duodenum
b) is supplied by branches of the superior mesenteric artery
c) venous drainage includes the blood from the lower third of the oesophagus
d) drains entirely into the splenic vein

Answer: C - venous drainage includes the blood from the lower third of the oesophagus

Explanation: The foregut includes the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum to the ampulla of Vater, and its venous drainage includes the lower third of the esophagus.

Question 39

The midgut:

a) is from the opening of the bile duct into the duodenum to the ileocecal junction
b) all venous drainage is to the superior mesenteric vein
c) superior mesenteric artery lies on the right side of the superior mesenteric vein
d) superior mesenteric artery originates off the aorta at L3

Answer: B - all venous drainage is to the superior mesenteric vein

Explanation: The midgut (from the duodenum distal to the ampulla to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon) drains venously via the superior mesenteric vein.

Question 40

The inferior mesenteric artery arises:

a) at L3
b) behind the inferior border of the third part of the duodenum
c) at the level of the umbilicus
d) 3-4cm above the aortic bifurcation
e) all of the above

Answer: E - all of the above

Explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery arises at L3, which is at the level of the umbilicus, behind the third part of the duodenum, and about 3-4cm above the aortic bifurcation.

Question 41

The nerve supply to the stomach:

a) the anterior vagal trunk alone controls the pyloric sphincter
b) the posterior vagal trunk alone controls the pyloric sphincter
c) secretion is controlled by sympathetic supply
d) the posterior vagal trunk is in contact with the left side of the esophagus

Answer: A - the anterior vagal trunk alone controls the pyloric sphincter

Explanation: The anterior vagal trunk provides the main parasympathetic control to the pyloric sphincter, though both vagal trunks contribute to gastric innervation.

Question 42

The liver:

a) lies from the 7th to the 11th left ribs along the midaxillary line
b) is normally completely under the costal margin
c) the upper margin is the 4th costal cartilage
d) blood supply divides into left and right supplying the lobes as divided by the falciform ligament

Answer: A - lies from the 7th to the 11th left ribs along the midaxillary line

Explanation: The liver extends from approximately the 7th to the 11th ribs along the midaxillary line on the left side.

Question 43

The spleen:

a) is a retroperitoneal organ
b) lies along the axis of the left 10th rib
c) lymphatics drain to the superior mesenteric paraaortic nodes
d) pain fibres accompany sympathetic fibres and pain may radiate in the distribution of thoracic dermatomes 6-10

Answer: B - lies along the axis of the left 10th rib

Explanation: The spleen lies along the axis of the left 10th rib in the left hypochondrium.

Question 44

Which nerve passes through psoas muscle and emerges anteriorly to run down the front of the muscle?

a) ilioinguinal
b) iliohypogastric
c) genitofemoral
d) lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

Answer: C - genitofemoral

Explanation: The genitofemoral nerve passes through the psoas major muscle and emerges on its anterior surface, then divides into genital and femoral branches.

Question 45

Regarding the anterior abdominal wall:

a) the arcuate lines lie midway between the symphysis pubis and umbilicus
b) between the umbilicus and the lateral margin transversus aponeurosis lies posterior the rectus
c) the inferior epigastric artery originates from the internal iliac
d) it gives support to the liver and spleen
e) the ilioinguinal nerve passes through the deep inguinal ring

Answer: B - between the umbilicus and the lateral margin transversus aponeurosis lies posterior the rectus

Explanation: Below the umbilicus, the aponeuroses of all three flat muscles pass anterior to the rectus abdominis, so the transversus aponeurosis lies posterior to the rectus only above the umbilicus.

Question 46

Pelvic joints and ligaments:

a) the sacroiliac joint is a fibrous joint between the auricular surfaces of the ilium and sacrum
b) the wedge shape of the sacrum contributes to its stability
c) the coccygeus muscle lies on the pelvic surface of the sacrotuberous ligament
d) the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments enclose the greater sciatic foramen
e) the iliolumbar ligament is V-shaped with the apex attached to L5

Answer: E - the iliolumbar ligament is V-shaped with the apex attached to L5

Explanation: The iliolumbar ligament is V-shaped with its apex attached to the transverse process of L5 and its two limbs extending to the iliac crest.

Question 47

Pelvic joints and ligaments:

a) muscles of pelvis include obturator externus and piriformis
b) piriformis arises from the lower third part of the sacrum
c) the sigmoid colon becomes the section at the level of the 4th part of the sacrum
d) the rectum has no mesentery
e) the pelvic brim follows the line of the pubic crest, pectineal line of pubis, iliac crests and ala and promontory of the sacrum

Answer: D - the rectum has no mesentery

Explanation: The rectum is a retroperitoneal structure and lacks a mesentery, unlike the sigmoid colon which has a mesentery.

Question 48

Perineum:

a) the lymphatic drainage from the scrotum goes to para-aortic nodes
b) lymphatic drainage from the rectum passes to internal iliac nodes from the upper part and to superficial inguinal group from the lower part
c) superior rectal branches of the pudendal nerves supply the external anal sphincter
d) the internal anal sphincter is compose

Anatomy Questions - Continued Series

Question 50

The portal vein: a) is formed by the union of the superior and inferior mesenteric veins
b) lies posterior to the bile duct in the porta hepatis
c) receives blood from the azygos system
d) is about 8cm long
e) drains directly into the right atrium

Answer: d
Explanation: The portal vein is approximately 8cm long and is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins behind the pancreas. It lies posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery in the porta hepatis.

Question 51

Regarding the inferior vena cava: a) it passes through the diaphragm at the level of T10
b) it lies to the left of the abdominal aorta
c) it receives the left gonadal vein directly
d) it is formed by the union of the common iliac veins at L4
e) it lies anterior to the right kidney

Answer: a
Explanation: The IVC passes through the diaphragm at T10 level through the caval opening. It lies to the right of the aorta, is formed at L5 level, and the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC.

Question 52

The spleen: a) is an intraperitoneal organ
b) lies between the 9th and 11th ribs
c) is supplied by the right gastric artery
d) has its hilum facing laterally
e) is drained by lymphatics to the para-aortic nodes

Answer: a
Explanation: The spleen is completely covered by peritoneum (intraperitoneal). It lies between the 9th-11th ribs, is supplied by the splenic artery, and its hilum faces medially. Lymphatic drainage is to the splenic nodes.

Question 53

Regarding the adrenal glands: a) both glands are supplied by three arteries
b) the right gland is triangular in shape
c) the left adrenal vein drains into the IVC
d) they lie outside the renal fascia
e) the cortex is derived from neural crest cells

Answer: a
Explanation: Both adrenal glands receive blood supply from three sources: superior (from phrenic), middle (from aorta), and inferior (from renal) adrenal arteries. The right gland is pyramidal, left is crescentic. The left adrenal vein drains to the left renal vein.

Question 54

The rectum: a) begins at the level of S2
b) has three lateral curvatures
c) is completely covered by peritoneum
d) receives its blood supply solely from the superior rectal artery
e) is 12cm long

Answer: e
Explanation: The rectum is approximately 12cm long, begins at S3 level, has three lateral curvatures (right, left, right), and only its upper third is covered by peritoneum. It receives blood from superior, middle, and inferior rectal arteries.

Question 55

Concerning the gallbladder: a) it lies at the tip of the 9th costal cartilage
b) it is completely covered by peritoneum
c) the cystic artery is usually a branch of the left hepatic artery
d) it can store up to 100ml of bile
e) Hartmann's pouch is at the neck

Answer: e
Explanation: Hartmann's pouch is a dilatation at the neck of the gallbladder where stones commonly lodge. The gallbladder lies at the tip of the 9th costal cartilage, is partially covered by peritoneum, and the cystic artery is usually from the right hepatic artery.

Question 56

The cisterna chyli: a) lies at the level of T10
b) is located anterior to the aorta
c) drains into the left subclavian vein
d) receives lymph from the lower limbs
e) is formed by the union of two lumbar trunks

Answer: d
Explanation: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from the lower limbs via the lumbar lymph trunks, the intestinal trunk, and other abdominal lymphatics. It lies at L1-L2 level, posterior to the aorta, and drains into the thoracic duct.

Question 57

Regarding the lumbar plexus: a) it is formed by the anterior rami of L1-L4
b) the obturator nerve supplies the adductor muscles
c) the femoral nerve has no cutaneous branches
d) the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causes meralgia paresthetica when compressed
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The lumbar plexus is formed by L1-L4 anterior rami, the obturator nerve supplies adductors, the femoral nerve has cutaneous branches, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression causes meralgia paresthetica.

Question 58

The psoas major muscle: a) arises from the bodies of L1-L5 vertebrae
b) passes under the inguinal ligament
c) inserts into the greater trochanter
d) is supplied by the obturator nerve
e) lies medial to the kidney

Answer: b
Explanation: Psoas major passes under the inguinal ligament to reach the thigh. It arises from T12-L5 vertebrae, inserts into the lesser trochanter, is supplied by lumbar plexus branches, and lies lateral to the vertebral bodies.

Question 59

The sympathetic trunk in the abdomen: a) lies anterior to the psoas muscle
b) has 5 lumbar ganglia
c) gives rise to the greater splanchnic nerve
d) provides preganglionic fibers to the adrenal medulla
e) lies medial to the psoas muscle

Answer: e
Explanation: The sympathetic trunk lies medial to the psoas muscle on the vertebral bodies. It typically has 4 lumbar ganglia, the greater splanchnic nerve arises from the thoracic sympathetic trunk, and it provides preganglionic fibers to various abdominal organs including the adrenal medulla.

Question 60

The azygos venous system: a) drains into the superior vena cava
b) the hemiazygos vein crosses at T8 level
c) provides collateral circulation between IVC and SVC
d) receives intercostal veins
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The azygos system drains into the SVC, hemiazygos crosses at T8, it provides important collateral circulation between systemic venous systems, and receives posterior intercostal veins.

Question 61

Regarding the diaphragm: a) the aortic hiatus is at T10 level
b) the esophageal hiatus is at T10 level
c) the inferior vena cava passes through at T8
d) the right crus is larger than the left
e) it receives blood supply from the intercostal arteries only

Answer: d
Explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm is larger and longer than the left. The aortic hiatus is at T12, esophageal hiatus at T10, and IVC hiatus at T8. Blood supply includes phrenic, intercostal, and other arteries.

Question 62

The obturator nerve: a) arises from the posterior divisions of L2-L4
b) passes through the obturator foramen
c) supplies the hip joint
d) may cause referred pain to the knee
e) supplies the gracilis muscle

Answer: b
Explanation: The obturator nerve passes through the obturator foramen to reach the medial thigh. It arises from anterior divisions of L2-L4, supplies the hip joint, can cause referred knee pain, and supplies gracilis among other adductor muscles.

Question 63

Concerning the femoral triangle: a) its boundaries are the inguinal ligament, adductor longus, and sartorius
b) it contains the femoral nerve, artery, and vein
c) the femoral vein lies lateral to the femoral artery
d) the deep inguinal lymph nodes lie within it
e) the femoral canal contains the femoral artery

Answer: a
Explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament superiorly, adductor longus medially, and sartorius laterally. The femoral vein lies medial to the artery, and the femoral canal contains lymphatics and fat, not the artery.

Question 64

The internal iliac artery: a) divides into anterior and posterior divisions
b) the posterior division gives rise to the superior gluteal artery
c) the anterior division gives rise to the internal pudendal artery
d) supplies the pelvic viscera
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The internal iliac artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The posterior division gives branches including the superior gluteal artery, while the anterior division supplies pelvic viscera and gives rise to the internal pudendal artery.

Question 65

Regarding the sacral plexus: a) it is formed by L4-S4 nerve roots
b) the sciatic nerve is its largest branch
c) the pudendal nerve arises from S2-S4
d) it lies on the posterior wall of the pelvis
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The sacral plexus is formed by L4-S4, gives rise to the sciatic nerve (largest nerve in the body), includes the pudendal nerve from S2-S4, and lies on the posterior pelvic wall.

Question 66

The prostate gland: a) lies below the bladder
b) is traversed by the prostatic urethra
c) has five lobes
d) is supplied by the inferior vesical artery
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The prostate lies below the bladder, is traversed by the prostatic urethra, traditionally described as having five lobes (though modern anatomy recognizes zones), and receives blood supply from the inferior vesical artery.

Question 67

Concerning the urinary bladder: a) it is lined by transitional epithelium
b) the trigone is formed by the ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice
c) the detrusor muscle is smooth muscle
d) it receives parasympathetic innervation from S2-S4
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The bladder is lined by transitional epithelium, the trigone is formed by the three orifices mentioned, the detrusor muscle is smooth muscle, and parasympathetic innervation comes from S2-S4 (pelvic splanchnic nerves).

Question 68

The rectovesical pouch: a) is the most dependent part of the male peritoneal cavity
b) lies between the rectum and bladder
c) may contain fluid in pathological conditions
d) is lined by peritoneum
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The rectovesical pouch is the most dependent part of the male peritoneal cavity, lies between rectum and bladder, can accumulate pathological fluid, and is lined by peritoneum.

Question 69

Regarding the pelvic fascia: a) it lines the pelvic cavity
b) it forms the lateral ligaments of the rectum
c) it supports the pelvic organs
d) it is continuous with the fascia of the pelvic floor muscles
e) all of the above are correct

Answer: e
Explanation: All statements are correct. The pelvic fascia lines the pelvic cavity, forms supporting ligaments including the lateral rectal ligaments, provides support to pelvic organs, and is continuous with the fascia of the levator ani and other pelvic floor muscles.

Abdominal Anatomy Multiple Choice Questions

Section 1: Anatomical Planes and Structures

Question 1

All but which are transected at the level of the transpyloric plane?

a) Superior mesenteric artery leaves aorta
b) Splenic vein joins superior mesenteric vein to become the portal vein
c) Hila of kidneys
d) Lower border L1 vertebra
e) Gall bladder

Answer: C - Hila of kidneys

Explanation: The transpyloric plane passes through L1 vertebra and includes the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta, the formation of the portal vein, and the fundus of the gallbladder. However, the hila of the kidneys lie at the level of L1-L2, with the left kidney hilum typically being slightly lower than the right, making it not consistently at the transpyloric plane level.

Question 2

The anterolateral abdominal muscles:

a) External oblique muscle arises by eight digitations from back of lower eight ribs and interdigitates with serratus anterior and pectoralis major
b) External oblique fibres run obliquely upwards and forwards
c) The lower border of external oblique forms the inguinal ligament
d) Internal oblique inserts into the linea alba from a single aponeurosis
e) Transversus abdominis runs anterior to rectus abdominis until the arcuate line

Answer: C - The lower border of external oblique forms the inguinal ligament

Explanation: The inguinal ligament is formed by the lower border of the external oblique aponeurosis extending from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. External oblique fibers run downward and forward (not upward), it has digitations but not exactly eight, and transversus abdominis runs posterior to rectus abdominis.

Question 3

The anterior abdominal wall:

a) The deep surface above the umbilicus has lymphatic drainage to mediastinal nodes
b) The deep surface below the umbilicus has lymphatic drainage to the internal iliac and para-aortic nodes
c) Rectus abdominis is supplied by lower intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12)
d) Internal oblique and transversus abdominis are supplied solely by the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves
e) The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the body of the rectus muscle

Answer: A - The deep surface above the umbilicus has lymphatic drainage to mediastinal nodes

Explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the anterior abdominal wall follows the "watershed" at the umbilicus. Above the umbilicus, lymphatics drain to the mediastinal and axillary nodes, while below the umbilicus they drain to the inguinal nodes. The rectus abdominis is supplied by T7-T12 nerves, and the epigastric arteries do anastomose within the rectus sheath.

Section 2: Inguinal Canal and Spermatic Cord

Question 4

Contents of the deep inguinal ring include all but:

a) Ilioinguinal nerve
b) Vas deferens
c) Cremasteric artery
d) Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
e) Obliterated remains of the processus vaginalis

Answer: A - Ilioinguinal nerve

Explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve does not pass through the deep inguinal ring. It enters the inguinal canal by piercing the internal oblique muscle and travels through the superficial inguinal ring. The deep inguinal ring contains the vas deferens, cremasteric vessels, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve, and processus vaginalis remnants.

Question 5

Regarding the inguinal canal:

a) The deep inguinal ring is an opening in internal oblique
b) The superior epigastric artery is located deep to the posterior wall medial to the deep ring
c) An indirect hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring
d) A direct hernia passes lateral to the deep inguinal ring
e) The floor of the inguinal canal is reinforced laterally by the lacunar ligament

Answer: C - An indirect hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring

Explanation: An indirect inguinal hernia follows the path of the spermatic cord, entering through the deep inguinal ring and potentially exiting through the superficial ring. The deep inguinal ring is in the transversalis fascia (not internal oblique), and direct hernias pass medial to the deep ring through Hesselbach's triangle.

Question 6

Contents of the spermatic cord include all of the following EXCEPT:

a) Ductus deferens
b) Testicular artery
c) Pampiniform plexus
d) Ilioinguinal nerve
e) Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve

Answer: D - Ilioinguinal nerve

Explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve travels alongside the spermatic cord but is not actually within it. The spermatic cord contains the vas deferens, testicular artery and veins (pampiniform plexus), lymphatics, and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.

Section 3: Genitourinary System

Question 7

Regarding the testis:

a) Leydig cells secrete testosterone
b) The epididymis is located posteromedially
c) Lymphatic drainage is to the inguinal lymph nodes
d) Arterial supply is from the aorta just above the renal arteries
e) The right testicular vein drains to the right renal vein

Answer: A - Leydig cells secrete testosterone

Explanation: Leydig cells (interstitial cells) are indeed responsible for testosterone production. The epididymis is located posterolaterally, lymphatic drainage is to para-aortic nodes, the testicular artery arises below the renal arteries, and the right testicular vein drains directly to the IVC (not the renal vein).

Question 8

Referred pain from which organ may be felt in the cutaneous distribution of the obturator nerve?

a) Bladder
b) Prostate
c) Ovary
d) Uterus
e) Sigmoid colon

Answer: C - Ovary

Explanation: The ovary shares nerve supply with the obturator nerve (L2-L4), so ovarian pathology can cause referred pain along the medial thigh in the distribution of the obturator nerve. This is a classic example of visceral referred pain.

Question 9

Regarding the urinary tract:

a) The narrowest points of the ureter are at the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and at the vesicoureteric junction
b) Kidney innervation is derived from segments L2-L5
c) The hilum of the right kidney lies just above the transpyloric plane 5 cm from the midline
d) The hilum of the right kidney lies lateral to the psoas
e) The left kidney lies over the tenth, eleventh and twelfth ribs

Answer: A - The narrowest points of the ureter are at the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and at the vesicoureteric junction

Explanation: These are the three classic anatomical narrowings of the ureter where stones commonly become impacted. Kidney innervation is from T12-L1, not L2-L5. The kidney hila lie at the level of L1-L2, and the left kidney typically lies over ribs 11-12.

Section 4: Gastrointestinal System

Question 10

The following structures are related to the transpyloric plane EXCEPT:

a) Celiac trunk
b) Tip of the 9th costal cartilage
c) Hilum of the kidney
d) Origin of the portal vein
e) Body of the pancreas

Answer: A - Celiac trunk

Explanation: The celiac trunk arises at the level of T12, which is above the transpyloric plane (L1). The transpyloric plane passes through the tips of the 9th costal cartilages, the kidney hila, portal vein origin, and the body of the pancreas.

Question 11

All of the following are retroperitoneal structures EXCEPT:

a) Cisterna chyli
b) Sympathetic trunk
c) Duodenum
d) Pancreas
e) Ureter

Answer: C - Duodenum

Explanation: While most of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, the first part (duodenal cap) is actually intraperitoneal, being suspended by the hepatoduodenal ligament. All other structures listed are completely retroperitoneal.

Question 12

The celiac trunk:

a) Supplies the gut from the entrance of the bile duct to the splenic flexure of the colon
b) Gives rise to the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery
c) Is the 1st branch of the abdominal aorta
d) Arises from the aorta at the level of L2
e) Supplies the lower part of the esophagus

Answer: E - Supplies the lower part of the esophagus

Explanation: The celiac trunk supplies the foregut, including the lower esophagus via the left gastric artery. It gives rise to the superior (not inferior) pancreaticoduodenal artery, arises at T12 (not L2), and while it's the first major branch, the phrenic arteries arise first.

Section 5: Vascular Anatomy

Question 13

The superior mesenteric artery:

a) Arises from the aorta at the level of T11
b) Passes anterior to the body of the pancreas
c) Passes anterior to the 3rd part of the duodenum
d) Gives the superior pancreaticoduodenal branch
e) Supplies the jejunum

Answer: E - Supplies the jejunum

Explanation: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, including the jejunum and ileum. It arises at L1 (not T11), passes posterior to the body of the pancreas, and crosses anterior to the 3rd part of the duodenum. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery.

Question 14

The inferior mesenteric artery:

a) Supplies the hindgut as far as the dentate line
b) Arises at the level of L1
c) Passes posterior to the 3rd part of the duodenum
d) Crosses the ureter at the pelvic brim
e) Gives rise to the right colic artery

Answer: A - Supplies the hindgut as far as the dentate line

Explanation: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut from the left colic flexure to the rectum, including the anal canal to the dentate line. It arises at L3 (not L1), and gives rise to the left colic artery (not right colic artery).

Question 15

The abdominal aorta:

a) Commences at T10 as it passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm
b) The first branch is the celiac trunk
c) It terminates at the level of L2
d) The gonadal arteries arise above the origin of the superior mesenteric artery
e) The median sacral artery is a small posterior branch just before bifurcation

Answer: E - The median sacral artery is a small posterior branch just before bifurcation

Explanation: The median sacral artery is indeed a small posterior branch that arises just before the aortic bifurcation. The aorta enters the abdomen at T12, the first branches are the phrenic arteries, it terminates at L4, and the gonadal arteries arise below the SMA.

Section 6: Hepatobiliary System

Question 16

Regarding the liver:

a) The caudate lobe is bounded by the ligamentum venosum and the inferior vena cava
b) The left lobe extends approximately 12cm to the left of the midline
c) The gall bladder is at the tip of the 11th costal cartilage
d) The bare area lies against the duodenum
e) Porta hepatis contains the hepatic and portal veins

Answer: A - The caudate lobe is bounded by the ligamentum venosum and the inferior vena cava

Explanation: The caudate lobe (segment I) is indeed bounded by the ligamentum venosum anteriorly and the IVC posteriorly. The gallbladder is at the tip of the 9th costal cartilage, and the bare area lies against the diaphragm, not the duodenum.

Question 17

Which is the correct order of structures in the porta hepatis (anterior-posterior):

a) Hepatic arteries, portal veins, hepatic ducts
b) Portal veins, hepatic ducts, hepatic arteries
c) Hepatic ducts, cystic duct, hepatic arteries, portal veins
d) Hepatic ducts, hepatic arteries, cystic duct, portal veins
e) Hepatic ducts, hepatic arteries, portal veins

Answer: E - Hepatic ducts, hepatic arteries, portal veins

Explanation: The anatomical arrangement from anterior to posterior in the porta hepatis is: hepatic ducts (most anterior), hepatic arteries (middle), and portal veins (most posterior). This can be remembered as "DAV" - Ducts, Arteries, Veins.

Section 7: Specialized Topics

Question 18

Within the anal canal are anal cushions (dilated venous spaces and arteriovenous anastomoses):

a) 3, 7 and 11 o'clock
b) 2, 6, and 10 o'clock
c) 3, 6 and 11 o'clock
d) 1, 7 and 12 o'clock
e) 1, 7 and 9 o'clock

Answer: A - 3, 7 and 11 o'clock

Explanation: The anal cushions are located at the 3, 7, and 11 o'clock positions when viewed in the lithotomy position. These are normal anatomical structures that contain arteriovenous anastomoses and help with anal continence.

Question 19

Lymph drainage of the testes are to:

a) The deep inguinal nodes
b) The mediastinal nodes
c) The para-aortic nodes
d) The pectoral group of axillary nodes
e) The external iliac nodes

Answer: C - The para-aortic nodes

Explanation: The testes develop in the abdomen and their lymphatic drainage follows their embryological origin, draining to the para-aortic lymph nodes at the level of L1-L2, where the testicular vessels arise from the aorta.

Question 20

Lymph drainage of the scrotum is to:

a) The superficial inguinal nodes
b) The internal iliac nodes
c) The deep inguinal nodes
d) The external iliac nodes
e) None of the above

Answer: A - The superficial inguinal nodes

Explanation: The scrotum, being part of the external genitalia and perineal skin, drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. This is different from the testicular lymphatic drainage, which goes to para-aortic nodes.

Section 8: Pancreatic and Duodenal Anatomy

Question 21

Regarding the duodenum:

a) All of the duodenum is retroperitoneal
b) The 3rd part receives the bile duct
c) The 2nd part passes over the hilum of the right kidney
d) The 3rd part is crossed by the superior mesenteric artery
e) The 4th part is 5 cm long

Answer: D - The 3rd part is crossed by the superior mesenteric artery

Explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum. The first part is intraperitoneal, the bile duct enters the second part (not third), the second part is anterior to the kidney hilum, and the fourth part is about 2-3 cm long.

Question 22

All of the following are relations of the body of the pancreas EXCEPT:

a) Left crus of diaphragm
b) Left psoas muscle
c) Left kidney hilum
d) Bile duct
e) Lesser sac

Answer: B - Left psoas muscle

Explanation: The body of the pancreas does not relate to the left psoas muscle. It lies across the posterior abdominal wall with relations including the left crus of diaphragm, left kidney and hilum, aorta, and the lesser sac anteriorly. The bile duct runs in the groove between the pancreatic head and duodenum.

Question 23

The duodenum:

a) Is a retroperitoneal structure
b) Is 25cm in length
c) Lies between the levels of L2-L4
d) In its fourth part lies to the right of the aorta
e) All of the above

Answer: B - Is 25cm in length

Explanation: The duodenum is approximately 25cm long and C-shaped. However, only parts 2-4 are retroperitoneal (part 1 is intraperitoneal), it lies between L1-L3 levels, and the fourth part lies to the left of the aorta as it ascends to the duodenojejunal flexure.

Question 24

The main vessel supplying the body of the pancreas is the:

a) Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery
b) Splenic artery
c) Left gastric artery
d) Left gastroepiploic artery
e) Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery

Answer: B - Splenic artery

Explanation: The splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas and gives multiple branches to supply the body and tail of the pancreas. The pancreaticoduodenal arteries supply the head of the pancreas, while the left gastric and gastroepiploic arteries have different distributions.

Question 25

The pancreas:

a) Lies at the level of the L1 vertebra
b) Body slopes downwards across the aorta
c) Receives its blood supply from the splenic artery
d) Is about 20cm long
e) Develops from three separate buds

Answer: C - Receives its blood supply from the splenic artery

Explanation: The pancreas receives blood supply from the splenic artery (body and tail) and pancreaticoduodenal arteries (head). It lies at L1-L2 level, is about 15cm long, develops from dorsal and ventral buds (not three), and the body slopes slightly upward, not downward.

Section 9: Renal and Urological Anatomy

Question 26

Regarding the kidneys:

a) Each weighs about 340 grams
b) The left kidney lies below the transpyloric plane
c) The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves lie behind the posterior surface of the kidney
d) Each kidney has six segments
e) The hilum is separated from the peritoneum on the right side by the 3rd part of the duodenum

Answer: A - Each weighs about 340 grams

Explanation: Adult kidneys weigh approximately 150g each, not 340g. The left kidney hilum is at the transpyloric plane, the subcostal nerve (T12) lies behind the kidney, kidneys have 5 segments, and the hilum relates to the second part of the duodenum.

Question 27

Regarding the ureters:

a) They exit the hilum behind the renal artery
b) They are a continuation of the renal pelvis which is formed by the union of 10 major calyces
c) They are each 40cm long
d) On a radiograph they run just lateral to the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae
e) The lower ends are supplied by the ureteric branch of the renal artery

Answer: A - They exit the hilum behind the renal artery

Explanation: The ureter exits the renal hilum posterior to the renal vessels. The renal pelvis is formed by 2-3 major calyces (not 10), ureters are 25cm long, run medial to the transverse processes, and the lower ends are supplied by vesical arteries.

Question 28

The ureter:

a) Passes anterior to genitofemoral nerve
b) Develops from the metanephric cap
c) Is represented by dermatome L2
d) In the male, is crossed anteriorly by the ductus deferens
e) Passes anterior to the uterine artery in the female

Answer: D - In the male, is crossed anteriorly by the ductus deferens

Explanation: The vas deferens crosses anterior to the ureter near the bladder - "water under the bridge." The ureter develops from the ureteric bud (not metanephric cap), is posterior to the genitofemoral nerve, and passes posterior to the uterine artery in females.

Question 29

The ureters:

a) Cross the gonadal vessels
b) Cross over the vas deferens
c) Are crossed by the genitofemoral nerve
d) Pass under the cover of the psoas muscle
e) Lie lateral to the lumbar transverse processes

Answer: A - Cross the gonadal vessels

Explanation: The ureters cross anterior to the gonadal vessels at the pelvic brim. The vas deferens crosses over the ureter (not vice versa), the genitofemoral nerve lies on psoas anterior to the ureter, and ureters lie medial to the transverse processes.

Question 30

Regarding the kidneys:

a) The hilum of the left kidney is just below that of the right
b) The hilum faces medially and somewhat posteriorly
c) The long axis is parallel with the lateral border of psoas
d) The perinephric fat is surrounded by the renal fascia
e) The renal artery lies in front of the renal vein

Answer: C - The long axis is parallel with the lateral border of psoas

Explanation: The kidney's long axis is indeed parallel to the lateral border of psoas major. The left hilum is slightly lower than the right, the hilum faces anteromedially, perinephric fat is within the renal fascia, and the renal vein lies anterior to the artery.

Section 10: Splenic Anatomy

Question 31

Regarding the spleen:

a) It lies between the 7th and 9th ribs
b) The tail is contained in the lienorenal ligament
c) The head is immediately anterior to the aorta
d) The tail lies in the transpyloric plane
e) The main blood supply is from the left gastric artery

Answer: B - The tail is contained in the lienorenal ligament

Explanation: The splenic vessels and tail of pancreas are contained within the lienorenal ligament. The spleen lies between ribs 9-11, doesn't have a "head" (that's the pancreas), and is supplied by the splenic artery, not the left gastric artery.

Section 11: Vascular System - Advanced

Question 32

All of the following about the abdominal aorta are correct EXCEPT:

a) It passes between crura of the diaphragm at the level of T12 vertebra and terminates at body of L4
