b) It is crossed by the splenic vein below the celiac trunk and above the superior mesenteric artery
c) It has the uncinate process of the pancreas lying anteriorly
d) It gives off 5 paired lumbar arteries
e) It continues as the median sacral artery

Answer: D - It gives off 5 paired lumbar arteries

Explanation: The abdominal aorta gives off 4 pairs of lumbar arteries (L1-L4), not 5. All other statements are correct: it enters at T12, is crossed by the splenic vein, has the uncinate process anterior to it, and continues as the median sacral artery.

Question 33

The abdominal aorta is crossed anteriorly by:

a) Left renal artery
b) Inferior mesenteric artery
c) Left renal vein
d) Right gonadal artery
e) Right renal vein

Answer: C - Left renal vein

Explanation: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The renal arteries arise from the aorta posterolaterally, the inferior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta itself, and the right gonadal artery doesn't cross the aorta.

Question 34

Which is true of the superior mesenteric artery and its branches?

a) Right colic artery is the main supply of the cecum
b) Superior mesenteric artery runs anterior to the 1st part of the duodenum
c) Right colic artery passes behind the right ureter
d) Superior mesenteric arises from aorta at level of L2
e) Main trunk of the superior mesenteric artery ends at the level of Meckel's diverticulum

Answer: E - Main trunk of the superior mesenteric artery ends at the level of Meckel's diverticulum

Explanation: The SMA terminates by dividing into ileal branches around the area where Meckel's diverticulum would be located. The ileocolic artery (not right colic) is the main supply to the cecum, SMA runs posterior to the duodenum, and arises at L1.

Question 35

Which is true of the inferior mesenteric artery and its branches?

a) Inferior mesenteric ends as the superior rectal artery
b) The main trunk crosses the left ureter, but its branches pass behind it
c) It arises from the aorta at the level of L2
d) The descending branch of the left colic supplies the sigmoid colon only
e) There is very little anastomosis between the branches

Answer: A - Inferior mesenteric ends as the superior rectal artery

Explanation: The IMA continues as the superior rectal artery after giving off the left colic and sigmoid branches. It arises at L3 (not L2), and there are good anastomoses between its branches through the marginal artery.

Question 36

Direct tributaries of the portal vein include all but:

a) Right gastric vein
b) Short gastric vein
c) Splenic vein
d) Superior pancreaticoduodenal vein
e) Left gastric vein

Answer: B - Short gastric vein

Explanation: The short gastric veins drain into the splenic vein, not directly into the portal vein. The portal vein receives direct tributaries from the right gastric, left gastric, splenic, and superior pancreaticoduodenal veins.

Question 37

Which is the correct portosystemic anastomosis?

a) Portal = tributary of inferior mesenteric vein, systemic = tributary of internal iliac vein
b) Portal = periumbilical vein, systemic = phrenic veins
c) Portal = intrahepatic portal branches, systemic = azygos vein
d) Portal = left gastric vein, systemic = IVC via esophageal veins
e) Portal = middle rectal vein, systemic = inferior rectal vein

Answer: A - Portal = tributary of inferior mesenteric vein, systemic = tributary of internal iliac vein

Explanation: This describes the rectal anastomosis where superior rectal vein (portal system via IMV) connects with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic via internal iliac). The esophageal anastomosis involves azygos veins, not direct IVC connection.

Section 12: Hepatic Anatomy

Question 38

Which is not true of the surface markings of the liver?

a) Lies below ribs 7-11 in the right midaxillary line
b) Highest point on right is 5th rib
c) Superior surface crosses the xiphisternal joint
d) Inferior margin lies level with right costal margin in most cases
e) Highest point on left is 6th intercostal space

Answer: E - Highest point on left is 6th intercostal space

Explanation: The highest point of the liver on the left is at the 5th intercostal space, not the 6th. The liver extends from the 5th intercostal space on the right to the 5th intercostal space on the left, though it's lower on the left side.

Question 39

The liver:

a) Is divided into superior and inferior lobes by the falciform ligament
b) Has a bare area inferiorly
c) Receives blood from portal and hepatic veins
d) Has a caudate lobe that lies within the lesser sac
e) Takes sympathetic nerve supply from paravertebral ganglia

Answer: D - Has a caudate lobe that lies within the lesser sac

Explanation: The caudate lobe (segment I) lies within the lesser sac and can be palpated through the lesser omentum. The liver is divided into right and left lobes, the bare area is posterosuperior, it receives blood from hepatic arteries and portal vein (not hepatic veins), and sympathetic supply is from the celiac plexus.

Section 13: Retroperitoneal Anatomy

Question 40

Which is not a structure of the retroperitoneum?

a) Kidney
b) Adrenal gland
c) Cisterna chyli
d) Spleen
e) Pancreas

Answer: D - Spleen

Explanation: The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ, suspended by the lienorenal and gastrosplenic ligaments. All other structures listed are retroperitoneal: kidneys, adrenals, cisterna chyli, and pancreas (except for the tail which is intraperitoneal).

Question 41

Which is not a structure in the transpyloric plane?

a) Pancreas
b) Superior mesenteric artery origin
c) Fundus of gallbladder
d) Tip of 9th costal cartilage
e) Lower pole of right kidney

Answer: E - Lower pole of right kidney

Explanation: The lower pole of the right kidney lies well below the transpyloric plane, around L3-L4 level. The transpyloric plane (L1) passes through the pancreatic neck, SMA origin, gallbladder fundus, and tips of the 9th costal cartilages.

Section 14: Inguinal Canal - Advanced

Question 42

Which of the following is INCORRECT?

a) The inguinal canal of the female contains the round ligament of the uterus
b) The deep inguinal ring is an opening in transversus muscle
c) The spermatic cord in the male emerges from the deep inguinal ring
d) The inguinal canal lies above the medial half of the inguinal ligament
e) The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by lower edges of internal oblique and transversus muscles

Answer: B - The deep inguinal ring is an opening in transversus muscle

Explanation: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia, not the transversus abdominis muscle. The transversalis fascia is the layer deep to the transversus abdominis muscle. All other statements are correct.

Question 43

Regarding the inguinal canal:

a) It has a roof formed by lower edges of internal oblique and transversus muscles
b) The ilioinguinal nerve enters the canal through the deep ring
c) Its posterior wall is formed by the external oblique aponeurosis
d) The conjoint tendon lies anterior to the superficial inguinal ring
e) The superior epigastric artery crosses the posterior wall medial to the deep inguinal ring

Answer: A - It has a roof formed by lower edges of internal oblique and transversus muscles

Explanation: The roof of the inguinal canal is indeed formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. The ilioinguinal nerve enters by piercing the internal oblique, the posterior wall is formed by transversalis fascia, and the conjoint tendon is posterior to the superficial ring.

Section 15: Gastric Anatomy

Question 44

Regarding the stomach:

a) The cardia is at the level of T8
b) The stomach is supplied by branches from the celiac trunk
c) The fundus is supplied by gastroepiploic vessels
d) The pyloric opening lies to the right of midline at T12
e) It has an outer longitudinal muscle layer and an inner oblique layer

Answer: B - The stomach is supplied by branches from the celiac trunk

Explanation: The stomach receives its arterial supply from branches of the celiac trunk: left gastric, splenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic), and common hepatic (right gastric and right gastroepiploic). The cardia is at T11, fundus is supplied by short gastric arteries, pylorus is at L1, and the stomach has three muscle layers.

Question 45

Which is not true of the stomach?

a) Completely invested by peritoneum
b) Cardia situated at T12
c) Pyloric opening at L1
d) Aorta to the left of lesser curve
e) Supplied by branches of the celiac trunk

Answer: B - Cardia situated at T12

Explanation: The cardia (gastroesophageal junction) is located at the level of T11, not T12. The stomach is completely covered by peritoneum, the pyloric opening is at L1, the aorta lies to the left of the lesser curve, and it's supplied by celiac trunk branches.

Question 46

Which does not pass through the transpyloric plane?

a) Splenic vein
b) Tips of the 9th costal cartilages
c) Lower border of L1
d) Spleen
e) Superior mesenteric artery

Answer: D - Spleen

Explanation: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium at the level of ribs 9-11, which is above the transpyloric plane. The transpyloric plane passes through the splenic vein, tips of 9th costal cartilages, lower border of L1, and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.

Question 47

All the following are veins which drain the stomach EXCEPT:

a) Gastroepiploic
b) Gastroduodenal
c) Right gastric
d) Left gastric
e) Short gastric

Answer: B - Gastroduodenal

Explanation: The gastroduodenal is an artery, not a vein. The gastroduodenal artery is a branch of the common hepatic artery. The stomach is drained by the right gastric, left gastric, short gastric, and gastroepiploic veins, all of which eventually drain into the portal system.

Section 16: Appendicular Anatomy

Question 48

Appendix:

a) Usually lies retrocecal in health
b) Drains to inguinal nodes
c) Has no mesentery
d) Has a tip constant in relation to the cecum
e) Opens into the cecum 2cm below the ileocecal valve

Answer: E - Opens into the cecum 2cm below the ileocecal valve

Explanation: The appendix opens into the cecum about 2-3cm below the ileocecal valve at the convergence of the teniae coli. It most commonly lies retrocecal (65%), drains to mesenteric nodes, has its own mesentery (mesoappendix), and has a variable tip position.

Question 49

Which of the following regarding the appendix is FALSE?

a) It has a base constant in relation to the cecum
b) It has its own mesentery
c) It is formed by teniae coli convergence
d) Varies in length between 2 and 25 cm
e) It always lies retro-ileal in presence of disease

Answer: E - It always lies retro-ileal in presence of disease

Explanation: The appendix does not always lie retro-ileal in disease. Its position can vary (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal, etc.) regardless of disease state. The appendix has a constant base where the teniae coli converge, has its own mesentery (mesoappendix), and varies in length from 2-25cm.

Question 50

Where does the appendix lie in health?

a) Retrocecal
b) Pelvic
c) Paracecal
d) Subcecal
e) Pre-ileal

Answer: A - Retrocecal

Explanation: The most common position of the appendix in health is retrocecal (behind the cecum), occurring in about 65% of people. Other positions include pelvic (30%), paracecal, subcecal, and pre-ileal, but retrocecal is the most frequent.

Section 17: Colonic Anatomy

Question 51

Which is true of colon?

a) Ascending is longer than descending
b) Only part suspended on mesentery is transverse colon
c) Marginal artery is weakest at hepatic flexure
d) Lymphatic drainage is via superior and inferior mesenteric lymph nodes
e) Cecum is the widest part

Answer: D - Lymphatic drainage is via superior and inferior mesenteric lymph nodes

Explanation: The colon's lymphatic drainage follows its arterial supply: right colon to superior mesenteric nodes, left colon to inferior mesenteric nodes. The descending colon is longer than ascending, sigmoid also has a mesentery, the marginal artery is weakest at the splenic flexure, and the cecum is indeed the widest part.

Question 52

Concerning the colon:

a) Appendices epiploicae are most frequent on the ascending colon
b) The transverse colon is normally shorter than the descending colon
c) The blood supply includes the superior mesenteric artery
d) Parasympathetic supply does not include the vagi
e) None of the above

Answer: C - The blood supply includes the superior mesenteric artery

Explanation: The right colon (cecum, ascending, and proximal transverse) is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery. Appendices epiploicae are most prominent on the sigmoid colon, the transverse colon is longer than the descending colon, and parasympathetic supply includes the vagus nerve for the right colon.

Section 18: Pelvic Anatomy

Question 53

The pelvic floor:

a) Consists of ischiococcygeus, iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus
b) Muscles have significant insertion into the sacrum
c) Creates a gutter that slopes downwards and backwards
d) Has the anococcygeal raphe as a superficial part
e) None of the above

Answer: A - Consists of ischiococcygeus, iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus

Explanation: The pelvic floor (levator ani) consists of three parts: pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and ischiococcygeus (coccygeus). The muscles insert into the coccyx and perineal body, create a gutter sloping downward and forward, and the anococcygeal raphe is a deep structure.

Question 54

The pelvic floor:

a) Muscles include obturator internus
b) Slopes down and forwards
c) Is supplied by S2, S3 and S4
d) Is relaxed during quiet respiration
e) Muscle iliococcygeus arises from the ilium

Answer: B - Slopes down and forwards

Explanation: The pelvic floor slopes downward and forward, creating a funnel shape. The obturator internus is a pelvic wall muscle, not part of the pelvic floor. The pelvic floor is supplied by S3-S4, contracts during inspiration, and iliococcygeus arises from the ischial spine and fascia.

Question 55

Regarding the vessels of the pelvis:

a) The inferior and superior gluteal arteries are branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery
b) The iliolumbar artery passes in front of the obturator nerve
c) The uterine artery passes above the ureter
d) The inferior vesical artery always supplies the lower end of the ureter
e) The obturator artery lies above the obturator nerve on the side wall of the pelvis

Answer: C - The uterine artery passes above the ureter

Explanation: The uterine artery crosses superior to the ureter - "water under the bridge" (ureter under uterine artery). The gluteal arteries are from the posterior division, but the statement about their specific origin needs verification. The obturator vessels run below the obturator nerve.

Section 19: Lymphatic Drainage

Question 56

Which lymph nodes drain the lower anal canal?

a) Superficial inguinal
b) External iliac
c) Deep inguinal
d) Para-aortic
e) Internal iliac

Answer: A - Superficial inguinal

Explanation: The lower anal canal (below the dentate line) drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, following the pattern of skin drainage. The upper anal canal drains to internal iliac and para-aortic nodes, following the pattern of visceral drainage.

Question 57

With regard to the blood supply of the rectum and anus:

a) It is principally the inferior rectal artery
b) The anal canal is a site of portosystemic anastomosis
c) The veins do not correspond to the arteries
d) The inferior mesenteric artery changes to the superior rectal artery at L3
e) The vessels do not supply the full thickness of the anal wall

Answer: B - The anal canal is a site of portosystemic anastomosis

Explanation: The anal canal is indeed a site of portosystemic anastomosis between the superior rectal vein (portal system) and the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic system). The principal supply is the superior rectal artery, veins correspond to arteries, and the IMA continues as the superior rectal artery.

Section 20: Final Questions

Question 58

Superior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains into:

a) Left gastric vein
b) Portal vein
c) Splenic vein
d) Superior mesenteric vein
e) IVC

Answer: B - Portal vein

Explanation: The superior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains directly into the portal vein, along with the gastric veins. The inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein drains into the superior mesenteric vein.

Question 59

The highest branch of the abdominal aorta is:

a) Right suprarenal artery
b) Celiac trunk
c) Left renal artery
d) Left gonadal artery
e) Superior mesenteric artery

Answer: B - Celiac trunk

Explanation: The celiac trunk is the highest (most superior) major branch of the abdominal aorta, arising at T12. While the phrenic arteries arise first, they're usually considered thoracic branches. The celiac trunk is the first major abdominal branch.

Question 60

The branches of the lumbar plexus include:

a) The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal which provide motor innervation to the internal and external oblique muscles
b) The genitofemoral nerve which is derived from L3 and L4
c) The femoral nerve which supplies the iliacus
d) The obturator nerve which is derived from L2,3 and 4 posterior divisions
e) The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve which supplies sensory and motor innervation to the lateral thigh

Answer: C - The femoral nerve which supplies the iliacus

Explanation: The femoral nerve does supply the iliacus muscle along with the quadriceps. The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves don't supply the oblique muscles significantly, the genitofemoral nerve is from L1-L2, the obturator nerve is from anterior divisions, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory.

Title: MKU Compiled Head and Neck Anatomy MCQs
Content:
Section 1: Head and Neck MCQs

Question 1

Regarding the superior orbital fissure, which is INCORRECT?

a) Its common tendinous ring binds the SOF content of nerves and muscles to the contents of the optic canal
b) The origin of levator palpebrae superioris is its bony upper margin
c) Lacrimal, frontal and trochlear nerves pass through it
d) The oculomotor, abducens and nasociliary nerves lie within the cone of the extraocular muscles

Answer: A

Explanation: The common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn) does not bind the superior orbital fissure contents to the optic canal contents. The tendinous ring is located around the optic canal and medial part of the superior orbital fissure, serving as the origin for the four rectus muscles. The other options are correct: levator palpebrae superioris does originate from the bony upper margin, the mentioned nerves do pass through the SOF, and the oculomotor, abducens, and nasociliary nerves are within the muscular cone.

Question 2

Regarding the extraocular muscles:

a) They all arise from a common tendinous ring around the superior orbital fissure
b) The rectus muscles all pass laterally to their point of insertion because of the angle of the orbital apex within the skull
c) The superior oblique muscle passes through the trochlear, a fibrocartilage loop attached to the frontal bone lateral margin, just behind the orbital margin
d) Except for superior oblique, all nerve supply to muscles enter from their optic side

Answer: D

Explanation: The nerve supply to extraocular muscles (except superior oblique) enters from the orbital/optic side. Option A is incorrect because not all muscles arise from the tendinous ring (superior oblique and inferior oblique don't). Option B is incorrect as the rectus muscles don't all pass laterally. Option C is incorrect because the trochlea is attached to the frontal bone's medial margin, not lateral margin.

Question 3

With regards to eye movement, which is INCORRECT?

a) The medial and lateral rectus evoke simple horizontal movement only
b) The inferior oblique turns the eye down and out
c) The superior rectus turns the eye up and in
d) The inferior rectus and superior oblique together produce vertical down gaze

Answer: B

Explanation: The inferior oblique turns the eye UP and OUT, not down and out. The inferior oblique elevates, abducts, and extorts the eye. The other options are correct: medial and lateral rectus produce pure horizontal movement, superior rectus elevates and adducts, and inferior rectus with superior oblique produce downward gaze.

Question 4

Which is INCORRECT?

a) In a 4th cranial nerve paralysis, the affected eye lies slightly inturned
b) In a 6th cranial nerve palsy, the lateral rectus is affected
c) In a 3rd nerve palsy, levator palpebrae is affected
d) In an oculomotor nerve palsy the eye looks down and out

Answer: A

Explanation: In 4th cranial nerve (trochlear) paralysis, the affected eye is typically slightly upturned and outturned, not inturned. The superior oblique muscle is paralyzed, leading to loss of its actions (depression, intorsion, and slight abduction). The other options are correct: 6th nerve palsy affects lateral rectus, 3rd nerve palsy affects levator palpebrae, and oculomotor palsy results in the eye looking down and out.

Question 5

With regards to the retina, which is CORRECT?

a) The retina covers the inner surface of the choroid and is light sensitive everywhere except at the corneal area
b) The optic disc contains retina that is completely free of blood vessels and is yellowish in color
c) The optic disc and fovea are of similar size
d) The fovea contains no blood vessels or cones, but a high concentration of rods

Answer: C

Explanation: The optic disc and fovea are indeed of similar size (approximately 1.5mm in diameter). Option A is incorrect because the retina doesn't extend to the corneal area. Option B is incorrect because the optic disc contains many blood vessels and is pale/pink, not yellowish. Option D is incorrect because the fovea contains a high concentration of cones, not rods, and has no blood vessels.

Question 6

The nasal septum consists of:

a) The maxilla
b) The vomer and ethmoid bones
c) The sphenoid and ethmoid bones
d) The frontal, zygoma and maxilla
e) The vomer and palatine bones

Answer: B

Explanation: The nasal septum is primarily formed by the vomer (posterior-inferior part) and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone (superior part). The septal cartilage forms the anterior part. The other bone combinations listed do not form the nasal septum.

Question 7

The ophthalmic artery:

a) Is a branch of the ECA
b) Enters through the superior orbital fissure
c) Does not penetrate the meninges of the optic nerve
d) Forms an anastomosis between ECA and ICA
e) Is an end artery

Answer: D

Explanation: The ophthalmic artery forms important anastomoses between the external carotid artery (ECA) and internal carotid artery (ICA) systems through its terminal branches. It is actually a branch of the ICA, enters through the optic canal (not superior orbital fissure), does penetrate the optic nerve meninges, and is not an end artery due to its anastomotic connections.

Question 8

Regarding the carotid sheath:

a) Ansa cervicalis lies behind the IJV
b) Is free to move in the neck
c) Contains the vagus and phrenic nerves
d) The sympathetic trunk lies outside the sheath
e) The CCA lies lateral to the IJV

Answer: D

Explanation: The sympathetic trunk lies outside the carotid sheath, posterior to it. The carotid sheath contains the common carotid artery (medially), internal jugular vein (laterally), and vagus nerve (posteriorly). The ansa cervicalis lies anterior to the IJV, the sheath is not freely mobile, it doesn't contain the phrenic nerve, and the CCA lies medial to the IJV.

Question 9

The contents of the jugular foramen include:

a) Superior petrosal sinus
b) Internal jugular vein
c) Vagus nerve
d) Hypoglossal nerve
e) All of the above

Answer: C

Explanation: The jugular foramen contains the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), vagus nerve (X), and accessory nerve (XI). The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen but the foramen itself doesn't contain the formed vein. The superior petrosal sinus and hypoglossal nerve do not pass through the jugular foramen. The hypoglossal nerve passes through the hypoglossal canal.

Question 10

The sensory innervation of the auricle of the ear includes:

a) Auriculotemporal nerve (V3)
b) Great auricular nerve (C2)
c) Facial nerve via tympanic plexus (VII)
d) Auricular branch of vagus (X)
e) All of the above

Answer: E

Explanation: The auricle receives sensory innervation from multiple sources: auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the anterior-superior part, great auricular nerve (C2,C3) supplies most of the external ear, facial nerve contributes through the tympanic plexus, and the auricular branch of vagus supplies the external acoustic meatus and part of the auricle.

Question 11

Regarding the abducent nerve (CN VI):

a) The nucleus lies in the medulla
b) Supplies superior oblique muscle
c) Enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure
d) Has no relation to the cavernous sinus
e) Carries autonomic fibers from Edinger-Westphal nucleus

Answer: C

Explanation: The abducent nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring. The nucleus lies in the pons (not medulla), it supplies the lateral rectus muscle (not superior oblique), it does pass through the cavernous sinus, and it carries no autonomic fibers (those come from the oculomotor nerve).

Question 12

Regarding the face, which is INCORRECT?

a) There is no deep fascia on the face
b) The bulk of orbicularis oris muscle comes from buccinator
c) The eyelid muscles are completely supplied by CN VII
d) The parotid duct pierces buccinator opposite the third upper molar tooth
e) The facial nerve supplies the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis

Answer: C

Explanation: The eyelid muscles are not completely supplied by CN VII. The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by CN III (oculomotor nerve), while the orbicularis oculi is supplied by CN VII. The superior tarsal muscle is supplied by sympathetic fibers. All other options are correct.

Question 13

Regarding the trigeminal nerve:

a) Branches emerge from the parotid gland
b) The mandibular nerve has three cutaneous branches
c) The supratrochlear nerve supplies midline forehead and scalp
d) The infratrochlear nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve
e) The bridge of the nose is supplied by the external nasal nerve

Answer: B

Explanation: The mandibular nerve has three main cutaneous branches: auriculotemporal, buccal, and mental nerves. Option A is incorrect (facial nerve branches emerge from parotid gland), option C is incorrect (supratrochlear supplies medial forehead, not midline), option D is incorrect (infratrochlear is a branch of nasociliary from ophthalmic), and option E is incorrect (external nasal is from ophthalmic division).

Question 14

Which structure does NOT pass through the parotid gland?

a) Retromandibular vein
b) Temporozygomatic branch of facial nerve
c) Cervicofacial branch of facial nerve
d) Internal jugular vein
e) External carotid artery

Answer: D

Explanation: The internal jugular vein does not pass through the parotid gland. It lies medial to the gland within the carotid sheath. The retromandibular vein, facial nerve branches, and external carotid artery all pass through the parotid gland substance.

Question 15

Which structure is NOT in the carotid sheath?

a) Internal jugular vein
b) Hypoglossal nerve
c) Glossopharyngeal nerve
d) External jugular vein
e) Internal carotid artery

Answer: D

Explanation: The external jugular vein is NOT in the carotid sheath. It runs superficially in the neck, crossing the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The carotid sheath contains the internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves are closely related to the sheath but not within it.

Question 16

Which is an intrinsic muscle of the tongue?

a) Superior longitudinal muscle
b) Genioglossus muscle
c) Hyoglossus muscle
d) Styloglossus muscle
e) Palatoglossus muscle

Answer: A

Explanation: The superior longitudinal muscle is one of the intrinsic muscles of the tongue (along with inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles). The intrinsic muscles alter the shape of the tongue. All other options are extrinsic muscles that move the tongue: genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, and palatoglossus.

Question 17

Which muscle abducts the vocal cords?

a) Cricothyroid
b) Oblique arytenoid
c) Posterior cricoarytenoid
d) Lateral cricoarytenoid
e) Thyroepiglottic

Answer: C

Explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal cords. It rotates the arytenoid cartilages outward, separating the vocal processes. The lateral cricoarytenoid adducts the cords, oblique arytenoid adducts and helps close the glottis, cricothyroid tenses the cords, and thyroepiglottic helps lower the epiglottis.

Question 18

Which laryngeal muscle is NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve?

a) Thyroarytenoid
b) Cricothyroid
c) Aryepiglottic
d) Oblique arytenoid
e) Posterior cricoarytenoid

Answer: B

Explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (thyroarytenoid, aryepiglottic, oblique arytenoid, and posterior cricoarytenoid) are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 19

The internal laryngeal nerve supplies:

a) Sensation to the vocal folds
b) Cricothyroid muscle
c) Sensation above the vocal folds
d) Transverse arytenoid muscle
e) Sensation below the vocal folds

Answer: C

Explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve) provides sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal folds, including the epiglottis and vestibular folds. Sensation below the vocal folds is provided by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, and laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Question 20

Which nerve does NOT supply skin to the upper eyelid?

a) Lacrimal
b) Supraorbital
c) Supratrochlear
d) Infratrochlear
e) Infraorbital

Answer: E

Explanation: The infraorbital nerve does not supply the upper eyelid; it supplies the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The upper eyelid is supplied by the lacrimal nerve (lateral part), supraorbital nerve (central part), supratrochlear nerve (medial part), and infratrochlear nerve (medial canthus area).

[hidden]

Question 21

Which extraocular muscle does NOT arise from the tendinous ring of the orbit?

a) Superior rectus
b) Superior oblique
c) Inferior rectus
d) Medial rectus
e) Lateral rectus

Answer: B

Explanation: The superior oblique muscle does not arise from the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn). It arises from the sphenoid bone above and medial to the optic foramen. The four rectus muscles (superior, inferior, medial, and lateral) all arise from the tendinous ring around the optic canal.

Question 22

Which structure passes through the tendinous ring of the orbit?

a) Ophthalmic artery
b) Inferior rectus muscle
c) Lacrimal nerve
d) Trochlear nerve
e) Superior oblique muscle

Answer: A

Explanation: The ophthalmic artery passes through the tendinous ring along with the optic nerve in the optic canal. The inferior rectus muscle arises from the ring but doesn't pass through it. The lacrimal, trochlear nerves, and superior oblique muscle pass outside the tendinous ring through the superior orbital fissure.

Question 23

Which bone is not part of the medial wall of the orbit?

a) Maxilla
b) Lacrimal bone
c) Sphenoid
d) Palatine bone
e) Ethmoid

Answer: D

Explanation: The palatine bone is not part of the medial wall of the orbit. The medial wall consists of the maxilla (frontal process), lacrimal bone, ethmoid bone (orbital plate), and sphenoid bone (body). The palatine bone contributes to the orbital floor, not the medial wall.

Question 24

Which muscle helps to open the jaw?

a) Medial pterygoid
b) Lateral pterygoid
c) Masseter
d) Temporalis
e) Buccinator

Answer: B

Explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle helps to open the jaw by pulling the mandible forward and downward. The medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporalis are all muscles of mastication that close the jaw. The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression that helps with chewing by keeping food between the teeth.

Question 25

Regarding the vertebral column:

a) Ligamentum flavum attaches adjacent pedicles
b) Lumbar vertebrae have foramen in their transverse processes
c) The intervertebral disc is a primary cartilaginous joint
d) Rotation is greatest in the thoracic region
e) The cruciform ligament holds the dens in place

Answer: E

Explanation: The cruciform ligament (cruciate ligament) holds the dens (odontoid process) of C2 in place against the anterior arch of C1. Option A is incorrect (ligamentum flavum connects adjacent laminae), option B is incorrect (cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina), option C is incorrect (intervertebral discs are secondary cartilaginous joints), and option D is incorrect (rotation is greatest in the cervical region).

Question 26

The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the:

a) Internal carotid artery
b) Middle cerebral artery
c) Maxillary artery
d) Deep temporal artery
e) Facial artery

Answer: C

Explanation: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (first part). It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater. It's clinically important because it can be torn in temporal bone fractures, causing epidural hematoma.

Question 27

The hyoid bone is at what level?

a) C2 vertebra
b) C3 vertebra
c) C4 vertebra
d) C5 vertebra
e) C6 vertebra

Answer: B

Explanation: The hyoid bone is located at the level of the C3 vertebra. This is an important anatomical landmark. Other key levels include: C4 (upper border of thyroid cartilage), C6 (cricoid cartilage), and C7 (vertebra prominens).

Section 2: Face, Blood Supply, Nerves

Question 1

The parotid gland:

a) Is the largest of the major salivary glands
b) Is a mainly mucous gland
c) Is a well organized, regular gland, clearly divided into lobes
d) Drains into the parotid duct on its posteromedial surface
e) Extends from the zygomatic arch to the lower level of the earlobe

Answer: A

Explanation: The parotid gland is indeed the largest of the major salivary glands. It is a mainly serous gland (not mucous), has an irregular shape without clear lobular divisions, drains via Stensen's duct from its anteromedial surface, and extends from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible (below the earlobe).

Question 2

Cutaneous sensation to the upper lip is supplied by the:

a) Zygomaticofacial nerve
b) Buccal nerve
c) Infraorbital nerve
d) Mental nerve
e) External nasal nerve

Answer: C

Explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of maxillary nerve) supplies cutaneous sensation to the upper lip, along with the lower eyelid and lateral nose. The mental nerve supplies the lower lip, the buccal nerve supplies the cheek, and the zygomaticofacial nerve supplies the cheek over the zygoma.

Question 3

Skin over the upper lateral eyelid is supplied by the:

a) Lacrimal nerve
b) Supraorbital nerve
c) Supratrochlear nerve
d) Zygomaticofacial nerve
e) Zygomaticotemporal nerve

Answer: A

Explanation: The lacrimal nerve supplies the skin over the upper lateral eyelid and lateral part of the upper eyelid. The supraorbital nerve supplies the central upper eyelid and forehead, the supratrochlear nerve supplies the medial upper eyelid, and the zygomatic nerves supply the cheek and temporal regions.

Question 4

The facial nerve:

a) Marginal mandibular branch supplies muscles of the upper and lower lips
b) Emerges through the stylomastoid foramen
c) Has four main branches that exit the parotid gland
d) Supplies the anterior belly of digastric
e) Divides into temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions just after it enters the parotid gland

Answer: B

Explanation: The facial nerve emerges from the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after passing through the temporal bone. Option A is incorrect (marginal mandibular branch supplies only lower lip muscles), option C is incorrect (there are five main terminal branches), option D is incorrect (anterior digastric is supplied by trigeminal nerve), and option E is incorrect (division occurs within the parotid gland, not just after entering).

Question 5

The facial artery:

a) Is a branch of the internal carotid artery
b) Crosses the angle of the jaw at the posterior border of masseter muscle
c) Courses along inferior margin of parotid duct
d) Lies in front of the facial vein
e) None of the above

Answer: D

Explanation: The facial artery lies in front of (anterior to) the facial vein in the face. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery, crosses the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle, and has no specific relationship to the parotid duct. Therefore, option D is correct.

Section 3: Head/Neck/CNS

Question 1

The cervical sympathetic trunk:

a) Lies anterior to scalenus anterior
b) Is enclosed in the carotid sheath
c) Is lateral to the vertebral artery
d) Each ganglion gives off a cardiac branch
e) Disruption causes miosis, ptosis and increased sweating

Answer: D

Explanation: Each cervical sympathetic ganglion gives off cardiac branches that contribute to the cardiac plexus. The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the carotid sheath, medial to scalenus anterior, medial to the vertebral artery, and disruption causes miosis, ptosis, and decreased sweating (Horner's syndrome).

Question 2

The oculomotor nerve:

a) Does not enter the cavernous sinus
b) Supplies the ciliary muscle
c) Emerges from the pons
d) Contains sympathetic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
e) Does not pass through the tendinous ring

Answer: B

Explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies the ciliary muscle through its parasympathetic fibers. It does enter the cavernous sinus, emerges from the midbrain (not pons), contains parasympathetic fibers (not sympathetic) from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus, and does pass through the tendinous ring.

Question 3

The chorda tympani carries:

a) Taste fibers for the posterior third of the tongue
b) Ordinary sensation for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
c) Taste fibers for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
d) Cervical sympathetic fibers
e) Motor fibers to the muscles of mastication

Answer: C

Explanation: The chorda tympani carries taste fibers for the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands. Taste for the posterior third comes from the glossopharyngeal nerve, ordinary sensation for anterior two-thirds comes from the lingual nerve, and motor fibers to mastication muscles come from the mandibular division of trigeminal nerve.

Question 4

Which is NOT a branch of the facial nerve?

a) Nerve to stapedius
b) Chorda tympani
c) Nerve to levator anguli oris
d) Greater superficial petrosal nerve
e) Auriculotemporal nerve

Answer: E

Explanation: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), not the facial nerve. All other options are branches of the facial nerve: nerve to stapedius, chorda tympani, nerve to levator anguli oris (via buccal branch), and greater superficial petrosal nerve.

Question 5

Regarding lymph drainage of head and neck, which is INCORRECT?

a) Superficial cervical nodes lie along the external jugular vein
b) Submandibular nodes are lateral to submental nodes
c) The left jugular lymph trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct
d) The jugulodigastric nodes lie on/near the tendon of omohyoid
e) Preauricular nodes are outside and within the capsule of the parotid gland

Answer: D

Explanation: The jugulodigastric nodes lie near the posterior belly of the digastric muscle and the internal jugular vein, not near the omohyoid tendon. The jugulo-omohyoid nodes are the ones associated with the omohyoid muscle. All other statements are correct.

Question 6

The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the:

a) Middle cerebral artery
b) Anterior cerebral artery
c) Internal carotid artery
d) Maxillary artery
e) Superficial temporal artery

Answer: D

Explanation: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery (first part). It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater. It runs in grooves on the inner surface of the temporal and parietal bones and is clinically significant in temporal bone fractures.

Question 7

Which is NOT a content of the posterior triangle of the neck?

a) Subclavian artery
b) Lymph nodes
c) Transverse cervical vein
d) Omohyoid muscle
e) Sternocleidomastoid muscle

Answer: E

Explanation: The sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior border of the posterior triangle, so it's not a content of the triangle itself. The posterior triangle contains the subclavian artery (third part), lymph nodes, transverse cervical vessels, and the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle crosses through it.

Question 8

Which laryngeal muscle abducts the vocal cords?

a) Posterior cricoarytenoid
b) Cricothyroid
c) Transverse arytenoid
d) Vocalis
e) Thyroarytenoid

Answer: A

Explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal cords. It rotates the arytenoid cartilages laterally, moving the vocal processes apart. The cricothyroid lengthens and tenses the cords, while the transverse arytenoid, vocalis, and thyroarytenoid muscles all help to adduct or modify the vocal cords.

Head and Neck Anatomy Questions - Study Guide

Section 1: Bones of the Skull

Question 1

Regarding the bones of the skull:

a) The middle cranial fossa does not extend to the posterior cranial vault
b) The temporal lobe rests on the bony rather than the membranous part of the middle cranial fossa
c) The posterior cranial fossa contains the cerebella and lies superior to the tentorium cerebelli
d) The floor of the anterior cranial fossa is formed from the orbital plate of the parietal bone
e) The cribriform plate lies in the midline and is formed from the roof of the sphenoid bone

Answer: B

Explanation: The temporal lobe indeed rests on the bony (greater wing of sphenoid) rather than the membranous part of the middle cranial fossa. Option A is incorrect because the middle cranial fossa does extend posteriorly. Option C is wrong as the posterior cranial fossa lies inferior (below) the tentorium cerebelli. Option D is incorrect as the anterior cranial fossa floor is formed by the orbital plate of the frontal bone, not parietal. Option E is wrong because the cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone, not sphenoid.

Question 2

Regarding the bones of the skull:

a) The anterior clinoid processes are formed by the lesser wings of the sphenoid
b) The posterior clinoid processes are formed from the occipital bone
c) The dorsum sellae is formed from the anterior part of the occipital bone
d) The petrous temporal bone forms the floor of the middle cranial fossa, but not the wall of the posterior cranial fossa
e) The inferior orbital fissure separates the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid

Answer: A

Explanation: The anterior clinoid processes are indeed formed by the lesser wings of the sphenoid bone. Option B is incorrect as posterior clinoid processes are formed from the sphenoid bone (dorsum sellae), not the occipital bone. Option C is wrong because the dorsum sellae is part of the sphenoid bone. Option D is incorrect as the petrous temporal bone does form part of the posterior cranial fossa wall. Option E is wrong because the inferior orbital fissure is between the greater wing of sphenoid and maxilla.

Section 2: Cervical Spine

Question 3

Regarding the cervical spine:

a) All seven cervical vertebrae have spinous processes
b) Rotatory movements of the head occur mostly at the atlanto-occipital joints
c) The odontoid process (peg) is encased by a bony canal in the axis
d) All seven cervical vertebrae have foramina transversaria for the vertebral artery to pass through
e) Spinous processes, where present, are all bifid except for C7

Answer: E

Explanation: The spinous processes of cervical vertebrae (C2-C6) are typically bifid, except for C7 which has a single, prominent spinous process. Option A is incorrect because C1 (atlas) has no spinous process. Option B is wrong as rotatory movements occur mainly at the atlantoaxial joint (C1-C2). Option C is incorrect as the odontoid process projects from the axis, not encased by it. Option D is wrong because the vertebral artery doesn't pass through the foramen transversarium of C7.

Question 8

The seventh cervical vertebra:

a) Is typical
b) Has a bifid spinous process
c) Transmits the vertebral artery through the foramen in the transverse process
d) Has the supra-pleural membrane attached to the anterior tubercle
e) Has a short spinous process

Answer: D

Explanation: C7 has the supra-pleural membrane (Sibson's fascia) attached to its anterior tubercle. Option A is incorrect as C7 is atypical. Option B is wrong because C7 has a single (non-bifid) spinous process. Option C is incorrect as the vertebral artery doesn't pass through C7's foramen transversarium. Option E is wrong because C7 has a long, prominent spinous process (vertebra prominens).

Question 9

The atlas:

a) Has no foramen in the transverse process
b) Is the narrowest cervical vertebra
c) Has a body
d) Has a posterior arch grooved by the vertebral artery
e) Has a short spinous process

Answer: D

Explanation: The atlas (C1) has a groove on its posterior arch where the vertebral artery passes. Option A is incorrect as the atlas does have foramina transversaria. Option B is wrong as it's not the narrowest. Option C is incorrect because the atlas has no body (the body forms the odontoid process of the axis). Option E is wrong because the atlas has no spinous process at all.

Section 3: Triangles of the Neck

Question 4

Regarding the triangles of the neck:

a) The posterior triangle is bound by trapezius, sternocleidomastoid and the middle quarter of clavicle
b) The anterior triangle is further divided into two smaller triangles, the carotid and submandibular triangles
c) The posterior belly of digastric (and stylohyoid) separates the carotid and submandibular triangles
d) The accessory nerve (CNXI) divides the posterior triangle into approximately two halves, and of these the lower contains little of importance
e) The investing fascia splits to enclose the sternomastoid and trapezius, but the parotid and submandibular glands lie deep to the fascia, in the anterior triangle

Answer: C

Explanation: The posterior belly of the digastric muscle (along with stylohyoid) does separate the carotid and submandibular triangles. Option A is incorrect as the posterior triangle is bounded by the posterior third of the clavicle. Option B is wrong because the anterior triangle is divided into four smaller triangles. Option D is incorrect as the lower part of the posterior triangle contains important structures. Option E is wrong because the parotid gland is not in the anterior triangle.

Section 4: Anatomical Landmarks

Question 5

Regarding anatomy of the neck landmarks:

a) The arch of the cricoid cartilage is palpable as it protrudes forward of the trachea
b) The cricoid cartilage marks the level of C5
c) The transverse process of the axis is the most prominent of the cervical transverse processes, and is palpable between angle of mandible and mastoid
d) The body of hyoid is not palpable because it is hidden behind the thyroid cartilage
e) The coracoid process of scapula is palpable within the deltopectoral triangle

Answer: A

Explanation: The cricoid cartilage's arch does protrude anteriorly and is palpable. Option B is incorrect as the cricoid is at the level of C6. Option C is wrong because the transverse process of the axis is not the most prominent. Option D is incorrect as the hyoid is palpable and lies above the thyroid cartilage. Option E is wrong because the coracoid process is palpable in the deltopectoral triangle but this is not a neck landmark.

Section 5: Fascia and Sheaths

Question 6

Regarding fascia and sheaths in the neck:

a) The pretracheal fascia contains both trachea and oesophagus, and also splits to envelop the lobes of the thyroid gland
b) The prevertebral fascia encloses vertebrae and muscles acting on the vertebrae, but does not contribute to the investment over the brachial plexus
c) The investing fascia encloses trapezius, sternomastoid and platysma muscles
d) The structures contained within the carotid sheath include carotid artery, sympathetic chain and jugular vein, but not phrenic nerve or vagus
e) Infection may track in the pretracheal space to mediastinum

Answer: A

Explanation: The pretracheal fascia does contain the trachea and oesophagus and splits to envelop the thyroid gland. Option B is incorrect as the prevertebral fascia does contribute to the axillary sheath. Option C is wrong because the investing fascia doesn't enclose platysma. Option D is incorrect as the carotid sheath contains the vagus nerve but not the sympathetic chain. Option E is true but not the best answer.

Section 6: Sternocleidomastoid Muscle

Question 7

For sternocleidomastoid, which is TRUE?

a) Contraction of one muscle rotates the head to the ipsilateral shoulder
b) It is crossed superficially by the external jugular vein
c) It is supplied by the transverse cervical nerve
d) Its clavicular fibres mainly insert into the superior nuchal line
e) It is superficial to the deep cervical fascia

Answer: B

Explanation: The external jugular vein does cross superficially over the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Option A is incorrect as contraction rotates the head to the contralateral side. Option C is wrong because it's supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI). Option D is incorrect as the clavicular fibers insert into the mastoid process. Option E is wrong because it lies deep to the investing fascia.

Section 7: Posterior Triangle Contents

Question 8

Which is NOT considered a content of the posterior triangle of the neck?

a) Subclavian artery
b) Trunks of the brachial plexus
c) Internal jugular vein
d) Branches of the cervical plexus
e) Accessory nerve

Answer: C

Explanation: The internal jugular vein is NOT in the posterior triangle; it lies in the carotid sheath in the anterior triangle. All other options (subclavian artery, brachial plexus trunks, cervical plexus branches, and accessory nerve) are contents of the posterior triangle.

Section 8: Thyroid Gland

Question 9

For the thyroid, which is TRUE?

a) The thyroid isthmus crosses the thyroid cartilage
b) The superior thyroid arteries are branches off the internal carotid arteries
c) The posterior surface lies on the carotid sheaths
d) The inferior thyroid arteries are branches off the external carotid arteries
e) The recurrent laryngeal nerves pass anteriorly to each lateral lobe

Answer: C

Explanation: The posterior surface of the thyroid gland does lie on the carotid sheaths. Option A is incorrect as the isthmus crosses the 2nd-4th tracheal rings. Option B is wrong because superior thyroid arteries branch from the external carotid. Option D is incorrect as inferior thyroid arteries branch from the thyrocervical trunk. Option E is wrong because recurrent laryngeal nerves pass posteriorly to the lateral lobes.

Section 9: Great Vessels of the Neck

Question 7 (Internal Jugular Vein)

The internal jugular vein:

a) Drains into the subclavian vein on the left
b) Lies in the carotid sheath with the carotid artery and the sympathetic trunk
c) Lies lateral to the internal carotid artery at the base of the skull
d) Lies lateral to the carotid artery in the lower neck
e) Lies anterior to the sternocleidomastoid

Answer: D

Explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the carotid artery in the lower neck. Option A is incorrect as it drains into the brachiocephalic vein. Option B is wrong because the sympathetic trunk is not in the carotid sheath. Option C is incorrect as it lies lateral to the internal carotid throughout. Option E is wrong because it lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid.

Question 10

Branches of the carotid artery include:

a) Inferior thyroid artery
b) Ascending pharyngeal artery
c) Internal thoracic
d) Superficial cervical
e) Thymic artery

Answer: B

Explanation: The ascending pharyngeal artery is a branch of the external carotid artery. Option A is incorrect as the inferior thyroid artery branches from the thyrocervical trunk. Options C, D, and E are branches of the subclavian artery, not the carotid.

Section 10: Nasal Cavity and Paranasal Sinuses

Question 1 (Little's Area)

The blood supply of Little's area (anteroinferior part of the septum) is best described by:

a) Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries from the ophthalmic artery
b) The sphenopalatine branch of the maxillary artery
c) Sphenopalatine artery and septal branch of the superior labial branch of the facial artery
d) All of the above
e) None of the above

Answer: C

Explanation: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) receives blood supply from multiple sources including the sphenopalatine artery and septal branch of the superior labial artery. This rich vascular supply from different arterial territories makes it prone to bleeding (epistaxis).

Question 18

Which opens into the inferior meatus of the nose:

a) Frontal sinus
b) Ethmoidal sinus
c) Maxillary sinus
d) Nasolacrimal duct
e) Auditory tube

Answer: D

Explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus of the nose. Option A is incorrect as the frontal sinus drains into the middle meatus. Option B is wrong as ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle and superior meatus. Option C is incorrect as the maxillary sinus drains into the middle meatus. Option E is wrong as the auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx.

Section 11: Larynx

Question 3 (Posterior Cricoarytenoid)

The posterior cricoarytenoid muscles:

a) Abduct the vocal cords
b) Adduct the vocal cords
c) Tensor of the vocal cords
d) Relaxors of the vocal cords
e) Act as a sphincter

Answer: A

Explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscles are the only muscles that abduct (open) the vocal cords. They are crucial for breathing as they open the airway. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles either adduct the vocal cords or adjust their tension.

Question 4 (Superior Laryngeal Nerve)

The superior laryngeal nerve:

a) Divides into internal and recurrent laryngeal nerves
b) Supplies the cricothyroid muscle via an external laryngeal branch
c) Supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx
d) Is sensory to larynx below the vocal cords
e) None of the above

Answer: B

Explanation: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into internal and external branches. The external laryngeal branch supplies the cricothyroid muscle. Option A is incorrect as it divides into internal and external branches, not recurrent. Option C is wrong because most intrinsic muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Option D is incorrect as it provides sensation above the vocal cords.

Section 12: Trachea

Question 5 (Trachea Surface Markings)

The surface markings of the trachea include:

a) Origin at lower end of the cricoid at C4 vertebra
b) Origin at C6 vertebra level
c) Termination at T2 at expiration
d) Termination at T4 level at maximal inspiration
e) 3rd to 5th rings covered anteriorly by isthmus of the thyroid

Answer: B

Explanation: The trachea begins at the level of C6 vertebra (lower border of cricoid cartilage). Option A is incorrect as it begins at C6, not C4. Option C is wrong as it terminates at T5 at expiration. Option D is incorrect as it terminates at T6 at maximal inspiration. Option E is wrong as the 2nd to 4th rings are covered by the thyroid isthmus.

Question 33

Which is true of the trachea?

a) Begins at the level of C7
b) Isthmus of the thyroid lies anterior to the 2nd, 3rd and 4th rings
c) Has 15-20 complete cartilaginous rings
d) Receives its blood supply from the inferior thyroid artery alone
e) Pulmonary artery bifurcates anterior to its lower end

Answer: B

Explanation: The thyroid isthmus typically lies anterior to the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th tracheal rings. Option A is incorrect as it begins at C6. Option C is wrong because the trachea has C-shaped cartilages, not complete rings. Option D is incorrect as it receives blood from multiple sources. Option E is wrong because the pulmonary trunk bifurcates, not the pulmonary artery.

Section 13: Foramina and Their Contents

Question 6 (Foramen Spinosum)

What runs through the foramen spinosum?

a) Internal carotid artery
b) Maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve
c) Mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve
d) Middle meningeal artery
e) Meningeal nerve

Answer: D

Explanation: The middle meningeal artery passes through the foramen spinosum. This is clinically important as fractures in this area can damage the artery, leading to epidural hematoma. Option A is incorrect as the internal carotid passes through the carotid canal. Options B and C are wrong as these nerves pass through different foramina. Option E is partially correct but the middle meningeal artery is the main structure.

Question 20 (Jugular Foramen)

All of the following structures pass through the jugular foramen EXCEPT:

a) Jugular vein
b) Glossopharyngeal nerve
c) Hypoglossal nerve
d) Accessory nerve
e) Vagus nerve

Answer: C

Explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal, NOT the jugular foramen. The jugular foramen transmits the internal jugular vein, glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), and accessory nerve (CN XI).

Section 14: Circle of Willis and Cerebral Circulation

Question 22

In the circle of Willis:

a) The basilar artery divides into right and left posterior cerebellar arteries
b) The middle cerebral arteries branch off and supply the motor but not sensory cortex
c) The anterior communicating artery unites the middle cerebral artery to the internal cerebral artery
d) It encircles the inferior brainstem at C2-3 level
e) The internal carotid artery gives off the ophthalmic artery before dividing into anterior and middle cerebral arteries

Answer: E

Explanation: The internal carotid artery does give off the ophthalmic artery before dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Option A is incorrect as the basilar artery divides into posterior cerebral arteries. Option B is wrong as middle cerebral arteries supply both motor and sensory cortex. Option C is incorrect as the anterior communicating artery connects the two anterior cerebral arteries. Option D is wrong as the circle of Willis is intracranial, not at C2-3 level.

Section 15: Facial Vein

Question 23

Regarding the facial vein, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

a) It drains into the internal jugular vein
b) It has no valves
c) It communicates with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic vein
d) It runs inferoposteriorly anterior to the facial artery
e) It communicates with the pterygoid plexus via the deep facial vein

Answer: D

Explanation: The facial vein runs inferoposteriorly but POSTERIOR to the facial artery, not anterior. This is important anatomically as "artery anterior, vein posterior" is a useful mnemonic. All other statements are correct: it drains into the internal jugular vein, has no valves (allowing bidirectional flow), communicates with the cavernous sinus, and connects to the pterygoid plexus.

Title: 🔹 Eukaryotic Transcription & Translation
Content:
🔹 EUKARYOTIC TRANSCRIPTION

Process: DNA → pre-mRNA → (processing) → mature mRNA
Location: Nucleus

1. Initiation Phase
  • Transcription starts when the enzyme RNA polymerase II needs to attach to the DNA at the start of a gene.
  • It looks for a special DNA sequence called the promoter.
  • Inside this promoter, there's a key signal called the TATA box, usually found about 25 bases before the actual starting point of transcription.
  • But RNA polymerase II can’t bind to the DNA by itself — it needs help.
  • First, a helper protein called TFIID comes in. Inside TFIID is a special subunit called TBP (TATA-binding protein) — this is the one that sticks to the TATA box.
  • After TFIID binds, more helper proteins join in — these are other transcription factors like TFIIA and TFIIB.
  • Together, all these proteins and RNA polymerase II form a group called the pre-initiation complex (PIC).
  • This complex makes sure that transcription starts at the correct point on the DNA.
2. Elongation Phase
  • Once the complex is ready, the DNA opens up at the transcription start site — this creates a bubble where transcription happens.
  • RNA polymerase II begins reading the template DNA strand from 3' to 5' direction.
  • It builds the new RNA strand in the 5' to 3' direction.
  • It adds free RNA building blocks called nucleoside triphosphates (NTPs) — these are:
    • ATP, UTP, GTP, and CTP.
  • These are added one by one, matching the DNA bases (A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G).
  • As RNA polymerase II moves along the DNA:
    • It unwinds the DNA ahead.
    • It closes it back behind, keeping the bubble moving forward.
3. Termination and Processing
  • Transcription ends when RNA polymerase II reaches a termination signal — this is a special sequence in the RNA: AAUAAA (called the polyadenylation signal).
  • At this point, the pre-mRNA is released — but it's not ready to be used yet.
  • It needs to go through processing steps to become mature mRNA:
    1. 5' Cap Addition:
      • A 7-methylguanosine cap is added to the 5' end.
      • This protects the RNA and helps it bind to ribosomes later.
    2. 3' Poly-A Tail Addition:
      • A long chain of adenine nucleotides (poly-A tail) is added to the 3' end.
      • This gives stability and helps in translation efficiency.
    3. Splicing:
      • Introns (non-coding parts) are cut out.
      • Exons (coding parts) are joined together.
  • The final mature mRNA now leaves the nucleus and goes to the cytoplasm for translation.
🔹 EUKARYOTIC TRANSLATION

Process: mRNA → protein
Location: Cytoplasm (on ribosomes)

1. Initiation Phase (Simplified)
  • Translation starts when the small ribosomal subunit (40S) binds to the 5' cap of the mature mRNA.
  • This step needs help from initiation factors called eIFs.
  • The 40S subunit moves along the mRNA from 5' to 3' direction, looking for the start codon (AUG).
  • AUG codes for the amino acid methionine — this marks the true starting point.
  • A special initiator tRNA, carrying methionine, binds to the AUG codon by base-pairing its anticodon to the mRNA codon.
  • Once everything is aligned, the large ribosomal subunit (60S) joins.
  • Together, they form the full 80S ribosome, which has 3 sites:
    • A site – where new tRNA with amino acid enters.
    • P site – where the growing protein chain is held.
    • E site – where empty tRNA exits the ribosome.
2. Elongation Phase
  • The ribosome reads the mRNA codon by codon.
  • For each codon:
    1. A matching aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site.
    2. A peptide bond forms between the new amino acid (in A site) and the existing chain (in P site).
      • This is done by peptidyl transferase, an enzyme built into the ribosome.
    3. The ribosome shifts forward by one codon (translocation).
      • The tRNA in P site moves to E site and exits.
      • The tRNA in A site moves to P site, carrying the growing protein.
  • This cycle repeats, adding one amino acid at a time to the chain.
3. Termination and Post-translational Processing
  • Translation ends when the ribosome reaches a stop codon — UAA, UAG, or UGA.
  • These codons don’t code for any amino acid.
  • Instead, special proteins called release factors (eRFs) bind to the A site.
  • These trigger the release of the finished polypeptide chain from the ribosome.
  • The ribosome then breaks apart, ready for another round of translation.
  • The new protein may still need processing before it's fully functional:
    1. Folding (with help from chaperone proteins).
    2. Cleavage of signal sequences.
    3. Chemical modifications:
      • Phosphorylation
      • Glycosylation
      • Acetylation
  • These steps help the protein get its final shape, proper location in the cell, and biological activity.
Quick Memory Aid:
DNA REPLICATION – STEP BY STEP

DNA replication is the process by which a cell makes an exact copy of its DNA before division. It is semi-conservative, meaning each new DNA molecule has one old (parental) strand and one new (daughter) strand.

🔹 GENERAL DNA REPLICATION STEPS (Eukaryotes)
Step 1: Initiation – DNA Unwinding

What happens:

  • The enzyme DNA helicase attaches to the origin of replication (a special DNA sequence).
  • Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds between base pairs (A-T and G-C) and unzips the DNA.
  • This creates a Y-shaped area called the replication fork.

Key points:

  • Origins are A-T rich (A-T has only 2 hydrogen bonds = easier to break).
  • Both strands separate and now act as templates.
  • Replication happens in both directions → bidirectional replication.
Step 2: Stabilization of Single Strands

What happens:

  • Single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) attach to the separated strands to keep them apart.
  • DNA gyrase (a type of topoisomerase) removes twists and relieves tension ahead of the fork.

Key points:

  • SSBs prevent strands from reannealing (coming back together).
  • Gyrase stops supercoiling, making it easier for helicase to move.
  • Keeps DNA open and stable for replication.
Step 3: Primer Synthesis

What happens:

  • RNA primase lays down short RNA primers (about 8–12 nucleotides).
  • These primers provide a 3’-OH end that DNA polymerase needs to begin synthesis.

Key points:

  • Primers are made of RNA, not DNA.
  • Leading strand → only one primer needed.
  • Lagging strand → needs many primers.
  • All new DNA is built in the 5’ to 3’ direction.
Step 4: DNA Synthesis – Leading Strand

What happens:

  • DNA polymerase starts adding DNA nucleotides to the 3’ end of the primer.
  • Synthesis goes continuously in the 5’ to 3’ direction, same direction as the fork.
  • DNA is copied smoothly into one long strand.

Key points:

  • Fast and efficient.
  • No breaks or fragments — just one continuous piece.
  • Reads template strand 3’ to 5’.
Step 5: DNA Synthesis – Lagging Strand

What happens:

  • DNA polymerase builds DNA in short segments called Okazaki fragments (1000–2000 bp long).
  • These are made away from the replication fork (still 5’ to 3’).
  • Multiple primers are needed — one for each fragment.

Key points:

  • Discontinuous synthesis.
  • Each fragment must be processed and joined later.
  • More complex than leading strand.
Step 6: Primer Removal and Gap Filling

What happens:

  • DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers.
  • At the same time, it fills in the gaps with new DNA nucleotides.

Key points:

  • RNA is completely replaced with DNA.
  • Ensures the DNA is pure and ready for sealing.
  • Leaves small “nicks” (unsealed bonds) between fragments.
Step 7: Ligation

What happens:

  • DNA ligase seals the final gaps by forming phosphodiester bonds between fragments.
  • This joins all Okazaki fragments into a single, continuous strand.

Key points:

  • Final sealing step.
  • Result = two identical DNA molecules.
  • Each new DNA has one original strand + one new strand → semi-conservative replication.

🧬 POLYMERASE CHAIN REACTION (PCR) – STEP BY STEP

PCR is a laboratory technique used to amplify specific DNA sequences exponentially in vitro.
Invented by Kary Mullis in 1983.
Requires DNA template, primers, Taq DNA polymerase, dNTPs, and a thermocycler.

PCR Steps (3 Main Phases – Repeated in Cycles)

Each cycle of PCR has three main steps:

🔹 1. Denaturation (94–96°C, ~30 seconds)

What happens:

  • The reaction mixture is heated to high temperature (usually 94–96°C).
  • This breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands of double-stranded DNA.
  • Result: The DNA denatures into two single strands.

Key points:

  • Mimics natural DNA melting during replication.
  • Provides single-stranded templates for primers to bind.
🔹 2. Annealing (50–65°C, ~30 seconds)

What happens:

  • The temperature is lowered to allow primers to bind (anneal) to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded DNA templates.
  • Two primers are used:
    • Forward primer binds to one strand.
    • Reverse primer binds to the opposite strand.

Key points:

  • Temperature depends on primer melting temperature (Tm).
  • Correct annealing ensures specificity of DNA amplification.
🔹 3. Extension / Elongation (72°C, ~30–60 seconds)

What happens:

  • The temperature is raised to the optimum temperature for Taq DNA polymerase (~72°C).
  • The enzyme adds dNTPs (A, T, G, C) to the 3' end of the primers, synthesizing new complementary strands.
  • DNA synthesis proceeds in the 5’ to 3’ direction.

Key points:

  • Taq polymerase is heat-stable, isolated from Thermus aquaticus.
  • Extension time depends on the length of the target DNA (typically ~1 kb/min).
🔁 Cycle Repetition
  • These three steps (denaturation, annealing, extension) are repeated for 20–40 cycles.
  • Each cycle doubles the amount of target DNA → leads to exponential amplification.
    • After n cycles: copies = 2ⁿ
    • E.g., 30 cycles = over 1 billion copies
🧪 PCR Requirements (Core Components)
🧩 Final PCR Product
  • At the end of all cycles, millions to billions of copies of the specific DNA region are produced.
  • The product can be analyzed using gel electrophoresis, cloning, sequencing, or diagnostic testing.
🧠 Memory Aid for PCR Steps:

D-A-E

  • Denaturation
  • Annealing
  • Extension
⚕️ Medical & Clinical Uses of PCR
  • Detecting genetic mutations (e.g., BRCA genes in breast cancer)
  • Diagnosing infectious diseases (e.g., HIV, COVID-19, TB)
  • DNA fingerprinting in forensic medicine
  • Prenatal diagnosis of genetic conditions
  • Quantitative PCR (qPCR) for measuring viral load or gene expression

Title: TRYPANOSOMA
Content:
TRYPANOSOMA

OVERVIEW

  • Type: Protozoan parasite (hemoflagellate)
  • Kingdom: Protista
  • Phylum: Sarcomastigophora
  • Class: Zoomastigophora
  • Order: Kinetoplastida
  • Family: Trypanosomatidae

GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS

  • Elongated, motile parasites with undulating membrane
  • Single flagellum arising from kinetoplast
  • Kinetoplast contains mitochondrial DNA
  • Polymorphic (different forms in different hosts)
  • Obligate parasites requiring two hosts for complete life cycle

MAIN SPECIES AND DISEASES

1. T. brucei gambiense → West African Sleeping Sickness (WASS)

2. T. brucei rhodesiense → East African Sleeping Sickness (EASS)

3. T. cruzi → Chagas Disease (American Trypanosomiasis)

AFRICAN TRYPANOSOMIASIS (SLEEPING SICKNESS)

CAUSATIVE AGENTS

T. brucei gambiense and T. brucei rhodesiense

MORPHOLOGY

  • Length: 15-30 μm
  • Width: 1.5-3.5 μm
  • Shape: Elongated with pointed ends
  • Flagellum: Single, arising from kinetoplast
  • Undulating membrane: Present along body length
  • Nucleus: Central, oval
  • Kinetoplast: Near posterior end

LIFE CYCLE - SIMPLE STEPS

IN HUMAN HOST:

  1. Infection: Metacyclic trypomastigotes injected by tsetse fly bite
  2. Multiplication: Parasites multiply in lymphatic system
  3. Blood invasion: Transform into slender blood trypomastigotes
  4. Tissue invasion: Spread to various organs including CNS
  5. Antigenic variation: Change surface proteins every 7-10 days

IN TSETSE FLY VECTOR:

  1. Ingestion: Fly takes blood meal containing trypomastigotes
  2. Midgut development: Transform into procyclic trypomastigotes
  3. Migration: Move to salivary glands
  4. Transformation: Become epimastigotes, then metacyclic trypomastigotes
  5. Transmission: Ready for injection into new host

Total cycle time: 3 weeks in vector

COMPARISON: T.b. gambiense vs T.b. rhodesiense

PATHOGENESIS AND CLINICAL FEATURES

STAGE I DISEASE (Systemic - No CNS involvement)

Signs & Symptoms:

  • Painless chancre at bite site (trypanosomal chancre)
  • Intermittent fever and chills
  • Rash
  • Anemia and weight loss
  • Headache
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Lymphadenopathy (especially posterior cervical - Winterbottom's sign)
  • Myocarditis (common in T.b. rhodesiense)

Laboratory findings:

  • Anemia
  • Moderate leucocytosis
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • High immunoglobulin M (IgM) levels

STAGE II DISEASE (CNS involvement - "Sleeping Sickness")

Signs & Symptoms:

  • Increasing headache
  • Mental dullness and apathy
  • Daytime sleepiness
  • Behavioral changes
  • Progressive coma
  • Death from asthenia (weakness)

Histopathology:

  • Chronic meningoencephalitis
  • Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and morula cells in meninges
  • Morula cells contain mulberry-shaped IgA masses
  • Perivascular cuffing of brain vessels
  • Neuronal degeneration
  • Microglial proliferation

CSF changes:

  • Raised intracranial pressure
  • Pleocytosis (increased WBC)
  • Raised protein levels

DIAGNOSIS

Non-specific findings:

  • Anemia and monocytosis
  • Raised ESR (due to increased gamma globulins)
  • Reversed albumin:globulin ratio
  • Increased CSF pressure, cells, and proteins

Specific diagnosis:

Demonstration of trypanosomes in:

  • Peripheral blood
  • Bone marrow
  • Lymph node aspirate
  • CSF
  • Chancre fluid

Methods:

  • Microscopy: Wet mount, Giemsa stain
  • Culture: Special media
  • Molecular: PCR
  • Imaging: CT (cerebral edema), MRI (white matter enhancement)

TREATMENT

STAGE I DISEASE:

  • T.b. gambiense: Pentamidine (3-4 mg/kg IM daily × 7-10 days)
  • T.b. rhodesiense: Suramin (20 mg/kg IV, 5 injections at 5-7 day intervals)

Note: Suramin doesn't cross blood-brain barrier but is nephrotoxic

STAGE II DISEASE:

  • T.b. gambiense: Eflornithine
  • T.b. rhodesiense: Melarsoprol (Mel-B) 2-3 mg/kg/day (max 40mg) × 3-4 days

Note: Melarsoprol crosses blood-brain barrier

AMERICAN TRYPANOSOMIASIS (CHAGAS DISEASE)

CAUSATIVE AGENT

Trypanosoma cruzi

HOSTS AND VECTORS

  • Definitive host: Humans
  • Vector: Reduviid bugs (triatomine bugs) - "kissing bugs"
  • Reservoir hosts: Armadillo, cats, dogs, pigs

MORPHOLOGY

  • Similar to T. brucei but smaller
  • Amastigote form: Oval, 2-4 μm (intracellular)
  • Trypomastigote form: C-shaped, 20 μm (in blood)
  • Epimastigote form: In vector gut

LIFE CYCLE - SIMPLE STEPS

IN HUMAN HOST:

  1. Infection: Metacyclic trypomastigotes from bug feces enter through skin/mucosa
  2. Cell invasion: Parasites enter cells and transform to amastigotes
  3. Multiplication: Amastigotes multiply in cells
  4. Transformation: Become trypomastigotes and rupture cells
  5. Blood circulation: Trypomastigotes in bloodstream
  6. Tissue invasion: Invade heart, digestive tract, nervous system

IN REDUVIID BUG:

  1. Ingestion: Bug takes blood meal with trypomastigotes
  2. Gut development: Transform to epimastigotes in midgut
  3. Multiplication: Epimastigotes multiply
  4. Transformation: Become metacyclic trypomastigotes
  5. Excretion: Passed in feces during feeding

INFECTION CYCLES

  1. Sylvatic cycle: Wild animals (armadillos, opossums)
  2. Peridomestic cycle: Domestic animals (dogs, cats)
  3. Domestic cycle: Humans

CLINICAL FEATURES

ACUTE CHAGAS DISEASE (1-4 months)

  • Incubation period: 1-2 weeks
  • Age group: Often children under 2 years
  • Chagoma: Subcutaneous lesion at inoculation site
  • Romana's sign: Unilateral, painless periocular edema (classical finding)
  • Generalized symptoms: Fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly
  • Complications: Acute myocarditis, meningoencephalitis
  • Resolution: Symptoms resolve in 4-8 weeks → asymptomatic phase

CHRONIC CHAGAS DISEASE (Years to decades later)

  • Age group: Adults and older children
  • Pathophysiology: Inflammatory response, cellular destruction, fibrosis
  • Target organs: Heart, esophagus, colon
  • Manifestations:
    • Cardiac myopathy
    • Megaesophagus
    • Megacolon

CONGENITAL INFECTION

  • Possible in both acute and chronic phases
  • Causes myocardial and neurological damage in fetus

DIAGNOSIS

  • Direct: Demonstration of T. cruzi in blood or tissues
  • Serology: Antibody detection
  • Microscopy: Peripheral blood film examination

TREATMENT

  • No highly effective treatment available
  • Drugs used:
    • Nifurtimox: 8-10 mg/kg (adults), 15 mg/kg (children)
    • Benznidazole: 5-10 mg/day × 60 days
  • Dosing: 4 divided doses daily for 90-120 days (Nifurtimox)
  • Limitation: Kill only extracellular forms, not intracellular

ANTIGENIC VARIATION (Important Concept)

MECHANISM

  • Trypanosomes change their surface glycoproteins
  • VSG (Variant Surface Glycoprotein) or VSSA (Variant Surface Specific Antigens)
  • Cyclical fluctuation every 7-10 days
  • Single trypanosome has 1,000+ VSG genes
  • Helps evade host immune response

PREVENTION AND CONTROL

For African Trypanosomiasis:

  • Vector control (tsetse fly elimination)
  • Protective clothing
  • Insect repellents
  • Clearing of vegetation around settlements
  • Mass screening and treatment

For Chagas Disease:

  • Vector control (improving housing conditions)
  • Insecticides
  • Screening blood donors
  • Education about the disease

KEY EXAMINATION POINTS

  1. Distinguish between the three main species
  2. Know the complete life cycles
  3. Understand antigenic variation
  4. Clinical staging of African trypanosomiasis
  5. Romana's sign and Winterbottom's sign
  6. Treatment differences for each stage and species
  7. Diagnostic methods
  8. Vectors and reservoirs for each species

MEMORY AIDS

  • WASS: West African Sleeping Sickness = T.b. gambiense = Glossina palpalis
  • EASS: East African Sleeping Sickness = T.b. rhodesiense = rapid course
  • Romana's sign: Romana = Reduviid bug = Right or left eye swelling
  • Winterbottom's sign: Winter = West African = W-shaped lymph nodes (posterior cervical)
  • Pentamidine: Pentamidine for palpalis (T.b. gambiense)
  • Suramin: Suramin for savanna (T.b. rhodesiense - found in East African savanna)

Title: LEISHMANIA
Content:
LEISHMANIA

1. INTRODUCTION & BASIC FACTS

What is Leishmania?

  • Flagellate protozoan parasite
  • Causes leishmaniasis (including Kala-azar)
  • Obligate intracellular parasite
  • Requires TWO hosts to complete life cycle

Key Classifications:

  • Definitive hosts: Humans, dogs, other mammals
  • Vector: Female sandfly (Phlebotomus & Lutzomyia species)
  • Infective form: Metacyclic promastigote

2. GLOBAL DISTRIBUTION & EPIDEMIOLOGY

Geographic Distribution:

  • Tropical and subtropical regions worldwide
  • Central & South America, North America (parts)
  • Central & Southeast Asia, India, China
  • Mediterranean region, Africa

Risk Factors:

  • Low socioeconomic status
  • Overcrowding and poor ventilation
  • Accumulation of organic material in houses
  • Poor sanitation

3. CLINICAL TYPES OF LEISHMANIASIS

A. VISCERAL LEISHMANIASIS (Kala-azar)

  • Causative agent: L. donovani complex
  • Organs affected: Liver, spleen, bone marrow
  • Most severe form

B. CUTANEOUS LEISHMANIASIS

  • Causative agents: L. tropica, L. major, L. aethiopica, L. mexicana complex
  • Affects: Skin only
  • Forms ulcerative lesions

C. MUCOCUTANEOUS LEISHMANIASIS

  • Causative agent: L. braziliensis complex
  • Affects: Skin and mucous membranes
  • Can cause facial disfigurement

4. MORPHOLOGY - TWO FORMS

A. AMASTIGOTE FORM (LD Body)

  • Location: Inside human/mammalian cells
  • Shape: Oval, small (2-4 μm)
  • Features:
    • No external flagellum
    • Nucleus and kinetoplast visible
