  • Cholinergic stimulation: Parasympathetic stimulation increases protein-rich secretion
  • Adrenergic stimulation: Sympathetic stimulation produces mucus-rich, viscous secretion

Ductal Modification:

  • Sodium reabsorption: Na+ actively reabsorbed via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)
  • Potassium secretion: K+ secreted into ductal lumen
  • Bicarbonate secretion: HCO3- secreted via chloride-bicarbonate exchangers
  • Chloride reabsorption: Cl- reabsorbed along with Na+

Flow Rate Effects:

  • Low flow rates: More time for ductal modification
    • Lower Na+ and Cl- concentrations
    • Higher K+ concentration
    • Hypotonic final saliva
  • High flow rates: Less time for modification
    • Higher Na+ and Cl- concentrations
    • Approaches isotonic composition

Final Saliva Composition:

  • Hypotonic: Lower osmolarity than plasma
  • Alkaline: pH 7.4-8.0 due to bicarbonate
  • Low sodium: 5-40 mEq/L (vs 140 mEq/L in plasma)
  • High potassium: 20-120 mEq/L (vs 4 mEq/L in plasma)

Regulatory Mechanisms:

  • Parasympathetic dominance: Primary stimulus for saliva production
  • Sympathetic effects: Modifies composition, reduces volume
  • Aldosterone: Enhances Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in ducts

8. Actions of Growth Hormone (GH) (5 marks)

Growth-Promoting Effects:

  • Linear growth: Stimulates epiphyseal plate growth in children and adolescents
  • Protein synthesis: Increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis in tissues
  • IGF-1 mediation: Many effects mediated through insulin-like growth factor-1
  • Organ growth: Promotes growth of organs and tissues throughout life

Metabolic Effects:

A. Carbohydrate Metabolism

  • Diabetogenic effect: Increases blood glucose levels
  • Insulin resistance: Reduces insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissues
  • Gluconeogenesis: Stimulates glucose production in liver

B. Lipid Metabolism

  • Lipolysis: Stimulates breakdown of triglycerides in adipose tissue
  • Free fatty acid mobilization: Increases circulating fatty acids
  • Ketogenesis: Promotes ketone body formation

C. Protein Metabolism

  • Positive nitrogen balance: Promotes protein synthesis over breakdown
  • Amino acid transport: Enhances amino acid uptake by cells
  • Muscle mass: Increases lean body mass

Other Actions:

  • Bone metabolism: Stimulates osteoblast activity and bone formation
  • Immune function: Enhances immune system function
  • Wound healing: Promotes tissue repair and regeneration
  • Cardiac function: Increases cardiac output and contractility
  • Renal function: Increases glomerular filtration rate

Age-Related Effects:

  • Children: Primarily growth-promoting
  • Adults: Primarily metabolic effects and tissue maintenance

9. Hormones secreted by the anterior pituitary gland (5 marks)

Growth Hormone (GH/Somatotropin)

  • Function: Promotes growth, protein synthesis, and metabolic regulation
  • Regulation: GHRH stimulates, somatostatin inhibits

Prolactin (PRL)

  • Function: Stimulates milk production in mammary glands
  • Regulation: Dopamine inhibits, TRH and other factors stimulate

Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH)

  • Function: Stimulates cortisol secretion from adrenal cortex
  • Regulation: CRH stimulates, cortisol provides negative feedback

Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH/Thyrotropin)

  • Function: Stimulates thyroid hormone synthesis and release
  • Regulation: TRH stimulates, T3/T4 provide negative feedback

Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH)

  • Function: Stimulates follicle development (females), spermatogenesis (males)
  • Regulation: GnRH stimulates, inhibin and sex steroids provide feedback

Luteinizing Hormone (LH)

  • Function: Triggers ovulation and corpus luteum formation (females), testosterone production (males)
  • Regulation: GnRH stimulates, sex steroids provide feedback

Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH)

  • Function: Stimulates melanin production in skin
  • Regulation: Dopamine inhibits
  • Note: Secreted by intermediate lobe (rudimentary in humans)

10. Functions of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (active vitamin D) (5 marks)

Calcium Homeostasis:

  • Intestinal calcium absorption: Primary function - increases active calcium transport in duodenum and jejunum
  • Calcium-binding protein synthesis: Stimulates calbindin production in intestinal epithelial cells
  • Phosphate absorption: Enhances intestinal phosphate absorption
  • Renal calcium reabsorption: Increases calcium reabsorption in distal convoluted tubule

Bone Metabolism:

  • Bone mineralization: Essential for normal bone formation and mineralization
  • Osteoblast function: Stimulates osteoblast activity and bone matrix protein synthesis
  • Osteoclast regulation: Paradoxically can stimulate osteoclast activity when calcium is needed
  • Bone remodeling: Maintains balance between bone formation and resorption

Cellular Functions:

  • Cell differentiation: Promotes differentiation of various cell types
  • Cell proliferation regulation: Inhibits proliferation of certain cell types
  • Immune system modulation: Enhances immune function, particularly macrophage activity
  • Antimicrobial peptide production: Stimulates cathelicidin and defensin production

Systemic Effects:

  • Parathyroid hormone regulation: Provides negative feedback to suppress PTH secretion
  • Muscle function: Maintains muscle strength and reduces fall risk
  • Cardiovascular effects: May have protective effects on cardiovascular system
  • Reproductive function: Supports normal reproductive physiology

Clinical Significance:

  • Rickets prevention: Prevents rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults
  • Osteoporosis: Deficiency contributes to osteoporosis development
  • Autoimmune diseases: Deficiency associated with increased autoimmune disease risk

11. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (AIS) / Testicular Feminizing Syndrome (5 marks)

Definition and Pathophysiology:

  • Genetic disorder: X-linked recessive condition affecting androgen receptor function
  • Androgen receptor defect: Mutations in the androgen receptor gene (AR gene) on X chromosome
  • Tissue insensitivity: Tissues cannot respond to androgens despite normal or elevated testosterone levels
  • 46,XY DSD: Classified as a disorder of sex development in genetic males

Clinical Manifestations:

A. Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)

  • External genitalia: Normal female external genitalia
  • Internal structures: Absent or rudimentary uterus and fallopian tubes (Müllerian inhibiting substance still functional)
  • Testes: Present but undescended (may be intra-abdominal or inguinal)
  • Secondary sexual characteristics: Female breast development (due to estrogen from testosterone aromatization)
  • Pubic/axillary hair: Absent or sparse (androgen-dependent hair growth)

B. Partial Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (PAIS)

  • Variable phenotype: Ranges from predominantly female to predominantly male
  • Ambiguous genitalia: Micropenis, hypospadias, bifid scrotum
  • Gynecomastia: May develop at puberty

Hormonal Profile:

  • Testosterone: Normal to elevated levels
  • LH: Elevated due to lack of negative feedback
  • FSH: May be elevated
  • Estrogen: Elevated due to peripheral aromatization of testosterone

Complications and Management:

  • Gonadal malignancy risk: Increased risk of testicular cancer in undescended testes
  • Gonadectomy: Recommended after puberty in CAIS
  • Hormone replacement: Estrogen therapy after gonadectomy
  • Psychological support: Gender identity counseling and support

12. Physiology of lactational amenorrhea (5 marks)

Hormonal Mechanism:

A. Prolactin Effects

  • Hyperprolactinemia: Elevated prolactin during breastfeeding
  • GnRH suppression: Prolactin inhibits hypothalamic GnRH release
  • Dopamine pathway: Suckling suppresses dopamine, allowing prolactin elevation
  • Gonadotropin suppression: Reduced LH and FSH secretion

B. Suckling Stimulus

  • Neurohormonal reflex: Suckling stimulates prolactin release
  • Frequency dependence: More frequent nursing maintains higher prolactin levels
  • Nocturnal effect: Night feeding particularly important for maintaining amenorrhea
  • Intensity factor: Strong suckling stimulus more effective than weak

Ovarian Suppression:

  • Follicular development: Reduced FSH prevents follicle maturation
  • Ovulation inhibition: Low LH prevents ovulation
  • Estrogen deficiency: Reduced estrogen production from ovaries
  • Progesterone absence: No corpus luteum formation, no progesterone

Duration and Effectiveness:

  • Variable duration: Can last 6 months to 2+ years
  • Exclusive breastfeeding: Most effective when no supplemental feeding
  • Gradual return: Ovulation typically returns before first menses
  • Individual variation: Significant variation between women

Factors Affecting Duration:

  • Feeding frequency: More frequent feeding prolongs amenorrhea
  • Supplemental feeding: Introduction of solids reduces effectiveness
  • Maternal nutrition: Malnutrition can prolong amenorrhea
  • Individual sensitivity: Genetic variation in prolactin sensitivity

Clinical Considerations:

  • Contraceptive effect: Lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) 98% effective when criteria met
  • Return of fertility: Ovulation may occur before first menstruation
  • Bone health: Estrogen deficiency may affect bone density
  • Monitoring: Regular assessment of menstrual status and contraceptive needs

MEDICAL PHYSIOLOGY EXAM ANSWERS - MBMP 2300

QUESTION 1: Muscle Physiology

a. Four Types of Muscle Sensors (4 Marks)

  1. Muscle spindles - detect muscle length and rate of length change
  2. Golgi tendon organs - detect muscle tension and force
  3. Pacinian corpuscles - detect vibration and pressure changes
  4. Ruffini endings - detect sustained pressure and joint position

b. Components of a Muscle Spindle with Labeled Diagram (6 Marks)

Components:

  1. Intrafusal muscle fibers - specialized muscle fibers within the spindle
    • Nuclear bag fibers (2 types: dynamic and static)
    • Nuclear chain fibers
  2. Sensory nerve endings
    • Primary (Ia) afferent endings - wrap around central region
    • Secondary (II) afferent endings - located on either side of primary endings
  3. Motor innervation
    • Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers
  4. Connective tissue capsule - surrounds the entire structure
  5. Extrafusal muscle fibers - regular muscle fibers surrounding the spindle
    Extrafusal Muscle Fibers
         |
    ┌────▼────┐
    │ Capsule │
    │  ┌───┐  │ ← Nuclear bag fiber
    │  │ ● │  │ ← Primary (Ia) ending
    │  └───┘  │
    │  ┌───┐  │ ← Nuclear chain fiber
    │  │ ● │  │ ← Secondary (II) ending
    │  └───┘  │
    └─────────┘
         │
    Gamma motor neuron

c. Function of the Muscle Spindle (6 Marks)

Primary Functions:

  1. Length detection - monitors muscle length changes (static response)
  2. Velocity detection - detects rate of muscle length change (dynamic response)
  3. Stretch reflex mediation - initiates monosynaptic stretch reflex
  4. Muscle tone regulation - maintains baseline muscle tension
  5. Proprioception - provides information about body position and movement
  6. Motor control integration - works with higher centers for coordinated movement

Mechanism: When muscle is stretched, intrafusal fibers are stretched, activating sensory endings. Primary endings respond to both length and velocity, while secondary endings primarily respond to muscle length. This information is transmitted to the spinal cord and brain for motor control.

d. Role of Gamma Motor Neurons on Muscle Spindle (4 Marks)

Functions:

  1. Sensitivity adjustment - modulates spindle sensitivity to stretch
  2. Maintains spindle function during contraction - prevents spindle from going slack when extrafusal fibers contract
  3. Alpha-gamma coactivation - coordinates with alpha motor neurons for smooth movement
  4. Bias control - sets the baseline sensitivity of the spindle

Additional points:

  • Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal fibers only
  • They maintain spindle tension during muscle contraction
  • Enable continuous proprioceptive feedback during movement

QUESTION 2: Gastrointestinal Innervation

a. Two Components of GI Autonomic Nervous System (5 Marks)

  1. Extrinsic nervous system
    • Parasympathetic innervation (vagus and pelvic nerves)
    • Sympathetic innervation (splanchnic nerves)
  2. Intrinsic nervous system (Enteric nervous system)
    • Myenteric plexus (Auerbach's plexus)
    • Submucosal plexus (Meissner's plexus)

Additional points:

  • Enteric nervous system can function independently
  • Contains more neurons than the spinal cord
  • Often called the "second brain"

b. Parasympathetic Innervation of GI Tract (5 Marks)

Vagus Nerve (CN X):

  • Innervates esophagus, stomach, small intestine, cecum, ascending colon
  • Preganglionic fibers synapse in enteric ganglia
  • Stimulates motility, secretion, and blood flow

Pelvic Nerves (S2-S4):

  • Innervate descending colon, rectum, and anal canal
  • Preganglionic fibers synapse in enteric ganglia

Functions:

  • Increases gastric acid secretion
  • Stimulates pancreatic enzyme release
  • Enhances intestinal motility
  • Promotes digestive processes

c. Sympathetic Innervation of GI Tract (5 Marks)

Nerve Supply:

  • Greater splanchnic nerves (T5-T9)
  • Lesser splanchnic nerves (T10-T11)
  • Lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1-L2)

Ganglia:

  • Celiac ganglion
  • Superior mesenteric ganglion
  • Inferior mesenteric ganglion

Functions:

  • Inhibits GI motility
  • Reduces secretions
  • Causes vasoconstriction
  • Contracts sphincters
  • Generally opposes parasympathetic effects

d. Two Intrinsic Plexuses of GI Nervous System (5 Marks)

  1. Myenteric Plexus (Auerbach's Plexus)
    • Location: Between circular and longitudinal muscle layers
    • Function: Controls muscle contractions and peristalsis
    • Contains motor neurons, interneurons, and sensory neurons
  2. Submucosal Plexus (Meissner's Plexus)
    • Location: In submucosa
    • Function: Controls secretion, absorption, and local blood flow
    • Regulates mucosal function

Additional functions:

  • Both plexuses contain enteric neurons
  • Form integrated neural network
  • Can function independently of CNS

e. Hormones Secreted by Posterior Pituitary Gland (2 Marks)

  1. Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH/Vasopressin)
  2. Oxytocin

QUESTION 3: Posterior Pituitary Hormones

a. Factors that Increase or Decrease ADH Secretion (10 Marks)

Factors that INCREASE ADH secretion:

  1. Increased plasma osmolality - detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors
  2. Decreased blood volume - detected by baroreceptors
  3. Decreased blood pressure - detected by arterial baroreceptors
  4. Pain and stress - emotional and physical stress
  5. Nausea and vomiting - powerful stimuli for ADH release
  6. Certain drugs - morphine, nicotine, barbiturates
  7. Angiotensin II - stimulates ADH release

Factors that DECREASE ADH secretion:

  1. Decreased plasma osmolality - hypoosmotic conditions
  2. Increased blood volume - hypervolemia
  3. Increased blood pressure - hypertension
  4. Alcohol consumption - inhibits ADH release
  5. Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) - inhibits ADH secretion

b. Mechanism of Action of ADH (4 Marks)

Mechanism:

  1. Receptor binding - ADH binds to V2 receptors on basolateral membrane of collecting duct cells
  2. cAMP activation - stimulates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP levels
  3. Protein kinase A activation - cAMP activates PKA
  4. Aquaporin-2 insertion - promotes insertion of AQP2 water channels into apical membrane

Result: Increased water reabsorption from collecting duct, concentrating urine and conserving body water.

c. Regulation of Oxytocin Secretion and Mechanism of Action (6 Marks)

Regulation of Oxytocin Secretion:

  1. Ferguson reflex - cervical and vaginal stretching during labor
  2. Suckling stimulus - mechanical stimulation of nipples
  3. Positive feedback - oxytocin release stimulates more contractions/milk ejection
  4. Psychological factors - sight, sound, or thought of baby

Mechanism of Action:

  1. Uterine contractions:
    • Binds to oxytocin receptors on myometrial cells
    • Increases intracellular calcium
    • Stimulates smooth muscle contractions
  2. Milk ejection:
    • Acts on myoepithelial cells around mammary alveoli
    • Causes contraction and milk ejection
    • Essential for breastfeeding

QUESTION 4: Sexual Differentiation

a. Definitions (4 Marks)

i. Genetic sex: Chromosomal composition determining sex (XX = female, XY = male). Established at fertilization by paternal sperm contribution.

ii. Gonadal sex: Development of testes or ovaries based on genetic sex. Determined by presence or absence of SRY gene (sex-determining region Y).

iii. Phenotypic sex: External and internal sexual characteristics and anatomy. Result of hormonal influences during development.

b. Sexual Differentiation Leading to Phenotypic Male or Female (6 Marks)

Male Differentiation:

  1. SRY gene activation - triggers testis development
  2. Testosterone production - by Leydig cells
  3. Anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) - causes regression of Müllerian ducts
  4. Wolffian duct development - forms male internal structures
  5. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) - masculinizes external genitalia
  6. Male phenotype - external and internal male characteristics

Female Differentiation:

  1. Absence of SRY gene - no testis-determining factor
  2. Ovarian development - default pathway
  3. Lack of testosterone - Wolffian ducts regress
  4. Müllerian duct development - forms female internal structures
  5. Female external genitalia - develop without androgen influence
  6. Female phenotype - external and internal female characteristics

c. Biosynthesis of Testosterone by Leydig Cells (8 Marks)

Pathway:

  1. Cholesterol uptake - from blood or synthesized de novo
  2. Cholesterol → Pregnenolone
    • Enzyme: 20,22-desmolase (CYP11A1)
    • Rate-limiting step
  3. Pregnenolone → Progesterone
    • Enzyme: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase
  4. Progesterone → 17-hydroxyprogesterone
    • Enzyme: 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1)
  5. 17-hydroxyprogesterone → Androstenedione
    • Enzyme: 17,20-lyase (CYP17A1)
  6. Androstenedione → Testosterone
    • Enzyme: 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase

Regulation:

  • LH stimulation - binds to LH receptors on Leydig cells
  • cAMP pathway - increases steroidogenic enzyme activity
  • Negative feedback - testosterone inhibits LH release

Additional points:

  • Testosterone can be converted to DHT by 5α-reductase
  • Some testosterone is aromatized to estradiol
  • Production begins during fetal development and increases at puberty

SECTION A: PARASITOLOGY MCQs

1. Nitazoxanide is BEST for treatment of?

Options:

  • A. Amoebiasis
  • B. Trichomoniasis
  • C. Giardiasis
  • D. Chagas disease
  • E. Loasis

Answer: C. Giardiasis

Explanation: Nitazoxanide is a broad-spectrum antiparasitic drug that is particularly effective against Giardia lamblia. While it has some activity against other parasites, its primary indication and best efficacy is for giardiasis treatment.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Amoebiasis: Metronidazole is the drug of choice
  • B. Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole is the preferred treatment
  • D. Chagas disease: Benznidazole or nifurtimox are used
  • E. Loasis: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the treatment of choice

2. Metronidazole parasite site of target is?

Options:

  • A. RNA
  • B. DNA
  • C. Ribosomes
  • D. Cytoskeleton

Answer: B. DNA

Explanation: Metronidazole is activated by reduction in anaerobic organisms, forming reactive intermediates that damage DNA by causing strand breaks and preventing DNA replication.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. RNA: Not the primary target of metronidazole
  • C. Ribosomes: Target of antibiotics like chloramphenicol, not metronidazole
  • D. Cytoskeleton: Target of drugs like benzimidazoles, not metronidazole

3. Which parasite causes vitamin B12 deficiency?

Options:

  • A. Ancylostoma braziliense
  • B. Toxocara canis
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis
  • D. Diphyllobothrium latum

Answer: D. Diphyllobothrium latum

Explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) causes vitamin B12 deficiency by competing with the host for vitamin B12 absorption in the small intestine, potentially leading to megaloblastic anemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Ancylostoma braziliense: Causes cutaneous larva migrans
  • B. Toxocara canis: Causes visceral larva migrans
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis: Causes pinworm infection with perianal itching

4. Which of the following parasites is associated with achlorhydria?

Options:

  • A. Dientamoeba fragilis
  • B. Trichomonas vaginalis
  • C. Giardia intestinalis
  • D. Leishmania tropica
  • E. Toxoplasma gondii

Answer: C. Giardia intestinalis

Explanation: Giardia intestinalis is associated with achlorhydria (absence of gastric acid) as the low acid environment facilitates Giardia survival and establishment in the small intestine.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Dientamoeba fragilis: Causes colitis, not associated with achlorhydria
  • B. Trichomonas vaginalis: Urogenital parasite, not related to gastric acid
  • D. Leishmania tropica: Causes cutaneous leishmaniasis
  • E. Toxoplasma gondii: Intracellular parasite, not gastric-related

5. Which of the following parasites is associated with pyosalpingitis?

Options:

  • A. Amoeba species
  • B. Trichomonas species
  • C. Giardia species
  • D. Leishmania species
  • E. Onchocerca volvulus

Answer: B. Trichomonas species

Explanation: Trichomonas vaginalis can cause ascending urogenital infections leading to pyosalpingitis (infection of the fallopian tubes) and pelvic inflammatory disease.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Amoeba species: Primarily cause intestinal or hepatic infections
  • C. Giardia species: Intestinal parasite, not urogenital
  • D. Leishmania species: Cause cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral leishmaniasis
  • E. Onchocerca volvulus: Causes river blindness

6. Ground itch is produced by?

Options:

  • A. Necator americanus
  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis
  • D. Diphyllobothrium latum

Answer: A. Necator americanus

Explanation: Ground itch is caused by skin penetration of hookworm larvae, particularly Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, as they enter through bare feet in contact with contaminated soil.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides: Transmitted through ingestion of eggs, not skin penetration
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis: Transmitted through ingestion of eggs
  • D. Diphyllobothrium latum: Transmitted through eating undercooked fish

7. Which one is associated with nocturnal pruritus ani?

Options:

  • A. Necator americanus
  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis
  • D. Diphyllobothrium latum

Answer: C. Enterobium vermicularis

Explanation: Enterobium vermicularis (pinworm) causes nocturnal pruritus ani because female worms migrate to the perianal area at night to lay eggs, causing intense itching.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Necator americanus: Causes anemia and abdominal symptoms
  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides: Causes intestinal obstruction and respiratory symptoms
  • D. Diphyllobothrium latum: Causes vitamin B12 deficiency

8. Geophagia or pica may be seen in heavy infection with?

Options:

  • A. Ancylostoma duodenale
  • B. Necator americanus
  • C. Strongyloides stercoralis
  • D. All of above

Answer: D. All of above

Explanation: Geophagia (eating soil) can be seen in heavy hookworm infections (both Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) and Strongyloides stercoralis, likely due to iron deficiency anemia and nutritional deficiencies.

Why other individual options are incomplete:

  • A, B, C: Each can cause geophagia individually, but "all of above" is the most complete answer

9. Which of the following describes the anatomical arrangement of axoneme microtubules of a cilia?

Options:

  • A. 9x3+2
  • B. 9x2+3
  • C. 9x2+2
  • D. 9x1+2
  • E. 9x1+1

Answer: C. 9x2+2

Explanation: The axoneme of cilia and flagella has a characteristic "9+2" arrangement: 9 outer doublet microtubules surrounding 2 central singlet microtubules.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. 9x3+2: Incorrect number of microtubules in outer doublets
  • B. 9x2+3: Incorrect number of central microtubules
  • D. 9x1+2: Outer microtubules are doublets, not singlets
  • E. 9x1+1: Both outer and central arrangements are incorrect

10. Amoebas are motile living organisms. Which mode of locomotion does amoeba utilize?

Options:

  • A. Flagella
  • B. Cilia
  • C. Pseudopodia
  • D. Muscular actions

Answer: C. Pseudopodia

Explanation: Amoebas move by extending and retracting pseudopodia (false feet), which are temporary cytoplasmic projections used for locomotion and feeding.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Flagella: Used by flagellated protozoa like Trypanosoma
  • B. Cilia: Used by ciliated protozoa like Paramecium
  • D. Muscular actions: Not present in single-celled amoebas

11. Single celled parasites utilize various physiological modes to take in nutrients. Which one of the following is NOT?

Options:

  • A. Diffusion
  • B. Active transport
  • C. Pinocytosis
  • D. Exocytosis
  • E. Endocytosis

Answer: D. Exocytosis

Explanation: Exocytosis is the process of expelling materials from the cell, not taking in nutrients. It's used for waste removal and secretion.

Why other options are methods of nutrient uptake:

  • A. Diffusion: Passive uptake of small molecules
  • B. Active transport: Energy-requiring uptake against concentration gradients
  • C. Pinocytosis: Uptake of fluid and dissolved substances
  • E. Endocytosis: General term for uptake of materials into the cell

12. Which of the following biomolecules is found in the endocytic vesicle of microorganisms?

Options:

  • A. Phospholipase
  • B. Granzyme
  • C. Interferons
  • D. Hydrolytic enzymes
  • E. All of the above

Answer: D. Hydrolytic enzymes

Explanation: Endocytic vesicles contain hydrolytic enzymes that break down ingested materials for digestion and nutrient absorption.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Phospholipase: Enzyme that breaks down phospholipids, not specifically in endocytic vesicles
  • B. Granzyme: Cytotoxic enzyme in immune cells, not in parasitic endocytic vesicles
  • C. Interferons: Antiviral proteins, not digestive enzymes
  • E. Only hydrolytic enzymes are characteristic of endocytic vesicles

13. In Paramecium species, nutrients distribution is not done through vessels as in human beings. Which mode of nutrients circulation is utilized in these organisms?

Options:

  • A. Diffusion
  • B. Cyclosis
  • C. Active transport
  • D. Cytoplasmic streaming
  • E. Endocytosis

Answer: D. Cytoplasmic streaming

Explanation: Cytoplasmic streaming (also called cyclosis) is the movement of cytoplasm that distributes nutrients and organelles throughout the cell in single-celled organisms like Paramecium.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Diffusion: Too slow for efficient distribution in larger cells
  • B. Cyclosis: Another term for cytoplasmic streaming, but "cytoplasmic streaming" is more specific
  • C. Active transport: Mechanism for crossing membranes, not for bulk distribution
  • E. Endocytosis: Mechanism for uptake, not distribution

14. In which form is Plasmodium falciparum picked from the human blood circulation system?

Options:

  • A. Sporozoites
  • B. Gametocytes
  • C. Trophozoites
  • D. Ookinete
  • E. Spores

Answer: B. Gametocytes

Explanation: Mosquitoes pick up gametocytes (sexual forms) from human blood during feeding. These are the only forms capable of continuing the life cycle in the mosquito.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Sporozoites: Injected by mosquito into humans, not picked up from blood
  • C. Trophozoites: Asexual forms that cannot survive in mosquito
  • D. Ookinete: Develops in mosquito gut, not in human blood
  • E. Spores: Not a stage in malaria life cycle

15. Malaria infection is characterized by paroxysms. What is the interval of these paroxysms in a Plasmodium malariae infection?

Options:

  • A. 24 hours
  • B. 96 hours
  • C. 48 hours
  • D. 72 hours
  • E. 12 hours

Answer: D. 72 hours

Explanation: Plasmodium malariae causes quartan malaria with fever paroxysms every 72 hours (every 4th day), corresponding to its longer erythrocytic cycle.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. 24 hours: Not characteristic of any malaria species
  • B. 96 hours: Too long for malaria cycles
  • C. 48 hours: Characteristic of P. vivax and P. ovale (tertian malaria)
  • E. 12 hours: Too short for malaria cycles

16. Which of the following species of Trypanosomes is found in the Eastern region of Africa and infects humans?

Options:

  • A. Trypanosoma brucei brucei
  • B. Trypanosoma brucei gambiense
  • C. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense
  • D. Trypanosoma cruzi
  • E. All of the above

Answer: C. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense

Explanation: T. b. rhodesiense causes East African sleeping sickness, found in Eastern and Southern Africa. It causes acute, rapidly progressive disease.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. T. b. brucei: Infects animals but not humans
  • B. T. b. gambiense: Causes West African sleeping sickness
  • D. T. cruzi: Causes Chagas disease in South America
  • E. Only T. b. rhodesiense is found in Eastern Africa and infects humans

17. The following statements are TRUE about sleeping sickness modes of transmission EXCEPT?

Options:

  • A. Can be through vectors
  • B. Can be through mother-to-child infection
  • C. Can be through blood contact
  • D. Can be through food fecal contamination
  • E. All of the above

Answer: D. Can be through food fecal contamination

Explanation: Sleeping sickness is NOT transmitted through food-fecal contamination. It's transmitted by tsetse fly vectors, blood transfusion, or congenitally.

Why other options are TRUE:

  • A. Vector transmission: Primary mode via tsetse flies
  • B. Mother-to-child: Congenital transmission can occur
  • C. Blood contact: Through transfusion or needle sharing
  • E. This is incorrect since D is false

18. Which of the following parasites can be diagnosed by cerebrospinal fluid biopsy?

Options:

  • A. Giardia lamblia
  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • C. Trichinella spiralis
  • D. Taenia solium
  • E. Leishmania aethiopica

Answer: D. Taenia solium

Explanation: Taenia solium can cause neurocysticercosis, where cysticerci lodge in the brain and can be detected in cerebrospinal fluid or brain biopsy.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Giardia lamblia: Intestinal parasite, not neurotropic
  • B. Ascaris lumbricoides: Intestinal parasite, doesn't typically affect CNS
  • C. Trichinella spiralis: Muscle parasite, not typically CNS
  • E. Leishmania aethiopica: Causes cutaneous leishmaniasis, not CNS disease

19. Bachman intradermal test and xenodiagnoses are best for?

Options:

  • A. Trichinella spiralis
  • B. Leishmania tropica
  • C. Trichuris trichiura
  • D. Taenia saginata

Answer: A. Trichinella spiralis

Explanation: The Bachman intradermal test is specifically used for diagnosing trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis infection). Xenodiagnosis can also be used for Trichinella.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Leishmania tropica: Diagnosed by skin biopsy, not these specific tests
  • C. Trichuris trichiura: Diagnosed by stool examination
  • D. Taenia saginata: Diagnosed by stool examination for eggs or proglottids

20. Trematodes require an intermediate host in order to complete their life cycle. Which one of the following is an example of these intermediate hosts?

Options:

  • A. Canines
  • B. Felines
  • C. Molluscs
  • D. Caprine
  • E. Bovines

Answer: C. Molluscs

Explanation: Molluscs (snails and other shellfish) serve as intermediate hosts for trematodes, where larval development occurs before infecting the definitive host.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Canines: Can be definitive hosts or reservoir hosts
  • B. Felines: Can be definitive hosts or reservoir hosts
  • D. Caprine (goats): Usually definitive hosts
  • E. Bovines (cattle): Usually definitive hosts

21. Which one of the following is the infective stage of Schistosoma haematobium?

Options:

  • A. Miracidium
  • B. Cercariae
  • C. Rediae
  • D. Sporocyst
  • E. Rhabditiform

Answer: B. Cercariae

Explanation: Cercariae are the infective larval stage that penetrate human skin from contaminated water to establish schistosomiasis infection.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Miracidium: Hatches from eggs and infects snails
  • C. Rediae: Developmental stage within snail intermediate host
  • D. Sporocyst: Developmental stage within snail intermediate host
  • E. Rhabditiform: Larval stage of nematodes, not schistosomes

22. Cestodes are intestinal parasites characterized by the presence of hooks and suckers on their scolex. Cestodes with four suckers on their scolex are called?

Options:

  • A. Cyclophyllid
  • B. Cycloplasms
  • C. Cytophyllic
  • D. Cyclocyllid
  • E. Cyclophyliae

Answer: A. Cyclophyllid

Explanation: Cyclophyllidean cestodes have four suckers on their scolex (e.g., Taenia species), distinguishing them from pseudophyllidean cestodes which have two bothria.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Cycloplasms: Not a taxonomic term for cestodes
  • C. Cytophyllic: Not a recognized taxonomic term
  • D. Cyclocyllid: Incorrect spelling/term
  • E. Cyclophyliae: Incorrect taxonomic term

23. Which of the following statements describe a "cellulose" cysticercus?

Options:

  • A. A cysticerci with no evident scolex
  • B. A cysticerci with fluid filled bladder
  • C. A cysticerci with fluid filled scolex
  • D. A cysticerci with an evident scolex
  • E. All of the above

Answer: A. A cysticerci with no evident scolex

Explanation: A "cellulose" cysticercus is a degenerate form where the scolex is not evident or has been resorbed, making it non-viable.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Fluid-filled bladder: Normal feature of viable cysticerci
  • C. Fluid-filled scolex: Not a characteristic of cellulose cysticerci
  • D. Evident scolex: Opposite of cellulose cysticerci
  • E. Only A correctly describes cellulose cysticerci

24. The main cause of creeping eruptions or cutaneous larva migrans is?

Options:

  • A. Ancylostoma braziliense
  • B. Strongyloides stercoralis
  • C. Toxocara canis
  • D. Enterobium vermicularis

Answer: A. Ancylostoma braziliense

Explanation: Ancylostoma braziliense (dog hookworm) is the primary cause of cutaneous larva migrans, creating serpentine tracks as larvae migrate through skin.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Strongyloides stercoralis: Can cause skin lesions but not typical creeping eruption
  • C. Toxocara canis: Causes visceral larva migrans, not cutaneous
  • D. Enterobium vermicularis: Causes perianal itching, not skin migration

25. The most common cause of visceral larval migrans is?

Options:

  • A. Ancylostoma braziliense
  • B. Strongyloides stercoralis
  • C. Toxocara canis
  • D. Enterobium vermicularis

Answer: C. Toxocara canis

Explanation: Toxocara canis (dog roundworm) is the most common cause of visceral larva migrans, where larvae migrate through organs causing inflammation.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Ancylostoma braziliense: Causes cutaneous larva migrans
  • B. Strongyloides stercoralis: Causes strongyloidiasis, not typical VLM
  • D. Enterobium vermicularis: Intestinal parasite, doesn't cause VLM

26. Which one produces autoinfection to man?

Options:

  • A. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • B. Ancylostoma duodenale
  • C. Strongyloides stercoralis
  • D. Trichuris trichiura

Answer: C. Strongyloides stercoralis

Explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis can undergo autoinfection where larvae develop into filariform larvae within the host's intestine and re-penetrate intestinal mucosa or perianal skin.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Ascaris lumbricoides: Requires external development of eggs
  • B. Ancylostoma duodenale: Requires soil development of larvae
  • D. Trichuris trichiura: Requires external development of eggs

27. Which parasite has a blood-lung phase in its life cycle?

Options:

  • A. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • B. Wuchereria bancrofti
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis
  • D. Taenia multiceps

Answer: A. Ascaris lumbricoides

Explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides larvae migrate from intestine to liver, then to lungs via blood circulation, are coughed up and swallowed to complete development in intestine.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Wuchereria bancrofti: Adult worms in lymphatics, not lung migration
  • C. Enterobium vermicularis: Direct development in intestine
  • D. Taenia multiceps: Cestode without lung migration phase

28. Which parasite may produce Loeffler's syndrome to man?

Options:

  • A. Ascaris lumbricoides
  • B. Wuchereria bancrofti
  • C. Gnathostoma spinigerum
  • D. Taenia multiceps

Answer: A. Ascaris lumbricoides

Explanation: Loeffler's syndrome is a transient pulmonary eosinophilia caused by larval migration through lungs, classically associated with Ascaris lumbricoides.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Wuchereria bancrofti: Causes lymphatic filariasis, not pulmonary eosinophilia
  • C. Gnathostoma spinigerum: Causes cutaneous gnathostomiasis
  • D. Taenia multiceps: Causes cerebral coenurosis, not pulmonary syndrome

29. Which of the following human parasites is NOT transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes?

Options:

  • A. Wuchereria bancrofti / Loa loa
  • B. Yellow fever virus
  • C. Dengue fever virus
  • D. West Nile virus
  • E. Onyong'nyong virus

Answer: A. Wuchereria bancrofti / Loa loa

Explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, and Loa loa is transmitted by Chrysops flies (deer flies), not Aedes mosquitoes.

Why other options ARE transmitted by Aedes:

  • B. Yellow fever virus: Transmitted by Aedes aegypti
  • C. Dengue fever virus: Transmitted by Aedes aegypti
  • D. West Nile virus: Can be transmitted by Aedes species
  • E. Onyong'nyong virus: Transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes (Note: This may be a distractor)

30. Arachnids are external parasites. Which of the following diseases is caused by members of this group of parasites?

Options:

  • A. Mange
  • B. Loa loa
  • C. Rift valley fever
  • D. Scrub typhus

Answer: A. Mange

Explanation: Mange is caused by mites (Sarcoptes scabiei), which are arachnids that parasitize skin causing scabies.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Loa loa: Caused by filarial nematode, not arachnid
  • C. Rift valley fever: Viral disease transmitted by mosquitoes
  • D. Scrub typhus: Caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by mites but the disease is bacterial

31. Which one of the following is an external parasite?

Options:

  • A. Pediculus humanus capitis
  • B. Trichomonas vaginalis
  • C. Entamoeba histolytica
  • D. Leishmania donovani

Answer: A. Pediculus humanus capitis

Explanation: Pediculus humanus capitis (head louse) is an external parasite that lives on the hair and scalp, feeding on blood.

Why other options are internal parasites:

  • B. Trichomonas vaginalis: Urogenital tract parasite
  • C. Entamoeba histolytica: Intestinal parasite
  • D. Leishmania donovani: Intracellular parasite causing visceral leishmaniasis

32. One of the following states Mesoparasite. Which one is it?

Options:

  • A. A parasite which is occasionally found in both intermediate and definitive host
  • B. A parasite which entirely lives in an intermediate host
  • C. A parasite which entirely lives in a definitive host
  • D. A parasite which partly lives in and on a host

Answer: D. A parasite which partly lives in and on a host

Explanation: A mesoparasite is one that has part of its body inside the host and part outside, like some copepods attached to fish.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. This describes a parasite with complex life cycle, not mesoparasite
  • B. This describes an intermediate host-specific parasite
  • C. This describes a definitive host-specific parasite

33. The following factors can be influenced by parasite host range EXCEPT?

Options:

  • A. Antigenic drifts
  • B. Morbidity
  • C. Drug resistance
  • D. Fecundity

Answer: A. Antigenic drifts

Explanation: Antigenic drift is primarily a viral phenomenon related to genetic mutations in surface proteins, not directly influenced by parasite host range.

Why other options are influenced by host range:

  • B. Morbidity: Broader host range can affect disease severity
  • C. Drug resistance: Host range affects selection pressure
  • D. Fecundity: Host range affects reproductive success

34. Which one of the following is NOT a role of parasites in an ecosystem?

Options:

  • A. Completion of life cycles
  • B. Modification of host responses
  • C. Genomic manipulation of an ecosystem
  • D. Reflect the "health" of an ecosystem

Answer: C. Genomic manipulation of an ecosystem

Explanation: Parasites don't manipulate the genome of entire ecosystems. They may affect individual host genetics but not ecosystem-wide genomic manipulation.

Why other options ARE roles of parasites:

  • A. Parasites complete their life cycles as part of ecosystem function
  • B. Parasites modify host behavior and physiology
  • D. Parasite diversity reflects ecosystem health

35. Bacterial fimbriae present on the outer cell surface are used for:

Options:

  • A. Cellular activity
  • B. Sexual reproduction
  • C. Cell wall synthesis
  • D. Adherence to surfaces
  • E. Adherence and exchange of genetic information

Answer: E. Adherence and exchange of genetic information

Explanation: Fimbriae serve dual functions: adherence to surfaces/cells and conjugation for genetic exchange (sex pili are specialized fimbriae).

Why other options are incomplete:

  • A. Too vague and non-specific
  • B. Partially correct but incomplete
  • C. Incorrect - not involved in cell wall synthesis
  • D. Correct but incomplete - doesn't include genetic exchange

36. The most important role of the prokaryotic cell wall is to:

Options:

  • A. Maintain the shape of the cell
  • B. Protect the cell from osmotic pressures
  • C. Prevent enzymes from leaking away from the cell
  • D. Block the effects of antibiotics like penicillin
  • E. All the above

Answer: B. Protect the cell from osmotic pressures

Explanation: The primary function of the bacterial cell wall is to prevent osmotic lysis by providing structural support against osmotic pressure differences.

Why other options are less important:

  • A. Shape maintenance is secondary to osmotic protection
  • C. Enzyme retention is not a primary cell wall function
  • D. Antibiotic resistance is not the primary purpose
  • E. Not all are equally important primary functions

37. Which of the following is NOT TRUE about capsules and slime layers?

Options:

  • A. They consist of secreted material lying outside of the bacterial cell wall
  • B. They can prevent desiccation of bacterial cells
  • C. They are required for bacteria to grow normally in culture
  • D. They help bacteria resist phagocytosis by macrophages
  • E. None of the above

Answer: C. They are required for bacteria to grow normally in culture

Explanation: Capsules and slime layers are NOT required for normal bacterial growth in culture. Many bacteria grow well without them in laboratory conditions.

Why other options are TRUE:

  • A. Capsules are extracellular secreted materials
  • B. They do protect against desiccation
  • D. They are major virulence factors preventing phagocytosis
  • E. Since C is false, this option is incorrect

38. Formation of endospores:

Options:

  • A. Can be triggered by adverse environmental conditions
  • B. Allows bacterial reproduction
  • C. Occurs when the cell has excess polyphosphate
  • D. Is called germination
  • E. Occurs in all bacterial cells

Answer: A. Can be triggered by adverse environmental conditions

Explanation: Endospore formation (sporulation) is triggered by adverse conditions like nutrient depletion, heat, or chemical stress as a survival mechanism.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Sporulation is for survival, not reproduction
  • C. Not related to excess polyphosphate
  • D. Germination is spore activation, not formation
  • E. Only certain bacteria (like Bacillus, Clostridium) form endospores

39. The presence of D-amino acids in the crosslinks of the peptidoglycan layer is most likely because:

Options:

  • A. Most peptidases can only cleave L-amino acids
  • B. D-amino acids fit the structural constraints of the cell wall better than L-amino acids
  • C. Most L-amino acids have already been used for protein synthesis
  • D. D-amino acids crosslink in the absence of ribosomes
  • E. They promote synthesis of much needed essential amino acids

Answer: A. Most peptidases can only cleave L-amino acids

Explanation: D-amino acids in peptidoglycan crosslinks provide protection against host peptidases and many bacterial enzymes, which are specific for L-amino acids, making the cell wall more resistant to degradation.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Structural fit is not the primary reason
  • C. Amino acid availability is not the determining factor
  • D. Ribosome presence/absence is irrelevant to crosslinking
  • E. They don't promote essential amino acid synthesis

40. The 70S prokaryotic ribosomes consist of:

Options:

  • A. Two 40S subunits
  • B. A 50S and a 30S subunit
  • C. A 40S and a 30S subunit
  • D. A 50S and a 20S subunit
  • E. A 20S and a 60S subunit

Answer: B. A 50S and a 30S subunit

Explanation: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S ribosomes composed of a large 50S subunit and a small 30S subunit. The S values don't add up arithmetically because they represent sedimentation coefficients.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. 40S subunits are found in eukaryotic ribosomes
  • C. 40S is eukaryotic, not prokaryotic
  • D. 20S subunit doesn't exist in standard ribosomes
  • E. 60S is the large subunit in eukaryotic ribosomes

41. Gram positive cells:

Options:

  • A. Have a second, outer membrane that helps retain the crystal violet stain
  • B. Have multiple layers of peptidoglycan that help retain the crystal violet stain
  • C. Have a thick capsule that traps the crystal violet stain
  • D. Have a periplasmic space that traps the crystal violet

Answer: B. Have multiple layers of peptidoglycan that help retain the crystal violet stain

Explanation: Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan layers (20-80 nm) that retain the crystal violet-iodine complex during the decolorization step of Gram staining.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Outer membrane is characteristic of Gram-negative bacteria
  • C. Capsule is not involved in Gram staining mechanism
  • D. Periplasmic space is prominent in Gram-negative bacteria

42. The use of antibiotics that inhibit or inactivate cellular ribosomes will result directly in the loss of which of the following functions:

Options:

  • A. ATP production
  • B. DNA replication
  • C. Phagocytosis
  • D. Protein synthesis
  • E. Cell division

Answer: D. Protein synthesis

Explanation: Ribosomes are the cellular machinery responsible for protein synthesis. Antibiotics that target ribosomes (like streptomycin, chloramphenicol) directly inhibit protein synthesis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. ATP production occurs in mitochondria/cell membrane, not ribosomes
  • B. DNA replication involves DNA polymerases, not ribosomes
  • C. Phagocytosis is a cellular process not dependent on ribosomes
  • E. Cell division may be affected secondarily but not directly

43. Resistance to Beta lactams:

Options:

  • A. Can be due to an efflux pump
  • B. Is most commonly due to modification of the target Penicillin-binding protein (PBPs)
  • C. Does not involve penetration of drug to target PBPs
  • D. Infers resistance only to penicillin
  • E. Can involve up to 5 different β-lactamases

Answer: B. Is most commonly due to modification of the target Penicillin-binding protein (PBPs)

Explanation: The most common mechanism of beta-lactam resistance is modification of PBPs (penicillin-binding proteins), which reduces the affinity of beta-lactams for their target.

Why other options are incorrect or less common:

  • A. Efflux pumps can contribute but are not the most common mechanism
  • C. Penetration issues do affect resistance
  • D. Resistance affects all beta-lactams, not just penicillin
  • E. While multiple β-lactamases exist, PBP modification is more common

44. All of the following inhibit nucleic acid synthesis EXCEPT:

Options:

  • A. Norfloxacin
  • B. Chloramphenicol
  • C. Trimethoprim
  • D. Rifampicin
  • E. Sulfasalazine

Answer: B. Chloramphenicol

Explanation: Chloramphenicol inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit, not nucleic acid synthesis.

Why other options inhibit nucleic acid synthesis:

  • A. Norfloxacin: Inhibits DNA gyrase (DNA synthesis)
  • C. Trimethoprim: Inhibits folate synthesis needed for DNA synthesis
  • D. Rifampicin: Inhibits RNA polymerase (RNA synthesis)
  • E. Sulfasalazine: Inhibits folate synthesis needed for DNA synthesis

45. Passive Prophylaxis is:

Options:

  • A. Administering antibodies formed in another host
  • B. Administering subunit vaccines
  • C. Giving vaccine booster
  • D. A combination of live attenuated and toxoid vaccines
  • E. None of the above

Answer: A. Administering antibodies formed in another host

Explanation: Passive prophylaxis involves administering pre-formed antibodies (from another host/source) to provide immediate but temporary protection.

Why other options are active prophylaxis:

  • B. Subunit vaccines stimulate active immunity
  • C. Vaccine boosters enhance active immunity
  • D. Live attenuated and toxoid vaccines induce active immunity
  • E. Option A is correct

46. When are Interferons synthesized?

Options:

  • A. Synthesized by the virus when infecting a cell
  • B. Synthesized by the host cell when infected by a virus
  • C. Synthesized by the defective particles during infection
  • D. Synthesized by the subviral agents during infection
  • E. A and B

Answer: B. Synthesized by the host cell when infected by a virus

Explanation: Interferons are host cell proteins synthesized in response to viral infection as part of the innate immune response.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Viruses don't synthesize interferons
  • C. Defective particles don't synthesize interferons
  • D. Subviral agents don't synthesize interferons
  • E. Only B is correct, not A

47. The virulence determining antigens of microorganisms may be:

Options:

  • A. Proteins and polysaccharides
  • B. Carbohydrate-protein complexes
  • C. Polysaccharide-phospholipid-protein complexes
  • D. All of these
  • E. None of the above

Answer: D. All of these

Explanation: Virulence antigens can be various molecular types including proteins, polysaccharides, and complex combinations of these molecules.

Why other options are incomplete:

  • A, B, C: Each represents only some types of virulence antigens
  • E: Incorrect since virulence antigens do exist

48. Which of the following is NOT a requirement for culturing bacteria on culture media?

Options:

  • A. Knowing the oxygen requirements
  • B. Knowing the nutrient requirements
  • C. Knowing the pH requirements
  • D. Knowing the UV requirements
  • E. None of the above

Answer: D. Knowing the UV requirements

Explanation: UV requirements are not typically needed for bacterial culture. Most bacteria are cultured in the dark or normal light, and UV is often harmful to bacteria.

Why other options ARE requirements:

  • A. Oxygen requirements determine aerobic/anaerobic conditions
  • B. Nutrient requirements determine media composition
  • C. pH requirements ensure proper growth conditions
  • E. Since D is not required, this is incorrect

49. Which of the following terms describes bacteria that can thrive in the cold?

Options:

  • A. Mesophiles
  • B. Thermophiles
  • C. Psychrophiles
  • D. Aerophiles
  • E. None of the above

Answer: C. Psychrophiles

Explanation: Psychrophiles are bacteria that grow optimally at low temperatures (typically below 15°C), thriving in cold environments.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Mesophiles: Grow at moderate temperatures (20-40°C)
  • B. Thermophiles: Grow at high temperatures (>45°C)
  • D. Aerophiles: Not a standard term; refers to oxygen preference, not temperature
  • E. Psychrophiles is the correct term

50. Select the pasteurization temperature of milk:

Options:

  • A. 72°C for 30 min
  • B. 63°C for 30 min
  • C. 63°C for 30 sec
  • D. 72°C for 30 sec
  • E. None of the above

Answer: B. 63°C for 30 min

Explanation: Low Temperature Long Time (LTLT) pasteurization uses 63°C for 30 minutes. High Temperature Short Time (HTST) uses 72°C for 15 seconds.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • A. Wrong time for 72°C
  • C. Wrong time for 63°C
  • D. Wrong time for 72°C (should be 15 seconds)
  • E. Option B is correct

51. Which of the following is used for isolating pure cultures of bacteria from pus?

Options:

  • A. Streak culture
  • B. Lawn culture
  • C. Stab culture
  • D. Stroke culture
  • E. None of the above

Answer: A. Streak culture

Explanation: Streak culture technique is used to isolate pure cultures by progressively diluting the specimen across the agar surface to obtain isolated colonies.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • B. Lawn culture: Creates confluent growth, not isolation
  • C. Stab culture: Used for anaerobic culture or storage
  • D. Stroke culture: Not a standard isolation technique
  • E. Streak culture is the correct method

SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (SAQs)

Parasitology SAQs

1. Outline the clinical manifestations of giardiasis infection (5 marks)

Answer:

  • Diarrhea - watery, foul-smelling, frothy stools
  • Abdominal pain - cramping, epigastric discomfort
  • Flatulence - excessive gas production
  • Malabsorption syndrome - fat, vitamin B12, folate deficiency
  • Weight loss - due to poor nutrient absorption
  • Nausea and vomiting - especially in acute cases
  • Chronic fatigue - in prolonged infections
  • Steatorrhea - fatty, greasy stools

Memory Technique: "GAFF-MAN"

  • Greasy stools, Abdominal pain, Flatulence, Fat malabsorption, Malaise, Anorexia, Nausea

2. Highlight the prophylaxis against filariasis (5 marks)

Answer:

  • Vector control - eliminating mosquito breeding sites
  • Personal protection - bed nets, repellents, protective clothing
  • Mass drug administration (MDA) - annual single-dose treatment
  • Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) - in non-onchocerciasis areas
  • Ivermectin + Albendazole - in onchocerciasis co-endemic areas
  • Environmental management - proper drainage, water storage
  • Community education - awareness about transmission

Memory Technique: "VAMP-DIE"

  • Vector control, Annual MDA, Mosquito nets, Personal protection, DEC, Ivermectin, Environmental management

3. Write short notes on prophylaxis against antenatal malaria in malaria endemic zones (5 marks)

Answer:

  • Intermittent Preventive Treatment (IPT) - sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine
  • Insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) - consistent use during pregnancy
  • Iron and folate supplementation - prevent anemia
  • Early antenatal care - regular checkups and screening
  • Prompt treatment - of symptomatic malaria
  • Indoor residual spraying (IRS) - in high-risk areas
  • Health education - about malaria prevention

Memory Technique: "HIPSTER"

  • Health education, IPT, Prompt treatment, Supplementation, Treated nets, Early care, Residual spraying

4. Outline the complications caused by Wuchereria bancrofti infection (8 marks)

Answer:

  • Lymphangitis - inflammation of lymphatic vessels
  • Lymphadenitis - swelling of lymph nodes
  • Elephantiasis - massive swelling of limbs/genitals
  • Hydrocele - fluid accumulation in scrotum
  • Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia - lung inflammation
  • Chyluria - lymphatic fluid in urine
  • Acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADLA) - skin inflammation
  • Secondary bacterial infections - due to compromised lymphatic drainage

Memory Technique: "HELPFUL"

  • Hydrocele, Elephantiasis, Lymphangitis, Pulmonary eosinophilia, Fluid in urine, Under skin inflammation, Lymphadenitis

5. Describe pathophysiology of sleeping sickness (9 marks)

Answer:

  • Initial bite - tsetse fly injects metacyclic trypomastigotes
  • Local chancre formation - at bite site with inflammation
  • Bloodstream invasion - parasites multiply in blood and lymph
  • Immune evasion - antigenic variation of surface glycoproteins
  • Hemolymphatic stage - fever, headache, lymphadenopathy
  • CNS invasion - parasites cross blood-brain barrier
  • Neurological stage - sleep cycle disruption, behavioral changes
  • Inflammatory cascade - cytokine release, astrocyte activation
  • Progressive neurodegeneration - leading to coma and death

Memory Technique: "BLIND-CHI"

  • Bite, Local chancre, Invasion, Neurological damage, Death, CNS crossing, Hemolymphatic stage, Immune evasion

6. Highlight treatment of Entamoeba histolytica (6 marks)

Answer:

  • Metronidazole - drug of choice for invasive amoebiasis
  • Tinidazole - alternative to metronidazole
  • Diloxanide furoate - for asymptomatic cyst passers
  • Paromomycin - luminal amoebicide
  • Supportive care - fluid replacement, electrolyte balance
  • Follow-up - stool examination to confirm cure

Memory Technique: "MT-DP-SF"

  • Metronidazole, Tinidazole, Diloxanide, Paromomycin, Supportive care, Follow-up

7. Outline laboratory diagnosis of Trichomonas vaginalis (6 marks)

Answer:

  • Wet mount preparation - direct microscopy of fresh sample
  • Motile trophozoites - characteristic jerky motility
  • Giemsa staining - for morphological details
  • Culture - Diamond's medium for increased sensitivity
  • Antigen detection - enzyme immunoassays
  • PCR - most sensitive and specific method

Memory Technique: "WET-GAP"

  • Wet mount, Enzyme immunoassay, Trophozoites, Giemsa stain, Antigen detection, PCR

8. Prescribe furazolidone against giardiasis in adults (6 marks)

Answer:

  • Drug name: Furazolidone
  • Dosage: 100mg four times daily
  • Duration: 7-10 days
  • Administration: Oral, with food
  • Contraindications: G6PD deficiency, pregnancy
  • Side effects: Nausea, vomiting, brown discoloration of urine
  • Monitoring: Complete blood count if prolonged use

Memory Technique: "FURA-100-4-7"

Microbiology SAQs

9. Discuss the roles of viral receptors in the occurrence of epidemic and pandemic infections (5 marks)

Answer:

  • Species specificity - determines host range and cross-species transmission
  • Tissue tropism - dictates which organs/tissues are infected
  • Transmission efficiency - affects person-to-person spread
  • Antigenic variation - changes in receptor binding can escape immunity
  • Virulence factors - receptor binding efficiency affects disease severity
  • Pandemic potential - novel receptor usage can lead to widespread susceptibility

Memory Technique: "STRAP-V"

  • Species specificity, Tissue tropism, Receptor binding, Antigenic variation, Pandemic potential, Virulence

10. Describe Koch's postulate and its impact on the development of medical microbiology (5 marks)

Answer: Koch's Four Postulates:

  1. Microorganism must be present in all cases of the disease
  2. Pure culture isolation from diseased host
  3. Disease reproduction when pure culture is inoculated into healthy host
  4. Re-isolation of same microorganism from experimentally infected host

Impact on Medical Microbiology:

  • Established scientific method for proving causation
  • Led to germ theory acceptance
  • Enabled systematic study of infectious diseases
  • Foundation for modern diagnostic microbiology
  • Antibiotic development through understanding pathogens

Memory Technique: "PPDR-GSDA"

  • Present, Pure culture, Disease reproduction, Re-isolation = Germ theory, Scientific method, Diagnostics, Antibiotics

SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (LAQs)

1. Discuss Toxoplasma gondii infection (20 marks)

i) Epidemiology (2 marks)

  • Worldwide distribution - most common parasitic infection globally
  • Cats as definitive hosts - oocyst shedding in feces
  • Multiple intermediate hosts - birds, mammals including humans
  • Transmission routes - ingestion of oocysts, undercooked meat, congenital

ii) Life cycle stages (6 marks)

  • Oocysts - resistant environmental stage, sporulated in cat feces
  • Sporozoites - infective stage released from oocysts
  • Tachyzoites - rapidly dividing stage in acute infection
  • Bradyzoites - slow-growing stage in tissue cysts
  • Sexual reproduction - occurs only in cat intestine
  • Asexual reproduction - occurs in all intermediate hosts

iii) Pathogenesis and clinical features (6 marks)

  • Immunocompetent hosts - usually asymptomatic or mild lymphadenopathy
  • Immunocompromised - severe encephalitis, chorioretinitis
  • Congenital infection - chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications
  • Ocular toxoplasmosis - retinochoroiditis, visual impairment
  • CNS involvement - encephalitis in AIDS patients
  • Pneumonitis - in severely immunocompromised

iv) Diagnosis (4 marks)

  • Serology - IgG/IgM antibodies (ELISA, IFA)
  • PCR - detection of DNA in body fluids
  • Histopathology - tachyzoites/bradyzoites in tissue
  • Imaging - CT/MRI for CNS lesions

v) Treatment (2 marks)

  • Sulfadiazine + Pyrimethamine + Folinic acid - standard therapy
  • Clindamycin - alternative for sulfa-allergic patients

Memory Technique: "TGIF-ESSP"

  • Toxoplasma Global Infection From cats = Epidemic, Stages, Symptoms, PCR diagnosis

2. Discuss Trichomonas under the following sub-headings (22 marks)

a) Etiology (2 marks)

  • Trichomonas vaginalis - flagellated protozoan parasite
  • Sexually transmitted - primarily affects urogenital tract

b) Morphology (2 marks)

  • Trophozoite stage only - no cyst formation
  • Pear-shaped - 10-20 μm in length
  • Four anterior flagella - plus one recurrent flagellum
  • Undulating membrane - extends halfway down the body

c) Pathogenesis (5 marks)

  • Adherence - to vaginal/urethral epithelium
  • Cytotoxic enzymes - cause tissue damage
  • pH alteration - disrupts normal vaginal flora
  • Inflammatory response - recruitment of neutrophils
  • Microulcerations - increase HIV transmission risk

d) Clinical manifestations (6 marks)

In Women:

  • Vaginal discharge - frothy, yellow-green, foul-smelling
  • Vulvar irritation - itching, burning sensation
  • Dysuria - painful urination
  • Strawberry cervix - punctate hemorrhages

In Men:

  • Often asymptomatic - may be carriers
  • Urethritis - discharge, dysuria
  • Complications - epididymitis, prostatitis

e) Diagnosis (4 marks)

  • Wet mount - motile trophozoites
  • Culture - Diamond's medium
  • Antigen detection - enzyme immunoassay
  • PCR - most sensitive method

f) Drug(s) of choice (3 marks)

  • Metronidazole - 2g single dose or 500mg BID x 7 days
  • Tinidazole - alternative, 2g single dose
  • Partner treatment - essential to prevent reinfection

Memory Technique: "TRICH-MFPAID"

  • Trichomonas Requires Immediate Care Help = Morphology, Flagella, Pathogenesis, Adherence, Inflammation, Diagnosis

3. Describe sleeping sickness (22 marks)

a) Etiology and vectors (2 marks)

  • Trypanosoma brucei gambiense - West African sleeping sickness
  • Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense - East African sleeping sickness
  • Vector: Tsetse fly (Glossina species)

b) Pathogenesis and clinical features (6 marks)

Stage I (Hemolymphatic):

  • Chancre - at bite site
  • Fever - intermittent, high-grade
  • Lymphadenopathy - Winterbottom's sign
  • Headache - severe, persistent
  • Hepatosplenomegaly - organ enlargement

Stage II (Neurological):

  • Sleep cycle disruption - daytime somnolence
  • Behavioral changes - personality alterations
  • Tremors - involuntary movements
  • Coma - eventual progression to death

c) Life cycle stages (4 marks)

  • Metacyclic trypomastigotes - infective stage in tsetse fly
  • Bloodstream trypomastigotes - dividing form in mammalian host
  • Procyclic trypomastigotes - multiplying form in tsetse midgut
  • Epimastigotes - form in tsetse salivary glands

d) Diagnosis (3 marks)

  • Microscopy - blood, lymph node aspirate, CSF
  • Serology - card agglutination test
  • PCR - molecular diagnosis

e) Control (3 marks)

  • Vector control - tsetse fly elimination
  • Case detection - active screening
  • Treatment - of infected individuals

f) Drug(s) of choice (4 marks)

Stage I:

  • Pentamidine - T.b. gambiense
  • Suramin - T.b. rhodesiense

Stage II:

  • NECT - Nifurtimox-eflornithine combination
  • Fexinidazole - new oral treatment

Memory Technique: "SLEEP-TIGHT"

  • Stage I/II, Lymphatics, East/West Africa, Etiologic agents, Pentamidine = Tsetse fly, Infective stages, Gambiense/rhodesiense, Hemolymphatic, Treatment

4. Discuss Schistosomiasis (22 marks)

i) Etiology (2 marks)

  • Schistosoma haematobium - urogenital schistosomiasis
  • Schistosoma mansoni - intestinal schistosomiasis
  • Schistosoma japonicum - Oriental schistosomiasis

ii) Pathogenesis (5 marks)

  • Cercarial dermatitis - skin penetration reaction
  • Acute schistosomiasis - Katayama fever
  • Chronic inflammation - egg deposition in tissues
  • Granuloma formation - around trapped eggs
  • Fibrosis - organ damage, portal hypertension

iii) Life cycle (6 marks)

  • Eggs - passed in urine/feces
  • Miracidium - hatches from egg in water
  • Snail intermediate host - Bulinus, Biomphalaria
  • Sporocyst stages - multiplication in snail
  • Cercariae - released from snail
  • Schistosomula - penetrate human skin

iv) Diagnosis (3 marks)

  • Microscopy - eggs in urine/stool
  • Serology - antibody detection
  • PCR - molecular methods

v) Control (3 marks)

  • Chemotherapy - mass drug administration
  • Snail control - intermediate host elimination
  • Sanitation - proper sewage disposal

vi) Drug(s) of choice (3 marks)

  • Praziquantel - single dose, all species
  • Dosage: 40mg/kg for S. haematobium/mansoni
  • Dosage: 60mg/kg for S. japonicum

Memory Technique: "SCHIST-EPIC"

  • Snail vector, Cercarial penetration, Hematobium/mansoni, Inflammation, Sporocyst, Tissue damage = Eggs, Praziquantel, Intermediate host, Control
