ANATOMY MUST KNOW ESSAYS
Content:
ANATOMY EXAMINATION QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS - COMPLETE

QUESTION 1 - Facial Nerve Lesions (10 Marks)

a) Difference in Clinical Presentation between Upper and Lower Motor Neuron Lesions of the Facial Nerve (3 marks)

Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Lesion:

  • Causes contralateral weakness of the lower half of the face
  • The forehead muscles are spared due to bilateral cortical innervation

Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Lesion:

  • Causes ipsilateral weakness of both the upper and lower facial muscles, including the forehead

Summary: UMN lesion = contralateral lower face weakness with forehead sparing; LMN lesion = ipsilateral complete facial paralysis.

b) Anatomical Basis for the Difference Between UMN and LMN Lesions (5 marks)

  1. Facial nucleus location: The facial nerve motor nucleus is located in the pons and gives rise to the lower motor neurons.
  2. Cortical innervation: The upper part of the facial nucleus (which controls the forehead) receives bilateral corticobulbar innervation, while the lower part (which controls the lower face) receives only contralateral corticobulbar innervation.
  3. UMN lesion (e.g., stroke): Since the upper facial muscles have bilateral input, they remain functional when one corticobulbar tract is damaged. However, the contralateral lower face loses its only source of cortical input, resulting in weakness.
  4. LMN lesion (e.g., Bell's palsy): The lesion affects the facial nerve after it exits the brainstem, disrupting all motor supply to ipsilateral facial muscles, both upper and lower.
  5. Resulting clinical difference: This anatomical pattern explains why UMN lesions spare the forehead, while LMN lesions cause complete ipsilateral facial paralysis.

c) Two Sensory Stimuli Conveyed by the Posterior Columns of the Spinal Cord (2 marks)

  1. Fine (discriminative) touch
  2. Proprioception (position sense)

QUESTION 2 - Esophagus (10 Marks)

a) Three Areas of Constriction (3 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Cervical constriction: At the origin of the esophagus, behind the cricoid cartilage (C6), caused by the cricopharyngeus muscle.
  2. Thoracic (broncho-aortic) constriction: Where the esophagus is crossed by the aortic arch and the left main bronchus (~T4–T5).
  3. Diaphragmatic constriction: Where the esophagus passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at T10.

b) Four Relations in the Superior Mediastinum (4 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Anteriorly: Trachea and left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
  2. Posteriorly: Vertebral column and thoracic duct.
  3. To the right: Azygos vein and right pleura/lung.
  4. To the left: Arch of the aorta, left subclavian artery, and left pleura/lung.

c) Lymphatic Drainage (3 marks)

The lymphatic drainage of the esophagus is segmental and drains into different nodal groups:

  1. Cervical part: Drains into deep cervical lymph nodes.
  2. Thoracic part: Drains into posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
  3. Abdominal part: Drains into left gastric and celiac lymph nodes.

QUESTION 3 - Jejunum vs Ileum and Inguinal Canal (10 Marks)

a) Name 4 Differences Between Jejunum and Ileum (4 Marks - 1 mark each)

b) Describe the Boundaries of the Inguinal Canal (6 Marks - 1.5 marks each for boundaries)

The inguinal canal is an oblique passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall, about 4 cm long, running from the deep to the superficial inguinal ring.

  1. Anterior Wall:
    • Mainly formed by the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle throughout
    • Reinforced laterally by internal oblique muscle fibers
  2. Posterior Wall:
    • Formed by the transversalis fascia
    • Reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon (fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses)
  3. Roof (Superior Wall):
    • Formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles
  4. Floor (Inferior Wall):
    • Formed by the inguinal ligament
    • Medially supported by the lacunar ligament

QUESTION 4 - Popliteal Fossa and Femoral Triangle (10 Marks)

a) Boundaries and Contents of the Popliteal Fossa (5 Marks)

Boundaries:

  1. Superolateral: Biceps femoris muscle
  2. Superomedial: Semimembranosus and semitendinosus muscles
  3. Inferolateral: Lateral head of gastrocnemius
  4. Inferomedial: Medial head of gastrocnemius
  5. Floor: Popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, and popliteus muscle
  6. Roof: Skin and deep fascia (popliteal fascia)

Contents (from superficial to deep/posterior to anterior):

  1. Tibial nerve
  2. Popliteal vein
  3. Popliteal artery
  4. Common peroneal (fibular) nerve
  5. Small saphenous vein (termination)
  6. Lymph nodes and fat

b) Boundaries and Contents of the Femoral Triangle (5 Marks)

Boundaries:

  1. Superior (base): Inguinal ligament
  2. Lateral: Sartorius muscle
  3. Medial: Adductor longus muscle
  4. Floor: Iliopsoas (laterally) and pectineus (medially)
  5. Roof: Fascia lata and skin

Contents (from lateral to medial - NAVEL mnemonic):

  1. Femoral Nerve
  2. Femoral Artery
  3. Femoral Vein
  4. Femoral canal (contains lymph node of Cloquet)
  5. Deep inguinal lymph nodes and fat

QUESTION 5 - Median Nerve (10 Marks)

A. Course of the Median Nerve in the Upper Limb

  1. Origin:
    • Formed by two roots from the medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus (C5–T1)
    • Roots unite anterior to the third part of the axillary artery
  2. In the Arm:
    • Runs lateral to the brachial artery initially, then crosses over to become medial to it near the mid-arm
    • Does not give any branches in the arm
  3. In the Cubital Fossa:
    • Enters the cubital fossa medial to the biceps tendon and brachial artery
    • Passes between the two heads of pronator teres
  4. In the Forearm:
    • Travels between flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP)
    • Gives off the anterior interosseous nerve (AION), supplying deep forearm muscles
    • At the wrist, it becomes superficial, passing through the carpal tunnel
  5. In the Hand:
    • Enters the hand deep to the flexor retinaculum (in the carpal tunnel)
    • Divides into recurrent branch (to thenar muscles) and digital branches (to lateral 3½ fingers for motor and sensory innervation)

B. Distribution of the Median Nerve

  1. Motor Supply:
    • Forearm muscles (anterior compartment): All except flexor carpi ulnaris and medial half of FDP
    • Thenar muscles: Abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
    • Lumbricals 1 and 2 (index and middle fingers)
  2. Sensory Supply:
    • Skin over the lateral palm
    • Palmar surface and dorsal tips of the lateral 3½ fingers (thumb, index, middle, and half of ring finger)

C. Deficits Following Median Nerve Injury

  1. At the Elbow (e.g., supracondylar fracture):
    • Loss of forearm pronation
    • Weak wrist flexion with ulnar deviation
    • Loss of flexion of the lateral fingers and thumb opposition
    • Hand of Benediction when attempting to make a fist (only ulnar-side fingers flex)
  2. At the Wrist (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome, laceration):
    • Thenar muscle wasting
    • Loss of thumb opposition
    • Sensory loss over lateral 3½ fingers
    • Ape hand deformity: Flattened thenar eminence, thumb held in same plane as fingers
  3. Anterior Interosseous Nerve Injury:
    • Weakness of flexor pollicis longus, FDP (lateral half), and pronator quadratus
    • Inability to make an "OK sign" (due to weak flexion of thumb and index finger tips)

QUESTION 6 - Stomach (10 Marks)

a) Blood Supply of the Stomach (4 Marks)

The stomach receives a rich arterial supply from branches of the celiac trunk:

  1. Lesser Curvature:
    • Left gastric artery (from the celiac trunk)
    • Right gastric artery (from the proper hepatic artery)
    • These anastomose along the lesser curvature
  2. Greater Curvature:
    • Left gastroepiploic artery (from splenic artery)
    • Right gastroepiploic artery (from gastroduodenal artery)
    • Anastomose along the greater curvature
  3. Fundus and Upper Body:
    • Short gastric arteries (from splenic artery)

Venous drainage: Corresponds to the arteries and drains into the portal vein via the left and right gastric veins, splenic vein, and superior mesenteric vein.

b) Innervation of the Stomach

  1. Parasympathetic Innervation:
    • From the vagus nerve (CN X)
    • Left vagus supplies the anterior wall, right vagus the posterior wall
    • Stimulates secretion, motility, and relaxation of sphincters
  2. Sympathetic Innervation:
    • From T6–T9 spinal segments via greater splanchnic nerves, synapsing in the celiac ganglion
    • Inhibits gastric motility and secretion; vasoconstrictive
  3. Visceral Afferents:
    • Pain fibers travel with the sympathetics, explaining epigastric pain in gastric pathology

c) Lymphatic Drainage of the Stomach

Lymph from the stomach drains into gastric and gastroepiploic lymph nodes, which eventually drain into celiac lymph nodes.

By region:

  1. Superior two-thirds (lesser curvature):
    • Drain into left and right gastric nodes → celiac nodes
  2. Greater curvature (inferior part):
    • Drain into right and left gastroepiploic nodes → pyloric or pancreaticosplenic nodes → celiac nodes
  3. Fundus and upper part of the body:
    • Drain into short gastric and pancreaticosplenic nodes → celiac nodes

QUESTION 7 - Cerebrospinal Fluid Flow (10 Marks)

1. Production of CSF

  • CSF is produced by the choroid plexuses located in the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and fourth ventricle
  • The majority is formed in the lateral ventricles
  • Approximately 500 mL/day is produced, but only about 150 mL circulates at a time due to continuous absorption

2. Flow of CSF through the Ventricular System

  1. From lateral ventricles → flows through the interventricular foramina (of Monro)
  2. Into the third ventricle
  3. Then passes via the cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius)
  4. Into the fourth ventricle

3. Exit from the Ventricles to the Subarachnoid Space

CSF exits the fourth ventricle through:

  1. One median aperture (foramen of Magendie)
  2. Two lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka)

These openings allow CSF to enter the subarachnoid space, particularly the cisterna magna.

4. Circulation in the Subarachnoid Space

CSF circulates around the brain and spinal cord within the subarachnoid space, cushioning neural structures and maintaining a stable environment.

5. Absorption of CSF

CSF is absorbed into the venous circulation through arachnoid granulations (villi) which protrude into the superior sagittal sinus and other dural venous sinuses. Absorption is pressure-dependent and helps maintain constant intracranial pressure.

Summary of Flow Pathway: Lateral ventricles → Foramina of Monro → Third ventricle → Cerebral aqueduct → Fourth ventricle → Foramina of Luschka and Magendie → Subarachnoid space → Arachnoid granulations → Superior sagittal sinus

Clinical note: Obstruction anywhere in this pathway can lead to hydrocephalus (accumulation of CSF with increased intracranial pressure).

QUESTION 8 - Male Sexual Response (10 Marks)

The Male Sexual Response Consists of Four Stages:

1. Excitement (Arousal Phase)

Description: Initiated by erotic stimuli (visual, tactile, psychological).

Anatomical Basis: Parasympathetic nervous system (S2–S4) via pelvic splanchnic nerves.

  • Causes vasodilation of arteries supplying the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum, leading to penile erection
  • Nitric oxide (NO) is released, relaxing smooth muscle and increasing blood flow
  • Bulbourethral glands secrete mucus for lubrication

2. Plateau Phase

Description: Sustained erection, increased muscle tone, and preparation for ejaculation.

Anatomical Basis: Continued parasympathetic activity maintains engorgement of erectile tissues.

  • Ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles (somatic via pudendal nerve) contract rhythmically, increasing pressure in erectile tissues

3. Orgasm (Ejaculation Phase)

Description: Release of semen through the urethra.

Anatomical Basis: Controlled by the sympathetic nervous system (T12–L2) via hypogastric nerves.

Two phases:

  1. Emission: Movement of sperm and glandular secretions into urethra via peristaltic contractions of vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate
  2. Ejaculation: Expulsion of semen by contraction of bulbospongiosus muscle (pudendal nerve)

Internal urethral sphincter contracts to prevent retrograde ejaculation into the bladder.

4. Resolution (Refractory Phase)

Description: Return to flaccid state and physiological recovery.

Anatomical Basis: Sympathetic vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to erectile tissues.

  • Venous outflow increases, leading to detumescence (loss of erection)
  • Temporary refractory period occurs, during which erection and orgasm cannot be repeated

Summary Table:

Mnemonic: "Point and Shoot" — Parasympathetic for erection (point), Sympathetic for ejaculation (shoot).

QUESTION 9 - Abdominal Wall Anatomy

i) State two muscles in the anterior abdominal wall that are vertically oriented

  1. Rectus abdominis
  2. Pyramidalis (present in ~80% of people)

ii) State the boundaries of the Triangle of Hesselbach (Inguinal Triangle)

  1. Medial border: Lateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle
  2. Lateral border: Inferior epigastric vessels
  3. Inferior border: Inguinal ligament

iii) State 3 modifications of Scarpa's fascia

  1. Forms the fundiform ligament of the penis/clitoris
  2. Continues into the perineum as Colles' fascia
  3. Contributes to the dartos fascia in the scrotum (in males)

iv) State the boundaries of the Epiploic Foramen of Winslow

  1. Anteriorly: Free edge of lesser omentum (contains portal triad: hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct)
  2. Posteriorly: Inferior vena cava
  3. Superiorly: Caudate lobe of the liver
  4. Inferiorly: First part of the duodenum

v) State the anatomical and functional division of the liver

  1. Anatomical division: By the falciform ligament into right and left lobes
  2. Functional division: By an imaginary line called Cantlie's line (from gallbladder to IVC), separating the liver into right and left functional lobes based on bile drainage and vascular supply

vi) State the boundaries of the Triangle of Calot (Cystohepatic Triangle)

  1. Medially: Common hepatic duct
  2. Laterally: Cystic duct
  3. Superiorly: Inferior surface of the liver

vii) Compare and Contrast Direct and Indirect Inguinal Hernias

viii) State the vertebral levels of the following branches of the abdominal aorta

a) Superior mesenteric artery: L1 b) Celiac artery: T12 c) Inferior mesenteric artery: L3

QUESTION 10 - Respiration and Related Anatomy

a) State the 3 Mechanisms of Ventilation and Their Anatomical Basis

  1. Pump Handle Movement
    • Anatomical Basis: Elevation of the upper ribs (mainly ribs 2–6) increases the anteroposterior diameter of the thoracic cavity. This movement is centered at the costovertebral and sternocostal joints.
  2. Bucket Handle Movement
    • Anatomical Basis: Elevation of the lower ribs (mainly ribs 7–10) increases the transverse diameter of the thoracic cavity. The curved ribs swing laterally like a bucket handle when lifted.
  3. Diaphragmatic Movement
    • Anatomical Basis: Contraction of the diaphragm flattens the dome, increasing the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity.

b) Branching Pattern of the Respiratory Tree and the Part of the Lung They Aerate

  1. Trachea – Begins at C6 and bifurcates at T4/T5 (sternal angle)
  2. Primary (Main) Bronchi
    • Right main bronchus: Wider, shorter, more vertical – enters right lung
    • Left main bronchus: Longer, narrower – enters left lung
    • Aerate entire lungs
  3. Secondary (Lobar) Bronchi
    • Right lung: 3 lobar bronchi (upper, middle, lower lobes)
    • Left lung: 2 lobar bronchi (upper and lower lobes)
    • Aerate each lobe
  4. Tertiary (Segmental) Bronchi
    • Right lung: 10 bronchopulmonary segments
    • Left lung: 8–10 segments
    • Aerate individual bronchopulmonary segments

c) State the Pattern of Fetal Circulation

  1. Oxygenated blood from placenta → through umbilical vein
  2. Most blood bypasses the liver via the ductus venosus → into inferior vena cava
  3. Blood enters the right atrium, most is shunted through the foramen ovale → left atrium
  4. From the left atrium → left ventricle → ascending aorta → body
  5. Blood that enters the right ventricle is pumped into the pulmonary artery, but most bypasses the lungs via ductus arteriosus → descending aorta
  6. Deoxygenated blood returns to the placenta via umbilical arteries

d) Course and Branches of the Vagus Nerve in the Neck (6 Marks)

Course:

  • Arises from the medulla oblongata, exits skull through the jugular foramen
  • Descends within the carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and internal/common carotid artery
  • Travels down to enter the thorax

Branches in the Neck:

  1. Auricular branch (Arnold's nerve): To external ear and external auditory canal
  2. Pharyngeal branches: Form pharyngeal plexus with cranial nerve IX and sympathetic fibers; innervates muscles of the pharynx (except stylopharyngeus) and soft palate (except tensor veli palatini)
  3. Superior laryngeal nerve:
    • External branch: Motor to cricothyroid muscle
    • Internal branch: Sensory to larynx above vocal cords
  4. Cardiac branches: Contribute to cardiac plexus in the thorax
  5. Recurrent laryngeal nerve (originates in root of neck):
    • Right loops under subclavian artery
    • Left loops under aortic arch
    • Ascends to supply larynx below vocal cords, and all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid

QUESTION 11 - Lower Limb and Development

a) Boundaries of the Femoral Triangle

  1. Superior (Base): Inguinal ligament
  2. Lateral: Sartorius muscle
  3. Medial: Adductor longus muscle
  4. Floor: Iliopsoas (laterally) and pectineus (medially)
  5. Roof: Fascia lata and skin

b) Contents of the Femoral Triangle and Their Clinical Relevance

Contents (from lateral to medial): Mnemonic: NAVEL

d) Write a Short Note on the Pericardium (5 Marks)

The pericardium is a double-walled fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels.

It has two main layers:

  1. Fibrous pericardium – Outer tough connective tissue layer that anchors the heart to surrounding structures (e.g., diaphragm and sternum).
  2. Serous pericardium – Inner layer further divided into:
    • Parietal layer (lines the fibrous pericardium)
    • Visceral layer (epicardium) – adheres to the heart surface

Between the layers is the pericardial cavity, which contains serous fluid that reduces friction during heart movements.

Functions: Protects the heart, prevents overdistension, and limits heart movement.

Clinical Note: Inflammation = pericarditis; fluid accumulation = pericardial effusion, which may cause cardiac tamponade.

e) Describe the Layers of the Epidermis and State the Cell Types in Each Layer (5 Marks)

The epidermis is the outermost layer of skin composed of keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, with five layers (from deep to superficial):

  1. Stratum basale (germinativum):
    • Single row of basal keratinocytes (actively dividing)

  2. Stratum spinosum:
    • Several layers of polyhedral keratinocytes connected by desmosomes
    • Langerhans cells (immune defense) also present
  3. Stratum granulosum:
    • 3–5 layers of flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules (precursors of keratin)
  4. Stratum lucidum: (only in thick skin)
    • Thin, translucent layer of dead keratinocytes
  5. Stratum corneum:
    • Outermost layer of dead, flattened keratinized cells (corneocytes) that provide waterproof protection

  1. Hair Follicles and Hair:

  1. Free Nerve Endings:

h) Outline 3 Effects of Luteinising Hormone (LH) on the Ovary

  1. Ovulation Trigger:

  2. Corpus Luteum Formation and Maintenance:

i) Define the Following Terms

a) Corpus Luteum: A temporary endocrine structure formed from the ruptured ovarian follicle after ovulation, responsible for secreting progesterone (and some estrogen) to support the luteal phase and potential implantation.

b) Corpus Albicans: A fibrous scar formed from the degenerated corpus luteum if fertilization does not occur; it is composed of collagen and is non-functional.

QUESTION 13 - Histological Organization of Long Bones and Blood Supply (20 Marks)

I. HISTOLOGICAL ORGANIZATION OF LONG BONES

Long bones (e.g., femur, humerus) consist of several distinct microanatomical features, visible under the light microscope. These include:

  1. Periosteum
    • Outer fibrous connective tissue layer covering the bone, except at joints
    • Contains fibroblasts, osteoprogenitor cells, and blood vessels
    • Inner layer (cambium layer) contains osteoblasts for bone growth and repair
  2. Compact (Cortical) Bone
    • Found in the diaphysis (shaft) of long bones
    • Composed of osteons (Haversian systems) with concentric lamellae around central Haversian canals
    • Contains:
      • Lamellae: Circular layers of mineralized bone matrix
      • Lacunae: Spaces housing osteocytes
      • Canaliculi: Small channels for nutrient exchange between osteocytes
      • Volkmann's canals: Perforating canals that connect Haversian canals transversely
  3. Spongy (Cancellous) Bone
    • Found in the epiphysis and inner regions of flat bones
    • Composed of trabeculae (bony struts) with interconnected spaces housing red bone marrow
    • Osteocytes reside in lacunae within the trabeculae
    • Site of hematopoiesis
  4. Endosteum
    • Thin vascular membrane lining the medullary cavity and Haversian canals
    • Contains osteoprogenitor cells for bone remodeling
  5. Bone Marrow
    • Red marrow (active hematopoiesis) – in children and flat bones
    • Yellow marrow (fat-storing) – predominates in adult long bones
  6. Epiphyseal Plate (in growing bones)
    • Region of hyaline cartilage between diaphysis and epiphysis
    • Site of endochondral ossification and longitudinal growth
    • Has distinct zones: resting, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, ossification
  7. Articular Cartilage
    • Hyaline cartilage covering the epiphyses at joint surfaces
    • Smooth, avascular, reduces friction during movement

II. BLOOD SUPPLY OF LONG BONES

  1. Nutrient Artery
    • Enters the bone via nutrient foramen, usually in the diaphysis
    • Divides into ascending and descending branches within the medullary cavity
    • Supplies inner 2/3 of cortex, medullary cavity, and marrow
  2. Periosteal Arteries
    • Arise from surrounding arteries
    • Supply the outer 1/3 of cortical bone via small channels (Volkmann's canals)
  3. Metaphyseal and Epiphyseal Arteries
    • Arise from adjacent joint and metaphyseal vessels
    • Supply the epiphysis, growth plate, and adjacent metaphysis
  4. Venous Drainage
    • Follows arteries through nutrient vein, periosteal veins, and epiphyseal veins
    • Drains into systemic venous circulation

QUESTION 14 - Formation of the Placenta (20 Marks)

The placenta is a temporary, highly vascular organ that forms during pregnancy. It facilitates exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes between maternal and fetal blood and produces hormones like hCG, progesterone, and estrogen.

It develops from both maternal and fetal tissues:

  • Fetal part: From chorion frondosum
  • Maternal part: From decidua basalis

I. FETAL COMPONENT OF THE PLACENTA

  1. Origin of the Chorion
    • Formed by: Extraembryonic mesoderm, Cytotrophoblast, Syncytiotrophoblast
    • These layers collectively form the chorionic membrane.
  2. Development of Chorionic Villi Occurs in three stages:
    • Primary villi (Day 13): Formed by cytotrophoblasts covered by syncytiotrophoblasts extending into maternal endometrium.
    • Secondary villi (Day 16): Mesodermal core invades primary villi.
    • Tertiary villi (Day 21): Formation of fetal capillaries within the mesoderm core, establishing early feto-placental circulation.
  3. Chorion Frondosum Formation
    • Villi adjacent to the decidua basalis proliferate and become chorion frondosum (fetal part of placenta)
    • Villi in other regions degenerate (forming chorion laeve)
  4. Formation of Umbilical Circulation
    • Two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from fetus to placenta
    • One umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus
    • These are enclosed in Wharton's jelly within the umbilical cord

II. MATERNAL COMPONENT OF THE PLACENTA

  1. Decidua Basalis
    • Derived from the endometrium of the uterus under the implanted embryo
    • Contains maternal spiral arteries, which supply blood to the intervillous spaces
  2. Intervillous Spaces
    • Formed by lacunae within the syncytiotrophoblast layer
    • Filled with maternal blood from spiral arteries
    • Fetal villi float in these spaces to allow exchange of substances across the placental barrier

III. PLACENTAL BARRIER

Separates maternal and fetal blood; composed of:

  1. Syncytiotrophoblast
  2. Cytotrophoblast (early)
  3. Basement membrane of trophoblast
  4. Mesenchyme of villus core
  5. Endothelium of fetal capillaries

Becomes thinner as pregnancy progresses to facilitate efficient exchange.

IV. FUNCTIONS OF THE PLACENTA

  1. Exchange of gases – O₂, CO₂ diffusion
  2. Nutrient transfer – Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids
  3. Waste removal – Urea, creatinine
  4. Hormone production – hCG, progesterone, estrogen, human placental lactogen (hPL)
  5. Immunological protection – Transfers maternal antibodies (IgG)

QUESTION 15 - Organization of Venous Vessels in the Lower Limb (20 Marks)

The venous system of the lower limb is organized into superficial, deep, and perforating veins. These veins are responsible for draining deoxygenated blood from the foot, leg, and thigh back to the heart. Valves are present throughout to prevent backflow, and muscular contractions assist in venous return (calf pump).

I. SUPERFICIAL VEINS

These veins lie in the subcutaneous tissue, superficial to deep fascia. They drain skin and superficial structures.

  1. Great Saphenous Vein
    • Origin: Medial side of dorsal venous arch of the foot
    • Course:
      • Ascends anterior to medial malleolus
      • Travels medial leg and thigh, accompanied by saphenous nerve
      • Passes through saphenous opening in fascia lata
      • Drains into femoral vein in the femoral triangle
    • Tributaries: Superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, external pudendal veins
    • Clinical Note: Commonly used for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)
  2. Small Saphenous Vein
    • Origin: Lateral side of dorsal venous arch
    • Course:
      • Ascends posterior to lateral malleolus
      • Travels in the midline of posterior leg
      • Pierces popliteal fascia and drains into the popliteal vein
      • Accompanied by the sural nerve

II. DEEP VEINS

Deep veins run with major arteries and are located beneath deep fascia. They have valves and are often paired (venae comitantes).

  1. Dorsal Foot and Leg
    • Anterior tibial vein – Accompanies anterior tibial artery; Drains dorsum of foot and anterior leg
  2. Posterior Compartment
    • Posterior tibial vein and fibular (peroneal) vein – Drain posterior leg and plantar foot
  3. Popliteal and Femoral Veins
    • Popliteal vein: Formed by union of anterior and posterior tibial veins; Becomes femoral vein at adductor hiatus
    • Femoral vein: Ascends in femoral triangle; receives deep femoral vein and great saphenous vein; Becomes external iliac vein after passing under inguinal ligament

III. PERFORATING VEINS

Connect superficial and deep veins, allowing blood to flow from superficial to deep. Contain valves to prevent reverse flow.

Examples:

  • Cockett's perforators – connect posterior arch vein (superficial) to posterior tibial vein
  • Boyd's perforator – near knee
  • Dodd's perforator – in thigh (Hunterian perforator)

IV. VENOUS VALVES AND MUSCLE PUMP

  • Valves ensure unidirectional blood flow toward the heart
  • Calf muscle pump: Contraction of leg muscles squeezes deep veins, propelling blood upward
  • Failure of valves can lead to varicose veins, especially in superficial system

V. CLINICAL CORRELATIONS

  1. Varicose veins – Due to incompetent valves in superficial veins (especially great saphenous vein)
  2. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) – Clots in deep veins, often in popliteal or femoral vein; risk of pulmonary embolism
  3. Venous ulcers – From chronic venous insufficiency, especially near medial malleolus

QUESTION 16 - Organization of Blood Supply in the Upper Limb (20 Marks)

The blood supply of the upper limb is provided primarily by the subclavian artery, which becomes the axillary artery, then the brachial artery, and further branches down to supply the forearm and hand. The arterial system ensures rich collateral circulation and follows a consistent anatomical path with key anastomoses at joints.

I. SUBCLAVIAN ARTERY

  • Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk (right side) or aortic arch (left side)
  • Becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib

Major branches relevant to upper limb:

  • Vertebral artery
  • Thyrocervical trunk – gives rise to suprascapular artery (important in scapular anastomosis)
  • Dorsal scapular artery – supplies medial border of scapula

II. AXILLARY ARTERY

Begins at lateral border of the first rib, ends at lower border of teres major. Divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle:

Branches:

  • First part (proximal to pectoralis minor):
    • Superior thoracic artery
  • Second part (posterior to pectoralis minor):
    • Thoracoacromial artery (has clavicular, deltoid, pectoral, and acromial branches)
    • Lateral thoracic artery
  • Third part (distal to pectoralis minor):
    • Subscapular artery (largest branch; gives rise to circumflex scapular artery and thoracodorsal artery)
    • Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries – encircle surgical neck of humerus

Clinical Note: Posterior circumflex humeral artery runs with axillary nerve in the quadrangular space

III. BRACHIAL ARTERY

  • Continuation of the axillary artery from lower border of teres major
  • Runs down the anterior arm, medial to biceps tendon
  • Ends in the cubital fossa where it divides into radial and ulnar arteries

Main Branches:

  • Profunda brachii (deep brachial artery): Travels with radial nerve in radial groove; Supplies posterior compartment of arm
  • Superior and Inferior ulnar collateral arteries: Participate in elbow anastomosis

IV. FOREARM BLOOD SUPPLY

Radial Artery:

  • Runs along lateral forearm
  • Supplies flexor muscles of lateral forearm, passes through anatomical snuffbox, enters palm to contribute to the deep palmar arch
  • Used for pulse at the wrist and for ABG (arterial blood gas) sampling

Ulnar Artery:

  • Runs along medial forearm, under flexor carpi ulnaris
  • Gives off common interosseous artery, which divides into:
    • Anterior interosseous artery – supplies deep flexors
    • Posterior interosseous artery – supplies extensor compartment
  • Continues to form the superficial palmar arch

V. BLOOD SUPPLY OF THE HAND

  1. Superficial Palmar Arch (mainly ulnar artery)
    • Gives rise to common palmar digital arteries, which divide into proper digital arteries
  2. Deep Palmar Arch (mainly radial artery)
    • Gives rise to palmar metacarpal arteries
    • Anastomoses with branches from the superficial arch
  3. Dorsal Carpal Arch
    • Formed by dorsal branches of radial and ulnar arteries
    • Supplies dorsum of hand

Clinical Note: The dual supply ensures collateral circulation, preventing ischemia in case of arterial blockage

VI. ANASTOMOSES AND COLLATERALS

Scapular anastomosis:

  • Suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery
  • Ensures blood reaches upper limb if axillary artery is occluded

Elbow anastomosis:

  • Brachial artery (ulnar collaterals) with radial and ulnar recurrent arteries

Palmar anastomosis:

  • Between superficial and deep palmar arches

QUESTION 17 - Thoracic Venous Drainage and Related Anatomy (20 Marks)

a) Describe the azygos/hemiazygos venous drainage (10 Marks)

The azygos system of veins provides venous drainage of the thoracic wall, posterior abdomen, and serves as a collateral pathway between the superior and inferior vena cava.

Azygos Vein:

  • Origin: Formed by the union of right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal vein (may receive contribution from IVC)
  • Course:
    • Ascends along the right side of the vertebral column, through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (T12)

    • Right posterior intercostal veins (5th–11th)

Hemiazygos Vein:

  • Origin: From left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein
  • Course:

  • Receives:
    • Left posterior intercostal veins (9th–11th)

Accessory Hemiazygos Vein:

  • Drains: Left posterior intercostal veins (5th–8th)
  • Course: Descends on the left side of the vertebrae, joins the azygos vein around T7–T8

  • Provides collateral venous return if either SVC or IVC is obstructed

Posterior Mediastinum:

a) Describe the blood and nerve supply to the perineum and related structures (10 Marks)

The perineum is the region below the pelvic diaphragm, bounded by the pubic symphysis anteriorly, ischial tuberosities laterally, and coccyx posteriorly.   • Deep dorsal vein of penis/clitoris drains into prostatic/vesical venous plexus

  • Superficial perineum structures: Superficial inguinal lymph nodes
  • Deep perineal structures: Internal iliac nodes
  • Glans penis/clitoris: Deep inguinal nodes

1. Pudendal Nerve – Main Nerve of the Perineum

  • Root Value: S2–S4 (ventral rami)

Branches:

  • Inferior rectal nerve: Anal sphincter, perianal skin
  • Perineal nerve: Superficial and deep perineal muscles, skin
  • Posterior scrotal/labial: Skin of posterior scrotum/labia

b) Describe the embryology of the midgut (10 Marks)

Origin: The midgut originates from the endoderm of the primitive gut tube. It extends from the distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

Blood Supply: Supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), which defines its vascular territory.

Physiological Herniation and Rotation: Around week 6, the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord due to rapid growth and limited abdominal space. It forms a U-shaped loop with:

  • Cranial limb → small intestine (jejunum and ileum)
  • Caudal limb → large intestine (cecum, ascending, proximal transverse colon)

Rotation:

  • The midgut undergoes a 270° counterclockwise rotation around the axis of the SMA
  • 90° during herniation → 180° upon return to abdominal cavity (~week 10)

Return to Abdomen:

  • The intestines retract into the abdominal cavity and assume their adult positions
  • Cecum is last to re-enter and temporarily lies in the right upper quadrant before descending to the iliac fossa

c) Describe the embryology of the hindgut (10 Marks)

Origin: The hindgut is derived from the caudal part of the primitive gut tube (endoderm). It extends from the distal 1/3 of transverse colon to the upper part of the anal canal.

Blood Supply: Supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).

Cloaca and Partitioning: The hindgut ends in the cloaca, a common cavity for the GI and urogenital tracts. A urorectal septum divides the cloaca into:

  • Anterior part → urogenital sinus
  • Posterior part → anorectal canal

The anal canal forms from two embryologic sources:

  • Upper 2/3: From endoderm (hindgut) – columnar epithelium
  • Lower 1/3: From ectoderm (proctodeum) – stratified squamous epithelium

The junction is marked by the pectinate line.

Failure of proper division may result in imperforate anus or fistulas.

8. Anatomical Basis for Bell's Palsy (3 Marks)

Bell's palsy is caused by lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve, often due to inflammation or viral infection (e.g., HSV). The facial nerve becomes compressed within the narrow facial canal in the temporal bone. Results in ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of all muscles of facial expression (forehead, eye, mouth), loss of taste on anterior tongue, hyperacusis due to stapedius paralysis, and dry eye (reduced lacrimation).

  • Taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue via chorda tympani

QUESTION 20 - Clinical Neuroanatomy Case (20 Marks)

Case Summary: A 20-year-old female presents with a 3-month history of:

  • Double vision (diplopia)
  • Sensitivity to light (photophobia)
  • Progressive ataxia
  • Medially fixed left eye
  • Vertical and horizontal nystagmus
  • Left-sided facial droop with mouth deviation to the right
  • Increased urinary frequency

The constellation of multifocal neurological symptoms involving cranial nerves, cerebellum, brainstem, and autonomic pathways, especially in a young adult, strongly suggests a central demyelinating disease such as Multiple Sclerosis (MS).

a) Anatomical Basis for Double Vision (Diplopia) (2 marks)

Likely due to disruption of conjugate gaze pathways, involving:

  • Cranial nerve VI (abducens) → lateral rectus palsy (eye fails to abduct)
  • Cranial nerve III (oculomotor) → impaired coordination of medial rectus

A classic lesion here is Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO), due to a demyelinating lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), disrupting communication between CN VI and CN III nuclei. Result: impaired horizontal gaze, leading to diplopia.

b) Anatomical Basis for Progressive Ataxia (2 marks)

Ataxia is likely due to a lesion in:

  • The cerebellar hemispheres or vermis
  • The cerebellar peduncles (especially the middle and inferior)

Alternatively, disruption of spinocerebellar or dorsal column pathways (proprioceptive fibers) in the brainstem or spinal cord. MS commonly affects cerebellar white matter, leading to truncal or limb ataxia.

c) Anatomical Basis for Medially Fixed Left Eye (2 marks)

Indicates left abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy:

  • CN VI innervates the lateral rectus muscle
  • Lesion prevents abduction of the left eye, leading to unopposed action of the medial rectus (CN III) → eye fixed medially

CN VI nucleus is located in the pons, making it vulnerable to pontine demyelinating lesions, as seen in MS.

d) Anatomical Basis for Nystagmus (2 marks)

Nystagmus can arise from:

  • Lesions in the vestibular nuclei (pons/medulla)
  • Cerebellum (especially flocculonodular lobe and vermis)
  • Disruption of the MLF (causing INO-related nystagmus)

In MS, INO is often associated with nystagmus in the abducting eye during attempted horizontal gaze.

e) Anatomical Basis for Facial Palsy & Type of Lesion (2 marks)

Left-sided facial droop with deviation to the right implies left facial muscle weakness. If entire half of the face is weak (including forehead), this is a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of CN VII.

Likely site: facial nucleus in the pons or fascicle of the facial nerve. MS commonly causes demyelination in the brainstem, affecting facial nerve pathways directly.

Note: If forehead were spared, that would imply an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, but full left-sided weakness indicates LMN.

f) Anatomical Basis for Increased Micturition Frequency (2 marks)

Suggests a neurogenic bladder due to loss of supraspinal inhibition of the sacral micturition reflex.

Possible lesions:

  • Pontine micturition center (Barrington's nucleus)
  • Descending spinal pathways (e.g., corticospinal tracts or periaqueductal gray to sacral spinal cord)

MS can cause demyelination of spinal cord tracts, particularly in cervical or thoracic cord, leading to detrusor overactivity → urgency and frequency.

g) With a reason, state the possible location of the lesion (2marks)

The lesion is most likely located in the left dorsal pons and may extend to involve adjacent brainstem structures and cerebellar connections.

Reason:

  • The medially fixed left eye indicates a left abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy, which localizes to the left pontine tegmentum where the abducens nucleus and fascicle reside.
  • The left-sided lower motor neuron facial weakness (entire side of face affected) suggests a lesion of the facial nerve nucleus or its fascicle, also located in the pons.
  • Nystagmus and diplopia are suggestive of a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)—a structure in the dorsal pons and midbrain—commonly affected in internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).
  • The progressive ataxia points to involvement of cerebellar pathways, especially the middle cerebellar peduncle, which connects the cerebellum to the pons.
  • The increased micturition frequency indicates disruption of descending supraspinal inhibitory pathways, likely involving the pontine micturition center or spinal projections traversing the brainstem.

QUESTION 21 - Tracheoesophageal Fistula (6 Marks)

Clinical Presentation: A newborn presents with choking during breastfeeding and is noted to turn blue in the hands and feet during the choking episodes. As the medical officer intern, you decide to put a nasogastric tube and you note that the tube is unable to advance. You order a plain chest radiograph and you see the coiling of the nasogastric tube. You suspect a tracheoesophageal fistula.

A. Likely Types of TEF Based on Clinical Presentation (3 marks)

A newborn with:

  • Choking and cyanosis during feeding
  • Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube
  • Coiling of the tube on chest X-ray

These findings strongly suggest Esophageal Atresia with Distal Tracheoesophageal Fistula (Gross Type C). Less likely but worth mentioning is H-type fistula (Type E).

Type C – Esophageal Atresia with Distal TEF (Most common: ~85–90%)

  • NG tube coiling in the upper esophageal pouch (due to proximal atresia)
  • Choking/cyanosis due to overflow of milk into trachea from the blind esophagus and possible reflux via distal fistula
  • Air in stomach seen on radiograph from air entering through the fistula

Type A – Pure Esophageal Atresia (No fistula)

  • NG tube coiling without gastric air
  • Cyanosis due to saliva aspiration, but no fistulous connection to trachea

Type E – H-type Fistula without Atresia (Rare)

  • Esophagus is patent, so NG tube should pass easily
  • Can cause choking/cyanosis due to a small fistula between esophagus and trachea, but coiling of NG tube is not expected, making it less likely in this case

B. Embryological Basis of TEF and Atresia (3 marks)

In week 4–5 of gestation, the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) arises from the ventral foregut. Normally, the tracheoesophageal septum divides the foregut into:

  • Dorsal part → esophagus
  • Ventral part → trachea and lungs

In TEF and EA: Abnormal partitioning of the foregut causes:

  • Esophageal atresia: due to failed elongation or recanalization of the dorsal foregut
  • Persistent fistula: from incomplete closure of the tracheoesophageal septum, creating an abnormal connection between esophagus and trachea

This defective separation leads to blind-ending upper esophagus and a distal communication with the trachea, as seen in Type C.

QUESTION 22 - Retinal Histology and Pancoast Tumor (20 Marks)

a) State the histological organization of the retina and the respective cell types seen on light microscopy (10 marks)

The retina is organized into ten histological layers, each containing specific cell types. From outermost (near choroid) to innermost (near vitreous body), these layers and their main cell types are:

  1. Retinal Pigment Epithelium (RPE)
    • Cells: Simple cuboidal epithelial cells containing melanin
    • Function: Absorbs stray light, phagocytoses photoreceptor outer segments, and forms part of the blood-retinal barrier
  2. Photoreceptor Layer
    • Cells: Rods and cones (light-sensitive cells)
    • Function: Capture light and initiate phototransduction
  3. External Limiting Membrane
    • Cells: Not a true membrane, but a line formed by adherens junctions between photoreceptors and Müller cells
  4. Outer Nuclear Layer
    • Cells: Nuclei of rods and cones
  5. Outer Plexiform Layer
    • Cells/processes: Synapses between photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and horizontal cells
  6. Inner Nuclear Layer
    • Cells: Bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glial cells (nuclei)
  7. Inner Plexiform Layer
    • Cells/processes: Synapses between bipolar cells and ganglion cells; also contains amacrine cell processes
  8. Ganglion Cell Layer
    • Cells: Cell bodies of ganglion cells (output neurons of the retina)
  9. Nerve Fiber Layer
    • Cells: Axons of ganglion cells that converge to form the optic nerve
  10. Internal Limiting Membrane
    • Cells: Formed by basal lamina of Müller cells

b) State the anatomical basis for the clinical presentation(s)/symptoms/signs seen in a patient with a large tumor of the apex of the lung (10 marks)

A large tumor at the apex of the lung (commonly referred to as a Pancoast tumor) can compress various adjacent anatomical structures, leading to specific clinical signs/symptoms:

  1. Involvement of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8–T1):
    • Clinical presentation: Pain radiating down the arm, weakness and muscle wasting in the hand, sensory loss in the medial forearm and hand
  2. Involvement of the sympathetic chain (stellate ganglion):
    • Clinical presentation: Horner's syndrome, characterized by:
      • Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
      • Miosis (constricted pupil)
      • Anhidrosis (loss of sweating on affected side)
      • Enophthalmos (sunken eye)
  3. Invasion of ribs and thoracic vertebrae:
    • Clinical presentation: Localized chest wall pain, especially in the shoulder or scapular area
  4. Invasion of recurrent laryngeal nerve (usually left side):
    • Clinical presentation: Hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis
  5. Compression of subclavian vessels (especially subclavian vein):
    • Clinical presentation: Edema of the upper limb or neck veins (venous congestion)
  6. Invasion of phrenic nerve (less common):
    • Clinical presentation: Ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis → dyspnea
  7. Proximity to spinal cord (in severe posterior invasion):
    • Clinical presentation: Neurological deficits, potentially leading to paraparesis or bladder dysfunction

  1. Sinoatrial (SA) node – Pacemaker, initiates impulse; located at SVC-RA junction
  2. Atrioventricular (AV) node – Delays impulse to allow atrial contraction
  3. AV bundle (Bundle of His) – Transmits impulse from AV node into ventricles

  5. Purkinje fibers – Distribute impulse to ventricular myocardium for contraction

  2. Left coronary artery (LCA) – Divides into:

    • Circumflex artery – Supplies lateral wall and part of LA
  3. Venous drainage – Via coronary sinus, which opens into right atrium
  4. Great cardiac vein – Follows LAD

  3. Lobar bronchi → Segmental (tertiary) bronchi – Aerate bronchopulmonary segments

Clinical significance:

  • Selective filtration barrier – blocks large and negatively charged proteins
  • Target in diseases like Goodpasture's syndrome and Alport syndrome

QUESTION 28 - Pain Pathways and Functional Neuroanatomy (50 Marks)

1. Describe the Pain Pathway (5 Marks)

  1. Nociceptors in skin/muscle detect pain
  2. Signal transmitted via A-delta or C fibers
  3. Enters dorsal root ganglion → dorsal horn
  4. Synapse with second-order neurons, decussate in spinal cord
  5. Ascend via spinothalamic tract to VPL of thalamus
  6. Thalamus → primary somatosensory cortex for perception

2. Boundaries and Contents of the Superior Mediastinum (5 Marks)

Boundaries:

  • Superior: Thoracic inlet
  • Inferior: Sternal angle (T4/T5)
  • Anterior: Manubrium
  • Posterior: T1–T4 vertebrae

Contents:

  • Aortic arch and branches
  • Brachiocephalic veins
  • SVC (upper part)
  • Trachea
  • Esophagus
  • Thymus
  • Phrenic, vagus, and left recurrent laryngeal nerves

3. Structures that Form the Stomach Bed (5 Marks)

  1. Pancreas
  2. Spleen
  3. Left kidney
  4. Left suprarenal gland
  5. Transverse mesocolon
  6. Splenic artery
  7. Diaphragm

4. Arrangement of Structures in Female Pelvis (Anterior to Posterior) (5 Marks)

  1. Urinary bladder
  2. Uterus and vagina
  3. Rectum and anal canal

5. Blood Supply to the Stomach (5 Marks)

Lesser curvature:

  • Left gastric (from celiac trunk)
  • Right gastric (from hepatic artery)

Greater curvature:

  • Left gastroepiploic (from splenic artery)
  • Right gastroepiploic (from gastroduodenal artery)

Fundus:

  • Short gastric arteries (from splenic)

6. Blood Supply to the Spinal Cord (5 Marks)

  1. Anterior spinal artery – from vertebral arteries; supplies anterior 2/3
  2. Posterior spinal arteries – from vertebral or PICA; supply posterior 1/3
  3. Radicular arteries – from segmental arteries (e.g., intercostals)
  4. Great anterior segmental medullary artery (of Adamkiewicz) – major lower thoracic/lumbar supply
  5. Venous drainage via internal vertebral venous plexus

7. Functional Areas in the Temporal Lobe (15 Marks)

a) Gyri (5 marks)

  • Superior temporal gyrus
  • Middle temporal gyrus
  • Inferior temporal gyrus
  • Medial temporal gyrus (includes hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus)
  • Fusiform gyrus (on the inferior surface)

b) Function of Each Area (5 marks)

c) Clinical Correlates of a Lesion in Each Area (5 marks)

8. Functional Areas in the Parietal Lobe (15 Marks)

a) Gyri (5 marks)

  • Postcentral gyrus
  • Superior parietal lobule
  • Inferior parietal lobule (includes supramarginal and angular gyri)
  • Precuneus (medial surface)
  • Intraparietal sulcus (separates superior and inferior lobules)

b) Function of Each Area (5 marks)

c) Clinical Correlates of Lesions (5 marks)

QUESTION 29 - Complex Anatomy and Physiology (50 Marks)

1. Anterior and Posterior Relations of the Rectum (10 marks)

Anterior Relations:

In males:

  • Sigmoid colon
  • Bladder
  • Seminal vesicles
  • Prostate
  • Vas deferens
  • Rectovesical pouch

In females:

  • Vagina (posterior wall)
  • Cervix
  • Rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas)
  • Uterus (via peritoneum)

Posterior Relations:

  • Sacrum and coccyx
  • Sacral vessels and nerves
  • Piriformis muscle
  • Coccygeus and levator ani muscles
  • Presacral fascia and lymph nodes

2. Micturition Reflex (10 marks)

  1. Bladder filling:
    • Stretch receptors in detrusor muscle activated as bladder fills
  2. Afferent signals:
    • Sent via pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) to spinal cord
  3. Spinal processing:
    • Reflex arc via sacral spinal cord initiates parasympathetic outflow
  4. Efferent signals:
    • Parasympathetic nerves (pelvic nerves) cause detrusor contraction
    • Internal urethral sphincter relaxes
  5. Voluntary control:
    • Pudendal nerve (S2–S4) maintains tone in external sphincter
    • Controlled by pontine micturition center
  6. Conscious initiation or inhibition:
    • Prefrontal cortex and periaqueductal gray regulate voluntary voiding

3. Blood Supply to the Spinal Cord (10 marks)

Arterial Supply:

  • 1 Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries) – anterior 2/3
  • 2 Posterior spinal arteries – posterior 1/3

Segmental spinal arteries from:

  • Intercostal arteries (thoracic region)
  • Lumbar arteries
  • Vertebral and deep cervical arteries
  • Artery of Adamkiewicz (large segmental artery in lower thoracic/lumbar)

Venous Drainage:

  • Internal vertebral venous plexus
  • External vertebral venous plexus

4. Arrangement of Structures in the True Female Pelvis (10 marks)

From anterior to posterior:

  1. Urinary bladder
  2. Uterus and vagina
  3. Rectum and anal canal

Laterally:

  • Broad ligament
  • Ureters
  • Ovaries and fallopian tubes
  • Internal iliac vessels
  • Pelvic floor muscles (levator ani)

Superiorly:

  • Peritoneal pouches: vesicouterine and rectouterine (Pouch of Douglas)

5. Pain Pathways (Reception to Perception) (10 marks)

  1. Nociceptors: Free nerve endings detect noxious stimulus
  2. First-order neurons: Aδ and C fibers → dorsal root ganglia
  3. Second-order neurons: Synapse in dorsal horn of spinal cord; Cross midline → ascend via spinothalamic tract
  4. Third-order neurons: In thalamus (VPL nucleus)
  5. Cortex: Signals relayed to somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus)

Also modulated by:

  • Reticular formation
  • Limbic system (emotional response)
  • Periaqueductal gray (descending inhibition)

COURSE INFORMATION

Course Title: Human Pathology

DEPARTMENTAL VISION, MISSION & VALUES

VISION

To be a global hub of excellence in education, research and innovation in Pathology.

MISSION

To provide world class education, research and innovation for global transformation and sustainable development in Pathology harnessing knowledge in applied sciences and technology for the service of humanity in line with the university quality policy and medical ethics.

CORE VALUES

  • Integrity
  • Professionalism
  • Innovation

1. COURSE PURPOSE

The course gives the student an overview on the use of chemical pathology and laboratory medicine in the interpretation of tests to make a diagnosis and management of diseases. It involves the study and use of chemical processes to measure levels of chemical components in body fluids and tissues.

2. QUALITY OBJECTIVES

2.1 Critical Thinking and Analysis

The ability to collect, analyze and evaluate information and formulate conclusions. Students develop and demonstrate the ability to think critically and analytically.

2.2 Communication and Technical Competency

To be competent in oral, written, quantitative, and technological skills. Students develop and demonstrate competency in oral and written communication as well as demonstrate scientific, quantitative and technological literacy.

2.3 Global Health Awareness

To allow the students acquire an understanding of economic, historical, political, geographic and environmental relationship, awareness, knowledge and appreciation of the diversity and commodity of cultures of health on a global platform.

2.4 Field Mastery

To enable the students gain a mastery of a field of knowledge and its multi-cultural and multinational application.

2.5 Community Service

A sense of being part of a community and a desire to be of service to it. Students are given opportunities to participate in community service, citizenship, or social action projects or activities.

2.6 Professional Ethics

As part of their growth and development, students formulate and articulate the ethical standards which will guide their professional and personal lives.

3. EXPECTED LEARNING OUTCOMES

3.1 Laboratory Test Knowledge

The student will be able to list the main chemical pathology laboratory tests that are done with regard to specific diseases of the various organ systems by understanding the role of the laboratory in patient management.

3.2 Clinical Interpretation

The student will be able to interpret clinical vignettes given in real disease scenarios by transforming the theory learnt into clinical practice by making a rational choice of relevant laboratory tests used to assess a patient.

3.3 Clinical Recommendations

The student will be able to make relevant recommendations for further laboratory testing and treatment.

3.4 Disease Management Application

The student will be able to apply knowledge of chemical pathology in the screening, monitoring, diagnosis, staging, prognostication and management of disease.

3.5 Curriculum Integration

The student will integrate and apply the knowledge learned to other disciplines within the MBChB training curriculum and participate effectively in the course delivery and evaluation to enhance the learning experience.

4. INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS

4.1 Interactive Learning

Lectures, PowerPoint presentations, and class discussions. A multifaceted approach will be used, employing mainly those methods that encourage active learning and stress on competency explaining principles and concepts, and explaining the difficult areas related to any discipline.

4.2 Laboratory Learning and Experiments

The lecturer, together with the laboratory technical staff, will take the students through practical sessions, demonstrating specific and practical aspects of what the students are currently studying. The students will thereafter be expected to use pre-formulated laboratory manuals to carry out various practical exercises and then write out their findings in their logbooks.

4.3 Multimedia Learning

Video demonstrations and/or CD-ROMs on Human Pathology when available, after the relevant topic has been covered.

4.4 Assignment Criteria

Students will be given individual or group research assignments on topics relevant to the course. These could include lectures, discovery learning, problem-based learning, experimental learning, group-based learning, independent studies, and e-learning.

Title: Chemical Pathology
Content:
Chemical Pathology Quiz

Quiz 1

Question 1

A 35-year-old man has no clinical evidence for bleeding and he feels fine. As part of a pre-operative workup for a hernia repair, laboratory studies show Hgb 14.8 g/dL, Hct 45%, MCV 96 fL, WBC count 8500/microliter, and platelet count 275,000/microliter. His prothrombin time is normal, but the partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. A deficiency of which of the following coagulation factors is most likely be associated with these findings?

Options: A) IX
B) VIII
C) XII
D) X
E) XIII

Answer: C) XII

Explanation: Factor XII deficiency causes prolonged PTT but normal PT, and importantly does not cause clinical bleeding symptoms. This fits the asymptomatic patient with isolated PTT prolongation.

Question 2

A 20-year-old man is actively bleeding from multiple sites during surgery. He has a CBC that shows a WBC count of 4500/microliter, Hgb 7.6 g/dL, Hct 23.9%, MCV 98 fL, and platelet count 75,000/microliter. His prothrombin time is 30 seconds and partial thromboplastin time 63 seconds. What is the best blood product to use for him in this situation?

Options: A) Whole blood
B) Cryoprecipitate (Cryo)
C) Packed red blood cells (PRBCs)
D) Granulocytes
E) Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

Answer: A) Whole blood

Explanation: The patient has multiple deficiencies: low Hgb/Hct (anemia), low platelets (thrombocytopenia), and prolonged PT/PTT (coagulopathy). Whole blood provides red cells, platelets, and clotting factors all in one product.

Question 3

A 31-year-old woman has oozing of blood from mucous membranes over the past 3 days. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 10,000/microliter. She receives 6 units of platelets. An hour following this transfusion, her platelet count is 2,000/microliter. What is the most probable explanation for the change in pre- to post-transfusion platelet count?

Options: A) Splenomegaly
B) Anti-HLA antibodies
C) Septicemia
D) Hemorrhage
E) Single donor source

Answer: B) Anti-HLA antibodies

Explanation: The platelet count actually decreased after transfusion, indicating platelet refractoriness most commonly due to anti-HLA antibodies that destroy transfused platelets.

Question 4

A 12-year-old boy has had multiple episodes of bleeding since infancy. It is characterized by hemarthroses and decreased joint mobility. His prothrombin time (PT) is normal, but the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) is elevated. When his plasma is mixed with normal plasma, the PTT is not elevated. His platelet count is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause for his illness?

Options: A) Acquired autoantibody
B) Congenital HIV infection
C) Repeated trauma
D) Inherited gene mutation
E) Chronic liver disease

Answer: D) Inherited gene mutation

Explanation: Classic presentation of hemophilia (Factor VIII or IX deficiency) with hemarthroses, prolonged PTT that corrects with mixing study, indicating factor deficiency rather than inhibitor. This is caused by inherited gene mutations.

Question 5

A 64-year-old nursing home patient receiving tube feedings is admitted with fever of two days' duration accompanied by a cough productive of yellowish sputum. On admission his temperature is 37.4°C. A sputum gram stain shows 4+ gram positive diplococci. He is also found to have a total serum protein of 9.4 g/dl with serum albumin of 3.8 g/dl. Which of the following underlying diseases do these findings most strongly suggest that he has?

Options: A) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
B) Chronic renal failure
C) Plasma cell dyscrasia
D) Diabetes mellitus
E) Hepatitis B virus infection

Answer: C) Plasma cell dyscrasia

Explanation: High total protein (9.4 g/dL) with normal albumin (3.8 g/dL) suggests elevated globulins, characteristic of plasma cell disorders like multiple myeloma. The large protein gap (9.4-3.8 = 5.6) is diagnostic.

Question 7

A 44-year-old man has had congestive heart failure for 2 years. His serum ferritin is markedly elevated. His CBC shows WBC count 6300/microliter, Hgb 7.8 g/dL, Hct 22.6%, MCV 69 fL, and platelet count 177,000/microliter. A hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals 2% Hgb A, 8% Hgb A2, and 90% Hgb F. Which of the following hematologic conditions is he most likely to have?

Options: A) Beta thalassemia major
B) Sickle cell anemia
C) Alpha thalassemia minor
D) Hemoglobin H disease
E) Hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin

Answer: A) Beta thalassemia major

Explanation: Very high HgbF (90%), elevated HgbA2 (8%), minimal HgbA (2%), severe microcytic anemia, and iron overload (high ferritin) are classic for beta thalassemia major.

Question 8

A study of blood product therapy is done. One product is identified that carries the greatest risk for infection. This blood product has the shortest shelf life, and it must be used as quickly as possible for transfusion. Which of the following products is best described by these findings?

Options: A) Platelets
B) Whole blood
C) Packed red blood cells
D) Cryoprecipitate
E) Fresh frozen plasma

Answer: A) Platelets

Explanation: Platelets are stored at room temperature (not refrigerated), have the shortest shelf life (5 days), and highest bacterial contamination risk due to room temperature storage.

Question 9

An 81-year-old previously healthy woman has had a 2 kg weight loss without dieting over the past 2 months. She reports no other problems. On examination there are no abnormal findings. Laboratory studies show a serum alkaline phosphatase of 200 U/L. Which of the following diseases is she most likely to have?

Options: A) Acute viral hepatitis
B) Bone metastases
C) Cholelithiasis
D) Intestinal obstruction
E) Osteoporosis

Answer: B) Bone metastases

Explanation: Elderly patient with unexplained weight loss and isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase suggests bone metastases from occult malignancy.

Question 11

A 17-year-old boy has developed a mild fever with sore throat over the past day. On physical examination he has generalized lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show a CD4 lymphocyte count of 375/microliter. He is most likely to be infected with which of the following agents?

Options: A) HTLV-1
B) HTLV-2
C) HIV-1
D) HIV-2
E) HHV-8

Answer: A) HTLV-1

Explanation: HTLV-1 can cause adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with lymphadenopathy and can affect CD4 counts. The acute presentation with lymphadenopathy fits HTLV-1 infection better than the other options.

Question 12

A 62-year-old healthy woman has a pre-operative workup for an elective surgery. A serum glucose is ordered and is of 120 mg/dl. Four hours later that day, another glucose test is ordered unnecessarily, and the value is noted to be 124 mg/dl. Which of the following best explains the difference in these two values on this woman?

Options: A) Diabetes mellitus
B) Laboratory error
C) Lack of test sensitivity
D) Blood removed by phlebotomy
E) Test coefficient of variation

Answer: E) Test coefficient of variation

Explanation: The small difference (4 mg/dL) between two glucose values is within normal analytical variation. Coefficient of variation describes this expected imprecision in laboratory testing.

Question 13

A healthy 27 year old male donates blood. He completes the questionnaire and interview with no exclusions noted. The presence of which of the following infectious agents will not routinely tested for on his blood collected for transfusion?

Options: A) Human immunodeficiency virus type 1
B) Hepatitis A virus
C) Human T lymphocytotrophic virus
D) Treponema pallidum
E) Hepatitis C virus

Answer: B) Hepatitis A virus

Explanation: Hepatitis A is not routinely tested in blood donors because it's primarily fecal-oral transmission, has short viremic period, and doesn't cause chronic infection. All other agents are routinely screened.

Question 14

A 33-year-old woman has had multiple episodes of deep venous thrombosis over the past year. Last week she had a transient ischemic attack. On examination there are no abnormal findings. Laboratory studies show a prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time. When her plasma is mixed in a ratio of 1:1 with normal plasma, neither the PT nor the PTT normalize. Which of the following conditions is she most likely to have?

Options: A) Antiphospholipid syndrome
B) Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
C) Protein C deficiency
D) Vitamin K deficiency
E) Hemophilia B

Answer: A) Antiphospholipid syndrome

Explanation: Recurrent thrombosis, prolonged PT/PTT that don't correct with mixing studies indicates presence of inhibitors (lupus anticoagulant), characteristic of antiphospholipid syndrome.

Question 15

A 5-year-old previously healthy child develops a mild watery diarrhea that lasts for 3 days. On physical examination the child has a low-grade fever. A stool for ova and parasites is negative. The child recovers without therapy and has no sequelae. What is the most likely infectious etiology for her diarrheal illness?

Options: A) Shigella flexneri
B) Adenovirus
C) Vibrio parahemolyticus
D) Rotavirus
E) Salmonella enterica

Answer: D) Rotavirus

Explanation: Self-limited watery diarrhea in a young child with low-grade fever, negative for parasites, is most commonly caused by rotavirus - the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis in children.

Question 16

During phlebotomy, there is difficulty obtaining blood for all of the test ordered. Not all of the collection tubes are completely filled. Of the following collection tubes, which is the only one that may be partially filled and not affect test results?

Options: A) Gray top for glucose
B) Light-blue top for protime
C) Purple top for CBC
D) Black top for sed rate
E) Red top for total protein

Answer: E) Red top for total protein

Explanation: Red top tubes (serum tubes) don't contain anticoagulants, so the blood-to-additive ratio isn't critical. Other tubes require specific ratios for accurate results (especially coagulation studies).

Question 17

A 30-year-old man experiences excessive bleeding following a wisdom tooth extraction. There is a family history of similar problems. His mother had menorrhagia. His sister has frequent nosebleeds. Laboratory findings show he has a normal PT, PTT, and platelet count. Which of the following coagulation disorders is this man most likely to have?

Options: A) Antiphospholipid antibody
B) von Willebrand disease
C) Vitamin K deficiency
D) Hemophilia B
E) Protein C deficiency

Answer: B) von Willebrand disease

Explanation: Family history of bleeding in both males and females, mucosal bleeding pattern, normal PT/PTT/platelet count suggests von Willebrand disease - the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

Question 18

A 47-year-old man has focal pain and swelling in his mouth for the past month. Physical exam reveals a large, firm area of induration starting from the gingiva and extending to the right floor of the mouth, with draining sinus tracts to skin. Mandibular osteomyelitis is present radiographically. There is some granular, yellowish-orange material in the exudate. Which of the following findings on a smear of the exudate is most likely to be seen microscopically?

Options: A) Short, broad, non-septate hyphae
B) Thin, branching, septate hyphae
C) Long gram positive filaments
D) Short acid fast bacilli
E) Long acid fast filaments

Answer: C) Long gram positive filaments

Explanation: Chronic osteomyelitis with draining sinuses and yellowish granules (sulfur granules) is characteristic of Actinomyces, which appears as long, branching, gram-positive filaments.

Question 19

A 34-year-old woman has developed malaise for the past 3 months. Over the past day she has becomes very ill with mental status changes. On examination areas of skin purpura are noted. Laboratory studies show Hgb 9.2, platelet count 225,000, and WBC count 44,500 with 18 segs, 5 bands, 2 metamyelocytes, 1 myelocytes, 67 promyelocytes, 5 lymphs, and 2 monos. A bone marrow biopsy shows myeloid hyperplasia with <5% blasts. Which of the following karyotypic findings is most likely present in cells from her biopsy?

Options: A) t(15;17)
B) t(8;14)
C) t(9;22)
D) t(14;18)
E) t(11;21)

Answer: A) t(15;17)

Explanation: High percentage of promyelocytes (67%) with acute clinical deterioration and purpura suggests acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), which is associated with t(15;17) translocation.

Question 20

A 58-year-old man with a history of unstable angina presents with chest pain that has been worsening for the past eight hours. The pain radiates down his left arm. On examination he is now diaphoretic, with tachycardia and an irregular cardiac rhythm. Which of the following is now the best laboratory test to order for this man?

Options: A) CK-MB
B) C-reactive protein
C) Troponin I
D) Total LDH
E) Myoglobin

Answer: C) Troponin I

Explanation: Troponin I is the most specific and sensitive marker for myocardial infarction, remaining elevated for days after the event. It's the gold standard cardiac biomarker.

Question 21

A 40-year-old veterinarian working near the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains in Southern California saw his physician because of marked axillary and inguinal lymph node swelling developing in only a day. On examination he has a high fever with tender right axillary node. There is a mall laceration on his right hand. A lymph node biopsy is obtained and shows marked necrosis with hemorrhage, and a Gram stain shows numerous gram-negative bacilli. With which of the following organisms is he most likely infected?

Options: A) Francisella tularensis
B) Leptospira interrogans
C) Borrelia burgdorferi
D) Yersinia pestis
E) Bacillus anthracis

Answer: D) Yersinia pestis

Explanation: Veterinarian in California with acute lymphadenitis, necrosis, hemorrhage, and gram-negative bacilli suggests plague (Yersinia pestis), which is endemic in California and affects animals and their handlers.

Question 22

While driving to his next clinic visit, a 52 year old man is involved in a vehicular accident in which his car is struck broadside at an intersection. Though the air bag inflates, the car rolls over, and the impact against the door results in a large laceration to his lower leg. After transport to a local hospital, he is found to have a Hct of 16%. Coagulation studies reveal a protime of 16 seconds and partial thromboplastin time of 24 seconds. His platelet count is 69,000/microliter. Which of the following blood products is most indicated for treatment of this man?

Options: A) Platelet packs
B) Packed red blood cells
C) Fresh frozen plasma
D) Cryoprecipitate
E) Whole blood

Answer: B) Packed red blood cells

Explanation: Severely low hematocrit (16%) indicates massive blood loss requiring immediate red cell replacement. While platelets are also low, the primary need is to restore oxygen-carrying capacity.

Question 23

A 25-year-old woman incurs a head injury from a skiing accident. She is now in stable condition and her vital signs are normal. Serum electrolytes now show Na 134 meq/L, K 7.6 meq/L, Cl 100 meq/L, and CO2 25 meq/L. What is the most likely etiology for these laboratory test findings?

Options: A) Hemolyzed specimen
B) Severe diarrhea
C) Mannitol infusion
D) Acute renal failure
E) Excess intravenous fluids

Answer: A) Hemolyzed specimen

Explanation: Stable patient with markedly elevated potassium (7.6) but normal other electrolytes suggests pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis during blood collection, releasing intracellular potassium.

Question 24

Seven children living in the same neighborhood develop perianal itching, most pronounced at night, over the past week. Their parents don't pay much attention to this until they also develop the same problem. The eggs recovered from the perianal region of affected children are 50 micron, flat, and embryonated. Which of the following infections are they most likely to have?

Options: A) Enterobius vermicularis
B) Ascaris lumbricoides
C) Trichuris trichiuria
D) Necator americanus
E) Strongyloides stercoralis

Answer: A) Enterobius vermicularis

Explanation: Perianal itching at night in children with family spread, and characteristic flat, embryonated eggs found in perianal area describes pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis) infection.

Question 25

A 45-year-old woman undergoes mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet tilting disk mechanical prosthesis as treatment for chronic rheumatic valvulitis with mitral stenosis. She is prescribed warfarin and the dosage is adjusted based upon prothrombin time testing. Which of the following ranges for international normalized ratio (INR) is most appropriate for this woman?

Options: A) 3 to 4
B) 2 to 3
C) 1 to 2
D) 0 to 1

Answer: B) 2 to 3

Explanation: For mechanical heart valves, the target INR is typically 2.5-3.5, but 2-3 is the most appropriate range listed. This provides adequate anticoagulation while minimizing bleeding risk.

Question 26

A 58-year-old woman has had malaise and a 2 kg weight loss over the past year. Laboratory studies show Hgb 10 g/dL, Hct 30.1%, MCV 88 fL, platelet count 200,000/microliter, and WBC count 7500/microliter. She has a decreased serum iron and total iron binding capacity (TIBC) in association with an increased serum ferritin. Which of the following conditions is she most likely to have?

Options: A) Sickle cell anemia
B) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
C) Atrophic gastritis
D) Colonic adenocarcinoma
E) Chronic hepatitis

Answer: D) Colonic adenocarcinoma

Explanation: Anemia of chronic disease pattern (low iron, low TIBC, high ferritin) with weight loss in older adult suggests underlying malignancy, commonly colorectal cancer.

Question 27

A 27-year-old G3 P2 woman gives birth at 35 weeks gestational age. On examination the infant has marked hydrops fetalis along with generalized icterus. The baby's peripheral blood smear demonstrates numerous nucleated RBC's, and the spun hematocrit is only 20%. Which of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be present in the mother of this infant?

Options: A) Antiphospholipid antibodies
B) Blood type O positive
C) Hemoglobin C
D) Positive Coombs test
E) Decreased haptoglobin

Answer: D) Positive Coombs test

Explanation: Hydrops fetalis with severe anemia and nucleated RBCs suggests hemolytic disease of the newborn, most commonly due to Rh incompatibility. The mother would have a positive indirect Coombs test.

Question 28

A 44-year-old man has increasing malaise and swelling of his legs and abdomen for the past year. On exam there is lower leg pitting edema and an abdominal fluid wave. Laboratory studies show an AST of 240 and an ALT of 155 U/L. The total serum bilirubin is 2.4 mg/dL with direct bilirubin of 1.6 mg/dL. His serum alkaline phosphatase is 55 U/L. The serum albumin is 2.6 g/dL with total serum protein of 4.9 g/dL. The serum lipase is 72 U/L. Which of the following diseases is he most likely to have?

Options: A) Chronic pancreatitis
B) Gilbert disease
C) Chronic alcoholism
D) Acute viral hepatitis
E) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

Answer: C) Chronic alcoholism

Explanation: Chronic liver disease with ascites, edema, low albumin, elevated transaminases (AST > ALT ratio suggests alcoholic liver disease), and low alkaline phosphatase pattern indicates chronic alcoholic liver disease.

Question 30

A 20-year-old woman is involved in a motor vehicle accident and has multiple bone fractures. On arrival in the emergency department her blood pressure is normal, with no orthostatic hypotension. her hematocrit is 27.4% after receiving crystalloids. Her platelet count is 115,000/microliter. Her partial thromboplastin time is 22 seconds and prothrombin time 15 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment strategy for this woman?

Options: A) Transfuse 2 units of packed RBC's
B) Transfuse 10 units of platelets
C) Transfuse 1 unit of whole blood
D) Transfuse 10 units of fresh frozen plasma
E) Not give a transfusion

Answer: E) Not give a transfusion

Explanation: Patient is hemodynamically stable with normal vital signs, hematocrit >25% (acceptable for young healthy patient), normal coagulation studies, and adequate platelet count. No immediate transfusion needed.

Title: Medical Bacteriology and Entomology
Content:
Medical Bacteriology and Entomology Quiz

Mount Kenya University - MBMM 3300

Question 1

A 22-year-old woman who works in a plant nursery presents with a history of fever and cough for 2 months. Over this period she has lost 5 kg. Chest radiography shows bilateral upper lobe infiltrates with cavities. A stain of her sputum shows acid-fast bacilli. The likely means by which the patient acquired her infection is:

A) Sexual activity
B) Ingesting the microorganisms in her food
C) Holding onto contaminated hand rails when she takes public transportation
D) Handling potting soil
E) Breathing aerosolized droplets containing the microorganism

Answer: E) Breathing aerosolized droplets containing the microorganism

Explanation: The clinical presentation (chronic cough, weight loss, bilateral upper lobe cavities, acid-fast bacilli in sputum) is classic for pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. TB is primarily transmitted through airborne droplets when infected individuals cough or sneeze.

Question 2

During a pandemic, 175 airline passengers flew from Lima, Peru, to Los Angeles. Lunch included crab salad eaten by two-thirds of passengers. Two passengers who stayed in Los Angeles developed severe watery diarrhea. The likely cause of the diarrhea is:

A) Escherichia coli O157:H7
B) Vibrio cholerae type O139
C) Shigella dysenteriae type 1
D) Campylobacter jejuni
E) Entamoeba histolytica

Answer: B) Vibrio cholerae type O139

Explanation: The severe watery diarrhea following consumption of seafood (crab salad) from Peru during a pandemic outbreak is characteristic of cholera. Vibrio cholerae is commonly associated with contaminated seafood and causes profuse watery diarrhea.

Question 3

A 65-year-old woman with a long-term central venous catheter develops fever and multiple blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus epidermidis. A biofilm is thought to be present on the catheter. Which statement about such an infection is correct?

A) The biofilm containing S. epidermidis is likely to wash off the catheter
B) Production of extracellular polysaccharide inhibits growth of S. epidermidis
C) The S. epidermidis in the biofilm are more susceptible to antimicrobial therapy
D) The quorum-sensing ability results in increased susceptibility to antimicrobial therapy
E) The complex molecular interactions within the biofilm make it difficult to provide effective antimicrobial therapy, and the catheter will likely need to be removed

Answer: E) The complex molecular interactions within the biofilm make it difficult to provide effective antimicrobial therapy, and the catheter will likely need to be removed
