Flail Chest: Multiple rib fractures creating an unstable chest wall segment that moves paradoxically, causing severe respiratory compromise and underlying pulmonary contusion.

2. State five (5) cytomorphologic features of malignant cells.

Nuclear Pleomorphism: Marked variation in nuclear size, shape, and staining characteristics within the cell population.

Increased Nuclear-to-Cytoplasmic Ratio: Enlarged nuclei relative to cytoplasmic volume, reflecting increased metabolic activity and DNA content.

Nuclear Hyperchromasia: Intensely staining, dark nuclei due to increased chromatin content and altered chromatin distribution pattern.

Prominent Nucleoli: Enlarged, irregular, and multiple nucleoli reflecting increased protein synthesis and ribosomal RNA production.

Abnormal Mitotic Figures: Increased mitotic activity with atypical, tripolar, or other abnormal mitotic configurations indicating genomic instability.

3. Outline the mediators of chronic inflammation and list their principal actions.

Interferon-γ (IFN-γ):

  • Activates macrophages enhancing their antimicrobial and antitumor activity
  • Promotes T-helper 1 (Th1) immune responses
  • Stimulates MHC class II expression on antigen-presenting cells

Interleukin-1 (IL-1):

  • Promotes T-lymphocyte activation and proliferation
  • Stimulates acute phase protein synthesis
  • Causes fever by acting on hypothalamic temperature regulation centers

Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α):

  • Activates endothelial cells and neutrophils
  • Promotes apoptosis in tumor cells and infected cells
  • Stimulates angiogenesis and tissue remodeling

Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β):

  • Promotes fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
  • Regulates angiogenesis and tissue remodeling
  • Has immunosuppressive effects on T-lymphocytes

Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF):

  • Stimulates fibroblast and smooth muscle cell proliferation
  • Promotes angiogenesis and wound healing
  • Attracts inflammatory cells to sites of injury

4. Briefly describe wound healing under granulation tissue formation and scar formation.

Granulation Tissue Formation: Granulation tissue represents the proliferative phase of wound healing, typically appearing 3-5 days after injury. It consists of proliferating fibroblasts, new capillary formation (angiogenesis), and inflammatory cells embedded in a loose extracellular matrix.

Characteristics:

  • Bright red, granular appearance grossly
  • Rich capillary network providing nutrients and oxygen
  • Active collagen synthesis by fibroblasts
  • Macrophages clearing debris and coordinating repair
  • Provides scaffold for epithelialization

Scar Formation (Maturation Phase): Beginning around day 21 and continuing for months to years, scar formation involves collagen remodeling and tissue reorganization.

Process:

  • Type III collagen is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen
  • Collagen fibers undergo cross-linking and realignment
  • Excess cells and blood vessels are removed
  • Tissue strength increases progressively
  • Final scar tissue has reduced cellularity and vascularity

5. Briefly outline the TNM classification of tumours.

The TNM system is an internationally standardized method for staging malignant tumors based on three key parameters:

T (Primary Tumor):

  • T0: No evidence of primary tumor
  • Tis: Carcinoma in situ
  • T1-T4: Increasing size and/or local extent of primary tumor
  • TX: Primary tumor cannot be assessed

N (Regional Lymph Nodes):

  • N0: No regional lymph node metastasis
  • N1-N3: Increasing involvement of regional lymph nodes
  • NX: Regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed

M (Distant Metastasis):

  • M0: No distant metastasis
  • M1: Distant metastasis present
  • MX: Distant metastasis cannot be assessed

Stage Grouping: TNM parameters are combined to assign overall stages (I-IV), with Stage I being early disease and Stage IV representing advanced disease with distant metastases.

6. Write short notes on Amyloidosis.

Definition: Amyloidosis is a group of diseases characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in a characteristic β-pleated sheet fibrillar configuration.

Types: AL Amyloidosis (Primary): Derived from immunoglobulin light chains, associated with plasma cell disorders including multiple myeloma.

AA Amyloidosis (Secondary): Derived from serum amyloid A protein, occurs secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Hereditary Amyloidosis: Various genetic mutations causing protein misfolding, including familial amyloid polyneuropathy and familial Mediterranean fever.

Morphology:

  • Amorphous, eosinophilic extracellular deposits in tissues
  • Characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light with Congo red staining
  • Electron microscopy shows non-branching fibrils 8-10 nm in diameter

Clinical Effects: Organ dysfunction depends on distribution - cardiac involvement causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, renal involvement leads to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, and neurologic involvement causes peripheral neuropathy.

SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS

1. Describe the vascular and cellular events of the acute inflammatory response. (10 Marks)

Definition: Acute inflammation is the immediate and early response to injurious agents, characterized by vascular changes, cellular recruitment, and molecular mediator release aimed at eliminating harmful stimuli and initiating repair.

Vascular Events:

Vasodilation:

  • Brief initial vasoconstriction (seconds) followed by sustained vasodilation
  • Affects arterioles and venules primarily
  • Mediated by histamine, prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2), and nitric oxide
  • Results in increased blood flow, tissue warmth, and redness

Increased Vascular Permeability: Immediate Response (0-30 minutes): Histamine and leukotrienes cause endothelial cell contraction, creating intercellular gaps that allow plasma protein extravasation.

Delayed Response (2-12 hours): Direct endothelial damage from severe injury, toxins, burns, or complement activation leads to prolonged leakage.

Hemodynamic Changes:

  • Initial increased blood flow followed by stasis as plasma extravasates
  • Hemoconcentration increases blood viscosity
  • Margination of leukocytes along vessel walls due to altered flow dynamics

Cellular Events:

Neutrophil Recruitment (Sequential Process):

Margination and Rolling: Decreased axial flow allows neutrophils to move toward vessel walls. Selectins (P-selectin, E-selectin) on activated endothelium bind to neutrophil ligands, creating rolling interactions.

Adhesion: Firm adhesion mediated by β2 integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1) on neutrophils binding to ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 on activated endothelium.

Transmigration (Diapedesis): Neutrophils migrate between endothelial cells through intercellular junctions, facilitated by PECAM-1 and other junctional molecules.

Chemotaxis: Directional migration toward injury site guided by chemoattractant gradients (C5a, LTB4, bacterial products).

Neutrophil Functions:

  • Phagocytosis of pathogens and debris
  • Degranulation releasing antimicrobial substances
  • Generation of reactive oxygen species (respiratory burst)
  • Formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)

Molecular Mediators: Cell-derived: Histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, platelet-activating factor Plasma-derived: Complement system, coagulation cascade, kinin system

Outcomes: Complete resolution, healing by scarring, chronic inflammation, or abscess formation.

2. Briefly discuss the aetiology, pathogenesis and morphologic features of atherosclerosis. (20 Marks)

Definition: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium-sized arteries characterized by the formation of atherosclerotic plaques (atheromas) in the vessel wall, leading to vessel narrowing and potential complications.

Aetiology:

Major Risk Factors: Hyperlipidemia: Elevated LDL cholesterol is the most important modifiable risk factor. Oxidized LDL plays a crucial role in atherogenesis.

Hypertension: Increased blood pressure causes endothelial dysfunction and promotes plaque formation, particularly at arterial bifurcations.

Diabetes Mellitus: Hyperglycemia causes advanced glycation end products, promoting inflammation and accelerated atherosclerosis.

Smoking: Tobacco products cause endothelial toxicity, promote thrombosis, and increase oxidative stress.

Non-modifiable Risk Factors:

  • Age and male gender
  • Genetic factors and family history
  • Postmenopausal status in women

Additional Risk Factors:

  • Physical inactivity and obesity
  • Chronic inflammatory conditions
  • Elevated homocysteine levels
  • Metabolic syndrome

Pathogenesis:

Response-to-Injury Hypothesis: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial injury and dysfunction, leading to a chronic inflammatory response in the arterial wall.

Initial Events: Endothelial Dysfunction: Risk factors cause endothelial activation, increased permeability, and loss of anticoagulant properties. This allows LDL cholesterol infiltration into the subendothelial space.

LDL Oxidation: Infiltrated LDL undergoes oxidation within the arterial wall, becoming highly atherogenic and triggering inflammatory responses.

Inflammatory Cell Recruitment:

  • Oxidized LDL stimulates endothelial expression of adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, ICAM-1)
  • Monocytes adhere to activated endothelium and migrate into the intima
  • Monocytes differentiate into macrophages under influence of M-CSF

Foam Cell Formation:

  • Macrophages express scavenger receptors that internalize oxidized LDL
  • Unlike normal LDL receptors, scavenger receptors are not downregulated
  • Continued uptake leads to lipid accumulation and foam cell formation

Plaque Development: Fatty Streak Formation: Earliest lesion consisting of subendothelial accumulation of foam cells and T-lymphocytes. These lesions are reversible and may be present in children.

Intermediate Lesions: Progressive accumulation of foam cells, smooth muscle cell migration from media to intima, and extracellular lipid deposition.

Advanced Atheroma: Mature plaques with well-defined fibrous caps overlying lipid-rich necrotic cores containing cholesterol crystals, foam cells, and inflammatory cells.

Smooth Muscle Cell Role:

  • Migration from media to intima stimulated by PDGF, FGF, and other growth factors
  • Proliferation and matrix synthesis contributing to fibrous cap formation
  • Phenotypic modulation from contractile to synthetic phenotype

Plaque Progression and Complications: Calcification: Dystrophic calcification occurs in advanced plaques, contributing to plaque stability but reducing vessel compliance.

Plaque Rupture: Vulnerable plaques with thin fibrous caps and large lipid cores are prone to rupture, exposing thrombogenic material.

Thrombosis: Plaque rupture triggers platelet aggregation and coagulation cascade activation, leading to acute vessel occlusion.

Morphologic Features:

Gross Pathology: Early Lesions: Fatty streaks appear as yellow, slightly raised intimal patches, most commonly at arterial bifurcations and branch points.

Advanced Lesions: Raised, firm, white-to-yellow plaques that may be circumferential or eccentric, causing significant luminal narrowing.

Complicated Lesions: Show ulceration, hemorrhage, calcification, or thrombosis. May present as total vessel occlusion.

Microscopic Features: Fibrous Cap: Composed of smooth muscle cells and dense collagen matrix, overlying the necrotic core. Cap thickness determines plaque stability.

Necrotic Core: Central area containing cholesterol crystals, foam cells, extracellular lipid, inflammatory cells, and cellular debris.

Inflammatory Infiltrate: Macrophages, T-lymphocytes, and occasional B-cells and neutrophils, particularly at plaque shoulders (junction of plaque with normal vessel wall).

Calcification: Dystrophic calcification may be punctate or extensive, sometimes forming "pipe-stem" rigidity in heavily affected vessels.

Neovascularization: Formation of new blood vessels within plaques, which may contribute to plaque progression and instability through intraplaque hemorrhage.

Distribution: Atherosclerosis preferentially affects:

  • Aorta (especially abdominal)
  • Coronary arteries
  • Carotid and cerebral arteries
  • Peripheral arteries (especially lower extremities)
  • Renal arteries

Clinical Complications:

  • Myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death
  • Stroke and transient ischemic attacks
  • Peripheral arterial disease
  • Abdominal aortic aneurysms
  • Renovascular hypertension

Natural History: Atherosclerosis is a progressive disease that begins in childhood and typically becomes clinically apparent in middle age, though the rate of progression varies significantly based on risk factor burden and genetic susceptibility.

Title: ONCOPATHOLOGY - MCQs WITH EXPLANATIONS
Content:
1. Cell Cycle Regulation

Q1. A cancer cell line shows hyperphosphorylated RB protein throughout the cell cycle, even in the absence of growth factors. Which of the following is the MOST likely underlying mechanism?

A) Loss of p53 function

B) Overexpression of cyclin D-CDK4 complex

C) Mutation in E2F transcription factor

D) Defective DNA damage checkpoints

E) Loss of p21 expression

Answer: B) Overexpression of cyclin D-CDK4 complex

Explanation: Hyperphosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing S-phase entry. The cyclin D-CDK4 complex is specifically responsible for RB phosphorylation. Overexpression would lead to constitutive RB phosphorylation regardless of growth signals, making cells growth factor-independent.

Q2. In normal cells, what happens immediately after RB protein becomes hyperphosphorylated?

A) Cell cycle arrest at G1/S checkpoint

B) Activation of p53-mediated apoptosis

C) Release of E2F transcription factor

D) Degradation of cyclin D

E) Activation of DNA repair mechanisms

Answer: C) Release of E2F transcription factor

Explanation: Hyperphosphorylated RB dissociates from the RB-E2F complex, releasing E2F. Free E2F then transcribes genes necessary for S-phase progression, including cyclins E and A, and DNA polymerases.

Q3. A patient's tumor shows complete loss of p16INK4a expression due to promoter hypermethylation. Which cell cycle transition would be MOST directly affected?

A) G0 to G1 transition

B) G1 to S transition

C) S to G2 transition

D) G2 to M transition

E) M to G1 transition

Answer: B) G1 to S transition

Explanation: p16INK4a normally competes with cyclin D for CDK4 binding, preventing RB phosphorylation. Loss of p16 allows uncontrolled cyclin D-CDK4 activity, leading to premature RB phosphorylation and unregulated G1/S transition.

Q4. Which of the following statements about the G1/S restriction point is MOST accurate?

A) It is primarily controlled by p53 activation

B) Once cells pass this point, they are committed to complete the cell cycle

C) It occurs after DNA replication has begun

D) Cyclin B-CDK1 is the primary regulator at this checkpoint

E) It can be bypassed without affecting cell viability

Answer: B) Once cells pass this point, they are committed to complete the cell cycle

Explanation: The G1/S restriction point (controlled by cyclin E-CDK2) is the "point of no return." Once cells pass this checkpoint, they are committed to completing S, G2, and M phases regardless of external growth signals.

Q5. A tumor sample shows high levels of cyclin D1 but normal levels of CDK4. The cells still show uncontrolled proliferation. What is the MOST likely explanation?

A) The CDK4 has gained kinase activity

B) There is concurrent loss of p16INK4a

C) The RB protein is mutated

D) p21 levels are elevated

E) E2F is constitutively active

Answer: B) There is concurrent loss of p16INK4a

Explanation: Even with normal CDK4 levels, high cyclin D1 can drive proliferation if p16INK4a (which competes with cyclin D for CDK4 binding) is lost. This is a common dual hit in cancer - cyclin D1 amplification plus p16 loss.

Q6. In cells exposed to DNA damage, which sequence of events occurs FIRST?

A) p21 transcription → CDK inhibition → cell cycle arrest

B) p53 phosphorylation → p53 stabilization → p21 activation

C) Apoptosis activation → caspase cascade → cell death

D) RB dephosphorylation → E2F sequestration → S-phase block

E) DNA repair protein recruitment → damage resolution

Answer: B) p53 phosphorylation → p53 stabilization → p21 activation

Explanation: DNA damage triggers immediate p53 phosphorylation and stabilization (preventing MDM2-mediated degradation). Stabilized p53 then acts as a transcription factor to upregulate p21, which subsequently inhibits CDKs and arrests the cell cycle.

2. Cyclins and CDK Inhibitors

Q7. A cancer cell line has a deletion in the gene encoding p27. Which of the following would be the PRIMARY consequence?

A) Inability to exit from G0 phase

B) Defective G2/M checkpoint

C) Accelerated G1/S transition

D) Impaired DNA repair

E) Enhanced apoptosis sensitivity

Answer: C) Accelerated G1/S transition

Explanation: p27 is a CDK inhibitor that normally restrains cyclin E-CDK2 and cyclin A-CDK2 complexes. Loss of p27 removes this brake, allowing accelerated progression through G1/S transition even in suboptimal growth conditions.

Q8. Which cyclin-CDK complex is responsible for the breakdown of the nuclear membrane during mitosis?

A) Cyclin D-CDK4

B) Cyclin E-CDK2

C) Cyclin A-CDK2

D) Cyclin B-CDK1

E) Cyclin D-CDK6

Answer: D) Cyclin B-CDK1

Explanation: Cyclin B-CDK1 (also called MPF - Maturation Promoting Factor) is activated by protein phosphatase at the G2/M transition and directly causes nuclear membrane breakdown and initiation of mitosis.

Q9. A pharmaceutical company develops a drug that specifically prevents cyclin E degradation. What would be the MOST likely cellular effect?

A) Permanent G1 arrest

B) Prolonged S phase

C) Enhanced G2/M checkpoint

D) Increased apoptosis

E) Accelerated mitosis

Answer: B) Prolonged S phase

Explanation: Cyclin E normally degrades after the G1/S transition to allow proper S-phase progression. Persistent cyclin E would maintain CDK2 activity throughout S phase, disrupting normal replication timing and potentially causing replication fork problems.

Q10. In which phase of the cell cycle would you expect to find the HIGHEST levels of cyclin A?

A) Early G1

B) Late G1

C) S phase and early mitosis

D) Late mitosis

E) G0 phase

Answer: C) S phase and early mitosis

Explanation: Cyclin A peaks during S phase (where it partners with CDK2 for replication) and continues into early mitosis (where it helps regulate mitotic prophase events). It's degraded before metaphase to allow proper mitotic progression.

3. Oncogenes and Growth Signaling

Q11. A lung cancer patient has a tumor with a point mutation in codon 12 of the KRAS gene. Which statement BEST describes the functional consequence?

A) RAS protein becomes permanently GDP-bound

B) RAS protein loses its GTPase activity

C) RAS protein cannot bind to downstream effectors

D) RAS protein is targeted for degradation

E) RAS protein becomes nuclear-localized

Answer: B) RAS protein loses its GTPase activity

Explanation: Codon 12 mutations in RAS (most common oncogenic mutation) impair the intrinsic and GAP-stimulated GTPase activity, keeping RAS in the active GTP-bound state. This leads to continuous growth signaling downstream.

Q12. Which of the following oncoproteins is MOST likely to be found in the nucleus of transformed cells?

A) Mutant RAS

B) BCR-ABL fusion protein

C) Overexpressed EGFR

D) MYC protein

E) Cyclin D1

Answer: D) MYC protein

Explanation: MYC is a transcription factor that functions in the nucleus to regulate genes controlling cell proliferation, protein synthesis, and apoptosis. While cyclin D1 can also be nuclear, MYC is the classic nuclear oncoprotein from the given options.

Q13. A breast cancer shows HER2 gene amplification but the patient doesn't respond to trastuzumab therapy. Which mechanism is MOST likely responsible for this resistance?

A) Loss of p53 function

B) Concurrent PIK3CA mutation

C) High expression of cyclin D1

D) Loss of estrogen receptors

E) Defective DNA repair mechanisms

Answer: B) Concurrent PIK3CA mutation

Explanation: PIK3CA mutations activate the PI3K/AKT pathway downstream of HER2, providing alternative survival signals that bypass HER2 inhibition. This is a well-documented mechanism of trastuzumab resistance.

Q14. In the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)], the breakpoint occurs within which genes?

A) BCR and RAS

B) ABL and MYC

C) BCR and ABL

D) ABL and BCL2

E) BCR and EGFR

Answer: C) BCR and ABL

Explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome results from translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, creating a BCR-ABL fusion gene. The BCR portion provides dimerization domains while ABL contributes constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.

Q15. Which statement about autocrine growth stimulation in cancer is MOST accurate?

A) It only occurs with growth factor receptor mutations

B) Cancer cells produce growth factors for which they lack receptors

C) It requires loss of tumor suppressor genes

D) Cancer cells produce growth factors to which they can respond

E) It is only seen in hematologic malignancies

Answer: D) Cancer cells produce growth factors to which they can respond

Explanation: Autocrine stimulation occurs when cancer cells produce growth factors (like PDGF, TGF-α) for which they have functional receptors, creating a self-stimulating loop that bypasses normal growth controls.

4. Cell Cycle Checkpoints and DNA Damage

Q16. A cell line with mutated p53 is exposed to high-dose radiation. Compared to normal cells, these cells would MOST likely:

A) Undergo immediate apoptosis

B) Show enhanced DNA repair

C) Continue proliferating with damaged DNA

D) Arrest permanently in G1

E) Activate alternative tumor suppressors

Answer: C) Continue proliferating with damaged DNA

Explanation: p53 is the "guardian of the genome." Without functional p53, cells cannot properly respond to DNA damage - they fail to arrest for repair and don't undergo apoptosis, leading to replication of damaged DNA and genomic instability.

Q17. The G2/M checkpoint is MOST important for preventing which outcome?

A) DNA replication errors

B) Chromosomal instability

C) Oncogene activation

D) Tumor suppressor loss

E) Growth factor independence

Answer: B) Chromosomal instability

Explanation: The G2/M checkpoint ensures complete DNA replication and checks for DNA damage before mitosis. Failure of this checkpoint leads to mitosis with incompletely replicated or damaged DNA, resulting in chromosomal instability and aneuploidy.

Q18. Which protein acts as the PRIMARY sensor of DNA double-strand breaks?

A) p53

B) ATM kinase

C) p21

D) BRCA1

E) MDM2

Answer: B) ATM kinase

Explanation: ATM (Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated) is recruited to DNA double-strand breaks and acts as the primary sensor. It then phosphorylates p53, leading to cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. ATM deficiency causes extreme radiation sensitivity.

Q19. A tumor suppressor gene is found to be silenced by promoter hypermethylation in 70% of colorectal cancers. This gene most likely encodes:

A) A growth factor receptor

B) A DNA repair enzyme

C) A cyclin protein

D) A CDK inhibitor

E) An oncogene activator

Answer: D) A CDK inhibitor

Explanation: This describes p16INK4a, which is frequently silenced by hypermethylation in many cancers including colorectal cancer. CDK inhibitors act as tumor suppressors, and their epigenetic silencing is a common mechanism of inactivation.

Q20. If a cell has defective spindle checkpoint machinery, what is the MOST likely outcome?

A) G1/S arrest

B) Apoptosis activation

C) Aneuploidy

D) DNA repair activation

E) Growth factor independence

Answer: C) Aneuploidy

Explanation: The spindle checkpoint (part of M phase) ensures proper chromosome attachment to spindle fibers before anaphase. Defective spindle checkpoints allow chromosome missegregation, leading to aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome numbers).

5. Integration and Clinical Applications

Q21. A cancer therapeutic strategy involves using CDK4/6 inhibitors. These drugs would be MOST effective against tumors with which characteristic?

A) p53 mutations

B) RAS activation

C) Functional RB pathway

D) EGFR overexpression

E) BCR-ABL fusion

Answer: C) Functional RB pathway

Explanation: CDK4/6 inhibitors work by preventing RB phosphorylation, keeping RB active to sequester E2F. This only works if the RB protein itself is functional. Tumors with RB mutations would be resistant to CDK4/6 inhibitors.

Q22. Which combination of alterations would be MOST likely to result in aggressive tumor behavior?

A) p53 mutation + RB loss

B) MYC amplification + p16 loss

C) EGFR overexpression + KRAS mutation

D) Cyclin D1 amplification + CDK4 mutation

E) BCR-ABL fusion + p21 overexpression

Answer: B) MYC amplification + p16 loss

Explanation: This combination provides both growth promotion (MYC drives proliferation, protein synthesis, angiogenesis) and removes growth restraint (p16 loss removes CDK4 inhibition). This dual hit is seen in many aggressive cancers.

Q23. A patient's tumor shows loss of both p53 and RB function. This tumor would be MOST resistant to which therapeutic approach?

A) DNA-damaging chemotherapy

B) Growth factor receptor inhibitors

C) Anti-angiogenic therapy

D) Immunotherapy

E) Targeted kinase inhibitors

Answer: A) DNA-damaging chemotherapy

Explanation: DNA-damaging agents rely on p53-mediated apoptosis for efficacy. Without p53 and RB (both key for DNA damage response and apoptosis), the tumor cannot respond properly to DNA damage, making it resistant to conventional chemotherapy.

Q24. In a research setting, cells are transfected with a constitutively active form of E2F. What would be the MOST predictable result?

A) G1 arrest due to checkpoint activation

B) Immediate entry into S phase

C) Enhanced apoptosis sensitivity

D) Decreased DNA synthesis

E) Loss of growth factor dependence

Answer: B) Immediate entry into S phase

Explanation: E2F is the master regulator of S-phase entry. Constitutively active E2F would bypass normal RB control, immediately transcribing S-phase genes (cyclins E and A, DNA polymerases) and driving cells into DNA synthesis.

Q25. Which statement about the relationship between cyclins and cancer is MOST accurate?

A) All cyclins act as tumor suppressors

B) Cyclin mutations are more common than cyclin overexpression

C) Cyclin D1 is the most frequently altered cyclin in human cancers

D) Cyclins cannot be therapeutic targets

E) Cyclin alterations only affect cell cycle timing

Answer: C) Cyclin D1 is the most frequently altered cyclin in human cancers

Explanation: Cyclin D1 is amplified in multiple cancer types (breast, esophageal, head/neck) and is the most clinically relevant cyclin alteration. It drives early cell cycle progression and bypasses normal growth controls.

6. Advanced Concepts and Mechanisms

Q26. A novel cancer drug specifically targets cells in S-phase. Which biomarker would be MOST useful for predicting response to this therapy?

A) p53 expression levels

B) Ki-67 proliferation index

C) Cyclin D1 amplification

D) RB phosphorylation status

E) EGFR expression levels

Answer: B) Ki-67 proliferation index

Explanation: Ki-67 is expressed in all active phases of the cell cycle (G1, S, G2, M) but not in G0. A high Ki-67 index indicates a high proliferation rate, meaning more cells are cycling and would be susceptible to S-phase targeting drugs.

Q27. Which mechanism would MOST likely lead to simultaneous activation of multiple oncogenes?

A) Point mutation in a single gene

B) Chromosomal amplification of a region

C) Viral integration near an oncogene

D) Loss of a tumor suppressor gene

E) Hypermethylation of gene promoters

Answer: B) Chromosomal amplification of a region

Explanation: Amplification of chromosomal regions (amplicons) can simultaneously increase copy numbers of multiple genes within that region, potentially activating several oncogenes at once. This is seen in many cancers and contributes to aggressive behavior.

Q28. A tumor shows high expression of both cyclin D1 and CDK4, but cells still respond normally to growth inhibitory signals. What is the MOST likely explanation?

A) The tumor has intact p16INK4a

B) RB protein is mutated

C) p21 levels are very low

D) E2F is constitutively active

E) DNA damage checkpoints are defective

Answer: A) The tumor has intact p16INK4a

Explanation: Despite high cyclin D1 and CDK4, intact p16INK4a can still compete for CDK4 binding and maintain some growth control. The tumor likely represents an early stage where oncogene activation hasn't yet been coupled with tumor suppressor loss.

Q29. Which alteration would make a cancer cell MOST dependent on continued oncogene expression for survival?

A) Loss of p53 function only

B) RB pathway inactivation only

C) Simultaneous MYC amplification and p53 loss

D) EGFR overexpression alone

E) p16 methylation only

Answer: C) Simultaneous MYC amplification and p53 loss

Explanation: This represents "oncogene addiction." MYC drives proliferation but also promotes apoptosis. p53 loss prevents the apoptosis, making cells absolutely dependent on continued MYC expression for survival. This creates a therapeutic vulnerability.

Q30. In analyzing a tumor's molecular profile, which finding would MOST strongly suggest defective DNA damage checkpoints?

A) High mutation rate throughout the genome

B) Overexpression of a single oncogene

C) Loss of a single tumor suppressor

D) Amplification of growth factor receptors

E) Activation of angiogenic pathways

Answer: A) High mutation rate throughout the genome

Explanation: Defective DNA damage checkpoints (usually from p53 loss or ATM deficiency) lead to genomic instability and accumulation of mutations throughout the genome. This "mutator phenotype" is a hallmark of checkpoint deficiency and creates the molecular signature of widespread genetic alterations.

Title: VITAL SIGNS ASSESSMENT
Content:
INTRODUCTION

Vital signs are objective measurements of the body's most basic physiological functions. They serve as indicators of health status, disease progression, and response to treatment. The six cardinal vital signs include: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respirations (R), Blood Pressure (BP), Oxygen Saturation (SpO2)- Not nessesarily a vital sign, and Pain.

1. BLOOD PRESSURE (BP)

Definition & Physiology

Blood pressure is the force exerted by circulating blood against arterial walls. It reflects cardiac output, peripheral vascular resistance, and blood volume.

Classification (American Heart Association Guidelines)

Pediatric Normal Values

  • Newborn: 65-95/30-60 mmHg
  • Infant (1-12 months): 80-100/55-65 mmHg
  • Toddler (1-2 years): 90-105/55-70 mmHg
  • Preschool (3-5 years): 95-110/60-75 mmHg
  • School age (6-12 years): 100-120/60-80 mmHg
  • Adolescent (13+ years): Adult values

Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)

Formula: MAP = Diastolic BP + 1/3(Systolic BP - Diastolic BP)

Clinical Significance:

  • Normal Range: 70-100 mmHg
  • Minimum for organ perfusion: 60 mmHg
  • Optimal for critically ill: 65-70 mmHg
  • Used to assess perfusion pressure to vital organs

Example Calculation: BP 120/80 → MAP = 80 + 1/3(120-80) = 80 + 13.3 = 93.3 mmHg

Assessment Technique

Equipment: Appropriately sized cuff, stethoscope, sphygmomanometer

Procedure:

  1. Patient seated/lying, arm at heart level
  2. Cuff covers 80% of arm circumference
  3. Palpate brachial artery, place cuff 2-3 cm above
  4. Inflate 20-30 mmHg above palpated systolic pressure
  5. Deflate at 2-3 mmHg/second
  6. Note first Korotkoff sound (systolic) and disappearance (diastolic)

Special Populations:

  • Elderly: May have pseudohypertension due to arterial stiffening
  • Pregnancy: Use appropriate pregnancy-specific values
  • Pediatric: Use age-appropriate cuff sizes and percentile charts

Factors Affecting Blood Pressure

Physiological:

  • Age, gender, race/ethnicity
  • Circadian rhythm (lower at night)
  • Physical activity, stress, pain
  • Body position, bladder fullness

Pathological:

  • Cardiovascular disease
  • Renal disease
  • Endocrine disorders
  • Medications

Hypertension Management

Non-Pharmacological (DASH Diet Approach):

  • Dietary: Reduce sodium (<2300mg/day), increase potassium
  • Weight: Maintain BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m²
  • Exercise: 150 minutes moderate aerobic activity/week
  • Alcohol: Limit to 2 drinks/day (men), 1 drink/day (women)
  • Smoking: Complete cessation
  • Stress: Relaxation techniques, meditation

Pharmacological Classes:

  • ACE Inhibitors: Block angiotensin-converting enzyme
  • ARBs: Angiotensin receptor blockers
  • Beta-blockers: Reduce heart rate and contractility
  • Calcium Channel Blockers: Vasodilation
  • Diuretics: Reduce blood volume

Hypotension Causes & Management

Causes:

  • Volume depletion: Hemorrhage, dehydration, burns
  • Cardiac: Heart failure, arrhythmias, MI
  • Vascular: Sepsis, anaphylaxis, medications
  • Neurogenic: Spinal cord injury, autonomic dysfunction

Assessment: Monitor for orthostatic changes (drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic)

2. PULSE/HEART RATE

Definition & Physiology

Pulse represents the rhythmic expansion and contraction of arteries with each heartbeat. Heart rate reflects the number of cardiac contractions per minute.

Normal Values by Age

Pulse Assessment Parameters

Rate:

  • Bradycardia: <60 bpm (adults)
  • Normal: 60-100 bpm (adults)
  • Tachycardia: >100 bpm (adults)

Rhythm:

  • Regular: Equal intervals between beats
  • Irregular: Unequal intervals (may be regularly irregular or irregularly irregular)

Quality/Amplitude:

  • 0: Absent, not palpable
  • 1+: Weak, thready, easily obliterated
  • 2+: Normal, easily palpable
  • 3+: Strong, bounding
  • 4+: Very strong, bounding, not easily obliterated

Pulse Sites:

  • Temporal: Side of forehead
  • Carotid: Neck (assess one at a time)
  • Brachial: Antecubital fossa
  • Radial: Wrist (most common)
  • Femoral: Groin
  • Popliteal: Behind knee
  • Dorsalis pedis: Top of foot
  • Posterior tibial: Behind medial malleolus

Assessment Technique

  1. Use fingertips (not thumb) - index and middle fingers
  2. Apply gentle pressure
  3. Count for 15 seconds × 4 (if regular) or 60 seconds (if irregular)
  4. Note rate, rhythm, and quality
  5. Assess bilateral pulses for comparison

Factors Affecting Heart Rate

Physiological Increases:

  • Exercise, fever, stress, anxiety
  • Pain, caffeine, nicotine
  • Pregnancy, hyperthyroidism
  • Age (infants/children have higher rates)

Physiological Decreases:

  • Sleep, physical fitness
  • Hypothermia, increased intracranial pressure
  • Medications (beta-blockers, digoxin)

Pathological Causes:

  • Tachycardia: Shock, hemorrhage, heart failure, arrhythmias, hyperthyroidism, anemia
  • Bradycardia: Heart block, increased ICP, hypothyroidism, medications

3. BODY TEMPERATURE

Definition & Physiology

Body temperature reflects the balance between heat production and heat loss. Core temperature is regulated by the hypothalamus.

Normal Values by Site

Temperature Classifications

  • Hypothermia: <36°C (96.8°F)
  • Normal: 36-37.5°C (96.8-99.5°F)
  • Low-grade fever: 37.5-38.3°C (99.5-101°F)
  • Moderate fever: 38.3-40°C (101-104°F)
  • High fever: >40°C (>104°F)
  • Hyperthermia: >41°C (>106°F)

Assessment Methods

Oral:

  • Most common, convenient
  • Wait 15-30 minutes after eating/drinking hot/cold substances
  • Contraindicated: unconscious, mouth breathing, oral surgery

Rectal:

  • Most accurate core temperature
  • Gold standard for infants <3 months
  • Insert 1.5-2.5 cm in adults, 1.25 cm in children
  • Contraindicated: rectal disorders, neutropenia

Axillary:

  • Safest, least invasive
  • Less accurate, reads 0.5°C lower than core
  • Hold arm against body for 5-10 minutes

Tympanic (Infrared):

  • Quick, convenient
  • Must ensure proper ear canal alignment
  • May be affected by earwax, otitis media

Temporal Artery:

  • Non-invasive, quick
  • Accurate reflection of core temperature
  • Not affected by eating/drinking

Factors Affecting Temperature

Age:

  • Neonates: Immature thermoregulation, higher baseline
  • Elderly: Decreased response to temperature changes
  • Children: Higher metabolic rate, more labile

Physiological:

  • Circadian rhythm (lowest 4-6 AM, highest 4-8 PM)
  • Menstrual cycle (rises after ovulation)
  • Exercise, environmental temperature
  • Medications, alcohol consumption

Pathological:

  • Infection, inflammation
  • Metabolic disorders
  • CNS disorders affecting hypothalamus

Fever Management (WHO Pain Ladder Concept Applied)

Step 1 - Mild Fever (37.5-38.3°C):

  • Comfort measures, increased fluids
  • Light clothing, room temperature control

Step 2 - Moderate Fever (38.3-40°C):

  • Antipyretics: Acetaminophen, NSAIDs
  • Tepid sponging (avoid alcohol baths)

Step 3 - High Fever (>40°C):

  • Aggressive cooling measures
  • IV fluids, intensive monitoring
  • Identify and treat underlying cause

4. RESPIRATIONS

Definition & Physiology

Respiration involves gas exchange between the atmosphere and body tissues. Assessment includes external respiration (breathing) and internal respiration (cellular level).

Normal Respiratory Rates by Age

Assessment Parameters

Rate:

  • Bradypnea: <12 breaths/minute (adults)
  • Normal: 12-20 breaths/minute (adults)
  • Tachypnea: >20 breaths/minute (adults)

Rhythm:

  • Regular: Even intervals between breaths
  • Irregular: Uneven pattern
  • Periodic: Cycles of increasing/decreasing depth (Cheyne-Stokes)

Depth:

  • Shallow: Minimal chest movement
  • Normal: Full chest expansion
  • Deep: Exaggerated chest movement

Quality/Effort:

  • Effortless: No visible work of breathing
  • Labored: Use of accessory muscles, retractions
  • Orthopnea: Difficulty breathing lying flat

Abnormal Breathing Patterns

Apnea: Absence of breathing >15-20 seconds Cheyne-Stokes: Periods of increasing/decreasing depth followed by apnea Kussmaul: Deep, rapid respirations (diabetic ketoacidosis) Biot's: Irregular depth and rate with sudden apneic periods

Assessment Technique

  1. Observe without patient awareness (count while appearing to take pulse)
  2. Watch chest rise and fall
  3. Count for full 60 seconds (30 seconds × 2 if regular)
  4. Note rate, rhythm, depth, and effort
  5. Listen for abnormal sounds (stridor, wheeze)

Factors Affecting Respiration

Physiological:

  • Age, physical fitness, altitude
  • Exercise, anxiety, pain
  • Medications (opioids decrease rate)
  • Body position

Pathological:

  • Respiratory diseases (asthma, COPD, pneumonia)
  • Cardiac conditions (CHF, pulmonary edema)
  • Metabolic disorders (acidosis, alkalosis)
  • Neurological conditions affecting respiratory center

5. OXYGEN SATURATION (SpO2)

Definition & Physiology

Oxygen saturation measures the percentage of hemoglobin molecules carrying oxygen. Pulse oximetry provides non-invasive assessment of oxygenation status.

Normal Values

  • Normal: 95-100%
  • Acceptable for healthy adults: ≥95%
  • COPD patients: 88-92% may be acceptable
  • Critical threshold: <90%

Assessment Technique

Equipment: Pulse oximeter with appropriate sensor

Procedure:

  1. Select appropriate sensor (finger, ear, toe)
  2. Ensure clean, dry application site
  3. Remove nail polish if using finger sensor
  4. Allow stabilization (30-60 seconds)
  5. Note waveform quality and alarm settings

Optimal Sites:

  • Adults: Index finger, middle finger
  • Infants: Great toe, thumb
  • Alternative sites: Ear lobe, forehead, bridge of nose

Factors Affecting Accuracy

Patient Factors:

  • Poor peripheral circulation
  • Hypothermia, hypotension
  • Excessive motion, shivering
  • Dark nail polish, artificial nails
  • Severe anemia (Hgb <5 g/dL)

Environmental/Technical:

  • Ambient light interference
  • Electrical interference
  • Improper sensor placement
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning (gives falsely high readings)

Clinical Significance

  • ≥95%: Generally adequate oxygenation
  • 90-94%: Mild hypoxemia, may need supplemental O2
  • 85-89%: Moderate hypoxemia, supplemental O2 indicated
  • <85%: Severe hypoxemia, immediate intervention required

6. PAIN ASSESSMENT

Definition

Pain is a subjective, multidimensional experience involving sensory, emotional, and cognitive components. It's considered the "5th vital sign."

Pain Scales

Numeric Rating Scale (0-10):

  • 0 = No pain
  • 1-3 = Mild pain
  • 4-6 = Moderate pain
  • 7-10 = Severe pain

Wong-Baker FACES Scale:

  • For children >3 years and adults with communication difficulties
  • 6 faces ranging from smiling to crying

FLACC Scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability):

  • For non-verbal patients, children <3 years
  • Each category scored 0-2, total 0-10

Critical Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT):

  • For critically ill, intubated patients
  • Assesses facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, ventilator compliance

Pain Assessment Framework (PQRST)

  • Provocation/Palliation: What makes it better/worse?
  • Quality: Sharp, dull, burning, cramping?
  • Region/Radiation: Where is it? Does it spread?
  • Severity: Rate 0-10
  • Timing: When did it start? Constant or intermittent?

Types of Pain

By Duration:

  • Acute: <3-6 months, identifiable cause
  • Chronic: >3-6 months, may persist beyond healing

By Origin:

  • Nociceptive: From tissue damage (somatic or visceral)
  • Neuropathic: From nerve damage
  • Mixed: Combination of both types

Cultural Considerations

  • Pain expression varies among cultures
  • Some cultures encourage stoicism
  • Religious/spiritual beliefs affect pain perception
  • Language barriers may complicate assessment

COMPREHENSIVE VITAL SIGNS DOCUMENTATION

Essential Components

  1. Date and time of assessment
  2. All vital sign values with units
  3. Patient position during assessment
  4. Site used for temperature, BP cuff size
  5. Oxygen delivery method if applicable
  6. Pain location and characteristics
  7. Patient activity level before assessment
  8. Any abnormal findings or patient symptoms

Sample Documentation

"VS: T 98.6°F (oral), P 82 regular and strong (radial), R 18 even and unlabored, BP 128/82 (left arm, sitting, adult cuff), SpO2 97% on room air. Patient reports 3/10 dull aching pain in lower back, present for 2 hours, relieved with position change. Patient ambulatory, no distress noted."

Trending and Analysis

  • Look for patterns over time, not isolated values
  • Compensatory mechanisms: Tachycardia with hypotension may indicate shock
  • Early warning signs: Subtle changes may precede deterioration
  • Medication effects: Consider timing of medications affecting vital signs

Critical Values Requiring Immediate Intervention

  • Temperature: >38.5°C (101.3°F) or <36°C (96.8°F)
  • Heart Rate: <50 or >120 bpm (adults)
  • Respirations: <10 or >30 breaths/minute (adults)
  • Blood Pressure: Systolic <90 or >180, Diastolic >110 mmHg
  • SpO2: <90% or 4% decrease from baseline
  • Pain: Sudden onset severe pain (8-10/10) or significant change

Age-Specific Considerations

Neonates/Infants:

  • More frequent assessment required
  • Different normal ranges
  • Behavioral cues important for pain assessment
  • Temperature regulation immature

Elderly:

  • May have altered baseline values
  • Medications affect vital signs
  • Slower response to changes
  • Higher pain tolerance, may underreport

Pediatric:

  • Age-appropriate equipment and techniques
  • Involve parents/caregivers
  • Developmental considerations for pain assessment
  • Higher anxiety may affect readings

Quality Assurance

  • Calibration: Ensure equipment accuracy
  • Technique: Use proper methods consistently
  • Training: Maintain competency in assessment skills
  • Documentation: Complete, timely, accurate records

CLINICAL PEARLS FOR NURSING PRACTICE

  1. Always assess vital signs in context - one abnormal value doesn't tell the whole story
  2. Trust your instincts - if a patient "looks sick," investigate further regardless of vital signs
  3. Trending is key - watch for patterns and changes from baseline
  4. Consider the whole patient - age, medications, medical history, current symptoms
  5. When in doubt, recheck - ensure accuracy before reporting critical values
  6. Pain is subjective - believe the patient's report of pain intensity
  7. Early detection saves lives - subtle changes may be the first sign of deterioration

Remember: Vital signs are tools to guide clinical decision-making, not replace critical thinking and comprehensive patient assessment.

Title: Mount Kenya University Pathology Q&A
Content:
MBChB III
UNIT TITLE: PATHOLOGY CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT
DATE: JULY 2021
TIME: 3 HOURS

Complete Question & Answer Guide

MBCHB III - July 2021

🎯 SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS & ANSWERS

Question 1

Malignant neoplasms show all the following features EXCEPT:

  • a) Disorganized cell structure
  • b) Encapsulation
  • c) Invasion of local and distant tissues
  • d) Rapid, erratic growth

Answer: b) Encapsulation
Explanation: Malignant neoplasms are characteristically non-encapsulated with irregular borders that allow invasion into surrounding tissues. Benign tumors are typically encapsulated.

Question 2

ONE of the following cells have LEAST capacity for regeneration:

  • a) Cardiac muscle
  • b) Skeletal muscle
  • c) Neuronal cells
  • d) Liver cells

Answer: c) Neuronal cells
Explanation: Neurons are post-mitotic cells with virtually no regenerative capacity in adults. While cardiac muscle has limited regeneration, neuronal tissue regeneration is essentially absent.

Question 3

The following are mediators of inflammation EXCEPT:

  • a) Interferons
  • b) Prostaglandins
  • c) Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF)
  • d) Myeloperoxidase enzyme

Answer: d) Myeloperoxidase enzyme
Explanation: Myeloperoxidase is an antimicrobial enzyme found in neutrophils, not a mediator of inflammation. Interferons, prostaglandins, and TNF are key inflammatory mediators.

Question 4

Metaplasia refers to:

  • a) Irregular, atypical proliferative changes in epithelial or mesenchymal cells
  • b) Loss of cell substance producing shrinkage of the cells
  • c) Replacement of one type of adult cell by another type of adult cell
  • d) None of the above

Answer: c) Replacement of one type of adult cell by another type of adult cell
Explanation: Metaplasia is adaptive cellular substitution - typically replacement of specialized cells with more resistant cell types (e.g., respiratory epithelium → squamous epithelium in smokers).

Question 5

Metastatic calcification is associated with:

  • a) Dead or dying tissues
  • b) Atherosclerosis
  • c) Abnormal calcium metabolism
  • d) Damaged heart valves

Answer: c) Abnormal calcium metabolism
Explanation: Metastatic calcification occurs due to hypercalcemia from various causes (hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, vitamin D excess), unlike dystrophic calcification in damaged tissues.

Question 6

Which of these is an endogenous pigment:

  • a) Melanin
  • b) Coal
  • c) Tattooing
  • d) Lipid

Answer: a) Melanin
Explanation: Melanin is an endogenous pigment produced by melanocytes. Coal and tattoo pigments are exogenous, while lipid is not a pigment but can cause tissue discoloration.

Question 7

Phagocytes include the following EXCEPT:

  • a) Neutrophils
  • b) Macrophages
  • c) Osteoclasts
  • d) Lymphocytes

Answer: d) Lymphocytes
Explanation: Lymphocytes are adaptive immune cells primarily involved in specific immunity, not phagocytosis. Neutrophils, macrophages, and osteoclasts are all phagocytic cells.

Question 8

Which of these is the commonest cause of infectious granulomas:

  • a) Tuberculosis
  • b) Fungal infections
  • c) Viral infections
  • d) Toxins

Answer: a) Tuberculosis
Explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the most common cause of infectious granulomas worldwide, forming characteristic epithelioid granulomas with central caseation.

Question 9

The most common fixative used to preserve tissue in histopathology is:

  • a) 10% Formalin
  • b) Ethylene Glycol
  • c) Haematoxylin
  • d) 95% Ethanol

Answer: a) 10% Formalin
Explanation: 10% neutral buffered formalin is the gold standard fixative, providing excellent morphological preservation through cross-linking proteins via formaldehyde.

Question 10

The following are oncogenic viruses in humans EXCEPT:

  • a) Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)
  • b) Epstein Barr Virus (EBV)
  • c) Hepatitis B virus
  • d) Polio Virus

Answer: d) Polio Virus
Explanation: Polio virus is not oncogenic. HPV causes cervical cancer, EBV causes Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and Hepatitis B causes hepatocellular carcinoma.

Question 11

RB gene, 'the guardian of the genome' regulates the cell cycle at:

  • a) G1/S Checkpoint
  • b) G2 Checkpoint
  • c) G0 restriction checkpoint
  • d) Intra-S Checkpoint

Answer: a) G1/S Checkpoint
Explanation: The RB gene product (pRb) controls the G1/S checkpoint, preventing cells from entering S phase until appropriate growth signals are received.

Question 12

TP53 is regulated and scavenged after completing its action by:

  • a) CDKN1A
  • b) MDM2
  • c) RAS
  • d) E6

Answer: b) MDM2
Explanation: MDM2 is the primary negative regulator of p53, promoting its degradation through ubiquitination once p53 has completed its cellular functions.

Question 13

Mutations in the TGF-Beta signaling pathway involving SMAD molecules usually result in the following type of cancer:

  • a) Colon Cancer
  • b) Stomach Cancer
  • c) Lung Cancer
  • d) Pancreatic cancer

Answer: d) Pancreatic cancer
Explanation: TGF-β/SMAD pathway mutations are particularly common in pancreatic adenocarcinoma, where SMAD4 is frequently inactivated.

Question 14

The most commonly mutated oncoprotein in all tumors and a key participant in abnormal signal transduction pathways is:

  • a) APC
  • b) TP53
  • c) BRAF
  • d) RAS

Answer: d) RAS
Explanation: RAS proteins are mutated in approximately 30% of all human cancers, making them the most commonly mutated oncoproteins. They control cell proliferation and differentiation.

Question 15

The 'Warburg' effect in tumor cellular metabolism refers to:

  • a) Oxidative phosphorylation in tumor cells
  • b) Aerobic glycolysis in tumor cells
  • c) Mutations and defects in enzymes that regulate the Krebs cycle
  • d) Defective Mitochondrial ATP synthesis

Answer: b) Aerobic glycolysis in tumor cells
Explanation: The Warburg effect describes the preference of cancer cells for glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen, rather than the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation.

Question 16

A Granuloma is comprised of:

  • a) Fibroblasts and capillaries
  • b) Capillaries and giant cells
  • c) Endothelial cells and neutrophils
  • d) Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes

Answer: d) Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes
Explanation: Granulomas are organized collections of epithelioid cells (activated macrophages), surrounded by lymphocytes, often with central necrosis and giant cells.

Question 17

During autopsy ONE of the following is NOT the role of the medical officer:

  • a) Identify the decedent
  • b) Ascertain the cause of death
  • c) Document evidence
  • d) Request for autopsy

Answer: d) Request for autopsy
Explanation: Medical officers perform autopsies but do not request them. Autopsy requests typically come from coroners, legal authorities, or family members.

Question 18

The postmortem interval can be estimated using the below EXCEPT:

  • a) Rigor Mortis
  • b) Algor Mortis
  • c) Mummification
  • d) Cadaveric spasms

Answer: d) Cadaveric spasms
Explanation: Cadaveric spasms occur at the moment of death and persist, but don't help estimate time since death. Rigor mortis, algor mortis, and mummification are time-dependent postmortem changes.

Question 19

Exhumation of human remains in Kenya may ONLY proceed on the authority of:

  • a) Valid Court Orders
  • b) The National Police Service
  • c) The Chief Government Pathologist
  • d) The Medical Superintendent

Answer: a) Valid Court Orders
Explanation: Exhumation is a legal procedure requiring judicial authorization through valid court orders to ensure proper legal oversight and protect human dignity.

Question 20

The following are chemical mediators of acute inflammation EXCEPT:

  • a) Leukotrienes
  • b) Complement proteins
  • c) Interleukins
  • d) Hormones

Answer: d) Hormones
Explanation: While some hormones can modulate inflammation, they are not considered primary chemical mediators. Leukotrienes, complement proteins, and interleukins are key inflammatory mediators.

Question 21

The characteristic cells of chronic inflammation are all EXCEPT:

  • a) Plasma cells
  • b) Macrophages
  • c) Lymphocytes
  • d) Polymorphonuclear Cells (PMNs)

Answer: d) Polymorphonuclear Cells (PMNs)
Explanation: PMNs (neutrophils) are characteristic of acute inflammation. Chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

Question 22

Which of the following is TRUE regarding the pathologic assessment of tumours:

  • a) Grading is the degree of macroscopic and microscopic differentiation
  • b) Staging is the extent of spread of tumours
  • c) TNM and AJCC systems can be used for staging malignant tumours
  • d) All of the above

Answer: d) All of the above
Explanation: All statements are correct. Grading assesses differentiation, staging evaluates spread, and both TNM and AJCC are standard staging systems.

Question 23

Complications of cutaneous wound healing include ONE of the following:

  • a) Wound dehiscence
  • b) Ulceration
  • c) Formation of contractures
  • d) Deficient scar formation

Answer: a) Wound dehiscence
Explanation: Wound dehiscence (separation of wound edges) is a direct complication of impaired wound healing. The others are more related to chronic wounds or healing disorders.

Question 24

ONE of the following statements is TRUE:

  • a) Large cutaneous wounds heal by first intention
  • b) Hormones such as glucocorticoids inhibit collagen synthesis
  • c) Defective inflammation may cause increased susceptibility to infection
  • d) Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory process

Answer: d) Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory process
Explanation: Atherosclerosis involves chronic inflammation in vessel walls. Large wounds heal by second intention, glucocorticoids do inhibit healing, and inflammation helps fight infection.

Question 25

The following statements are TRUE of ischaemia:

  • a) Results from critical lack of blood supply to an area
  • b) May occur in atherosclerosis
  • c) May be reversible when blood supply is restored
  • d) All the above

Answer: d) All the above
Explanation: All statements are correct. Ischemia results from inadequate blood supply, commonly occurs in atherosclerosis, and can be reversible if circulation is restored before irreversible damage.

✍️ SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (35 MARKS)

Question 1: Define the following terms (5 Marks)

a) Oncogene: A mutated or overexpressed version of a normal gene (proto-oncogene) that promotes cell growth and division, contributing to cancer development. Examples include MYC, RAS, and HER2.

b) Oncoprotein: The abnormal protein product of an oncogene that promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation and transformation. These proteins often function in growth signaling pathways.

c) Proto-oncogene: Normal cellular genes that regulate cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis. When mutated or abnormally expressed, they become oncogenes and contribute to malignant transformation.

Question 2: Compare and contrast Apoptosis and Necrosis (5 Marks)

Question 3: Steps in Cytology Specimen Preparation (5 Marks)

  1. Collection: Obtain cells through scraping, brushing, or aspiration
  2. Fixation: Immediate alcohol fixation or air-drying depending on staining method
  3. Processing: Cell preparation on slides through smearing or cytocentrifugation
  4. Staining: Papanicolaou stain for cervical smears, Giemsa for FNA
  5. Mounting: Cover slip application and labeling for microscopic examination

Question 4: Short Notes on Amyloidosis (5 Marks)

Definition: Amyloidosis is the extracellular deposition of misfolded proteins in a characteristic β-pleated sheet configuration.

Types:

  • AL amyloidosis: Light chain proteins (associated with plasma cell disorders)
  • AA amyloidosis: Serum amyloid A protein (chronic inflammatory conditions)
  • Aβ amyloidosis: Beta-amyloid protein (Alzheimer's disease)

Diagnosis: Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light

Clinical significance: Organ dysfunction due to protein deposits in heart, kidney, liver, and nervous system.

Question 5: Principal Mediators of Acute Inflammation (5 Marks)

  1. Histamine: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability from mast cells
  2. Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2): Vasodilation, pain, fever
  3. Leukotrienes (LTB4, LTC4): Vasoconstriction, increased permeability, neutrophil chemotaxis
  4. Complement (C3a, C5a): Vasodilation, increased permeability, opsonization
  5. Cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α): Fever, acute phase response, leukocyte activation
  6. Nitric oxide: Vasodilation and antimicrobial effects

Question 6: Cytomorphologic Features of Malignant Cells (5 Marks)

  1. Nuclear pleomorphism: Variation in nuclear size and shape
  2. Increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio: Large nuclei relative to cytoplasm
  3. Hyperchromatism: Increased nuclear staining intensity
  4. Prominent nucleoli: Enlarged, irregular nucleoli
  5. Abnormal mitotic figures: Atypical mitoses and increased mitotic activity

Question 7: Major Steps in Autopsy Conduction (5 Marks)

  1. External examination: Body identification, external injuries, and abnormalities
  2. Internal examination: Systematic organ removal and examination
  3. Organ dissection: Detailed examination of individual organs
  4. Histological sampling: Tissue collection for microscopic examination
  5. Documentation: Detailed recording of findings and cause of death determination

📝 SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (40 MARKS)

Question 1a: Neoplasia and Malignant Transformation (10 Marks)

Definition of Neoplasia: Neoplasia is the abnormal, autonomous proliferation of cells that persists after cessation of the stimulus that initiated the change. It represents a fundamental disturbance in cellular growth control mechanisms.

Process of Malignant Transformation:

1. Initiation (2-3 marks)

  • Initial genetic damage to DNA by carcinogens (chemical, physical, viral)
  • Mutations in critical genes controlling cell cycle, apoptosis, DNA repair
  • Formation of initiated cells with altered growth potential

2. Promotion (2-3 marks)

  • Clonal expansion of initiated cells
  • Additional genetic alterations accumulate
  • Selective advantage allows mutated cells to outcompete normal cells
  • Development of premalignant lesions

3. Progression (2-3 marks)

  • Acquisition of additional mutations (tumor suppressor genes, oncogenes)
  • Development of invasive and metastatic capabilities
  • Angiogenesis induction for tumor vascularization
  • Ability to evade immune surveillance

4. Metastasis (2-3 marks)

  • Local invasion through basement membrane
  • Intravasation into blood/lymphatic vessels
  • Survival in circulation and extravasation
  • Establishment of secondary tumor sites

Question 1b: Cutaneous Wound Healing and Repair (10 Marks)

1. Hemostasis Phase (2-3 marks)

  • Immediate vasoconstriction to reduce blood loss
  • Platelet aggregation and activation
  • Coagulation cascade activation forming fibrin clot
  • Formation of stable hemostatic plug

2. Inflammatory Phase (2-3 marks)

  • Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
  • Neutrophil infiltration (24-48 hours) for debris removal
  • Macrophage recruitment for phagocytosis and growth factor release
  • Preparation of wound bed for repair

3. Proliferative Phase (2-3 marks)

  • Angiogenesis: new blood vessel formation
  • Fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
  • Re-epithelialization: keratinocyte migration and proliferation
  • Granulation tissue formation

4. Remodeling Phase (2-3 marks)

  • Collagen reorganization and cross-linking
  • Tissue tensile strength improvement
  • Excess collagen removal and scar tissue formation
  • Can continue for months to years

Factors Affecting Healing:

  • Age, nutrition, oxygenation, infection, medications

Question 2: Vascular and Cellular Events of Acute Inflammation (20 Marks)

VASCULAR EVENTS (10 marks)

1. Changes in Vascular Flow and Caliber (3-4 marks)

  • Initial transient vasoconstriction (seconds): Immediate response to injury
  • Vasodilation (minutes): Mediated by histamine, NO, and prostaglandins
  • Increased blood flow: Results in heat and redness (calor and rubor)
  • Stasis: Eventually leads to sluggish flow and potential thrombosis

2. Increased Vascular Permeability (3-4 marks)

  • Mechanism: Endothelial cell contraction creating gaps
  • Mediators: Histamine, leukotrienes, complement, PAF
  • Result: Protein-rich fluid extravasation (exudate formation)
  • Clinical significance: Tissue swelling (tumor) and loss of function

3. Changes in Blood Flow (3-4 marks)

  • Margination: Leukocytes move from central to peripheral circulation
  • Rolling: Selectin-mediated loose attachment to endothelium
  • Adhesion: Firm attachment via integrin-ICAM interactions
  • Transmigration: Leukocyte passage through vessel wall

CELLULAR EVENTS (10 marks)

1. Neutrophil Response (3-4 marks)

  • Recruitment: First cells to arrive (6-24 hours)
  • Chemotaxis: Directed migration following chemical gradients
  • Activation: Release of granule contents and reactive oxygen species
  • Functions: Phagocytosis, bacterial killing, debris removal

2. Monocyte/Macrophage Response (3-4 marks)

  • Timing: Peak at 24-48 hours, persist longer than neutrophils
  • Functions: Phagocytosis, antigen presentation, tissue repair initiation
  • Secretory products: Cytokines, growth factors, complement components
  • Resolution role: Removal of apoptotic neutrophils

3. Other Cellular Participants (3-4 marks)

  • Mast cells: Histamine and mediator release
  • Platelets: Hemostasis and inflammatory mediator release
  • Endothelial cells: Barrier function changes, adhesion molecule expression
  • Tissue-resident cells: Local response initiation and amplification

MOLECULAR MEDIATORS ORCHESTRATING THESE EVENTS:

  • Plasma-derived: Complement, coagulation factors, kinins
  • Cell-derived: Prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines, chemokines
  • Function: Coordinate vascular and cellular responses for effective inflammation

🎯 SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS

CHOOSE THE SINGLE BEST ANSWER TO EACH QUESTION

Question 1

Name the response that best categorizes cells:

  • a) Labile cells
  • b) Stable cells
  • c) Permanent cells
  • d) Semi permeable cells
  • e) A, B, and C

Answer: e) A, B, and C
Explanation: Cells are categorized into three types based on their proliferative capacity: labile cells (continuously dividing), stable cells (divide when stimulated), and permanent cells (non-dividing post-mitotic cells).

Question 2

All the granulomatous diseases EXCEPT:

  • a) Tuberculosis
  • b) Sarcoidosis
  • c) Schistosomiasis
  • d) Syphilis
  • e) Asthma

Answer: e) Asthma
Explanation: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by eosinophilia and smooth muscle hypertrophy, not granulomatous inflammation. The others all cause granulomatous reactions.

Question 3

The following are chemical mediators of chronic inflammation EXCEPT:

  • a) Leukotrienes
  • b) Complement proteins
  • c) Interleukins
  • d) Cytokines
  • e) Hormones

Answer: e) Hormones
Explanation: While hormones can modulate inflammatory responses, they are not considered primary chemical mediators of chronic inflammation. Leukotrienes, complement, interleukins, and cytokines are key inflammatory mediators.

Question 4

The most important cell in chronic inflammation is:

  • a) Macrophages
  • b) Monocyte
  • c) Lymphocyte
  • d) Fibroblast
  • e) Smooth Muscle Cell

Answer: a) Macrophages
Explanation: Macrophages are the hallmark cells of chronic inflammation, responsible for phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and secretion of inflammatory mediators and growth factors.

Question 5

The following are causes of pathological atrophy EXCEPT:

  • a) Reduced nervous supply
  • b) Ischaemia
  • c) Malnutrition
  • d) Muscle disease
  • e) None of the above

Answer: e) None of the above
Explanation: All listed options (denervation, ischemia, malnutrition, and muscle disease) are valid causes of pathological atrophy - reduction in cell size and organ mass.

Question 6

The following are functions of cellular adaptations EXCEPT:

  • a) Phagocytosis
  • b) Antigen processing
  • c) Secretion of inflammatory substances
  • d) Lysis
  • e) None of the above

Answer: e) None of the above
Explanation: All listed functions can be part of cellular adaptations. Cells can adapt to perform various functions including phagocytosis, antigen processing, secretion, and lysis in response to environmental changes.

Question 7

Mechanisms of cell injury include all EXCEPT:

  • a) Damaged mitochondrial functions
  • b) Leaky cell membrane
  • c) Normal protein synthesis
  • d) Deranged calcium homeostasis
  • e) Leakage of lysosomal enzymes

Answer: c) Normal protein synthesis
Explanation: Normal protein synthesis is a sign of cellular health, not injury. Cell injury involves mitochondrial dysfunction, membrane damage, calcium dysregulation, and lysosomal enzyme leakage.

Question 8

A tuberculous granuloma is comprised of:

  • a) Fibroblasts and capillaries
  • b) Capillaries and giant cells
  • c) Endothelial cells and neutrophils
  • d) Young capillaries
  • e) Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes

Answer: e) Central necrotic area, epithelioid cells and lymphocytes
Explanation: Tuberculous granulomas are characterized by central caseating necrosis surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and a peripheral layer of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Question 9

Events surrounding chronic inflammation include all EXCEPT:

  • a) Infiltration with macrophages
  • b) Angiogenesis
  • c) Attempts at repair
  • d) Tissue destruction
  • e) Infiltration with neutrophils

Answer: e) Infiltration with neutrophils
Explanation: Neutrophil infiltration is characteristic of acute inflammation. Chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophage infiltration, angiogenesis, repair attempts, and tissue destruction.

Question 10

The heart and kidneys are prone to this type of cellular adaptation:

  • a) Dysplasia
  • b) Hyperplasia
  • c) Hypertrophy
  • d) Atrophy
  • e) Anaplasia

Answer: c) Hypertrophy
Explanation: Heart and kidney cells are primarily post-mitotic, so they respond to increased workload by increasing cell size (hypertrophy) rather than cell number (hyperplasia).

Question 11

Low albumin results in:

  • a) Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
  • b) Decreased colloid osmotic pressure
  • c) Decrease in capillary hydrostatic pressure
  • d) Decrease in interstitial pressure
  • e) None of the above

Answer: b) Decreased colloid osmotic pressure
Explanation: Albumin is the major contributor to plasma oncotic pressure. Low albumin (hypoalbuminemia) decreases colloid osmotic pressure, leading to fluid extravasation and edema.

Question 12

White blood cells attach to endothelial cells in the inflammatory process using their surface receptors called:

  • a) Integrins
  • b) E-Selection
  • c) P-Selection
  • d) XCAMS
  • e) CD35

Answer: a) Integrins
Explanation: Integrins on leukocytes bind to adhesion molecules (like ICAM-1) on endothelial cells, allowing firm adhesion before transmigration. Selectins mediate rolling, not firm adhesion.

Question 13

A white blood cell that is involved in the acute inflammatory response is:

  • a) Neutrophil
  • b) T-lymphocyte
  • c) B-lymphocyte
  • d) Fibroblast
  • e) Platelet

Answer: a) Neutrophil
Explanation: Neutrophils are the first and most numerous leukocytes recruited during acute inflammation, arriving within hours to perform phagocytosis and antimicrobial functions.

Question 14

In the process of phagocytosis, the oxidative arm produces the following EXCEPT:

  • a) Collagenases
  • b) Elastases
  • c) O2-
  • d) NO3
  • e) Iodine

Answer: a) Collagenases
Explanation: Collagenases are non-oxidative enzymes. The oxidative arm of phagocytosis produces reactive oxygen species like superoxide (O2-), nitrates, and hypohalites (including iodine compounds).

Question 15

Wound healing involves all the processes outlined below EXCEPT:

  • a) Induction of an acute inflammatory response
  • b) Parenchymal cell regeneration
  • c) Migration and proliferation
  • d) Synthesis of intracellular proteins (ICM)
  • e) Remodeling of parenchymal elements to restore function and strength

Answer: d) Synthesis of intracellular proteins (ICM)
Explanation: Wound healing involves extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, not intracellular proteins. The process includes inflammation, cell regeneration, migration/proliferation, and tissue remodeling.

Question 16

Which of the following is the correct response to describe how secondary healing differs from primary healing:

  • a) Large tissue defects in secondary healing
  • b) Inflammatory response is more intense
  • c) Larger amounts of granulation tissues are observed
  • d) Wound contraction is a distinguishing feature
  • e) All of the above

Answer: e) All of the above
Explanation: Secondary healing (healing by second intention) involves all these features compared to primary healing: larger defects, more intense inflammation, extensive granulation tissue, and significant wound contraction.

Question 17

Wound healing is affected by all of the following EXCEPT:

  • a) Infection
  • b) Malnutrition
  • c) Poor blood vessel supply
  • d) Absence of glucocorticoids
  • e) Type and location of tissue

Answer: d) Absence of glucocorticoids
Explanation: The absence of glucocorticoids would actually improve wound healing, as glucocorticoids impair healing by suppressing inflammation and collagen synthesis. The other factors all negatively affect healing.

Question 18

Haemorrhage can result in one of the following:

  • a) Cardiogenic Shock
  • b) Septic Shock
  • c) Neurogenic Shock
  • d) Anaphylactic Shock
  • e) Hypovolaemic Shock

Answer: e) Hypovolaemic Shock
Explanation: Hemorrhage leads to blood volume loss, resulting in hypovolemic shock. The other shock types have different etiologies: cardiac dysfunction, infection, neurological injury, and allergic reactions respectively.

Question 19

The most common cause of oedema in the developing world secondary to reduced plasma colloid oncotic pressure is:

  • a) Protein losing renal syndrome
  • b) Liver cirrhosis
  • c) Excessive protein loss from the gut
  • d) Malnutrition
  • e) Acute and chronic inflammatory

Answer: d) Malnutrition
Explanation: In developing countries, protein-energy malnutrition (kwashiorkor) is the most common cause of hypoproteinemic edema due to inadequate protein intake leading to low albumin synthesis.

Question 20

One of the following is not associated with the pathophysiology of oedema:

  • a) Increased Hydrostatic Pressure
  • b) Reduced Plasma Oncotic Pressure
  • c) Lymphatic obstruction
  • d) Potassium retention
  • e) Inflammation

Answer: d) Potassium retention
Explanation: Potassium retention doesn't directly cause edema. Edema results from increased hydrostatic pressure, decreased oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, increased vascular permeability (inflammation), and sodium retention.

✍️ SECTION B: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (5 MARKS EACH)

Question 1: Define the following terms:

a) Hypoxia: Reduced oxygen availability to tissues despite adequate perfusion. Can result from respiratory disease, anemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, or high altitude. Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism leading to lactic acidosis.

b) Necrosis: Pathological cell death characterized by cellular swelling, membrane disruption, organelle destruction, and inflammatory response. Results from severe cell injury and is irreversible, unlike apoptosis.

c) Apoptosis: Programmed cell death characterized by cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, membrane blebbing without rupture, and phagocytosis by macrophages without inflammation. Energy-dependent process crucial for development and homeostasis.

d) Anoxia: Complete absence of oxygen in tissues. More severe than hypoxia, rapidly leading to irreversible cell damage and death. Can occur in situations like drowning, strangulation, or complete vascular occlusion.

Question 2:

A) Briefly describe what is meant by a chronic inflammatory process:

Chronic inflammation is a prolonged inflammatory response lasting weeks to years, characterized by:

  • Infiltration by macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells
  • Tissue destruction and attempts at healing occurring simultaneously
  • Angiogenesis and fibroblast proliferation
  • Can result from persistent acute inflammation, autoimmune reactions, or prolonged exposure to toxic agents

B) Discuss how a granuloma is formed:

Granuloma formation occurs when macrophages cannot eliminate persistent irritants:

  1. Macrophage activation: Persistent antigen activates macrophages
  2. Epithelioid transformation: Activated macrophages transform into epithelioid cells
  3. Giant cell formation: Fusion of epithelioid cells forms multinucleated giant cells
  4. Lymphocyte recruitment: T-cells surround the central core
  5. Fibroblast proliferation: Peripheral fibrosis may develop

Question 3: List 4 biological properties of the complement system:

  1. Opsonization: C3b coating of pathogens enhances phagocytosis
  2. Membrane Attack Complex (MAC): C5b-9 complex creates pores in target cell membranes
  3. Inflammation: C3a and C5a act as anaphylatoxins causing vasodilation and increased permeability
  4. Chemotaxis: C5a attracts neutrophils and macrophages to infection sites

Question 4: Differentiate between benign and malignant conditions:

Question 5: Give 3 examples of metaplasia:

  1. Respiratory metaplasia: Ciliated respiratory epithelium → stratified squamous epithelium (smoking)
  2. Barrett's esophagus: Stratified squamous epithelium → columnar epithelium (acid reflux)
  3. Bladder metaplasia: Transitional epithelium → stratified squamous epithelium (chronic irritation)

📝 SECTION C: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (20 MARKS EACH)

Question 1: Compare and contrast healing by primary and secondary intention (20 Marks)

PRIMARY INTENTION HEALING (10 marks)

Characteristics:

  • Clean, well-approximated wound edges
  • Minimal tissue loss and contamination
  • Surgical incisions are typical examples

Process:

  1. Hemostasis (0-24 hours): Blood clot formation seals the wound
  2. Inflammation (24-72 hours): Minimal inflammatory response, neutrophil infiltration
  3. Proliferation (3-21 days):
    • Epithelialization occurs rapidly within 24-48 hours
    • Minimal granulation tissue formation
    • Fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
  4. Remodeling (weeks-months): Collagen reorganization, minimal scar formation

Advantages:

  • Faster healing (7-10 days)
  • Minimal scarring
  • Lower infection risk
  • Preserved function

SECONDARY INTENTION HEALING (10 marks)

Characteristics:

  • Large tissue defects with wide separation
  • Significant tissue loss or contamination
  • Infected wounds, pressure sores, chronic ulcers

Process:

  1. Hemostasis: Similar to primary healing but more extensive
  2. Inflammation (prolonged): More intense and prolonged inflammatory response
  3. Proliferation (extended period):
    • Extensive granulation tissue formation
    • Wound contraction is prominent
    • Re-epithelialization from wound edges (slower)
    • Angiogenesis more pronounced
  4. Remodeling: Extended period with significant scar tissue formation

Key Differences:

  • Granulation tissue: Extensive in secondary healing
  • Wound contraction: Major feature of secondary healing
  • Time: Secondary healing takes weeks to months
  • Scarring: More pronounced in secondary healing
  • Infection risk: Higher in secondary healing

Question 2: List 4 metabolic pigmentation disorders. Select one and discuss it briefly (20 Marks)

FOUR METABOLIC PIGMENTATION DISORDERS (8 marks)

  1. Hemosiderosis/Hemochromatosis - Iron accumulation
  2. Jaundice (Icterus) - Bilirubin accumulation
  3. Ochronosis - Homogentisic acid accumulation (Alkaptonuria)
  4. Melanosis - Excessive melanin deposition

DETAILED DISCUSSION: JAUNDICE (ICTERUS) (12 marks)

Definition: Jaundice is the yellow discoloration of tissues due to elevated bilirubin levels (>2.5 mg/dL) in blood and tissues.

Bilirubin Metabolism:

  • Red blood cell breakdown releases hemoglobin
  • Hemoglobin → heme → unconjugated bilirubin (indirect)
  • Liver conjugates bilirubin with glucuronic acid → conjugated bilirubin (direct)
  • Conjugated bilirubin excreted in bile → intestines → urobilinogen

Types and Causes:

1. Pre-hepatic Jaundice (Hemolytic):

  • Cause: Excessive RBC destruction
  • Bilirubin type: Predominantly unconjugated
  • Examples: Hemolytic anemia, malaria, transfusion reactions
  • Laboratory: ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin

2. Hepatic Jaundice (Hepatocellular):

  • Cause: Liver cell dysfunction
  • Bilirubin type: Mixed (conjugated and unconjugated)
  • Examples: Hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug toxicity
  • Laboratory: ↑ both bilirubin types, ↑ liver enzymes

3. Post-hepatic Jaundice (Obstructive):

  • Cause: Biliary obstruction
  • Bilirubin type: Predominantly conjugated
  • Examples: Gallstones, pancreatic cancer, biliary atresia
  • Laboratory: ↑ direct bilirubin, ↑ alkaline phosphatase, dark urine

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Yellow discoloration of skin, sclera, mucous membranes
  • Dark urine (conjugated bilirubin)
  • Pale stools (obstructive jaundice)
  • Pruritus (bile salt deposition)

Complications:

  • Kernicterus in neonates (unconjugated bilirubin crosses blood-brain barrier)
  • Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (obstructive jaundice)

Title: 50 Multiple Choice Questions
Content:
Cellular Responses to Stress and Toxic Insults

Robbins Pathology - Chapter 1

SECTION 1: CELLULAR ADAPTATIONS

Question 1

Which of the following best describes physiologic hypertrophy?

A. Enlargement of skeletal muscle in bodybuilders
B. Cardiac enlargement in hypertension
C. Prostatic enlargement in elderly men
D. Thyroid enlargement in Graves' disease

Answer: A

Explanation: Physiologic hypertrophy occurs in response to normal stimuli like exercise or hormonal stimulation during pregnancy. Skeletal muscle enlargement with exercise is a classic example. Option B represents pathologic hypertrophy due to increased workload from disease.

Question 2

Barrett esophagus is an example of:

A. Hyperplasia
B. Metaplasia
C. Dysplasia
D. Anaplasia

Answer: B

Explanation: Barrett esophagus represents metaplasia where normal stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells in response to chronic acid reflux. This is an adaptive response to chronic injury.

Question 3

Which cellular adaptation is reversible upon removal of the stimulus?

A. Atrophy
B. Metaplasia
C. Dysplasia
