EXPLANATION: FMRP is an RNA-binding protein transported from cytoplasm to nucleus, where it binds specific mRNAs and transports them to axons and dendrites, regulating translation at synapses.

QUESTION 11

What condition affects approximately 30% of females carrying the fragile X premutation?

A) Mental retardation
B) Premature ovarian failure before age 40
C) Breast cancer
D) Diabetes

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Approximately 30% of females carrying the premutation have premature ovarian failure (before age 40), indicating that premutations are not benign though abnormalities are milder.

QUESTION 12

What syndrome develops in approximately one-third of premutation-carrying males in their sixth decade?

A) Alzheimer disease
B) Parkinson disease
C) Fragile X-associated tremor-ataxia
D) Multiple sclerosis

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: About one-third of premutation-carrying males exhibit fragile X-associated tremor-ataxia starting in their sixth decade, characterized by intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia, potentially progressing to parkinsonism.

QUESTION 13

In Huntington disease, when does conversion from premutation to full mutation occur?

A) During oogenesis
B) During spermatogenesis
C) During mitosis
D) During fertilization

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Unlike fragile X syndrome where expansion occurs during oogenesis, in Huntington disease and some other trinucleotide repeat disorders, premutations are converted to full mutations during spermatogenesis.

QUESTION 14

What type of mutation occurs when trinucleotide repeats affect coding regions?

A) Loss of function
B) Toxic gain of function
C) Silent mutation
D) Neutral mutation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: When mutations affect coding regions (like in Huntington disease), they give rise to misfolded proteins that interfere with normal protein function, called toxic gain-of-function mutations.

QUESTION 15

What are diseases involving CAG repeat expansions in coding regions commonly called?

A) Fragile site disorders
B) Polyglutamine diseases
C) Mitochondrial diseases
D) Imprinting disorders

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Diseases involving CAG repeats that encode polyglutamine tracts are referred to as "polyglutamine diseases," which primarily affect the nervous system and feature accumulation of misfolded protein aggregates.

QUESTION 16

Why does maternal inheritance occur in mitochondrial diseases?

A) Mothers have more mitochondria
B) Ova contain mitochondria while spermatozoa contain few or none
C) Mitochondrial DNA is X-linked
D) Fathers cannot transmit any organelles

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Ova contain mitochondria within their abundant cytoplasm, whereas spermatozoa contain few if any mitochondria. The mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is therefore derived entirely from the ovum.

QUESTION 17

Which organs are most affected by mitochondrial diseases?

A) Skin and hair
B) Liver and kidneys
C) Skeletal muscle, heart, and brain
D) Lungs and spleen

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Because mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes for oxidative phosphorylation, diseases from mitochondrial mutations affect organs most dependent on oxidative phosphorylation: skeletal muscle, heart, and brain.

QUESTION 18

What is the prototypical mitochondrial disease?

A) Fragile X syndrome
B) Leber hereditary optic neuropathy
C) Huntington disease
D) Prader-Willi syndrome

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is the prototypical mitochondrial disorder, manifesting as progressive bilateral loss of central vision leading to blindness.

QUESTION 19

What is genomic imprinting?

A) DNA replication errors
B) Differential inactivation of genes during gametogenesis
C) Chromosome translocation
D) Gene duplication

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process whereby certain genes are differentially inactivated during paternal and maternal gametogenesis, creating functional differences between maternal and paternal gene copies.

QUESTION 20

What molecular mechanism is associated with genomic imprinting?

A) Point mutations
B) Methylation of gene promoter
C) Gene deletion
D) Chromosome inversion

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: At the molecular level, imprinting is associated with methylation of the gene promoter, as well as histone protein modifications, which silence the gene.

QUESTION 21

What chromosomal region is deleted in both Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes?

A) Chromosome 15q11-q13
B) Chromosome 7q11
C) Chromosome 22q11
D) Chromosome Xq27

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: Both Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes involve deletion of band q12 in the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q11-q13), but the parent of origin differs.

QUESTION 22

In Prader-Willi syndrome, which parental chromosome is deleted?

A) Maternal
B) Paternal
C) Either maternal or paternal
D) Both

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In Prader-Willi syndrome, the deletion affects the paternally derived chromosome 15 in all cases, demonstrating parent-of-origin effects on gene function.

QUESTION 23

What clinical features characterize Prader-Willi syndrome?

A) Ataxia, seizures, and inappropriate laughter
B) Mental retardation, obesity, small hands/feet, hypogonadism
C) Vision loss and blindness
D) Tremors and parkinsonism

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Prader-Willi syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, short stature, hypotonia, obesity, small hands and feet, and hypogonadism.

QUESTION 24

In Angelman syndrome, which parental chromosome is deleted?

A) Maternal
B) Paternal
C) Either maternal or paternal
D) Both

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: In Angelman syndrome, the deletion affects the maternally derived chromosome 15, in contrast to Prader-Willi syndrome where the paternal chromosome is deleted.

QUESTION 25

What clinical features characterize Angelman syndrome?

A) Obesity and hypogonadism
B) Mental retardation, ataxic gait, seizures, inappropriate laughter
C) Vision loss
D) Muscle weakness only

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Angelman syndrome patients are mentally retarded and present with ataxic gait, seizures, and inappropriate laughter, giving rise to the name "happy puppet syndrome."

QUESTION 26

What is uniparental disomy?

A) Having three copies of a chromosome
B) Inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent
C) Deletion of one chromosome
D) Translocation between chromosomes

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Uniparental disomy is the inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from one parent. In Prader-Willi syndrome, this can occur when both copies of chromosome 15 are from the mother.

QUESTION 27

What gene is responsible for Angelman syndrome?

A) FMR1
B) HTT
C) UBE3A
D) FMRP

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The Angelman syndrome gene is UBE3A, which encodes a ligase in the ubiquitin-proteasome proteolytic pathway and is expressed primarily from the maternal allele in specific brain regions.

QUESTION 28

What does maternal imprinting mean?

A) The paternal allele is inactivated
B) The maternal allele is inactivated
C) Both alleles are active
D) Neither allele is active

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Maternal imprinting refers to transcriptional silencing of the maternal allele, whereas paternal imprinting means the paternal allele is inactivated.

QUESTION 29

How many CGG repeats define a full mutation in fragile X syndrome?

A) 52-100
B) 100-200
C) 200-4000
D) Over 5000

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Full mutations in fragile X syndrome are characterized by 200 to 4000 CGG repeats, which arise through expansion of premutations (52-200 repeats).

QUESTION 30

Why can Prader-Willi syndrome result from maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15?

A) Maternal genes are overexpressed
B) Patient lacks functional genes from nonimprinted paternal chromosome
C) Maternal genes are deleted
D) Chromosome is duplicated

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Maternal uniparental disomy means the patient has both copies from the mother and lacks functional genes from the nonimprinted paternal chromosome 15, resulting in the same effect as paternal deletion.

QUESTION 31

Approximately how many diseases are now known to be caused by trinucleotide repeat mutations?

A) About 10
B) About 20
C) About 40
D) About 100

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: About 40 diseases are now known to be caused by trinucleotide repeat mutations, and all disorders discovered so far are associated with neurodegenerative changes.

QUESTION 32

What percentage of Prader-Willi syndrome cases show an interstitial deletion detectable by standard cytogenetics?

A) 20-40%
B) 40-50%
C) 60-75%
D) 90-100%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In 60% to 75% of Prader-Willi syndrome cases, an interstitial deletion of band q12 in chromosome 15—del(15)(q11;q13)—can be detected. Many others have smaller deletions detectable by FISH.

QUESTION 33

Which technique can detect smaller deletions in Prader-Willi syndrome not visible by standard cytogenetics?

A) PCR
B) Western blot
C) FISH analysis
D) Karyotyping

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In patients without detectable cytogenetic abnormality, FISH (Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization) analysis can reveal smaller deletions within the same chromosomal region.

QUESTION 34

Where is FMRP most highly expressed in normal tissues?

A) Liver and kidney
B) Brain and testis
C) Heart and lung
D) Skin and muscle

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: FMRP is widely expressed in normal tissues, but higher levels are found in the brain and the testis, which correlates with the clinical manifestations of fragile X syndrome.

QUESTION 35

What is the original diagnostic method that gave fragile X syndrome its name?

A) PCR analysis
B) Western blotting
C) Culturing cells in folate-deficient medium showing X chromosome discontinuity
D) DNA sequencing

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The syndrome gets its name from culturing patient cells in folate-deficient medium, which revealed a discontinuity of staining or constriction in the long arm of the X chromosome. This method is now replaced by DNA-based analysis.

QUESTION 36

What is the chromosomal location of the FMR1 gene?

A) Xp21
B) Xq27.3
C) Xp11
D) Xq21

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The FMR1 gene maps to Xq27.3 on the long arm of the X chromosome, and mutations in this gene result in fragile X syndrome.

QUESTION 37

Can mothers transmit mitochondrial DNA to their sons?

A) No, only to daughters
B) Yes, to both sons and daughters
C) Yes, but only sons can transmit further
D) No, mitochondrial DNA is not inherited

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Mothers transmit mitochondrial genes to all their offspring, both male and female; however, only daughters (not sons) transmit the DNA further to their progeny.

QUESTION 38

What is the net effect of having genes from the nonimprinted paternal chromosome 15 in Prader-Willi syndrome?

A) Gene overexpression
B) No functional genes available since maternal copies are imprinted
C) Normal gene expression
D) Mixed expression patterns

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Genes on the maternal chromosome 15 are imprinted (silenced), so the only functional alleles come from the paternal chromosome. Loss of these leads to Prader-Willi syndrome.

QUESTION 39

What happens when the number of trinucleotide repeats exceeds approximately 230 in the FMR1 gene?

A) Gene is overexpressed
B) DNA becomes abnormally methylated
C) Protein is mutated
D) Chromosome breaks

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: When CGG repeats exceed approximately 230, the DNA of the entire 5' region becomes abnormally methylated, extending to the promoter region, resulting in transcriptional suppression.

QUESTION 40

In trinucleotide repeat disorders affecting noncoding regions, what is the typical outcome?

A) Toxic gain of function
B) Loss of function due to suppressed protein synthesis
C) Increased protein expression
D) No effect on protein

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: When mutations affect noncoding regions (like in fragile X syndrome), there is loss of function since protein synthesis is suppressed, in contrast to coding region mutations that cause toxic gain of function.

QUESTION 41

What common feature is seen in polyglutamine diseases?

A) Gene deletion
B) Accumulation of misfolded proteins in cytoplasmic aggregates
C) Chromosomal translocations
D) Mitochondrial dysfunction only

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in aggregates within the cytoplasm is a common feature of polyglutamine diseases resulting from CAG repeat expansions in coding regions.

QUESTION 42

Why is Prader-Willi syndrome thought to result from loss of multiple genes rather than a single gene?

A) Multiple chromosomes are affected
B) Several genes in the region are lost, unlike Angelman which involves one gene
C) It is not a genetic disorder
D) Genes are duplicated

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Prader-Willi syndrome, unlike Angelman syndrome, probably is caused by loss of function of several genes located on chromosome 15 between q11 and q13, which are still being fully characterized.

QUESTION 43

When is imprinting established?

A) During fertilization
B) In ovum or sperm and then stably transmitted to all somatic cells
C) After birth
D) During adolescence

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Imprinting occurs in ovum or sperm (during gametogenesis) and is then stably transmitted to all somatic cells derived from the zygote.

QUESTION 44

What type of disorders are predominantly associated with trinucleotide repeat mutations?

A) Cardiac disorders
B) Neurodegenerative disorders
C) Immune disorders
D) Metabolic disorders

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: All trinucleotide repeat disorders discovered so far are associated with neurodegenerative changes, affecting primarily the nervous system.

QUESTION 45

In normal individuals, which regions of the brain primarily express UBE3A from the maternal allele?

A) All brain regions equally
B) Specific regions of the brain
C) No brain regions
D) Only the cerebellum

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: UBE3A is expressed primarily from the maternal allele in specific regions of the normal brain. In Angelman syndrome, UBE3A is not expressed in these areas, causing neurologic manifestations.

QUESTION 46

What is the threshold number of CGG repeats above which abnormal methylation occurs in fragile X syndrome?

A) Approximately 52
B) Approximately 100
C) Approximately 230
D) Approximately 500

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: When the number of trinucleotide repeats in the FMR1 gene exceeds approximately 230, the DNA of the entire 5' region becomes abnormally methylated, leading to gene silencing.

QUESTION 47

What is the role of FMRP-mRNA complexes in synapses?

A) DNA replication
B) Regulating translation of specific mRNAs
C) Protein degradation
D) Lipid synthesis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In synapses, FMRP-mRNA complexes perform critical roles in regulating the translation of specific mRNAs. The absence of this finely coordinated shuttle function underlies fragile X syndrome.

QUESTION 48

What distinguishes the clinical presentation of males versus females with fragile X syndrome?

A) Males are never affected
B) Females cannot be carriers
C) Males have moderate to severe mental retardation; 30-50% of carrier females are affected
D) Clinical features are identical

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Clinically affected males have moderate to severe mental retardation, while 30-50% of carrier females are affected (mentally retarded), much higher than typical X-linked recessive disorders.

QUESTION 49

What happens during the conversion of premutation to full mutation in fragile X syndrome?

A) CGG repeats decrease
B) Further amplification of CGG repeats occurs
C) Gene is deleted
D) Chromosome breaks

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: During oogenesis, premutations (52-200 repeats) can be converted to full mutations (200-4000 repeats) by further amplification of the CGG repeats.

QUESTION 50

Why do Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes demonstrate "parent-of-origin" effects?

A) Diseases are X-linked
B) Different genes are imprinted on maternal versus paternal chromosomes
C) Mutations differ between parents
D) Chromosomes are structurally different

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: These syndromes demonstrate parent-of-origin effects because different genes within the same region are imprinted on maternal versus paternal chromosomes, so deletion of maternal or paternal chromosome 15 produces distinct clinical syndromes.

Title: TUMOR SUPPRESSOR GENES & CELL CYCLE CONTROL MCQs
Content:
50 COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1

What is the chromosomal location of the RB gene?

A) 13q11
B) 13q14
C) 17p13
D) 5q21

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The RB gene, the first tumor suppressor gene to be discovered, is located at chromosomal locus 13q14.

QUESTION 2

According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, how many mutations are required to develop retinoblastoma?

A) One mutation is sufficient
B) Two hits (mutations) are required
C) Three mutations are needed
D) Four or more mutations

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis states that two hits are required to develop retinoblastoma - both copies of the RB tumor suppressor gene must be dysfunctional.

QUESTION 3

In familial retinoblastoma, what is the origin of the first hit?

A) Both mutations are somatic
B) One mutation is inherited (germline), second is somatic
C) Both mutations are inherited
D) Mutations occur after birth

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In familial cases, one hit (mutation) is inherited in the germline and the second hit develops when the normal Rb gene is lost by somatic mutation in retinoblasts.

QUESTION 4

What is the critical cell cycle checkpoint controlled by the RB gene?

A) G2/M transition
B) M/G1 transition
C) G1/S transition
D) S/G2 transition

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The Rb gene exerts antiproliferative effects by controlling the G1/S transition of the cell cycle, preventing cells from entering S phase inappropriately.

QUESTION 5

In its active tumor suppressor form, what is the phosphorylation state of RB protein?

A) Hyperphosphorylated
B) Hypophosphorylated
C) Unphosphorylated
D) Dephosphorylated then rephosphorylated

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In its active form, Rb is hypophosphorylated and binds to E2F transcription factor, preventing transcription of genes required for DNA replication like cyclin E.

QUESTION 6

What transcription factor does hypophosphorylated RB bind to?

A) p53
B) E2F
C) NF-κB
D) AP-1

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Hypophosphorylated Rb binds to E2F transcription factor, preventing E2F from activating transcription of genes required for cell cycle progression and DNA replication.

QUESTION 7

What percentage of tumors demonstrate biallelic loss of TP53?

A) 30%
B) 50%
C) 70%
D) 90%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Approximately 70% of tumors demonstrate biallelic loss of TP53, highlighting its critical role as a tumor suppressor and "guardian of the genome."

QUESTION 8

Which syndrome is associated with germline mutation in one TP53 allele?

A) Lynch syndrome
B) Li-Fraumeni syndrome
C) Familial adenomatous polyposis
D) Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Li-Fraumeni syndrome involves inheritance of one defective TP53 allele in the germline, with the second defect occurring in somatic cells, predisposing to multiple cancers.

QUESTION 9

What is p53 commonly referred to as due to its critical role in genomic stability?

A) Governor of the cell cycle
B) Guardian of the genome
C) Master regulator
D) Cell cycle brake

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: p53 is called the "guardian of the genome" because it serves as the central monitor of cellular stress and can initiate responses to maintain genomic integrity.

QUESTION 10

Which stresses can activate p53 protein?

A) Anoxia, oncogene signaling, and DNA damage
B) Nutrient excess only
C) Normal cell growth
D) Mitosis

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: p53 is the central monitor of stress in the cell and can be activated by anoxia, inappropriate oncogene signaling, or DNA damage.

QUESTION 11

What mechanism activates p53 in response to DNA damage?

A) Dephosphorylation
B) Phosphorylation
C) Acetylation only
D) Ubiquitination

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: DNA damage leads to activation of p53 by phosphorylation, which stabilizes the protein and activates its transcriptional functions.

QUESTION 12

What gene does activated p53 drive transcription of to cause G1-S cell cycle block?

A) CDK4
B) Cyclin E
C) CDKN1A (p21)
D) Cyclin D

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Activated p53 drives transcription of CDKN1A (which encodes p21), a CDK inhibitor that prevents Rb phosphorylation, thereby causing a G1-S block in the cell cycle.

QUESTION 13

What is the purpose of the G1-S cell cycle block induced by p53?

A) To promote cell division
B) To allow cells to repair DNA damage
C) To induce immediate apoptosis
D) To accelerate cell growth

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The pause in cell cycle progression allows cells time to repair DNA damage. If damage cannot be repaired, p53 then induces cellular senescence or apoptosis.

QUESTION 14

If DNA damage cannot be repaired, what outcomes can p53 induce?

A) Continued proliferation
B) Cellular senescence or apoptosis
C) Enhanced DNA synthesis
D) Increased telomerase activity

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: If DNA damage cannot be repaired despite the cell cycle pause, p53 induces either cellular senescence (permanent growth arrest) or apoptosis (programmed cell death).

QUESTION 15

How do oncogenic DNA viruses like HPV disable RB and p53 function?

A) By deleting the genes
B) By encoding proteins that bind to RB and p53
C) By preventing gene transcription
D) By inducing mutations

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Oncogenic DNA viruses like HPV encode proteins that bind to RB and p53, rendering them non-functional and allowing uncontrolled cell proliferation.

QUESTION 16

What percentage of pancreatic cancers have mutations in at least one component of the TGF-β pathway?

A) 50%
B) 70%
C) 83%
D) 100%

ANSWER: D

EXPLANATION: In 100% of pancreatic cancers and 83% of colon cancers, at least one component of the TGF-β pathway is mutated, highlighting its critical role as a growth inhibitor.

QUESTION 17

In most normal epithelial, endothelial, and hematopoietic cells, what is the effect of TGF-β?

A) Potent promoter of proliferation
B) Potent inhibitor of proliferation
C) No effect on proliferation
D) Variable effect depending on cell type

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In most normal epithelial, endothelial, and hematopoietic cells, TGF-β is a potent inhibitor of proliferation, transmitting antiproliferative signals.

QUESTION 18

What cellular process does TGF-β activate in late-stage tumors that promotes metastasis?

A) Apoptosis
B) Senescence
C) Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)
D) Differentiation

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In late-stage tumors, TGF-β signaling can paradoxically activate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), promoting migration, invasion, and metastasis.

QUESTION 19

What does TGF-β signaling activate that has growth-suppressing activity?

A) Cyclins
B) CDK inhibitors (CDKIs)
C) Growth factor receptors
D) Oncogenes

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: TGF-β signaling leads to transcriptional activation of CDK inhibitors (CDKIs) with growth-suppressing activity, while also repressing growth-promoting genes like MYC and cyclins.

QUESTION 20

Which genes does TGF-β signaling repress?

A) Tumor suppressor genes
B) DNA repair genes
C) MYC, CDK2, CDK4, and cyclins A and E
D) Apoptosis genes

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: TGF-β signaling represses growth-promoting genes such as MYC, CDK2, CDK4, and those encoding cyclins A and E, contributing to its antiproliferative effects.

QUESTION 21

What cellular behavior is abolished in cancer cells, allowing them to pile on top of one another?

A) Apoptosis
B) Contact inhibition
C) Senescence
D) Differentiation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Contact inhibition is abolished in cancer cells, allowing them to pile on top of one another and continue proliferating despite cell-cell contact.

QUESTION 22

Which molecule maintains contact inhibition and is lost in malignant cells?

A) N-cadherin
B) E-cadherin
C) Integrin
D) Selectin

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: E-cadherin maintains contact inhibition, which is lost in malignant cells, allowing them to overcome this normal growth-limiting mechanism.

QUESTION 23

What protein does the NF2 tumor suppressor gene produce?

A) E-cadherin
B) β-catenin
C) Neurofibromin-2 (merlin)
D) APC

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The NF2 tumor suppressor gene produces neurofibromin-2 (merlin), which facilitates E-cadherin-mediated contact inhibition.

QUESTION 24

How does the APC gene exert antiproliferative actions?

A) By activating p53
B) By regulating destruction of cytoplasmic β-catenin
C) By inhibiting RB phosphorylation
D) By blocking TGF-β receptors

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The APC gene exerts antiproliferative actions by regulating the destruction of cytoplasmic β-catenin, preventing its nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity.

QUESTION 25

What happens when APC is mutated and lost?

A) β-catenin is destroyed
B) β-catenin accumulates, translocates to nucleus, acts as growth-promoting transcription factor
C) Cell cycle arrest occurs
D) Apoptosis is induced

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: With APC mutation and loss, β-catenin is not destroyed, accumulates in the cytoplasm, translocates to the nucleus, and acts as a growth-promoting transcription factor.

QUESTION 26

What syndrome is associated with germline mutation of the APC gene?

A) Lynch syndrome
B) Li-Fraumeni syndrome
C) Familial adenomatous polyposis
D) Hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome involves inheritance of a germline mutation in the APC gene, with sporadic loss of the normal allele causing development of hundreds of colonic polyps at a young age.

QUESTION 27

What percentage of sporadic colon cancers show somatic loss of both APC alleles?

A) 30%
B) 50%
C) 70%
D) 90%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Somatic loss of both alleles of the APC gene is seen in approximately 70% of sporadic colon cancers, demonstrating its importance in colorectal carcinogenesis.

QUESTION 28

What are the two main pathways that can initiate apoptosis?

A) Intrinsic and extrinsic pathways
B) Mitochondrial and nuclear pathways
C) Early and late pathways
D) Fast and slow pathways

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: Apoptosis can be initiated through extrinsic (death receptor) or intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathways, both resulting in activation of a proteolytic caspase cascade.

QUESTION 29

What regulates mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization in apoptosis?

A) p53 only
B) Balance between pro-apoptotic (BAX, BAK) and anti-apoptotic molecules (BCL2, BCL-XL)
C) Caspases only
D) DNA damage sensors

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization is regulated by the balance between pro-apoptotic molecules (e.g., BAX, BAK) and anti-apoptotic molecules (BCL2, BCL-XL).

QUESTION 30

What is the role of BH3-only proteins in apoptosis?

A) Inhibit apoptosis
B) Regulate balance between pro- and anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members
C) Directly destroy cells
D) Repair DNA damage

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: BH3-only proteins (BAD, BID, and PUMA) regulate the balance between pro- and anti-apoptotic members of the BCL2 family, tilting it in favor of pro-apoptotic molecules to activate apoptosis.

QUESTION 31

How do BH3-only molecules activate apoptosis?

A) By inhibiting pro-apoptotic molecules
B) By tilting balance in favor of pro-apoptotic molecules
C) By directly activating caspases
D) By preventing mitochondrial function

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: BH3-only molecules activate apoptosis by tilting the balance in favor of the pro-apoptotic molecules, promoting mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and caspase activation.

QUESTION 32

What is autophagy?

A) Cell death pathway
B) Stress-induced process where cells consume their own components
C) Cell division process
D) DNA repair mechanism

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Autophagy is a stress-induced process where cells consume their own components, which cancer cells may avoid through mutations or corrupt to provide parts for continued growth.

QUESTION 33

How can cancer cells manipulate autophagy?

A) Always activate it
B) Always inhibit it
C) Accumulate mutations to avoid it or corrupt it to support growth
D) Have no interaction with autophagy

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Cancer cells may accumulate mutations to avoid autophagy (which could lead to cell death), or may corrupt the process to provide cellular components for continued growth.

QUESTION 34

What happens to telomeres in normal cells with each cell division?

A) They lengthen
B) They shorten
C) They remain unchanged
D) They duplicate

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Telomeres shorten with each cell division in normal cells due to incomplete replication of chromosome ends, eventually activating cell cycle checkpoints leading to senescence.

QUESTION 35

What is the consequence of shortened telomeres in normal cells with intact checkpoints?

A) Unlimited proliferation
B) Senescence
C) Apoptosis immediately
D) Increased growth rate

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Shortened telomeres in normal cells with intact checkpoints eventually activate cell cycle checkpoints, leading to senescence and placing a limit on the number of divisions.

QUESTION 36

What happens when cells have disabled checkpoints and shortened telomeres?

A) Immediate cell death
B) Senescence
C) Massive chromosomal instability and mitotic crisis
D) Normal cell function

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In cells with disabled checkpoints, DNA repair pathways are inappropriately activated by shortened telomeres, leading to massive chromosomal instability and mitotic crisis.

QUESTION 37

How do tumor cells achieve immortality?

A) By preventing cell division
B) By reactivating telomerase
C) By stopping DNA replication
D) By increasing apoptosis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Tumor cells reactivate telomerase, thus staving off mitotic catastrophe from critically shortened telomeres and achieving unlimited replicative potential (immortality).

QUESTION 38

What is the fundamental characteristic of tumor suppressor genes?

A) They promote cell proliferation
B) They apply brakes to cell proliferation
C) They have no effect on cell growth
D) They only affect cell migration

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The proteins encoded by tumor suppressor genes apply brakes to cell proliferation. Disruptions of such genes render cells refractory to growth inhibition.

QUESTION 39

How many copies of a tumor suppressor gene must be dysfunctional for tumor development?

A) One copy is sufficient
B) Both copies must be dysfunctional
C) Either one or both
D) Three copies

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Unlike oncogenes (which require only one mutated copy), both copies of a tumor suppressor gene must be dysfunctional for tumor development to occur.

QUESTION 40

What is the clinical consequence of heterozygosity at the RB locus?

A) Aggressive cancer
B) Mild cancer
C) Not neoplastic
D) Increased cancer risk only

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Heterozygosity at the Rb locus (one normal, one mutated allele) is not neoplastic. Both alleles must be lost for tumor development, illustrating the two-hit hypothesis.

QUESTION 41

What cancers besides retinoblastoma show homozygous loss of RB gene?

A) Only retinoblastoma
B) Multiple other cancers
C) No other cancers
D) Only eye cancers

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Homozygous loss or mutation of the Rb gene is seen in retinoblastoma and many other cancers, demonstrating its broader role as a tumor suppressor beyond its tissue of discovery.

QUESTION 42

Almost all cancers have a disabled G1 checkpoint due to what?

A) Only RB mutations
B) RB mutation or mutations affecting RB function (cyclin D, CDK4, CDKIs)
C) Only p53 mutations
D) Only cyclin mutations

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Almost all cancers have a disabled G1 checkpoint due to either RB mutation or mutations in genes that affect Rb function, such as cyclin D, CDK4, and CDK inhibitors.

QUESTION 43

What is the relationship between TGF-β receptors I and II in signal transduction?

A) They function independently
B) They form a complex upon ligand binding
C) Only receptor I is active
D) They antagonize each other

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: TGF-β regulates cellular processes by binding to a complex composed of TGF-β receptors I and II. Dimerization of the receptors upon ligand binding initiates the signaling cascade.

QUESTION 44

In sporadic retinoblastoma, what is the origin of both hits?

A) Both are inherited
B) One inherited, one somatic
C) Both are somatic mutations in one retinoblast
D) Environmental factors only

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In sporadic cases, both normal RB alleles are lost by somatic mutation in one retinoblast, requiring two independent mutational events in the same cell.

QUESTION 45

What members of the BCL2 family are pro-apoptotic?

A) BCL2 and BCL-XL
B) BAX and BAK
C) BH3-only proteins only
D) All BCL2 family members

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic members of the BCL2 family that promote mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, while BCL2 and BCL-XL are anti-apoptotic.

QUESTION 46

What members of the BCL2 family are anti-apoptotic?

A) BAX and BAK
B) BCL2 and BCL-XL
C) BH3-only proteins
D) Caspases

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: BCL2 and BCL-XL are anti-apoptotic molecules that prevent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and inhibit apoptosis, opposing the actions of BAX and BAK.

QUESTION 47

What inevitably happens to polyps in familial adenomatous polyposis?

A) They remain benign forever
B) They spontaneously regress
C) One or more evolve into colonic cancer
D) They never change

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In familial adenomatous polyposis, patients develop hundreds of colonic polyps at a young age, and inevitably one or more of these polyps evolve into colonic cancer.

QUESTION 48

Which genes does activated p53 control in response to stress?

A) Only cell cycle genes
B) Genes involved in cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, senescence, and apoptosis
C) Only apoptosis genes
D) Only DNA repair genes

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Activated p53 controls the expression and activity of genes involved in multiple protective responses: cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, cellular senescence, and apoptosis.

QUESTION 49

What is the functional consequence of RB binding to E2F?

A) Activation of S phase genes
B) Prevention of transcription of genes required for DNA replication
C) Enhanced cell proliferation
D) Immediate apoptosis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: When hypophosphorylated Rb binds to E2F transcription factor, it prevents E2F from activating transcription of genes required for DNA replication, such as cyclin E, thus blocking cell cycle progression.

QUESTION 50

What fundamental process in carcinogenesis involves failure of growth inhibition?

A) Enhanced apoptosis
B) Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals
C) Increased differentiation
D) Reduced mutation rate

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Failure of growth inhibition (insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals) is fundamental in carcinogenesis. Disruption of tumor suppressor genes renders cells refractory to growth inhibition and mimics growth-promoting effects.

Title: LIPID AND LIPOPROTEIN DISORDERS MCQs
Content:
40 COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1

Which lipoprotein is responsible for transporting dietary triglycerides from the intestines to tissues?

A) VLDL
B) LDL
C) Chylomicrons
D) HDL

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Chylomicrons are the largest lipoproteins and transport dietary triglycerides from the intestines to other tissues. They are primarily involved in the transport of dietary fats.

QUESTION 2

What is the primary function of HDL cholesterol?

A) Transport cholesterol to peripheral tissues
B) Transport cholesterol from cells back to the liver for excretion
C) Transport dietary fats from intestines
D) Store triglycerides

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: HDL (High-Density Lipoprotein) transports cholesterol from cells and tissues back to the liver for excretion, earning it the name "good cholesterol." High HDL levels are associated with lower cardiovascular risk.

QUESTION 3

Which enzyme is responsible for breaking down triglycerides in adipose tissue during lipolysis?

A) Lipoprotein lipase
B) Hormone-sensitive lipase
C) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
D) Fatty acid synthase

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Hormone-sensitive lipase breaks down triglycerides into glycerol and free fatty acids, primarily in adipose tissue during lipolysis in response to hormonal signals.

QUESTION 4

What happens to VLDL as it loses triglycerides?

A) It becomes chylomicrons
B) It transforms into LDL
C) It becomes HDL
D) It is excreted

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: VLDL (Very-Low-Density Lipoprotein) carries triglycerides from the liver to tissues. As VLDL loses triglycerides through lipoprotein lipase action, it transforms into LDL.

QUESTION 5

Which hormone promotes lipogenesis and inhibits lipolysis?

A) Glucagon
B) Epinephrine
C) Insulin
D) Cortisol

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Insulin promotes lipogenesis (fat synthesis) and inhibits lipolysis (fat breakdown), while glucagon and epinephrine have opposite effects, stimulating lipolysis.

QUESTION 6

What is the genetic defect in familial hypercholesterolemia?

A) Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase
B) Mutation in LDL receptor genes
C) Apolipoprotein E defect
D) HDL receptor mutation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Familial hypercholesterolemia results from mutations affecting LDL receptors, leading to elevated LDL cholesterol. Heterozygous form has one mutated allele; homozygous has both alleles mutated.

QUESTION 7

Which clinical sign consists of yellowish nodules commonly found on the Achilles tendon in hypercholesterolemia?

A) Xanthelasma
B) Tendon xanthomas
C) Eruptive xanthomas
D) Arcus senilis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Tendon xanthomas are yellowish nodules on tendons, commonly around the Achilles tendon or hands, characteristic of severe hypercholesterolemia, particularly familial hypercholesterolemia.

QUESTION 8

What condition can severe hypertriglyceridemia lead to?

A) Stroke
B) Acute pancreatitis
C) Hypothyroidism
D) Renal failure

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Severe hypertriglyceridemia can lead to acute pancreatitis, presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. This is a serious complication of markedly elevated triglyceride levels.

QUESTION 9

What is lipemia retinalis?

A) Fatty deposits on eyelids
B) Milky appearance of retina due to extremely elevated triglycerides
C) Vision loss from cholesterol
D) Retinal hemorrhage

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Lipemia retinalis is a rare condition where triglycerides are extremely elevated (usually >2000-4000 mg/dL), leading to a milky appearance of the retinal vessels during eye examination.

QUESTION 10

Which statin is commonly used to lower LDL cholesterol?

A) Fenofibrate
B) Atorvastatin
C) Ezetimibe
D) Niacin

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Atorvastatin is a statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) that is the primary treatment for lowering LDL cholesterol. Other statins include simvastatin and rosuvastatin.

QUESTION 11

What is the primary metabolic pathway for fatty acid breakdown in mitochondria?

A) De novo lipogenesis
B) Beta-oxidation
C) Lipolysis
D) Glycolysis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Beta-oxidation is the process where free fatty acids are transported to mitochondria and converted into acetyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle for energy production.

QUESTION 12

Which apolipoprotein defect is responsible for familial dysbetalipoproteinemia?

A) Apolipoprotein A1
B) Apolipoprotein B
C) Apolipoprotein E
D) Apolipoprotein C

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia results from genetic defects in apolipoprotein E, leading to elevated IDL (Intermediate-Density Lipoprotein) cholesterol and premature atherosclerosis.

QUESTION 13

What is the characteristic clinical finding of palmar xanthomas?

A) Found in familial hypertriglyceridemia
B) Associated with familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
C) Seen only in children
D) Present in hypothyroidism

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Palmar xanthomas (yellowish deposits on the palms) along with tuberous xanthomas on elbows and knees are characteristic of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.

QUESTION 14

Which medication class primarily lowers triglycerides and sometimes raises HDL?

A) Statins
B) Fibrates
C) Bile acid sequestrants
D) PCSK9 inhibitors

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Fibrates (such as fenofibrate and gemfibrozil) are primarily used to lower triglycerides and can sometimes raise HDL cholesterol levels.

QUESTION 15

What is Type I hyperlipoproteinemia characterized by?

A) Elevated LDL only
B) Elevated chylomicrons due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency
C) Elevated HDL
D) Low triglycerides

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Type I hyperlipoproteinemia is characterized by elevated chylomicrons due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency, leading to severe hypertriglyceridemia.

QUESTION 16

When do heart attacks typically occur in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia?

A) In childhood
B) Before age 50 years
C) After age 70 years
D) Never occur

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, early-onset cardiovascular disease with heart attacks or strokes often occurs at a younger age, typically before 50 years.

QUESTION 17

What is the mechanism of action of ezetimibe?

A) Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase
B) Reduces cholesterol absorption in the intestine
C) Increases bile acid excretion
D) Activates lipoprotein lipase

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption inhibitor that lowers LDL cholesterol by reducing cholesterol absorption in the intestine.

QUESTION 18

Which secondary condition is associated with elevated triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol?

A) Hypothyroidism
B) Diabetes mellitus (diabetic dyslipidemia)
C) Nephrotic syndrome
D) Liver cirrhosis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Diabetic dyslipidemia is characterized by elevated triglycerides and low HDL cholesterol due to insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus.

QUESTION 19

What laboratory test measures Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and Triglycerides?

A) Complete blood count
B) Lipid profile
C) Liver function tests
D) Renal panel

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A lipid profile (or lipid panel) is the standard test that measures total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides to assess lipid status.

QUESTION 20

In homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, when do heart attacks typically occur?

A) After age 60
B) In childhood or adolescence
C) In middle age (40-50 years)
D) They don't occur

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia presents with extremely high LDL cholesterol and severe atherosclerosis, with heart attacks occurring in childhood or adolescence.

QUESTION 21

What is xanthelasma?

A) Nodules on tendons
B) Yellowish patches on eyelids or around the eyes
C) Deposits on palms
D) Ring around the cornea

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Xanthelasma refers to yellowish patches on the eyelids or around the eyes, which are cholesterol deposits commonly seen in hypercholesterolemia.

QUESTION 22

Which class of drugs works by binding bile acids in the intestine to lower LDL cholesterol?

A) Statins
B) Fibrates
C) Bile acid sequestrants
D) PCSK9 inhibitors

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Bile acid sequestrants (like cholestyramine and colesevelam) lower LDL cholesterol by binding bile acids in the intestine, forcing the liver to use cholesterol to make more bile acids.

QUESTION 23

What is the recommended duration of moderate-intensity exercise per week for lipid management?

A) 30 minutes
B) 60 minutes
C) 150 minutes
D) 300 minutes

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Regular physical activity of at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week (such as brisk walking or cycling) is recommended for improving lipid profiles.

QUESTION 24

Which lipoprotein is a transitional form between VLDL and LDL?

A) Chylomicrons
B) HDL
C) IDL (Intermediate-Density Lipoprotein)
D) Lipoprotein (a)

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: IDL (Intermediate-Density Lipoprotein) is a transitional form between VLDL and LDL, involved in lipid metabolism as VLDL loses triglycerides.

QUESTION 25

What enzyme is key in lipogenesis (fatty acid synthesis)?

A) Hormone-sensitive lipase
B) Lipoprotein lipase
C) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase
D) Carnitine palmitoyltransferase

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is a key enzyme in lipogenesis, catalyzing the first committed step in fatty acid synthesis by converting acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA.

QUESTION 26

Which condition is characterized by edema and elevated cholesterol/triglycerides due to protein loss in urine?

A) Hypothyroidism
B) Nephrotic syndrome
C) Diabetes
D) Liver cirrhosis

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Nephrotic syndrome presents with edema (swelling of legs, ankles, face) due to protein loss in urine, accompanied by elevated cholesterol and triglycerides.

QUESTION 27

What are PCSK9 inhibitors particularly useful for?

A) Lowering triglycerides only
B) Raising HDL only
C) Significantly lowering LDL cholesterol in familial hypercholesterolemia
D) Treating diabetes

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: PCSK9 inhibitors (like alirocumab and evolocumab) significantly lower LDL cholesterol and are especially useful for patients with familial hypercholesterolemia or those not achieving target levels with statins alone.

QUESTION 28

What is Type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia characterized by?

A) Elevated triglycerides only
B) Elevated LDL cholesterol
C) Elevated HDL only
D) Elevated chylomicrons

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia is characterized by elevated LDL cholesterol due to various genetic or environmental factors, increasing cardiovascular risk.

QUESTION 29

Which prescription omega-3 fatty acid is used to lower triglyceride levels?

A) Atorvastatin
B) Icosapent ethyl
C) Ezetimibe
D) Cholestyramine

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Icosapent ethyl is a prescription form of omega-3 fatty acid used specifically to lower triglyceride levels in patients with hypertriglyceridemia.

QUESTION 30

What lipid abnormality is associated with hypothyroidism?

A) Low LDL and low total cholesterol
B) Elevated total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol
C) High HDL only
D) Low triglycerides

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Hypothyroid dyslipidemia is characterized by elevated total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol due to decreased LDL receptor activity caused by thyroid hormone deficiency.

QUESTION 31

Where does de novo lipogenesis primarily occur?

A) Muscle and brain
B) Liver and adipose tissue
C) Kidney and spleen
D) Lungs and heart

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: De novo lipogenesis, the conversion of excess carbohydrates and proteins into fatty acids, primarily occurs in the liver and adipose tissue.

QUESTION 32

What is Type V hyperlipoproteinemia characterized by?

A) Low cholesterol
B) Elevated chylomicrons and VLDL
C) Elevated HDL only
D) Normal lipid levels

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Type V hyperlipoproteinemia is characterized by elevated chylomicrons and VLDL, often due to lipoprotein lipase deficiency or genetic conditions, leading to severe hypertriglyceridemia.

QUESTION 33

Which dietary modification is recommended to lower LDL cholesterol?

A) Increase saturated fats
B) Reduce saturated and trans fats
C) Eliminate all fats
D) Increase red meat consumption

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Reducing intake of saturated and trans fats (found in red meat, processed foods, and high-fat dairy products) is recommended to lower LDL cholesterol levels.

QUESTION 34

What is familial combined hyperlipidemia associated with?

A) Elevated LDL cholesterol only
B) Elevated LDL cholesterol and triglycerides
C) Low HDL only
D) Normal lipid levels

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Familial combined hyperlipidemia is characterized by elevated levels of both LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, often associated with premature cardiovascular disease.

QUESTION 35

What is the main form of stored energy in the body?

A) Cholesterol
B) Phospholipids
C) Triglycerides
D) Fatty acids

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Triglycerides are the main form of stored energy in the body, stored primarily in adipose tissue and released during lipolysis when energy is needed.

QUESTION 36

Which medications can induce secondary dyslipidemia?

A) Antibiotics only
B) Corticosteroids and antiretrovirals
C) Antihypertensives only
D) Analgesics

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Certain drugs such as corticosteroids and antiretrovirals can induce dyslipidemia as a side effect, requiring monitoring and potential lipid management.

QUESTION 37

What is the role of fatty acid synthase?

A) Breaks down fatty acids
B) Multi-enzyme complex that synthesizes fatty acids from acetyl-CoA
C) Transports fatty acids
D) Oxidizes fatty acids

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Fatty acid synthase is a multi-enzyme complex that synthesizes fatty acids from acetyl-CoA during lipogenesis, building long-chain fatty acids through repeated cycles.

QUESTION 38

What clinical sign is arcus senilis?

A) Yellowish deposits on eyelids
B) Ring around the cornea
C) Nodules on tendons
D) Deposits on palms

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Arcus senilis is a ring around the cornea that can be a sign of hyperlipidemia, particularly in younger individuals, though it may also occur normally with aging.

QUESTION 39

What percentage of sporadic colon cancers might be affected by lipid metabolism through APC gene mutations?

A) This question is incorrectly placed - APC relates to cancer, not lipid disorders
B) 50%
C) 70%
D) 100%

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: This appears to be a question error. APC gene mutations relate to colorectal cancer pathogenesis (from the oncology material), not lipid disorders. The documents should not be mixed in question formation.

QUESTION 40

Which lipoprotein primarily carries cholesterol from the liver to peripheral cells?

A) HDL
B) LDL
C) Chylomicrons
D) VLDL

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: LDL (Low-Density Lipoprotein) primarily carries cholesterol from the liver to cells throughout the body. High levels of LDL can lead to plaque buildup in arteries, earning it the name "bad cholesterol."

Title: INTRODUCTION TO NEOPLASIA MCQs
Content:
40 COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1

What is the definition of neoplasia?

A) Inflammation of tissues
B) Formation of new, abnormal growth of tissue
C) Repair of damaged tissue
D) Normal tissue regeneration

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Neoplasia is defined as the formation of new, abnormal growth of tissue. The term comes from "neo" (new) and "plasia" (growth or formation).

QUESTION 2

What does the term "tumour" originally mean?

A) Cancer
B) Malignant growth
C) Swelling in inflammation
D) Abnormal cell division

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The term "tumour" originally meant swelling in inflammation before it came to be associated with neoplastic growths. It derives from the Latin word for swelling.

QUESTION 3

What is the origin of the word "cancer"?

A) Greek word for growth
B) Latin word for crab
C) Latin word for swelling
D) Greek word for tumor

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Cancer comes from the Latin word for crab. It is the common term for all malignant tumours, possibly named because of the crab-like spreading pattern of some cancers.

QUESTION 4

What suffix is typically used to designate benign neoplasms?

A) -sarcoma
B) -carcinoma
C) -oma
D) -plasia

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Benign neoplasms are typically designated with the suffix "-oma" added to the cell of origin, such as fibroma, lipoma, or chondroma.

QUESTION 5

What is a benign neoplasm of adipose tissue called?

A) Liposarcoma
B) Lipoma
C) Adenoma
D) Fibroma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A benign neoplasm of adipose (fat) tissue is called a lipoma. The suffix "-oma" indicates it is benign, and "lipo-" refers to fat.

QUESTION 6

What is a malignant neoplasm of mesenchymal origin generally called?

A) Carcinoma
B) Adenoma
C) Sarcoma
D) Papilloma

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Malignant neoplasms of mesenchymal origin are usually called sarcomas, such as liposarcoma (malignant fat tumor) or fibrosarcoma (malignant fibrous tumor).

QUESTION 7

What is a malignant neoplasm of epithelial origin called?

A) Sarcoma
B) Carcinoma
C) Lymphoma
D) Melanoma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Malignant neoplasms of epithelial origin are called carcinomas, such as squamous cell carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma.

QUESTION 8

What is a benign neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin called?

A) Adenoma
B) Adenocarcinoma
C) Papilloma
D) Fibroma

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: A benign neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin is called an adenoma (solid) or cystadenoma (if it forms large cysts).

QUESTION 9

What is a malignant neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin called?

A) Adenoma
B) Squamous cell carcinoma
C) Adenocarcinoma
D) Sarcoma

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: A malignant neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin is called an adenocarcinoma, indicating both its glandular nature and malignant behavior.

QUESTION 10

What term describes a benign neoplasm with finger-like or warty projections?

A) Adenoma
B) Papilloma
C) Fibroma
D) Lipoma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A papilloma is a benign neoplasm characterized by finger-like or warty projections, commonly seen on skin or mucosal surfaces.

QUESTION 11

How many new cancer cases were there globally in the year 2000?

A) 5 million
B) 10 million
C) 15 million
D) 20 million

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: In the year 2000, there were 10 million new cancer cases globally, with 6 million cancer deaths that year.

QUESTION 12

How many new cancer cases were there globally in 2020?

A) 10.1 million
B) 15.5 million
C) 18.1 million
D) 20.5 million

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In 2020, there were 18.1 million new cancer cases globally, showing a significant increase from 10 million in 2000.

QUESTION 13

What proportion of global deaths in 2020 were due to cancer?

A) 1 in 10
B) 1 in 8
C) 1 in 6
D) 1 in 4

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In 2020, cancer caused 10 million deaths globally, accounting for 1 in 6 deaths worldwide, highlighting its massive public health impact.

QUESTION 14

In Kenya, how many new cancer cases were there in 2012?

A) 28,500
B) 32,987
C) 37,000
D) 47,887

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In Kenya in 2012, there were 37,000 new cancer cases and 28,500 deaths from cancer.

QUESTION 15

In Kenya in 2018, what was cancer's ranking as a cause of death?

A) Leading cause
B) 2nd leading cause
C) 3rd leading cause
D) 5th leading cause

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: In Kenya in 2018, cancer was the 3rd leading cause of death, with 47,887 new cases and 32,987 deaths.

QUESTION 16

What is the term for the study of tumors?

A) Pathology
B) Oncology
C) Cytology
D) Histology

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Oncology is the study of tumors, derived from the Greek word "oncos" meaning tumor. It encompasses the study of cancer diagnosis, treatment, and prevention.

QUESTION 17

What is a benign neoplasm of fibrous connective tissue called?

A) Fibrosarcoma
B) Fibroma
C) Lipoma
D) Chondroma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A benign neoplasm of fibrous connective tissue is called a fibroma. The malignant counterpart would be a fibrosarcoma.

QUESTION 18

What is a benign neoplasm of cartilage called?

A) Osteoma
B) Chondrosarcoma
C) Chondroma
D) Fibroma

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: A benign neoplasm of cartilage is called a chondroma. The malignant version is called chondrosarcoma.

QUESTION 19

Which of the following is an example of an "oddly named" neoplasm that doesn't follow standard nomenclature?

A) Fibroma
B) Adenoma
C) Melanoma
D) Lipoma

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Melanoma is oddly named because despite having the "-oma" suffix typically used for benign tumors, it is actually malignant. Seminoma is another example of unusual nomenclature.

QUESTION 20

What aspect of neoplasia deals with the study of disease distribution in populations?

A) Aetiology
B) Epidemiology
C) Pathogenesis
D) Morphology

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Epidemiology deals with the study of disease distribution, patterns, and determinants in populations, including cancer incidence, prevalence, and risk factors.

QUESTION 21

What aspect of neoplasia deals with the study of disease causation?

A) Aetiology
B) Epidemiology
C) Morphology
D) Treatment

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: Aetiology (or etiology) is the study of disease causation, examining factors that cause or contribute to the development of neoplasms.

QUESTION 22

What term describes the mechanism by which disease develops?

A) Aetiology
B) Epidemiology
C) Pathogenesis
D) Morphology

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Pathogenesis refers to the mechanism or sequence of events by which a disease develops, including the molecular and cellular changes that occur.

QUESTION 23

What is a malignant neoplasm of fat tissue called?

A) Lipoma
B) Liposarcoma
C) Adenoma
D) Fibrosarcoma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A malignant neoplasm of fat (adipose) tissue is called a liposarcoma. The benign counterpart is a lipoma.

QUESTION 24

What type of carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium?

A) Adenocarcinoma
B) Squamous cell carcinoma
C) Basal cell carcinoma
D) Transitional cell carcinoma

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium and is a malignant neoplasm of epithelial origin, commonly found in skin, lung, and other organs.

QUESTION 25

Between 2012 and 2018 in Kenya, by approximately how much did new cancer cases increase?

A) 5,000
B) 10,887
C) 15,000
D) 20,000

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: New cancer cases in Kenya increased from 37,000 in 2012 to 47,887 in 2018, an increase of approximately 10,887 cases, representing about a 29% increase.

QUESTION 26

What is the significance of studying morphological changes in neoplasia?

A) To understand disease distribution
B) To identify structural/microscopic characteristics for diagnosis
C) To determine treatment costs
D) To calculate survival rates

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Studying morphological changes involves examining the structural and microscopic characteristics of neoplasms, which is crucial for accurate diagnosis and classification.

QUESTION 27

What is a cystadenoma?

A) Malignant glandular tumor
B) Benign glandular tumor forming large cysts
C) Benign fibrous tumor
D) Malignant cystic tumor

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A cystadenoma is a benign neoplasm of glandular epithelial origin that forms large cysts, as opposed to an adenoma which is solid.

QUESTION 28

What does the study of clinical features in neoplasia involve?

A) Laboratory investigations only
B) Symptoms, signs, and manifestations of the disease
C) Statistical analysis
D) Genetic testing

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The study of clinical features involves examining the symptoms, signs, and manifestations that patients with neoplasms present with, which aids in diagnosis and management.

QUESTION 29

What is the increase in global cancer deaths from 2000 to 2020?

A) 2 million
B) 4 million
C) 6 million
D) 8 million

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Global cancer deaths increased from 6 million in 2000 to 10 million in 2020, an increase of 4 million deaths, representing about a 67% increase.

QUESTION 30

Why are preventive strategies important in neoplasia?

A) To reduce treatment costs only
B) To reduce incidence and mortality of cancer
C) To improve diagnostic techniques
D) To increase research funding

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Preventive strategies are crucial for reducing the incidence and mortality of cancer by addressing modifiable risk factors, implementing screening programs, and promoting healthy lifestyles.

QUESTION 31

What is the origin tissue for a benign bone tumor called osteoma?

A) Cartilage
B) Bone
C) Muscle
D) Fat

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: An osteoma is a benign neoplasm of bone tissue. The malignant counterpart would be an osteosarcoma.

QUESTION 32

What percentage increase in new cancer cases occurred globally from 2000 to 2020?

A) 50%
B) 61%
C) 81%
D) 100%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: New cancer cases increased from 10 million in 2000 to 18.1 million in 2020, an increase of 8.1 million, which represents an 81% increase.

QUESTION 33

What does the term "neoplasm" literally mean?

A) Old growth
B) New growth
C) Abnormal cell
D) Tissue damage

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Neoplasm literally means "new growth," derived from "neo" (new) and "plasm" (formation or growth), referring to abnormal tissue proliferation.

QUESTION 34

Which of the following is NOT a typical area of significance in studying neoplasia?

A) Aetiology
B) Pathogenesis
C) Agricultural production
D) Clinical features

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Agricultural production is not relevant to the study of neoplasia. The significant areas include aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, morphological changes, clinical features, investigations, treatments, complications, and preventive strategies.

QUESTION 35

What is a malignant neoplasm of fibrous connective tissue called?

A) Fibroma
B) Fibrosarcoma
C) Fibroadenoma
D) Fibrocartilage

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A malignant neoplasm of fibrous connective tissue is called a fibrosarcoma. The benign version is called a fibroma.

QUESTION 36

What distinguishes benign from malignant neoplasms in nomenclature for mesenchymal tumors?

A) Cell size
B) Addition of "sarcoma" for malignant tumors
C) Location only
D) Growth rate

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: For mesenchymal tumors, benign tumors use the suffix "-oma" (e.g., lipoma, fibroma), while malignant tumors use "sarcoma" (e.g., liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma).

QUESTION 37

What is the primary reason for studying investigations in neoplasia?

A) To increase healthcare costs
B) For accurate diagnosis and staging
C) For legal documentation only
D) To delay treatment

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Studying investigations (laboratory tests, imaging, biopsies) is crucial for accurate diagnosis, staging, and determining appropriate treatment strategies for neoplasms.

QUESTION 38

Between 2012 and 2018 in Kenya, approximately how much did cancer deaths increase?

A) 2,487
B) 4,487
C) 6,487
D) 8,487

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Cancer deaths in Kenya increased from 28,500 in 2012 to 32,987 in 2018, an increase of 4,487 deaths, representing about a 16% increase.

QUESTION 39

Why is understanding complications important in neoplasia study?

A) For research purposes only
B) To anticipate and manage treatment-related and disease-related complications
C) For statistical analysis
D) To increase patient costs

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Understanding complications helps clinicians anticipate and manage both disease-related complications (e.g., metastases, organ failure) and treatment-related complications (e.g., chemotherapy side effects).

QUESTION 40

What is the fundamental difference between "tumor" and "neoplasm" in modern usage?

A) Tumor is always malignant; neoplasm is always benign
B) Tumor originally meant swelling; neoplasm specifically refers to abnormal new growth
C) They mean exactly the same thing
D) Tumor refers to epithelial; neoplasm to mesenchymal

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: While the terms are often used interchangeably, "tumor" originally meant any swelling (including inflammatory swelling), whereas "neoplasm" specifically refers to abnormal new tissue growth, though both terms now commonly refer to neoplastic growths.

Title: INTRODUCTION TO GENETIC DISORDERS AND MUTATIONS MCQs
Content:
40 COMPREHENSIVE QUESTIONS

QUESTION 1

What is the lifetime frequency of genetic disease per 1000 individuals?

A) 250
B) 450
C) 670
D) 850

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The lifetime frequency of genetic disease is thought to be 670 per 1000 individuals, which is higher than widely appreciated, meaning approximately 67% of people will develop some genetic-related condition.

QUESTION 2

Approximately how many genes do human beings have?

A) 10,000
B) 20,000
C) 30,000
D) 50,000

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Human beings have approximately 30,000 genes, though less than 2% of these actually code for proteins, with more than half being repetitive nucleotide sequences.

QUESTION 3

What percentage of human DNA codes for proteins?

A) Less than 2%
B) About 10%
C) About 25%
D) More than 50%

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: Less than 2% of human DNA codes for proteins. More than half of the genome consists of repetitive nucleotide sequences of mysterious function.

QUESTION 4

What percentage of DNA sequence do individuals share with each other?

A) 90.0%
B) 95.5%
C) 99.0%
D) 99.9%

ANSWER: D

EXPLANATION: Individuals share 99.9% of their DNA sequence with each other, with only 0.1% (about 3 million base pairs) accounting for the diversity in the human race.

QUESTION 5

Approximately what percentage of early pregnancy miscarriages have demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities?

A) 25%
B) 35%
C) 50%
D) 75%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Approximately 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages have demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities, highlighting the significant impact of genetic disorders on early development.

QUESTION 6

What percentage of individuals under 25 years develop a serious disease with significant genetic component?

A) 1%
B) 5%
C) 10%
D) 15%

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Approximately 5% of individuals under 25 years of age develop a serious disease with a significant genetic component, demonstrating the clinical impact of genetic disorders in young populations.

QUESTION 7

What is a point mutation?

A) Deletion of entire chromosome
B) Substitution of a single nucleotide base by a different base
C) Addition of three nucleotides
D) Inversion of chromosome segment

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A point mutation is the substitution of a single nucleotide base by a different base, resulting in substitution of an amino acid within a protein, such as in sickle cell anemia.

QUESTION 8

What type of mutation is exemplified by sickle cell anemia?

A) Frameshift mutation
B) Point mutation
C) Trinucleotide repeat mutation
D) Chromosomal deletion

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation where a single nucleotide substitution leads to the replacement of glutamic acid with valine in the β-globin chain.

QUESTION 9

What is a frameshift mutation?

A) Substitution of one base
B) Insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs altering the reading frame
C) Amplification of three nucleotides
D) Chromosomal translocation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A frameshift mutation involves insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs that alters the reading frame of the DNA strand, changing all subsequent amino acids in the protein.

QUESTION 10

What type of mutation involves dynamic amplification of a sequence of three nucleotides?

A) Point mutation
B) Frameshift mutation
C) Trinucleotide repeat mutation
D) Missense mutation

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Trinucleotide repeat mutations involve dynamic amplification of a sequence of three nucleotides (often guanine and cytosine), with the degree of amplification increasing at gametogenesis.

QUESTION 11

Which disorder is an example of trinucleotide repeat mutation?

A) Sickle cell anemia
B) Down syndrome
C) Fragile X syndrome
D) Cystic fibrosis

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Fragile X syndrome is the classic example of a trinucleotide repeat mutation, involving expansion of CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene.

QUESTION 12

What are the three major categories of genetic disorders?

A) Infectious, inflammatory, neoplastic
B) Mutant genes, multifactorial inheritance, chromosomal aberrations
C) Congenital, acquired, hereditary
D) Autosomal, X-linked, mitochondrial

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The three major categories of genetic disorders are: diseases related to mutant genes of large effect, diseases with multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance, and diseases arising from chromosomal aberrations.

QUESTION 13

Which type of mutation affects germ cells?

A) Somatic mutations only
B) Mutations transmitted to progeny causing inherited diseases
C) Mutations causing cancer
D) Mutations causing congenital malformations only

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Mutations affecting germ cells are transmitted to progeny and cause inherited diseases, unlike somatic mutations which are not transmitted to offspring.

QUESTION 14

What do somatic cell mutations typically cause?

A) Inherited diseases only
B) Chromosomal aberrations
C) Cancers and some congenital malformations
D) Nothing - they are harmless

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Mutations affecting somatic cells are not transmitted to progeny but can cause cancers and some congenital malformations in the affected individual.

QUESTION 15

What is functional cloning (classic approach) in molecular genetics?

A) Random gene isolation
B) Starting with known affected protein to isolate and clone normal gene
C) Mapping disease to chromosome location
D) Gene therapy technique

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Functional cloning starts with a known affected protein (clinical phenotype), then isolates and clones the normal gene, and determines molecular changes affecting the gene.

QUESTION 16

What is positional cloning (candidate gene approach)?

A) Starting with known protein
B) Random gene selection
C) Mapping disease phenotype to chromosome location and cloning DNA from region
D) Mitochondrial gene analysis

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Positional cloning involves mapping a disease phenotype to a particular chromosome location, cloning several DNA pieces from the region in vitro, and identifying aberrant proteins from mutated genes.

QUESTION 17

Which of the following is produced using recombinant DNA technology by inserting genes into bacteria?

A) Antibiotics only
B) Growth hormone and erythropoietin
C) Vitamins
D) Natural killer cells

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Human biologically active agents like soluble TNF receptor, tissue plasminogen activator, growth hormone, and erythropoietin are produced by inserting requisite genes into bacteria or suitable cells in tissue culture.

QUESTION 18

What is gene therapy?

A) Use of antibiotics
B) Treating genetic diseases by transfer of somatic cells transfected with normal genes
C) Surgical correction of defects
D) Chemotherapy for cancer

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Gene therapy involves treating genetic diseases by transferring somatic cells that have been transfected with normal genes, though questions remain about whether benefits outweigh risks.

QUESTION 19

What is a missense mutation?

A) Silent mutation with no effect
B) Point mutation resulting in amino acid substitution
C) Mutation creating stop codon
D) Deletion of chromosome

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A missense mutation is a type of point mutation where nucleotide substitution results in a different amino acid being incorporated into the protein, potentially affecting protein function.

QUESTION 20

What is a nonsense mutation?

A) Point mutation with no effect
B) Point mutation creating premature stop codon
C) Frameshift mutation
D) Trinucleotide repeat

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: A nonsense mutation is a point mutation that creates a premature stop codon, leading to truncated protein production and usually loss of protein function.

QUESTION 21

Which diseases are now considered to have genetic components beyond "classic" genetic disorders?

A) Only single-gene disorders
B) Cardiovascular diseases, immunity disorders, cancers
C) Infectious diseases only
D) Nutritional deficiencies

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Beyond classic genetic disorders, cardiovascular diseases, disorders of immunity, and cancers are now recognized to have significant genetic components.

QUESTION 22

What characterizes diseases with multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance?

A) Single gene defect
B) Multiple genes plus environmental factors
C) Chromosomal abnormality only
D) Mitochondrial mutation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Diseases with multifactorial or polygenic inheritance result from the interaction of multiple genes along with environmental factors, rather than a single gene defect.

QUESTION 23

What is the key characteristic of trinucleotide repeat mutations?

A) They remain stable
B) They are dynamic with amplification increasing at gametogenesis
C) They only affect somatic cells
D) They cannot be inherited

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Trinucleotide repeat mutations are dynamic, meaning the degree of amplification increases during gametogenesis, which can lead to anticipation (worsening severity in successive generations).

QUESTION 24

What is genomic imprinting?

A) Random gene expression
B) Epigenetic influences where gene expression depends on parent of origin
C) Gene deletion
D) Chromosomal translocation

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon where the expression of certain genes depends on whether they were inherited from the mother or father, affecting disease transmission.

QUESTION 25

Which category of genetic disorders involves mitochondrial DNA mutations?

A) Major category
B) Other category beyond three major types
C) Not a recognized category
D) Same as chromosomal aberrations

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Diseases resulting from mutations in mitochondrial DNA constitute a separate category beyond the three major categories, with unique maternal inheritance patterns.

QUESTION 26

How can molecular probes be used in disease diagnosis?

A) Only for genetic diseases
B) For both genetic and nongenetic (e.g., infectious) diseases
C) Only for chromosomal disorders
D) Only for cancer

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Molecular probes can be used in diagnosis of both genetic diseases and nongenetic diseases such as infectious diseases, making them versatile diagnostic tools.

QUESTION 27

What is a permanent change in DNA called?

A) Transcription
B) Translation
C) Mutation
D) Replication

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Mutations are permanent changes in the DNA sequence that can be transmitted to progeny (if in germ cells) or cause disease in the individual (if in somatic cells).

QUESTION 28

What percentage of DNA is responsible for human diversity?

A) 0.1%
B) 1.0%
C) 5.0%
D) 10.0%

ANSWER: A

EXPLANATION: Only 0.1% of DNA (approximately 3 million base pairs) accounts for diversity in the human race, while individuals share 99.9% of their DNA sequence.

QUESTION 29

Which nucleotides are typically involved in trinucleotide repeat mutations?

A) Adenine and thymine
B) Guanine and cytosine
C) Adenine and guanine
D) Cytosine and thymine

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Trinucleotide repeat mutations typically involve sequences containing guanine and cytosine nucleotides, such as CGG repeats in Fragile X syndrome.

QUESTION 30

What application of genetics involves producing tissue plasminogen activator?

A) Gene therapy
B) Disease diagnosis
C) Production of human biologically active agents
D) Positional cloning

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Tissue plasminogen activator is a human biologically active agent produced using recombinant DNA technology by inserting genes into bacteria or tissue culture cells.

QUESTION 31

What is the extremity range of genetic disorders?

A) All are equally severe
B) Varies from mild/hidden to severe/lethal
C) All are mild
D) All are lethal

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The extremity of genetic disorders varies widely - some may be mild or remain hidden, while others cause early miscarriage or serious disease in young individuals.

QUESTION 32

What is the main difference between functional and positional cloning?

A) No difference
B) Functional starts with protein; positional starts with chromosome location
C) Functional is newer
D) Positional is obsolete

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Functional (classic) cloning starts with a known affected protein and works toward the gene, while positional (candidate gene) cloning starts by mapping disease to a chromosome location and works toward the protein.

QUESTION 33

What proportion of human genes consists of repetitive nucleotide sequences?

A) Less than 10%
B) About 25%
C) More than 50%
D) Exactly 75%

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: More than half (>50%) of human genes consist of repetitive nucleotide sequences of mysterious function, with less than 2% actually coding for proteins.

QUESTION 34

What raises the question "Do the benefits outweigh the risks?" in medical genetics?

A) Disease diagnosis
B) Gene therapy
C) Functional cloning
D) Molecular probes

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Gene therapy raises important ethical and safety questions about whether the benefits of treating genetic diseases by transferring normal genes outweigh the potential risks.

QUESTION 35

What happens in a frameshift mutation involving deletion of two base pairs?

A) No change in protein
B) Only one amino acid changes
C) Reading frame altered affecting all downstream amino acids
D) Gene is duplicated

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Deletion of two base pairs in a frameshift mutation alters the reading frame, changing the coding of all amino acids downstream from the mutation site, usually severely affecting protein function.

QUESTION 36

Which genetic disorder category includes diseases like Down syndrome?

A) Mutant genes of large effect
B) Multifactorial inheritance
C) Chromosomal aberrations
D) Mitochondrial mutations

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a disease arising from chromosomal aberrations, specifically having an extra copy of chromosome 21.

QUESTION 37

What is the significance of unknown genetic disorders being mild or hidden?

A) They are not important
B) True burden of genetic disease may be underestimated
C) They don't exist
D) They cannot be diagnosed

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: The fact that an unknown number of genetic disorders may be mild or remain hidden suggests that the true burden of genetic disease is likely higher than currently recognized.

QUESTION 38

What type of cells must be affected for a mutation to be inherited?

A) Somatic cells
B) Germ cells
C) Liver cells
D) Muscle cells

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Only mutations affecting germ cells (sperm or egg cells) can be transmitted to progeny and cause inherited diseases. Somatic cell mutations affect only the individual.

QUESTION 39

Which application of genetics helps in understanding the molecular basis of human disease?

A) Gene therapy only
B) Functional and positional cloning approaches
C) Production of biologics only
D) None of the above

ANSWER: B

EXPLANATION: Both functional cloning and positional cloning approaches help understand the molecular basis of human disease by identifying genes and proteins involved in disease processes.

QUESTION 40

What is the clinical implication of 50% of early miscarriages having chromosomal abnormalities?

A) Chromosomal abnormalities are rare
B) Most chromosomal abnormalities are compatible with life
C) Chromosomal abnormalities are major cause of pregnancy loss
D) All miscarriages are genetic

ANSWER: C

EXPLANATION: The fact that approximately 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages have demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities indicates that chromosomal abnormalities are a major cause of early pregnancy loss and many are incompatible with continued development.

Title: COMPLEX MULTIGENIC AND CYTOGENETIC DISORDERS - 50 MCQs
Content:
Comprehensive MCQ Practice Examination

Total Questions: 50
Time Suggested: 75 minutes
Instructions: Select the BEST answer for each question

SECTION A: GENETIC POLYMORPHISMS & COMPLEX DISORDERS (Questions 1-10)

Question 1

What is the minimum population frequency required for a genetic variant to be classified as a polymorphism?

A. 0.1%
B. 1%
C. 5%
D. 10%

Answer: B

Explanation: A polymorphism is defined as a genetic variant that has at least two alleles and occurs in at least 1% of the population.

Question 2

In complex multigenic disorders, what percentage of type 1 diabetes risk is contributed by a few HLA alleles?

A. 25%
B. 40%
C. More than 50%
D. 75%

Answer: C

Explanation: Of the 20 to 30 genes implicated in type 1 diabetes, a few HLA alleles contribute more than 50% of the risk, demonstrating that different polymorphisms vary significantly in their contribution.

Question 3

Which environmental factor is most commonly associated with unmasking the genetic trait in type 2 diabetes mellitus?

A. Smoking
B. Obesity
C. Alcohol consumption
D. Stress

Answer: B
