Title: MEDICAL ENTOMOLOGY PAST PAPER
Content:
DANIEL ROSASI - Comprehensive Study Guide

SECTION A: LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (20 Marks Each)

Question 1: Life Cycle of a Three-Host Tick (20 Marks)

With an illustration, outline the life cycle of a three-host tick

Answer:

Life Cycle Stages:

  1. Egg Stage (Fall)
    • Adult females drop off the third host after feeding, usually in the fall
    • Females lay eggs in the environment
    • Eggs hatch into six-legged larvae
    • Larvae overwinter in this stage
  2. Larval Stage (Spring - First Host)
    • In spring, larvae seek out and attach to the first host, usually a small rodent
    • Larvae feed on the first host
    • Later in summer, engorged larvae leave the first host
    • Larvae molt into nymphs, usually in fall
    • Ticks overwinter in the nymphal stage
  3. Nymphal Stage (Following Spring - Second Host)
    • During the following spring, nymphs seek out and attach to the second host
    • Second host is usually another rodent or lagomorph
    • Nymphs feed on the second host and drop off later in summer
    • Nymphs molt into adults off the host in late summer or fall
    • Adults overwinter in this stage
  4. Adult Stage (Next Spring - Third Host)
    • The next spring, adults seek out and attach to a third host
    • Third host is usually a larger herbivore (cervids, bovids), carnivore, or human
    • Adults feed and mate on the third host during summer
    • Females drop off the host in fall to continue the cycle
    • Females may reattach and feed multiple times

Important Notes:

  • The three hosts do not necessarily have to be different species or different individuals
  • Humans may serve as first, second, or third hosts

Question 2: Myiasis (20 Marks)

Discuss myiasis under the following sub-headings

A. AETIOLOGY (3 Marks)

  • Myiasis is the invasion of organs and tissues of humans or other vertebrates by fly larvae
  • Fly larvae feed on living or dead tissues or, in intestinal myiasis, on the host's ingested food
  • Flies in several genera may cause myiasis in humans

Important Species:

  • Dermatobia hominis - Primary human bot fly
  • Cochliomyia hominivorax - Primary screwworm fly (New World)
  • Chrysomya bezziana - Old World screwworm
  • Cordylobia anthropophaga - Tumbu fly
  • Cuterebra, Oestrus, Wohlfahrtia - Animal parasites that occasionally infect humans

B. PATHOGENESIS (5 Marks)

Types of Myiasis:

1. Accidental Myiasis

  • Usually involves eating food contaminated by eggs or larvae of non-parasitic flies (e.g., house flies)
  • Larvae may survive for some time in the intestine
  • No flies are specially adapted to cause intestinal myiasis in humans
  • Symptoms: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, blood discharge, vomiting
  • Living larvae may be passed in excreta or vomit

2. Obligatory Myiasis

  • Occurs in other mammals, not typically humans
  • Essential for fly maggots to live on a live host for at least part of their life
  • Examples: Larvae of Cordylobia anthropophaga, Cochliomyia hominivorax, Chrysomya bezziana, Dermatobia hominis, Wohlfahrtia magnifica
  • All obligatory parasites of humans and other vertebrates

3. Facultative Myiasis

  • Larvae are normally free-living, often attacking carcasses
  • Under certain conditions may infect living hosts
  • Urogenital myiasis: Occasionally occurs in humans, usually involving larvae of Musca or Fannia species
  • Ovipositing flies attracted to unhygienic discharges lay eggs near genital orifices
  • Hatching larvae enter genital orifice and pass up urogenital tract
  • Considerable pain may be caused during urination
  • Larvae may obstruct passages, causing discharge of mucus, blood, and eventually larvae

Different Terms for Myiasis by Body Part:

  • Dermal myiasis - Affects different parts of the body
  • Cutaneous myiasis - Skin infection
  • Intestinal/enteric/gastrointestinal myiasis - Digestive system
  • Ophthalmic myiasis - Eyes
  • Creeping myiasis - When larvae burrow under skin surface producing creeping eruption
  • Traumatic myiasis - When wounds become infested

C. DIAGNOSIS (3 Marks)

  • Diagnosis made by finding fly larvae in tissue
  • Identification to genus/species level involves comparing morphological structures:
    • Anterior and posterior spiracles
    • Mouthparts
    • Cephalopharyngeal skeleton
    • Cuticular spines
  • Travel history can be helpful for genus/species identification

D. TREATMENT (4 Marks)

  • Simple removal: When larvae occur in wounds, sores, dermal or subdermal tissues, removal under aseptic conditions is usually relatively simple
  • Complex removal: When larvae are deeply embedded in underlying tissues or have penetrated mucous membranes, eyes, frontal sinuses, or cavities, removal is more difficult
  • Surgery may be needed for deeply embedded larvae

E. CONTROL (6 Marks)

  1. Ash/salt on tables/latrines to discourage landing of flies
  2. Curtains to entrances of eateries to prevent fly entry
  3. Screens on windows to prevent fly entry
  4. Use of insecticides to kill flies
  5. Cover food and water during storage to avoid contamination
  6. Washing of fruits and vegetables
  7. Use of electric fly traps (emit purple light to attract and electrocute flies)

Question 4: Genetic-Based Control Methods for Vector-Borne Diseases (20 Marks)

Introduction

  • Insects are responsible for transmission of major infectious diseases
  • Recent advances in insect genomics and transformation technology provide new strategies for control
  • Genetic modification offers alternatives to conventional insect-based control strategies

Advantages of Genetic Control

  • Offers several advantages over conventional insecticide-based strategies
  • Caution required: Great caution needed regarding:
    • Safety after release into environment
    • Acceptance by target populations

Current Control Limitations

  • Current control measures heavily depend on insecticides
  • Adverse environmental effects
  • Prolonged use results in development of insecticide resistance

Two Broad Categories of Genetic Approach

1. Genetic Suppression of Vector Competence

  • Suppress ability of vectors to transmit pathogens
  • Specific to control of diseases transmitted by vectors (e.g., mosquitoes)

2. Genetic Suppression of Insect Populations

  • Suppress female-specific populations by releasing male-sterile or dominant lethal genes into environment
  • Applicable to control of any insects where genetic manipulation is feasible

Genetic Control of Mosquitoes

Two Main Approaches:

Approach 1: Sterile Male Release

  • Release laboratory-reared male mosquitoes sterilized by various techniques:
    • Ionizing radiation
    • Crossing closely related species to produce infertile hybrid males
    • Introducing chemosterilants into insectary rearing programs (makes both sexes sterile)
  • Large numbers of sterile males released into field populations
  • Compete with natural fertile males for female mates
  • Results in large numbers of infertile inseminations
  • Eggs laid by such females are sterile and fail to hatch

Question 5: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) for Vector Control (20 Marks)

Definition and Mechanism

  • IRS involves coating walls and other surfaces of a house with residual insecticide
  • For several months, insecticide kills mosquitoes and other insects contacting these surfaces
  • Does NOT directly prevent people from being bitten
  • Usually kills mosquitoes AFTER they have fed if they rest on sprayed surfaces
  • Prevents transmission of infection to other persons

Effectiveness Requirements

To be effective, IRS must:

  1. Be applied to a very high proportion of households in an area
  2. Target areas where mosquitoes rest inside dwellings after blood meals

Application Process

  • IRS is the process of spraying insecticide to the inside of dwellings to kill mosquitoes that spread malaria
  • Dilute solution of insecticide sprayed on inside walls of certain dwelling types:
    • Walls made from porous materials (mud or wood)
    • NOT plaster as in city dwellings
  • Mosquitoes are killed or repelled by the spray, preventing disease transmission

Target Vectors

  • Many malaria vectors are "endophilic"
  • Mosquito vectors rest inside houses after taking blood meal
  • These mosquitoes particularly susceptible to IRS control

WHO Recommendations

WHO recommends IRS as one of three primary means of malaria control:

  1. Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS)
  2. Use of Insecticide-Treated Bednets (ITNs)
  3. Prompt treatment of confirmed cases with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapies (ACTs)

Historical Context

  • WHO previously recommended IRS in areas of stable, endemic transmission
  • In 2006, began recommending IRS only in areas of unstable transmission

Conditions for IRS Effectiveness

For IRS to be effective, three conditions must be met:

  1. High Coverage
    • Must be high percentage of sprayable surfaces within each dwelling
  2. Vector Behavior
    • Vector (mosquitoes) must feed or rest indoors
  3. Susceptibility
    • Targeted vectors must be susceptible (i.e., not resistant) to insecticides being sprayed

Question 6: Medical Importance of Fleas (20 Marks)

1. PLAGUE

Types of Plague:

  • Three main types: bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic
  • All caused by bacterium Yersinia pestis
  • Medically most important is bubonic plague (worldwide distribution)

Bubonic Plague Transmission:

  • Bubonic plague is a zoonosis, primarily a disease of wild animals (especially rodents)
  • Transmission cycle between wild rodents termed "sylvatic, campal, rural or enzootic plague"
  • Many different flea species bite rodents and maintain plague transmission

Wild to Human Transmission:

  • When people hunt wild animals (e.g., trappers), they risk getting bitten by rodent fleas
  • Infected wild animals can transmit plague to people

Urban Plague:

  • Important form where plague circulates among wild rodents
  • Transmitted to commensal rats
  • Maintained in rat populations by fleas:
    • Xenopsylla cheopis (Europe, Asia, Africa, Americas)
    • X. astia (Southeast Asia)
    • X. brasiliensis (Africa, South America, India)

Human Infection Pathway:

  • When rats living in close association with humans (in rat-infested slums, garbage) become infected with plague, they rapidly develop septicemia and die
  • On death, infected fleas leave rats and feed on humans
  • Rat fleas spread bubonic plague to human populations

Alternative Infection Methods:

  • Flea feces rubbed into skin abrasions or contact with mucous membranes
  • Plague bacilli remain infective in flea feces for up to 3 years
  • Occasionally tonsils become infected by crushing infected fleas between teeth

Other Plague Forms:

  • Septicaemic plague: Bacilli in blood
  • Pneumonic plague: Bacilli invade lungs
  • Very occasionally septicaemic plague transmitted mechanically by fleas

2. MURINE TYPHUS

Distribution:

  • Also known as endemic typhus or Mexican typhus
  • Occurs almost worldwide

Causative Agent:

  • Caused by bacterium Rickettsia typhi
  • Infected when flea takes blood meal
  • Transmission occurs when infected feces are scratched/rubbed into abrasions or contact mucous membranes
  • Also by release of rickettsiae from crushed fleas

Persistence:

  • Under laboratory conditions, they remain infective for 4.5-9 years
  • Under more dry conditions they remain infective for many months

Transmission:

  • Rickettsiae of murine typhus can pass to eggs, larvae, adults of flea (i.e., transovarial and transstadial transmission)

3. CESTODES (Tapeworms)

Dipylidium caninum:

  • Commonest tapeworm of dogs and cats
  • Occasionally occurs in children
  • Transmitted by fleas (C. felis, C. canis, P. irritans) to pets and humans

Life Cycle:

  1. Proglottids containing eggs excreted by pet, crawl away and dry
  2. Larval fleas feeding on organic debris bite into dried proglottids, releasing and swallowing eggs
  3. Larval worms hatch, penetrate gut wall of larval flea, enter body cavity (coelom)
  4. Remain trapped, pass to pupa, then to adult flea
  5. Encapsulate and become cysticercoids (infective larvae)

Human/Animal Infection:

  • Animals infected by licking coats during grooming and swallowing infected adult fleas
  • Young children infected by fondling/kissing dogs and cats, swallowing fleas
  • Can be licked by dogs which have crushed infected fleas, liberating infective cysticercoids

Other Tapeworms:

  • Rat tapeworms Hymenolepis diminuta and H. nana have similar life cycles

4. FLEAS AS NUISANCE

General Impact:

  • Although fleas can be important disease vectors, most widespread complaint is discomfort and irritation from bites

Most Common Nuisance Flea:

  • Cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) - worldwide distribution
  • Most common nuisance flea globally

Biting Patterns:

  • Frequently bite ankles and legs
  • At night, sleeping person may be bitten on any part of body

Allergic Reactions:

  • People who become hypersensitive to flea bites can suffer from:
    • Dermatitis
    • Inhalation of flea feces

Age Sensitivity:

  • Children under 10 years tend to experience greater discomfort from flea bites than older people

Behavioral Impact:

  • People can spend sleepless nights alternately scratching themselves and trying to catch fleas

Question 7: Medical Importance of Ixodes Species (20 Marks)

1. TICK PARALYSIS AND ALLERGIES

Tick Paralysis:

  • Symptoms appear 4-7 days after a tick (usually female) has commenced feeding
  • Earliest symptoms: Patient unable to walk, paralysis affecting first legs, then arms
  • After first symptoms, there follows difficulty in:
    • Speaking
    • Swallowing
    • Breathing
  • Symptoms painless, rarely any rise in patient's temperature

Recovery:

  • Removal of ticks can result in complete recovery after 48 hours
  • In severe cases, recovery may take few days or up to about 6 weeks

Species Variation:

  • Different tick species vary markedly in ability to produce tick paralysis
  • Same species may differ in different populations of humans and animals

Allergies:

  • Some people may become allergic to tick bites
  • Can cause nausea, vomiting, and sometimes serious consequences
  • Includes: skin rashes, itchy skin, dermatitis

Question 8: Differentiate Terminologies in Medical Entomology (6 Marks)

A. PROPAGATIVE

  • Only the number of pathogens increases
  • Developmental stage remains constant
  • Examples: Plague and typhus are good examples of propagative disease transmission

B. CYCLO-DEVELOPMENTAL

  • Only the developmental stage (form) of the pathogen changes (small to big, immature to mature stage, etc.)
  • Number of disease pathogenic organisms remains constant
  • Example: Filariasis

C. CYCLOPROPAGATIVE

  • This type of disease transmission is a combination of both propagative and cyclo-developmental
  • Both number and developmental form (stage) change within the vector
  • Example: Malaria

Question 12: Development of Filarial Nematodes in Vectors (6 Marks)

Developmental Stages in Mosquito:

  1. Blood Meal Ingestion
    • When vector mosquito feeds on carrier mosquito, microfilariae are taken in with blood meal
  2. Migration to Thoracic Muscles (2-6 hours)
    • Within 2-6 hours, they cast off their sheaths (exsheating)
    • Penetrate stomach wall, migrate to thoracic muscles where they undergo further development
  3. First-Stage Larva (Next 2 Days)
    • During next 2 days, metamorphose into first-stage larva
    • Sausage-shaped with spiky tail
  4. Second-Stage Larva (Within a Week)
    • Within a week, moults once or twice
    • Increases in size
    • Becomes second-stage larva
  5. Third-Stage Larva (In Another Week)
    • In another week, develops internal structures
    • Becomes elongated L3 (infective form)
    • Actively motile
    • Is the infective form
  6. Human Infection
    • Enters persons who are the proboscis sheath of mosquito
    • Awaits opportunity for infecting humans

  39. Simulotoxicosis is A NEGATIVE REACTION TO THE SALIVA OF BLACK FLIES
  40. Insecticide resistance develops by:
    • USING LOW DOSES OF INSECTICIDES
    • USING HIGH OR PROLONGED DOSES OF INSECTICIDES
  41. SIMULIUM DAMNOSUM is the pathogen that causes river blindness (NOTE: This is actually the VECTOR, not pathogen. The pathogen is Onchocerca volvulus)
  42. Culex larvae are found in ALL OF THE ABOVE (freshwater marshes, salt marshes, wet muddy areas around cattails or near water tanks)
  43. Integrated pest management RELIES SOLELY ON PESTICIDES and RELIES SOLELY ON BIOLOGICAL AND NATURAL CONTROL (NOTE: This seems contradictory - IPM actually combines multiple methods)
  44. The stage of Leishmania that develops in the sandfly and is transmitted to humans is PROMASTIGOTE
  45. PHLEBOTOMINAE is not a subfamily in the family Culicidae
  46. Epidemic typhus and Chagas disease can both be vectored via:
    • THE SALIVA OF A VECTOR
    • FECES (FRASS) OF A VECTOR
  47. FUSCA GROUP of Glossina species is insignificant in the transmission of Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense
  48. CLOGGED DRAINAGE DITCH is the most likely place for mosquito larvae to live
  49. ALL OF THESE ATTRACT MOSQUITOES (carbon dioxide, host odors, and the color white) to the host
  50. BLATTELLA are organisms that have the characteristics to be an effective mechanical vector of human disease
  51. ALL OF THE ABOVE (between the head board of the bed and the wall, between the mattress and the box springs, in the bed frame cavities) are places where you might look if you suspected bedbugs have infested your house
  52. Malaria-infected patients experience MEROZOITES ARE SYNCHRONOUSLY EMERGING FROM RED BLOOD CELLS, WHERE THEY BRIEFLY STIMULATE A STRONG IMMUNE REACTION BEFORE THEY DISAPPEAR INTO NEW RED BLOOD CELLS - this explains cycles of extreme fever followed by brief period of recovery
  53. NONE OF THE ABOVE (cockroaches, lice, true flies, and fleas) are included in the order Diptera (NOTE: True flies ARE in Diptera)
  54. BULINUS is not a mechanical vector, while Fannia, Musca, and Blatta are mechanical vectors
  55. Q-FEVER is a disease that can be effectively controlled by use of acaricides
  56. LEPTOTROMBIDIUM is a biological vector of scrub typhus pathogens
  57. ORIENTIA TSUTSUGAMUSHI is a pathogen that can be transovarially transmitted by its biological vector
  58. BENZYL BENZOATE is the best treatment for scabies
  59. LIQUID TETRACYCLINE can be used in the diagnosis of mite infection
  60. Indoor residual spraying is best effective against ENDOPHILIC insect vectors of pathogens
  61. BOOPHILUS vectors utilize ONE HOST in its life cycle and pathogen transmission
  62. PERIPLANETA SPECIES vectors of pathogens are best controlled by using BORIC ACID POWDER (e.g., Borax)

EXAMINATION TIPS AND KEY CONCEPTS

Important Disease-Vector Relationships to Remember

Key Terminology

Vector Types:

  • Biological Vector: Pathogen develops/multiplies in vector
  • Mechanical Vector: Pathogen transported without development
  • Anthropophilic: Prefers human hosts
  • Zoophilic: Prefers animal hosts
  • Endophilic: Rests indoors
  • Exophilic: Rests outdoors
  • Endophagic: Feeds indoors
  • Exophagic: Feeds outdoors

Transmission Types:

  • Propagative: Pathogen multiplies, no development
  • Cyclo-developmental: Pathogen develops, no multiplication
  • Cyclopropagative: Both multiplication and development
  • Transovarial: Pathogen passed through eggs
  • Transstadial: Pathogen passed between life stages

Control Methods Summary

1. Chemical Control:

  • Organophosphates
  • Organochlorides (DDT)
  • Pyrethroids
  • Carbamates

2. Biological Control:

  • Predatory fish
  • Bacillus thuringiensis (Bti)
  • Parasitic nematodes
  • Fungi and protozoans

3. Environmental Control:

  • Drainage
  • Source reduction
  • Habitat modification

4. Genetic Control:

  • Sterile Insect Technique (SIT)
  • Gene modification

5. Personal Protection:

  • Bed nets (ITNs)
  • Repellents (DEET)
  • Protective clothing
  • Screens and barriers

6. Integrated Vector Management (IVM):

  • Combines multiple methods
  • Sustainable approach
  • Reduces resistance development

END OF PAST PAPER

Study Recommendations:

  1. Focus on disease-vector-pathogen relationships
  2. Understand life cycles thoroughly
  3. Master control methods for each vector
  4. Know morphological identification features
  5. Remember geographic distributions
  6. Understand transmission mechanisms

Good Luck with Your Studies!

Title: BND 3104 NUTRITION AND DIETETICS
Content:
Exam Questions and Answers

SECTION A: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS

1. Differentiate between essential and non-essential amino acids (4 Marks)

Answer:

Essential Amino Acids are amino acids that the body cannot synthesize or produces in insufficient amounts. Therefore, they must be obtained through diet. Examples include:

  • Leucine
  • Isoleucine
  • Valine
  • Lysine

Non-Essential Amino Acids are amino acids that the body can synthesize in sufficient amounts, so they do not necessarily need to be supplied by the diet. Examples include:

  • Alanine
  • Glutamine
  • Glycine
  • Tyrosine

2. Explain the importance of dietary fiber (5 Marks)

Answer:

Dietary fiber is crucial for maintaining optimal health for several reasons:

  1. Digestive Health: Fiber promotes regular bowel movements and prevents constipation by adding bulk to stool and facilitating its passage through the digestive tract.
  2. Weight Management: High-fiber foods increase satiety and help control appetite, leading to reduced calorie intake and better weight management.
  3. Blood Sugar Control: Soluble fiber slows down the absorption of sugar, helping to regulate blood glucose levels and reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.
  4. Cardiovascular Health: Fiber, particularly soluble fiber, helps lower blood cholesterol levels by binding to cholesterol particles and removing them from the body, reducing the risk of heart disease.
  5. Colon Health: Fiber promotes healthy gut bacteria and may reduce the risk of colorectal cancer and other gastrointestinal disorders.

3. Differentiate between major minerals and trace minerals (6 Marks)

Answer:

Major Minerals (also called macrominerals):

  • Required by the body in amounts greater than 100 mg per day
  • Present in the body in larger quantities (more than 5 grams)
  • Examples include: Calcium, Phosphorus, Magnesium, Sodium, Potassium, Chloride, and Sulfur
  • Functions: Building bones and teeth, maintaining fluid balance, nerve transmission, and muscle contraction

Trace Minerals (also called microminerals):

  • Required by the body in amounts less than 100 mg per day
  • Present in the body in very small quantities (less than 5 grams)
  • Examples include: Iron, Zinc, Iodine, Selenium, Copper, Manganese, Fluoride, and Chromium
  • Functions: Enzyme activation, hormone production, immune function, and antioxidant activities

4. Suggest five benefits of breastfeeding to infants (5 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Optimal Nutrition: Breast milk provides the perfect balance of nutrients specifically designed for infant growth and development, including proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals in ideal proportions.
  2. Immune Protection: Breast milk contains antibodies, white blood cells, and antimicrobial factors that protect infants from infections, including respiratory infections, ear infections, and diarrheal diseases.
  3. Digestive Health: Breast milk is easily digestible and promotes the development of healthy gut bacteria, reducing the risk of gastrointestinal problems like colic and constipation.
  4. Cognitive Development: Breastfeeding has been associated with improved cognitive development and higher IQ scores due to the presence of essential fatty acids like DHA.
  5. Reduced Risk of Chronic Diseases: Breastfed infants have lower rates of obesity, type 1 and 2 diabetes, asthma, allergies, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

5. Distinguish between soluble and insoluble fiber with examples of sources (5 Marks)

Answer:

Soluble Fiber:

  • Dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance
  • Helps lower blood cholesterol and glucose levels
  • Slows digestion and promotes satiety
  • Sources: Oats, barley, beans, lentils, apples, citrus fruits, carrots, psyllium

Insoluble Fiber:

  • Does not dissolve in water
  • Adds bulk to stool and helps food pass through the digestive system
  • Prevents constipation and promotes regular bowel movements
  • Sources: Whole wheat products, wheat bran, brown rice, vegetables (cauliflower, green beans), nuts, seeds, potato skins

6. Explain the limitations of early introduction of complementary feeds to infants (5 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Immature Digestive System: Infants under 6 months have an immature digestive system that cannot properly digest complex foods, leading to gastrointestinal discomfort, diarrhea, or malabsorption.
  2. Increased Risk of Infections: Early introduction of complementary foods may expose infants to contaminated food and water, increasing the risk of infections and diarrheal diseases.
  3. Nutritional Displacement: Complementary foods may replace breast milk, which is nutritionally superior, leading to inadequate nutrient intake and potential malnutrition.
  4. Allergic Reactions: Early introduction increases the risk of developing food allergies, particularly to common allergens like eggs, peanuts, and wheat.
  5. Choking Hazard: Infants may not have developed adequate oral motor skills for chewing and swallowing solid foods, increasing the risk of choking.

SECTION B: ESSAY QUESTIONS

7a. Examine five principles of diet planning (10 Marks)

Answer:

1. Adequacy An adequate diet provides sufficient energy and all essential nutrients in amounts necessary to prevent deficiencies and maintain health. This is achieved by consuming a variety of nutrient-rich foods from all food groups. An adequate diet meets the Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDAs) or Adequate Intakes (AIs) for all nutrients.

2. Balance A balanced diet supplies appropriate amounts of nutrients from each food group in the correct proportions. Balance is achieved by consuming foods from all food groups (grains, proteins, fruits, vegetables, dairy) without overemphasizing one group at the expense of others. This ensures that no single nutrient is consumed in excess while others are lacking.

3. Calorie Control This principle ensures that energy intake matches energy expenditure to maintain a healthy body weight. Calorie intake should be appropriate for age, sex, body size, and physical activity level. Consuming more calories than needed leads to weight gain, while consuming too few results in weight loss and potential nutrient deficiencies.

4. Moderation Moderation involves avoiding excessive consumption of any food or nutrient, particularly those that may be harmful in large amounts. This principle is especially important for foods high in saturated fats, added sugars, sodium, and alcohol. It also applies to supplements of vitamins and minerals to prevent toxicity.

5. Nutrient Density This principle emphasizes choosing foods that provide substantial amounts of nutrients relative to their calorie content. Nutrient-dense foods deliver maximum nutrition with minimal calories. For example, choosing fresh fruit over sugary soda, or choosing whole grains over refined grains provides more nutrients per calorie consumed.

7b. Explain the ABCD of Nutrition assessment (10 Marks)

Answer:

The ABCD approach is a comprehensive method for assessing nutritional status:

A - Anthropometric Measurements This involves measuring physical dimensions and body composition:

  • Weight: Measured using bathroom scales or specialized scales; indicates overall nutritional status
  • Height/Length: Measured using stadiometer (adults/children who can stand) or infantometer (infants); used to calculate growth and BMI
  • Head Circumference: Measured in infants to assess brain development, taken from supraorbital ridge to the occipital bone
  • Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC): Measured using specialized tape with color indicators (red: severely malnourished, yellow: moderately malnourished, green: normal); used for children and pregnant women
  • Waist-Hip Ratio: Indicates body fat distribution and risk of chronic diseases
  • BMI (Body Mass Index): Calculated as weight(kg)/height(m)² to classify nutritional status

B - Biochemical Tests Laboratory analysis of body fluids and tissues:

  • Blood Tests: Measure levels of nutrients (vitamins, minerals), metabolites (glucose, cholesterol), and proteins (albumin, hemoglobin)
  • Urine Tests: Detect nutrient deficiencies or excesses, metabolic disorders
  • Examples include: serum calcium, potassium, sodium levels, blood sugar levels, vitamin A levels
  • These tests provide objective data on internal nutritional status

C - Clinical Examination Physical examination for signs and symptoms of malnutrition:

  • Skin: Dryness, scaling, pallor, edema
  • Hair: Thinness, brittleness, discoloration, easy pluckability
  • Eyes: Pale conjunctiva (anemia), night blindness, Bitot's spots (vitamin A deficiency)
  • Mouth: Angular stomatitis, glossitis, dental caries
  • Nails: Spooning (koilonychia), pallor
  • General appearance: Muscle wasting, subcutaneous fat loss, edema

D - Dietary Data/History Assessment of food intake patterns:

  • 24-Hour Dietary Recall: Patient recalls all foods and beverages consumed in the previous 24 hours
  • Food Frequency Questionnaire: Assesses how often specific foods are consumed over a period
  • Food Diary: Patient records all food intake for 3-7 days
  • Dietary History: Comprehensive assessment of usual eating patterns, food preferences, restrictions, and cultural practices This information helps determine nutrient intake adequacy and identify dietary problems.

8a. Explain the vicious cycle of illness and malnutrition (10 Marks)

Answer:

The vicious cycle of illness and malnutrition describes the bidirectional relationship where illness leads to malnutrition, and malnutrition predisposes to illness, creating a continuous cycle:

How Illness Causes Malnutrition:

  1. Reduced Food Intake: Illness causes loss of appetite, nausea, and difficulty eating or swallowing, leading to decreased nutrient intake.
  2. Increased Nutrient Losses: Diseases like diarrhea and vomiting cause significant loss of nutrients and fluids. Fever increases metabolic demands and nutrient losses through perspiration.
  3. Malabsorption: Illness, particularly gastrointestinal diseases, impairs the body's ability to absorb nutrients even when food is consumed, resulting in nutrient deficiencies.
  4. Increased Metabolic Demands: During illness, the body requires more energy and nutrients for immune response, tissue repair, and fighting infection, but intake is often reduced.

How Malnutrition Causes Illness:

  1. Weakened Immune System: Malnutrition impairs immune function, reducing the body's ability to fight infections. This makes the person more susceptible to bacterial, viral, and parasitic infections.
  2. Impaired Tissue Repair: Inadequate protein and micronutrients slow wound healing and tissue regeneration, prolonging recovery from illness or injury.
  3. Reduced Physical Capacity: Malnutrition causes muscle wasting and weakness, reducing physical activity and further compromising health.
  4. Increased Disease Susceptibility: Malnourished individuals are more prone to developing infections and chronic diseases. Specific nutrient deficiencies lead to specific illnesses (e.g., vitamin A deficiency increases risk of measles severity).

The Perpetual Cycle: Once established, this cycle is self-reinforcing. Malnourished individuals who become ill experience more severe and prolonged illness, leading to further nutritional deterioration. The weakened state makes them vulnerable to additional infections before fully recovering, creating a downward spiral. Breaking this cycle requires simultaneous treatment of both the illness and nutritional rehabilitation, along with prevention strategies like vaccination, improved sanitation, and nutrition education.

8b. Describe the feeding problems in infancy (10 Marks)

Answer:

1. Breastfeeding Problems:

  • Poor Latch: Infant fails to properly attach to the breast, leading to inadequate milk transfer and nipple pain
  • Insufficient Milk Supply: Mother may produce inadequate milk due to stress, poor nutrition, or inadequate stimulation
  • Breast Engorgement: Painful swelling of breasts making it difficult for infant to latch
  • Mastitis: Breast infection causing pain and reduced milk production
  • Inverted or Flat Nipples: Makes it difficult for infant to latch properly

2. Bottle Feeding Problems:

  • Improper Formula Preparation: Over-dilution leads to malnutrition; under-dilution causes dehydration and digestive problems
  • Contamination: Improper sterilization of bottles and nipples leads to infections
  • Nipple Confusion: Infant may refuse breast after being introduced to bottle
  • Overfeeding: Easier to overfeed with bottles, potentially leading to obesity

3. Colic:

  • Excessive crying (more than 3 hours per day) in otherwise healthy infants
  • Causes include immature digestive system, gas, food allergies, or overfeeding
  • Leads to feeding difficulties and parental stress

4. Reflux (Gastroesophageal Reflux):

  • Frequent spitting up or vomiting after feeding
  • Causes discomfort and may lead to inadequate weight gain
  • Infant may refuse feeding due to pain

5. Food Allergies and Intolerances:

  • Lactose Intolerance: Inability to digest lactose causing diarrhea, gas, and abdominal pain
  • Cow's Milk Protein Allergy: Causes vomiting, diarrhea, skin rashes, and respiratory problems
  • May require specialized formulas or elimination diets

6. Oral-Motor Problems:

  • Poor sucking reflex in premature infants
  • Weak muscle tone affecting ability to suck and swallow
  • Tongue thrust reflex interfering with feeding

7. Underfeeding/Overfeeding:

  • Underfeeding: Leads to failure to thrive, poor growth, and developmental delays
  • Overfeeding: May cause excessive weight gain, vomiting, and digestive discomfort
  • Both result from misreading infant hunger cues or improper feeding schedules

8. Introduction of Solids:

  • Starting too early causes digestive problems and allergies
  • Starting too late may lead to nutrient deficiencies and feeding difficulties
  • Improper texture or inappropriate foods pose choking hazards

9. Dehydration:

  • Can occur rapidly in infants due to small body size
  • Caused by inadequate fluid intake, diarrhea, vomiting, or fever
  • Requires immediate medical attention

10. Parental Factors:

  • Lack of knowledge about proper feeding techniques
  • Anxiety and stress affecting feeding relationship
  • Postpartum depression affecting mother's ability to respond to infant cues
  • Conflicting advice from multiple sources causing confusion

Additional Topics

Functions of Proteins in the Body (5 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Structural Component: Proteins serve as building blocks for body tissues, including muscles, skin, hair, nails, and organs. They are essential for growth, maintenance, and repair of body tissues.
  2. Enzymatic Function: Proteins act as enzymes that catalyze various biochemical reactions in the body, including digestion, metabolism, and energy production.
  3. Immune Function: Proteins form antibodies that protect the body from foreign invaders such as bacteria, viruses, and other pathogens, playing a crucial role in immune defense.
  4. Hormonal Function: Some proteins function as hormones that regulate various body processes. For example, insulin controls blood glucose levels, and growth hormone regulates growth and development.
  5. Energy Source: When carbohydrates and fats are insufficient, proteins can be broken down and used as an energy source, providing 4 calories per gram.

Importance of Pre-conception Nutrition (6 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Prevention of Congenital Abnormalities: Adequate nutrition, particularly folic acid, before conception reduces the risk of neural tube defects and other birth defects. Folic acid deficiency can cause serious developmental problems.
  2. Reduced Risk of Infertility: Proper nutrition improves reproductive health and increases fertility in both men and women, ensuring healthy gametes (sperm and egg) are produced.
  3. Maternal Health: Good nutritional status before pregnancy ensures the mother enters pregnancy in optimal health, reducing risks of complications such as anemia, gestational diabetes, and hypertension.
  4. Healthy Pregnancy Outcomes: Pre-conception nutrition reduces the risk of pregnancy complications such as miscarriage, preterm birth, low birth weight, and premature delivery.
  5. Fetal Development: Adequate nutrient stores before conception ensure the developing fetus has access to essential nutrients during critical early developmental stages, particularly in the first trimester.
  6. Preparation for Pregnancy Demands: Pre-conception nutrition helps build adequate nutrient reserves to meet the increased demands of pregnancy, ensuring a smooth pregnancy journey.

Complications During Pregnancy (6 Marks)

Answer:

1. Hyperemesis Gravidarum:

  • Severe nausea and vomiting occurring around 4 weeks of pregnancy
  • More severe than normal morning sickness
  • Complications include: Severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, ketoacidosis, and nutritional deficiencies
  • May require hospitalization for intravenous fluids and medications

2. Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension (Preeclampsia):

  • High blood pressure developing after 20 weeks of pregnancy (systolic ≥140 mmHg and/or diastolic ≥90 mmHg)
  • Accompanied by proteinuria (protein in urine)
  • Can lead to serious complications including eclampsia (seizures), stroke, organ damage, and placental abruption
  • Requires close monitoring and may necessitate early delivery

3. Gestational Diabetes:

  • Develops during pregnancy due to hormonal changes affecting insulin function
  • Increases risk of macrosomia (large baby), birth complications, cesarean delivery
  • Can lead to type 2 diabetes later in life for mother
  • Requires dietary management and possibly insulin therapy

Factors Influencing Nutrient Requirements (5 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Age: Different life stages have varying nutrient needs. Children and adolescents require more nutrients for growth, while elderly people may need adjusted amounts due to decreased absorption and activity.
  2. Physiological State: Pregnancy and lactation significantly increase nutrient requirements to support fetal development and milk production.
  3. Health Status: Illness and disease increase nutrient requirements for immune function and tissue repair. Chronic diseases may also affect nutrient absorption and utilization.
  4. Sex: Males typically require more energy and certain nutrients due to larger muscle mass and higher metabolic rates compared to females.
  5. Geographic Location: People living in areas with food insecurity or specific environmental conditions may have different nutrient requirements or availability.

Nutritional Deficiency Disorders (3 Marks)

Answer:

  1. Vitamin C Deficiency: Causes Scurvy, characterized by bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and weakness
  2. Iron Deficiency: Causes Anemia, resulting in fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity
  3. Iodine Deficiency: Causes Goiter (thyroid gland enlargement) and can lead to hypothyroidism and developmental problems

End of Document

Title: EPIDEMIOLOGY CASE STUDY
Content:
Questions and Comprehensive Answers

CASE SCENARIO: TYPHOID FEVER OUTBREAK

Background Information:

  • Typhoid fever manifests clinically with high fever and headache
  • A person infected with the typhoid fever agent works in a café but shows no manifestation of disease (asymptomatic carrier)
  • This person serves 20 people in one day at the café
  • 5 people got infected with typhoid fever
  • Only 3 of the 5 infected people developed disease symptoms
  • Among the 3 who developed typhoid: 2 recovered and 1 died

QUESTION 1

From the given information, who is likely the mode of transmission?

ANSWER:

The Infected Food Handler (Asymptomatic Carrier) is the source of transmission.

Mode of Transmission: Fecal-Oral Route (Indirect Contact)

Explanation:

  1. Source/Reservoir: The café worker is an asymptomatic carrier (also called a healthy carrier). This person is infected with Salmonella typhi but shows no clinical symptoms while still shedding the bacteria.
  2. Mode of Transmission:
    • Primary Mode: Contaminated food and water (fecal-oral route)
    • The infected food handler likely contaminated food/beverages served at the café through poor hand hygiene after using the toilet
    • Customers consumed the contaminated food/drinks, leading to infection
  3. Chain of Infection:
    • Agent: Salmonella typhi bacteria
    • Reservoir: The asymptomatic food handler
    • Portal of Exit: Feces of the infected person
    • Mode of Transmission: Indirect contact via contaminated food/water
    • Portal of Entry: Mouth of the customers (ingestion)
    • Susceptible Host: The 20 customers served

Public Health Significance: Asymptomatic carriers are particularly dangerous in food service settings because they can unknowingly spread disease to many people. This is similar to the famous case of "Typhoid Mary" in New York.

QUESTION 2

Each of the affected persons are what type of case, and each one is what? (Clarification: Identify case types and infection outcomes)

ANSWER:

Classification of the Affected Individuals:

The Food Handler (Index Case):

  • Type: Asymptomatic Carrier (Subclinical Case/Inapparent Infection)
  • Status: Infected but shows no clinical symptoms
  • Role: Primary source of the outbreak

The 5 Infected People:

Group 1: Two who remained asymptomatic (5 infected - 3 who developed disease = 2 asymptomatic)

  • Type: Subclinical Cases/Inapparent Infections
  • Status: Infected with Salmonella typhi but did not develop clinical symptoms
  • Outcome: Remain healthy despite infection

Group 2: Three who developed disease symptoms

  1. First Person (Recovered)
    • Type: Clinical Case (Confirmed/Probable Case)
    • Outcome: Recovery
  2. Second Person (Recovered)
    • Type: Clinical Case (Confirmed/Probable Case)
    • Outcome: Recovery
  3. Third Person (Died)
    • Type: Clinical Case (Confirmed/Probable Case)
    • Outcome: Fatal Case
    • Significance: Death from typhoid fever

The 15 People Who Were Not Infected:

  • Type: Exposed but Not Infected (Contacts)
  • Status: Either immune or did not consume contaminated items
  • Outcome: No infection, no disease

Summary Table:

Attack Rate Calculation:

  • Attack Rate = (Number who developed disease / Number exposed) × 100
  • Attack Rate = (3/20) × 100 = 15%

Case Fatality Rate:

  • CFR = (Number of deaths / Number of cases) × 100
  • CFR = (1/3) × 100 = 33.3%

QUESTION 3

Can you group the 20 people who were served at the café into the 4 stages of natural history of communicable disease?

ANSWER:

The Natural History of Disease has 4 main stages. Here's how the 20 customers fit into each stage:

STAGE 1: STAGE OF SUSCEPTIBILITY (Pre-pathogenesis Period)

Number of People: 15 people

Characteristics:

  • These individuals were exposed to the contaminated food/water but did NOT get infected
  • They remain susceptible but the agent did not establish infection
  • Reasons they didn't get infected:
    • May have natural immunity
    • Did not consume contaminated items
    • Consumed insufficient infectious dose
    • Good immune system defense

Intervention at this stage: Primary prevention (health education, food safety, hand hygiene)

STAGE 2: STAGE OF SUBCLINICAL DISEASE (Early Pathogenesis)

Number of People: 2 people + 1 food handler = 3 people total

Characteristics:

  • These individuals are infected with Salmonella typhi
  • The pathogen has entered the body and is multiplying
  • NO clinical symptoms are present (asymptomatic)
  • They may be carriers capable of transmitting disease
  • Disease is in the incubation period
  • The person is infected but appears healthy

Intervention at this stage: Secondary prevention (screening, early detection through laboratory tests)

STAGE 3: STAGE OF CLINICAL DISEASE

Number of People: 3 people

Characteristics:

  • These individuals developed clinical manifestations of typhoid fever
  • Symptoms include: high fever, headache, abdominal pain, weakness
  • Disease is now apparent and diagnosable
  • Patient seeks medical care
  • This stage includes:
    • Early symptomatic stage: When symptoms first appear
    • Advanced stage: Full manifestation of disease

Breakdown of the 3 clinical cases:

  • 2 people with symptoms who will recover
  • 1 person with symptoms who will die

Intervention at this stage: Secondary prevention (early diagnosis and prompt treatment), Tertiary prevention (treatment to prevent complications)

STAGE 4: STAGE OF RECOVERY, DISABILITY, OR DEATH (Resolution)

Number of People: 3 people (same as Stage 3, representing outcomes)

Characteristics: This stage represents the outcome of clinical disease:

A. Complete Recovery: 2 people

  • Successfully treated
  • Return to normal health
  • May develop immunity to typhoid

B. Disability: 0 people

  • None in this case
  • (In typhoid, disability could include intestinal perforation sequelae, chronic carrier state)

C. Death: 1 person

  • Fatal outcome
  • Death from typhoid complications (possibly sepsis, intestinal perforation, or multi-organ failure)

Intervention at this stage: Tertiary prevention (rehabilitation, preventing recurrence, managing carrier state)

SUMMARY TABLE: Distribution of 20 People + Food Handler

Note: The same 3 people appear in both Stage 3 and Stage 4 as these stages represent disease progression and outcome.

QUESTION 4

How would you classify Pulmonary TB using Epidemiological methods and what is the main importance of such classification?

ANSWER:

EPIDEMIOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION OF PULMONARY TUBERCULOSIS

Pulmonary TB can be classified using various epidemiological methods:

A. CLASSIFICATION BY TIME (Temporal Classification)

1. Epidemic

  • Large number of TB cases occurring in excess of expected levels
  • Example: TB outbreak in a prison, school, or hospital
  • Requires immediate public health response

2. Endemic

  • TB occurs consistently at baseline levels in a community
  • Regular, expected occurrence
  • Example: TB is endemic in many Sub-Saharan African countries

3. Pandemic

  • TB occurring over a very wide geographic area affecting large populations
  • Historically, TB has been pandemic globally

B. CLASSIFICATION BY PLACE (Spatial Classification)

1. Urban TB

  • Higher prevalence in crowded urban settings
  • Related to overcrowding and poor living conditions

2. Rural TB

  • May have limited access to diagnosis and treatment
  • Different transmission patterns

3. Geographic Distribution

  • High-burden countries (e.g., India, China, Indonesia, Philippines)
  • Low-burden countries (e.g., Western Europe, North America)

C. CLASSIFICATION BY PERSON (Host Characteristics)

1. By Age:

  • Childhood TB (higher risk of disseminated disease)
  • Adult TB (most common form)
  • Elderly TB (reactivation common)

2. By Sex:

  • Male vs. Female distribution
  • Males typically have higher rates

3. By Immune Status:

  • HIV-positive TB (TB-HIV co-infection)
  • Immunocompromised TB (diabetes, malnutrition, immunosuppressive therapy)
  • Immunocompetent TB

4. By Occupation:

  • Healthcare workers (occupational exposure)
  • Miners
  • Prison inmates
  • General population

5. By Socioeconomic Status:

  • High-risk: poverty, homelessness, malnutrition
  • Low-risk: adequate living conditions, good nutrition

D. CLASSIFICATION BY CASE DEFINITION

1. Bacteriologically Confirmed TB

  • Sputum smear-positive
  • Culture-positive
  • GeneXpert (molecular test) positive

2. Clinically Diagnosed TB

  • Based on clinical symptoms, X-ray findings
  • When bacteriological confirmation not available

3. New Cases

  • Never received TB treatment or received treatment for <1 month

4. Relapse Cases

  • Previously treated and declared cured, now with TB again

5. Treatment After Failure

  • TB patient whose treatment failed

6. Treatment After Loss to Follow-up

  • Patients who interrupted treatment ≥2 months

E. CLASSIFICATION BY DRUG RESISTANCE

1. Drug-Susceptible TB

  • Responds to standard first-line drugs

2. Multi-Drug Resistant TB (MDR-TB)

  • Resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin

3. Extensively Drug-Resistant TB (XDR-TB)

  • MDR-TB + resistance to fluoroquinolones and second-line injectables

4. Rifampicin-Resistant TB (RR-TB)

  • Resistant to rifampicin (with or without other drug resistance)

F. CLASSIFICATION BY INFECTIOUSNESS

1. Infectious (Transmissible) TB

  • Sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB
  • Can transmit to others
  • High public health priority

2. Non-infectious TB

  • Sputum smear-negative
  • Extrapulmonary TB
  • Lower transmission risk

IMPORTANCE OF EPIDEMIOLOGICAL CLASSIFICATION OF TB

1. Disease Surveillance and Monitoring

  • Track disease trends over time
  • Identify high-risk populations and areas
  • Monitor disease burden and distribution
  • Detect outbreaks early

2. Resource Allocation

  • Prioritize areas and populations needing intervention
  • Allocate diagnostic tools, medications, and healthcare workers
  • Plan budget based on disease burden
  • Ensure equitable distribution of resources

3. Designing Control Programs

  • Develop targeted interventions for specific populations
  • Create appropriate treatment protocols
  • Implement contact tracing strategies
  • Design vaccination programs (BCG)

4. Treatment Planning

  • Determine appropriate treatment regimen based on drug resistance
  • Plan duration of treatment
  • Identify need for directly observed therapy (DOT)
  • Manage complications

5. Evaluation of Interventions

  • Assess effectiveness of control programs
  • Measure treatment outcomes
  • Monitor success rates
  • Identify program gaps

6. Research and Policy Development

  • Identify risk factors
  • Understand transmission dynamics
  • Develop evidence-based policies
  • Guide research priorities

7. Prevention Strategies

  • Identify contacts requiring prophylaxis
  • Target high-risk groups for screening
  • Implement infection control measures in healthcare facilities
  • Address social determinants of health

8. Predicting Future Trends

  • Forecast disease burden
  • Anticipate drug resistance patterns
  • Plan long-term healthcare needs
  • Prepare for epidemics

9. International Reporting

  • Standardized reporting to WHO
  • Compare TB burden across countries
  • Track progress toward End TB Strategy goals
  • Facilitate international collaboration

10. Public Health Action

  • Inform health education campaigns
  • Guide contact investigation
  • Implement quarantine when necessary
  • Protect public health

QUESTION 5

Suppose in a certain rainy season, you diagnose malaria in several people who come to seek treatment and you undertake the following measures:

  1. Treat each patient with appropriate antimalarial drug
  2. Mobilize the community to eradicate breeding sites of mosquitoes
  3. Give health education on proper use of insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs)

Which factor in the chain of disease transmission is each measure targeting?

ANSWER:

The Chain of Infection consists of six links:

  1. Infectious Agent
  2. Reservoir
  3. Portal of Exit
  4. Mode of Transmission
  5. Portal of Entry
  6. Susceptible Host

Let's analyze each intervention:

MEASURE 1: Treat each patient with appropriate antimalarial drug

Target: INFECTIOUS AGENT & RESERVOIR

Explanation:

  • Infectious Agent Targeted: Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae)
  • The antimalarial drug kills or inhibits the malaria parasites in the patient's bloodstream
  • This reduces the parasitemia (parasite load in blood)

How it breaks the chain:

  • Eliminates the agent: Drugs like artemisinin-based combinations, chloroquine, or quinine destroy the parasites
  • Reduces the reservoir: Treating infected humans decreases the reservoir of infection in the community
  • Prevents transmission: When parasites are cleared from blood, mosquitoes cannot pick up parasites when they bite the treated person
  • Prevents complications: Early treatment prevents severe malaria and death

Type of Prevention: Secondary Prevention (Treatment of existing cases)

MEASURE 2: Mobilize the community to eradicate breeding sites of mosquitoes

Target: MODE OF TRANSMISSION (Vector Control)

Explanation:

  • Vector Targeted: Female Anopheles mosquitoes (the transmitting vector)
  • Breeding sites include stagnant water in puddles, containers, ponds, etc.

How it breaks the chain:

  • Eliminates mosquito breeding: Removing stagnant water prevents mosquito larvae from developing into adult mosquitoes
  • Reduces vector population: Fewer mosquitoes = fewer opportunities for disease transmission
  • Interrupts transmission cycle: Without vectors, the malaria parasite cannot move from infected to susceptible individuals

Specific Actions Include:

  • Draining stagnant water
  • Filling puddles and ditches
  • Covering water storage containers
  • Improving drainage systems
  • Environmental management
  • Larviciding (killing mosquito larvae)

Type of Prevention: Primary Prevention (Preventing occurrence of disease)

Environmental Factor: This measure also targets environmental factors in the chain of disease transmission by modifying the environment to make it unsuitable for mosquito breeding.

MEASURE 3: Give health education on proper use of insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs)

Target: SUSCEPTIBLE HOST & MODE OF TRANSMISSION

Explanation:

A. Protecting the Susceptible Host:

  • ITNs create a physical barrier between mosquitoes and sleeping humans
  • Reduces human-vector contact
  • Protects vulnerable individuals (children, pregnant women) from mosquito bites
  • Reduces the probability of transmission to susceptible individuals

B. Interrupting Mode of Transmission:

  • The insecticide on the nets kills or repels mosquitoes
  • Reduces vector population in the household
  • Prevents mosquitoes from feeding on humans
  • Decreases the number of bites on both infected and uninfected individuals

How it breaks the chain:

  • Blocks portal of entry: Mosquitoes cannot reach human skin to inject parasites
  • Protects susceptible hosts: Uninfected people are shielded from mosquito bites
  • Reduces transmission: Even if mosquitoes are present, they cannot transmit disease
  • Community protection: Widespread use provides community-level protection

Education Component:

  • Proper hanging of nets
  • Ensuring nets are tucked under mattresses
  • Regular retreatment or replacement
  • Using nets consistently every night
  • Repairing torn nets

Type of Prevention: Primary Prevention (Preventing disease occurrence in healthy individuals)

SUMMARY TABLE: Measures and Targeted Links

COMPLETE CHAIN OF INFECTION FOR MALARIA

Understanding how these measures interrupt the chain:

  1. Infectious Agent: Plasmodium species → Measure 1 targets this
  2. Reservoir: Infected humans → Measure 1 targets this
  3. Portal of Exit: Infected human's blood (taken by mosquito)
  4. Mode of Transmission: Female Anopheles mosquito bite → Measures 2 & 3 target this
  5. Portal of Entry: Skin (mosquito bite) → Measure 3 targets this
  6. Susceptible Host: Uninfected humans → Measure 3 targets this

INTEGRATED APPROACH

These three measures represent a comprehensive malaria control strategy:

  • Treatment (Case management)
  • Vector control (Environmental management)
  • Personal protection (Behavioral change)

This multi-pronged approach is essential for effective malaria prevention and control, as recommended by WHO's Global Malaria Programme. Breaking multiple links in the chain of transmission provides the best chance of controlling and eliminating malaria.

ADDITIONAL CONCEPT: EPIDEMIOLOGICAL RATIOS

Definition and Use of Epidemiological Ratios

Formula for Prevalence Rate:

Prevalence Rate = (Number of existing cases / Total population at risk) × 1000

Example Calculation from scenario:

= (468 / 1150) × 1000
= 407 per 1000 population

This means 407 out of every 1000 people in the population have the disease at that particular time.

End of Document

Title: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Content:
GROUP 1: CHARACTERISTICS & EPIDEMIOLOGY

Bacterial Characteristics

Classification:

  • Gram-positive diplococcus
  • Encapsulated
  • Facultative anaerobe
  • Alpha-hemolytic on blood agar

Morphology:

  • Lancet-shaped (pointed ends)
  • Occurs in pairs (diplococci)
  • Polysaccharide capsule (major virulence factor)

Key Identifying Features:

  • Optochin sensitive
  • Bile soluble
  • Quellung reaction positive (capsular swelling)

Epidemiology

Global Burden:

  • Leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia worldwide
  • Major cause of bacterial meningitis
  • Most common cause of otitis media in children

Prevalence:

  • Colonizes 5-10% of healthy adults
  • Up to 20-40% of healthy children carry it asymptomatically
  • Higher carriage rates in daycare settings and overcrowded conditions

Geographic Distribution:

  • Found worldwide
  • Higher disease burden in developing countries
  • Seasonal variation (more common in winter/spring)

Transmission:

  • Person-to-person via respiratory droplets
  • Close contact facilitates spread
  • Asymptomatic carriers serve as reservoir

At-Risk Populations:

Age Groups:

  • Children <2 years (immature immunity)
  • Adults >65 years (declining immunity)

Immunocompromised:

  • HIV/AIDS
  • Organ transplant recipients
  • Chemotherapy patients
  • Asplenia or splenic dysfunction
  • Primary immunodeficiencies

Chronic Conditions:

  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Chronic heart disease
  • Chronic lung disease (COPD, asthma)
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Liver cirrhosis

Lifestyle Factors:

  • Smoking (damages respiratory epithelium)
  • Alcohol abuse (impairs immunity)
  • IV drug use

Environmental:

  • Crowded living conditions
  • Institutional settings (nursing homes, military barracks)

Serotype Distribution:

  • Over 100 capsular serotypes identified
  • 10-15 serotypes cause most invasive disease
  • Serotype distribution varies by region and age
  • Common invasive serotypes: 1, 3, 4, 5, 6A, 6B, 7F, 9V, 14, 18C, 19A, 19F, 23F

Disease Patterns:

  • Peaks after viral respiratory infections (especially influenza)
  • Co-infection with influenza increases mortality
  • Outbreaks in closed populations

Mortality:

  • Pneumonia: 5-7% (higher in elderly and immunocompromised)
  • Meningitis: 15-20%
  • Sepsis: Up to 30-40%

Prevention Impact:

  • Pneumococcal vaccines (PCV13, PPSV23) have reduced invasive disease
  • Herd immunity from childhood vaccination programs
  • Serotype replacement observed (non-vaccine types emerging)

GROUP 2: MECHANISM OF ENTRY & VIRULENCE FACTORS

Mechanism of Entry

Step 1: Transmission

  • Respiratory droplets from coughing, sneezing, talking
  • Bacteria land in nasopharynx

Step 2: Adhesion (Colonization)

Phosphorylcholine-PAFr Binding:

  • Bacterial phosphorylcholine binds to platelet-activating factor receptor (PAFr)
  • Primary mechanism for epithelial attachment

PsaA (Pneumococcal Surface Adhesin A):

  • Binds to E-cadherin at epithelial cell junctions
  • Maintains colonization at tight junctions

Neuraminidase:

  • Cleaves sialic acid from cell surfaces
  • Exposes more binding sites for adhesins
  • Releases sugars as nutrients

Step 3: Biofilm Formation

  • Bacteria form protective communities
  • Resistance to mucociliary clearance
  • Asymptomatic carriage for weeks to months
  • Altered gene expression and increased antibiotic resistance

Step 4: Local Spread

To Middle Ear (Otitis Media):

  • Route: Nasopharynx → Eustachian tube → Middle ear
  • Trigger: Eustachian tube obstruction during URI
  • Results in inflammation, fluid, pain, fever

To Sinuses (Sinusitis):

  • Route: Nasopharynx → Paranasal sinuses
  • Trigger: Impaired drainage, mucus accumulation
  • Results in facial pain, headache, discharge

Step 5: Lung Invasion (Pneumonia)

Entry via Microaspiration:

  • Oropharyngeal secretions aspirated during sleep
  • Risk increased when defenses impaired

Risk Factors:

  • Viral infections (damage cilia)
  • Smoking (impairs clearance)
  • Alcohol (suppresses reflexes)
  • Chronic lung disease

Three Phases in Lungs:

Phase 1 - Adhesion:

  • CbpA binds to pneumocytes
  • Pneumolysin damages cells, disrupts tight junctions, activates complement

Phase 2 - Growth:

  • Rapid multiplication
  • Capsule prevents phagocytosis
  • Toxins cause fluid leakage into alveoli

Phase 3 - Inflammation:

  • Massive neutrophil infiltration
  • Alveoli fill with exudate, pus, RBCs
  • Lobar consolidation develops

Step 6: Bloodstream Entry (Bacteremia)

Four Routes:

  1. Paracellular - through damaged tight junctions
  2. Transcellular - inside vacuoles through cells
  3. Direct invasion - through damaged tissue
  4. Trojan horse - hidden in phagocytes

Step 7: Brain Invasion (Meningitis)

Requirements:

  • High bacteremia
  • Compromised blood-brain barrier

Three Routes Into CNS:

  1. Transcellular - endocytosis and transport through endothelial cells
  2. Paracellular - through damaged tight junctions
  3. Trojan horse - inside infected monocytes

In the Brain:

  • CSF has low immunity
  • Rapid bacterial multiplication
  • Inflammation damages neurons
  • Causes edema, increased pressure, neuronal death

Step 8: Other Sites

  • Heart → Endocarditis (valve infection)
  • Joints → Septic arthritis
  • Peritoneum → Peritonitis (especially dialysis patients)

Virulence Factors

1. Capsular Polysaccharide (Most Important)

Structure:

  • Thick polysaccharide layer outside cell wall
  • Over 100 different serotypes based on capsule composition

Functions:

  • Antiphagocytic - prevents complement C3b binding
  • Blocks neutrophil recognition
  • Inhibits opsonization
  • Essential for invasive disease

Clinical Relevance:

  • Unencapsulated strains rarely cause invasive disease
  • Serotype determines virulence level
  • Target of pneumococcal vaccines

2. Pneumolysin (Major Toxin)

Type:

  • Cholesterol-dependent cytolysin
  • Pore-forming toxin

Mechanisms:

  • Forms pores in cell membranes → cell lysis
  • Disrupts epithelial and endothelial barriers
  • Activates complement cascade
  • Triggers inflammatory cytokine release
  • Inhibits ciliary beating
  • Suppresses immune cell function

Effects:

  • Direct cytotoxicity to pneumocytes
  • Increases vascular permeability
  • Facilitates bacterial invasion
  • Contributes to tissue damage

3. Surface Proteins

PspA (Pneumococcal Surface Protein A):

  • Inhibits complement activation
  • Interferes with C3 deposition
  • Reduces opsonophagocytosis

PspC (Choline-Binding Protein A/CbpA):

  • Binds to complement factor H
  • Prevents complement activation on bacterial surface
  • Mediates adhesion to cells

Pili (Fimbriae):

  • Long protein appendages
  • Mediate adhesion to epithelial cells
  • Important for biofilm formation
  • Facilitate colonization

4. Enzymes

Neuraminidase (NanA, NanB, NanC):

  • Cleaves sialic acid residues
  • Exposes cryptic receptors
  • Provides nutrition
  • Facilitates adhesion

Hyaluronidase:

  • Degrades hyaluronic acid in connective tissue
  • Facilitates spread through tissues

IgA1 Protease:

  • Cleaves secretory IgA antibodies
  • Evades mucosal immunity

Autolysin (LytA):

  • Degrades peptidoglycan
  • Releases pneumolysin and other intracellular components
  • Contributes to inflammation

5. Hydrogen Peroxide Production

  • Generates oxidative stress
  • Damages host tissues
  • Particularly important in early colonization

6. Phase Variation

  • Bacteria alter surface protein expression
  • Adapts to different host environments
  • Helps evade immune recognition
  • Switches between colonization and invasive phenotypes

7. Immune Evasion Strategies

Molecular Mimicry:

  • Phosphorylcholine resembles host PAF
  • Reduces immune recognition

Complement Resistance:

  • Multiple mechanisms block complement
  • Capsule, PspA, PspC all contribute

Biofilm Formation:

  • Protection from antibodies
  • Reduced antibiotic penetration
  • Altered metabolism

GROUP 3: TREATMENT & RESISTANCE

Treatment

Antibiotic Therapy

First-Line Agents (Susceptible Strains):

Penicillins:

  • Penicillin G (IV for severe infections)
  • Amoxicillin (oral for mild-moderate infections)
  • Mechanism: Inhibits cell wall synthesis

Dosing Considerations:

  • High-dose therapy may overcome intermediate resistance
  • Amoxicillin: 1g three times daily (standard) or 2g twice daily (high-dose)

Alternative Agents:

Cephalosporins:

  • Ceftriaxone (IV) - for severe infections, meningitis
  • Cefotaxime (IV) - alternative to ceftriaxone
  • Cefuroxime - oral option

Macrolides:

  • Azithromycin
  • Clarithromycin
  • Often combined with beta-lactams for pneumonia

Fluoroquinolones:

  • Levofloxacin
  • Moxifloxacin
  • Respiratory quinolones with excellent pneumococcal coverage

Vancomycin:

  • Reserved for penicillin-resistant strains
  • Especially in meningitis
  • IV administration required

Linezolid:

  • Alternative for resistant strains
  • Oral bioavailability

Treatment by Disease Type

Community-Acquired Pneumonia:

  • Outpatient: Amoxicillin or macrolide
  • Inpatient: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin OR respiratory fluoroquinolone
  • Duration: 5-7 days (may extend to 7-10 days for severe cases)

Meningitis:

  • Ceftriaxone + vancomycin (empiric therapy)
  • Add dexamethasone to reduce inflammation
  • Duration: 10-14 days
  • May add rifampin for resistant strains

Otitis Media:

  • High-dose amoxicillin
  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate if no improvement
  • Duration: 5-10 days

Bacteremia/Sepsis:

  • Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
  • Add vancomycin if resistance suspected
  • Duration: 7-14 days depending on source

Supportive Care

  • Oxygen therapy for pneumonia
  • IV fluids for dehydration
  • Antipyretics for fever
  • Drainage for empyema or abscess

Antibiotic Resistance

Mechanisms of Resistance

1. Penicillin Resistance (Most Common)

Mechanism:

  • Alterations in penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
  • Mutations reduce antibiotic affinity
  • Mosaic PBPs acquired from other streptococci

Levels:

  • Susceptible: MIC ≤0.06 μg/mL
  • Intermediate: MIC 0.12-1 μg/mL
  • Resistant: MIC ≥2 μg/mL

Clinical Impact:

  • Intermediate resistance often overcome with high-dose therapy
  • High-level resistance requires alternative agents

2. Macrolide Resistance

Mechanisms:

  • erm genes: ribosomal methylation (cross-resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, streptogramins)
  • mef genes: efflux pumps (macrolide-specific)

Prevalence:

  • Up to 30-40% in some regions

3. Fluoroquinolone Resistance

Mechanism:

  • Mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC)
  • Stepwise accumulation of mutations

Prevalence:

  • Still relatively low (<5%) but increasing

4. Multi-Drug Resistance (MDR)

Definition:

  • Resistance to ≥3 antibiotic classes

Concern:

  • Limits treatment options
  • Associated with certain serotypes (especially 19A)

Factors Driving Resistance

Antibiotic Pressure:

  • Widespread antibiotic use selects for resistant strains
  • Prophylactic antibiotic use in children

Horizontal Gene Transfer:

  • Transformation (uptake of DNA from environment)
  • Acquisition of resistance genes from other bacteria

Geographic Variation:

  • Higher resistance in areas with high antibiotic use
  • Asia, Southern Europe, and Latin America particularly affected

Serotype-Specific:

  • Certain serotypes more likely to be resistant (e.g., 19A, 6A, 9V, 14)
  • Non-vaccine serotypes may show higher resistance

Healthcare Settings:

  • Hospitals and long-term care facilities are reservoirs

Global Resistance Patterns

Penicillin Resistance:

  • Non-meningeal isolates: 10-30% resistance globally
  • Meningeal isolates: Higher concern due to poor CNS penetration

Regional Variations:

  • North America: ~20-30% non-susceptible
  • Europe: Variable (5-40% depending on country)
  • Asia: Up to 70-80% in some countries
  • Africa: Data limited but concerning trends

Impact of Vaccination on Resistance

PCV7 (2000):

  • Reduced disease from vaccine serotypes
  • Many vaccine serotypes had high resistance rates

PCV13 (2010):

  • Included serotype 19A (highly resistant)
  • Overall decrease in resistant infections

Serotype Replacement:

  • Non-vaccine serotypes emerging
  • Some with resistance patterns (e.g., 15A, 35B)

Strategies to Combat Resistance

Antimicrobial Stewardship:

  • Appropriate antibiotic selection
  • Correct dosing and duration
  • Avoid unnecessary antibiotic use

Vaccination:

  • PCV13 for children
  • PPSV23 for adults and high-risk groups
  • Reduces overall disease burden and antibiotic use

Infection Control:

  • Hand hygiene
  • Respiratory etiquette
  • Isolation of infected patients

Surveillance:

  • Monitor resistance patterns
  • Track emerging serotypes
  • Guide empiric therapy recommendations

Treatment Modifications for Resistance

For Penicillin-Resistant Pneumonia:

  • Use respiratory fluoroquinolone
  • OR ceftriaxone (high-dose)
  • Vancomycin for treatment failures

For Penicillin-Resistant Meningitis:

  • Ceftriaxone + vancomycin
  • Consider adding rifampin
  • May need CSF sterilization monitoring

For MDR Strains:

  • Combination therapy
  • Linezolid or newer agents
  • Consult infectious disease specialist

Future Directions

New Antibiotics:

  • Lefamulin (pleuromutilin) - approved 2019
  • Ceftaroline (5th generation cephalosporin)
  • Delafloxacin (fluoroquinolone)

Novel Approaches:

  • Anti-virulence therapy (targeting toxins)
  • Immunotherapy
  • Bacteriophage therapy (experimental)

Vaccine Development:

  • Broader coverage vaccines
  • Protein-based vaccines (serotype-independent)
  • Next-generation conjugate vaccines

Key Takeaway Messages

Group 1 (Characteristics & Epidemiology):

  • S. pneumoniae is a major global pathogen with significant morbidity and mortality
  • Certain populations at higher risk
  • Vaccination has changed epidemiology

Group 2 (Mechanism & Virulence):

  • Multistep process from colonization to invasive disease
  • Capsule and pneumolysin are key virulence factors
  • Multiple mechanisms enable immune evasion

Group 3 (Treatment & Resistance):

  • Beta-lactams remain first-line when susceptible
  • Resistance is increasing globally
  • Vaccination and stewardship are critical control measures

Title: BASIC PHARMACOLOGY -  STUDY GUIDE
Content:
Course Code: DBS 3103 / MBPL3611
Institution: Mount Kenya University
Program: Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery
Assessment: Continuous Assessment Test (CAT) 3
Duration: 1 Hour

SECTION A: MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQs)

GENERAL PHARMACOLOGY

Question 1

Pharmacodynamics includes the study of:

A. Mechanisms of drug action
B. Biotransformation of drugs in the organism
C. Distribution of drugs in the organism
D. Excretion of drugs in the organism
E. All of the above

Answer: A

Explanation: Pharmacodynamics specifically studies the mechanisms of drug action and the biochemical and physiological effects of drugs on the body. Options B, C, and D describe pharmacokinetic processes (what the body does to the drug), while pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body.

Question 2

Which of the following physiological changes in the elderly may lead to the need to reduce the dose of a prescribed medication?

A. Increased rate of drug absorption
B. Increased rate of hepatic drug biotransformation
C. Decreased efficiency in drug biotransformation
D. Decreased total body fluid as a proportion of body mass
E. None of the above

Answer: C

Explanation: Elderly patients experience decreased hepatic enzyme activity and reduced liver blood flow, leading to decreased drug biotransformation. This results in prolonged drug half-life and increased drug accumulation, necessitating dose reduction to prevent toxicity.

Question 3

What does the term "affinity" mean?

A. A measure of how tightly a drug binds to plasma proteins
B. A measure of how tightly a drug binds to a receptor
C. A measure of the inhibitory potency of a drug
D. A measure of the bioavailability of a drug

Answer: B

Explanation: Affinity refers to the strength of the interaction between a drug and its receptor. High affinity means the drug binds strongly to the receptor, requiring lower concentrations to achieve binding. This is distinct from efficacy, which describes the ability to produce an effect once bound.

Question 4

A pharmacological antagonist is a drug that:

A. Binds to the receptor and initiates changes in cell function, producing a suboptimal effect
B. Binds to the receptor and initiates changes in cell function, producing an optimal effect
C. Interacts with plasma proteins but does not produce any effect
D. Binds to the receptors without directly altering their function

Answer: D

Explanation: An antagonist binds to a receptor but does not activate it. Instead, it blocks the receptor site, preventing endogenous ligands or agonists from binding and producing their effects. Antagonists have affinity but no intrinsic activity (efficacy).

Question 5

Irreversible inhibition is due to:

A. Ionic bond
B. Covalent bond
C. Hydrogen bond
D. All of the above

Answer: B

Explanation: Irreversible inhibition occurs through covalent bond formation between the drug and its target. Covalent bonds are very strong and permanent, making the inhibition essentially irreversible. The effect only diminishes when new enzymes or receptors are synthesized.

Question 6

Which of the following parameters is used to indicate the ability of a drug to produce the desired effect?

A. Potency
B. Intrinsic activity
C. Therapeutic index
D. Efficacy

Answer: D

Explanation: Efficacy refers to the maximum response a drug can produce, regardless of dose. It indicates the drug's ability to produce the desired therapeutic effect. Potency refers to the dose required to produce a given effect, while efficacy describes the magnitude of that effect.

Question 7

Drug receptors are found on:

A. Plasma membranes only
B. Plasma membranes and plasma proteins
C. Plasma proteins only
D. Plasma membranes and intracellular structures

Answer: D

Explanation: Drug receptors are located on plasma membranes (G-protein coupled receptors, ion channels, enzyme-linked receptors) and intracellularly (nuclear receptors for steroid hormones, thyroid hormones). This allows drugs to interact with various cellular components to produce therapeutic effects.

AUTONOMIC NERVOUS SYSTEM

Question 8

Nicotinic receptor sites do not include which of the following?

A. Bronchial smooth muscle
B. Adrenal medullary cells
C. Parasympathetic ganglia
D. Skeletal muscle end plates
E. Sympathetic ganglia

Answer: A

Explanation: Bronchial smooth muscle contains muscarinic receptors (M3), not nicotinic receptors. Nicotinic receptors are found at neuromuscular junctions (skeletal muscle), autonomic ganglia (both sympathetic and parasympathetic), and adrenal medulla.

Question 9

Which of the following is the neurotransmitter agent normally released in the sinoatrial node (SAN) of the heart in response to an increase in blood pressure?

A. Acetylcholine
B. Dopamine
C. Epinephrine
D. Glutamine
E. Norepinephrine

Answer: A

Explanation: When blood pressure increases, baroreceptors activate parasympathetic (vagal) output to the heart. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine at the SA node, which binds to M2 muscarinic receptors, causing bradycardia and reduced cardiac output to lower blood pressure.

Question 10

Which of the following drugs facilitates catecholamine transmitter release from adrenergic nerve endings?

A. Dopamine
B. Epinephrine
C. Amphetamine
D. Norepinephrine
E. Reserpine

Answer: C

Explanation: Amphetamine is an indirect sympathomimetic that enters adrenergic nerve terminals and displaces stored norepinephrine, causing its release into the synaptic cleft. This mechanism is responsible for amphetamine's stimulant effects. Reserpine, in contrast, depletes catecholamine stores.

Question 11

Full activation of the sympathetic nervous system, as in the fight-or-flight reaction, may occur during maximal exercise. Which of the following effects is most likely to occur?

A. Bronchoconstriction
B. Increased intestinal motility
C. Decreased renal blood flow
D. Miosis
E. Bradycardia

Answer: C

Explanation: During sympathetic activation, blood is redirected from non-essential organs (including kidneys and GI tract) to skeletal muscles, heart, and brain. This causes decreased renal blood flow. Other sympathetic effects include bronchodilation, decreased GI motility, mydriasis (pupil dilation), and tachycardia.

Question 12

Mr. Otieno has been diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. You are considering treatment with pyridostigmine and neostigmine. Which adverse effect is associated with these two drugs?

A. Bronchoconstriction
B. Irreversible action
C. Constipation
D. Diarrhea
E. Reduced gastric secretions

Answer: D

Explanation: Pyridostigmine and neostigmine are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors that increase acetylcholine levels at all cholinergic sites, including the GI tract. This leads to increased GI motility and secretions, causing diarrhea. Other cholinergic effects include bronchoconstriction, increased secretions, and bradycardia.

Question 13

Probable signs of atropine overdose in toddlers include which one of the following?

A. Gastrointestinal smooth muscle cramping
B. Tachycardia
C. Increased gastric secretion
D. Pupillary constriction

Answer: B

Explanation: Atropine is an antimuscarinic that blocks parasympathetic effects. Overdose presents with "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter." Tachycardia results from blockade of vagal (M2) receptors in the heart. Other signs include mydriasis, decreased secretions, and hyperthermia.

Question 14

Which of the following is the most dangerous effect of belladonna alkaloids in infants and toddlers?

A. Dehydration
B. Hallucinations
C. Hyperthermia
D. Hypertension
E. Intraventricular heart block

Answer: C

Explanation: Hyperthermia is the most life-threatening effect in children because belladonna alkaloids (atropine) block sweat glands, preventing heat dissipation. Children have less efficient thermoregulation and higher metabolic rates, making them particularly vulnerable to dangerous temperature elevations.

Question 15

Which is the treatment of choice in a child with signs of anaphylaxis after being stung by three bees?

A. Diphenhydramine
B. Ephedrine
C. Epinephrine
D. Dexamethasone
E. Isoproterenol

Answer: C

Explanation: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis. It acts on α1 receptors (vasoconstriction to reverse hypotension), β1 receptors (increased cardiac output), and β2 receptors (bronchodilation). It also stabilizes mast cells, preventing further mediator release. Route: IM into anterolateral thigh.

Question 16

Epinephrine causes a decrease in:

A. Cyclic AMP in heart muscle
B. Free fatty acids in blood
C. Glucose in blood
D. Lactate in blood
