Answer: C) Phospholipid

Explanation: PAF is chemically acetyl-glyceryl-ether-phosphocholine, making it a phospholipid derivative. Despite its small size compared to eicosanoids, it has potent biological activities including platelet aggregation, inflammation, and increased vascular permeability at very low concentrations (nanomolar range).

Title: Medical Parasitology
Content:
MEDICAL ENTOMOLOGY

Vector Control Methods

1. Physical/Mechanical Control

  • Screened windows and doors
  • Mosquito nets on walls
  • Draining pools of water
  • Removing long grass
  • Emptying containers

2. Biological Control

  • Using living organisms to control vectors
  • Toxorhynchites mosquito species - larvae feed on larvae of Anopheles, Culex, and Aedes
  • Gambusia affinis (fish) - feeds on mosquito larvae
  • Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt bacteria) - bacterial form
  • Bacillus sphaericus
  • Other predators

3. Genetic Engineering

  • Sterile male technique
  • Refractory vectors - modifying genes of vectors so that pathogens cannot develop
  • Result: change in target site

4. Chemical Control - Insecticides

Classification Based on Toxicity (LD50):
  • LD50 1-50: Extremely toxic/dangerous
  • LD50 50-500: Moderately toxic
  • LD50 >5000: Safe
Types of Insecticides:

A) Chlorinated Hydrocarbons

  • Relatively stable
  • Act as nerve poisons
  • Lipid/fat soluble
  • Disrupt Na+ channels
  • Most are banned (e.g., DDT) due to long persistence and bioaccumulation in fatty tissues
  • Examples: DDT, Dieldrin, Endrin

B) Organophosphates (OP)

  • Less persistent, don't accumulate in fatty tissues
  • Block cholinesterase (acetylcholine won't be broken down)
  • Examples: Malathion, Chlorpyrifos, Parathion, Diazinon, Dimethoate

C) Carbamates

  • MOA similar to organophosphates
  • Bind to acetylcholinesterase
  • Better biodegradability, availability, and solubility
  • Examples: Carbaryl, Propoxur, Bendiocarb
  • Lower mammalian/human toxicity
  • Advantage over OP: Chronic exposure to carbamates is less likely to cause illness than organophosphates; inhibiting action is reversible

D) Pyrethroids

  • Synthetic/semi-natural compounds
  • Examples: Permethrin (used in ITNs, LLINs), Deltamethrin
  • They bind to voltage gated sodium channels and delay their inactivation. increasing permeability
  • Results in excitation, lack of coordination, and paralysis
  • Relatively safe for outdoor use
  • Effect is rapid (knockdown effect)

E) Insect Growth Regulators (IGRs)

  • Block insect sugar/chitin biosynthesis pathway
  • Example: Pyriproxyfen, Diflubenzuron

F) Formamidines

  • Mimic activity of octopamine (neurotransmitter/neurohormone/neuromodulator)
  • They bind to octopamine receptors in insects, leading to disordered neuronal excitation and death
  • MOA is different, useful in resistant insects
  • Example: Amitraz
  • Effective against mites and ticks
  • Examples: Chlordimeform, Amitraz

G) Avermectins

  • Cause paralysis and death by inhibiting transmission of nerve impulses
  • Narrow spectrum, active only against specific invertebrates
  • Can also be used against parasitic nematodes
  • Example: Abamectin

H) Neonicotinoids

  • Both systemic and contact activity against sucking insects
  • Mimic nicotine
  • Example: Imidacloprid

I) Miticides

  • Effective against mites
  • Examples: Bromopropylate, Cyhexatin, Tetradifon
Types of Insecticides by Application:
  • Contact poison
  • Fumigant
  • Systemic
  • Stomach poison
  • Respiratory poison

MOSQUITO-BORNE DISEASES

Family: CULICIDAE

Genus: ANOPHELES

Key Species:

  • Anopheles gambiae complex (supervector)
  • An. funestus
  • An. arabiensis - zoophilic
  • An. melas
  • An. stephensi - supervector, transmits malaria mostly in Asia; recently reported in Africa (unlike other African species, can withstand high temperatures and arid conditions)

Behavior:

  • Anthropophilic
  • Endophagic (feeds indoors)
  • Endophilic (rests indoors)

Life Cycle:

  • Complete metamorphosis (holometabolous)
  • Duration depends on temperature (optimal 25°C) and humidity (78%)

Breeding:

  • Stagnant water with vegetation and algae
  • Eggs laid singly and laid one at a time
  • Float on water surface

Larval Stage:

  • 4 instars (L1-L4)
  • Larva lies parallel to water surface (breathes through spiracles on body side)
  • Feeding stage

Pupal Stage:

  • Resting stage
  • Comma-shaped
  • Emerges after 2-3 days

Adult Stage:

  • Emerges and mates post-emergence
  • Females: Feed on sugar solutions AND blood (require blood meal for egg development - anautogenous)
  • Males: Only feed on sugar solutions
  • Parthenogenesis possible (egg development without fertilization)

Identification:

  • Resting position: 45° angle to surface
  • Antennae: Males - bushy/plumose; Females - smooth/pilose
  • Feeding: Only females take blood meals
  • Both sexes feed on sugar solutions

Geographic Distribution:

  • Determined by location of parasite

Medical Importance:

  • Primary: Transmission of malaria (genus Plasmodium)

Control Measures:

  1. Chemical: Larvicides, breeding site treatment
  2. Biological: Toxorhynchites species (T. rutilus) prey on mosquito larvae
  3. Genetic: Refractory index - use of endosymbionts/bacteria that kill mosquito, preventing Plasmodium survival
  4. Physical/Mechanical:
    • Draining/removal of containers
    • Mosquito nets
    • IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying)
    • Trans-ovarian light traps
    • Screening windows
    • Cutting tall grass/weeds
    • Mesh on walls

Genus: CULEX

Key Species:

  • Culex quinquefasciatus

Behavior:

  • Exophagic (feeds outdoors)
  • Exophilic (rests outdoors)
  • Feeding time: 3pm-6pm, nocturnal
  • Diurnal feeding: 10am

Breeding:

  • Contaminated water (sewage, drains)

Life Cycle:

  • Complete metamorphosis
  • Eggs, larvae, pupae, adult stages
  • Eggs: Laid simultaneously, attached to each other forming a raft; float on water as a raft
  • Larvae: Breathe via siphon; feed on particles and algae; hang at 45° angle to surface (unlike Anopheles)

Host Detection:

  • Eyes and olfactory cues

Medical Importance:

  • Transmission of filarial nematodes (Wuchereria bancrofti)
  • Transmission of arboviruses (Rift Valley fever, West Nile virus)
  • Can transmit virus from female to eggs (transovarial transmission), so adults emerge with virus

Control:

  1. Breeding site management: Improving sanitation, installing proper sewage systems
  2. Chemical: Insecticides on larval habitats (spray over 7-10 days; oils/films less effective in presence of organic matter)
  3. Genetic engineering: Light traps
  4. Physical: Wire mesh screens

Genus: AEDES

Key Species:

  • Aedes aegypti
  • Aedes albopictus

Appearance:

  • Black color with white spots
  • Painful biters

Behavior:

  • "Container breeders" - prefer breeding in clean containers
  • Biting time: Early morning and late evening
  • Bimodal biting behavior

Breeding:

  • Clean containers, tires, flower vases
  • Both males and females take blood meals during oviposition

Life Cycle:

  • Similar to Culex
  • Complete metamorphosis

Medical Importance: Both species transmit:

  • Dengue fever
  • Chikungunya
  • Zika virus
  • Yellow fever
  • O'nyong-nyong
  • Japanese encephalitis
  • Arboviruses transmitted vertically (transovarial)
  • Rift Valley fever (mechanical transmission)

Control:

  1. Physical: Remove vegetation, predators, drain containers; straighten rivers and remove obstructing material to increase water velocity
  2. Chemical:
    • Insecticides on water surfaces (15-30 min duration)
    • Use of Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis)
  3. Biological: Light traps, mosquito-eating fish

Family: PSYCHODIDAE (Sandflies)

Subfamily: PHLEBOTOMINAE

Distribution:

  • Worldwide
  • Old World: Mediterranean, Indian subcontinent, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia
  • New World: Central and South America

Genera:

  1. Phlebotomus (Old World) - 4 subgenera
  2. Lutzomyia (New World) - Lutzomyia umbratilis (Brazil)
  3. Sergentomyia (zoophilic)

Bionomics:

  • Oviposition in small cracks, holes in ground, base of termite mounds
  • Can breed in chicken coops, poultry houses, animal burrows, rubbish heaps
  • Prefer high humidity areas; cannot withstand desiccation
  • Complete life cycle

Behavior:

  • Females require blood meal
  • Some species are autogenous
  • Anthropophilic
  • Weak fliers
  • Short mouthparts
  • Bite exposed body parts
  • Bimodal biting pattern: feeding times in early morning and early evening

Medical Importance:

  • Transmission of leishmaniasis (3 forms):
    • Leishmania donovani - visceral leishmaniasis
    • Leishmania tropica - cutaneous leishmaniasis (Old World)
    • Leishmania braziliensis complex - mucocutaneous leishmaniasis
  • Transmission of Carrion's disease (Bartonella bacilliformis)
  • Sandfly fever virus (Phlebovirus)

Control:

  1. Physical:
    • Removal of termite mounds
    • Personal protection
    • Applying efficient insect repellents (DEET, Picaridin)
    • Protective clothing
    • Timing outdoor activities
  2. Chemical:
    • Spraying insecticides on cracks in walls, termite mounds, animal burrows
  3. Habitat Control:
    • Attempts to destroy reservoir hosts (rodents are reservoir hosts involved in zoonotic transmission)

Family: CERATOPOGONIDAE (Biting Midges)

Common Name: Biting midges, "no-see-ums"

Distribution:

  • Worldwide in tropics, subtropics, Caribbean, Pacific

Genera:

  1. Leptoconops - tropics and continents
  2. Culicoides - worldwide distribution

Breeding:

  • Prefer ovipositing in wet mud/sand (both salt and fresh water)
  • Pupae in soil or mud

Behavior:

  • Both diurnal and nocturnal
  • Very active in wind
  • Females prefer feeding on exposed body parts
  • Both exophagic and exophilic
  • Some Culicoides are autogenous

Medical Importance:

  • Transmission of Mansonella ozzardi (filarial nematode)
  • In Africa, monkey acts as reservoir host
  • Painful bites
  • Culicoides are biting pests with larvae found in various habitats

Control:

  • Difficult to achieve by insecticides
  • Can be achieved by avoiding activity during peak times
  • Personal protection with repellents
  • Use of screens/netting

Family: SIMULIIDAE (Black Flies)

Common Name: Black flies

Distribution: Worldwide

Breeding:

  • Along riverbanks in fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water

Genera:

  • Simulium
  • Prosimulium
  • Cnephia

Bionomics:

  • Both males and females feed on plant juices
  • Females require blood meal for egg viability
  • Few members are autogenous
  • Bimodal biting pattern: early morning and early evening (diurnal)
  • Exophilic and exophagic
  • Prefer feeding on exposed body parts (head and arms more than legs)

Medical Importance:

  • Transmission of Onchocerca volvulus (causes river blindness/onchocerciasis)
  • Simulium metallicum can transmit Mansonella ozzardi (non-pathogenic)
  • Bites cause bleeding of skin; wounds predispose to secondary bacterial infection

Control:

  1. Physical:
    • Protection by wearing clothing that covers exposed parts
    • Application of repellents
    • Timing outdoor activities (avoid early morning/evening)
  2. Chemical:
    • Spraying insecticides on larval breeding sites and resting areas
    • Applying larvicides on water surfaces (15-30 min duration)
    • Use of Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis)
  3. Physical habitat modification:
    • Straightening rivers
    • Remove obstructing material to increase water velocity

Family: TABANIDAE (Horse Flies, Deer Flies)

Common Name: Horse flies, deer flies

Genera:

  1. Tabanus (horse fly) - green head, breeds in swamps
  2. Chrysops (deer fly) - yellow/brown
  3. Haematopota (clegs)

Bionomics:

  • Females feed during day in bright sunlight
  • Locate host by sight and olfactory cues
  • Purely exophagic except Chrysops silacea (attracted by darkness, must hang from objects)
  • Diurnal; sight plays major role in attraction along with olfactory cues
  • Large object detectors
  • Painful bites due to large mouthparts

Medical Importance:

  • Tabanus implicated in transmission of Bacillus anthracis (anthrax)
  • Also Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease - though primarily tick-borne)
  • Chrysops transmits Loa loa in West and Central Africa (C. silacea and C. dimidiata)

Control:

  1. Physical:
    • Creating barriers
    • Use of traps (canopy traps)
  2. Chemical:
    • Aerial sprays
    • Spraying usually in dry season
  3. Habitat management:
    • Efficient drainage of larval habitats
    • Might be problematic due to large areas
    • Often cost-prohibitive
  4. Personal protection:
    • Insect repellents
    • Use of tags/protective clothing

Family: GLOSSINIDAE (Tsetse Flies)

Common Name: Tsetse flies

Distribution: Sub-Saharan Africa (tropical Africa between 15°N and 20°S)

Classification by Habitat Groups:

1. Forest Group (Fusca group)

  • Inhabit forested areas
  • Key species:
    • G. palpalis - riverine forest, West, Central, and Southern Africa
    • G. tachinoides - drier forested areas
    • G. fuscipes - Central and West Africa
  • Except Glossina longipennis, G. fusca, and G. brevipalpis

2. Savanna Group (Morsitans group)

  • Ecology: savanna regions of West, Central, and East Africa
  • Key species:
    • G. morsitans - most widely distributed in East and Southern Africa
    • G. swynnertoni - in dry thickets
    • G. pallidipes - savanna of East and Southern Africa
    • G. longipalpis - smallest species

3. Riverine Group (Palpalis group)

  • Inhabit vegetation along rivers, lakes, swamps in moist/humid coastal areas
  • Key species:
    • G. palpalis
    • G. tachinoides - near permanent rivers in West Africa, humid areas
    • G. fuscipes - Central and West Africa

Bionomics:

  • Unique reproduction: Adenotrophic viviparity (larviparous)
    • Uterus supplied by accessory gland (milk gland)
    • Larva deposited in shaded areas, soil, cracks (2.5cm deep)
    • Pupates immediately; adults emerge after 4-5 weeks
  • Feeding:
    • Both males and females feed on blood every 2-3 days
    • Diurnal feeders; sight plays major role in host detection along with olfactory cues
    • Attracted to dark moving objects
  • Resting:
    • At night, prefer resting on vegetation
    • During day, rest at lower levels
    • Resting takes place 23 hours/day

Medical Importance:

  • African Trypanosomiasis (Sleeping Sickness)
    • G. palpalis and G. tachinoides - transmit West African (Gambian) trypanosomiasis (T. brucei gambiense)
    • G. morsitans, G. swynnertoni, G. pallidipes - transmit East African (Rhodesian) trypanosomiasis (T. brucei rhodesiense)
    • G. longipalpis causes dermatitis in Angola

Control:

  1. Physical/Mechanical:
    • Creating barriers
    • Aerial sprays (especially in dry season)
    • Use of traps (Ngu trap)
  2. Habitat Management:
    • Clearing vegetation
    • Bush clearing along rivers
  3. Chemical:
    • Insecticides
    • Targets for insecticide application
  4. Biological:
    • Sterile insect technique

KEY CONCEPTS IN VECTOR BIOLOGY

Vector Types and Transmission

Based on Maturation of Pathogen:

  1. Cyclopropagative
    • Disease agent undergoes cyclic development AND multiplies in vector
    • Pathogen number increases and develops
  2. Cyclodevelopment
    • Disease agent undergoes cyclic development when fertilized by vector
    • Cyclic change but does not multiply in vector body
  3. Propagative
    • Only multiplication stage of disease transmission
    • No development, only pathogen number increases

Passive Vectors:

  • Mechanical - no biological development
  • Composed of outdoor components only
  • Non-living vectors (fomites)

Development of Resistance

Theme is development of resistance by vectors, leading to:

  • Change of target site
  • Behavioral resistance

Sensitivity and Specificity

In relation to thin vs thick blood smears for parasite detection

Anthrophilic vs Zoophilic

  • Anthropophilic - preference for human blood meals
  • Zoophilic - preference for animal blood meals

Feeding and Resting Behavior

  • Endophagic - feeds indoors
  • Exophagic - feeds outdoors
  • Endophilic - rests indoors
  • Exophilic - rests outdoors

Mosquito Egg Development

  • Autogenous - can develop eggs without blood meal
  • Anautogenous - requires blood meal for egg development

Reproduction

  • Parthenogenesis - form of asexual reproduction where offspring develop without fertilization

Medical Parasitology (Continued)

MUSCIDAE, FANNIIDAE, AND STOMOXYDAE FAMILIES

Five Genera:

  1. Common Housefly - Musca domestica
  2. Greater Housefly - Muscina stabulans
  3. Stable Fly - Stomoxys calcitrans
  4. Lesser Housefly - Fannia canicularis
  5. Latrine Fly - Fannia scalaris

Epidemiology

  • Worldwide distribution in areas of poor hygiene conditions
  • Mechanical vectors in transmission of enteropathogens

Pathogen Transmission

Pathogens can be transmitted in 3 possible routes:

  1. By flies' body hairs and mouthparts
  2. By flies regurgitating on food during feeding (which they do frequently)
  3. By flies' defecation - most important route of transmission

Medical Importance

  • However, Stomoxys are biting pests and can cause:
    • Dermatitis
    • Secondary bacterial infection
  • Muscidae and Fanniidae biologically transmit Thelazia spp. (eyeworms)

Control

  1. Light bulb insect traps - attract flies which are then electrocuted
  2. Air curtains/barriers - found in entrances of some shops; reduces number of flies entering premises
  3. Source reduction - optimizing/cleaning the larval habitats:
    • Domestic garbage should be placed either in bins/receptacles or in plastic bags with openings tightly closed

THELAZIA SPP. (Eyeworms)

Vector: Tabanus spp.

MYIASIS

Definition: The invasion of organs and tissues of humans and animals by fly larvae

Larvae feed on:

  • Living tissues
  • Dead tissues of host
  • Ingested food (in case of intestinal myiasis)

Types of Myiasis

1. Accidental Myiasis

  • Occurs when an individual consumes food contaminated with eggs or larvae of flies that are not parasitic mammals, such as houseflies
  • Larvae may survive for some time in the intestine and result in pathological effects:
    • Diarrhea
    • Dysentery
    • Abdominal pain
    • Vomiting
  • Larvae may be passed alive or vomited
  • No species is adapted to cause intestinal myiasis in humans

2. Obligatory Myiasis

  • Occurs in mammals, not just humans
  • Maggots/larvae must live in a live host for at least part of their life cycle

3. Facultative Myiasis

  • Larvae are free-living
  • Attack carcasses but can infect living tissues

Pathogenic Forms

A) Urogenital Myiasis

  • Flies are attracted to distal areas which are dirty (in hospital areas, especially)
  • Fly deposits eggs, which hatch immediately and larvae enter urethra

B) Cutaneous/Dermal Myiasis (Furuncular Myiasis)

  • Also called "creeping eruption"
  • Boil-like inflammation of wound infected with larvae
  • Only wounds attract flies which lay eggs; eggs hatch and larvae develop under skin

Treatment: Remove larvae under aseptic conditions

C) Ophthalmic/Ocular Myiasis

  • Flies are attracted to eyes which are dirty
  • Can cause larvae (maggots) to invade and develop in eyes in both humans and animals
  • Fly deposits eggs on/near the eye, the larvae feed on host's living eye tissues
  • Symptoms: Lacrimation, redness, pain
  • Treatment:
    • Removal of larvae
    • If larvae deeply embedded in tissues or mucous membranes, eyes may need to be enucleated
    • If damage by larvae is irreversible, result is eye removal
  • Prevention: Personal hygiene, eyewear

D) Nasopharyngeal Myiasis

  • Major route is nose
  • Larvae crawl down to nasopharynx and can cause:
    • Tonsillitis
    • Tonsillar irritation

E) Intestinal Myiasis

  • Route of entry is mouth
  • Food contaminated with eggs/larvae is swallowed

Maggot Therapy

Application: Live and sterile larvae of Lucilia sericata used in wound management

  • Larvae clean the wounds by feeding on dead tissue

RELEVANT QUESTIONS/CONCEPTS

  1. Give relevant examples of medical importance of flies
  2. Differentiate stable fly and housefly in terms of size and behavior
  3. What is the significance of partially digested blood meals?
  4. How do fleas move?

ORDER: SIPHONAPTERA (Fleas)

Distribution

  • Worldwide distribution
  • Associated with people and animals

Medical Importance - Key Genera:

  1. Xenopsylla cheopis
  2. Ctenocephalides (C. felis, C. canis)
  3. Tunga penetrans (chigoe/jigger flea)
  4. Pulex irritans (human flea)

1. XENOPSYLLA CHEOPIS

  • Vector for Yersinia pestis (plague)
  • Common in the tropics due to warm temperature
  • Also transmits Rickettsia typhi (murine typhus)

2. CTENOCEPHALIDES

Species: C. felis (cat flea), C. canis (dog flea)

Medical Importance:

  • Fleas of this genus may be intermediate hosts of cestodes:
    • Dipylidium caninum
    • Hymenolepis diminuta
  • Also transmit bacteria causing cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae)

3. TUNGA PENETRANS

  • Also known as "chigoe" or "jigger flea"
  • Burrows into people's feet
  • The gravid female flea penetrates the host and deposits eggs in the dermis

4. PULEX IRRITANS

  • Human flea
  • Parasite causing dermatitis in allergic individuals

Bionomics (General for Fleas)

Feeding:

  • Both sexes feed on blood
  • Both are ectoparasites

Life Cycle:

  1. Egg Stage:
    • Female flea locates the host and deposits eggs in the debris/dust in the habitat/dwelling places (e.g., rodent burrow)
    • For human or domestic animal fleas, they lay eggs while still on the host
    • Since the eggs are sticky, they soon fall off the host and are found in areas where host spends their time
  2. Larval Stage:
    • Eggs hatch into larvae (feed on any organic matter/debris)
    • To successfully achieve full development to adulthood, the larvae must feed on partly digested blood meal regurgitated from alimentary canal of adult fleas or feces
    • At the end of larval period, the larvae spin a silken cocoon from protein secreted by its salivary gland
    • Being sticky, it becomes covered with fine particles of dust and debris/sand picked up from floor of host's dwelling
  3. Pupal Stage:
    • 4-12 days (duration 7-8 days) is spent in pupal stage inside the cocoon
    • Time is dependent on temperature and stimulus
  4. Adult Stage:
    • Emerges and seeks host

Host Preference:

  • Although feeding preference and host blood type keeps flea alive, their fertility is determined by preferred host
  • Some can withstand considerable hunger/starvation
  • When no suitable host is available, they rapidly abandon their (dead) hosts in search of living host
  • Presenting a new wave of plague transmission
  • Portions move and feed on horses/livestock in absence of humans

Movement:

  • On the host, they move rapidly by crawling
  • Have a protein called resilin in their legs - highly compressed, produces rapid expansion by the compressed state, giving the power of jumping

Medical Importance of Fleas

1. Flea Nuisance

  • Cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) and dog flea bite people on ankles/lower legs or any exposed body part
  • Hypersensitive people develop dermatitis
  • Inhalation of flea feces causes allergic reactions

2. Plague

  • Medically most important: bubonic plague
  • People have contracted plague when they are hunters handling wild mammals infected with plague

3. Murine Typhus (Rickettsia typhi)

  • Transmitted by rodent fleas, especially X. cheopis

4. Tularemia (Francisella tularensis)

  • Can be transmitted by examining the site

Control of Fleas

  1. Repellents - DEET on clothing
  2. Rodent fleas and larvae - use hand-operated dusters to apply insecticidal dusts such as:
    • Carbaryl
    • Pyrethroids
    • Organophosphates applied to animals/pets
  3. For cat and dog fleas: Insecticides (pyrethroids and OPs) are applied to animals

ORDER: PHTHIRAPTERA (Sucking Lice)

Discuss:

  1. Define pediculosis
  2. Describe the group of lice
  3. Discuss types of blood-sucking lice in humans
  4. Can be located in hairy parts of the body
  5. Identified by pigmented abdomen

Three types of blood-sucking lice in humans:

  1. Body Louse - Pediculus humanus corporis
  2. Head Louse - Pediculus humanus capitis
  3. Pubic/Crab Louse - Pthirus pubis

BODY LOUSE (Pediculus humanus corporis)

Epidemiology

  • Worldwide distribution
  • Common in densely populated slums
  • Associated with poor hygiene conditions

Medical Importance

  1. Pediculosis - condition known as "lousy disease"
    • They feed on blood due to repeated injection of saliva when they bite
    • Bite several times a day
    • Results in intense itchiness/irritability or pessimistic mood
    • Dermatitis, severe itching
    • May have some type of asthma or bronchitis
  2. Risk of secondary bacterial infection such as impetigo (which is contagious)
  3. Results into fever due to lateral scratching
  4. Vector-borne diseases transmitted transcutaneously:
    • Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii)
    • Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis)
    • Trench fever (Bartonella quintana)

Control of Body Louse

  1. Louse-infested clothing is subjected to washing or ironing
  2. Dry cleaning
  3. Impregnation of clothing with pyrethroid insecticides may provide long-lasting protection (permethrin)
  4. Trials have shown that orally administered ivermectin kills lice

HEAD LOUSE (Pediculus humanus capitis)

Medical Importance

  • Causes pediculosis capitis
  • Can result in loss of hair (alopecia)

Control

  1. Regular combing of hair
  2. Shaving of head hair
  3. Use of insecticidal formulas/lotions/shampoos

PUBIC/CRAB LOUSE (Pthirus pubis)

Description

  • Eggs are attached to lice and composed of both louse attached to hair shaft
  • Unlike head lice, crab lice may be laid on a single hair strand
  • Can be found on:
    • Beard
    • Armpits
    • Occasionally chest hair

Medical Importance

  • Cause pediculosis pubis (pubic lice infestation)
  • Due to deposition of feces around genital area
  • Small blue spots/maculae may appear on infested part of skin

Control

  1. Shaving pubic hair
  2. Insecticidal formulations:
    • Dusts
    • Lotions
    • Emulsions (not alcohol-based in genital region)
    • Malathion (may cause irritation in genital area)
  3. On eyelashes: Apply small amount of petroleum jelly twice a day for 8-10 days
  4. After pubic lice treatment, spray/dust or apply emulsion/wash affected areas with water, then iron and dry in sunlight

SCABIES

Causative Agent

Sarcoptes scabiei - worldwide distribution, causes mange

ORDER: HEMIPTERA

Family: CIMICIDAE (Bedbugs)

Key Species:

  1. Cimex lectularius - widely distributed in tropical and non-tropical countries
  2. Cimex hemipterus - commonly found in old and new world tropics; although C. lectularius is found in warm areas of some non-tropical countries (e.g., Florida)
  3. Leptocimex - found mainly in Africa; also recorded in Asia

Epidemiology

Increase in bedbug infestation due to:

  • Global resistance to insecticides
  • Warmer temperatures

Bionomics

Feeding:

  • Both sexes take blood meals
  • They prefer to feed during the night
  • During sunshine, they often hide
  • However, in temperate regions, they may remain active

Resting:

  • During the day, adults and nymphs hide underneath:
    • Loose wallpaper
    • Mattresses
    • Beds
    • Cracks in walls
  • They rest as a group

Medical Importance

  1. Cause restless/sleepless nights
  2. Repeated and vigorous feeding can contribute to iron deficiency, especially in:
    • Infants
    • Young children
    • Elderly people
  3. Hepatitis B
    • But no evidence that they transmit any disease to people

Control

  1. Mechanical transmission of enteropathogens (Shigella, E. coli, Salmonella)
  2. Undergo ecdysis (molting) - can trigger allergic reactions or asthma in people allergic to cockroaches
  3. Cast-off skins or excreta - about 10% of non-asthmatic people exhibit cockroach allergies
    • Symptoms: Sneezing, skin rash, sore eyes, respiratory distress
    • In extreme cases: shortness of breath

Family: REDUVIIDAE (Triatomine Bugs/Kissing Bugs)

Key Genera and Species:

  1. Triatoma - T. infestans, T. dimidiata
  2. Rhodnius - R. prolixus
  3. Panstrongylus - P. megistus

Medical Importance

  • Involved in vector-borne transmission of Trypanosoma cruzi which causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis)
  • Bugs feed on blood, then defecate
  • The feces contain parasites
  • When bugs bite in large numbers, can cause anemia
  • Some people exhibit hypersensitivity, shown by:
    • Edema
    • Pruritus
    • Erythema

Control

  • Spraying the interior surfaces of walls and floors of houses
  • Prefer warm areas like chicken sheds and goat pens
  • Clean pyrethrin only works during feeling of house out/fumigation
  • Reduction of hiding places
  • Prefer dark places

COCKROACHES

Key Genera and Species:

  1. Blattella - B. germanica (German cockroach)
  2. Blatta - B. orientalis (Oriental cockroach)
  3. Periplaneta - P. americana (American cockroach)
  4. Supella - S. longipalpa

Medical Importance

  1. Mechanical transmission of enteropathogens:
    • Shigella
    • E. coli
    • Salmonella
  2. Undergo ecdysis (molting) - can trigger allergic reactions or asthma in people allergic to cockroaches
  3. Allergy - about 10% of non-asthmatic people exhibit cockroach allergies
    • Symptoms:
      • Sneezing
      • Skin rash
      • Sore eyes
      • Respiratory distress
      • In extreme cases: shortness of breath

Control

  1. Use insect growth regulators (IGRs) - inhibit development
  2. Use contact poisons:
    • Boric acid powder (also stomach poison)
  3. Spraying interior surfaces of walls and floors
  4. Reduction of hiding places
  5. Sanitation and good hygiene

CLASS: ARACHNIDA

General Characteristics

  • 8 legs
  • No antennae
  • Undergo incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetabolous) - from larval stage to adult stage
  • Have chelicerae on mouthparts
  • Body divided into:
    • Cephalothorax (prosoma)
    • Abdomen (opisthosoma)

TICKS

Two Main Families:

  1. ARGASIDAE (Soft Ticks)
  2. IXODIDAE (Hard Ticks)

ARGASIDAE (Soft Ticks)

Key Genera:

  • Ornithodoros - O. moubata
  • Argas

Distribution

  • Found in warm areas
  • Vector of tick-borne relapsing fever (Borrelia duttoni)

Characteristics

Nidicolous Ticks:

  • As opposed to non-nidicolous (hard ticks) which quest from the host environment
  • Nymphs and adults are blood-feeding stages
  • Remain for short period of time (hours) on host compared to hard ticks
  • Have multiple host types - called "multi-host tick"
  • Multiple nymphal stages (N1, N2, N3, N4) - usually 4 or 5 nymphal instars

Medical Importance

  1. Transmit bacteria Borrelia (relapsing fever)
  2. Transmission of spirochetes
  3. Viruses
  4. Tick paralysis due to injection of toxins in saliva

Control

  1. Repellents - DEET
  2. Impregnated nets with permethrin
  3. Use of acaricides on furniture/walls which harbor ticks

IXODIDAE (Hard Ticks)

Distribution

  • Worldwide but most common in temperate regions

Key Genera:

  1. Dermacentor
  2. Amblyomma
  3. Haemaphysalis
  4. Rhipicephalus
  5. Hyalomma
  6. Boophilus (1-host tick)

Characteristics

Life Cycle:

  • Hemimetabolous (incomplete metamorphosis)
  • Non-nidicolous
  • 1 nymphal stage
  • Host stays on host for longer period compared to soft ticks

Tick Types Based on Host Number:

3-Host Tick
  • Eggs → Larvae → Nymphs → Adult
  • Each stage feeds on different host
  • Examples: Dermacentor, Amblyomma, Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma
2-Host Tick
  • Eggs hatch into larvae
  • Larvae molt into nymphs on first host
  • Nymphs drop off and seek second host
  • Examples: Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma
1-Host Tick
  • Eggs hatch into larvae on the host
  • Larvae molt into nymphs on host
  • Nymphs molt into adults on host
  • Example: Boophilus

Questing Behavior:

  • Larvae have questing behavior
  • Climb up vegetation (grass, stems, limbs)
  • Wait for host fur contact
  • Drop onto host

Medical Importance

  1. Tick paralysis - toxins in female saliva pumped into host during feeding period
    • Followed by difficulties in:
      • Breathing
      • Swallowing
      • Speaking
  2. Transmission of arboviruses:
    • Q fever
    • Tick-borne encephalitis
    • In people with allergies - can cause poliomyelitis
  3. Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)

Control

  1. Repellents - DEET
  2. Regular dipping of livestock with acaricides
  3. Regular spraying of gardens
  4. Proper removal - pulling it out carefully
  5. Impregnated clothing with permethrin

Why are ticks hard to control?

  1. Nutrient requirements - can survive long periods without feeding
  2. Host adaptability - ticks have the ability to adapt to various host types
  3. This increases their chances of survival as parasites
  4. Vectors for getting hosts for endurance

MITES

Family: SARCOPTIDAE

Causative Agent: Sarcoptes scabiei - scabies mite

Distribution

  • Worldwide distribution
  • Causes mange in animals
  • Causes scabies in humans

Characteristics

  • Are arachnids
  • Don't have teeth on the hypostome of their mouth
  • Have setae (bristles) on body structures for sensing

Diagnosis

By detection of:

  1. Female mites burrowing into the skin to deposit eggs
  2. Narrow, twisting tunnels on the skin may be visible as dark pepper-like tracks
  3. On dark skin: Smear a drop of ink on suspected area
    • After a few minutes when ink is wiped off, tunnels will be visible
  4. Alternative: Use liquid tetracycline under UV light - tunnels fluoresce bright yellow-green

Types of Scabies

1. Classic Scabies Rash

  • Papular eruption (non-painful)
  • Mainly affects interdigital web spaces
  • Also affects:
    • Wrists
    • Elbows
    • Armpits
    • Genitals
    • Other body parts
  • Does NOT appear at sites above the head

Response produced: Due to bite of the burrowing mite

After first exposure:

  • A few number of mites can cause rash
  • One may have severe pruritus (itching) followed by:
    • Constant itching and scratching, especially at night
    • Worse after taking hot bath
    • Scratching can lead to secondary bacterial infections

Control: Use of scabicide on surface layer

2. Crusted/Norwegian Scabies

  • Highly contagious
  • As a result, numerous numbers of mites on skin
  • Skin becomes scaly and hyperkeratotic
  • Can spread to other people easily
  • Mite adheres to patients and infects others

Scraping: Affected skin areas with a scalpel can reveal the mites

Treatment of Scabies

1. Creams and Emulsions

A) Permethrin Cream (5%):

  • Careful application (2 applications - one now, one later)
  • Apply from neck downwards
  • Wash off after 8-12 hours
  • For complicated cases: Re-application after 24 hours

B) Benzyl Benzoate:

  • Apply, then wash after 24 hours for parent/adult
  • Re-application then wash on 2nd and 3rd day, then cure

C) Crotamiton Cream/Lotion:

  • 5 daily applications for one week
  • Can be used in young children and pregnant women

D) Ivermectin:

  • Single dose
  • Topical application

Control of Scabies

  1. It's contagious - treat all family members/community members
  2. Clothes and bedding should be disinfected:
    • Dry cleaning
    • Dusting the clothes/beddings with insecticides
  3. Bed linen, clothes, and infant mattresses:
    • Wash with hot water
    • Then iron and dry in sunlight
    • Can also be wiped in sealed plastic bag and placed in freezer for 48 hours to kill the bedbugs
  4. Antihistamines to control itching
  5. Proper construction of houses

QUESTIONS TO ADDRESS:

  1. Differentiate between Argasidae and Ixodidae
    • Nidicolous vs. non-nidicolous
    • Multi-host vs specific hosts
  2. Highlight on medical importance of Argasidae
  3. Illustrate that Argasidae are multi-host ticks
  4. Medical importance of Argasidae
  5. Distribution of Ixodidae - widespread, mostly in temperate regions of Europe and Asia; less in tropical areas
  6. Differentiate between 3-host, 2-host, and 1-host ticks
  7. Examples of each type
  8. Medical importance of Ixodidae
  9. Why are ticks hard to control?
    • Nutrient requirements
    • Host adaptability
    • Ability to adapt to various host types
  10. Differentiate between crusted and classic scabies
  11. Write short notes on:
    • Infection
    • Describe key features
    • Classic vs. crusted scabies
  12. Highlight on scabies
  13. Outline the medical importance of mites
  14. Describe the class Arachnida
  15. Medical importance of Sarcoptidae

Family: TROMBICULIDAE (Chigger Mites)

Key Species:

  • Leptotrombidium deliense
  • L. akamushi
  • L. fletcheri
  • Eutrombicula alfreddugesi (red bug)
  • Trombicula autumnalis (harvest mite)

Life Cycle

Adults:

  • Adults bite and feed on vertebrates inhabiting arthropod-rich areas
  • Female lays 1-5 spherical eggs in moist but well-drained soil (e.g., riverbank)

Larval Stage:

  • Only larvae are parasitic
  • Attach to small mammals so they will have hosts on which to feed
  • Rodents are important local hosts

Nymphs and Adults:

  • Free-living
  • Inhabit habitats containing suitable small arthropods for feeding

Ecology

  • Humans are accidental hosts, important in aiding dispersal of larvae to other areas
  • Support for larvae away from vegetation
  • Mites are frequently found in agricultural areas/pastures which create scrub vegetation following agricultural processes

Medical Importance

  1. Nuisance: Harvest mites (Trombicula autumnalis), red bugs (Eutrombicula alfreddugesi) cause:
    • Intense irritation
    • Itchy welts/rash
  2. Transmission of scrub typhus (caused by Rickettsia tsutsugamushi/Orientia tsutsugamushi)

Control

  1. Repellents: DEET, benzyl benzoate
  2. Clothing impregnated/sprayed with repellents or permethrin
  3. Burning scrub vegetation
  4. Insecticidal applications by aircraft

KEY CONCEPTS

Transgenic Vectors

Definition: Include into an organism's genome a foreign gene

Purpose:

  • To create GMOs (Genetically Modified Organisms)
  • Gene therapy

Applications in Vector Control:

  • Reducing vector competence
  • Mosquito population suppression (sterile insect technique)
  • Resistance to pathogens
  • Altering vector behavior

IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying)

Definition: Application of insecticides on interior walls of houses and other structures

Challenges:

  • Insecticide resistance
  • Requires trained personnel
  • Health concerns
  • Bottlenecks in implementation

Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt)

  • Bacterial biopesticide
  • Used for mosquito larval control
  • Different strains for different vectors

SUMMARY TABLE: PARASITES AND VECTORS

Title: COMPREHENSIVE BASIC PHARMACOLOGY - 120 CHALLENGING MCQs
Content:
COMPREHENSIVE BASIC PHARMACOLOGY - 120 CHALLENGING MCQs

SECTION A: PHARMACOKINETICS (25 Questions)

1. Bioavailability is BEST defined as:

  • A) Rate of drug absorption
  • B) Fraction of unchanged drug reaching systemic circulation
  • C) Drug concentration at receptor sites
  • D) Degree of protein binding

Answer: B Bioavailability (F) is the percentage of administered drug that reaches systemic circulation unchanged. IV route has 100% bioavailability by definition.

2. A drug that undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism will show:

  • A) Increased oral bioavailability
  • B) Reduced oral bioavailability
  • C) No effect on bioavailability
  • D) Increased half-life

Answer: B First-pass metabolism in the liver reduces the amount of drug reaching systemic circulation, decreasing oral bioavailability. Examples include nitroglycerin and propranolol.

3. A patient with hepatic cirrhosis requires a drug with high first-pass metabolism. Which pharmacokinetic parameter change would you most expect?

  • A) Decreased bioavailability
  • B) Increased bioavailability
  • C) No change in bioavailability
  • D) Decreased volume of distribution

Answer: B Hepatic cirrhosis reduces first-pass metabolism, so less drug is metabolized before reaching systemic circulation, resulting in increased bioavailability and risk of toxicity.

4. Volume of distribution (Vd) increases when a drug is:

  • A) Highly protein-bound
  • B) Highly water soluble
  • C) Highly lipid soluble
  • D) Administered intravenously

Answer: C Lipid-soluble drugs penetrate cell membranes easily and distribute widely into tissues, resulting in large Vd values.

5. A drug has a volume of distribution (Vd) of 400L in a 70kg patient. What does this indicate?

  • A) Drug is confined to plasma
  • B) Drug is confined to extracellular fluid
  • C) Drug is highly tissue-bound
  • D) Drug has poor absorption

Answer: C A Vd of 400L (much larger than total body water ~42L) indicates the drug is extensively distributed and bound to tissues outside the vascular compartment.

6. Clearance is defined as:

  • A) Fraction metabolized per hour
  • B) Volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time
  • C) Rate of drug absorption
  • D) Protein binding capacity

Answer: B Clearance (CL) represents the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time (mL/min or L/hr), reflecting elimination efficiency.

7. The major determinant of half-life (t½) is:

  • A) Bioavailability
  • B) Clearance and Vd
  • C) Protein binding only
  • D) Route of administration

Answer: B Half-life = (0.693 × Vd) / CL. It depends on both volume of distribution and clearance. Changes in either parameter affect t½.

8. If a drug's half-life is 6 hours, approximately how long will it take to reach 97% steady-state concentration with continuous dosing?

  • A) 12 hours
  • B) 18 hours
  • C) 24 hours
  • D) 30 hours

Answer: D Steady state is reached after approximately 5 half-lives (5 × 6 = 30 hours), which achieves about 97% of the final steady-state concentration.

9. Zero-order kinetics means:

  • A) A constant fraction is eliminated
  • B) A constant amount is eliminated
  • C) Elimination is concentration dependent
  • D) Drug never reaches steady state

Answer: B In zero-order kinetics, a fixed amount (not fraction) of drug is eliminated per unit time, regardless of concentration. Occurs with enzyme saturation (e.g., high-dose aspirin, alcohol, phenytoin).

10. Which statement about zero-order kinetics is TRUE?

  • A) A constant fraction of drug is eliminated per unit time
  • B) Half-life remains constant regardless of dose
  • C) Elimination rate is independent of drug concentration
  • D) Doubling the dose doubles the time to eliminate the drug

Answer: C In zero-order kinetics, a constant AMOUNT (not fraction) is eliminated per unit time, regardless of concentration. This occurs when elimination mechanisms are saturated.

11. Steady-state concentration in continuous infusion mainly depends on:

  • A) Loading dose
  • B) Half-life
  • C) Clearance
  • D) Route of administration

Answer: C Steady-state concentration (Css) = Infusion rate / Clearance. It's determined by the balance between input rate and elimination (clearance), not by Vd or t½.

12. A loading dose is required to:

  • A) Maintain steady state
  • B) Rapidly achieve therapeutic concentration
  • C) Reduce toxicity
  • D) Increase bioavailability

Answer: B Loading doses rapidly achieve therapeutic concentrations without waiting 5 half-lives. Loading dose = (Vd × Target concentration) / Bioavailability.

13. A drug is 95% protein-bound. In a patient with hypoalbuminemia, what is the most likely consequence?

  • A) Decreased total drug concentration, increased free drug concentration
  • B) Increased total drug concentration, decreased free drug concentration
  • C) Both total and free drug concentrations decrease
  • D) Decreased total drug concentration, unchanged free drug concentration

Answer: D With less protein available for binding, total drug decreases, but the body maintains free (active) drug concentration through homeostatic mechanisms and increased clearance.

14. Which organ is MOST responsible for Phase I metabolism?

  • A) Kidney
  • B) Liver
  • C) Lungs
  • D) Spleen

Answer: B The liver contains the highest concentration of CYP450 enzymes responsible for Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis).

15. Phase II reactions mainly involve:

  • A) Oxidation
  • B) Reduction
  • C) Conjugation
  • D) Hydrolysis

Answer: C Phase II metabolism involves conjugation reactions (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation) that increase water solubility for excretion.

16. A drug undergoes phase II metabolism. What does this typically involve?

  • A) Oxidation reactions via CYP450
  • B) Reduction reactions
  • C) Hydrolysis reactions
  • D) Conjugation reactions

Answer: D Phase II metabolism involves conjugation reactions (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) that make drugs more water-soluble for excretion. Phase I involves oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis.

17. Oral absorption is most affected by:

  • A) Plasma protein binding
  • B) Intestinal motility
  • C) Renal blood flow
  • D) Hepatic clearance

Answer: B Intestinal motility affects contact time with absorptive surfaces. Increased motility (diarrhea) reduces absorption; decreased motility increases it.

18. A lipophilic drug with pKa of 8.4 is administered orally. In which environment will it be most absorbed?

  • A) Stomach (pH 2)
  • B) Duodenum (pH 6)
  • C) Jejunum (pH 7.5)
  • D) Ileum (pH 8)

Answer: D For a weak base (pKa 8.4), the drug is more unionized in less acidic environments. At pH 8, closer to its pKa, more drug is in the lipophilic unionized form, favoring absorption.

19. Drugs excreted unchanged by kidney tend to be:

  • A) Highly lipid soluble
  • B) Highly water soluble
  • C) Highly protein bound
  • D) Administered intramuscularly

Answer: B Water-soluble (polar) drugs cannot be reabsorbed from renal tubules and are excreted unchanged. Lipid-soluble drugs are reabsorbed or metabolized first.

20. Enterohepatic circulation tends to:

  • A) Shorten half-life
  • B) Prolong half-life
  • C) Cause rapid elimination
  • D) Decrease bioavailability

Answer: B Enterohepatic circulation (drug excreted in bile, reabsorbed in intestine, returned to liver) recycles drug, prolonging presence in the body and increasing half-life.

21. Which increases the half-life of a renally cleared drug?

  • A) Increased blood pressure
  • B) Reduced GFR
  • C) Increased metabolism
  • D) Increased renal clearance

Answer: B Reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR) decreases renal clearance, increasing half-life. This is critical in elderly patients and those with renal disease.

22. A drug with high first-pass effect is best avoided via:

  • A) Oral route
  • B) Sublingual route
  • C) IV route
  • D) IM route

Answer: A Oral drugs undergo first-pass metabolism in the liver. Alternative routes (sublingual, IV, IM, transdermal) bypass or reduce first-pass effect.

23. Two drugs are co-administered. Drug A inhibits CYP3A4, and Drug B is a CYP3A4 substrate. What is the expected outcome?

  • A) Decreased plasma levels of Drug B
  • B) Increased plasma levels of Drug B
  • C) No change in Drug B levels
  • D) Increased metabolism of Drug B

Answer: B Inhibiting CYP3A4 decreases the metabolism of Drug B, leading to increased plasma levels and potential toxicity. Common with grapefruit juice, ketoconazole, erythromycin.

24. Which factor would LEAST affect the rate of drug absorption from an intramuscular injection site?

  • A) Blood flow to the muscle
  • B) Drug lipid solubility
  • C) Muscle mass
  • D) First-pass metabolism

Answer: D First-pass metabolism occurs when drugs pass through the liver after oral absorption. IM injections bypass the GI tract and enter systemic circulation directly, avoiding first-pass metabolism.

25. A drug has a clearance of 120 mL/min and a volume of distribution of 50L. What is its half-life?

  • A) 2.9 hours
  • B) 4.8 hours
  • C) 6.2 hours
  • D) 8.5 hours

Answer: B Half-life = (0.693 × Vd) / CL = (0.693 × 50,000 mL) / 120 mL/min = 289 minutes ≈ 4.8 hours.

SECTION B: PHARMACODYNAMICS (25 Questions)

26. Efficacy refers to:

  • A) Ability to produce maximal response
  • B) Strength of binding to receptor
  • C) Dose needed to achieve 50 percent response
  • D) Toxic dose

Answer: A Efficacy (Emax) is the maximal effect a drug can produce, regardless of dose. It's related to intrinsic activity and differs from potency.

27. Potency refers to:

  • A) Maximal effect
  • B) Amount of drug required to produce effect
  • C) Duration of action
  • D) Therapeutic index

Answer: B Potency is the dose or concentration required to produce a specific effect (usually EC50). A more potent drug requires less dose to achieve the same effect.

28. Which statement best describes potency?

  • A) The maximum effect a drug can produce
  • B) The dose required to produce 50% of maximal effect
  • C) The ability of a drug to produce a harmful effect
  • D) The duration of drug action

Answer: B Potency refers to the concentration or dose required to produce a specific effect (typically EC50 or ED50). A more potent drug requires less dose to achieve the same effect.

29. A competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve:

  • A) Rightward, same maximal effect
  • B) Leftward, reduced maximal effect
  • C) Downward, same potency
  • D) Upward and to the left

Answer: A Competitive antagonists bind reversibly to the same site as the agonist, requiring more agonist to achieve the same effect (rightward shift), but maximal effect remains achievable.

30. Which type of antagonism can be overcome by increasing the agonist concentration?

  • A) Non-competitive antagonism
  • B) Irreversible antagonism
  • C) Competitive antagonism
  • D) Chemical antagonism

Answer: C Competitive antagonism is reversible and surmountable. Increasing agonist concentration can outcompete the antagonist for receptor binding, restoring the maximal effect.

31. An irreversible antagonist:

  • A) Reduces efficacy
  • B) Increases potency
  • C) Has no effect on efficacy
  • D) Is always competitive

Answer: A Irreversible antagonists bind covalently or very tightly, permanently reducing the number of available receptors, thereby reducing maximal response (efficacy) that cannot be overcome.

32. A noncompetitive antagonist causes:

  • A) Parallel shift right
  • B) Decreased maximal response
  • C) Increased potency
  • D) No change in efficacy

Answer: B Non-competitive antagonists reduce the maximal effect (efficacy) by binding to allosteric sites or irreversibly, and this cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration.

33. A partial agonist is administered to a patient already taking a full agonist at the same receptor. What effect would you expect?

  • A) Increased effect compared to full agonist alone
  • B) Decreased effect compared to full agonist alone
  • C) No change in effect
  • D) Complete blockade of the receptor

Answer: B A partial agonist has lower intrinsic activity than a full agonist. When both are present, the partial agonist competes for receptors but produces less effect, resulting in decreased overall response.

34. A partial agonist:

  • A) Produces no effect
  • B) Produces maximal effect
  • C) Produces lower maximal effect than full agonist
  • D) Cannot act as antagonist

Answer: C Partial agonists bind to receptors but have lower intrinsic activity, producing submaximal responses even at full receptor occupancy. Can act as antagonists in presence of full agonists.

35. An inverse agonist differs from an antagonist because it:

  • A) Binds to a different receptor site
  • B) Produces an effect opposite to the agonist by reducing constitutive receptor activity
  • C) Has no effect on basal receptor activity
  • D) Only works in the presence of an agonist

Answer: B Inverse agonists bind to receptors and reduce constitutive (baseline) activity below normal levels, whereas competitive antagonists simply block agonist binding without affecting basal activity.

36. Therapeutic index (TI) indicates:

  • A) Binding affinity
  • B) Margin of safety
  • C) Rate of clearance
  • D) Genetic polymorphism

Answer: B TI = TD50/ED50 or LD50/ED50. A higher TI indicates a wider margin between therapeutic and toxic doses, meaning greater safety.

37. A drug has an ED50 of 10mg and a TD50 of 100mg. What is its therapeutic index?

  • A) 0.1
  • B) 1
  • C) 10
  • D) 90

Answer: C Therapeutic Index = TD50/ED50 = 100/10 = 10. A higher therapeutic index indicates a wider margin of safety between therapeutic and toxic doses.

38. A drug with narrow TI requires:

  • A) No monitoring
  • B) Widely variable dosing
  • C) Therapeutic drug monitoring
  • D) Increased dosing interval

Answer: C Drugs with narrow TI (small difference between therapeutic and toxic doses) require therapeutic drug monitoring to ensure safety and efficacy (e.g., warfarin, digoxin, phenytoin, lithium).

39. Agonists activate receptors by binding to:

  • A) Allosteric sites
  • B) Orthosteric sites
  • C) Lipid bilayer
  • D) DNA

Answer: B Orthosteric sites are the primary binding sites where endogenous ligands bind. Agonists bind here to activate receptors. Allosteric sites are secondary binding sites.

40. Tachyphylaxis is:

  • A) Delayed drug effect
  • B) Rapidly decreasing response to drug
  • C) Increased sensitivity
  • D) Long-term receptor upregulation

Answer: B Tachyphylaxis is acute, rapid tolerance that develops quickly (minutes to hours) with repeated administration, such as with ephedrine, nitrates, or amphetamines.

41. Tachyphylaxis is best described as:

  • A) Gradual decrease in drug response over days to weeks
  • B) Rapid decrease in drug response after repeated doses
  • C) Increased sensitivity to a drug over time
  • D) Drug effect that persists after drug elimination

Answer: B Tachyphylaxis is acute, rapid tolerance that develops quickly (minutes to hours) with repeated administration, such as with ephedrine or nitrates.

42. Desensitization of receptors occurs due to:

  • A) Increased bioavailability
  • B) Prolonged stimulation
  • C) Reduced metabolism
  • D) Increased potency

Answer: B Prolonged receptor stimulation leads to desensitization through receptor phosphorylation, internalization, or uncoupling from signaling pathways (e.g., beta-receptor desensitization with chronic beta-agonist use).

43. Desensitization of receptors typically involves:

  • A) Decreased receptor synthesis
  • B) Receptor phosphorylation and internalization
  • C) Increased receptor affinity
  • D) Conversion to spare receptors

Answer: B Acute desensitization often involves receptor phosphorylation (e.g., by G protein-coupled receptor kinases) followed by receptor internalization or uncoupling from signaling pathways.

44. The median effective dose (ED50) is:

  • A) Dose that kills half population
  • B) Dose that produces effect in half population
  • C) Maximum safe dose
  • D) Minimum toxic dose

Answer: B ED50 is the dose that produces the desired therapeutic effect in 50% of the population. It's a measure of drug potency.

45. The median toxic dose (TD50) is:

  • A) Dose that produces effect in 50 percent
  • B) Dose that kills 50 percent
  • C) Dose that produces toxicity in 50 percent
  • D) Lethal dose

Answer: C TD50 is the dose that produces a specified toxic effect in 50% of the population. Used to calculate therapeutic index: TI = TD50/ED50.

46. Intrinsic activity refers to:

  • A) Binding affinity
  • B) Ability to activate receptor
  • C) Ability to resist metabolism
  • D) Lipid solubility

Answer: B Intrinsic activity (efficacy) is the ability of a drug-receptor complex to produce a response. Full agonists have high intrinsic activity; antagonists have zero.

47. A drug-receptor interaction shows a Kd of 10 nM. What does this indicate?

  • A) High affinity of the drug for the receptor
  • B) Low affinity of the drug for the receptor
  • C) High efficacy of the drug
  • D) The drug is a partial agonist

Answer: A Kd (dissociation constant) represents the concentration at which 50% of receptors are occupied. A lower Kd (like 10 nM) indicates higher affinity (tighter binding).

48. The concept of "spare receptors" means:

  • A) Maximal response can be achieved without occupying all receptors
  • B) Some receptors have no function
  • C) Extra receptors are stored intracellularly
  • D) Only 50% of receptors are functional

Answer: A Spare receptors exist when the system can produce a maximal response with less than 100% receptor occupancy, indicating high receptor reserve and amplification in the signaling cascade.

49. A drug produces its effect through a G-protein coupled receptor. Which is the correct signaling sequence?

  • A) Receptor → Effector enzyme → G-protein → Second messenger
  • B) Receptor → G-protein → Effector enzyme → Second messenger
  • C) Receptor → Second messenger → G-protein → Effector enzyme
  • D) G-protein → Receptor → Effector enzyme → Second messenger

Answer: B The correct GPCR cascade: Agonist binds receptor → Receptor activates G-protein → G-protein modulates effector enzyme (e.g., adenylyl cyclase) → Enzyme produces second messenger (e.g., cAMP).

50. Idiosyncratic reactions are due to:

  • A) Predictable pharmacology
  • B) Genetic variations
  • C) Overdose
  • D) Drug interactions

Answer: B Idiosyncratic reactions are unpredictable, unusual responses often due to genetic polymorphisms (e.g., G6PD deficiency causing hemolysis with certain drugs, or malignant hyperthermia).

SECTION C: ROUTES OF ADMINISTRATION (18 Questions)

51. The route that completely avoids first-pass metabolism:

  • A) Oral
  • B) Rectal
  • C) Sublingual
  • D) Intramuscular

Answer: C Sublingual administration allows absorption directly into the systemic circulation via veins draining into the superior vena cava, completely bypassing the liver.

52. Sublingual administration bypasses first-pass metabolism because:

  • A) The drug is not absorbed systemically
  • B) Venous drainage is directly into the superior vena cava
  • C) The oral mucosa has no blood supply
  • D) The drug is metabolized in the mouth

Answer: B Sublingual drugs are absorbed into veins that drain into the superior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic portal system and avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism (e.g., nitroglycerin).

53. Which route of administration has the FASTEST onset of action?

  • A) Oral
  • B) Intramuscular
  • C) Subcutaneous
  • D) Intravenous

Answer: D IV administration delivers drug directly into systemic circulation, providing immediate onset. All other routes require absorption time.

54. Intravenous route has:

  • A) Slow absorption
  • B) Incomplete bioavailability
  • C) Immediate 100 percent bioavailability
  • D) Extensive first-pass effect

Answer: C IV administration places the entire dose directly into blood, giving 100% bioavailability with no absorption phase. Used as the reference (F=1.0) for calculating bioavailability of other routes.

55. Bioavailability is ALWAYS 100% with which route?

  • A) Oral
  • B) Intramuscular
  • C) Subcutaneous
  • D) Intravenous

Answer: D By definition, IV administration has 100% bioavailability as the entire dose enters systemic circulation directly without absorption barriers.

56. Inhalational route advantage:

  • A) Slow onset
  • B) Large surface area and rapid absorption
  • C) High first-pass effect
  • D) Avoids systemic action

Answer: B The lungs provide enormous surface area (~70m²), rich blood supply, and thin alveolar-capillary membrane, enabling rapid absorption (e.g., anesthetics, bronchodilators).

57. Inhalation is the preferred route for asthma medications because:

  • A) Complete systemic absorption is achieved
  • B) High local drug concentrations with minimal systemic effects
  • C) First-pass metabolism enhances efficacy
  • D) Faster than IV administration

Answer: B Inhalation delivers high drug concentrations directly to the lungs (site of action) while minimizing systemic exposure and side effects (e.g., albuterol, corticosteroids).

58. Subcutaneous injection is unsuitable for:

  • A) Peptides
  • B) Lipid-soluble drugs
  • C) Large volumes
  • D) Vaccines

Answer: C SC injections are limited to small volumes (<2 mL) to avoid pain and tissue damage. Used for insulin, heparin, vaccines, but not large-volume infusions.

59. Topical administration aims for:

  • A) Systemic effects
  • B) Local effects
  • C) High bioavailability
  • D) Rapid distribution

Answer: B Topical application targets local effects at the site of application (skin, eyes, nose) while minimizing systemic absorption, used for dermatologic conditions, conjunctivitis, nasal congestion.

60. The rectal route avoids first pass by:

  • A) Superior rectal vein
  • B) Middle and inferior rectal veins
  • C) Hepatic artery
  • D) Portal vein

Answer: B The middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the portal circulation. The superior rectal vein does go to the portal system. About 50% of rectal dose avoids first-pass.

61. Rectal administration is particularly useful when:

  • A) Patient requires immediate effect
  • B) Patient is vomiting or unconscious
  • C) Maximum bioavailability is needed
  • D) Large volumes need to be administered

Answer: B Rectal route is valuable when oral route is unavailable (vomiting, unconscious, seizures) or for local effects. About 50% avoids first-pass metabolism (e.g., diazepam for seizures, antiemetics).

62. Oral drugs must be:

  • A) Highly lipophilic
  • B) Highly hydrophilic
  • C) Only water soluble
  • D) Resistant to proteolytic enzymes

Answer: A Oral drugs must be sufficiently lipophilic to cross intestinal membranes, stable in gastric acid and digestive enzymes, and suitable for first-pass metabolism.

63. Intradermal route mainly used for:

  • A) Analgesics
  • B) Diagnostic testing
  • C) Insulin
  • D) Sedatives

Answer: B Intradermal injections (into dermis, 10-15° angle) are used for diagnostic testing (tuberculin test, allergy testing) and local anesthesia, not systemic therapy.

64. The transdermal route provides:

  • A) Rapid peaks
  • B) Slow and sustained release
  • C) Low compliance
  • D) High first-pass effect

Answer: B Transdermal patches provide controlled, sustained drug release over hours to days, improving compliance and maintaining steady plasma levels (e.g., nicotine, fentanyl, nitroglycerin, estrogen).

65. Which drug formulation is specifically designed for sustained release?

  • A) Elixir
  • B) Suspension
  • C) Transdermal patch
  • D) Syrup

Answer: C Transdermal patches are designed to release drug slowly over extended periods (hours to days), providing sustained therapeutic levels and reducing dosing frequency.

66. Which factor MOST limits drug absorption through the skin?

  • A) Blood flow to the skin
  • B) Stratum corneum barrier
  • C) Surface area
  • D) Skin temperature

Answer: B The stratum corneum (outermost layer of epidermis) is a lipid-rich barrier that significantly limits transdermal drug penetration. Only lipophilic, small molecules (<500 Da) penetrate effectively.

67. A drug destroyed by gastric acid should be given:

  • A) Oral
  • B) Rectal
  • C) Intravenous
  • D) Sublingual

Answer: C Drugs destroyed by stomach acid (peptides, proteins like insulin) must be given parenterally (IV, IM, SC) or via non-oral routes that bypass the GI tract.

68. Which statement about intrathecal administration is TRUE?

  • A) It is used for drugs that readily cross the blood-brain barrier
  • B) It delivers drugs directly into the cerebrospinal fluid
  • C) It has slower onset than oral administration
  • D) It is the same as epidural administration

Answer: B Intrathecal administration delivers drugs directly into CSF within the subarachnoid space, bypassing the blood-brain barrier, useful for spinal anesthesia or treating CNS infections/cancer.

SECTION D: RATIONAL PRESCRIBING (10 Questions)

69. The first step in rational prescribing is:

  • A) Choose the drug
  • B) Define the patient's problem
  • C) Start treatment immediately
  • D) Determine cost

Answer: B The WHO six-step approach starts with: 1) Define the patient's problem, 2) Specify therapeutic objective, 3) Select treatment strategy, 4) Select appropriate drug, 5) Verify suitability, 6) Give information/instructions.

70. When applying the WHO Guide to Good Prescribing, what is the FIRST step?

  • A) Choose a treatment strategy
  • B) Select appropriate drug therapy
  • C) Define the patient's problem
  • D) Write a prescription

Answer: C The rational prescribing process starts with defining the patient's problem through diagnosis before considering any treatment options.

71. Essential drugs are selected based on:

  • A) Marketing
  • B) Cost-effectiveness and safety
  • C) Patient preference only
  • D) Hospital availability

Answer: B WHO Essential Medicines List criteria: efficacy, safety, quality, cost-effectiveness, and ability to satisfy priority healthcare needs of populations.

72. An essential medicine is defined as one that:

  • A) Is the most expensive option available
  • B) Satisfies priority healthcare needs of the population
  • C) Is available only in hospitals
  • D) Requires specialist prescription

Answer: B The WHO defines essential medicines as those satisfying priority healthcare needs, selected for efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness, forming the basis of national formularies.

73. Polypharmacy mostly increases risk of:

  • A) Improved compliance
  • B) Drug interactions
  • C) Reduced side effects
  • D) Increased efficacy

Answer: B Polypharmacy (typically ≥5 medications) increases risks of drug-drug interactions, adverse effects, non-adherence, medication errors, and healthcare costs, especially in elderly.

74. Polypharmacy increases the risk of:

  • A) Improved treatment outcomes
  • B) Reduced medication costs
  • C) Drug-drug interactions and adverse effects
  • D) Better patient compliance

Answer: C Polypharmacy (use of multiple medications) increases the risk of drug interactions, adverse effects, medication errors, and non-compliance, particularly in elderly patients.

75. A prescription must legally include:

  • A) Diagnosis
  • B) Dose, frequency, duration
  • C) Patient insurance
  • D) Lab results

Answer: B Legal prescription requirements: patient name/details, date, drug name (generic preferred), strength, dose, frequency, duration, route, quantity, prescriber signature and credentials.

76. A drug contraindication means:

  • A) Relative benefit
  • B) Must not be used in specific condition
  • C) Can be used with caution
  • D) Always safe

Answer: B Contraindications are conditions where drug use poses unacceptable risk. Absolute contraindications prohibit use; relative contraindications require careful risk-benefit assessment.

77. A patient requires treatment for hypertension but also has asthma. Which antihypertensive should be AVOIDED?

  • A) Calcium channel blockers
  • B) ACE inhibitors
  • C) Non-selective beta-blockers
  • D) Thiazide diuretics

Answer: C Non-selective beta-blockers (like propranolol) can block β2-receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchoconstriction and worsening asthma. Use cardioselective β1-blockers if needed.

78. The most important factor for dosage adjustments in renal failure is:

  • A) Half-life
  • B) Route of administration
  • C) Drug clearance
  • D) Vd

Answer: C Renal failure reduces drug clearance. Drugs primarily eliminated by kidneys require dose adjustment based on creatinine clearance/GFR to prevent accumulation and toxicity.

79. When prescribing for elderly patients, which pharmacokinetic change is MOST important to consider?

  • A) Increased gastric acid production
  • B) Decreased renal function
  • C) Increased hepatic metabolism
  • D) Enhanced drug absorption

Answer: B *Elderly patients often have reduced renal function (decreased GFR), which impairs drug elimination and increases risk of accumulation and toxicity, especially for renally-excreted drugs. Also consider decreased hepatic metabolism, altered body composition, and polypharmacy.*

80. Elderly patients require dose adjustments due to:

  • A) Increased renal function
  • B) Reduced metabolism and clearance
  • C) Increased cardiac output
  • D) Increased protein binding

Answer: B Elderly have decreased hepatic metabolism (reduced CYP450 activity, liver blood flow), reduced renal clearance, decreased lean body mass, increased fat, and reduced albumin—all affecting pharmacokinetics.

81. Therapeutic drug monitoring is required for drugs with:

  • A) Short half-lives
  • B) High safety margin
  • C) Narrow therapeutic index
  • D) Rapid metabolism

Answer: C TDM is essential for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices where small changes in concentration can lead to toxicity or treatment failure (e.g., digoxin, phenytoin, lithium, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, warfarin).

82. What is the PRIMARY goal of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)?

  • A) To reduce healthcare costs
  • B) To optimize individual dosing for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices
  • C) To detect drug abuse
  • D) To replace clinical assessment

Answer: B TDM is used for drugs with narrow therapeutic indices, significant inter-patient variability, or where clinical effects are difficult to monitor (e.g., phenytoin, digoxin, aminoglycosides).

83. Failure to adhere to prescriptions leads to:

  • A) Good patient outcome
  • B) Subtherapeutic effect
  • C) Lower toxicity
  • D) None

Answer: B Non-adherence results in subtherapeutic drug levels, treatment failure, disease progression, increased morbidity, hospitalizations, and healthcare costs.

84. A patient is non-compliant with medication. Which factor is LEAST likely to improve adherence?

  • A) Simplifying the dosing regimen
  • B) Providing patient education about the condition
  • C) Prescribing the most expensive brand
  • D) Addressing side effects

Answer: C Cost is actually a barrier to compliance. Using affordable medications, along with simplified regimens, patient education, and managing side effects, improves adherence.

85. Best way to reduce medication error:

  • A) Poor handwriting
  • B) Use generic names and clarity
  • C) Verbal instructions
  • D) Avoid documentation

Answer: B Error prevention: use generic names, clear legible writing/electronic prescribing, avoid abbreviations, double-check calculations, include indication, patient education, and proper documentation.

86. A pregnant woman in her first trimester requires drug therapy. Which FDA pregnancy category represents the HIGHEST risk?

  • A) Category A
  • B) Category C
  • C) Category D
  • D) Category X

Answer: D Category X drugs have demonstrated fetal abnormalities and risks that clearly outweigh any possible benefit (e.g., isotretinoin, thalidomide). They are contraindicated in pregnancy.

SECTION E: DRUG CLASSIFICATION (13 Questions)

87. ACE inhibitors are classified based on their:

  • A) Chemical structure
  • B) Mechanism of action
  • C) Route of administration
  • D) Side effect profile

Answer: B ACE (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme) inhibitors are classified by their mechanism—they inhibit the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing blood pressure.

88. Beta-lactam antibiotics include all EXCEPT:

  • A) Penicillins
  • B) Cephalosporins
  • C) Carbapenems
  • D) Aminoglycosides

Answer: D Beta-lactams (containing a β-lactam ring) include penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin) are a different structural class inhibiting protein synthesis.

89. NSAIDs are classified together because they:

  • A) Have identical chemical structures
  • B) Inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes
  • C) Are all derived from salicylic acid
  • D) Have the same half-life

Answer: B NSAIDs (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs) are grouped by their mechanism of inhibiting COX-1 and/or COX-2 enzymes, despite having diverse chemical structures (e.g., aspirin, ibuprofen, celecoxib).

90. Which class of drugs acts primarily on voltage-gated sodium channels?

  • A) Beta-blockers
  • B) Local anesthetics
  • C) ACE inhibitors
  • D) Proton pump inhibitors

Answer: B Local anesthetics (like lidocaine, bupivacaine) block voltage-gated sodium channels in neuronal membranes, preventing action potential propagation and causing reversible loss of sensation.

91. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are used primarily as:

  • A) Antihypertensives
  • B) Antidepressants
  • C) Antiemetics
  • D) Bronchodilators

Answer: B SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine) inhibit serotonin reuptake in the CNS, increasing synaptic serotonin levels, and are first-line treatments for depression and anxiety disorders.

92. Statins are classified as:

  • A) Antihypertensives
  • B) Anticoagulants
  • C) Lipid-lowering agents
  • D) Antiarrhythmics

Answer: C Statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin) are HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors that lower cholesterol by inhibiting cholesterol synthesis in the liver, used for cardiovascular disease prevention.

93. Which drug class works by blocking H2 receptors in the stomach?

  • A) Proton pump inhibitors
  • B) Antacids
  • C) H2 receptor antagonists
  • D) Prostaglandin analogs

Answer: C H2 receptor antagonists (ranitidine, famotidine, cimetidine) block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion for ulcer treatment.

94. Benzodiazepines primarily enhance the action of which neurotransmitter?

  • A) Dopamine
  • B) GABA
  • C) Serotonin
  • D) Norepinephrine

Answer: B Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam) enhance GABAergic neurotransmission by binding to GABA-A receptors, increasing chloride channel opening frequency, producing anxiolytic, sedative, and anticonvulsant effects.

95. Drugs are often classified based on:

  • A) Colour
  • B) Mechanism of action
  • C) Packaging
  • D) Price

Answer: B Drug classification systems include: mechanism of action (most common and useful), therapeutic use, chemical structure, target organ/system. Mechanism provides understanding of effects and interactions.

96. A "prodrug" is:

  • A) A drug in its active form
  • B) An inactive compound converted to active drug in the body
  • C) The first drug developed in a class
  • D) A drug used professionally

Answer: B Prodrugs are inactive or less active compounds that are metabolized in vivo to the active drug form (e.g., enalapril→enalaprilat, codeine→morphine), often to improve absorption, distribution, or reduce side effects.

97. A prodrug is designed to:

  • A) Be inactive
  • B) Improve absorption and bioavailability
  • C) Increase toxicity
  • D) Reduce metabolism

Answer: B Prodrugs are designed to overcome pharmaceutical or pharmacokinetic barriers: improve oral absorption, increase lipophilicity to cross BBB, target specific tissues, or reduce first-pass metabolism.

98. An "orphan drug" is one that:

  • A) Has been discontinued from the market
  • B) Is developed for rare diseases affecting small populations
  • C) Has no patent protection
  • D) Is available without prescription

Answer: B Orphan drugs treat rare diseases (affecting <200,000 people in US, <1 in 2,000 in EU), receiving special regulatory incentives (tax credits, market exclusivity) for development due to limited market profitability.

99. An orphan drug treats:

  • A) Common diseases
  • B) Rare diseases
  • C) Infections only
  • D) Psychiatric disorders only

Answer: B Orphan drugs are developed for rare/orphan diseases with small patient populations, where development costs may exceed potential revenue without regulatory incentives.

SECTION F: DRUG DISCOVERY & DEVELOPMENT (11 Questions)

100. Lead compounds are:

  • A) Marketed drugs
  • B) Prototype molecules for modification
  • C) Final therapeutic molecules
  • D) Clinical trial drugs

Answer: B Lead compounds show promising biological activity and acceptable properties, serving as starting points for chemical optimization to improve potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics, and safety.

101. A "lead compound" in drug discovery refers to:

  • A) The final marketed drug
  • B) A compound with promising activity selected for optimization
  • C) The first drug in a therapeutic class
  • D) A compound that failed clinical trials

Answer: B A lead compound shows desired biological activity and acceptable properties, serving as a starting point for chemical modification (medicinal chemistry) to improve potency, selectivity, and drug-like properties.

102. High-throughput screening (HTS) in drug discovery is used to:

  • A) Test one compound at a time in detail
  • B) Rapidly test thousands of compounds for biological activity
  • C) Determine drug safety in humans
  • D) Package drugs for market

Answer: B HTS uses automated robotic systems to rapidly screen large chemical libraries (thousands to millions of compounds) against biological targets to identify "hits" with desired activity.

103. High-throughput screening is used to:

  • A) Select patients
  • B) Rapidly identify active compounds
  • C) Manufacture large volumes
  • D) Increase Vd

Answer: B HTS is an early drug discovery technique using automation to test large compound libraries against disease targets, identifying potential lead compounds for further development.

104. Phase I clinical trials test:

  • A) Efficacy
  • B) Toxicity and safety in healthy volunteers
  • C) Comparison with standard therapy
  • D) Post-marketing surveillance

Answer: B Phase I (first-in-human, FIH) trials assess safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (ADME), and pharmacodynamics in 20-80 healthy volunteers (except in oncology, where cancer patients are used).

105. The PRIMARY purpose of Phase I clinical trials is to:

  • A) Determine drug efficacy
  • B) Assess safety and pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers
  • C) Compare with existing treatments
  • D) Monitor long-term side effects

Answer: B Phase I trials (first-in-human) assess safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics, usually in small groups of healthy volunteers (20-80 subjects), establishing safe dose ranges.

106. Phase II trials mainly test:

  • A) Market viability
  • B) Dose-response and efficacy in patients
  • C) Long term safety
  • D) Distribution

Answer: B Phase II trials (proof-of-concept) evaluate therapeutic efficacy, dose-response relationships, and short-term safety in 100-300 patients with the target disease, determining optimal dosing.

107. Phase III trials are:

  • A) First human studies
  • B) Large-scale comparative studies
  • C) Animal testing
  • D) Toxicology studies only

Answer: B Phase III trials are large (1,000-3,000+ patients), randomized, controlled studies comparing new drug with standard treatment or placebo, confirming efficacy and monitoring adverse events before regulatory approval.

108. Which phase of clinical trials typically involves the LARGEST number of patients?

  • A) Phase I
  • B) Phase II
  • C) Phase III
  • D) Phase IV

Answer: C Phase III trials involve thousands of patients to confirm efficacy, monitor adverse effects, and compare with standard treatments before regulatory approval (pivotal trials).

109. The "investigational new drug" (IND) application is submitted:

  • A) After Phase III trials
  • B) Before beginning human trials
  • C) Only if animal studies show toxicity
  • D) After the drug is marketed
