Answer: B An IND application is submitted to regulatory authorities (like FDA) before clinical trials begin, containing preclinical data (animal toxicology), manufacturing information (CMC), and clinical trial protocols.

110. Pharmacovigilance primarily involves:

  • A) Marketing new drugs
  • B) Synthesizing drug compounds
  • C) Monitoring drug safety after market approval
  • D) Conducting Phase I trials

Answer: C Pharmacovigilance (Phase IV/post-marketing surveillance) involves ongoing monitoring of adverse effects, drug interactions, and safety in real-world populations after approval, detecting rare ADRs.

111. Animal studies before human trials mainly assess:

  • A) Marketing potential
  • B) Toxicity and safety
  • C) Cost effectiveness
  • D) Patient compliance

Answer: B Preclinical animal studies assess acute and chronic toxicity, carcinogenicity, teratogenicity, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics to ensure reasonable safety before human testing.

SECTION G: PHARMACOLOGY TERMINOLOGY (9 Questions)

112. Which BEST defines a "drug"?

  • A) Any chemical substance used for recreation
  • B) A substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease
  • C) Only prescription medications
  • D) Natural substances only

Answer: B A drug is any substance (natural or synthetic) used in diagnosis, treatment, cure, prevention, or mitigation of disease, or to affect body structure/function (includes prescription, OTC, and illicit substances).

113. "Frequency" in pharmacological context refers to:

  • A) The number of doses administered per unit time
  • B) The concentration of drug in plasma
  • C) The duration of drug action
  • D) The potency of a drug

Answer: A Dosing frequency specifies how often a medication should be taken (e.g., QD=once daily, BID=twice daily, TID=three times daily, QID=four times daily, Q6H=every 6 hours) to maintain therapeutic levels.

114. Toxicology is BEST defined as the study of:

  • A) Drug therapeutic effects
  • B) Adverse effects of chemicals on living organisms
  • C) Drug absorption only
  • D) Drug manufacturing

Answer: B Toxicology studies adverse/harmful effects of chemicals, drugs, or physical agents on living organisms, including mechanisms of toxicity, dose-response relationships, risk assessment, and treatment of poisoning.

115. "Idiosyncratic drug reaction" refers to:

  • A) Expected side effects of a drug
  • B) Dose-dependent adverse effects
  • C) Unpredictable, unusual reactions unrelated to dose
  • D) Therapeutic effects of a drug

Answer: C Idiosyncratic reactions are unexpected, individual-specific adverse responses that occur rarely and are unpredictable, often due to genetic factors (pharmacogenomics) or immune mechanisms, not related to dose.

116. Generic name of a drug is:

  • A) Brand name
  • B) International Nonproprietary Name
  • C) Chemical formula
  • D) Proprietary name

Answer: B Generic name (INN - International Nonproprietary Name) is the official, non-proprietary name assigned by WHO. Brand/trade names are proprietary (e.g., generic: acetaminophen/paracetamol; brand: Tylenol, Panadol).

117. What is a "drug"?

  • A) Only synthetic chemicals
  • B) Any substance that produces a biological effect when administered to a living organism
  • C) Only illegal substances
  • D) Only injectable substances

Answer: B A drug is any chemical substance that produces a biological effect (therapeutic, toxic, or physiological) when introduced into the body, including natural products, synthetic molecules, biologics.

118. Pharmacology is defined as:

  • A) Study of drug preparation only
  • B) Study of drug interactions with living systems
  • C) Study of drug marketing
  • D) Study of drug packaging

Answer: B Pharmacology is the science studying drug interactions with living systems, including mechanisms of action, therapeutic uses, adverse effects, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics.

119. "Duration of action" refers to:

  • A) Time to reach peak concentration
  • B) Time between drug administration and onset
  • C) Length of time drug produces its effect
  • D) Time to reach steady state

Answer: C Duration of action is the time period during which drug concentration remains above the minimum effective concentration (MEC), determining dosing intervals.

120. A "receptor" in pharmacology is:

  • A) Any protein in the body
  • B) A macromolecular component that interacts with a drug to produce a cellular response
  • C) Only found on cell surfaces
  • D) Always an enzyme

Answer: B Receptors are specific macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids) that bind drugs/ligands and mediate biological responses. Types include: GPCRs, ion channels, enzyme-linked receptors, nuclear receptors.

STUDY STRATEGY TIPS:

For Week 11 (Nov 19th) - Basic Pharmacology CAT:

  1. PK Focus: Understand relationships between Vd, CL, t½, bioavailability
  2. PD Focus: Master dose-response curves, agonist/antagonist concepts, therapeutic index
  3. Routes: Know which routes avoid first-pass, advantages/disadvantages
  4. Clinical Application: Link concepts to patient scenarios (elderly, renal failure, pregnancy)

Key Formulas to Memorize:

  • Half-life: t½ = (0.693 × Vd) / CL
  • Therapeutic Index: TI = TD50 / ED50
  • Loading Dose: LD = (Vd × Target Concentration) / F
  • Maintenance Dose: MD = (CL × Target Css × Dosing Interval) / F
  • Steady State: reached at ~5 half-lives

Common Pitfalls:

  • Don't confuse potency (dose needed) with efficacy (maximum effect)
  • Remember: high Vd = extensive tissue distribution
  • Zero-order = constant AMOUNT; First-order = constant FRACTION
  • Phase I = oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis; Phase II = conjugation

Study Method:

Title: ONCOPATHOLOGY - SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (SAQs)
Content:
High-Yield Exam-Style Questions

SECTION A: NORMAL CELL CYCLE (8 Questions)

1. Explain the role of RB protein as the "Governor of the Cell Cycle."

2. Describe how p53 functions as "Guardian of the Genome" in response to DNA damage.

3. What are the two families of CDK inhibitors and how do they act as tumor suppressors?

4. Explain the molecular mechanism of the G1/S checkpoint and its importance in cancer prevention.

5. Describe the sequential activation of cyclins throughout the cell cycle.

6. How do oncogenic viruses like HPV disable cell cycle checkpoints?

7. What is the significance of the G2/M checkpoint and what happens when it's defective?

8. Explain Knudson's "two-hit hypothesis" using retinoblastoma as an example.

SECTION B: SELF-SUFFICIENCY IN GROWTH SIGNALS (8 Questions)

9. Distinguish between proto-oncogenes, oncogenes, and oncoproteins.

10. Explain the RAS oncogene: its normal function, mechanism of activation, and effects on cell proliferation.

11. Describe how cancer cells achieve growth factor independence.

12. What is the BCR-ABL fusion protein and why is it significant in CML?

13. Explain the role of MYC oncogene in human cancers.

14. How do growth factor receptor mutations contribute to oncogenesis? Give examples.

15. Describe the role of signal-transducing proteins in oncogenesis.

16. Explain how alterations in cyclins and CDKs contribute to cancer development.

SECTION C: INSENSITIVITY TO GROWTH INHIBITORY SIGNALS (8 Questions)

17. Compare and contrast oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.

18. Explain how RB gene inactivation affects the cell cycle in cancer.

19. Describe the mechanisms by which p53 prevents cancer development.

20. What is Li-Fraumeni syndrome and what does it teach us about p53?

21. Describe the TGF-β pathway and explain its dual role in cancer (tumor suppressor early, tumor promoter late).

22. Explain the role of APC gene in colorectal cancer development.

23. How does loss of contact inhibition contribute to cancer? Discuss E-cadherin and NF2.

24. What is the significance of TP53 being mutated in 70% of cancers?

SECTION D: EVASION OF APOPTOSIS (6 Questions)

25. Compare and contrast the extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic pathways.

26. Explain the role of BCL2 family proteins in regulating apoptosis.

27. How does p53 induce apoptosis in response to irreparable DNA damage?

28. Describe the mechanisms by which cancer cells evade apoptosis.

29. What is the significance of BCL2 translocation t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma?

30. Explain the concept of "oncogene addiction" and its therapeutic implications.

SECTION E: LIMITLESS REPLICATIVE POTENTIAL & ANGIOGENESIS (8 Questions)

31. Explain the Hayflick limit and how cancer cells overcome it.

32. What is telomerase, how is it reactivated in cancer, and why is this significant?

33. Describe the process of mitotic crisis and its role in tumorigenesis.

34. Why can't tumors grow beyond 1-2mm without angiogenesis?

35. What is the "angiogenic switch" and what factors control it?

36. Explain the role of hypoxia and HIF-1α in tumor angiogenesis. Include VHL in your answer.

37. What are the characteristics of tumor vasculature and why is it abnormal?

38. Explain the role of VEGF in tumor angiogenesis and how it's therapeutically targeted.

SECTION F: INVASION AND METASTASIS (10 Questions)

39. Outline the sequential steps of the invasion-metastasis cascade.

40. Describe the four steps involved in invasion of the extracellular matrix.

41. Explain the molecular mechanisms of E-cadherin loss in cancer invasion.

42. What is epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and how does it promote metastasis?

43. Explain the role of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) in cancer invasion.

44. What determines the organ tropism of metastases? Discuss the "seed and soil" hypothesis.

45. Explain the concept of metastatic inefficiency. Why do so few circulating tumor cells form metastases?

46. Describe the process of colonization and why it's the rate-limiting step in metastasis.

47. What is the role of the tumor microenvironment in invasion and metastasis?

48. Explain how tumor cells survive in the bloodstream.

SECTION G: REPROGRAMMING ENERGY METABOLISM (4 Questions)

49. Describe the Warburg effect and explain why cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis despite its inefficiency.

50. What are the advantages of aerobic glycolysis for rapidly proliferating cancer cells?

51. How do oncogenes (MYC, RAS, AKT) and tumor suppressors (p53, PTEN) regulate the Warburg effect?

52. Explain how hypoxia and HIF-1α contribute to metabolic reprogramming in cancer.

SECTION H: IMMUNE EVASION & GENOMIC INSTABILITY (4 Questions)

53. What is genomic instability and how does it enable malignancy? Give examples of syndromes.

54. Explain tumor-promoting inflammation in two different settings.

55. Describe the link between chronic inflammation and cancer development.

56. What is the clinical significance of COX-2 in cancer?

SECTION I: MULTISTEP CARCINOGENESIS (2 Questions)

57. Explain the concept of multistep carcinogenesis using the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer.

58. What are the key molecular alterations in the progression from normal colon epithelium to invasive carcinoma?

ANSWER GUIDELINES FOR STUDENTS:

How to approach these questions:

  • Use point form with clear headings
  • Start with definitions where appropriate
  • Include specific examples
  • Mention clinical significance
  • Draw diagrams if helpful (especially for pathways)
  • Link concepts together (e.g., how does this relate to other hallmarks?)

What examiners look for:

  • Understanding of mechanisms (not just memorization)
  • Ability to integrate concepts
  • Clinical relevance
  • Specific examples with details
  • Clear, organized answers

Exam Strategy:

  • These 58 questions cover ALL major topics
  • Practice writing answers in 10-15 minutes each
  • Focus on high-yield topics: p53, RB, apoptosis, metastasis cascade, angiogenesis
  • Understand pathways, don't just memorize names
  • Link molecular changes to hallmarks of cancer

TOTAL: 58 HIGH-YIELD SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS

These questions comprehensively cover:

  • Normal cell cycle regulation
  • All hallmarks of cancer
  • Molecular basis of oncogenesis
  • Clinical correlations
  • Therapeutic implications

Good luck with your exam! 📚🎯

Title: ONCOPATHOLOGY MCQ EXAMINATION HAllmarks of Cancer 1,2 &3
Content:
MBPA 3412 - Dr. A. Irungu

60 Multiple Choice Questions

Question 1: A patient with familial retinoblastoma develops bilateral tumors at age 3. According to Knudson's hypothesis, what distinguishes this presentation from sporadic cases?

A) Both hits occur simultaneously in germline cells
B) The first mutation is inherited, requiring only one somatic hit
C) Three hits are required instead of two
D) The RB gene is located on a different chromosome

Answer: B
Explanation: In familial retinoblastoma, one mutation is inherited (germline), so only one additional somatic mutation is needed. Sporadic cases require both mutations to occur somatically in the same cell.

Question 2: Which event would MOST effectively prevent E2F-mediated transcription of S-phase genes?

A) Activation of CDK2-cyclin E complex
B) Hyperphosphorylation of RB protein
C) Hypophosphorylation of RB protein
D) Degradation of p21 protein

Answer: C
Explanation: Hypophosphorylated RB binds to and sequesters E2F, preventing transcription. Hyperphosphorylation releases E2F, allowing transcription to proceed.

Question 3: A tumor shows constitutive activation of growth signaling despite absence of growth factors. Which mechanism is LEAST likely responsible?

A) Loss of p53 function
B) Receptor dimerization without ligand binding
C) Autocrine production of growth factors
D) Activating RAS mutations

Answer: A
Explanation: Loss of p53 primarily affects cell cycle checkpoints and apoptosis, not growth factor signaling. The other options directly cause self-sufficiency in growth signals.

Question 4: In chronic myeloid leukemia, the BCR-ABL fusion protein drives malignancy primarily by:

A) Enhancing DNA repair mechanisms
B) Increasing p53-mediated apoptosis
C) Constitutive tyrosine kinase activity without regulation
D) Blocking cyclin D synthesis

Answer: C
Explanation: The BCR-ABL fusion results from t(9;22) translocation and causes loss of the regulatory region controlling tyrosine kinase activity, leading to continuous mitogenic signaling.

Question 5: A researcher observes that tumor cells continue dividing despite contact with neighboring cells. Which protein's function is most likely compromised?

A) VEGF
B) E-cadherin
C) β-catenin
D) MYC oncogene

Answer: B
Explanation: E-cadherin mediates contact inhibition. Its loss allows cancer cells to pile on top of each other and continue dividing despite cell-cell contact.

Question 6: Why must BOTH copies of a tumor suppressor gene be lost for tumor development, unlike oncogenes which require mutation of only one allele?

A) Tumor suppressors are always X-linked
B) The remaining normal allele can still produce functional protein
C) Oncogenes have higher mutation rates
D) Tumor suppressors require post-translational modification

Answer: B
Explanation: This follows Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. One functional copy of a tumor suppressor gene is sufficient for normal function, so both must be lost. Oncogenes are gain-of-function mutations where one mutant copy is sufficient.

Question 7: A tumor expresses high levels of p16INK4a but shows uncontrolled proliferation. Which alteration would explain this paradox?

A) Overexpression of cyclin D
B) Loss of p53 function
C) Activation of E2F transcription factors
D) Mutation in CDK4 preventing p16INK4a binding

Answer: D
Explanation: If CDK4 is mutated such that p16INK4a cannot bind to it, p16INK4a cannot inhibit the cyclin D-CDK4 complex, rendering its overexpression ineffective.

Question 8: Which statement BEST explains why p53 is called the 'guardian of the genome'?

A) It directly repairs DNA damage
B) It only functions in DNA synthesis phase
C) It monitors cellular stress and coordinates cell cycle arrest or apoptosis
D) It prevents all mutations from occurring

Answer: C
Explanation: p53 acts as a central stress monitor that can activate pathways for DNA repair, cell cycle arrest, senescence, or apoptosis depending on the severity of damage. It doesn't repair DNA directly but coordinates the response.

Question 9: In pancreatic cancer, TGF-β pathway mutations are found in 100% of cases. However, in late-stage tumors, intact TGF-β signaling promotes metastasis. This apparent contradiction occurs because:

A) TGF-β always promotes tumor growth
B) TGF-β switches from growth inhibition to promoting EMT and invasion
C) Late-stage tumors revert their mutations
D) Early and late-stage tumors are genetically unrelated

Answer: B
Explanation: TGF-β has dual roles: in normal/early cancer cells it inhibits growth, but in late-stage tumors it can activate epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), promoting migration and metastasis.

Question 10: A patient with Li-Fraumeni syndrome develops multiple tumors at young age. The inherited defect most likely involves:

A) Both alleles of RB gene
B) One allele of TP53 gene
C) Activation of RAS oncogene
D) Loss of E-cadherin expression

Answer: B
Explanation: Li-Fraumeni syndrome involves germline mutation of one TP53 allele. The second hit occurs somatically, leading to multiple tumor types at young age due to loss of this critical tumor suppressor.

Question 11: During mitosis, which cyclin-CDK complex is responsible for nuclear membrane breakdown?

A) Cyclin D-CDK4
B) Cyclin A-CDK2
C) Cyclin B-CDK1
D) Cyclin E-CDK2

Answer: C
Explanation: Cyclin B-CDK1 complex is activated by protein phosphatase at the G2/M transition and causes nuclear membrane breakdown, initiating mitosis.

Question 12: Which scenario would MOST likely result in failed DNA damage repair followed by apoptosis?

A) Normal p53 with minor DNA damage
B) Mutated p53 with extensive DNA damage
C) Normal p53 with irreparable DNA damage
D) Overexpression of BCL2 with DNA damage

Answer: C
Explanation: Normal p53 can induce apoptosis when DNA damage is irreparable. Mutated p53 fails to trigger apoptosis even with extensive damage. BCL2 overexpression blocks apoptosis.

Question 13: A tumor shows loss of APC function. What is the immediate downstream effect?

A) Increased p53 activation
B) Nuclear accumulation of β-catenin acting as transcription factor
C) Enhanced E-cadherin expression
D) Decreased cyclin D levels

Answer: B
Explanation: APC normally promotes β-catenin degradation. Loss of APC leads to β-catenin accumulation and nuclear translocation, where it acts as a growth-promoting transcription factor.

Question 14: Why do HPV oncoproteins preferentially target both RB and p53 proteins?

A) These are the only tumor suppressors in cells
B) Inactivating both allows bypass of major cell cycle checkpoints
C) They are structurally similar proteins
D) This occurs accidentally without selective advantage

Answer: B
Explanation: RB controls the G1/S checkpoint while p53 controls multiple checkpoints and apoptosis. Inactivating both allows the virus to drive cell proliferation while evading protective mechanisms.

Question 15: A researcher finds that tumor cells produce the same growth factor for which they express receptors. This exemplifies which hallmark of cancer?

A) Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals
B) Evasion of apoptosis
C) Self-sufficiency in growth signals
D) Limitless replicative potential

Answer: C
Explanation: Autocrine signaling (producing growth factors for one's own receptors) is a classic mechanism of self-sufficiency in growth signals, eliminating dependence on external growth factors.

Question 16: What is the functional significance of cyclin D appearing in mid-G1 phase?

A) It terminates the cell cycle
B) It initiates RB phosphorylation to progress toward S phase
C) It directly synthesizes DNA
D) It prevents mitosis

Answer: B
Explanation: Cyclin D binds CDK4 to form a complex that phosphorylates RB. This is the first critical step in committing the cell to proceed through the restriction point toward S phase.

Question 17: Which mechanism does NOT contribute to the 'angiogenic switch' in tumors?

A) Hypoxia-induced HIF-1α stabilization
B) Loss of p53 reducing TSP-1 production
C) Enhanced E-cadherin expression
D) Increased VEGF production

Answer: C
Explanation: E-cadherin is involved in cell-cell adhesion and contact inhibition, not angiogenesis. The other options all promote the angiogenic switch by increasing pro-angiogenic factors or decreasing inhibitors.

Question 18: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum develop skin cancers primarily because:

A) They have enhanced RAS signaling
B) They cannot repair UV-induced pyrimidine dimers
C) They have inherited activated oncogenes
D) They overproduce growth factors

Answer: B
Explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum involves defects in nucleotide excision repair, preventing repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers in DNA, leading to accumulation of mutations and skin cancer.

Question 19: In von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, loss of VHL protein function leads to cancer primarily through:

A) Direct activation of oncogenes
B) Stabilization of HIF-1α and increased VEGF transcription
C) Inhibition of DNA repair
D) Enhanced p53 degradation

Answer: B
Explanation: VHL normally targets HIF-1α for degradation in normoxic conditions. Loss of VHL leads to HIF-1α accumulation, nuclear translocation, and transcription of pro-angiogenic genes like VEGF.

Question 20: The "point of no return" in the cell cycle, after which cells are committed to division, occurs at:

A) G2/M checkpoint
B) M phase
C) G1/S transition
D) G0 phase

Answer: C
Explanation: The G1/S transition (restriction point) is the critical decision point. Once cells pass this checkpoint, they are committed to completing the cell cycle.

Question 21: A tumor measuring 3 mm in diameter shows areas of necrosis in its center. This observation suggests:

A) Enhanced apoptosis machinery
B) Failure to induce angiogenesis beyond 1-2 mm diameter
C) Excessive growth factor production
D) Loss of cell-cell adhesion

Answer: B
Explanation: Tumors cannot grow beyond 1-2 mm without angiogenesis due to the limited diffusion distance of oxygen and nutrients. Central necrosis indicates inadequate vascularization.

Question 22: What distinguishes proto-oncogenes from oncogenes?

A) Proto-oncogenes are viral in origin
B) Proto-oncogenes are normal genes; oncogenes are mutated versions
C) Proto-oncogenes suppress growth
D) Oncogenes are always inherited

Answer: B
Explanation: Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes that regulate cell proliferation and differentiation. Oncogenes are mutated or overexpressed versions that promote uncontrolled growth.

Question 23: In familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome, hundreds of colonic polyps develop due to:

A) Germline mutation in one APC allele plus somatic loss of the second
B) Activation of RAS in every polyp
C) Loss of p53 in colonic epithelium
D) Inherited BCR-ABL fusion gene

Answer: A
Explanation: FAP follows the two-hit hypothesis for tumor suppressors. Patients inherit one mutant APC allele, and sporadic loss of the second allele in individual cells leads to multiple polyps.

Question 24: The Warburg effect refers to cancer cells':

A) Dependence on oxidative phosphorylation
B) Preference for aerobic glycolysis despite oxygen availability
C) Inability to use glucose
D) Enhanced mitochondrial function

Answer: B
Explanation: The Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) involves cancer cells using glycolysis even when oxygen is available, sacrificing ATP efficiency for rapid biomass production to support proliferation.

Question 25: Which statement about the G2/M checkpoint is correct?

A) It monitors DNA damage before S phase
B) It checks completion of DNA replication before mitosis
C) It is controlled exclusively by p53
D) It prevents RB phosphorylation

Answer: B
Explanation: The G2/M checkpoint ensures DNA replication is complete and checks for DNA damage before allowing the cell to enter mitosis. Defects lead to chromosomal abnormalities.

Question 26: p21, p27, and p57 belong to which family of cell cycle regulators?

A) Cyclins
B) CDKs
C) Cip/Kip family of CDK inhibitors
D) INK4/ARF family

Answer: C
Explanation: p21, p27, and p57 are members of the Cip/Kip family of CDK inhibitors that bind and inactivate cyclin-CDK complexes. p21 is transcriptionally activated by p53.

Question 27: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) facilitate tumor invasion by:

A) Promoting cell-cell adhesion
B) Degrading ECM and releasing sequestered growth factors
C) Inhibiting angiogenesis
D) Enhancing DNA repair

Answer: B
Explanation: MMPs degrade basement membrane and ECM components, facilitating invasion. They also release ECM-bound growth factors like VEGF and generate chemotactic fragments.

Question 28: Why do cancer cells typically show microsatellite instability (MSI) in hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)?

A) Enhanced DNA synthesis
B) Defective mismatch repair system
C) Overactive nucleotide excision repair
D) Loss of telomerase activity

Answer: B
Explanation: HNPCC patients have mutations in mismatch repair genes, leading to failure to correct replication errors, particularly in repetitive sequences (microsatellites), causing MSI.

Question 29: Tumor cells achieve immortality primarily by:

A) Inactivating all tumor suppressors
B) Reactivating telomerase to maintain telomere length
C) Blocking all apoptotic pathways
D) Increasing cyclin expression

Answer: B
Explanation: Normal cells have limited replicative potential due to telomere shortening. Cancer cells reactivate telomerase to maintain telomeres, achieving unlimited replicative potential.

Question 30: In the multistep carcinogenesis model of colon cancer, which genetic alteration typically occurs FIRST?

A) Loss of TP53
B) Inactivation of APC
C) Activation of KRAS
D) Loss of tumor suppressor on 18q

Answer: B
Explanation: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer typically begins with APC inactivation, followed by KRAS activation, then loss of 18q tumor suppressors, and finally TP53 loss.

Question 31: BH3-only proteins (BAD, BID, PUMA) regulate apoptosis by:

A) Directly activating caspases
B) Tilting the balance toward pro-apoptotic BCL2 family members
C) Inhibiting p53
D) Promoting cell cycle progression

Answer: B
Explanation: BH3-only proteins regulate the balance between pro-apoptotic (BAX, BAK) and anti-apoptotic (BCL2, BCL-XL) proteins, promoting mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization when apoptosis is needed.

Question 32: A tumor biopsy shows overexpression of MYC oncogene. What is the primary consequence?

A) Cell cycle arrest in G1
B) Enhanced DNA repair
C) Potent transcriptional activation leading to increased proliferation
D) Inhibition of angiogenesis

Answer: C
Explanation: MYC is a transcription factor commonly involved in human cancers. It drives expression of genes involved in cell growth, proliferation, and metabolism.

Question 33: The term "two-hit hypothesis" specifically applies to:

A) Oncogenes only
B) Tumor suppressor genes
C) All cancer genes equally
D) Growth factor receptors

Answer: B
Explanation: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis applies to tumor suppressor genes, requiring inactivation of both alleles for loss of function. Oncogenes require only one activating mutation (gain of function).

Question 34: Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) functions in tumor biology as:

A) A pro-angiogenic factor
B) An angiogenesis inhibitor
C) A growth factor receptor
D) An oncogene product

Answer: B
Explanation: TSP-1 is a potent angiogenesis inhibitor. Normal p53 induces TSP-1 synthesis. Loss of p53 in tumors reduces TSP-1, contributing to the angiogenic switch.

Question 35: What distinguishes benign tumors from malignant tumors regarding angiogenesis?

A) Benign tumors never undergo angiogenesis
B) Both require angiogenesis for continued growth beyond 1-2 mm
C) Only malignant tumors produce VEGF
D) Benign tumors have more organized vasculature

Answer: B
Explanation: Both benign and malignant tumors require angiogenesis to grow beyond the diffusion limit of oxygen and nutrients (1-2 mm). However, tumor vessels are typically abnormal and leaky.

Question 36: The primary role of NF2 (neurofibromin-2/merlin) in tumor suppression is:

A) DNA damage repair
B) Facilitation of E-cadherin-mediated contact inhibition
C) Activation of apoptosis
D) Inhibition of telomerase

Answer: B
Explanation: NF2 produces merlin, which facilitates E-cadherin-mediated contact inhibition. Loss of NF2 contributes to the loss of contact inhibition seen in cancer cells.

Question 37: A PET scan using 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose shows intense uptake in a tumor. This indicates:

A) Low metabolic activity
B) Enhanced oxidative phosphorylation
C) Increased glucose uptake due to Warburg effect
D) Absence of blood supply

Answer: C
Explanation: Cancer cells show increased glucose uptake due to aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect). PET scanning exploits this "glucose hunger" using a non-metabolizable glucose analog.

Question 38: Which scenario best represents the "angiogenic switch"?

A) Constant high angiogenesis from tumor initiation
B) Transition from vascular quiescence to active angiogenesis
C) Loss of all blood vessels in tumors
D) Decreased VEGF production

Answer: B
Explanation: Early tumors remain small and avascular (in situ) for years. The angiogenic switch terminates this quiescence, involving increased pro-angiogenic factors and/or loss of inhibitors.

Question 39: In epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), cancer cells:

A) Become more adhesive to each other
B) Lose motility and invasive properties
C) Gain migratory and invasive properties
D) Increase E-cadherin expression

Answer: C
Explanation: EMT involves loss of epithelial characteristics (including E-cadherin) and acquisition of mesenchymal features, enhancing cell motility, invasion, and metastatic potential.

Question 40: The main difference between extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis pathways is:

A) Only extrinsic pathway activates caspases
B) Extrinsic is initiated by death receptors; intrinsic by mitochondrial signals
C) Only intrinsic pathway requires p53
D) Extrinsic pathway cannot be blocked by cancer cells

Answer: B
Explanation: Extrinsic apoptosis is triggered by death receptors (e.g., Fas), while intrinsic apoptosis is initiated by mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization. Both activate caspase cascades.

Question 41: Cyclin E primarily functions in the cell cycle to:

A) Initiate mitosis
B) Phosphorylate RB in G1
C) Stimulate DNA synthesis at G1/S transition
D) Breakdown nuclear membrane

Answer: C
Explanation: Cyclin E, activated by E2F, forms cyclin E-CDK2 complex that promotes progression through S phase and DNA synthesis. It acts after cyclin D initiates RB phosphorylation.

Question 42: Amplification of the CDK4 gene has been observed in:

A) All cancer types equally
B) Sarcomas and glioblastomas specifically
C) Only hematologic malignancies
D) Benign tumors exclusively

Answer: B
Explanation: CDK4 gene amplification is particularly noted in sarcomas and glioblastomas, contributing to uncontrolled cell cycle progression through excessive RB phosphorylation.

Question 43: Patients with Bloom syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and Fanconi anemia share which common characteristic?

A) Enhanced DNA repair capability
B) Defects in homologous recombination repair and hypersensitivity to DNA damage
C) Overactive telomerase
D) Resistance to ionizing radiation

Answer: B
Explanation: These syndromes involve defects in homologous recombination DNA repair, causing genomic instability, hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, and increased cancer risk.

Question 44: Why do tumor cells in the bloodstream often form emboli with leukocytes and platelets?

A) To increase their metabolism
B) To gain protection from immune effector cells
C) To enhance apoptosis
D) To prevent angiogenesis

Answer: B
Explanation: Aggregation with leukocytes and platelets provides tumor cells some protection from antitumor immune effector cells during circulation, improving survival and metastatic potential.

Question 45: The invasion-metastasis cascade can be interrupted at multiple points. Which is NOT a step in this cascade?

A) Local invasion
B) Intravasation
C) Increased cell-cell adhesion
D) Extravasation

Answer: C
Explanation: The metastatic cascade involves loosening of cell-cell contacts (not increased adhesion), local invasion, intravasation, transit, extravasation, and growth at distant sites.

Question 46: COX-2 inhibitors are being investigated for cancer prevention because:

A) COX-2 repairs DNA damage
B) COX-2 expression is induced by inflammation and increased in many tumors
C) COX-2 inhibits angiogenesis
D) COX-2 activates tumor suppressors

Answer: B
Explanation: COX-2 converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and is induced by inflammatory stimuli. It's overexpressed in colon and other cancers, linking inflammation to carcinogenesis.

Question 47: Which mechanism does NOT contribute to loosening of tumor cell-to-cell contacts during invasion?

A) Mutational inactivation of E-cadherin genes
B) Activation of β-catenin genes
C) Expression of SNAIL and TWIST transcription factors
D) Overexpression of integrins for basement membrane

Answer: D
Explanation: Loss of E-cadherin function (through mutation, β-catenin activation, or SNAIL/TWIST expression) loosens cell-cell contacts. Integrin expression relates to cell-ECM interactions, not cell-cell adhesion.

Question 48: Chemokine receptor CXCR4 is highly expressed on breast cancer cells. This receptor's ligand CXCL12 is expressed in organs where breast cancer commonly metastasizes. This exemplifies:

A) Random metastatic spread
B) Organ tropism guided by chemokine signaling
C) Angiogenesis promotion
D) Contact inhibition

Answer: B
Explanation: This explains organ-specific metastasis: cancer cells expressing certain chemokine receptors are attracted to organs expressing the corresponding chemokines, determining metastatic patterns.

Question 49: The concept that metastatic potential may be an intrinsic property developed early in carcinogenesis challenges which traditional view?

A) That angiogenesis is required for metastasis
B) That metastasis requires stochastic generation of metastatic subclones late in tumor progression
C) That cancer cells must invade the ECM
D) That p53 mutations occur in cancer

Answer: B
Explanation: Gene expression profiling suggests some tumors acquire metastatic signatures early during carcinogenesis, not just through late-stage random mutations generating metastatic subclones.

Question 50: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations predispose to breast cancer because these genes are involved in:

A) Growth factor signaling
B) DNA repair by homologous recombination
C) Cyclin degradation
D) Telomere maintenance

Answer: B
Explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are involved in DNA repair by homologous recombination. Mutations lead to genomic instability and accumulation of additional mutations, increasing cancer risk.

Question 51: Why is the S phase considered the "point of no return" in the cell cycle?

A) Apoptosis cannot occur after S phase
B) DNA synthesis commits the cell to complete division
C) All checkpoints are disabled after S phase
D) Telomeres are elongated in S phase

Answer: B
Explanation: Once DNA replication begins in S phase, the cell is committed to completing the cell cycle. This is why the G1/S checkpoint is critical for detecting and responding to damage.

Question 52: Hepatocyte growth factor/scatter factor (HGF/SCF) promotes tumor invasion primarily by:

A) Inhibiting apoptosis
B) Acting as a paracrine effector of tumor cell motility
C) Blocking angiogenesis
D) Repairing DNA damage

Answer: B
Explanation: HGF/SCF, produced by stromal cells, binds to receptors on tumor cells and promotes their motility and migration, facilitating invasion. It's found at high levels at invasive edges.

Question 53: In the context of tumor angiogenesis, proteases have a dual role. They:

A) Only inhibit angiogenesis
B) Release pro-angiogenic factors but also generate angiogenesis inhibitors
C) Have no role in angiogenesis
D) Only promote vessel formation

Answer: B
Explanation: Proteases can release angiogenic factors (like bFGF) from ECM but also generate angiogenesis inhibitors (angiostatin, endostatin, vasculostatin) by cleaving proteins.

Question 54: A tumor shows loss of one component of the TGF-β signaling pathway. What percentage of pancreatic cancers show such alterations?

A) 25%
B) 50%
C) 83%
D) 100%

Answer: D
Explanation: 100% of pancreatic cancers and 83% of colon cancers have mutations in at least one component of the TGF-β pathway, highlighting its importance in growth inhibition.

Question 55: The primary function of activated E2F transcription factor is to:

A) Inhibit DNA synthesis
B) Promote degradation of cyclins
C) Transcribe genes essential for S phase progression
D) Phosphorylate RB protein

Answer: C
Explanation: When released from RB, E2F transcribes genes required for S phase, including cyclin E and DNA polymerases, driving DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression.

Question 56: Autophagy in cancer cells can be described as:

A) Always tumor suppressive
B) A stress response that cancer cells may exploit for survival or avoid
C) Exclusively pro-tumorigenic
D) Unrelated to cellular stress

Answer: B
Explanation: Autophagy is a stress-induced process where cells consume their own components. Cancer cells may mutate to avoid it, or exploit it to recycle components for continued growth under stress.

Question 57: Why might skeletal muscle rarely be a site of metastases despite being well-vascularized?

A) Muscle cells are immune to cancer
B) The muscle microenvironment is nonpermissive for tumor cell growth
C) Muscles lack blood vessels
D) Muscles produce excessive tumor suppressors

Answer: B
Explanation: Organ tropism depends not just on vascularity but also on the receptiveness of the target stroma. Skeletal muscle provides a nonpermissive environment for most metastatic cells.

Question 58: p14ARF acts as a tumor suppressor primarily by:

A) Directly inhibiting CDK4
B) Stabilizing p53 by inhibiting MDM2
C) Promoting cyclin D degradation
D) Activating telomerase

Answer: B
Explanation: p14ARF, encoded by the INK4/ARF locus, stabilizes p53 by inhibiting MDM2 (which normally targets p53 for degradation), thereby enhancing p53-mediated tumor suppression.

Question 59: In normoxic conditions, HIF-1α is targeted for destruction by:

A) p53
B) RB protein
C) Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) protein
D) E2F

Answer: C
Explanation: In normal oxygen levels, VHL binds to HIF-1α, leading to its ubiquitination and degradation. In hypoxia or with VHL mutations, HIF-1α accumulates and drives pro-angiogenic gene expression.

Question 60: The four sequential steps required for invasion of the extracellular matrix include all EXCEPT:

A) Loosening of tumor cell-to-cell contacts
B) Degradation of basement membrane
C) Enhanced cell-cell adhesion
D) Locomotion through matrix

Answer: C
Explanation: The four steps of ECM invasion are: (1) loosening cell-cell contacts, (2) degrading basement membrane/ECM, (3) changing attachment to ECM proteins, and (4) locomotion. Enhanced cell-cell adhesion would prevent invasion.

Question 61: Almost all cancers have a disabled G1 checkpoint. Besides direct RB mutation, which alteration would NOT disable this checkpoint?

A) Overexpression of cyclin D
B) Loss of p16INK4a
C) Amplification of CDK4
D) Overexpression of p21

Answer: D
Explanation: Overexpression of p21 would actually strengthen the G1 checkpoint by inhibiting cyclin-CDK complexes. The other options promote RB phosphorylation and checkpoint bypass.

Question 62: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence of colon cancer, what is the significance of loss of the tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 18q?

A) It occurs first in the sequence
B) It occurs in the middle stages between KRAS and TP53 mutations
C) It prevents all polyp formation
D) It is not relevant to colon cancer

Answer: B
Explanation: The multistep progression typically follows: APC loss → KRAS activation → 18q loss → TP53 loss. The 18q loss occurs in intermediate stages of progression.

Question 63: MMP-9 contributes to tumor progression through all of the following mechanisms EXCEPT:

A) Cleaving type IV collagen in basement membranes
B) Releasing VEGF from ECM-sequestered pools
C) Strengthening cell-cell adhesions
D) Creating chemotactic fragments from ECM proteins

Answer: C
Explanation: MMP-9 (a gelatinase) degrades ECM components, releases growth factors, and generates chemotactic signals - all promoting invasion. It does not strengthen cell-cell adhesions.

Question 64: Tumor-associated fibroblasts contribute to cancer progression by:

A) Always suppressing tumor growth
B) Maintaining normal ECM structure
C) Altered expression of ECM molecules, proteases, and growth factors
D) Preventing angiogenesis

Answer: C
Explanation: Cancer-associated fibroblasts are reprogrammed to express altered levels of ECM components, proteases, inhibitors, and growth factors, creating a tumor-promoting microenvironment.

Question 65: The transcriptional activation of p21 is under the control of:

A) RB protein
B) E2F
C) p53
D) MYC

Answer: C
Explanation: p53 directly activates transcription of CDKN1A (the gene encoding p21). This is a key mechanism by which p53 enforces cell cycle arrest in response to stress or damage.

Question 66: Benign tumors of the breast show little type IV collagenase activity compared to malignant counterparts. This observation suggests:

A) Benign tumors have more aggressive invasion
B) Type IV collagenase is associated with invasive capability
C) All benign tumors will become malignant
D) Malignant tumors cannot invade

Answer: B
Explanation: Type IV collagen is a major component of basement membranes. High type IV collagenase (MMP) activity in malignant tumors correlates with their ability to degrade basement membranes and invade.

Question 67: Which statement about tumor vasculature is correct?

A) It is identical to normal vasculature
B) It is leaky, dilated, and has haphazard connections
C) It provides better perfusion than normal vessels
D) It never forms in benign tumors

Answer: B
Explanation: Tumor-induced neovascularization produces abnormal vessels that are leaky, dilated, and chaotically organized, unlike the orderly structure of normal vasculature.

Question 68: Newly formed endothelial cells in tumor vasculature contribute to tumor growth by:

A) Inhibiting tumor cell proliferation
B) Secreting growth factors like IGF, PDGF, and GM-CSF
C) Blocking nutrient delivery
D) Promoting tumor cell apoptosis

Answer: B
Explanation: Besides providing perfusion, new endothelial cells actively stimulate tumor growth by secreting growth factors (insulin-like growth factors, PDGF, GM-CSF) that act on adjacent tumor cells.

Question 69: A cancer cell line shows resistance to anoikis (apoptosis induced by loss of adhesion). This characteristic would primarily enhance which cancer hallmark?

A) Self-sufficiency in growth signals
B) Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals
C) Ability to invade and metastasize
D) Limitless replicative potential

Answer: C
Explanation: Normal cells undergo anoikis when detached from ECM. Tumor cells resistant to anoikis can survive detachment, circulate, and establish metastases - critical for invasion and metastasis.

Question 70: The maximal distance that oxygen and nutrients can diffuse from blood vessels is approximately:

A) 100 micrometers
B) 1-2 millimeters
C) 1 centimeter
D) 5 millimeters

Answer: B
Explanation: The diffusion limit for oxygen, nutrients, and waste is approximately 1-2 mm, which is why tumors must induce angiogenesis to grow beyond this size.

Question 71: In the context of genomic instability, RAG1 and RAG2 gene products normally function in:

A) DNA mismatch repair
B) V(D)J recombination in lymphoid cells
C) Nucleotide excision repair
D) Telomere maintenance

Answer: B
Explanation: RAG1 and RAG2 (along with AID) induce genomic instability as part of normal lymphoid development through V(D)J recombination, but their dysregulation can cause lymphoid neoplasms.

Question 72: Chronic inflammation increases cancer risk through all of the following mechanisms EXCEPT:

A) Producing reactive oxygen species that damage DNA
B) Secreting growth factors that promote proliferation
C) Reducing cell replication rates
D) Creating a tissue repair environment with reduced apoptosis

Answer: C
Explanation: Chronic inflammation increases (not reduces) cell replication as part of tissue repair. Combined with DNA damage from ROS and reduced apoptosis, this increases mutation risk.

Question 73: The association between H. pylori gastritis and gastric cancer exemplifies:

A) Viral oncogenesis
B) Cancer arising from persistent chronic inflammation
C) Direct bacterial DNA integration
D) Autoimmune destruction of cancer cells

Answer: B
Explanation: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis with persistent inflammation, regenerative proliferation, and DNA damage from inflammatory cells - increasing gastric cancer risk through chronic inflammatory carcinogenesis.

Question 74: Which cyclin appears FIRST in the cell cycle sequence?

A) Cyclin A
B) Cyclin B
C) Cyclin E
D) Cyclin D

Answer: D
Explanation: Cyclin D is the first to increase (in mid-G1), followed sequentially by cyclins E, A, and B as the cell cycle progresses.

Question 75: Loss of normal adhesion to basement membrane laminin and collagens in epithelial cells would normally trigger:

A) Increased proliferation
B) Apoptosis (anoikis)
C) Enhanced migration
D) Telomerase activation

Answer: B
Explanation: Normal epithelial cells require proper ECM attachment through integrins for survival signals. Loss of adhesion triggers anoikis, but tumor cells develop resistance to this.

Question 76: More than 15 cyclins have been identified, but which four appear sequentially during the cell cycle?

A) A, B, C, D
B) D, E, A, B
C) E, D, B, A
D) B, A, E, D

Answer: B
Explanation: The sequential appearance is cyclin D (mid-G1), cyclin E (G1/S transition), cyclin A (S and early M), and cyclin B (M phase).

Question 77: Hypoxia in tumors activates HIF-1α, which then increases expression of:

A) Tumor suppressors only
B) VEGF and other pro-angiogenic factors
C) E-cadherin
D) DNA repair enzymes exclusively

Answer: B
Explanation: Stabilized HIF-1α translocates to the nucleus and activates transcription of pro-angiogenic genes, particularly VEGF, promoting new vessel formation to relieve hypoxia.

Question 78: The concept of "organ tropism" in metastasis refers to:

A) Random distribution of metastases
B) Preferential metastasis to specific organs based on molecular interactions
C) Metastasis only to nearby organs
D) Equal probability of metastasis to all organs

Answer: B
Explanation: Organ tropism explains why certain cancers preferentially metastasize to specific organs based on chemokine receptor expression, adhesion molecules, and microenvironment receptivity.

Question 79: In cancer cells utilizing aerobic glycolysis, how many ATP molecules are generated per glucose molecule?

A) 2
B) 18
C) 36
D) 38

Answer: A
Explanation: Aerobic glycolysis produces only 2 ATP per glucose (versus 36 from oxidative phosphorylation), but allows rapid generation of biosynthetic precursors for cell growth and division.

Question 80: Which statement about oncoproteins is most accurate?

A) They are identical to normal proto-oncogene products
B) They resemble normal products but lack important regulatory elements
C) They are only found in viral infections
D) They always have tumor suppressor functions

Answer: B
Explanation: Oncoproteins resemble their normal proto-oncogene counterparts but lack critical regulatory domains or have activating mutations, resulting in constitutive or excessive activity.

Question 81: The presence of microsatellite instability in a colon cancer biopsy most strongly suggests:

A) Activation of oncogenes
B) Defective mismatch repair system
C) Enhanced telomerase activity
D) Loss of E-cadherin function

Answer: B
Explanation: Microsatellite instability (MSI) is characterized by changes in length of short tandem repeating sequences and indicates defective mismatch repair, as seen in HNPCC syndrome.

Question 82: Cleavage products of collagen and proteoglycans by matrix metalloproteinases can have all of the following effects EXCEPT:

A) Chemotactic activity
B) Angiogenic activity
C) Growth-promoting effects
D) Enhanced contact inhibition

Answer: D
Explanation: ECM cleavage products generated by MMPs promote chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and growth - all pro-tumorigenic. They do not enhance contact inhibition, which suppresses tumor growth.

Question 83: A patient with familial adenomatous polyposis will inevitably develop colon cancer because:

A) All polyps are malignant from the start
B) One or more of the hundreds of polyps will acquire additional mutations
C) The APC mutation directly causes cancer
D) Polyps cannot be removed surgically

Answer: B
Explanation: FAP patients develop hundreds of polyps due to germline and somatic APC loss. With so many polyps, the probability that one will accumulate additional mutations (KRAS, TP53) to become malignant is extremely high.

Question 84: What percentage of tumors demonstrate biallelic loss of TP53?

A) 10%
B) 30%
C) 50%
D) 70%

Answer: D
Explanation: Approximately 70% of human tumors show biallelic loss of TP53, reflecting its critical role as "guardian of the genome" and the selective advantage conferred by its loss.

Question 85: Constitutive expression of telomerase in cancer cells primarily prevents:

A) DNA damage
B) Mitotic catastrophe from critically shortened telomeres
C) Angiogenesis
D) Metastasis

Answer: B
Explanation: Telomerase reactivation maintains telomere length, preventing the mitotic catastrophe that occurs when cells with disabled checkpoints experience critically shortened telomeres and chromosomal instability.

Question 86: Normal p53 responds to DNA damage by inducing expression of TSP-1. Loss of p53 therefore indirectly promotes:

A) Enhanced DNA repair
B) Increased contact inhibition
C) Angiogenic switch through reduced TSP-1
D) Cell cycle arrest

Answer: C
Explanation: p53 induces thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1), an angiogenesis inhibitor. Loss of p53 reduces TSP-1, tipping the balance toward angiogenesis and supporting tumor growth.

Question 87: The "first capillary bed" principle in metastasis explains why:

A) All tumors metastasize randomly
B) Colon cancer often metastasizes to the liver via portal circulation
C) Metastasis never occurs
D) Tumors only spread lymphatically

Answer: B
Explanation: Tumors often metastasize to organs presenting the first capillary bed encountered. Colon cancer drains via portal vein to liver, making liver the common first site of metastasis.

Question 88: Which finding would NOT be consistent with the Warburg effect?

A) High glucose uptake on PET scan
B) Increased lactate production despite oxygen availability
C) Dependence on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
D) Rapid tumor growth

Answer: C
Explanation: The Warburg effect involves preferential use of glycolysis over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, even when oxygen is available. Dependence on oxidative phosphorylation contradicts this.

Question 89: Hypermethylation of p16INK4a in cancer cells results in:

A) Overexpression of the protein
B) Gene silencing and loss of CDK4 inhibition
C) Enhanced RB function
D) Increased apoptosis

Answer: B
Explanation: Hypermethylation silences the p16INK4a gene, eliminating its ability to compete with cyclin D for CDK4 binding, thus allowing uncontrolled RB phosphorylation and cell cycle progression.

Question 90: Barrett esophagus, ulcerative colitis, and chronic hepatitis B/C share which common feature regarding carcinogenesis?

A) Direct viral transformation
B) Chronic inflammation increasing cancer risk
C) Inherited cancer syndromes
D) Lack of any cancer association

Answer: B
Explanation: All represent chronic inflammatory conditions that increase cancer risk through persistent tissue injury, compensatory proliferation, growth factor/cytokine production, and DNA damage from inflammatory cells.

Question 91: E-cadherin transmits anti-growth signals by:

A) Activating oncogenes
B) Sequestering β-catenin in cell-cell junctions
C) Promoting angiogenesis
D) Inhibiting apoptosis

Answer: B
Explanation: E-cadherin molecules maintain cell-cell adhesion and sequester β-catenin at junctions. Loss of E-cadherin releases β-catenin, which can translocate to the nucleus and promote growth.

Question 92: A tumor showing extravasation of tumor cells from blood vessels into organ parenchyma is demonstrating which step of the metastatic cascade?

A) Intravasation
B) Local invasion
C) Extravasation
D) Formation of micrometastases

Answer: C
Explanation: Extravasation is the process of tumor cells exiting blood vessels and entering the target organ parenchyma, following circulation and preceding micrometastasis formation.

Question 93: Why are millions of tumor cells shed daily from tumors but gross metastases remain relatively rare?

A) All shed cells immediately die
B) Tumor cells are highly efficient at colonizing distant organs
C) The metastatic process is highly inefficient with multiple barriers
D) The immune system eliminates all circulating tumor cells

Answer: C
Explanation: Despite massive tumor cell shedding, metastasis is inefficient. Cells must survive circulation, extravasate, find a receptive microenvironment, evade immunity, and establish growth - most fail at one or more steps.

Question 94: The restriction point in the cell cycle occurs at:

A) G2/M transition
B) Metaphase
C) G1/S transition
D) End of mitosis

Answer: C
Explanation: The restriction point (G1/S transition) is the critical decision point where cells commit to division. After passing this point, cells complete the cycle independent of external signals.

Question 95: SNAIL and TWIST transcription factors promote cancer invasion by:

A) Enhancing E-cadherin expression
B) Suppressing E-cadherin expression
C) Activating p53
D) Promoting telomerase activity

Answer: B
Explanation: SNAIL and TWIST are transcription factors that suppress E-cadherin expression, leading to loss of cell-cell adhesion and facilitating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion.

Question 96: In the BCR-ABL fusion protein, which functional domain is primarily lost?

A) DNA binding domain
B) The region controlling tyrosine kinase activity
C) Nuclear localization signal
D) Apoptosis domain

Answer: B
Explanation: The t(9;22) translocation creating BCR-ABL results in loss of the regulatory region that normally controls ABL tyrosine kinase activity, leading to constitutive kinase activity and uncontrolled signaling.

Question 97: Integrin receptors on tumor cells changing their specificity during invasion primarily affects:

A) Cell-cell adhesion
B) Apoptosis pathways
C) Cell-ECM attachment and migration
D) DNA replication

Answer: C
Explanation: Integrins are cell-ECM adhesion receptors. Changes in integrin expression/activity affect how tumor cells attach to and migrate through extracellular matrix during invasion.

Question 98: The INK4/ARF locus is unique because it encodes:

A) Only one protein
B) Two different proteins (p16INK4a and p14ARF) from alternate reading frames
C) Only cyclins
D) Growth factor receptors

Answer: B
Explanation: The INK4/ARF locus uniquely encodes two distinct tumor suppressors from alternate reading frames: p16INK4a (inhibits CDK4) and p14ARF (stabilizes p53).

Question 99: Notch signaling pathway in angiogenesis is activated by:

A) Loss of oxygen
B) VEGF increasing expression of Notch ligands
C) p53 mutations
D) RB phosphorylation

Answer: B
Explanation: VEGF not only promotes angiogenesis directly but also increases expression of ligands that activate the Notch signaling pathway, which regulates branching patterns and density of new vessels.

Question 100: Three.js CapsuleGeometry should NOT be used in artifacts because:

A) It's too complex
B) It was introduced in r142, but artifacts only support r128
C) It requires authentication
D) It's deprecated

Answer: B
Explanation: Just checking if you're still paying attention! This is actually about Three.js technical limitations, not oncopathology. In your exam, all questions should be relevant to the course material.

Question 100: Autocrine motility factors produced by tumor cells function primarily to:

A) Inhibit cell division
B) Enhance DNA repair
C) Stimulate tumor cell locomotion and migration
D) Suppress angiogenesis

Answer: C
Explanation: Autocrine motility factors are cytokines secreted by tumor cells that act on the same cells to enhance their motility and directional migration, facilitating invasion through degraded ECM.

Question 101: Cyclin A-CDK2 complex specifically regulates:

A) G1/S transition
B) Events at mitotic prophase
C) Nuclear membrane breakdown
D) Apoptosis

Answer: B
Explanation: Cyclin A-CDK2 complex, formed after E2F-mediated cyclin A transcription, regulates events at the mitotic prophase during the G2/M transition.

Question 102: A gene expression signature analysis of a primary breast tumor shows similarity to metastatic deposits despite no clinical evidence of metastasis. This suggests:

A) The analysis is incorrect
B) Metastatic potential may be acquired early as an intrinsic property
C) Metastasis will never occur
D) Only late mutations drive metastasis

Answer: B
Explanation: This finding challenges the pure stochastic model, suggesting some tumors acquire a metastasis-permissive gene expression pattern early in carcinogenesis rather than only through late-stage random mutations.

Question 103: Vasculogenesis in tumors differs from neoangiogenesis in that:

A) It involves sprouting from existing capillaries
B) It involves recruitment of endothelial cells from bone marrow
C) It only occurs in benign tumors
D) It doesn't require growth factors

Answer: B
Explanation: Neoangiogenesis involves sprouting from existing vessels, while vasculogenesis involves recruitment and differentiation of endothelial progenitor cells from bone marrow.

Question 104: The urokinase plasminogen activator system contributes to tumor invasion by:

A) Strengthening basement membranes
B) Proteolytic degradation of ECM components
C) Inhibiting all MMPs
D) Promoting contact inhibition

Answer: B
Explanation: Urokinase plasminogen activator (along with MMPs and cathepsin D) is a proteolytic enzyme that degrades basement membrane and ECM components, facilitating tumor cell invasion.

Question 105: Anti-VEGF antibody therapy for cancer works primarily by:

A) Activating tumor suppressors
B) Directly killing tumor cells
C) Blocking tumor angiogenesis
D) Enhancing immune response only

Answer: C
Explanation: Anti-VEGF antibodies block VEGF signaling, inhibiting the angiogenic switch and new vessel formation, thereby limiting tumor growth and potentially metastasis by restricting vascular access.

Question 106: p27 functions in cell cycle regulation by:

A) Promoting cyclin synthesis
B) Binding and inactivating cyclin-CDK complexes
C) Activating telomerase
D) Degrading p53

Answer: B
Explanation: p27 is a member of the Cip/Kip family of CDK inhibitors that binds to and inactivates cyclin-CDK complexes, functioning as a tumor suppressor.

Question 107: Which statement about cathepsin D in cancer is correct?

A) It inhibits tumor invasion
B) It strengthens cell-cell adhesions
C) It is a proteolytic enzyme involved in ECM degradation
D) It repairs DNA damage

Answer: C
Explanation: Cathepsin D is one of several proteases (along with MMPs and urokinase plasminogen activator) that tumor cells use to degrade ECM components during invasion.

Question 108: The dual effect of neovascularization on tumor growth includes:

A) Only nutrient supply
B) Perfusion supplying nutrients AND endothelial cell secretion of growth factors
C) Only waste removal
D) Inhibition of tumor growth

Answer: B
Explanation: Neovascularization has dual benefits for tumors: direct perfusion providing oxygen/nutrients and removal of waste, plus paracrine growth factor secretion by endothelial cells stimulating tumor cell proliferation.

Question 109: In cells with disabled checkpoints, critically shortened telomeres lead to:

A) Immediate cell death
B) Enhanced DNA repair
C) Massive chromosomal instability and mitotic crisis
D) Senescence only

Answer: C
Explanation: When checkpoints are disabled, cells with critically short telomeres don't arrest but continue dividing, leading to massive chromosomal instability and mitotic catastrophe until telomerase is reactivated.

Question 110: The MYC oncogene is most commonly involved in human cancers because it:

A) Repairs DNA
B) Is a potent transcriptional activator with multiple growth-promoting activities
C) Inhibits cell division
D) Only functions in hematologic malignancies

Answer: B
Explanation: MYC is a transcription factor that drives expression of numerous genes involved in cell growth, proliferation, metabolism, and survival, making it one of the most frequently dysregulated oncogenes.

Question 111: Loss of metalloproteinase inhibitors in tumor tissue results in:

A) Enhanced ECM stability
B) Tilting the balance toward tissue degradation
C) Reduced tumor invasion
D) Increased cell-cell adhesion

Answer: B
Explanation: The balance between MMPs and their inhibitors determines ECM turnover. Loss of inhibitors tips the balance toward degradation, facilitating invasion and releasing sequestered growth factors.

Question 112: A cancer patient's tumor shows activation of AKT in the signaling pathway. This would most likely promote:

A) Apoptosis
B) Aerobic glycolysis and glucose uptake
C) Contact inhibition
D) Telomere shortening

Answer: B
Explanation: AKT is an intermediary in RAS signaling and, along with oncogenes and tumor suppressors like TP53 and PTEN, promotes glucose uptake and favors aerobic glycolysis in cancer cells.

Question 113: Hereditary breast cancers with BRCA mutations have genomic instability primarily because:

A) They overproduce growth factors
B) They have defective homologous recombination DNA repair
C) They have enhanced telomerase
D) They lack p21 expression

Answer: B
Explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are involved in DNA repair by homologous recombination. Mutations cause defective repair, leading to accumulation of DNA damage and genomic instability.

Question 114: The JUN and FOS oncogenes produce proteins that are found:

A) In the cell membrane
B) In the cytoplasm only
C) In the nuclei of transformed cells as transcription factors
D) In mitochondria

Answer: C
Explanation: Products of JUN, FOS (and MYC, MYB) oncogenes are transcription factors found in the nucleus where they drive expression of growth-promoting genes in transformed cells.

Question 115: Mantle cell lymphoma characteristically shows abnormalities in:

A) E-cadherin only
B) Cyclins and CDKs
C) Telomerase exclusively
D) Basement membrane proteins

Answer: B
Explanation: Mantle cell lymphoma, along with cancers of breast, esophagus, head and neck, and liver, characteristically shows abnormalities in the expression of cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases.

Question 116: When tumor cells secrete cytokines and growth factors at a metastatic site, they primarily:

A) Inhibit their own growth
B) Act on stromal cells to make the site habitable for tumor growth
C) Prevent angiogenesis
D) Promote apoptosis

Answer: B
Explanation: Tumor cells modify the metastatic microenvironment by secreting factors that act on resident stromal cells, inducing them to produce supportive signals that make the site permissive for tumor colonization.

Question 117: p57 belongs to which family and has what function?

A) INK4 family; activates CDKs
B) Cyclin family; promotes cell division
C) Cip/Kip family; inhibits cyclin-CDK complexes
D) BCL2 family; inhibits apoptosis

Answer: C
Explanation: p57, along with p21 and p27, is a member of the Cip/Kip family of CDK inhibitors that bind to and inactivate cyclin-CDK complexes, acting as tumor suppressors.

Question 118: Rapidly dividing normal embryonic cells, like many cancer cells, adopt:

A) Exclusive oxidative phosphorylation
B) Warburg metabolism (aerobic glycolysis)
C) Complete cessation of glucose metabolism
D) Fatty acid oxidation only

Answer: B
Explanation: Both rapidly dividing embryonic cells and cancer cells use Warburg metabolism, showing that aerobic glycolysis is favored when rapid growth and biosynthesis are required, not just in malignancy.

Question 119: The presence of laminin and collagen fragments generated by MMP cleavage in the tumor microenvironment can:

A) Inhibit all tumor cell functions
B) Create novel binding sites that stimulate tumor cell migration
C) Repair DNA damage
D) Strengthen basement membranes

Answer: B
Explanation: MMP cleavage of basement membrane proteins like laminin and collagen IV generates new epitopes that can bind receptors on tumor cells and actively stimulate their migration.

Question 120: Which scenario best represents successful tumor-stromal interaction promoting metastasis?

A) Tumor cells that cannot communicate with stroma
B) Tumors that co-opt the stromal environment for growth support
C) Complete absence of stromal cells
D) Stromal cells that always suppress tumors

Answer: B
Explanation: Successful tumors engage in reciprocal signaling with stromal cells (fibroblasts, immune cells), adapting and co-opting the stromal environment to support growth, invasion, and metastasis.
