Title: GENETIC DISORDERS SAQs EXAMINATION
Content:
GENETIC DISORDERS - 30 KEY SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS

Comprehensive coverage: Mutations, Mendelian Disorders, and Inheritance Patterns

SECTION A: INTRODUCTION & APPLICATIONS OF GENETICS (4 Questions)

1. What is the lifetime frequency of genetic disease and why is it higher than commonly appreciated?

Answer:

  • Lifetime frequency: 670 per 1000 individuals
  • Higher than appreciated because includes:
    • "Classic" genetic disorders (single gene, chromosomal)
    • Cardiovascular diseases with genetic components
    • Disorders of immunity
    • Cancers (genetic mutations in somatic cells)
    • Variable expressivity (mild/hidden presentations)
  • ~50% of early pregnancy miscarriages have chromosomal abnormalities
  • ~5% of individuals <25 years develop serious disease with significant genetic component
  • Many mild genetic disorders remain undiagnosed

2. Explain the human genome composition and genetic diversity.

Answer: Genome composition:

  • Approximately 30,000 genes in human genome
  • <2% code for proteins (protein-coding genes)
  • >50% are repetitive sequences of unknown function
  • Includes regulatory sequences, introns, non-coding RNAs

Genetic diversity:

  • Humans share 99.9% of DNA sequence
  • 0.1% difference = ~3 million base pairs
  • This 0.1% accounts for:
    • Individual variations
    • Disease susceptibility
    • Physical characteristics
    • Drug responses
    • Ethnic diversity

3. Compare functional cloning and positional cloning approaches.

Answer: Functional (Classic) Cloning:

  • Start with: Known affected protein/clinical phenotype
  • Steps:
    • Identify abnormal protein through clinical/biochemical studies
    • Isolate and clone normal gene
    • Determine molecular changes in disease
  • Example: Sickle cell anemia (abnormal hemoglobin identified first)

Positional (Candidate Gene) Cloning:

  • Start with: Chromosome location of disease
  • Steps:
    • Map disease phenotype to chromosome location (linkage analysis)
    • Clone multiple DNA pieces from that region
    • Identify aberrant proteins from mutated genes
    • Work backwards from location to function
  • Example: Huntington disease (location found before gene function known)

4. Describe four major applications of genetics in medicine.

Answer: 1. Molecular basis of human disease:

  • Understanding disease mechanisms at genetic level
  • Both approaches: functional and positional cloning

2. Production of biologically active agents:

  • Insert genes into bacteria/tissue culture cells
  • Examples: TNF receptor, tissue plasminogen activator, growth hormone, erythropoietin, insulin

3. Gene therapy:

  • Transfer of somatic cells with normal genes
  • Treat genetic diseases at source
  • Ethical considerations: benefits vs risks

4. Disease diagnosis:

  • Molecular probes for genetic diseases
  • Prenatal diagnosis
  • Carrier detection
  • Diagnosis of infectious diseases (pathogen DNA detection)
  • Personalized medicine approaches

SECTION B: TYPES AND CATEGORIES OF MUTATIONS (7 Questions)

5. Define mutation and distinguish between germline and somatic mutations.

Answer: Mutation:

  • Permanent change in DNA sequence
  • Can affect single base pairs to large chromosomal segments

Germline mutations:

  • Occur in germ cells (sperm/egg)
  • Transmitted to progeny
  • Present in all cells of offspring
  • Cause inherited/hereditary diseases
  • Examples: Hemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease

Somatic mutations:

  • Occur in body (somatic) cells
  • NOT transmitted to progeny
  • Present only in affected tissue/cell lineage
  • Cause: cancers, some congenital malformations
  • Examples: Most cancers, some birthmarks

6. Describe the three major categories of mutations.

Answer: 1. Genome mutations:

  • Affect whole chromosome number
  • Monosomies: Loss of one chromosome (e.g., Turner syndrome 45,X)
  • Trisomies: Gain of one chromosome (e.g., Down syndrome, trisomy 21)
  • Result from nondisjunction during meiosis

2. Chromosome mutations:

  • Rearrangement of genetic material
  • Visible structural changes under microscope
  • Types: deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations
  • Example: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in CML

3. Gene mutations:

  • Changes within individual genes
  • May involve:
    • Single base pair (point mutations)
    • Small deletions/insertions
    • Partial or complete gene deletion
  • NOT visible cytogenetically

7. Explain point mutations and their three types.

Answer: Point mutations: Substitution of single nucleotide base

1. Missense mutations:

  • Change one amino acid to another
  • Conservative: Similar amino acid (minimal effect)
  • Non-conservative: Different amino acid properties (significant effect)
  • Example: Sickle cell anemia (glutamic acid → valine)

2. Nonsense mutations:

  • Change amino acid codon to stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA)
  • Premature termination of translation
  • Truncated, non-functional protein
  • Usually severe effect

3. Silent mutations:

  • Change nucleotide but same amino acid (genetic code redundancy)
  • No change in protein sequence
  • Generally no clinical effect

8. What are frameshift mutations and their consequences?

Answer: Definition:

  • Insertion or deletion of nucleotides NOT divisible by 3
  • Alters reading frame of DNA

Mechanism:

  • Genetic code read in triplets (codons)
  • Insertion/deletion of 1 or 2 base pairs shifts reading frame
  • All downstream amino acids changed
  • Usually encounter premature stop codon

Consequences:

  • Completely different amino acid sequence after mutation
  • Non-functional protein
  • Usually severe phenotype
  • Example: Some forms of Tay-Sachs disease

Note: Deletions/insertions of 3 or multiples of 3:

  • Do NOT cause frameshift
  • Result in missing/extra amino acids
  • May be less severe

9. Explain trinucleotide repeat mutations and their unique characteristics.

Answer: Definition:

  • Dynamic amplification of sequence of 3 nucleotides
  • Usually involves guanine (G) and cytosine (C)

Unique characteristics: 1. Dynamic nature:

  • Degree of amplification increases during gametogenesis
  • Each generation may have more repeats

2. Anticipation:

  • Earlier onset in successive generations
  • More severe phenotype in offspring

3. Threshold effect:

  • Normal: small number of repeats
  • Disease: exceeds threshold number

Examples:

  • Fragile X syndrome: CGG repeats in FMR1 gene
  • Huntington disease: CAG repeats in huntingtin gene
  • Myotonic dystrophy: CTG repeats

10. Describe mutations affecting non-coding sequences.

Answer: Promoter and enhancer mutations:

  • Affect regulatory sequences
  • Interfere with transcription factor binding
  • Result: Reduced or absent transcription
  • Normal gene present but not expressed properly
  • Example: Some hereditary hemolytic anemias (thalassemias)

Splice site mutations:

  • Affect intron-exon boundaries
  • Abnormal mRNA splicing
  • Aberrant proteins or no protein

Effects:

  • May be as severe as coding sequence mutations
  • Difficult to detect without sequencing
  • Important in disease diagnosis

11. What are the three main categories of genetic disorders?

Answer: 1. Diseases related to mutant genes of large effect:

  • Single gene (Mendelian) disorders
  • Autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked
  • Clear inheritance patterns
  • Examples: Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, hemophilia

2. Diseases with multifactorial (polygenic) inheritance:

  • Multiple genes + environmental factors
  • No clear Mendelian pattern
  • Examples: Diabetes, hypertension, coronary artery disease, cleft lip/palate

3. Chromosomal disorders:

  • Abnormalities in chromosome number or structure
  • Examples: Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Turner syndrome (45,X), Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)

Other important categories:

  • Trinucleotide repeat disorders
  • Mitochondrial DNA disorders
  • Disorders with genomic imprinting

SECTION C: MENDELIAN DISORDERS - GENERAL CONCEPTS (5 Questions)

12. Define Mendelian disorders and key genetic concepts.

Answer: Mendelian disorders:

  • Fall under mutations in single genes of large effect
  • Follow Mendel's laws of inheritance
  • Clear inheritance patterns

Key statistics:

  • Every person carries 5-8 deleterious genes
  • Most are recessive
  • 80% familial (inherited)
  • 20% de novo (new mutations)

Important concepts: Gene expression:

  • Dominant, recessive, or co-dominant

Pleiotropy:

  • Single mutant gene → multiple end effects
  • Example: Marfan syndrome affects eyes, skeleton, cardiovascular system

Genetic heterogeneity:

  • Mutations at different loci → same trait/disease
  • Example: Osteogenesis imperfecta (multiple different genes)

13. Explain penetrance and expressivity in genetic disorders.

Answer: Penetrance:

  • Definition: Percentage of individuals with mutation who show disease phenotype
  • Complete penetrance (100%): All with mutation are affected
  • Reduced/incomplete penetrance (<100%): Some with mutation appear normal
  • Example: BRCA1 mutation (70% develop breast cancer, not 100%)

Expressivity:

  • Definition: Degree/severity of phenotype among affected individuals
  • Variable expressivity: Same mutation, different severity
  • All with mutation show trait but expressed differently
  • Example: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (mild café-au-lait spots in some, severe tumors in others)

Clinical importance:

  • Complicates genetic counseling
  • Affects risk prediction
  • Important for family screening

14. What is the biochemical and molecular basis of Mendelian disorders?

Answer: Major mechanisms:

1. Enzyme defects:

  • Most common in autosomal recessive disorders
  • Complete/partial enzyme deficiency
  • Accumulation of substrates or deficiency of products
  • Example: Phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency)

2. Defects in receptors:

  • Inability to respond to signals
  • Example: Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor defect)

3. Defects in transport systems:

  • Impaired movement across membranes
  • Example: Cystic fibrosis (CFTR chloride channel)

4. Alterations in non-enzyme proteins:

  • Structural proteins affected
  • Example: Sickle cell disease (hemoglobin), Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin)

5. Defects in hemostasis:

  • Coagulation factor deficiencies
  • Example: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency)

6. Defects in growth regulation:

  • Abnormal cell growth/differentiation
  • Example: Neurofibromatosis (tumor suppressor defect)

7. Adverse drug reactions:

  • Genetically determined (pharmacogenetics)
  • Example: G6PD deficiency (hemolysis with certain drugs)

15. Distinguish between familial and de novo mutations.

Answer: Familial mutations:

  • 80% of Mendelian disorders
  • Inherited from one or both parents
  • Present in parental germline
  • May trace through multiple generations
  • Family history positive
  • Example: Familial hypercholesterolemia passed through generations

De novo mutations:

  • 20% of Mendelian disorders
  • New mutation in parental gamete
  • Not present in either parent's somatic cells
  • Parents phenotypically normal
  • No family history
  • Child is first affected in family
  • Can be transmitted to subsequent generations

Risk factors for de novo mutations:

  • Advanced paternal age (especially for autosomal dominant)
  • Environmental mutagens
  • Random errors in DNA replication

16. What is the difference between genetic heterogeneity and pleiotropy?

Answer: Genetic heterogeneity:

  • Mutations at several different genetic loci → same phenotype/trait
  • "Many genes, one disease"
  • Locus heterogeneity
  • Example: Osteogenesis imperfecta (mutations in COL1A1, COL1A2, or other collagen genes)
  • Example: Retinitis pigmentosa (>50 different genes can cause)

Clinical importance:

  • Complicates genetic testing
  • May explain phenotypic variation
  • Different mutations may respond differently to treatment

Pleiotropy:

  • Single mutant gene → multiple different effects
  • "One gene, many effects"
  • Example: Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation affects):
    • Skeletal system (tall stature, arachnodactyly)
    • Ocular (lens dislocation)
    • Cardiovascular (aortic aneurysm)
  • Example: Sickle cell disease (single HBB mutation causes):
    • Anemia
    • Pain crises
    • Organ damage
    • Increased infection risk

SECTION D: AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT DISORDERS (4 Questions)

17. List and explain the key characteristics of autosomal dominant disorders.

Answer: 1. Inheritance pattern:

  • Typically at least one parent affected (vertical transmission)
  • Exception: De novo mutations (especially with advanced paternal age)

2. Gender distribution:

  • Affects both males and females equally
  • Both sexes can transmit to offspring

3. Transmission:

  • 50% risk for each child of affected parent
  • Affected individuals usually heterozygous
  • Homozygous state often lethal or more severe

4. Clinical features modified by:

  • Reduced penetrance: Not all with mutation show disease
  • Variable expressivity: Different severity among affected

5. Age of onset:

  • Many have delayed onset (manifest in adulthood)
  • Example: Huntington disease (symptoms in 30s-40s)

6. Family pattern:

  • Horizontal AND vertical transmission through pedigree
  • Male-to-male transmission occurs (distinguishes from X-linked)

17. What are the two main molecular mechanisms of autosomal dominant disorders?

Answer: 1. Haploinsufficiency:

  • 50% of normal gene product insufficient for normal function
  • Reduced production from one normal allele
  • Loss-of-function mutation
  • Example: Familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor deficiency)

Mechanism:

  • One mutant allele produces no protein
  • One normal allele produces 50% of normal amount
  • 50% insufficient for normal cellular function

2. Dominant-negative effect:

  • Mutant protein interferes with normal protein function
  • Abnormal protein produced, not just reduced amount
  • More severe than simple haploinsufficiency
  • Common with multimeric proteins

Example: Osteogenesis imperfecta

  • Abnormal collagen α-chains
  • Incorporate into triple helix with normal chains
  • Disrupt entire collagen molecule structure
  • One abnormal chain ruins multiple molecules

3. Gain-of-function mutations (less common):

  • Mutant protein acquires new, harmful activity
  • Example: Some forms of familial cancer syndromes

19. Explain why many autosomal dominant disorders show delayed onset.

Answer: Reasons for delayed onset:

1. Cumulative damage:

  • Normal allele initially compensates
  • Over time: accumulated cellular damage
  • Eventually exceeds compensatory capacity
  • Example: Adult polycystic kidney disease

2. Age-related decline in cellular function:

  • Compensation adequate in youth
  • Aging reduces cellular reserves
  • Mutation effects become apparent
  • Example: Huntington disease

3. Threshold effects:

  • Disease manifests only after reaching critical threshold
  • Takes years to accumulate
  • Example: Some familial cancers

4. Secondary insults:

  • Environmental factors over time
  • "Two-hit" mechanism in some cases

Clinical implications:

  • Reproductive decisions made before diagnosis
  • Challenges for genetic counseling
  • Importance of predictive testing
  • Psychological impact of waiting for symptoms

20. Compare homozygous and heterozygous states in autosomal dominant disorders.

Answer: Heterozygous state:

  • Most affected individuals are heterozygous (Aa)
  • One mutant allele, one normal allele
  • Disease manifests (by definition of "dominant")
  • Clinical expression variable
  • Compatible with reproduction
  • Examples: Most familial hypercholesterolemia patients

Homozygous state:

  • Two mutant alleles (AA) - rare
  • Usually much more severe or lethal
  • Often incompatible with life
  • May be embryonic lethal

Examples:

  • Familial hypercholesterolemia:
    • Heterozygous: Cholesterol 300-500 mg/dL, heart disease in 30s-40s
    • Homozygous: Cholesterol >1000 mg/dL, heart disease in childhood, often fatal
  • Achondroplasia:
    • Heterozygous: Dwarfism, viable
    • Homozygous: Lethal, severe skeletal abnormalities

Why rare:

  • Requires both parents affected (uncommon)
  • Homozygous state often lethal
  • Reduced reproductive fitness

SECTION E: AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE DISORDERS (5 Questions)

21. List and explain the key characteristics of autosomal recessive disorders.

Answer: 1. Parental status:

  • Parents usually phenotypically normal (carriers/heterozygotes)
  • Both parents must be carriers for affected children

2. Inheritance pattern:

  • Horizontal transmission (siblings affected, not parents)
  • 25% recurrence risk for each subsequent pregnancy
  • No vertical transmission through generations (typically)

3. Gender distribution:

  • Affects both males and females equally

4. Clinical expression:

  • More uniform than autosomal dominant disorders
  • Complete penetrance is common
  • Less variable expressivity

5. Age of onset:

  • Onset frequently early in life (childhood)
  • Often present at birth or infancy

6. Consanguinity:

  • Increased frequency in consanguineous marriages
  • Rare alleles more likely to be homozygous

7. Disease category:

  • Include almost all inborn errors of metabolism
  • Enzyme deficiencies most common

22. Explain why autosomal recessive disorders are the largest category of Mendelian disorders.

Answer: Reasons for large numbers:

1. Carrier advantage (heterozygote advantage):

  • Carriers may have selective advantage
  • Natural selection maintains mutant alleles
  • Example: Sickle cell trait protects against malaria

2. Concealed in heterozygotes:

  • Carriers phenotypically normal
  • Mutations not eliminated by selection
  • Persist in population at low frequency

3. Enzyme defects mechanism:

  • 50% enzyme activity usually sufficient (in carriers)
  • Only homozygotes (<50% activity) show disease
  • Most metabolic pathways have excess capacity

4. High mutation rates:

  • Some genes more prone to mutation
  • New mutations constantly arising

5. Founder effects:

  • Common in isolated populations
  • Genetic drift increases frequency

6. Consanguinity:

  • Common in some populations
  • Increases likelihood of rare allele pairing

23. What is consanguinity and why does it increase risk of autosomal recessive disorders?

Answer: Consanguinity:

  • Marriage/reproduction between blood relatives
  • Share common ancestor(s)
  • Share proportion of genes "identical by descent"

Degree of relationship:

  • First cousins: Share 1/8 (12.5%) of genes
  • Second cousins: Share 1/32 of genes

Why increases AR disorder risk:

1. Shared rare alleles:

  • Related individuals more likely to carry same rare mutant alleles
  • Inherited from common ancestor
  • Higher probability both parents are carriers

2. Mathematical risk:

  • General population: Carrier frequency for rare disorder = low
  • Consanguineous couple: BOTH carriers = much higher
  • Increases probability of homozygous affected children

3. Multiple rare disorders:

  • Risk applies to ALL recessive disorders
  • Consanguineous couples at higher risk for multiple different AR conditions

Prevalence:

  • Common in some populations (Middle East, North Africa, South Asia)
  • Legal restrictions in some countries
  • Important for genetic counseling

24. Why do autosomal recessive disorders show complete penetrance and uniform expression?

Answer: Complete penetrance (nearly always):

  • Homozygotes have complete absence or severe reduction of gene product
  • No normal allele to compensate
  • Threshold for normal function crossed
  • All homozygotes manifest disease

More uniform expression:

1. No normal allele modulation:

  • Heterozygotes: Variable compensation by normal allele
  • Homozygotes: Consistently absent/minimal function
  • Less variation in disease severity

2. Metabolic basis:

  • Most AR disorders are enzyme deficiencies
  • Complete/near-complete loss of enzyme
  • Predictable biochemical consequences
  • Substrate accumulation or product deficiency consistent

3. Earlier onset:

  • Severe from birth/early life
  • Less time for environmental modulation
  • Less acquired factors affecting expression

Exceptions:

  • Some variation exists due to:
    • Different mutations in same gene (compound heterozygotes)
    • Modifier genes
    • Environmental factors
  • But generally MORE uniform than AD disorders

25. Explain why most inborn errors of metabolism are autosomal recessive.

Answer: Metabolic pathway characteristics:

1. Enzyme redundancy/excess capacity:

  • Most metabolic pathways have >50% excess enzyme capacity
  • Heterozygotes (50% activity): Still sufficient for normal function
  • Homozygotes (<50% activity): Below threshold → disease

2. Loss-of-function mutations:

  • Most metabolic disorders due to enzyme deficiency
  • Loss-of-function = recessive
  • Need both alleles defective for disease

3. Threshold effects:

  • Minimum enzyme activity required
  • One normal allele usually produces enough
  • Only when both defective: Below threshold

Examples:

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU):
    • Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency
    • Heterozygotes (50% activity): Normal
    • Homozygotes (<5% activity): Mental retardation without treatment
  • Tay-Sachs disease:
    • Hexosaminidase A deficiency
    • Heterozygotes: Asymptomatic
    • Homozygotes: Fatal neurodegeneration

Contrast with dominant:

  • Structural proteins often dominant
  • Dominant-negative effects
  • Haploinsufficiency for some non-enzymatic functions

SECTION F: X-LINKED DISORDERS (5 Questions)

26. List and explain the key characteristics of X-linked recessive disorders.

Answer: 1. Affected individuals:

  • Males predominantly affected (hemizygous - only one X)
  • Females rarely affected (need two mutant X chromosomes)

2. Transmission pattern:

  • No male-to-male transmission (fathers give Y to sons)
  • Affected male's daughters: ALL carriers
  • Affected male's sons: ALL unaffected
  • Carrier females: 50% sons affected, 50% daughters carriers

3. Inheritance through females:

  • Passed through carrier females
  • Mothers of affected males usually carriers
  • Diagonal pattern in pedigree (uncle-nephew through carrier sister)

4. Carrier females:

  • Usually asymptomatic or mild symptoms
  • May show manifestations due to:
    • Skewed X-inactivation (Lyonization)
    • Unfavorable X-inactivation pattern

5. Prevalence:

  • More common in males
  • Rare in females (requires affected father AND carrier mother)

Examples:

  • Hemophilia A and B
  • Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy
  • Fragile X syndrome
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Color blindness

27. Explain X-inactivation (Lyonization) and its effects on carrier females.

Answer: X-inactivation (Lyonization):

  • In females: One X chromosome randomly inactivated in each cell
  • Occurs early in embryonic development
  • Forms Barr body (inactive X)
  • Ensures dosage compensation (equal X gene expression in males/females)

Process:

  • Random: Either maternal or paternal X inactivated
  • Early embryonic: ~Day 16 of development
  • Permanent: Same X stays inactive in all descendant cells
  • Mosaic: Females are mosaics of two cell populations

Effects on carrier females:

1. Usually asymptomatic:

  • Random inactivation: ~50% cells have normal X active
  • Sufficient for normal function in most cases

2. Variable manifestations (sometimes):

  • Unfavorable skewing: More cells with normal X inactivated
  • Symptoms appear (mild to moderate)
  • Example: Some carriers of Duchenne muscular dystrophy have muscle weakness

3. Examples of manifesting carriers:

  • Hemophilia carriers: Occasional mild bleeding
  • G6PD deficiency: Hemolysis in some carriers
  • Fragile X carriers: Learning difficulties in some

28. Describe X-linked dominant disorders and give examples.

Answer: Characteristics:

  • Rare compared to X-linked recessive
  • Affect both males and females
  • Females more commonly affected (2:1 ratio)
  • Often more severe in males (hemizygous)

Inheritance pattern:

  • Affected male: ALL daughters affected, NO sons affected
  • Affected female: 50% children (both sexes) affected
  • Male-to-male transmission does NOT occur

Clinical features:

  • Often lethal in affected males (embryonic/early life)
  • Survivors are mostly females
  • Variable severity in females (X-inactivation)

Examples:

1. Vitamin D-resistant rickets (hypophosphatemic rickets):

  • Defect in phosphate reabsorption
  • Both sexes affected
  • Males often more severe

2. Rett syndrome:

  • MECP2 gene mutation
  • Almost exclusively females (lethal in males)
  • Progressive neurological disorder

3. Incontinentia pigmenti:

  • Usually lethal in males
  • Skin pigmentation abnormalities in females

4. Fragile X syndrome (some features):

  • Predominantly affects males
  • Carrier females may have learning difficulties

29. Why don't affected males with X-linked recessive disorders transmit the disease to their sons?

Answer: Sex chromosome inheritance:

Males (XY):

  • Receive X from mother
  • Receive Y from father
  • Sons get father's Y chromosome, mother's X

Affected male (XᵐY):

  • Has mutant X chromosome (Xᵐ)
  • Passes Y to ALL sons
  • Sons cannot receive father's X
  • Therefore: No male-to-male transmission

Daughters of affected male:

  • Receive father's Xᵐ
  • Receive mother's X (normal)
  • ALL daughters are obligate carriers (XᵐX)
  • Usually phenotypically normal (have one normal X)

Carrier females (XᵐX):

  • Pass Xᵐ or normal X to children (50% each)
  • Sons who inherit Xᵐ: Affected (XᵐY)
  • Daughters who inherit Xᵐ: Carriers (XᵐX)

Pedigree pattern:

  • Diagonal pattern: Uncle to nephew through carrier sister
  • Never father to son
  • Distinguishes X-linked from autosomal inheritance

30. Explain why some carrier females manifest symptoms of X-linked disorders.

Answer: Mechanisms of manifesting carriers:

1. Skewed (non-random) X-inactivation:

  • Normally: 50:50 inactivation of each X
  • Skewed: >75% of cells have same X inactive
  • Unfavorable skewing: Normal X preferentially inactivated
  • Most cells express mutant X
  • Insufficient normal gene product
  • Example: Duchenne carrier with 90% normal X inactivated → muscle weakness

2. Turner syndrome (45,X):

  • Female with only one X chromosome
  • If that X carries mutation: Manifests disease
  • No second X to compensate
  • Example: Hemophilia in Turner syndrome female with mutant X

3. X-autosome translocations:

  • Translocation between X and autosome
  • Preferential inactivation of normal X
  • Mutant X remains active
  • Manifests disease

4. Compound heterozygotes (X-linked dominant):

  • Two different mutations on each X
  • Manifests features of both

5. Homozygous state (rare):

  • Affected father + carrier mother
  • Daughter inherits mutant X from both
  • Manifests disease (often severe)

Clinical examples:

  • Hemophilia carriers: 10-15% have bleeding tendency
  • Duchenne carriers: 8-10% have muscle weakness
  • G6PD carriers: May have hemolysis with oxidant drugs
  • Fragile X carriers: 30-50% have learning difficulties

STUDY TIPS FOR GENETIC DISORDERS:

High-Yield Concepts:

  1. Inheritance patterns - Practice drawing pedigrees
  2. Penetrance vs expressivity - Understand the difference
  3. Germline vs somatic mutations - Different implications
  4. X-inactivation - Critical for understanding carrier manifestations
  5. Consanguinity - Why it increases AR disorder risk

Must-Know Examples:

  • AD: Familial hypercholesterolemia, Marfan syndrome, Huntington disease
  • AR: Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, PKU, Tay-Sachs
  • XLR: Hemophilia, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Fragile X
  • XLD: Vitamin D-resistant rickets

Common Exam Patterns:

  • Pedigree interpretation (determine inheritance pattern)
  • Risk calculations for offspring
  • Mechanism-based questions
  • Clinical correlation with molecular basis
  • Distinguishing between inheritance patterns

Key Formulas:

  • AR disorder risk (both parents carriers): 25% affected, 50% carriers, 25% normal
  • AD disorder risk (one affected parent): 50% affected, 50% normal
  • XLR carrier female: 50% sons affected, 50% daughters carriers

Good luck with your Genetic Disorders studies! 🧬📚

Title: GENETIC DISORDERS MCQ EXAMINATION
Content:
MBPA 3413 - General Pathology III

60 Multiple Choice Questions

Question 1: A couple has a child with an autosomal recessive disorder. Neither parent is affected. What is the probability that their next child will be affected?

A) 50%
B) 25%
C) 75%
D) 100%

Answer: B
Explanation: In autosomal recessive inheritance, two carrier parents have a 25% chance with each pregnancy of having an affected child (homozygous recessive), 50% chance of a carrier, and 25% chance of being unaffected and not a carrier.

Question 2: An estimated 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages have which underlying cause?

A) Maternal infection
B) Demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities
C) Autosomal dominant disorders
D) Environmental toxins exclusively

Answer: B
Explanation: Approximately 50% of early pregnancy miscarriages are associated with demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities, highlighting the importance of genomic integrity in fetal development.

Question 3: What percentage of human DNA codes for proteins?

A) Less than 2%
B) 50%
C) 25%
D) 98%

Answer: A
Explanation: Less than 2% of human DNA actually codes for proteins. More than half consists of repetitive nucleotide sequences whose functions are not fully understood.

Question 4: A patient has a genetic condition that shows different severity among affected family members despite having the same mutation. This phenomenon is called:

A) Reduced penetrance
B) Variable expressivity
C) Genetic heterogeneity
D) Pleiotropy

Answer: B
Explanation: Variable expressivity occurs when a trait is seen in all individuals with the mutation but is expressed differently in terms of severity or manifestation. Reduced penetrance refers to some individuals not showing the trait at all.

Question 5: Sickle cell anemia results from which type of mutation?

A) Frameshift mutation
B) Nonsense mutation
C) Point mutation (non-conservative missense)
D) Trinucleotide repeat mutation

Answer: C
Explanation: Sickle cell anemia results from a single nucleotide substitution (point mutation) that causes a non-conservative missense mutation, replacing glutamic acid with valine in the beta-globin chain.

Question 6: Which approach to understanding genetic disease starts with identifying a known affected protein, then isolating the normal gene?

A) Positional cloning
B) Functional cloning
C) Gene therapy
D) Genomic imprinting

Answer: B
Explanation: Functional cloning (classic approach) begins with a known affected protein from the clinical phenotype, then isolates and clones the normal gene before determining molecular changes.

Question 7: A mutation that changes an amino acid codon to a chain terminator is classified as:

A) Missense mutation
B) Silent mutation
C) Nonsense mutation
D) Conservative mutation

Answer: C
Explanation: Nonsense mutations convert an amino acid codon into a stop codon (chain terminator), resulting in premature termination of protein synthesis and usually a non-functional truncated protein.

Question 8: How many deleterious genes does the average person carry?

A) 0-1
B) 2-3
C) 5-8
D) 15-20

Answer: C
Explanation: It is estimated that every person carries 5 to 8 deleterious genes, most being recessive. About 80% are familial and the remainder are acquired de novo.

Question 9: In X-linked recessive disorders, an affected male will:

A) Transmit the disorder to all his sons
B) Transmit the disorder to all his daughters
C) Not transmit to sons; daughters will be carriers
D) Transmit equally to sons and daughters

Answer: C
Explanation: In X-linked recessive disorders, affected males pass their Y chromosome to sons (who are unaffected) and their X chromosome to daughters (who become carriers).

Question 10: Fragile X syndrome is caused by which type of mutation?

A) Point mutation
B) Frameshift mutation
C) Trinucleotide repeat mutation
D) Chromosomal translocation

Answer: C
Explanation: Fragile X syndrome results from dynamic amplification of a trinucleotide repeat sequence (typically CGG repeats), with the degree of amplification increasing during gametogenesis.

Question 11: What percentage of individuals under 25 years develop a serious disease with significant genetic component?

A) 1%
B) 5%
C) 10%
D) 25%

Answer: B
Explanation: Approximately 5% of individuals under 25 years develop a serious disease with a significant genetic component, demonstrating the considerable impact of genetic disorders in young populations.

Question 12: A single mutant gene leading to multiple, seemingly unrelated effects is an example of:

A) Genetic heterogeneity
B) Incomplete dominance
C) Pleiotropy
D) Codominance

Answer: C
Explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single mutant gene leads to many different end effects, affecting multiple organ systems or producing various manifestations from one genetic defect.

Question 13: Which category represents the largest group of Mendelian disorders?

A) Autosomal dominant
B) Autosomal recessive
C) X-linked dominant
D) Y-linked

Answer: B
Explanation: Autosomal recessive disorders constitute the largest category of Mendelian disorders and include almost all inborn errors of metabolism.

Question 14: Mutations in promoter and enhancer sequences primarily affect:

A) Translation of mRNA
B) DNA replication only
C) Binding of transcription factors and gene transcription
D) Post-translational modifications

Answer: C
Explanation: Mutations in regulatory sequences (promoters and enhancers) interfere with binding of transcription factors, leading to reduced or absent transcription of the gene, as seen in some hereditary hemolytic anemias.

Question 15: In 2020, how many deaths worldwide were attributed to cancer?

A) 6 million
B) 8 million
C) 10 million
D) 15 million

Answer: C
Explanation: In 2020, there were approximately 10 million cancer deaths globally (representing 1 in 6 deaths), up from 6 million in 2000, showing an increasing cancer burden.

Question 16: A deletion or insertion of two base pairs in a coding sequence would most likely result in:

A) Silent mutation
B) Conservative missense mutation
C) Frameshift mutation
D) No effect on protein

Answer: C
Explanation: Insertion or deletion of one or two base pairs (not divisible by 3) causes a frameshift mutation, altering the reading frame and typically producing a non-functional protein.

Question 17: When mutations at several different genetic loci produce the same clinical trait, this is called:

A) Pleiotropy
B) Genetic heterogeneity
C) Variable expressivity
D) Incomplete penetrance

Answer: B
Explanation: Genetic heterogeneity occurs when mutations at different genetic loci can produce the same phenotype or disease trait, explaining why the same disease can result from different genetic defects.

Question 18: Which inheritance pattern typically shows that the trait does not affect parents but may affect siblings?

A) Autosomal dominant
B) Autosomal recessive
C) X-linked dominant
D) Mitochondrial

Answer: B
Explanation: Autosomal recessive inheritance typically shows unaffected parents (both carriers) with affected siblings, as the trait requires two copies of the mutant allele to manifest.

Question 19: Complete penetrance is most commonly seen in:

A) Autosomal dominant disorders
B) Autosomal recessive disorders
C) Multifactorial disorders
D) X-linked dominant disorders

Answer: B
Explanation: Complete penetrance is common in autosomal recessive disorders, where expression of the defect tends to be more uniform than in autosomal dominant disorders which often show variable penetrance.

Question 20: The lifetime frequency of genetic disease is estimated to be:

A) 100 per 1000
B) 250 per 1000
C) 670 per 1000
D) 900 per 1000

Answer: C
Explanation: The lifetime frequency of genetic disease is thought to be approximately 670 per 1000, which is higher than widely appreciated, including cardiovascular diseases, immune disorders, and cancers with genetic components.

Question 21: Individuals share what percentage of their DNA sequence with other humans?

A) 90%
B) 95%
C) 99.9%
D) 100%

Answer: C
Explanation: Humans share 99.9% of their DNA sequence, with only 0.1% (about 3 million base pairs) accounting for genetic diversity among individuals in the human race.

Question 22: A frameshift mutation would NOT occur with an insertion or deletion of:

A) 1 base pair
B) 2 base pairs
C) 3 base pairs
D) 5 base pairs

Answer: C
Explanation: Insertions or deletions of 3 base pairs (or multiples of 3) do not cause frameshift mutations because they maintain the reading frame, though they result in abnormal proteins missing or gaining amino acids.

Question 23: In autosomal dominant disorders, de novo mutations are more commonly associated with:

A) Younger mothers
B) Older fathers
C) Consanguinity
D) Environmental toxins exclusively

Answer: B
Explanation: De novo mutations in autosomal dominant disorders are more frequently associated with relatively older fathers, as mutations accumulate in spermatogonial cells over time.

Question 24: Which statement about autosomal recessive disorders is INCORRECT?

A) They include almost all inborn errors of metabolism
B) Onset is frequently early in life
C) Parents are usually affected
D) 25% recurrence risk for each birth

Answer: C
Explanation: In autosomal recessive disorders, parents are typically NOT affected but are carriers. The trait manifests in children who inherit two mutant alleles.

Question 25: Positional cloning approach involves:

A) Starting with a known abnormal protein
B) Mapping disease phenotype to chromosome location first
C) Direct sequencing of all genes
D) Only studying protein function

Answer: B
Explanation: Positional cloning (candidate gene approach) starts by mapping the disease phenotype to a particular chromosome location, then cloning DNA pieces from that region to identify aberrant proteins.

Question 26: Conservative missense mutations differ from non-conservative ones in that they:

A) Always produce normal proteins
B) Substitute chemically similar amino acids
C) Create stop codons
D) Cause frameshift

Answer: B
Explanation: Conservative missense mutations substitute an amino acid with another that has similar chemical properties, potentially having less severe effects than non-conservative mutations that substitute chemically different amino acids.

Question 27: Vitamin D-resistant rickets represents which unusual inheritance pattern?

A) Autosomal recessive
B) Mitochondrial
C) X-linked dominant
D) Y-linked

Answer: C
Explanation: Vitamin D-resistant rickets is one of the few X-linked dominant conditions, making it an exception to the rule that almost all X-linked disorders are recessive.

Question 28: Gene therapy aims to treat genetic diseases by:

A) Editing all germline cells
B) Transfer of somatic cells transfected with normal genes
C) Removing all mutant DNA
D) Preventing all mutations

Answer: B
Explanation: Gene therapy involves treating genetic diseases by transferring somatic cells that have been transfected with normal genes, though questions remain about whether benefits outweigh risks.

Question 29: In Kenya (2018), cancer was which leading cause of death?

A) 1st
B) 2nd
C) 3rd
D) 5th

Answer: C
Explanation: In Kenya in 2018, cancer was the 3rd leading cause of death, with 47,887 new cases and 32,987 deaths reported, showing a significant increase from 2012 figures.

Question 30: Mutations affecting somatic cells result in:

A) Inherited diseases only
B) Conditions transmitted to progeny
C) Cancers and some congenital malformations
D) No phenotypic changes

Answer: C
Explanation: Somatic cell mutations are not transmitted to progeny but can result in cancers and some congenital malformations in the affected individual.

Question 31: The term "reduced penetrance" means:

A) All individuals with mutation show the trait
B) Some percentage show the trait, others are phenotypically normal despite having the mutation
C) The trait shows variable severity
D) Multiple genes are involved

Answer: B
Explanation: Reduced penetrance refers to the phenomenon where a certain percentage of individuals with a mutation are affected while others remain phenotypically normal despite carrying the mutation.

Question 32: Which biologically active agent can be produced by inserting requisite genes into bacteria?

A) Chromosomes
B) Erythropoietin
C) DNA polymerase exclusively
D) Ribosomes

Answer: B
Explanation: Human biologically active agents like erythropoietin, growth hormone, tissue plasminogen activator, and soluble TNF receptor can be produced by inserting genes into bacteria or cultured cells.

Question 33: Approximately how many genes do humans have?

A) 10,000
B) 20,000
C) 30,000
D) 50,000

Answer: C
Explanation: Human beings have approximately 30,000 genes, though less than 2% of total DNA codes for proteins, with much of the genome consisting of repetitive sequences.

Question 34: In autosomal dominant inheritance, both males and females:

A) Can be affected but only males can transmit
B) Can be affected and can transmit the disorder
C) Are affected equally often but females cannot transmit
D) Show the disorder only if homozygous

Answer: B
Explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders affect both males and females equally, and both sexes can transmit the disorder to their offspring, requiring only one copy of the mutant allele.

Question 35: Trinucleotide repeat mutations are described as "dynamic" because:

A) They change rapidly during mitosis
B) The degree of amplification increases during gametogenesis
C) They only occur in somatic cells
D) They repair themselves

Answer: B
Explanation: Trinucleotide repeat mutations are dynamic because the degree of amplification (expansion) of the repeat sequence increases during gametogenesis, often leading to more severe disease in successive generations (anticipation).

Question 36: Which category of genetic disorders involves visible structural changes in chromosomes?

A) Gene mutations
B) Genome mutations
C) Chromosome mutations
D) Point mutations

Answer: C
Explanation: Chromosome mutations involve rearrangement of genetic material resulting in visible structural changes in chromosomes, distinct from gene mutations or whole chromosome gains/losses.

Question 37: A mutation in an enhancer sequence would most likely affect:

A) mRNA splicing
B) Protein folding
C) Gene transcription levels
D) DNA replication fidelity

Answer: C
Explanation: Enhancer sequences are regulatory elements that increase transcription. Mutations in enhancers affect the level of gene transcription by interfering with transcription factor binding.

Question 38: Monosomies and trisomies are examples of:

A) Point mutations
B) Genome mutations
C) Frameshift mutations
D) Missense mutations

Answer: B
Explanation: Monosomies (loss of a chromosome) and trisomies (gain of a chromosome) are genome mutations involving the loss or gain of whole chromosomes.

Question 39: Which mechanism is NOT typically involved in autosomal dominant disorders?

A) Reduced production of gene product
B) Production of inactive protein
C) Requirement for two mutant alleles
D) Dominant negative effects

Answer: C
Explanation: Autosomal dominant disorders manifest with only one mutant allele (heterozygous state). Requiring two mutant alleles is characteristic of recessive disorders.

Question 40: The concept of delayed onset is particularly characteristic of:

A) Autosomal recessive disorders
B) Many autosomal dominant disorders
C) All X-linked disorders
D) Chromosomal abnormalities

Answer: B
Explanation: Many autosomal dominant conditions have delayed onset, manifesting in adulthood rather than early in life, which is an important feature distinguishing them from many recessive disorders.

Question 41: What percentage of deleterious genes carried by individuals are familial versus de novo?

A) 50% familial, 50% de novo
B) 80% familial, 20% de novo
C) 20% familial, 80% de novo
D) 100% familial

Answer: B
Explanation: Of the 5-8 deleterious genes carried by each person, approximately 80% are familial (inherited) and the remainder (20%) are acquired de novo.

Question 42: Molecular probes in disease diagnosis can be used for:

A) Only genetic diseases
B) Only infectious diseases
C) Both genetic and non-genetic diseases including infections
D) Only cancer diagnosis

Answer: C
Explanation: Molecular probes are used in diagnosis of both genetic diseases and non-genetic diseases, including infectious diseases, making them versatile diagnostic tools.

Question 43: In which type of disorder would consanguinity most likely increase disease prevalence?

A) Autosomal dominant
B) Autosomal recessive
C) X-linked dominant
D) Mitochondrial

Answer: B
Explanation: Consanguinity (marriage between related individuals) significantly increases the risk of autosomal recessive disorders because related individuals are more likely to carry the same recessive mutations.

Question 44: A silent mutation would most likely result from:

A) Nucleotide change that doesn't alter amino acid due to genetic code degeneracy
B) Nonsense mutation
C) Frameshift mutation
D) Large deletion

Answer: A
Explanation: Silent mutations are nucleotide substitutions that don't change the amino acid due to the degeneracy of the genetic code (multiple codons for same amino acid), having no effect on the protein.

Question 45: Almost all inborn errors of metabolism follow which inheritance pattern?

A) Autosomal dominant
B) Autosomal recessive
C) X-linked
D) Mitochondrial

Answer: B
Explanation: Almost all inborn errors of metabolism are autosomal recessive disorders, where enzyme deficiencies manifest only in the homozygous recessive state.

Question 46: Between 2000 and 2020, global new cancer cases increased by approximately:

A) 2 million
B) 5 million
C) 8 million
D) 12 million

Answer: C
Explanation: New cancer cases increased from 10 million in 2000 to 18.1 million in 2020, representing an increase of approximately 8 million cases, highlighting the growing cancer burden globally.

Question 47: Which biochemical/molecular basis is NOT listed as a mechanism for Mendelian disorders?

A) Enzyme defects
B) Defects in receptors
C) Prion protein misfolding
D) Defects in transport systems

Answer: C
Explanation: The listed mechanisms include enzyme defects, receptor defects, transport defects, structural protein alterations, hemostasis defects, and growth regulation defects. Prion diseases are not typical Mendelian disorders.

Question 48: Gene expression in Mendelian disorders may be:

A) Only dominant
B) Only recessive
C) Dominant, recessive, or co-dominant
D) Always co-dominant

Answer: C
Explanation: Gene expression in Mendelian disorders can be dominant (one mutant allele sufficient), recessive (two mutant alleles needed), or co-dominant (both alleles expressed).

Question 49: A patient has a disorder that shows genetic heterogeneity. This means:

A) One gene affects multiple traits
B) Multiple genes can cause the same disease
C) The disease skips generations
D) Only males are affected

Answer: B
Explanation: Genetic heterogeneity means that mutations at several different genetic loci can produce the same trait or disease phenotype, explaining why clinically similar diseases can have different genetic causes.

Question 50: The main difference between benign and malignant neoplasms is:

A) Size only
B) Growth rate only
C) Ability to invade and metastasize
D) Presence of blood supply

Answer: C
Explanation: The fundamental difference is that malignant neoplasms can invade adjacent tissues and metastasize to distant sites, while benign tumors remain localized despite potentially growing large.

Question 51: Melanoma and seminoma are described as "oddly named" neoplasms because:

A) They end in -oma but are malignant
B) They are always benign
C) They cannot be classified
D) They are viral in origin

Answer: A
Explanation: These neoplasms are oddly named because they end in -oma (typically denoting benign tumors) but are actually malignant neoplasms, breaking the standard nomenclature convention.

Question 52: A lipoma is a benign tumor of:

A) Epithelial origin
B) Glandular tissue
C) Mesenchymal origin (adipose tissue)
D) Neural tissue

Answer: C
Explanation: Lipoma is a benign tumor of mesenchymal origin, specifically from adipose (fat) tissue, following the nomenclature rule of adding -oma to the cell of origin.

Question 53: Malignant tumors of epithelial origin are generally called:

A) Sarcomas
B) Carcinomas
C) Lymphomas
D) Melanomas

Answer: B
Explanation: Malignant tumors of epithelial origin are called carcinomas (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma), while sarcomas arise from mesenchymal tissues.

Question 54: A cystadenoma is characterized by:

A) Solid glandular growth only
B) Large cystic spaces within glandular epithelial tumor
C) Mesenchymal origin
D) Always being malignant

Answer: B
Explanation: Cystadenomas are benign tumors of glandular epithelial origin that contain large cystic spaces, distinguishing them from solid adenomas.

Question 55: Defects in hemostasis as a basis for Mendelian disorders would most likely involve:

A) Structural proteins exclusively
B) Clotting factors and related proteins
C) Growth regulators only
D) Enzyme inhibitors exclusively

Answer: B
Explanation: Defects in hemostasis involve abnormalities in clotting factors and related proteins involved in blood coagulation, such as in hemophilia.

Question 56: Genetically determined adverse reactions to drugs represent:

A) Somatic mutations only
B) A biochemical/molecular basis of some Mendelian disorders
C) Environmental factors exclusively
D) Acquired immunity

Answer: B
Explanation: Genetically determined adverse drug reactions (pharmacogenetics) represent one of the biochemical/molecular bases of Mendelian disorders, where genetic variations affect drug metabolism or response.

Question 57: A papilloma is characterized by:

A) Cystic spaces
B) Adipose tissue
C) Finger-like or warty projections
D) Cartilaginous matrix

Answer: C
Explanation: Papillomas are benign epithelial neoplasms characterized by finger-like or warty projections, named for their distinctive architectural pattern.

Question 58: Alterations in structure, function, or quantity of non-enzyme proteins can cause:

A) Only malignancies
B) Only metabolic disorders
C) Various Mendelian disorders
D) No disease states

Answer: C
Explanation: Alterations in non-enzyme proteins (structural, transport, regulatory) represent an important biochemical/molecular basis for various Mendelian disorders beyond enzyme deficiencies.

Question 59: In Kenya, the increase in cancer cases from 2012 to 2018 represents approximately:

A) 5,000 new cases
B) 10,000 new cases
C) 11,000 new cases
D) 20,000 new cases

Answer: C
Explanation: Cancer cases in Kenya increased from 37,000 in 2012 to 47,887 in 2018, representing an increase of approximately 10,887 (nearly 11,000) new cases over 6 years.

Question 60: The suffix "-sarcoma" typically indicates a malignant tumor of:

A) Epithelial origin
B) Mesenchymal origin
C) Glandular origin
D) Neural origin only

Answer: B
Explanation: Sarcomas are malignant tumors of mesenchymal origin, including liposarcoma (fat), fibrosarcoma (fibrous tissue), chondrosarcoma (cartilage), and osteosarcoma (bone).

END OF EXAMINATION

Title: GENETIC DISORDERS MCQ EXAMINATION (PART 2)
Content:
MBPA 3413 - Complex Multigenic and Cytogenetic Disorders

60 Multiple Choice Questions

Question 1: A genetic variant with at least two alleles occurring in at least 1% of the population is termed:

A) Mutation
B) Polymorphism
C) Deletion
D) Translocation

Answer: B
Explanation: A polymorphism is defined as a genetic variant that has at least two alleles and occurs in at least 1% of the population, distinguishing it from rare mutations.

Question 2: In type 1 diabetes, approximately how many genes contribute most significantly to disease risk?

A) 2-3 genes
B) 6-7 genes
C) 15-20 genes
D) Over 50 genes

Answer: B
Explanation: While 20-30 genes are implicated in type 1 diabetes, only 6-7 are most important, with a few HLA alleles contributing more than 50% of the risk.

Question 3: Which environmental factor commonly unmasks the genetic trait in type 2 diabetes mellitus?

A) Cold exposure
B) Obesity and weight gain
C) High altitude
D) Vitamin deficiency

Answer: B
Explanation: Type 2 diabetes has features of a complex multigenic disorder where obesity and weight gain often unmask the diabetic genetic trait, demonstrating gene-environment interaction.

Question 4: Approximately what percentage of first-trimester spontaneous abortions have chromosomal abnormalities?

A) 10%
B) 25%
C) 50%
D) 75%

Answer: C
Explanation: Approximately 50% of first-trimester spontaneous abortions have demonstrable chromosomal abnormalities, highlighting the importance of chromosomal integrity for fetal development.

Question 5: The G-banding technique uses which stain to visualize chromosomes?

A) Hematoxylin
B) Wright stain
C) Giemsa stain
D) Gram stain

Answer: C
Explanation: The G-banding (Giemsa banding) technique is widely used to stain chromosomes, producing distinctive patterns of alternating light and dark bands that allow identification of each chromosome.

Question 6: A chromosome number of 69 (3n) would be classified as:

A) Euploid and polyploid
B) Aneuploid
C) Diploid
D) Monosomic

Answer: A
Explanation: 69 chromosomes (3n) is an exact multiple of the haploid number (n=23), making it euploid. Since it's a multiple other than 2n, it's also polyploid (specifically triploid).

Question 7: The chief cause of aneuploidy is:

A) Viral infection
B) Radiation exposure
C) Nondisjunction during meiosis
D) Balanced translocation

Answer: C
Explanation: Nondisjunction of homologous chromosomes during the first meiotic division or failure of sister chromatids to separate during the second meiotic division is the chief cause of aneuploidy.

Question 8: Monosomy involving an autosome is:

A) Compatible with life with minor defects
B) Incompatible with life
C) The most common chromosomal abnormality
D) Only seen in males

Answer: B
Explanation: Monosomy involving an autosome is incompatible with life, whereas trisomies of certain autosomes and monosomy of sex chromosomes can be compatible with life.

Question 9: Mosaicism is defined as:

A) Presence of extra chromosomes in all cells
B) Presence of two or more populations of cells with different chromosome complements
C) Complete loss of one chromosome
D) Balanced translocation

Answer: B
Explanation: Mosaicism is the presence of two or more populations of cells with different complements of chromosomes in the same individual, usually resulting from postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction.

Question 10: In cytogenetic notation, "p" denotes:

A) The long arm of a chromosome
B) The short arm of a chromosome
C) The centromere
D) A point mutation

Answer: B
Explanation: In cytogenetic shorthand, "p" (from French "petit") denotes the short arm of a chromosome, while "q" denotes the long arm.

Question 11: The notation 46,XX,t(2;5)(q31;p14) indicates:

A) Normal female karyotype
B) Trisomy 2
C) Reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 2 and 5
D) Deletion of chromosome 5

Answer: C
Explanation: This notation indicates a reciprocal translocation involving the long arm of chromosome 2 at region 3 band 1, and the short arm of chromosome 5 at region 1 band 4.

Question 12: Robertsonian translocation typically involves:

A) Two metacentric chromosomes
B) Two acrocentric chromosomes
C) Sex chromosomes only
D) Multiple chromosomes simultaneously

Answer: B
Explanation: Robertsonian (centric) fusion is a reciprocal translocation between two acrocentric chromosomes, involving the short arm of one and long arm of the other, forming one large and one very small chromosome.

Question 13: The most common isochromosome in live births involves:

A) Short arm of chromosome 21
B) Long arm of the X chromosome [i(Xq)]
C) Short arm of the Y chromosome
D) Long arm of chromosome 13

Answer: B
Explanation: The most common isochromosome in live births is i(Xq), involving the long arm of the X chromosome, resulting in monosomy for Xp genes and trisomy for Xq genes.

Question 14: An isochromosome results from:

A) Vertical division of the centromere
B) Horizontal division of the centromere
C) Complete chromosome deletion
D) Reciprocal translocation

Answer: B
Explanation: Isochromosomes result when the centromere divides horizontally (rather than vertically), leading to loss of one arm and duplication of the other, creating two identical arms.

Question 15: Which statement about chromosomal abnormalities is correct?

A) Loss of chromosomal material is better tolerated than gain
B) Gain of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than loss
C) Loss of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than gain
D) Loss and gain produce identical effects

Answer: C
Explanation: In general, loss of chromosomal material produces more severe defects than does gain of chromosomal material, which is why monosomies are typically more severe than trisomies.

Question 16: Sex chromosome imbalances compared to autosomal imbalances are:

A) Always lethal
B) Tolerated much better
C) More severe
D) Never occur

Answer: B
Explanation: Imbalances of sex chromosomes (excess or loss) are tolerated much better than similar imbalances of autosomes, often producing subtle abnormalities.

Question 17: Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) include all of the following EXCEPT:

A) Hair color
B) Height
C) Down syndrome
D) Intelligence

Answer: C
Explanation: QTLs are normal phenotypic characteristics governed by multigenic inheritance showing continuous variation, including hair color, eye color, height, and intelligence. Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder.

Question 18: The most common chromosomal disorder is:

A) Turner syndrome
B) Klinefelter syndrome
C) Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
D) Edwards syndrome

Answer: C
Explanation: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the most common chromosomal disorder, occurring with notable frequency compared to other chromosomal abnormalities.

Question 19: In about 95% of Down syndrome cases, the extra chromosome 21 is of:

A) Paternal origin
B) Maternal origin
C) Equal maternal and paternal origin
D) Unknown origin

Answer: B
Explanation: In approximately 95% of trisomy 21 cases, the extra chromosome is of maternal origin, resulting from meiotic nondisjunction in the ovum.

Question 20: Maternal age has the strongest correlation with which type of Down syndrome?

A) Translocation form
B) Mosaic form
C) Meiotic nondisjunction form
D) All forms equally

Answer: C
Explanation: Maternal age has a strong influence on Down syndrome due to meiotic nondisjunction (95% of cases), with incidence increasing dramatically with advancing maternal age.

Question 21: The translocation form of Down syndrome accounts for approximately what percentage of cases?

A) 1%
B) 4%
C) 10%
D) 25%

Answer: B
Explanation: About 4% of trisomy 21 patients have the extra chromosomal material as a translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to chromosome 22 or 14, often familial.

Question 22: Mosaic Down syndrome accounts for approximately what percentage of cases?

A) 1%
B) 4%
C) 10%
D) 25%

Answer: A
Explanation: Approximately 1% of trisomy 21 patients are mosaics with a mixture of 46- and 47-chromosome cells, resulting from mitotic nondisjunction during early embryogenesis.

Question 23: Which cardiac defect is most common in Down syndrome?

A) Coarctation of aorta
B) Tetralogy of Fallot
C) Endocardial cushion defects
D) Patent ductus arteriosus

Answer: C
Explanation: Approximately 40% of Down syndrome patients have congenital heart disease, most commonly endocardial cushion defects including atrial and ventricular septal defects.

Question 24: Children with trisomy 21 have what increased risk of developing acute leukemia?

A) 2- to 5-fold
B) 5- to 10-fold
C) 10- to 20-fold
D) No increased risk

Answer: C
Explanation: Children with trisomy 21 have a 10- to 20-fold increased risk of developing acute leukemia, including both acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemias.

Question 25: Most Down syndrome patients older than 40 develop neuropathologic changes characteristic of:

A) Parkinson disease
B) Alzheimer disease
C) Multiple sclerosis
D) Huntington disease

Answer: B
Explanation: Virtually all patients with trisomy 21 older than age 40 develop neuropathologic changes characteristic of Alzheimer disease.

Question 26: The current median age at death for persons with Down syndrome is:

A) 25 years
B) 35 years
C) 47 years
D) 60 years

Answer: C
Explanation: Improved medical care has increased longevity in Down syndrome from a median of 25 years in 1983 to currently 47 years.

Question 27: Most Down syndrome patients have an IQ in which range?

A) 10 to 25
B) 25 to 50
C) 50 to 70
D) 70 to 85

Answer: B
Explanation: Down syndrome is a leading cause of severe mental retardation; approximately 80% have an IQ of 25 to 50.

Question 28: Trisomy 18 is also known as:

A) Patau syndrome
B) Edwards syndrome
C) Turner syndrome
D) Down syndrome

Answer: B
Explanation: Trisomy 18 is also known as Edwards syndrome, occurring less commonly than trisomy 21 and associated with severe malformations and early death.

Question 29: Trisomy 13 is also known as:

A) Patau syndrome
B) Edwards syndrome
C) Turner syndrome
D) Klinefelter syndrome

Answer: A
Explanation: Trisomy 13 is also known as Patau syndrome, associated with increased maternal age, severe malformations, and death usually within the first year of life.

Question 30: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome was previously thought to represent which two separate disorders?

A) Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome
B) DiGeorge syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome
C) Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome
D) Patau syndrome and cri du chat syndrome

Answer: B
Explanation: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome encompasses what were previously believed to be two different disorders: DiGeorge syndrome and velocardiofacial syndrome.

Question 31: Which gene on chromosome 22 is suspected to be responsible for DiGeorge syndrome features?

A) BCR
B) ABL
C) TBX1
D) TP53

Answer: C
Explanation: The transcription factor gene TBX1 in the 22q11.2 region is suspected to be responsible for DiGeorge syndrome features, as its loss correlates with syndrome occurrence.

Question 32: Patients with 22q11.2 deletion are at particularly high risk for:

A) Diabetes mellitus
B) Psychoses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
C) Hepatic failure
D) Renal disease

Answer: B
Explanation: In addition to malformations, patients with 22q11.2 deletion are at particularly high risk for developing psychoses such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

Question 33: The diagnosis of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is established by:

A) Standard karyotype
B) Blood glucose testing
C) Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)
D) Serum electrophoresis

Answer: C
Explanation: While diagnosis may be suspected clinically, it can only be established by detection of the deletion using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

Question 34: Clinical features of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome include all EXCEPT:

A) Congenital heart disease affecting outflow tracts
B) Thymic hypoplasia with impaired T cell immunity
C) Parathyroid hypoplasia with hypocalcemia
D) Hepatomegaly with cirrhosis

Answer: D
Explanation: Features include cardiac defects, palate abnormalities, facial dysmorphism, developmental delay, thymic hypoplasia, and parathyroid hypoplasia. Hepatic involvement is not characteristic.

Question 35: When T cell immunodeficiency and hypocalcemia dominate in 22q11.2 deletion, the patient is said to have:

A) Velocardiofacial syndrome
B) DiGeorge syndrome
C) Down syndrome
D) Turner syndrome

Answer: B
Explanation: When T cell immunodeficiency and hypocalcemia are dominant features, patients are said to have DiGeorge syndrome, while velocardiofacial syndrome has pronounced dysmorphology and cardiac defects.

Question 36: According to the common disease-common variant hypothesis, complex disorders occur when:

A) A single gene is mutated
B) Many polymorphisms with modest effects are co-inherited
C) Chromosomes are duplicated
D) Only environmental factors interact

Answer: B
Explanation: Complex multigenic disorders occur when many polymorphisms, each with modest effect and low penetrance, are co-inherited, according to the common disease-common variant hypothesis.

Question 37: A ring chromosome forms when:

A) Centromere divides horizontally
B) Two chromosomes fuse
C) Segments are lost from each end and arms unite
D) Material is transferred to another chromosome

Answer: C
Explanation: A ring chromosome is a variant of deletion where, after loss of segments from each end of the chromosome, the remaining arms unite to form a ring structure.

Question 38: Deletion of which chromosome's short arm causes cri du chat syndrome?

A) Chromosome 4
B) Chromosome 5
C) Chromosome 13
D) Chromosome 21

Answer: B
Explanation: Cri du chat syndrome results from partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-), named for the characteristic cat-like cry of affected infants.

Question 39: An inversion occurs when:

A) A chromosome segment is lost
B) Two interstitial breaks occur and segment reunites after turnaround
C) Centromere divides abnormally
D) Material transfers to another chromosome

Answer: B
Explanation: Inversions occur when there are two interstitial breaks in a chromosome and the segment between them reunites after rotating 180 degrees (complete turnaround).

Question 40: A balanced reciprocal translocation involves:

A) Loss of genetic material
B) Gain of genetic material
C) Exchange with no net gain or loss of genetic material
D) Duplication of one chromosome

Answer: C
Explanation: Balanced reciprocal translocations involve exchange of chromosomal material between two chromosomes with no net gain or loss of genetic material, potentially causing problems during meiosis.

Question 41: Which best describes complex multigenic disorders?

A) Caused by single gene mutations only
B) Caused by interactions between gene variants and environmental factors
C) Always follow Mendelian inheritance
D) Never show familial clustering

Answer: B
Explanation: Complex multigenic (or multifactorial/polygenic) disorders are caused by interactions between variant forms of genes and environmental factors.

Question 42: Anaphase lag can lead to aneuploidy through:

A) Duplication of all chromosomes
B) Failure of pairing followed by random assortment
C) Horizontal centromere division
D) Reciprocal translocation

Answer: B
Explanation: Failure of pairing of homologous chromosomes followed by random assortment (anaphase lag) can lead to aneuploidy, in addition to nondisjunction.

Question 43: Mosaicism affecting which chromosomes is most common?

A) Autosomes
B) Sex chromosomes
C) Equally common in both
D) Never occurs

Answer: B
Explanation: Mosaicism affecting sex chromosomes is common, whereas autosomal mosaicism is relatively uncommon.

Question 44: In most chromosomal disorders, the parents are:

A) Always affected
B) Usually carriers
C) Normal with de novo changes in offspring
D) Both homozygous for mutations

Answer: C
Explanation: In most cases, chromosomal disorders result from de novo changes (parents are normal and risk of recurrence in siblings is low), with translocation Down syndrome being an important exception.

Question 45: Fertilization of a gamete with an extra chromosome (n+1) by a normal gamete produces:

A) Monosomic zygote (2n-1)
B) Trisomic zygote (2n+1)
C) Normal diploid zygote
D) Polyploid zygote

Answer: B
Explanation: Fertilization of a gamete containing an extra chromosome (n+1) by a normal gamete (n) results in a trisomic zygote with 2n+1 chromosomes.

Question 46: Polyploidy (3n, 4n) generally results in:

A) Normal development
B) Minor birth defects
C) Spontaneous abortion
D) Enhanced viability

Answer: C
Explanation: Polyploidy, where chromosome numbers are 3n or 4n (exact multiples of the haploid number other than 2n), generally results in spontaneous abortion.

Question 47: Which THREE autosomal trisomies were among the first chromosomal abnormalities identified?

A) 13, 18, and 21
B) 8, 13, and 18
C) 15, 18, and 21
D) 13, 15, and 21

Answer: A
Explanation: Trisomies 21, 18, and 13 were among the first chromosomal abnormalities identified, along with cri du chat syndrome (5p deletion).

Question 48: The incidence of Down syndrome in women younger than 20 years is approximately:

A) 1 in 25 live births
B) 1 in 100 live births
C) 1 in 500 live births
D) 1 in 1550 live births

Answer: D
Explanation: Down syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 1550 live births in women younger than 20 years, increasing dramatically to 1 in 25 in women older than 45 years.

Question 49: The immune dysfunction in Down syndrome primarily affects:

A) B cell function exclusively
B) Mainly T cell function
C) Complement system only
D) Natural killer cells only

Answer: B
Explanation: Patients with Down syndrome demonstrate abnormal immune responses with abnormalities affecting mainly T cell functions, predisposing to infections and thyroid autoimmunity.

Question 50: In the translocation form of Down syndrome, the translocated chromosome is most commonly inherited from:

A) De novo mutation only
B) A parent who is a carrier of a robertsonian translocation
C) Maternal grandmother
D) Never inherited, always sporadic

Answer: B
Explanation: The translocation form is frequently (but not always) familial, with the translocated chromosome inherited from a parent who is typically a carrier of a robertsonian translocation.

Question 51: Variable expressivity in complex traits can be confused with:

A) Penetrance of single genes
B) Chromosomal abnormalities
C) Environmental factors only
D) None of the above

Answer: A
Explanation: Variable expressivity and reduced penetrance of single mutant genes can account for severity variation, making it sometimes difficult to distinguish mendelian from multifactorial disorders.

Question 52: Assigning a disease to complex multigenic inheritance depends first on:

A) Molecular testing
B) Familial clustering and exclusion of mendelian/chromosomal transmission
C) Environmental factors only
D) Age of onset

Answer: B
Explanation: Attribution to complex multigenic inheritance depends first on familial clustering and the exclusion of mendelian and chromosomal modes of transmission.

Question 53: Approximately what percentage of newborns have some form of chromosomal abnormality?

A) 1 in 50
B) 1 in 100
C) 1 in 200
D) 1 in 500

Answer: C
Explanation: It is estimated that 1 in 200 newborn infants has some form of chromosomal abnormality, though many more embryos with abnormalities result in spontaneous abortion.

Question 54: In HLA-associated diseases, a few HLA alleles can contribute what percentage of the risk in type 1 diabetes?

A) Less than 10%
B) About 25%
C) More than 50%
D) 100%

Answer: C
Explanation: In type 1 diabetes, a few HLA alleles contribute more than 50% of the genetic risk, demonstrating that different polymorphisms vary significantly in their contributions.

Question 55: Some polymorphisms in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases are:

A) Always disease-specific
B) Common to multiple diseases of the same type
C) Never shared between diseases
D) Only found in single diseases

Answer: B
Explanation: Some polymorphisms are common to multiple diseases of the same type (e.g., various immune-mediated inflammatory diseases), while others are disease-specific.

Question 56: Two interstitial breaks with reunion of proximal and distal segments results in:

A) Translocation
B) Inversion
C) Loss of intermediate segment (deletion)
D) Duplication

Answer: C
Explanation: Two interstitial breaks with reunion of proximal and distal segments result in loss of the intermediate segment (deletion), with the isolated fragment lacking a centromere typically being lost.

Question 57: Sex chromosomal disorders often produce abnormalities that are:

A) Immediately fatal
B) Always severe
C) Subtle and sometimes not detected at birth
D) Never clinically significant

Answer: C
Explanation: Sex chromosomal disorders often produce subtle abnormalities that may not be detected at birth, with infertility being a common manifestation that cannot be diagnosed until adolescence.

Question 58: Which statement about Down syndrome mosaics is correct?

A) They always have severe phenotype
B) Clinical manifestations are variable and often milder
C) They have worse outcomes than non-mosaics
D) They cannot have normal intelligence

Answer: B
Explanation: Mosaic Down syndrome patients (1% of cases) have variable and milder clinical manifestations depending on the proportion of abnormal cells; some mosaics have normal or near-normal intelligence.

Question 59: Cardiac problems in Down syndrome are responsible for:

A) Most psychiatric symptoms
B) Majority of deaths in infancy and early childhood
C) Intellectual disability
D) Alzheimer changes

Answer: B
Explanation: Cardiac problems, particularly endocardial cushion defects, are responsible for the majority of deaths in infancy and early childhood in Down syndrome patients.

Question 60: In a Robertsonian translocation, the extremely small chromosome that forms is usually:

A) The most important for survival
B) Retained in all cells
C) Lost
D) Duplicated

Answer: C
Explanation: In Robertsonian translocation, transfer of segments between acrocentric chromosomes leads to formation of one abnormally large chromosome and one extremely small one, with the latter usually being lost.

END OF EXAMINATION

Title: MBPL3621 Introduction to Pharmacology Quiz 1
Content:
Sep/Dec 2022/23

Question 1

Which process involves the transfer of a drug from its site of administration to the blood stream?

Choices:

  • A. Absorption
  • B. Metabolism
  • C. Excretion
  • D. Distribution

Answer: A. Absorption

Explanation: Absorption is the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream. This process is essential for the drug to reach systemic circulation and eventually its site of action.

Question 2

Receptor agonists result in a drug response.

Choices:

  • A. True
  • B. False

Answer: A. True

Explanation: Receptor agonists bind to receptors and activate them, producing a biological response. This is the mechanism by which many drugs exert their therapeutic effects.

Question 3

Glomerular filtration of a drug is affected by its:

Choices:

  • A. Rate of tubular secretion
  • B. Plasma protein binding
  • C. Lipid solubility
  • D. Degree of ionization

Answer: B. Plasma protein binding

Explanation: Only free (unbound) drug molecules can be filtered through the glomerulus. Drugs bound to plasma proteins are too large to pass through the glomerular membrane, so plasma protein binding directly affects glomerular filtration.

Question 4

For the calculation of the volume of distribution (Vd) one must take into account:

Choices:

  • A. Therapeutic window of the drug
  • B. Concentration of a substance in plasma
  • C. The dose of the drug
  • D. Concentration of substance in urine

Answer: B. Concentration of a substance in plasma

Explanation: Volume of distribution (Vd) is calculated using the formula: Vd = Dose / Plasma concentration. It represents the theoretical volume needed to contain the total amount of drug at the same concentration as in plasma.

Question 5

This illustration below is concerned with which factor that influences the response to drug therapy.

Choices:

  • A. Patient compliance
  • B. Rate of metabolism and excretion
  • C. Drug-receptor interaction
  • D. Placebo effects

Answer: B. Rate of metabolism and excretion

Explanation: The illustration focuses on pharmacokinetics (how the body processes the drug), not pharmacodynamics (drug effects). Metabolism and excretion are pharmacokinetic processes that determine drug concentration over time.

Question 6

Increasing the dose of the drug will increase the strength of the bond the drug has with its receptor. As a result, the response will increase.

Choices:

  • A. False
  • B. True

Answer: A. False

Explanation: Increasing the dose does not change the strength of drug-receptor binding (affinity). Instead, it increases the number of receptors occupied, which may increase the response up to a maximum effect (efficacy).

Question 7

The strength of the drug is related to the dose of the drug.

Choices:

  • A. True
  • B. False

Answer: A. True

Explanation: Strength refers to the amount of drug in a dosage form (e.g., 500 mg tablet). Higher doses contain more drug and therefore have greater strength, though this is different from potency, which is a comparative measure.

Question 8

What does "pharmacokinetics" include?

Choices:

  • A. Influence of drugs on metabolism processes
  • B. Drug biotransformation in the organism
  • C. Complications of drug therapy
  • D. Influence of drugs on genes

Answer: B. Drug biotransformation in the organism

Explanation: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to the drug, including absorption, distribution, metabolism (biotransformation), and excretion (ADME).

Question 9

Drugs which undergo high degree of first-pass metabolism in liver:

Choices:

  • A. Are contraindicated in liver disease
  • B. Go through elimination
  • C. Have low oral bioavailability
  • D. Are excreted primarily in bile

Answer: C. Have low oral bioavailability

Explanation: First-pass metabolism occurs when orally administered drugs are metabolized in the liver before reaching systemic circulation, reducing the amount of active drug available and thus decreasing oral bioavailability.

Question 10

Bioavailability of drug refers to:

Choices:

  • A. All the choices
  • B. Ratio of drug excreted unchanged in urine to that excreted as metabolites
  • C. None of the choices
  • D. Ratio of orally administered drug to that excreted in the faeces
  • E. Percentage of administered dose that reaches systemic circulation in the changed form
  • F. Ratio of oral dose to parenteral dose

Answer: C. None of the choices

Explanation: Bioavailability is the percentage of administered dose that reaches systemic circulation in the UNCHANGED (active) form, not "changed form" as stated in option E. None of the provided options correctly defines bioavailability.

Question 11

Receptor antagonists result in a drug response.

Choices:

  • A. False
  • B. True

Answer: A. False

Explanation: Receptor antagonists bind to receptors but do not activate them. They block the receptor and prevent agonists from binding, thereby inhibiting a response rather than producing one.

Question 12

Which of the following are sources for making drugs?

Choices:

  • A. Animals
  • B. Plants
  • C. None of the choices
  • D. Synthetic
  • E. All the choices

Answer: E. All the choices

Explanation: Drugs can be derived from multiple sources including animals (e.g., insulin), plants (e.g., morphine), and synthetic/chemical synthesis (e.g., aspirin). Modern pharmaceuticals use all these sources.

Question 13
