c) Discuss the management options for this condition, including both acute treatment and definitive therapy. (6 marks)

Short Answer Questions

Question 4.2

a) What is the formula for corrected calcium? (1 mark)

b) List three causes of hypocalcemia. (3 marks)

c) Name two ECG changes seen in hypocalcemia. (1 mark)

Question 4.3

A patient with malignancy has a serum calcium of 3.4 mmol/L.

a) Name two malignancy-related mechanisms of hypercalcemia. (2 marks)

b) List three immediate management steps for severe hypercalcemia. (3 marks)

SECTION 5: RENAL FUNCTION

Long Essay Question

Question 5.1

A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with fatigue and nausea. His GP noted elevated creatinine on routine blood work.

Investigations:

  • Serum Creatinine: 450 μmol/L
  • Serum Urea: 28 mmol/L
  • eGFR: 12 mL/min/1.73m²
  • Serum Potassium: 6.1 mmol/L
  • Serum Bicarbonate: 16 mmol/L
  • Serum Calcium: 1.95 mmol/L
  • Serum Phosphate: 2.1 mmol/L
  • Hemoglobin: 89 g/L

Urinalysis: Protein 3+, Blood 2+

a) What stage of chronic kidney disease does this patient have? Justify your answer. (3 marks)

b) Explain the pathophysiology of FOUR biochemical abnormalities observed in this patient. (8 marks)

c) Discuss the indications for renal replacement therapy in chronic kidney disease. (4 marks)

Short Answer Questions

Question 5.2

a) Define glomerular filtration rate (GFR). (1 mark)

b) Name two equations used to estimate GFR. (2 marks)

c) List two limitations of using serum creatinine alone to assess renal function. (2 marks)

Question 5.3

Distinguish between pre-renal, intrinsic renal, and post-renal causes of acute kidney injury by completing the table for:
a) Urine sodium (3 marks)
b) Fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) (3 marks)

SECTION 6: LIVER FUNCTION

Long Essay Question

Question 6.1

A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol excess presents with jaundice, ascites, and confusion. He has spider nevi and palmar erythema on examination.

Laboratory results:

  • Total Bilirubin: 185 μmol/L
  • Conjugated Bilirubin: 140 μmol/L
  • ALT: 85 U/L
  • AST: 195 U/L
  • Alkaline Phosphatase: 145 U/L
  • Albumin: 26 g/L
  • INR: 2.8
  • Ammonia: 150 μmol/L (elevated)

a) Classify the pattern of liver injury based on the enzyme results. (3 marks)

b) Explain the pathophysiology of hepatic encephalopathy and the role of ammonia. (5 marks)

c) Discuss the biochemical basis for the following features in chronic liver disease:

  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Prolonged INR
  • Hyperbilirubinemia (7 marks)

Short Answer Questions

Question 6.2

a) What is the AST:ALT ratio typically seen in alcoholic liver disease? (1 mark)

b) List three causes of an isolated elevated alkaline phosphatase. (3 marks)

c) Name one test to differentiate bone from liver origin of raised ALP. (1 mark)

Question 6.3

a) Describe the difference between conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. (2 marks)

SECTION 7: DIABETES & GLUCOSE METABOLISM

Long Essay Question

Question 7.1

A 52-year-old obese man undergoes routine health screening. He has a family history of type 2 diabetes.

Results:

  • Fasting Plasma Glucose: 6.8 mmol/L
  • HbA1c: 44 mmol/mol (6.2%)
  • Total Cholesterol: 6.2 mmol/L
  • HDL Cholesterol: 0.9 mmol/L

a) Based on WHO/ADA criteria, how would you classify this patient's glucose status? (3 marks)

b) Explain the concept of metabolic syndrome and assess whether this patient meets the criteria. (5 marks)

c) Discuss the advantages and limitations of using HbA1c versus fasting glucose for diabetes diagnosis and monitoring. (7 marks)

Question 7.2

A patient presents with plasma glucose of 2.2 mmol/L, elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.

Long Essay Question

Question 8.1

A 35-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, and tremor. On examination, she has a diffuse goiter, lid lag, and a fine tremor.

Thyroid function tests:

  • TSH: <0.01 mIU/L (low)
  • Free T4: 42 pmol/L (elevated)

A patient on amiodarone has TSH 8.5 mIU/L, Free T4 18 pmol/L (normal).

A 58-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction 2 years ago attends for cardiovascular risk assessment.

  • Total Cholesterol: 7.8 mmol/L

Title: MBMM3311 – MEDICAL BACTERIOLOGY
Content:
DEPARTMENT OF MEDICAL MICROBIOLOGY

MBMM3311 – MEDICAL BACTERIOLOGY
BACHELOR OF MEDICINE AND BACHELOR OF SURGERY (MBChB)

YR:2021

INSTRUCTIONS: Answer all questions in Section A and Section B. Answer only ONE question in Section C.

SECTION A – MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (40 MARKS)

1. The heat-labile toxin of Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) acts through which mechanism?

A. Attachment and effacement
B. Activation of adenylyl cyclase
C. Aggregative adherence
D. Ribosomal dysfunction

Answer: B

Explanation: The heat-labile toxin (LT) of ETEC functions similarly to cholera toxin by activating adenylyl cyclase, which increases intracellular cAMP levels, leading to secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen and causing watery diarrhea.

2. Which of the following statements regarding Pseudomonas aeruginosa is correct?

A. P. aeruginosa is typically susceptible to penicillin G
B. P. aeruginosa grows readily in anaerobic blood cultures
C. P. aeruginosa penetrates intact skin using the enzyme "invasin"
D. P. aeruginosa seldom causes pneumonia
E. P. aeruginosa possesses fimbriae that promote attachment to epithelial cells

Answer: E

Explanation: P. aeruginosa has fimbriae (pili) that facilitate adherence to epithelial cells, which is crucial for colonization and infection. The organism is resistant to penicillin G, requires oxygen (obligate aerobe), does not penetrate intact skin, and is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia.

3. Long-term carriage and chronic shedding are most likely after gastrointestinal infection with:

A. Escherichia coli O157:H7
B. Shigella dysenteriae
C. Vibrio cholerae
D. Campylobacter jejuni
E. Salmonella typhi

Answer: E

Explanation: Salmonella typhi can establish chronic carriage in the gallbladder, with persistent shedding in feces for months to years after acute infection. This is particularly important in typhoid fever transmission. The other organisms listed rarely cause chronic carriage.

4. A patient presents with acute non-bloody diarrhea for 12 hours. He lives in Thika and has not traveled recently. Which organism is least likely to cause his illness?

A. Salmonella typhimurium
B. Campylobacter jejuni
C. Shigella sonnei
D. Vibrio cholerae

Answer: D

Explanation: Vibrio cholerae is endemic to specific regions with poor sanitation and contaminated water sources. In Kenya, cholera outbreaks occur sporadically but are not common causes of sporadic acute diarrhea in non-endemic areas like Thika without recent travel history.

5. A 19-year-old man has urethral discharge. Culture shows Neisseria gonorrhoeae that is β-lactamase positive and highly resistant to tetracycline. Which statement is correct?

A. Both β-lactamase and tetracycline resistance genes are plasmid-mediated
B. β-lactamase is chromosomal, tetracycline resistance is plasmid-mediated
C. β-lactamase is plasmid-mediated, tetracycline resistance is chromosomal
D. Both β-lactamase and tetracycline resistance genes are chromosomal

Answer: C

Explanation: In N. gonorrhoeae, β-lactamase production is typically encoded by plasmid-mediated genes (TEM-1 type), while high-level tetracycline resistance is usually due to chromosomal mutations in ribosomal protection proteins or efflux pumps.

6. Which Neisseria gonorrhoeae structure mediates attachment to host epithelial cells?

A. Lipooligosaccharide
B. Fimbriae
C. IgA1 protease
D. Outer membrane porin proteins
E. Iron-binding proteins

Answer: B

Explanation: Fimbriae (pili) are the primary adhesion structures of N. gonorrhoeae that mediate initial attachment to mucosal epithelial cells. This is the critical first step in colonization and infection.

7. A 6-year-old boy develops fever, headache, and neck stiffness. CSF culture grows Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B. What should be recommended for household contacts?

A. No prophylaxis needed
B. Pilin vaccine
C. Serogroup B polysaccharide capsule vaccine
D. Rifampin prophylaxis
E. Sulfonamide prophylaxis

Answer: D

Explanation: Close contacts of meningococcal meningitis cases should receive chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent secondary cases. Serogroup B polysaccharide vaccine is poorly immunogenic, and sulfonamide resistance is common.

8. An 18-year-old woman with fever and pelvic pain is diagnosed with gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease. A common long-term complication is:

A. Cervical cancer
B. Urethral stricture
C. Uterine fibroids
D. Infertility
E. Vaginal–rectal fistula

Answer: D

Explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can lead to scarring and adhesions of the fallopian tubes, resulting in tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. This is one of the most serious long-term complications of untreated or inadequately treated gonococcal infection.

9. Which statement best describes the pathogenesis of Clostridium botulinum?

A. Toxin inhibits acetylcholine release at cholinergic synapses
B. Exotoxin is a lecithinase causing tissue necrosis
C. Capsule inhibits phagocytosis and aids CNS invasion
D. Toxin suppresses release of inhibitory neurotransmitters
E. Produces leukotoxin leading to abscess formation

Answer: A

Explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions by cleaving SNARE proteins required for vesicle fusion. This prevents muscle contraction, leading to flaccid paralysis characteristic of botulism.

10. A 47-year-old woman with cavitary lung disease grows a photochromogenic acid-fast bacillus (produces orange pigment on light exposure). The organism is:

A. Mycobacterium tuberculosis
B. Mycobacterium kansasii
C. Mycobacterium gordonae
D. Mycobacterium avium complex
E. Mycobacterium fortuitum

Answer: B

Explanation: Mycobacterium kansasii is a photochromogenic (Runyon Group I) nontuberculous mycobacterium that produces yellow-orange pigment when exposed to light. It can cause pulmonary disease resembling tuberculosis, particularly in patients with underlying lung disease.

11. A 31-year-old Asian woman has fever, weight loss, and granulomas with acid-fast bacilli in liver and bone marrow. Chest X-ray is normal. Most likely organism:

A. Mycobacterium leprae
B. Mycobacterium fortuitum
C. Mycobacterium ulcerans
D. Mycobacterium gordonae
E. Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Answer: E

Explanation: This presentation is consistent with disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis, which can occur without prominent pulmonary findings on chest X-ray. M. tuberculosis commonly causes extrapulmonary disease involving liver, bone marrow, and other organs, especially in immunocompromised patients.

12. A concern for the patient above is infection with a strain that is:

A. Susceptible only to isoniazid
B. Resistant to streptomycin
C. Resistant to clarithromycin
D. Resistant to isoniazid and rifampin
E. Enterotoxin-producing E. coli

Answer: D

Explanation: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), defined as resistance to both isoniazid and rifampin, is a major concern as these are the two most effective first-line anti-TB drugs. MDR-TB requires prolonged treatment with second-line drugs and has worse outcomes.

13. A 10-week pregnant woman previously treated for syphilis has RPR non-reactive and TP-PA reactive. The most correct interpretation is:

A. Previous treatment was effective
B. Baby is at high risk for congenital syphilis
C. Mother requires re-treatment
D. Mother needs lumbar puncture for neurosyphilis evaluation
E. None of the above

Answer: A

Explanation: A non-reactive RPR (non-treponemal test) with a reactive TP-PA (treponemal test) indicates past treated syphilis. The treponemal test remains positive for life, while the non-treponemal test becomes negative after successful treatment. The baby is at low risk if treatment was adequate.

14. A 20-year-old woman has a 2-cm painless ulcer with raised border on the labia majora. The most likely pathogen is:

A. Haemophilus ducreyi
B. Papillomavirus
C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
D. Chlamydia trachomatis
E. All of the above

Answer: A (Note: The classic description fits syphilitic chancre caused by Treponema pallidum, but this was not listed as an option)

Explanation: The description of a painless ulcer with raised border is classic for a primary syphilitic chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. However, since this option is not provided, among the given choices, none perfectly fit. H. ducreyi causes painful ulcers (chancroid), not painless ones. This question has an issue with the answer choices.

15. A 19-year-old man develops community-acquired pneumonia. Which organism is a common cause?

A. Legionella pneumophila
B. Chlamydia pneumoniae
C. Streptococcus pneumoniae
D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae
E. All of the above

Answer: E

Explanation: All listed organisms are recognized causes of community-acquired pneumonia in young adults. S. pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause overall, while M. pneumoniae and C. pneumoniae are common causes of atypical pneumonia. L. pneumophila can occur in certain exposures.

16. A 15-year-old girl has profuse "rice-water" diarrhea without fever. Most likely cause:

A. Clostridium difficile enterotoxin
B. Vibrio cholerae toxin (A/B subunits)
C. Shigella dysenteriae type 1 (Shiga toxin)
D. ETEC producing heat-labile and heat-stable toxins
E. Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin F

Answer: B

Explanation: The characteristic "rice-water" appearance of profuse watery diarrhea without fever is pathognomonic for cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae. The cholera toxin (with A/B subunits) activates adenylyl cyclase, causing massive fluid secretion.

17. Mechanism of action of diphtheria toxin:

A. Forms pores in red cells → hemolysis
B. Degrades lecithin in membranes
C. Causes release of tumor necrosis factor
D. Inhibits elongation factor-2
E. Increases adenylate cyclase activity

Answer: D

Explanation: Diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating and inactivating elongation factor-2 (EF-2), which is essential for ribosomal translocation during translation. This leads to cell death, particularly affecting heart and nerve tissues.

18. A man develops toxic shock 8 hours after nasal tampon placement. The illness is caused by:

A. Lipopolysaccharide
B. Peptidoglycan
C. A superantigen toxin
D. A toxin with A/B subunits
E. Lecithinase (alpha toxin)

Answer: C

Explanation: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by superantigen toxins (such as TSST-1 and enterotoxins) that bypass normal antigen processing and cause massive, non-specific T-cell activation, leading to cytokine storm and systemic shock.

19. The most likely organism responsible for the disease in Question 18 is:

A. Escherichia coli
B. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
C. Clostridium perfringens
D. Neisseria meningitidis
E. Staphylococcus aureus

Answer: E

Explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the primary cause of toxic shock syndrome, particularly associated with tampon use (menstrual TSS) or wound infections (non-menstrual TSS). The organism produces superantigen toxins like TSST-1.

20. All of the following are characteristic of Bacillus anthracis EXCEPT:

A. Motility
B. Medusa-head colonies
C. Poly-D-glutamic acid capsule
D. Susceptibility to penicillin in vitro
E. Non-hemolytic on sheep blood agar

Answer: A

Explanation: Bacillus anthracis is non-motile, which distinguishes it from other Bacillus species. It characteristically produces large colonies with irregular edges (medusa-head appearance), has a poly-D-glutamic acid capsule, is susceptible to penicillin, and is non-hemolytic.

SECTION B – SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (15 MARKS)

1. Outline the virulence factors of Streptococcus pyogenes. (5 marks)

Answer:

Streptococcus pyogenes possesses multiple virulence factors:

Surface components:

  • M protein: Inhibits phagocytosis by preventing complement C3b deposition and binding factor H; also mediates adherence to epithelial cells
  • Lipoteichoic acid and F protein: Facilitate adherence to host cells
  • Capsule (hyaluronic acid): Antiphagocytic, mimics host tissue

Enzymes:

  • Streptokinase: Dissolves fibrin clots, facilitating spread
  • Streptodornases (DNases): Liquefy pus by degrading DNA
  • Hyaluronidase: Breaks down connective tissue, promoting spread
  • C5a peptidase: Degrades complement component C5a, impairing neutrophil chemotaxis

Toxins:

  • Streptolysins O and S: Lyse red blood cells, neutrophils, and other cells
  • Pyrogenic (erythrogenic) exotoxins: Act as superantigens causing scarlet fever and toxic shock
  • Streptolysin O is oxygen-labile and antigenic; Streptolysin S is oxygen-stable and non-antigenic

These factors collectively enable the organism to adhere, evade immune responses, spread through tissues, and cause local and systemic disease.

2. Differentiate a syphilitic chancre from a Haemophilus ducreyi chancroid. (5 marks)

Answer:

Syphilitic chancre (Treponema pallidum):

  • Painless ulcer
  • Single lesion (usually)
  • Clean, indurated base with raised, firm borders
  • Non-purulent discharge
  • Regional lymphadenopathy: bilateral, firm, non-tender, non-suppurative
  • Appears 10-90 days (average 21 days) after exposure
  • Heals spontaneously in 3-6 weeks
  • Highly infectious

Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi):

  • Painful ulcer
  • Multiple lesions common
  • Soft, non-indurated base with ragged, undermined edges
  • Purulent exudate
  • Regional lymphadenopathy: unilateral, tender, may suppurate and form buboes
  • Appears 4-7 days after exposure
  • Does not heal spontaneously without treatment
  • Infectious but less so than chancre

Key differentiating features: Pain (chancroid is painful, chancre is not), ulcer consistency (soft vs. hard/indurated), and lymph node characteristics (suppurative vs. non-suppurative).

3. Explain the mechanism of action of Clostridium tetani toxin. (5 marks)

Answer:

Tetanospasmin mechanism:

Clostridium tetani produces tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin), a potent neurotoxin that causes the characteristic spastic paralysis of tetanus.

Steps:

  1. Production and release: Tetanospasmin is produced at the wound site during vegetative bacterial growth under anaerobic conditions
  2. Binding and uptake: The toxin binds to receptors (gangliosides and glycoproteins) at neuromuscular junctions and enters motor neurons via receptor-mediated endocytosis
  3. Retrograde transport: The toxin is transported retrograde (backwards) through axons to the spinal cord and brainstem
  4. Trans-synaptic migration: Tetanospasmin crosses synapses to reach inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells)
  5. Cleavage of SNARE proteins: The toxin's light chain (a zinc metalloprotease) cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP), a SNARE protein essential for vesicle fusion
  6. Block of inhibitory neurotransmitter release: This prevents release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA and glycine) from Renshaw cells onto motor neurons
  7. Result: Unopposed motor neuron stimulation leads to sustained muscle contraction (spastic paralysis), causing trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, and generalized muscle spasms

Unlike botulinum toxin which causes flaccid paralysis by blocking acetylcholine release, tetanus toxin causes spastic paralysis by blocking inhibitory signals.

SECTION C – LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS (20 MARKS)

ANSWER ONLY ONE QUESTION

Question 1

An 8-year-old boy presents with bloody diarrhea and fever after a camping trip. Gram stain shows curved Gram-negative rods.

a. Identify the most likely organism.

Answer:
The most likely organism is Campylobacter jejuni. The clinical presentation of bloody diarrhea with fever following camping (suggesting exposure to contaminated food or water), combined with the characteristic curved (comma-shaped or spiral) Gram-negative rods on microscopy, is highly suggestive of Campylobacter infection. C. jejuni is the most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis worldwide.

b. Describe possible routes of exposure.

Answer:

  • Contaminated food: Undercooked poultry (chicken is the primary reservoir), unpasteurized milk, contaminated water used for drinking or food preparation
  • Contaminated water: Drinking untreated stream or lake water during camping; swimming in contaminated water
  • Animal contact: Direct contact with infected animals (pets, farm animals, especially puppies with diarrhea)
  • Cross-contamination: Poor food handling practices during food preparation
  • Person-to-person: Fecal-oral transmission (rare but possible in young children)

c. Explain how food or water becomes contaminated.

Answer:

  • Poultry contamination: Campylobacter colonizes the intestinal tract of chickens and other birds asymptomatically. During slaughter and processing, intestinal contents contaminate carcasses
  • Water contamination: Animal and bird feces containing Campylobacter contaminate surface water sources (streams, lakes, wells). Without proper treatment or boiling, water remains infectious
  • Milk contamination: Occurs through fecal contamination during milking or from infected udders
  • Cross-contamination in food preparation: Raw poultry juices contaminate other foods, cutting boards, or utensils
  • Environmental persistence: The organism can survive in moist, cool environments (refrigeration temperatures), allowing persistence in food and water

d. State potential complications and explain their pathogenesis.

Answer:

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS):

  • Most serious complication, occurring in approximately 1 in 1,000 infections
  • Pathogenesis: Molecular mimicry between Campylobacter lipooligosaccharide (LOS) and gangliosides (GM1, GD1a) on peripheral nerve myelin
  • Cross-reactive antibodies attack peripheral nerves, causing demyelination
  • Results in ascending flaccid paralysis, potentially requiring mechanical ventilation

Reactive arthritis:

  • Occurs 1-3 weeks post-infection
  • Pathogenesis: Immune-mediated inflammation triggered by bacterial antigens deposited in joints
  • Affects large joints (knees, ankles), may be part of Reiter's syndrome with urethritis and conjunctivitis

Bacteremia:

  • Rare, more common in immunocompromised patients, infants, and elderly
  • Can lead to extraintestinal infections (meningitis, endocarditis, septic arthritis)

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS):

  • Rare complication
  • Post-infectious thrombotic microangiopathy affecting kidneys

e. Name an antibiotic that shortens severe disease.

Answer:
Azithromycin (a macrolide antibiotic) is the drug of choice. Alternative agents include erythromycin and fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), though resistance to fluoroquinolones is increasing. Antibiotics are most effective when given early in illness (within first 3-4 days) and are particularly indicated for severe disease, immunocompromised patients, or bloody diarrhea. For mild, self-limited cases, supportive care with hydration is often sufficient.

Question 2

A 17-year-old male presents with urethral discharge. Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci.

a. Identify the disease and causative organism.

Answer:
Disease: Gonorrhea (gonococcal urethritis)
Causative organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The presence of Gram-negative diplococci (kidney bean-shaped, in pairs) within neutrophils on urethral discharge Gram stain is diagnostic of gonococcal infection. This is the most common cause of purulent urethral discharge in sexually active males.

b. Explain why his sexual partners require examination.

Answer:
Sexual partners require examination for several critical reasons:

  • High transmission rate: Gonorrhea has a transmission rate of 20-50% per sexual contact, meaning partners are likely infected
  • Asymptomatic infection in women: Up to 50% of infected women are asymptomatic but can still transmit infection and develop complications
  • Prevention of reinfection: Treating the patient alone without treating partners leads to "ping-pong" reinfection
  • Prevention of complications: Untreated infection in partners can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), infertility, ectopic pregnancy in women, and epididymitis in men
  • Break transmission chain: Contact tracing and treatment prevent further spread in the community
  • Public health requirement: Most jurisdictions require partner notification and treatment for gonorrhea as it is a reportable disease

c. State other organisms for which he is at increased risk and why.

Answer:
Patients with gonorrhea are at increased risk for:

Chlamydia trachomatis:

  • Coinfection occurs in 30-50% of cases
  • Both are sexually transmitted and share similar risk factors
  • Often asymptomatic, can cause non-gonococcal urethritis
  • CDC recommends routine testing and empiric treatment for both

HIV:

  • Gonorrhea causes urethral inflammation and disruption of mucosal barriers
  • Increased genital tract HIV shedding in coinfected patients
  • Enhanced HIV transmission and acquisition due to inflammatory response
  • Behavior indicating unprotected sex increases risk for both

Syphilis (Treponema pallidum):

  • Shares transmission routes and risk factors
  • Genital ulcers increase HIV transmission risk
  • May have concurrent infection

Other STIs: Herpes simplex virus, hepatitis B, trichomonas

Why: All share the common risk factor of unprotected sexual contact, and the presence of one STI indicates high-risk sexual behavior and increased likelihood of exposure to others.

d. Explain the significance of the absence of inguinal lymphadenopathy and testicular pain.

Answer:

Absence of inguinal lymphadenopathy suggests:

  • Not chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi): Would cause painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with possible bubo formation
  • Not lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV - Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3): Would cause prominent inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy with groove sign
  • Consistent with uncomplicated gonorrhea: N. gonorrhoeae typically does not cause significant lymphadenopathy in urethritis

Absence of testicular pain suggests:

  • No epididymitis: Inflammation has not spread to epididymis, which would cause testicular pain, swelling, and tenderness
  • Uncomplicated infection: Disease is limited to anterior urethra
  • Good prognosis: Less likely to have ascending infection or complications
  • Early presentation: Patient sought care before development of complications

However, the clinician should still palpate for subtle epididymal tenderness and counsel about warning signs requiring return visit.

e. State the recommended antibiotics.

Answer:
Current CDC recommendations (2021) for uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis:

Single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone 500 mg (250 mg if <150 kg body weight)

PLUS (for presumptive chlamydial coinfection):

Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
OR
Azithromycin 1 gram orally single dose (though doxycycline is now preferred due to concerns about azithromycin-resistant Mycoplasma genitalium)

Rationale:

  • Ceftriaxone addresses increasing fluoroquinolone resistance
  • Dual therapy covers likely chlamydial coinfection (30-50% of cases)
  • Single-dose IM therapy ensures compliance
  • Alternative for ceftriaxone allergy: cefixime 800 mg PO single dose or gentamicin 240 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g PO

Additional management: Partner notification and treatment, test of cure if symptoms persist, HIV and syphilis testing, counseling on safe sex practices.

Question 3

A 33-year-old HIV-positive man has fever, weight loss, rust-colored sputum, and abnormal chest X-ray. A tuberculin test is performed.

a. Why was a chest X-ray requested?

Answer:
A chest X-ray was requested to:

  • Evaluate for pulmonary tuberculosis: The clinical presentation (fever, weight loss, productive cough with rust-colored sputum) is highly suggestive of active pulmonary TB
  • Assess extent of disease: Determine if disease is localized or disseminated, identify cavitary lesions, infiltrates, or miliary pattern
  • Identify characteristic findings: Look for upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion typical of TB
  • Screen for complications: Detect pneumothorax, empyema, or extensive parenchymal involvement
  • Differentiate from other conditions: Rule out other causes of respiratory symptoms in HIV patients (bacterial pneumonia, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Kaposi's sarcoma, fungal infections)
  • Assess HIV-related patterns: HIV patients may show atypical radiographic features (lower lobe disease, diffuse infiltrates, absence of cavitation)
  • Guide treatment decisions: Severity of radiographic findings influences treatment approach and monitoring
  • Baseline for follow-up: Provides baseline to monitor treatment response

b. Why was a sputum sample collected?

Answer:
Sputum was collected to:

Microbiological diagnosis:

  • Direct microscopy: Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine-rhodamine staining to visualize acid-fast bacilli (AFB), providing rapid preliminary diagnosis
  • Culture: Gold standard for definitive diagnosis; identifies Mycobacterium tuberculosis and allows drug susceptibility testing
  • Molecular testing: GeneXpert MTB/RIF provides rapid detection of TB and rifampin resistance within 2 hours
  • Species identification: Distinguishes M. tuberculosis from non-tuberculous mycobacteria

Assess infectiousness:

  • Sputum smear positivity indicates higher bacterial load and greater infectiousness, requiring isolation precautions

Monitor treatment:

  • Serial sputum samples (at 2, 4, 6 months) assess treatment response and bacteriological cure
  • Conversion from positive to negative indicates treatment success

Drug resistance testing:

  • Culture allows phenotypic and genotypic drug susceptibility testing to detect MDR-TB or XDR-TB

c. Describe the appearance of a positive tuberculin skin test.

Answer:
A positive tuberculin (Mantoux) skin test appears as:

Physical characteristics:

  • Induration (not erythema): A raised, firm, palpable swelling at the injection site on the volar surface of the forearm
  • Size: Measured as transverse diameter of induration (perpendicular to long axis of forearm) at 48-72 hours post-injection
  • Shape: Usually circular or oval
  • Color: Skin may appear pale or slightly erythematous, but only induration is measured
  • Texture: Firm to palpation, distinct from surrounding soft tissue
  • Border: Well-demarcated edge distinguishing induration from normal skin

Measurement:

  • Use fingertips or ballpoint pen to palpate edges
  • Measure widest transverse diameter in millimeters
  • Record actual measurement; do not record as simply "positive" or "negative"

d. Interpret the meaning of such a result.

Answer:
Interpretation depends on induration size and patient risk factors:

For this HIV-positive patient:

  • ≥5 mm is positive: HIV infection significantly lowers threshold for positivity
  • Indicates cell-mediated immune response to tubercular antigens (PPD)
  • Suggests latent TB infection (LTBI) or active TB disease

Positive TST indicates:

  • Previous exposure to M. tuberculosis
  • Immune response to mycobacterial antigens
  • Does NOT distinguish between latent infection and active disease
  • Does NOT confirm diagnosis of active TB (requires clinical, radiographic, and microbiological evidence)

In HIV patients, special considerations:

  • Reduced sensitivity: Anergy (inability to mount immune response) common with low CD4 counts (<200 cells/μL)
  • False negatives common: Severe immunosuppression may prevent induration despite TB infection
  • IGRA tests preferred: Interferon-gamma release assays (QuantiFERON, T-SPOT) are more specific and not affected by BCG vaccination

Clinical context: Given this patient's symptoms, abnormal CXR, and HIV status, a positive TST (or any suspicion) warrants aggressive workup for active TB disease, not just LTBI.

e. Identify the disease and its causative agent.

Answer:
Disease: Pulmonary tuberculosis (active TB disease)
Causative agent: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis is an acid-fast, aerobic bacillus that causes chronic granulomatous disease. It is an obligate aerobe, explaining its predilection for oxygen-rich apical lung regions. The rust-colored (blood-tinged) sputum, constitutional symptoms, and radiographic abnormalities are classic for pulmonary TB.

f. Explain how he likely acquired the infection.

Answer:
Mode of transmission: Airborne transmission

Mechanism:

  • Inhalation of droplet nuclei: M. tuberculosis is transmitted via airborne particles (1-5 μm diameter) containing bacteria
  • Source: Generated when individuals with active pulmonary/laryngeal TB cough, sneeze, speak, or sing
  • Droplet nuclei characteristics: Remain suspended in air for hours, can travel long distances on air currents, small enough to bypass upper airway defenses and reach alveoli
    Deposition in alveoli: Once inhaled, droplet nuclei deposit in terminal alveoli, particularly in well-ventilated upper lung zones
    Likely scenarios for acquisition:
    Household contact: Close, prolonged contact with person with active TB (family member, roommate)
    Congregate settings: Exposure in crowded environments (healthcare facilities, shelters, prisons, dormitories)
    Community exposure: Contact in poorly ventilated spaces (public transport, workplaces, churches)
    Geographic factors: Living in or traveling to high TB prevalence areas
    Risk factors increasing acquisition in this patient:
    HIV infection: Impaired cell-mediated immunity increases susceptibility to TB infection and progression
    Socioeconomic factors: May include poverty, homelessness, malnutrition, substance abuse
    Healthcare exposure: Possible nosocomial transmission in HIV care settings
    Reactivation possibility: Could represent reactivation of latent infection acquired years earlier, now progressing due to HIV-related immunosuppression
    Infection process:
    Inhalation of droplet nuclei containing tubercle bacilli
    Deposition in alveoli
    Phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages
    In immunocompetent individuals: Granuloma formation contains infection (90-95% remain latent)
    In HIV patients: Impaired T-cell function prevents effective granuloma formation, leading to progressive primary disease or rapid reactivation
    g. State why the agent is more virulent in HIV-infected patients.
    Answer:
    M. tuberculosis is more virulent in HIV-infected patients due to profound immunological defects:
    1. Impaired Cell-Mediated Immunity (CMI):
    CD4+ T-cell depletion: HIV progressively destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which are essential for TB control
    Loss of Th1 response: Reduced production of interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), IL-2, and TNF-α needed to activate macrophages
    Impaired macrophage function: Without adequate T-cell help, macrophages cannot effectively kill or contain intracellular mycobacteria
    Critical threshold: TB risk dramatically increases when CD4 count falls below 200 cells/μL
    2. Defective Granuloma Formation:
    Granulomas are critical: Normally contain TB infection in organized structures with activated macrophages, epithelioid cells, and giant cells
    HIV disrupts architecture: Without functional CD4+ cells and cytokines, granulomas are poorly formed or absent
    Unrestricted bacterial replication: Mycobacteria multiply freely without containment
    Dissemination: Bacteria spread hematogenously to multiple organs (miliary TB, extrapulmonary TB)
    3. Increased Reactivation Risk:
    Latent TB progression: HIV patients with LTBI have 10% annual risk of reactivation vs. 5-10% lifetime risk in immunocompetent individuals
    Rapid progression: Primary infection more likely to progress directly to active disease without latency period
    4. Altered Disease Manifestations:
    Atypical presentations: Lower lobe infiltrates, diffuse disease, absence of cavitation
    Higher mycobacterial burden: More organisms in tissues and sputum
    Extrapulmonary disease: More common (40-60% vs. 15-20% in HIV-negative patients)
    Miliary TB: Disseminated disease more frequent
    5. Impaired Protective Cytokine Networks:
    TNF-α deficiency: Essential for granuloma maintenance; HIV reduces TNF-α production
    IL-12/IFN-γ axis disruption: Critical pathway for macrophage activation is compromised
    Reduced chemokine production: Impairs recruitment of immune cells to infection sites
    6. Synergistic Pathogenesis:
    TB accelerates HIV progression: TB increases HIV viral load and accelerates CD4 decline
    HIV accelerates TB progression: Creates vicious cycle of mutual enhancement
    Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS): Starting antiretroviral therapy (ART) can paradoxically worsen TB symptoms due to restored but dysregulated immune response
    7. Increased Mortality:
    Higher fatality rates: Even with treatment, mortality is 2-3 times higher than in HIV-negative TB patients
    Drug interactions: Rifampin induces cytochrome P450, reducing effectiveness of protease inhibitors and NNRTIs
    Overlapping toxicities: Both TB drugs and antiretrovirals can cause hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy
    Clinical implications:
    Aggressive screening: All HIV patients should be screened for TB at initial presentation and regularly
    Lower diagnostic thresholds: Earlier empiric treatment for suspected TB
    Prophylaxis essential: Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) for HIV patients with latent TB
    Integrated treatment: Coordinate TB therapy with ART initiation (usually start TB treatment first, then ART 2-8 weeks later depending on CD4 count)
    Prolonged therapy: May require longer treatment duration
    Close monitoring: For treatment response, adverse effects, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome
    Summary: The virulence of M. tuberculosis in HIV patients stems fundamentally from the loss of CD4+ T-cell-mediated immunity, which is the cornerstone of host defense against intracellular pathogens. Without effective CMI, the balance tips decisively in favor of the pathogen, allowing unchecked bacterial replication, dissemination, and severe clinical disease.

    END OF EXAMINATION
    Instructions for grading:
    Section A: 2 marks per question × 20 questions = 40 marks
    Section B: 5 marks per question × 3 questions = 15 marks
    Section C: Answer ONE question = 20 marks
    Total: 75 marks
    Time allowed: 2 hours

Title: Yr3 Medical Entomology Questions | COMPLETE SET
Content:
Dr. Ngala (Must Know)

Vector Control Methods

1. Explain how Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) works as a biological control agent and why it's preferred over chemical insecticides.

Answer: Bt is a bacterial biopesticide that blocks insect chitin biosynthesis pathways, killing mosquito larvae. It's preferred over chemical insecticides because:

  • Specific to target insects (narrow spectrum)
  • Doesn't persist in the environment
  • No bioaccumulation in fatty tissues
  • Minimal impact on non-target organisms

2. Compare and contrast organophosphates and carbamates in terms of mechanism of action and safety profile.

Answer:

  • Mechanism: Both block/bind to acetylcholinesterase, preventing acetylcholine breakdown
  • Safety differences:
    • Carbamates have lower mammalian/human toxicity
    • Carbamates have better biodegradability
    • Carbamate inhibition is reversible
    • Chronic carbamate exposure less likely to cause illness than organophosphates

3. Why were chlorinated hydrocarbons like DDT banned despite their effectiveness? Discuss two specific concerns.

Answer:

  1. Long environmental persistence - Relatively stable, don't break down easily
  2. Bioaccumulation - Lipid/fat soluble, accumulate in fatty tissues through the food chain, reaching toxic levels in top predators

4. Describe the sterile male technique and explain why it's considered a genetic engineering approach to vector control.

Answer: Sterile males are produced and released to mate with wild females, resulting in no viable offspring and population reduction. It's considered genetic engineering because it modifies the reproductive capacity of the vector population, changing the target site/genetic makeup without using chemicals.

5. Explain the mechanism of action of pyrethroids and why they are commonly used in ITNs and LLINs.

Answer: Pyrethroids bind to voltage-gated sodium channels and delay their inactivation, increasing membrane permeability. This results in excitation, lack of coordination, and paralysis (knockdown effect). They're used in ITNs/LLINs because:

  • Relatively safe for humans
  • Rapid action (knockdown effect)
  • Effective at low doses
  • Example: Permethrin, Deltamethrin

6. What is IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying) and why is it effective against endophilic mosquitoes?

Answer: IRS is the application of insecticides on interior walls of houses and structures. It's effective against endophilic mosquitoes (those that rest indoors) because:

  • Mosquitoes rest on walls after blood feeding
  • Contact with treated surfaces kills them
  • Provides long-lasting protection (weeks to months)
  • Targets mosquitoes when they're most vulnerable

7. Describe how Toxorhynchites species function as biological control agents.

Answer: Toxorhynchites mosquito larvae (e.g., T. rutilus) are predators that feed on larvae of disease-transmitting mosquitoes including Anopheles, Culex, and Aedes. Adults feed only on sugar solutions (not blood), making them non-vectors. They provide natural population control without chemicals.

8. What are Insect Growth Regulators (IGRs) and how do they control vector populations?

Answer: IGRs are chemicals that block insect sugar/chitin biosynthesis pathways, disrupting normal development and molting. Examples include Pyriproxyfen and Diflubenzuron. They prevent larvae from developing into adults, reducing vector populations without killing adult mosquitoes directly.

Mosquito Biology and Control

9. Explain why Anopheles mosquitoes are more efficient malaria vectors than Culex or Aedes species. Include at least two behavioral characteristics.

Answer: Anopheles behavioral characteristics that enhance malaria transmission:

  • Anthropophilic - Prefer human blood meals
  • Endophagic - Feed indoors where humans sleep
  • Endophilic - Rest indoors after feeding These behaviors maximize human-mosquito contact and facilitate Plasmodium parasite transmission.

10. How can you distinguish between Anopheles and Culex larvae in their aquatic habitat?

Answer:

  • Anopheles larvae: Lie parallel to water surface, breathe through spiracles on body side
  • Culex larvae: Hang at 45° angle to surface, breathe via a siphon

11. Describe the bimodal biting pattern of Aedes mosquitoes and explain its significance for disease transmission.

Answer: Aedes mosquitoes have two peak feeding times:

  • Early morning
  • Late evening

Significance: This pattern increases disease transmission because mosquitoes bite multiple hosts during peak human activity periods, facilitating arbovirus spread (dengue, Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever).

12. What is transovarial transmission? Provide one example of a disease transmitted this way.

Answer: Transovarial transmission is when a pathogen passes from infected female mosquito to her eggs, so adults emerge already infected with the virus.

Examples:

  • Culex: Rift Valley fever, West Nile virus
  • Aedes: Dengue, Zika, yellow fever, chikungunya

13. Compare the breeding sites of Anopheles, Culex, and Aedes mosquitoes.

Answer:

  • Anopheles: Stagnant water with vegetation and algae; clean natural water bodies
  • Culex: Contaminated water (sewage, drains); polluted water
  • Aedes: Clean containers (tires, flower vases, artificial containers) - "container breeders"

14. Describe the egg-laying behavior of Anopheles, Culex, and Aedes mosquitoes.

Answer:

  • Anopheles: Eggs laid singly, one at a time; float individually on water surface
  • Culex: Eggs laid simultaneously, attached to each other forming a raft; float as a raft
  • Aedes: Eggs laid in containers; can survive desiccation

15. What is the significance of An. stephensi being recently reported in Africa?

Answer: An. stephensi is a supervector that:

  • Transmits malaria primarily in Asia
  • Unlike other African Anopheles species, can withstand high temperatures and arid conditions
  • Its presence in Africa threatens malaria control because it can breed in urban areas and drought-prone regions where other vectors cannot
  • Expands malaria transmission to new geographic areas

16. Explain the complete metamorphosis (holometabolous) life cycle of mosquitoes.

Answer: Complete metamorphosis includes four distinct stages:

  1. Egg - Laid on/in water
  2. Larva - 4 instars (L1-L4); aquatic, feeding stage
  3. Pupa - Aquatic, resting/non-feeding stage; comma-shaped; emerges after 2-3 days
  4. Adult - Terrestrial, flying, reproductive stage Duration depends on temperature (optimal 25°C) and humidity (78%)

17. Why do female mosquitoes require blood meals while males do not?

Answer:

  • Females: Require blood meals for egg development (protein needed for oogenesis) - they are anautogenous
  • Males: Feed only on sugar solutions (plant nectar) for energy
  • Both sexes feed on sugar solutions, but only females need blood for reproduction

18. Describe the resting position and antenna characteristics that distinguish male from female Anopheles mosquitoes.

Answer:

  • Resting position: Both rest at 45° angle to surface (unlike Culex at nearly parallel)
  • Antennae:
    • Males: Bushy/plumose (feathery)
    • Females: Smooth/pilose (few hairs)
  • Feeding: Only females take blood meals

Sandflies and Phlebotominae

19. Describe the characteristics that make sandflies (Phlebotominae) important disease vectors.

Answer:

  • Weak fliers - stay close to breeding sites
  • Short mouthparts - bite exposed body parts
  • Bimodal biting - early morning and evening
  • Prefer high humidity - cannot withstand desiccation
  • Anthropophilic - prefer human blood
  • Transmit leishmaniasis, Carrion's disease, and sandfly fever

20. Differentiate between Old World and New World sandfly genera and their geographic distribution.

Answer:

  • Old World: Phlebotomus (4 subgenera) - Mediterranean, Indian subcontinent, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia
  • New World: Lutzomyia (e.g., L. umbratilis in Brazil) - Central and South America
  • Sergentomyia - Zoophilic species found in both regions

21. Name the three clinical forms of leishmaniasis and their causative agents.

Answer:

  1. Visceral leishmaniasis - Leishmania donovani (affects internal organs)
  2. Cutaneous leishmaniasis - Leishmania tropica (Old World) - skin lesions
  3. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis - Leishmania braziliensis complex - affects mucous membranes (nose, mouth)
[paywall]

22. Describe the breeding and oviposition sites preferred by sandflies.

Answer: Sandflies oviposit in:

  • Small cracks and holes in ground
  • Base of termite mounds
  • Chicken coops and poultry houses
  • Animal burrows
  • Rubbish heaps
  • Require high humidity areas; cannot withstand desiccation

23. What control measures are effective against sandflies?

Answer:

  • Physical: Removal of termite mounds, personal protection, timing outdoor activities
  • Repellents: DEET, Picaridin on exposed skin
  • Protective clothing: Cover exposed body parts
  • Chemical: Spray insecticides on cracks in walls, termite mounds, animal burrows
  • Habitat control: Destroy reservoir hosts (rodents involved in zoonotic transmission)

Biting Midges (Ceratopogonidae)

24. What are "no-see-ums" and why are they medically important?

Answer: "No-see-ums" are biting midges (Family Ceratopogonidae, genus Culicoides and Leptoconops). They're medically important because:

  • Transmit Mansonella ozzardi (filarial nematode)
  • Very small size makes them difficult to see
  • Painful bites
  • Active in wind (unlike other vectors)
  • Both diurnal and nocturnal feeders

25. Describe the breeding preferences of biting midges.

Answer: Biting midges prefer:

  • Wet mud/sand for oviposition
  • Both salt and fresh water habitats
  • Pupae develop in soil or mud
  • Found in tropics, subtropics, Caribbean, and Pacific regions

26. Why is control of biting midges difficult to achieve?

Answer:

  • Very small size makes them hard to target
  • Difficult to control with insecticides effectively
  • Control achieved mainly through:
    • Avoiding activity during peak biting times
    • Personal protection with repellents
    • Use of fine-mesh screens/netting (regular screens don't work)

Black Flies (Simuliidae)

27. What is onchocerciasis and which vector transmits it?

Answer: Onchocerciasis (river blindness) is caused by the filarial nematode Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by Simulium species (black flies). The disease causes:

  • Skin manifestations
  • Eye lesions leading to blindness
  • Associated with fast-flowing rivers where black flies breed

28. Describe the breeding habitat requirements of black flies.

Answer: Black flies breed:

  • Along riverbanks
  • In fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water
  • Larvae attach to rocks and vegetation in streams
  • Require clean, moving water (unlike mosquitoes)

29. What are the feeding behaviors and biting patterns of black flies?

Answer:

  • Both sexes feed on plant juices
  • Females require blood meal for egg viability
  • Bimodal biting: Early morning and early evening (diurnal)
  • Exophilic and exophagic (outdoor feeders and resters)
  • Prefer feeding on exposed body parts (head and arms more than legs)
  • Few members are autogenous

30. Describe control measures for black flies.

Answer:

  • Physical: Wear clothing covering exposed parts, apply repellents, time outdoor activities
  • Chemical:
    • Spray insecticides on larval breeding sites and resting areas
    • Larvicides on water surfaces (15-30 min duration)
    • Use of Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis)
  • Habitat modification:
    • Straighten rivers
    • Remove obstructions to increase water velocity

Horse Flies and Deer Flies (Tabanidae)

31. Distinguish between Tabanus, Chrysops, and Haematopota in the family Tabanidae.

Answer:

  • Tabanus (horse fly): Green head, breeds in swamps, larger size
  • Chrysops (deer fly): Yellow/brown color, smaller than Tabanus
  • Haematopota (clegs): European species All have painful bites due to large mouthparts

32. What diseases do Chrysops species transmit and in which geographic regions?

Answer: Chrysops transmits Loa loa (African eye worm) in West and Central Africa. Key species:

  • C. silacea (attracted by darkness, must hang from objects)
  • C. dimidiata The parasite causes loiasis (Calabar swellings and eye migration)

33. Describe the feeding behavior and host detection methods of tabanid flies.

Answer:

  • Females feed during day in bright sunlight
  • Diurnal feeders
  • Locate hosts by:
    • Sight (visual cues) - large object detectors
    • Olfactory cues (smell)
  • Purely exophagic (except C. silacea)
  • Painful bites due to large mouthparts

34. Why is habitat management for tabanid control often cost-prohibitive?

Answer: Tabanid larvae breed in:

  • Large swampy areas
  • Wetlands covering extensive geographic areas
  • Efficient drainage of these large larval habitats requires:
    • Massive infrastructure
    • High costs
    • Environmental concerns
  • Often impractical for widespread implementation

Tsetse Flies (Glossinidae)

35. What is adenotrophic viviparity and which vector exhibits this unique reproductive strategy?

Answer: Adenotrophic viviparity (larviparous reproduction) is found in tsetse flies (Glossinidae). The larva develops inside the mother's uterus, nourished by an accessory milk gland. A single mature larva is deposited and immediately pupates in soil/shaded areas (2.5cm deep). Adults emerge after 4-5 weeks.

36. Describe the three habitat groups of tsetse flies with examples.

Answer:

  1. Forest Group (Fusca): G. palpalis, G. tachinoides, G. fuscipes - forested areas
  2. Savanna Group (Morsitans): G. morsitans, G. swynnertoni, G. pallidipes - savanna regions of East and Southern Africa
  3. Riverine Group (Palpalis): G. palpalis, G. tachinoides, G. fuscipes - vegetation along rivers, lakes, swamps in humid coastal areas

37. Which tsetse fly species transmit West African vs. East African trypanosomiasis?

Answer:

  • West African (Gambian) trypanosomiasis (T. brucei gambiense):
    • G. palpalis
    • G. tachinoides
  • East African (Rhodesian) trypanosomiasis (T. brucei rhodesiense):
    • G. morsitans
    • G. swynnertoni
    • G. pallidipes

38. Describe the feeding and resting behavior of tsetse flies.

Answer:

  • Feeding:
    • Both males and females feed on blood every 2-3 days
    • Diurnal feeders
    • Host detection by sight and olfactory cues
    • Attracted to dark moving objects
  • Resting:
    • Rest 23 hours/day
    • At night: prefer resting on vegetation
    • During day: rest at lower levels

39. What control measures are used against tsetse flies?

Answer:

  • Physical/Mechanical:
    • Creating barriers
    • Aerial sprays (especially in dry season)
    • Use of traps (Ngu trap)
  • Habitat Management:
    • Clearing vegetation
    • Bush clearing along rivers
  • Chemical: Insecticides, targets for insecticide application
  • Biological: Sterile insect technique (SIT)

40. Where are tsetse flies geographically distributed?

Answer: Tsetse flies are found only in Sub-Saharan Africa (tropical Africa between 15°N and 20°S latitude). They do not occur outside Africa, making African trypanosomiasis a geographically restricted disease.

Houseflies and Related Families

41. Name the five genera in Muscidae, Fanniidae, and Stomoxydae families and their common names.

Answer:

  1. Musca domestica - Common housefly
  2. Muscina stabulans - Greater housefly
  3. Stomoxys calcitrans - Stable fly
  4. Fannia canicularis - Lesser housefly
  5. Fannia scalaris - Latrine fly

42. Describe the three routes by which flies mechanically transmit enteropathogens.

Answer:

  1. Body hairs and mouthparts - Pathogens stick to external surfaces
  2. Regurgitation - Flies vomit on food during feeding (they do this frequently)
  3. Defecation - Most important route; flies defecate while feeding on food

43. What is the medical importance of Stomoxys (stable fly) compared to other Muscidae?

Answer: Unlike other Muscidae that are mechanical vectors, Stomoxys are biting pests that:

  • Cause dermatitis
  • Cause secondary bacterial infection from bites
  • Have painful bites
  • Both males and females bite (unlike most flies where only females bite)

44. Describe control measures for houseflies.

Answer:

  • Light bulb insect traps - Attract and electrocute flies
  • Air curtains/barriers - At shop entrances to reduce fly entry
  • Source reduction:
    • Domestic garbage in closed bins/receptacles
    • Plastic bags with openings tightly closed
    • Optimize/clean larval habitats
  • Sanitation and hygiene

Myiasis

45. Define myiasis and list the three types.

Answer: Myiasis is the invasion of organs and tissues of humans and animals by fly larvae that feed on living/dead tissues or ingested food.

Types:

  1. Accidental myiasis - Consuming food contaminated with eggs/larvae of non-parasitic flies
  2. Obligatory myiasis - Larvae must live in live host for at least part of life cycle
  3. Facultative myiasis - Free-living larvae that attack carcasses but can infect living tissues

46. Describe cutaneous (furuncular) myiasis and its treatment.

Answer:

  • Also called "creeping eruption"
  • Boil-like inflammation of wound infected with larvae
  • Only wounds attract flies which lay eggs
  • Eggs hatch and larvae develop under skin
  • Treatment: Remove larvae under aseptic conditions

47. What is ophthalmic myiasis and what are its consequences?

Answer: Ophthalmic (ocular) myiasis occurs when:

  • Flies attracted to dirty eyes deposit eggs on/near the eye
  • Larvae (maggots) invade and feed on living eye tissues
  • Symptoms: Lacrimation, redness, pain
  • Treatment:
    • Removal of larvae
    • If deeply embedded, eyes may need enucleation (removal)
    • If damage irreversible, results in eye removal
  • Prevention: Personal hygiene, eyewear

48. Describe intestinal myiasis including route of entry and symptoms.

Answer:

  • Route: Mouth - food contaminated with eggs/larvae is swallowed
  • Occurs in: Accidental myiasis (no species adapted to cause intestinal myiasis in humans)
  • Symptoms:
    • Diarrhea
    • Dysentery
    • Abdominal pain
    • Vomiting
  • Larvae may be passed alive in stool or vomited

49. What is maggot therapy and what fly species is used?

Answer: Maggot therapy uses live, sterile larvae of Lucilia sericata for wound management. The larvae:

  • Clean wounds by feeding on dead/necrotic tissue (debridement)
  • Leave healthy tissue intact
  • Promote healing
  • Reduce bacterial load

50. Describe nasopharyngeal myiasis and its complications.

Answer:

  • Major route: Nose
  • Larvae crawl down to nasopharynx
  • Can cause:
    • Tonsillitis
    • Tonsillar irritation
    • Discomfort and pain

Fleas (Siphonaptera)

51. Describe the life cycle of fleas with emphasis on larval feeding requirements.

Answer:

  • Eggs: Female deposits eggs in debris/dust in host habitat; eggs fall off host
  • Larvae: Feed on organic matter/debris BUT must feed on partly digested blood meal regurgitated from adult fleas or their feces to successfully develop
  • Pupae: Larvae spin silken cocoon (4-12 days, avg 7-8 days); cocoon covered with dust/debris
  • Adults: Emerge and seek host; duration dependent on temperature and stimulus

52. What is the medical importance of Xenopsylla cheopis?

Answer: X. cheopis (rat flea) is the primary vector for:

  1. Yersinia pestis (bubonic plague) - Most important
  2. Rickettsia typhi (murine typhus)
  • Common in tropics due to warm temperatures
  • Feeds on rats and humans

53. Describe the unique behavior of Tunga penetrans (jigger flea).

Answer: Tunga penetrans (chigoe/jigger flea):

  • Burrows into people's feet
  • Gravid female flea penetrates the host
  • Deposits eggs in the dermis
  • Causes painful swelling and secondary infections
  • Common in sandy, tropical areas

54. What cestode parasites use Ctenocephalides fleas as intermediate hosts?

Answer: Ctenocephalides (C. felis - cat flea; C. canis - dog flea) are intermediate hosts for:

  1. Dipylidium caninum (dog tapeworm)
  2. Hymenolepis diminuta (rat tapeworm) Also transmit Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease)

55. Explain why fleas rapidly abandon dead hosts and the significance for plague transmission.

Answer: When no suitable (living) host is available:

  • Fleas rapidly abandon their dead hosts in search of living hosts
  • This behavior presents a new wave of plague transmission
  • Dead plague-infected rodents release infected fleas
  • Fleas seek new hosts (including humans)
  • Creates epidemic spread

56. Describe the jumping mechanism of fleas.

Answer: Fleas have a protein called resilin in their legs:

  • Highly compressed state
  • Produces rapid expansion from compressed state
  • Gives power for jumping (can jump 150x their body length)
  • On host, move rapidly by crawling

57. What control measures are used against fleas?

Answer:

  • Repellents: DEET on clothing
  • Rodent fleas and larvae: Hand-operated dusters with insecticidal dusts:
    • Carbaryl
    • Pyrethroids
    • Organophosphates applied to animals/pets
  • Cat/dog fleas: Insecticides (pyrethroids, OPs) applied directly to animals
  • Environmental: Treat carpets, bedding, animal resting areas

Lice (Phthiraptera)

58. Name the three types of blood-sucking lice in humans and their preferred locations.

Answer:

  1. Pediculus humanus corporis - Body louse (lives in clothing)
  2. Pediculus humanus capitis - Head louse (scalp hair)
  3. Pthirus pubis - Pubic/crab louse (pubic hair, beard, armpits, chest hair)

59. What is pediculosis and what are its symptoms?

Answer: Pediculosis is the condition of lice infestation ("lousy disease"). Symptoms include:

  • Intense itching/irritability
  • Pessimistic mood
  • Dermatitis and severe itching
  • May cause asthma or bronchitis
  • Risk of secondary bacterial infection (impetigo - contagious)
  • Fever from scratching

60. Name three vector-borne diseases transmitted transcutaneously by body lice.

Answer:

  1. Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii)
  2. Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis)
  3. Trench fever (Bartonella quintana)

Transmission: Pathogens in louse feces are scratched into skin

61. Describe control measures for body lice.

Answer:

  • Louse-infested clothing subjected to:
    • Washing or ironing
    • Dry cleaning
  • Impregnation of clothing with pyrethroid insecticides (permethrin) for long-lasting protection
  • Oral ivermectin kills lice (trials shown effective)
  • Improved personal hygiene

62. What are the medical importance and control of head lice?

Answer: Medical importance:

  • Causes pediculosis capitis
  • Can result in hair loss (alopecia)
  • Intense itching

Control:

  • Regular combing of hair
  • Shaving of head hair
  • Insecticidal formulas/lotions/shampoos

63. Describe the appearance and control of pubic lice.

Answer: Appearance:

  • Eggs attached to hair shaft (can be laid on single hair strand)
  • Crab-shaped body
  • Found on pubic hair, beard, armpits, occasionally chest hair

Control:

  • Shaving pubic hair
  • Insecticidal formulations (dusts, lotions, emulsions - NOT alcohol-based in genital area)
  • Malathion (may cause irritation)
  • For eyelashes: Petroleum jelly twice daily for 8-10 days
  • Wash affected areas, iron clothing, dry in sunlight

Bedbugs (Hemiptera: Cimicidae)

64. Name the key bedbug species and their geographic distribution.

Answer:

  1. Cimex lectularius - Widely distributed in tropical and non-tropical countries
  2. Cimex hemipterus - Old and New World tropics; also warm areas of non-tropical countries (e.g., Florida)
  3. Leptocimex - Mainly Africa; also recorded in Asia

65. Describe the feeding and resting behavior of bedbugs.

Answer: Feeding:

  • Both sexes take blood meals
  • Prefer to feed at night
  • During sunshine, often hide
  • In temperate regions, may remain active during day

Resting:

  • Hide during day underneath:
    • Loose wallpaper
    • Mattresses and beds
    • Cracks in walls
  • Rest as a group

66. What are the medical consequences of bedbug infestations?

Answer:

  • Cause restless/sleepless nights
  • Repeated vigorous feeding can contribute to iron deficiency anemia, especially in:
    • Infants
    • Young children
    • Elderly people
  • Possible Hepatitis B transmission (under investigation)
  • No confirmed evidence of disease transmission to humans

67. Why has there been an increase in bedbug infestations?

Answer:

  1. Global resistance to insecticides - Bedbugs developed resistance
  2. Warmer temperatures - Climate change favors bedbug survival
  3. Increased international travel
  4. Reduced use of effective (but banned) insecticides

Triatomine Bugs (Reduviidae)

68. What disease do triatomine bugs transmit and what is the mechanism of transmission?

Answer: Triatomine bugs (kissing bugs) transmit Trypanosoma cruzi, causing Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis).

Mechanism:

  • Bugs feed on blood, then defecate near bite site
  • Feces contain T. cruzi parasites
  • Person scratches bite, rubbing feces (with parasites) into wound
  • Parasites enter through skin or mucous membranes

69. Name three genera of triatomine bugs and key species.

Answer:

  1. Triatoma - T. infestans, T. dimidiata
  2. Rhodnius - R. prolixus
  3. Panstrongylus - P. megistus

70. Describe the medical importance of triatomine bug bites.

Answer:

  • Vector transmission of Chagas disease (T. cruzi)
  • When bugs bite in large numbers, can cause anemia
  • Some people exhibit hypersensitivity:
    • Edema (swelling)
    • Pruritus (itching)
    • Erythema (redness)

71. What control measures are effective against triatomine bugs?

Answer:

  • Spraying interior surfaces of walls and floors of houses
  • Target preferred warm areas:
    • Chicken sheds
    • Goat pens
  • Pyrethrin works during house fumigation
  • Reduction of hiding places (prefer dark places)
  • Housing improvement: Seal cracks, improve construction

Cockroaches

72. Name four medically important cockroach species.

Answer:

  1. Blattella germanica - German cockroach
  2. Blatta orientalis - Oriental cockroach
  3. Periplaneta americana - American cockroach
  4. Supella longipalpa

73. What are the medical importance and health consequences of cockroach infestations?

Answer: Mechanical transmission of enteropathogens:

  • Shigella
  • E. coli
  • Salmonella

Allergies:

  • Ecdysis (molting) triggers allergic reactions/asthma
  • ~10% of non-asthmatic people have cockroach allergies
  • Symptoms: Sneezing, skin rash, sore eyes, respiratory distress
  • Extreme cases: shortness of breath

74. Describe control measures for cockroaches.

Answer:

  • Insect Growth Regulators (IGRs) - Inhibit development
  • Contact poisons:
    • Boric acid powder (also stomach poison)
  • Spraying interior surfaces of walls and floors
  • Reduction of hiding places
  • Sanitation and good hygiene - Remove food sources and water
  • Seal cracks and crevices

Ticks - General

75. What are the general characteristics of Class Arachnida?

Answer:

  • 8 legs (4 pairs)
  • No antennae
  • Incomplete metamorphosis (hemimetabolous) - larval stage to adult stage directly
  • Have chelicerae on mouthparts
  • Body divided into:
    • Cephalothorax (prosoma)
    • Abdomen (opisthosoma)

Soft Ticks (Argasidae)

Medical Entomology Short Answer Questions - CONTINUED

Soft Ticks (Argasidae) - Continued

76. Differentiate between Argasidae (soft ticks) and Ixodidae (hard ticks) in terms of feeding behavior and host preferences.

Answer:

77. What is the medical importance of Ornithodoros moubata?

Answer: Ornithodoros moubata (soft tick) is the vector of:

  • Tick-borne relapsing fever caused by Borrelia duttoni (spirochete bacteria)
  • Transmits viruses
  • Can cause tick paralysis due to injection of toxins in saliva
  • Found in warm areas of Africa

78. Explain the term "nidicolous ticks" and give an example.

Answer: Nidicolous ticks are ticks that remain in the nest/dwelling of their host rather than questing from vegetation.

  • Example: Argasidae (soft ticks) like Ornithodoros
  • As opposed to non-nidicolous (hard ticks) which quest from the host environment
  • Nymphs and adults are blood-feeding stages

79. Describe the life cycle characteristics unique to Argasidae.

Answer:

  • Multiple nymphal stages - Usually 4 or 5 instars (N1, N2, N3, N4)
  • Multi-host tick - Different hosts for different stages
  • Nymphs and adults are blood-feeding stages
  • Remain for short period of time (hours) on host compared to hard ticks
  • Nidicolous behavior - stay in host nests/burrows

80. What control measures are used against soft ticks?

Answer:

  • Repellents: DEET on skin
  • Impregnated nets with permethrin
  • Acaricides on furniture/walls which harbor ticks
  • Environmental management: Clean animal burrows and nesting sites
  • Personal protection: Avoid sleeping in infested dwellings

Hard Ticks (Ixodidae)

81. Name five genera of hard ticks (Ixodidae).

Answer:

  1. Dermacentor
  2. Amblyomma
  3. Haemaphysalis
  4. Rhipicephalus
  5. Hyalomma
  6. Boophilus (1-host tick)

82. Explain what questing behavior is and which tick family exhibits it.

Answer: Questing behavior is exhibited by Ixodidae (hard ticks), particularly the larvae:

  • Climb up vegetation (grass, stems, limbs)
  • Wait with extended front legs for potential host
  • When host brushes against vegetation, tick drops onto or grasps host's fur/skin
  • Use chemical and physical cues to detect hosts

83. Differentiate between 1-host, 2-host, and 3-host ticks with examples.

Answer:

3-Host Tick:

  • Each stage (larva, nymph, adult) feeds on different host
  • Drop off after each feeding to molt
  • Examples: Dermacentor, Amblyomma, Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma

2-Host Tick:

  • Larvae molt into nymphs on first host
  • Nymphs drop off and seek second host
  • Molt to adults on second host
  • Examples: Some Rhipicephalus, Hyalomma species

1-Host Tick:

  • All stages remain on same host
  • Larvae molt to nymphs on host
  • Nymphs molt to adults on host
  • Example: Boophilus

84. What is tick paralysis and how does it occur?

Answer: Tick paralysis occurs due to:

  • Toxins in female tick saliva pumped into host during feeding period
  • Results in ascending paralysis
  • Followed by difficulties in:
    • Breathing
    • Swallowing
    • Speaking
  • Can be fatal if tick not removed
  • Symptoms resolve after tick removal

85. Name four diseases transmitted by hard ticks (Ixodidae).

Answer:

  1. Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi)
  2. Tick-borne encephalitis (arbovirus)
  3. Q fever (Coxiella burnetii)
  4. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii)
  • Can cause poliomyelitis in people with allergies

86. Why are ticks difficult to control? Provide two reasons.

Answer:

  1. Nutrient requirements: Can survive long periods without feeding (months to years)
  2. Host adaptability: Ticks can adapt to various host types, increasing survival chances as parasites
  3. Multiple habitats: Found in diverse environments
  4. Resistance: Developing resistance to acaricides

87. Describe proper tick removal technique.

Answer:

  • Pull carefully and slowly with tweezers close to skin
  • Grasp tick near head/mouthparts, not body
  • Pull straight out with steady, even pressure
  • Don't twist or jerk (can leave mouthparts in skin)
  • Don't squeeze tick body
  • Clean area with antiseptic after removal
  • Save tick for identification if needed

88. What control measures are used against hard ticks?

Answer:

  • Repellents: DEET on exposed skin
  • Regular dipping of livestock with acaricides
  • Regular spraying of gardens and vegetation
  • Proper removal techniques
  • Impregnated clothing with permethrin
  • Environmental management: Keep grass short, remove leaf litter
  • Personal protection: Wear long sleeves/pants, tuck pants into socks

Mites - Scabies (Sarcoptidae)

89. What is the causative agent of scabies and its distribution?

Answer:

  • Causative agent: Sarcoptes scabiei (scabies mite)
  • Distribution: Worldwide
  • Causes mange in animals
  • Causes scabies in humans
  • Family: Sarcoptidae

90. Describe the diagnostic features of scabies.

Answer: Diagnosis by detection of:

  • Female mites burrowing into skin to deposit eggs
  • Narrow, twisting tunnels on skin (visible as dark pepper-like tracks)
  • Burrows most common in web spaces between fingers

Diagnostic tests:

  • Dark skin: Smear ink on suspected area; after wiping, tunnels visible
  • Alternative: Use liquid tetracycline under UV light - tunnels fluoresce bright yellow-green
  • Skin scraping: Can reveal mites under microscope

91. Describe the difference between classic scabies and crusted (Norwegian) scabies.

Answer:

Classic Scabies:

  • Few mites present (10-15 mites)
  • Papular eruption (non-painful)
  • Affects interdigital web spaces, wrists, elbows, armpits, genitals
  • Does NOT appear above the head
  • Severe itching, worse at night and after hot bath
  • Not highly contagious

Crusted (Norwegian) Scabies:

  • Numerous mites on skin (thousands to millions)
  • Highly contagious
  • Skin becomes scaly and hyperkeratotic (thick, crusty)
  • Easily spreads to others
  • Often occurs in immunocompromised individuals
  • Mites adhere to patients and infect others easily
  • Skin scraping reveals many mites

92. What are the characteristics of Sarcoptes scabiei mites?

Answer:

  • Are arachnids (Class Arachnida)
  • Don't have teeth on hypostome of mouthparts
  • Have setae (bristles) on body structures for sensing
  • Female burrows into skin to lay eggs
  • Eggs hatch in 3-4 days
  • Complete life cycle in 10-14 days

93. Describe the symptoms and response produced by classic scabies.

Answer:

After first exposure:

  • Few mites can cause rash
  • Severe pruritus (itching) especially at night
  • Worse after taking hot bath
  • Papular eruption at affected sites
  • Constant itching and scratching
  • Scratching can lead to secondary bacterial infections
  • May see linear burrow tracks

Sites affected:

  • Interdigital web spaces
  • Wrists, elbows
  • Armpits
  • Genitals
  • Does NOT appear above head in adults (except in infants)

94. What treatments are available for scabies?

Answer:

A) Permethrin Cream (5%):

  • Apply from neck downwards
  • 2 applications (one now, one later)
  • Wash off after 8-12 hours
  • For complicated cases: re-apply after 24 hours

B) Benzyl Benzoate:

  • Apply, wash after 24 hours for adults
  • Re-application, then wash on 2nd and 3rd day

C) Crotamiton Cream/Lotion:

  • 5 daily applications for one week
  • Safe for young children and pregnant women

D) Ivermectin:

  • Single oral dose
  • Can also use topical application

95. Describe control measures for scabies in households.

Answer:

  • It's contagious - Treat all family/community members simultaneously
  • Clothes and bedding disinfection:
    • Dry cleaning
    • Dusting with insecticides
    • Wash with hot water (>50°C)
    • Iron and dry in sunlight
  • Sealed plastic bag method: Place items in sealed bag, freeze for 48 hours to kill mites
  • Antihistamines to control itching
  • Proper construction of houses
  • Avoid skin-to-skin contact during treatment period

Chigger Mites (Trombiculidae)

96. Name four species of chigger mites and their common names.

Answer:

  1. Leptotrombidium deliense
  2. L. akamushi
  3. L. fletcheri
  4. Eutrombicula alfreddugesi - "red bug"
  5. Trombicula autumnalis - "harvest mite"

97. Describe the life cycle of chigger mites, emphasizing which stage is parasitic.

Answer:

Adults:

  • Free-living
  • Bite and feed on small arthropods
  • Female lays 1-5 spherical eggs in moist, well-drained soil (e.g., riverbank)

Larval Stage:

  • ONLY larvae are parasitic (feed on vertebrates)
  • Attach to small mammals to feed
  • Rodents are important reservoir hosts

Nymphs and Adults:

  • Free-living
  • Inhabit habitats with suitable small arthropods for feeding
  • Not parasitic

98. What is the medical importance of chigger mites?

Answer:

Nuisance:

  • Harvest mites (T. autumnalis) and red bugs (E. alfreddugesi) cause:
    • Intense irritation
    • Itchy welts/rash ("chigger bites")

Disease transmission:

  • Scrub typhus (caused by Rickettsia tsutsugamushi/Orientia tsutsugamushi)
  • Transmitted by Leptotrombidium species
  • Common in Asia-Pacific region ("tsutsugamushi triangle")

99. Where are chigger mites commonly found and who are accidental hosts?

Answer:

Ecology:

  • Agricultural areas/pastures
  • Scrub vegetation following agricultural processes
  • Moist but well-drained soil areas

Accidental hosts:

  • Humans are accidental hosts
  • Important in aiding dispersal of larvae to other areas
  • Provide support for larvae away from vegetation

100. What control measures are effective against chigger mites?

Answer:

  • Repellents: DEET, benzyl benzoate on exposed skin
  • Clothing: Impregnated/sprayed with repellents or permethrin
  • Burning scrub vegetation in endemic areas
  • Insecticidal applications by aircraft in large areas
  • Personal protection: Long sleeves, pants, tucked in
  • Avoid sitting on ground in endemic areas

Vector Biology Concepts

101. Define and differentiate between cyclopropagative, cyclodevelopmental, and propagative transmission.

Answer:

Cyclopropagative:

  • Disease agent undergoes cyclic development AND multiplies in vector
  • Both development and increase in pathogen number
  • Example: Plasmodium in Anopheles

Cyclodevelopmental:

  • Disease agent undergoes cyclic development when transmitted by vector
  • Cyclic change but does NOT multiply in vector body
  • Example: Filarial worms in mosquitoes

Propagative:

  • Only multiplication stage of disease transmission
  • No development, only pathogen number increases
  • Example: Some viruses in mosquitoes

102. What are passive vectors and give an example?

Answer: Passive vectors:

  • Mechanical transmission - No biological development of pathogen in vector
  • Composed of outdoor components only
  • Non-living vectors (fomites) can also act as passive vectors
  • Example: Houseflies carrying bacteria on their feet/mouthparts

103. Define the following terms: anthropophilic vs zoophilic.

Answer:

  • Anthropophilic: Preference for human blood meals (e.g., Anopheles gambiae)
  • Zoophilic: Preference for animal blood meals (e.g., An. arabiensis)

This affects vector competence and disease transmission efficiency.

104. Define the following mosquito behavioral terms: endophagic, exophagic, endophilic, exophilic.

Answer:

  • Endophagic: Feeds indoors
  • Exophagic: Feeds outdoors
  • Endophilic: Rests indoors
  • Exophilic: Rests outdoors

These behaviors determine effectiveness of control measures like IRS and ITNs.

105. What is the difference between autogenous and anautogenous mosquitoes?

Answer:

  • Autogenous: Can develop eggs without a blood meal (e.g., some Culex species)
  • Anautogenous: Requires blood meal for egg development (e.g., Anopheles females, most mosquitoes)

Blood provides protein necessary for egg production (vitellogenesis).

106. Define parthenogenesis in the context of mosquito reproduction.

Answer: Parthenogenesis is a form of asexual reproduction where:

  • Offspring develop without fertilization
  • Eggs develop into viable adults without male involvement
  • Possible in some mosquito species
  • Results in female-only or clonal populations

107. What is behavioral resistance in vectors?

Answer: Behavioral resistance occurs when vectors change their behavior to avoid control measures:

  • Shift from endophagic to exophagic (feed outdoors to avoid IRS)
  • Shift from endophilic to exophilic (rest outdoors to avoid treated walls)
  • Change biting times to avoid ITNs
  • Results from selection pressure by control interventions
  • Makes existing control methods less effective

108. What is a supervector and give two examples?

Answer: Supervector: A highly efficient disease vector with characteristics that maximize transmission:

  • High anthropophilic behavior
  • High population density
  • Close association with humans
  • Long lifespan
  • High vectorial capacity

Examples:

  1. Anopheles gambiae complex - Malaria in Africa
  2. An. stephensi - Malaria in Asia, recently in Africa

109. What is vectorial capacity?

Answer: Vectorial capacity is a measure of disease transmission potential that includes:

  • Vector density relative to host
  • Vector biting rate
  • Vector competence (ability to transmit pathogen)
  • Vector survival/longevity
  • Extrinsic incubation period of pathogen
  • Mathematical measure of transmission risk

110. Define transgenic vectors and their purpose in vector control.

Answer: Transgenic vectors: Include a foreign gene into vector's genome to create GMOs (Genetically Modified Organisms).

Purpose:

  • Gene therapy
