  • Reducing vector competence (make vectors unable to transmit disease)
  • Mosquito population suppression (sterile insect technique)
  • Resistance to pathogens (vectors that cannot support pathogen development)
  • Altering vector behavior (making them less attracted to humans)

Control Methods and Concepts

111. What is IRS (Indoor Residual Spraying) and what are its challenges?

Answer: IRS is the application of insecticides on interior walls of houses and structures where vectors rest.

Challenges:

  • Insecticide resistance - Vectors developing resistance
  • Requires trained personnel - Proper application techniques needed
  • Health concerns - Toxicity to humans and pets
  • Bottlenecks in implementation - Logistics, cost, coverage
  • Behavioral resistance - Vectors changing resting behavior
  • Community acceptance - Concerns about chemicals in homes

112. Describe the role of Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) in vector control.

Answer: Bt is a bacterial biopesticide used for mosquito larval control:

  • Produces toxins that kill insect larvae
  • Different strains for different vectors:
    • Bti (B. thuringiensis israelensis) - Most effective for mosquitoes and black flies
    • Bt - General use
  • Blocks chitin biosynthesis
  • Environmentally safe
  • Specific to target insects
  • No resistance issues (when used properly)

113. What are the advantages of using ITNs (Insecticide-Treated Nets) and LLINs (Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets)?

Answer:

Advantages:

  • Physical barrier against mosquito bites
  • Insecticide kills/repels mosquitoes on contact
  • Protects sleeping individuals (when mosquitoes most active)
  • LLINs: Insecticide incorporated into fibers, lasts 3-5 years
  • Community protection effect
  • Reduces disease transmission
  • Cost-effective

Common insecticide: Permethrin (pyrethroid)

114. What is the purpose of canopy traps in vector control?

Answer: Canopy traps are used for:

  • Monitoring and controlling tabanid flies (horse flies, deer flies)
  • Traps placed in open areas
  • Exploit tabanids' attraction to:
    • Large dark objects
    • Movement
    • Visual cues
  • Effective for surveillance and population reduction
  • Non-chemical control method

115. Describe the concept of integrated vector management (IVM).

Answer: IVM combines multiple control strategies:

Components:

  • Chemical: Insecticides (IRS, larvicides)
  • Biological: Predators (fish, Toxorhynchites), Bt
  • Physical/Mechanical: Nets, screens, habitat modification
  • Genetic: Sterile insect technique, transgenic vectors
  • Environmental: Source reduction, sanitation
  • Community participation: Education, behavior change

Benefits:

  • Reduces reliance on single method
  • Delays resistance development
  • More sustainable
  • Cost-effective

116. What is the Ngu trap and for which vector is it used?

Answer: Ngu trap is used for tsetse fly (Glossina spp.) control:

  • Exploits tsetse attraction to:
    • Dark moving objects
    • Blue/black colors
    • Visual and olfactory cues
  • Traps placed strategically in tsetse habitats
  • Cost-effective surveillance and control method
  • Part of integrated tsetse management

117. Explain the sterile insect technique (SIT) and its application.

Answer: SIT involves:

  • Mass rearing of target insect
  • Sterilization (usually by radiation)
  • Release of sterile males into wild population
  • Sterile males mate with wild females
  • No viable offspring produced
  • Population gradually declines

Applications:

  • Tsetse flies - African trypanosomiasis control
  • Mosquitoes - Aedes, Anopheles programs
  • Success: Depends on releasing enough sterile males to overwhelm wild males

118. What is the refractory index in genetic vector control?

Answer: Refractory index refers to:

  • Use of endosymbionts/bacteria (e.g., Wolbachia) that:
    • Kill mosquitoes, OR
    • Prevent Plasmodium parasite survival/development in mosquito
  • Creates "refractory vectors" - mosquitoes that cannot transmit disease
  • Genetically modified vectors resistant to pathogen infection
  • Example: Wolbachia-infected Aedes for dengue control

119. Why is source reduction important in mosquito control?

Answer: Source reduction eliminates/modifies larval breeding sites:

Importance:

  • Prevents mosquito production at source
  • Most cost-effective long-term strategy
  • Reduces need for insecticides
  • Environmentally sustainable
  • No resistance development

Methods:

  • Drain stagnant water
  • Remove/empty containers
  • Fill ditches
  • Improve drainage
  • Community participation essential

120. What is the knockdown effect of pyrethroids?

Answer: Knockdown effect:

  • Rapid paralysis of insects upon contact with pyrethroid insecticides
  • Insects fall from surfaces quickly
  • May or may not lead to death (depending on dose)
  • Makes pyrethroids ideal for:
    • Space sprays
    • Aerosols
    • ITNs/LLINs
  • Provides immediate protection
  • Visible effect shows insecticide is working

Disease-Vector-Pathogen Relationships

121. Complete the following: Malaria is transmitted by _______ genus, specifically _______ species are most important.

Answer: Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles genus, specifically:

  • An. gambiae complex (supervector - most important in Africa)
  • An. funestus
  • An. stephensi (Asia, recently Africa)
  • An. arabiensis

Causative agent: Plasmodium species (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi)

122. What vector transmits lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) and what is the causative agent?

Answer:

  • Vector: Culex quinquefasciatus (also Anopheles, Aedes in some regions)
  • Causative agent: Wuchereria bancrofti (filarial nematode)
  • Disease: Lymphatic filariasis/elephantiasis
  • Worms block lymphatic vessels causing massive swelling

123. Match the following arboviruses with their vectors: Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, Yellow fever.

Answer: All four are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes:

  • Aedes aegypti (primary vector)
  • Aedes albopictus (secondary vector)

Arboviruses:

  1. Dengue fever - Dengue virus
  2. Chikungunya - Chikungunya virus
  3. Zika - Zika virus
  4. Yellow fever - Yellow fever virus

All show transovarial transmission.

124. What is the vector and causative agent of river blindness?

Answer:

  • Disease: River blindness (Onchocerciasis)
  • Vector: Simulium species (black flies)
  • Causative agent: Onchocerca volvulus (filarial nematode)
  • Geographic distribution: Africa, Yemen, Central/South America
  • Pathology: Microfilariae in skin and eyes cause blindness

125. What diseases do Glossina palpalis and G. morsitans transmit?

Answer:

G. palpalis and G. tachinoides:

  • West African (Gambian) trypanosomiasis
  • Causative agent: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense
  • Chronic form (sleeping sickness)

G. morsitans, G. swynnertoni, G. pallidipes:

  • East African (Rhodesian) trypanosomiasis
  • Causative agent: Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense
  • Acute form (sleeping sickness)

126. What vector transmits Loa loa and where is it found?

Answer:

  • Vector: Chrysops species (deer flies) - C. silacea, C. dimidiata
  • Causative agent: Loa loa (African eye worm)
  • Geographic distribution: West and Central Africa
  • Disease: Loiasis - worm migrates through subcutaneous tissues and across eye (conjunctiva)
  • Causes Calabar swellings

127. What are the vectors and causative agents of the three types of leishmaniasis?

Answer:

Vector: Sandflies (Phlebotomus - Old World; Lutzomyia - New World)

Types:

  1. Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar):
    • Leishmania donovani
    • Affects internal organs (spleen, liver)
  2. Cutaneous leishmaniasis:
    • Leishmania tropica (Old World)
    • Skin lesions/ulcers
  3. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis:
    • Leishmania braziliensis complex
    • Affects mucous membranes (nose, mouth)

128. What is the causative agent and vector of Chagas disease?

Answer:

  • Disease: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis)
  • Vector: Triatomine bugs (kissing bugs) - Triatoma, Rhodnius, Panstrongylus
  • Causative agent: Trypanosoma cruzi
  • Distribution: Central and South America
  • Transmission: Through infected bug feces rubbed into bite wound

129. What disease does Xenopsylla cheopis transmit and what is the reservoir host?

Answer:

  • Vector: Xenopsylla cheopis (rat flea)
  • Primary disease: Bubonic plague
  • Causative agent: Yersinia pestis
  • Reservoir host: Rats (Rattus rattus, R. norvegicus)
  • Also transmits: Murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi)

130. What diseases are transmitted by body lice and through what route?

Answer:

Vector: Pediculus humanus corporis (body louse)

Diseases (all transmitted transcutaneously):

  1. Epidemic typhus - Rickettsia prowazekii
  2. Louse-borne relapsing fever - Borrelia recurrentis
  3. Trench fever - Bartonella quintana

Route: Scratching infected louse feces into bite wounds

131. What tick-borne diseases affect humans and what are their vectors?

Answer:

Soft ticks (Argasidae):

  • Tick-borne relapsing fever - Borrelia duttoni (Ornithodoros)

Hard ticks (Ixodidae):

  • Lyme disease - Borrelia burgdorferi (Ixodes)
  • Rocky Mountain spotted fever - Rickettsia rickettsii (Dermacentor)
  • Tick-borne encephalitis - Virus (Ixodes)
  • Q fever - Coxiella burnetii (various)
  • Ehrlichiosis - Ehrlichia spp. (Amblyomma)

132. What disease is transmitted by Leptotrombidium mites and where is it endemic?

Answer:

  • Disease: Scrub typhus
  • Causative agent: Rickettsia tsutsugamushi (Orientia tsutsugamushi)
  • Vector: Leptotrombidium species (L. deliense, L. akamushi, L. fletcheri)
  • Endemic region: Asia-Pacific ("tsutsugamushi triangle") - Southeast Asia, Japan, northern Australia
  • Reservoir: Rodents

133. What vector transmits Rift Valley fever and what is unique about its transmission?

Answer:

  • Vector: Aedes and Culex mosquitoes
  • Causative agent: Rift Valley fever virus (Phlebovirus)
  • Unique transmission:
    • Transovarial transmission - virus passed to eggs
    • Mechanical transmission - also by Aedes
  • Geographic distribution: Africa, Arabian Peninsula
  • Also affects: Livestock (major economic impact)

134. What enteropathogens are mechanically transmitted by houseflies?

Answer: Musca domestica (housefly) mechanically transmits:

  • Shigella (bacillary dysentery)
  • E. coli (diarrhea)
  • Salmonella typhi (typhoid fever)
  • Vibrio cholerae (cholera)
  • Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery)
  • Various intestinal parasites (Giardia, helminth eggs)

Route: Body hairs, mouthparts, regurgitation, defecation

135. What intermediate host role do Ctenocephalides fleas play?

Answer: Ctenocephalides (C. felis - cat flea; C. canis - dog flea) are intermediate hosts for:

Cestodes (tapeworms):

  1. Dipylidium caninum (dog tapeworm)
  2. Hymenolepis diminuta (rat tapeworm)

Bacteria: 3. Bartonella henselae (cat scratch disease)

Humans (especially children) infected by accidentally ingesting infected fleas.

Additional Clinical and Applied Questions

136. A patient presents with itchy, linear burrow tracks between fingers. What is the likely diagnosis and causative agent?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Classic scabies
  • Causative agent: Sarcoptes scabiei
  • Characteristic features:
    • Linear burrow tracks (tunnels)
    • Interdigital web spaces most affected
    • Severe pruritus, worse at night
    • Worse after hot bath
  • Diagnosis confirmed by: Skin scraping showing mites, eggs, or fecal pellets

137. Why are Anopheles mosquitoes most efficiently controlled by IRS and ITNs?

Answer: Because Anopheles are:

  • Endophagic - Feed indoors (ITNs protect during feeding)
  • Endophilic - Rest indoors after feeding (IRS kills resting mosquitoes)
  • Nocturnal - Feed when people are sleeping under nets
  • These behaviors make them highly vulnerable to indoor interventions
  • Other mosquitoes (Culex, Aedes) are more exophilic/exophagic, so less affected

138. A farmer in East Africa presents with subcutaneous swellings that appear and disappear. He reports seeing a worm cross his eye. What is the diagnosis and vector?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Loiasis (Loa loa infection)
  • Vector: Chrysops species (C. silacea, C. dimidiata) - deer flies
  • Characteristic features:
    • Calab

Medical Entomology Short Answer Questions - CONTINUED

Additional Clinical and Applied Questions - Continued

138. A farmer in East Africa presents with subcutaneous swellings that appear and disappear. He reports seeing a worm cross his eye. What is the diagnosis and vector?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Loiasis (Loa loa infection)
  • Vector: Chrysops species (C. silacea, C. dimidiata) - deer flies
  • Characteristic features:
    • Calabar swellings (transient subcutaneous swellings)
    • Adult worm migrates through conjunctiva (visible crossing eye)
    • Geographic distribution: West and Central Africa
  • Treatment: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC), surgical removal of adult worm from eye

139. Why is transovarial transmission important in arbovirus epidemiology?

Answer: Transovarial transmission is important because:

  • Virus maintenance: Virus survives in vector population between transmission seasons
  • Adults emerge already infected: No need to acquire virus from host
  • Amplifies transmission: Increases infected vector population
  • Overwintering mechanism: Virus survives in eggs during dry/cold seasons
  • Rapid outbreak potential: Large numbers of infected vectors can emerge simultaneously
  • Example: Rift Valley fever, dengue, Zika in Aedes mosquitoes

140. A patient in South America develops facial swelling and cardiomyopathy years after being bitten by a "kissing bug." What is the diagnosis and why is it called a "kissing bug"?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis)
  • Causative agent: Trypanosoma cruzi
  • Vector: Triatomine bugs (Triatoma, Rhodnius, Panstrongylus)
  • Called "kissing bug" because:
    • Prefer to bite around mouth/face area
    • Bite painlessly at night while person sleeps
    • Feed on exposed facial areas
  • Clinical features: Acute phase → Chronic phase (cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus, megacolon)

141. Why are container-breeding mosquitoes (Aedes) difficult to control with traditional larvicides?

Answer:

  • Dispersed breeding sites: Countless small containers in urban areas
  • Artificial containers: Tires, vases, buckets, bottle caps - hard to locate all
  • Indoor breeding: Many containers inside homes, inaccessible to outdoor spraying
  • Frequent refilling: Rain refills containers, requiring repeated treatment
  • Community participation needed: Source reduction requires household cooperation
  • Better strategy: Community-based source reduction (emptying containers)

142. A child presents with fever, headache, and a black eschar (tache noire) on the leg. Patient recently went camping in tall grass in Asia. What is the likely diagnosis?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Scrub typhus
  • Causative agent: Orientia tsutsugamushi (Rickettsia tsutsugamushi)
  • Vector: Leptotrombidium species (chigger mite larvae)
  • Characteristic feature: Black eschar (necrotic lesion) at bite site
  • Geographic distribution: Asia-Pacific ("tsutsugamushi triangle")
  • Risk factors: Walking through scrub vegetation where larvae quest
  • Treatment: Doxycycline

143. Why is An. stephensi considered a major threat to malaria control in Africa?

Answer: An. stephensi is a threat because:

  • Supervector from Asia now established in Africa
  • Urban adaptation: Breeds in artificial water containers (unlike rural African vectors)
  • Arid adaptation: Can withstand high temperatures and drought conditions
  • Year-round transmission: Not dependent on seasonal rainfall
  • Insecticide resistance: May carry resistance genes
  • Expands malaria range: Threatens urban areas previously malaria-free
  • High vectorial capacity: Efficient malaria transmitter

144. Explain why removing a tick incorrectly (by squeezing the body) can increase disease transmission risk.

Answer:

  • Squeezing tick body forces:
    • Regurgitation of gut contents into wound
    • Injection of more saliva (containing pathogens)
    • Increased pathogen transfer
  • Correct removal: Grasp near head with tweezers, pull straight out steadily
  • Don't squeeze, twist, or burn tick
  • Pathogens in tick gut/saliva: Borrelia, Rickettsia, viruses
  • Risk increases with: Duration of attachment and manipulation during removal

145. A rural community in West Africa wants to reduce tsetse fly populations. What integrated control strategy would you recommend?

Answer:

Integrated Tsetse Management:

1. Physical/Mechanical:

  • Deploy Ngu traps (blue/black targets)
  • Targets impregnated with insecticides

2. Habitat Management:

  • Selective clearing of riverine vegetation
  • Bush clearing along water sources
  • Maintain some vegetation for ecological balance

3. Chemical:

  • Aerial spraying in dry season
  • Pour-on insecticides on livestock (attract tsetse)

4. Biological:

  • Sterile Insect Technique (SIT)
  • Release sterile males

5. Community Participation:

  • Education on tsetse habitat
  • Livestock management
  • Reporting sick animals

146. Why do some mosquito species become resistant to pyrethroids used in ITNs, and what are the resistance mechanisms?

Answer:

Resistance Mechanisms:

1. Target site resistance:

  • Mutation in voltage-gated sodium channel (kdr - knockdown resistance)
  • Changes binding site so pyrethroid cannot attach
  • Most common mechanism

2. Metabolic resistance:

  • Increased detoxification enzymes (P450s, esterases, GSTs)
  • Break down pyrethroid before it acts
  • Overexpression of metabolic genes

3. Behavioral resistance:

  • Shift to exophagic/exophilic behavior
  • Avoid contact with treated surfaces
  • Feed/rest outdoors

Why it develops:

  • Selection pressure from widespread ITN use
  • High pyrethroid usage (only class approved for ITNs)
  • Genetic selection over generations

147. A patient with HIV/AIDS presents with thick, crusted skin lesions crawling with mites. What type of scabies is this and why is it highly contagious?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies
  • Why highly contagious:
    • Thousands to millions of mites on skin (vs. 10-15 in classic scabies)
    • Mites easily shed from hyperkeratotic crusts
    • Direct skin contact spreads massive numbers of mites
    • Fomites (bedding, clothes) heavily contaminated
    • Patient often immunocompromised (reduced immune response)
  • Risk factors: HIV/AIDS, elderly, immunosuppressed, institutionalized patients
  • Treatment: Multiple applications of scabicide, ivermectin, treat all contacts

148. Why is source reduction considered the most sustainable mosquito control strategy?

Answer:

Advantages of Source Reduction:

1. Environmental sustainability:

  • No chemicals or insecticides needed
  • No environmental pollution
  • Safe for humans and non-target organisms

2. No resistance development:

  • Physical removal of breeding sites
  • Cannot develop biological resistance

3. Cost-effective long-term:

  • One-time infrastructure improvements
  • Reduces need for ongoing insecticide purchases
  • Community-based, low-tech

4. Reduces multiple vector species:

  • Targets breeding sites of Anopheles, Culex, Aedes
  • Not species-specific

5. Community empowerment:

  • Engages communities in their own protection
  • Education and behavior change
  • Sustainable beyond project duration

Challenges: Requires sustained community participation and behavior change

149. Explain why black fly control is achieved by treating fast-flowing rivers rather than stagnant water.

Answer:

  • Black fly breeding habitat: Fast-flowing, well-oxygenated water
  • Larvae attach to: Rocks and vegetation in streams/rivers
  • Require: High oxygen levels (unlike mosquitoes)
  • Larvicide application: Applied to water surfaces, flows downstream
  • Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis): Applied to rivers, kills larvae for 15-30 minutes as it flows
  • Habitat modification: Straighten rivers, remove obstructions to increase flow velocity
  • Different from mosquitoes: Mosquitoes breed in stagnant water, black flies in moving water

150. A blood smear shows microfilariae with diurnal periodicity. The patient lives in West Africa. What is the diagnosis and vector?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Loiasis (Loa loa infection)
  • Vector: Chrysops species (deer flies) - diurnal feeders
  • Microfilariae characteristics:
    • Diurnal periodicity: Peak levels in blood during day (matches vector feeding time)
    • Sheathed microfilariae
  • Clinical features: Calabar swellings, eye worm migration
  • Contrast with:
    • W. bancrofti - nocturnal periodicity (Culex feeds at night)
    • Onchocerca - in skin, not blood

151. Why are ITNs less effective against Aedes mosquitoes compared to Anopheles?

Answer:

Behavioral differences:

Anopheles:

  • Nocturnal feeders (peak midnight-dawn)
  • Endophagic/endophilic
  • People protected under nets during feeding times
  • ITNs highly effective

Aedes:

  • Diurnal feeders (early morning, late afternoon)
  • Bimodal biting pattern
  • Exophagic/exophilic
  • People active and outdoors during Aedes feeding times
  • Not protected by ITNs during peak biting

Better Aedes control:

  • Source reduction (remove containers)
  • Personal protection (repellents, long sleeves)
  • Larvicides in containers
  • Community-based container management

152. Describe the "fly belt" of Africa and its significance for African trypanosomiasis.

Answer:

"Fly Belt" or "Tsetse Belt":

  • Region of Sub-Saharan Africa between 15°N and 20°S latitude
  • Geographic distribution of tsetse flies (Glossina spp.)
  • Covers ~10 million km² across 37 African countries

Significance:

  • Sleeping sickness endemic zone: Human African trypanosomiasis limited to this area
  • Animal trypanosomiasis (nagana): Major constraint to livestock development
  • Economic impact: Limits cattle raising, agriculture, development
  • No tsetse outside Africa: Disease geographically restricted

Habitat types within belt:

  • Forest (palpalis group)
  • Savanna (morsitans group)
  • Riverine (palpalis group)

153. A homeless person presents with severe itching, fever, and multiple bite marks. Lice are found in clothing seams. What diseases should you be concerned about?

Answer:

Diagnosis: Body louse infestation (pediculosis corporis)

Vector-borne diseases to screen for:

1. Epidemic typhus:

  • Rickettsia prowazekii
  • Most serious concern
  • Symptoms: High fever, headache, rash

2. Louse-borne relapsing fever:

  • Borrelia recurrentis
  • Relapsing fevers

3. Trench fever:

  • Bartonella quintana
  • Chronic bacteremia

Risk factors: Homelessness, poor hygiene, crowded conditions, refugees, disasters

Management:

  • Treat patient with appropriate antibiotics
  • Delousing: Wash/iron clothing, ivermectin
  • Address underlying social conditions

154. Why is the pupal stage of mosquitoes a non-feeding stage and what are the implications for larval control?

Answer:

Pupal characteristics:

  • Non-feeding (resting) stage
  • Comma-shaped
  • Mobile but doesn't feed
  • Metamorphosis occurring inside
  • Lasts 2-3 days
  • Resistant to larvicides (doesn't ingest)

Implications for control:

  • Larvicides ineffective against pupae: Must target earlier larval stages
  • Timing critical: Apply larvicides when larvae present (L1-L4)
  • Pupae near emergence: Source reduction still effective (physically remove)
  • Why target larvae: Feeding stages vulnerable to stomach poisons and Bti
  • Pupae as indicators: Presence indicates imminent adult emergence

155. What is the "knockdown resistance" (kdr) mutation and why is it a concern for malaria control?

Answer:

kdr (knockdown resistance) mutation:

  • Mutation in voltage-gated sodium channel gene
  • Target site of pyrethroid and DDT insecticides
  • Changes amino acid sequence (L1014F, L1014S mutations common)
  • Prevents insecticide binding

Concern for malaria control:

  • Pyrethroids only class approved for ITNs/LLINs
  • Widespread: kdr found in Anopheles across Africa, Asia
  • Reduces ITN effectiveness: Mosquitoes survive contact with nets
  • Cross-resistance: Affects both pyrethroids and DDT
  • Limited alternatives: Few insecticide classes safe for ITNs
  • Threatens control gains: Malaria resurgence risk

Mitigation strategies:

  • Rotate insecticide classes (for IRS)
  • Combination nets (pyrethroid + PBO synergist)
  • New insecticide development
  • Non-chemical methods (source reduction)

156. Explain why removing termite mounds is an effective control measure against sandflies.

Answer:

Sandfly biology:

  • Oviposit in small cracks and holes in ground
  • Base of termite mounds is preferred breeding site
  • Also breed in termite mound crevices
  • Require high humidity (termite mounds provide this)

Why termite mound removal works:

  • Eliminates breeding habitat
  • Reduces humidity microhabitats
  • Removes resting sites for adults
  • Disrupts life cycle

Additional sandfly control:

  • Spray insecticides on cracks in walls
  • Target animal burrows
  • Remove rubbish heaps
  • Personal protection (repellents, clothing)

Challenge: Labor-intensive, termite mounds widespread in endemic areas

157. A patient presents with a painful boil-like lesion on the arm. Examination reveals a small breathing hole in the center and movement inside. What is the diagnosis?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Cutaneous (furuncular) myiasis
  • Also called "creeping eruption"
  • Cause: Fly larvae developing under skin
  • Common flies: Dermatobia hominis (human botfly), Cordylobia anthropophaga (tumbu fly)

Characteristics:

  • Boil-like inflammation
  • Small hole (spiracle) for larva to breathe
  • Movement/sensation of something crawling inside
  • Pain, itching
  • Secondary bacterial infection risk

Treatment:

  • Remove larvae under aseptic conditions
  • Methods: Occlusion (petroleum jelly blocks spiracle, forces larva out), surgical extraction
  • Antibiotics if secondary infection
  • Tetanus prophylaxis

158. Why do Culex mosquitoes breed in polluted water while Anopheles prefer clean water?

Answer:

Larval adaptations:

Culex:

  • Tolerate organic pollution: Sewage, drains, pit latrines
  • Feed on bacteria and organic particles
  • Siphon allows breathing at surface despite scum
  • Ecological niche: Exploits polluted urban water
  • High organic matter supports larval nutrition

Anopheles:

  • Require cleaner water: Vegetated, sunlit pools
  • Feed on algae and microorganisms
  • Lie parallel to surface (need clear water)
  • Ecological niche: Natural, rural water bodies
  • Presence of algae and vegetation essential

Control implications:

  • Culex: Sanitation, proper sewage systems
  • Anopheles: Source reduction, drainage of clean pools
  • Different breeding sites require different strategies

159. Describe the epidemiological significance of zoophilic mosquitoes in disease transmission.

Answer:

Zoophilic species (e.g., An. arabiensis):

Reduced human disease transmission:

  • Prefer feeding on animals over humans
  • Zooprophylaxis: Animals act as "dead-end" hosts for human pathogens
  • Diverts mosquito bites away from humans
  • Lower vectorial capacity for human diseases

Applications in control:

  • Livestock as barriers: Place animals between humans and mosquito breeding sites
  • Cattle pens: Attract zoophilic vectors away from houses
  • Can treat animals with insecticides (pour-ons)

Limitations:

  • Opportunistic feeding still occurs
  • Some pathogens cycle in animal reservoirs
  • May still transmit zoonotic diseases
  • Anthropophilic species (An. gambiae) remain primary vectors

Contrast: Anthropophilic vectors (human-preferring) are most efficient disease transmitters

160. Why is maggot therapy making a comeback in modern wound care?

Answer:

Benefits of maggot therapy (Lucilia sericata larvae):

1. Selective debridement:

  • Larvae feed only on dead/necrotic tissue
  • Leave healthy tissue intact
  • More precise than surgical debridement

2. Antimicrobial effects:

  • Secrete antimicrobial substances
  • Reduce bacterial load in wounds
  • Effective against MRSA and other resistant bacteria

3. Promotes healing:

  • Stimulates granulation tissue formation
  • Growth factors in secretions
  • Improves wound healing rates

4. Cost-effective:

  • Less expensive than multiple surgeries
  • Reduces hospital stay
  • Outpatient application possible

5. Antibiotic resistance era:

  • Alternative to antibiotics
  • Effective against resistant bacteria
  • No resistance development to maggots

Applications: Diabetic ulcers, pressure sores, post-surgical wounds, burns

Preparation: Sterile, laboratory-reared larvae used

161. Explain the concept of extrinsic incubation period (EIP) and its importance in vector-borne disease transmission.

Answer:

Extrinsic Incubation Period (EIP):

  • Time from vector ingesting pathogen to when vector can transmit
  • Period pathogen needs to develop in vector to infectious stage
  • Temperature-dependent (warmer = shorter EIP)

Importance:

1. Vector must survive EIP to transmit:

  • If vector dies before EIP complete, no transmission
  • Longer EIP = lower transmission (more vectors die)

2. Temperature effects:

  • Warmer climates: Shorter EIP, more transmission
  • Climate change: Expanding disease ranges as EIP shortens

3. Examples:

  • Malaria (Plasmodium): 10-14 days in mosquito
  • Dengue: 8-12 days
  • West Nile virus: 10-14 days

4. Control implications:

  • Reducing vector longevity very effective
  • Adult mosquito control critical
  • Insecticides targeting resting adults

Formula component: EIP affects vectorial capacity calculations

162. A traveler returns from Brazil with skin lesions that start as papules but progress to destructive lesions of the nasal mucosa. What is the diagnosis and vector?

Answer:

  • Diagnosis: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (espundia)
  • Causative agent: Leishmania braziliensis complex
  • Vector: Lutzomyia species (New World sandflies)
  • Geographic distribution: Central and South America

Clinical progression:

  • Primary cutaneous lesion (papule/ulcer)
  • Months to years later: metastatic spread to mucosa
  • Destructive lesions of nose, mouth, pharynx
  • Can cause disfigurement
  • Secondary bacterial infections

Diagnosis: Parasite identification, PCR, serology

Treatment: Antimonials, amphotericin B (more difficult to treat than cutaneous form)

163. Why is community participation essential for sustainable vector control programs?

Answer:

Reasons community participation is essential:

1. Source reduction requires household action:

  • Empty containers, cover water storage
  • Cannot be done by external programs alone
  • Individual households control breeding sites

2. Sustainability:

  • Programs end, but community behavior continues
  • Self-reliance reduces dependence on external resources
  • Cost-effective long-term

3. Local knowledge:

  • Communities know local breeding sites
  • Understand local practices and barriers
  • Cultural appropriateness

4. Ownership and empowerment:

  • Communities invested in their own health
  • Behavior change more likely with participation
  • Social mobilization amplifies impact

5. Integrated approaches:

  • Combines with chemical/biological control
  • Multiple strategies more effective
  • Reduces insecticide dependence

Challenges:

  • Requires sustained motivation
  • Education and awareness campaigns needed
  • May need incentives initially

Examples: Container management for Aedes control, use of ITNs, environmental sanitation

164. Describe the concept of "refractory vectors" in malaria control using Wolbachia.

Answer:

Refractory vectors:

  • Mosquitoes that cannot transmit malaria parasites
  • Genetically or biologically altered to block Plasmodium development

Wolbachia approach:

Mechanism:

  • Wolbachia bacteria infect mosquito
  • Blocks Plasmodium development in mosquito gut/salivary glands
  • Parasite cannot complete life cycle
  • Mosquito becomes transmission-incompetent

Advantages:

  • Self-sustaining: Wolbachia passed to offspring (cytoplasmic inheritance)
  • Population replacement: Infected mosquitoes gradually replace wild population
  • No insecticides: Biological control
  • No resistance concern: Not killing mosquitoes, just blocking transmission

Challenges:

  • Wolbachia naturally infects some mosquitoes but not all Anopheles
  • Technical challenges in establishing stable infections
  • Regulatory and ethical considerations

Success in other diseases: Wolbachia-infected Aedes effective against dengue

Alternative approaches: Transgenic mosquitoes, gene drives

**165. Why do some arbov

iruses show seasonality in their transmission?**

Answer:

Factors causing seasonal arbovirus transmission:

1. Vector population dynamics:

  • Rainy season: Increased breeding sites, more mosquitoes
  • Temperature: Warmer temperatures = faster mosquito development
  • Vector abundance peaks seasonally

2. Extrinsic Incubation Period (EIP):

  • Temperature-dependent: Warmer = shorter EIP
  • Cold temperatures slow/stop virus replication in vector
  • Transmission efficiency varies by season

3. Vector behavior:

  • Activity levels: Higher biting rates in warm weather
  • Some vectors less active in cold/dry seasons
  • Diapause in winter (temperate regions)

4. Host behavior:

  • Human: More outdoor activity in warm weather = more exposure
  • Amplification hosts: Migratory birds seasonal

5. Rainfall patterns:

  • Creates breeding sites (mosquitoes)
  • Floods can wash away larvae (complex relationship)

Examples:

  • West Nile virus: Summer/fall peaks in temperate regions
  • Dengue: Rainy season in tropics
  • Rift Valley fever: Heavy rains trigger outbreaks

Control implications: Target interventions before/during transmission season

Q1. Define the following terminologies (3 marks)

i. Zoophilic Vectors that prefer feeding on animal blood rather than human blood.

ii. Endophagic Vectors that prefer feeding indoors (inside buildings/houses).

iii. Fomite Non-living objects capable of transmitting infectious pathogens from one host to another.

Q2. With examples, outline five (5) medical importances of arthropods (10 marks)

1. Biological vectors of disease

  • Transmit pathogens that multiply/develop in them
  • Example: Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria; tsetse flies transmit sleeping sickness

2. Mechanical vectors

  • Carry pathogens on body parts without pathogen development
  • Example: Houseflies and cockroaches transmit cholera, typhoid

3. Direct causative agents

  • Cause disease through infestation
  • Example: Scabies mite (Sarcoptes scabiei), head lice

4. Venomous effects

  • Cause injury through bites/stings
  • Example: Scorpions, spiders, bees cause envenomation

5. Nuisance and allergic reactions

  • Cause irritation and hypersensitivity
  • Example: Mosquito bites, bed bugs, dust mites trigger allergies

Q3. Using an illustration, discuss the life cycle of a three-host tick (15 marks)

Three-Host Tick Life Cycle (e.g., Rhipicephalus appendiculatus)

Stages:

  1. Eggs → Laid on ground by engorged female (2,000-20,000 eggs)
  2. Larvae (6-legged) → Hatch, climb vegetation, attach to HOST 1 (small mammals/birds), feed 3-7 days, drop off, molt to nymph
  3. Nymph (8-legged) → Climb vegetation, attach to HOST 2 (medium mammals), feed 4-7 days, drop off, molt to adult
  4. Adult (8-legged) → Climb vegetation, attach to HOST 3 (large mammals/cattle), mate on host, female feeds 7-14 days, drops off, lays eggs, dies

Key feature: Each stage feeds on a different host and drops to ground to molt.

Duration: Complete cycle takes 6 months to 3 years depending on conditions.

Title: ONCOPATHOLOGY & HISTOPATHOLOGY ANSWERS
Content:
1. Differentiate between benign and malignant tumours.

Benign tumours:

  • Well differentiated
  • Encapsulated and well circumscribed
  • Do not invade locally or metastasize
  • Remain at primary site
  • Slow growth rate
  • Amenable to surgical removal

Malignant tumours:

  • Most are anaplastic; variable differentiation
  • Non-encapsulated
  • Locally invasive, cause tissue damage
  • Ability to metastasize from primary site
  • Rapid growth rate
  • Surgical intervention less effective

2. Define differentiation, anaplasia, pleomorphism, and dysplasia.

  • Differentiation: How similar tumour parenchymal cells are to normal parenchymal cells in morphology and function
  • Anaplasia: Lack of cellular differentiation
  • Pleomorphism: Differences in cell appearance (shape, size, features)
  • Dysplasia: Disorderly cellular growth

3. Give two examples each of:

a) Carcinomas:

  • Adenocarcinomas
  • Squamous cell carcinomas

b) Sarcomas:

  • Fibrosarcomas
  • Osteosarcomas

4. Define choristoma and hamartoma.

  • Choristoma: Group of cells found in locations where they are not normally found (ectopic cells)
  • Hamartoma: Group of cells clumped together in an unusual way

5. List the hallmarks of cancer.

  1. Self-sufficiency in growth signals
  2. Insensitivity to growth inhibitory signals
  3. Limitless replicative potential
  4. Evasion of apoptosis
  5. Altered cellular metabolism
  6. Sustained angiogenesis
  7. Ability to invade and metastasize
  8. Evasion of the immune system
  9. Genomic instability
  10. Tumour-enabling inflammation

6. Name five oncogenic viruses and the cancers they cause.

  1. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) - Burkitt Lymphoma, Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  2. Human T-cell Leukemia Virus (HTLV) - Adult T-cell Leukemia
  3. Hepatitis B Virus - Hepatocellular carcinoma
  4. Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) - Cervical cell carcinoma, Anal carcinoma
  5. Human Herpes Virus 8/Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpes Virus - Kaposi Sarcoma

7. Define tumour markers.

Substances whose presence indicates the presence of a neoplasm in the body. They can be enzymes produced in elevated amounts, proteins only produced in embryogenesis, or ectopic hormones from tumours.

8. Give examples of tumour markers and the conditions they indicate.

  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) - Liver, yolk sac tumours
  • Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA) - Various carcinomas
  • CA-125 - Ovarian cancer
  • CA 19-9 - Pancreatic cancer
  • CA 15-3 - Breast cancer

9. State the uses of tumour markers.

  1. Diagnosis of malignancy
  2. Prognosis of malignancy
  3. Detection of minimal residual disease
  4. Determination of therapy
  5. Investigation of drug resistance

10. Define cytopathology.

The study of the effect of diseases on individual cells morphologically. Includes the changes cells go through as a result of disease.

11. Define histopathology.

A branch of pathology that deals with the study of the effects of diseases on individual tissues.

12. What is a laboratory request form?

An official form of communication between a clinician and laboratory staff. Contains details on the procedures requested by the clinician for the laboratory staff to perform.

13. Define tissue fixation.

A histological method of preservation of tissue specimens that includes physical and chemical methods that stop vital cellular processes while maintaining tissue shape and volume for further histologic/cytologic examination.

14. Define tissue decalcification.

The process of removal of minerals from calcified tissues to allow preparation of thin tissue sections for examinations.

15. Define fine needle aspiration (FNA).

A method of sample collection in which a superfine needle is used to collect cells from the body. These cells are aspirated and placed on a slide for examination.

16. Define aspiration cytology.

A minimally invasive procedure in which study of cells is obtained by invading body organs minimally and collecting specific cells which are taken out and further examined.

17. Define exfoliative cytology.

Study of cells obtained from skin and mucous membranes. Could be obtained by brushing or washing of membranes.

18. Define immunohistochemistry.

The use of specific antibodies to identify and illustrate antigens. An immunologic reaction whereby antibodies specific to certain antigens are used to show their presence in tissues.

19. What are frozen sections?

Tissue samples prepared using a cryostat to cut and freeze them for the purpose of rapid diagnosis. Can be done during an operation.

20. List the components of a laboratory request form.

Patient's information:

  • Full name of patient, age, gender, requesting clinician's name

Specimen information:

  • Type of procedure requested (e.g., biopsy)
  • Location of specimen (e.g., laparoscopy left breast)

Clinical information:

  • Should be clearly written by clinician
  • Should include previous reports on any procedure performed on the patient
  • Drawings can be used for further illustration

Laboratory test required:

  • Can be ticked from various choices or written down

Laboratory information:

  • Filled by laboratory staff
  • Contains time and date when specimen was received
  • Rejection criteria if conditions not met (e.g., insufficient specimen)

21. Define fixatives and give examples.

Fixatives are chemicals used in histology to preserve tissue specimens. They work by arresting vital cellular processes while maintaining shape and volume of cells for further histologic/cytologic examination.

Examples:

  • Chemical fixatives: Formalin (10%), aldehydes (formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde), oxidizing agents (potassium dichromate, potassium permanganate), protein denaturing agents (methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, acetic acid)
  • Physical fixatives: Heat, microwave

22. State the functions of tissue fixation.

  1. Prevent autolysis and bacterial infections
  2. Maintain shape and volume of cells for further processes such as staining
  3. Keep cells as close to their living state as possible

23. Give examples of chemical fixatives.

  1. Aldehydes - Formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde (make covalent bonds between proteins to maintain cell structure)
  2. Oxidizing agents - Potassium dichromate, potassium permanganate (mostly used as secondary fixatives)
  3. Protein denaturing agents - Methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, acetic acid (denature cellular proteins)
  4. Miscellaneous fixatives: Mercury chloride (unsafe as it causes kidney damage)

24. Give examples of physical fixatives.

  1. Heat
  2. Microwave - Allows use of controlled heat; low heat leads to poor staining, high heat leads to vacuolization and overstaining of cytoplasm; rapid, non-chemical technique

25. Define decalcification and state tissues that require it.

Decalcification is the process of removing minerals from calcified tissues to enable preparation of thin sections for examinations. It enables a microtome to cut through tissue such as bone.

Tissues requiring decalcification:

  • Bone
  • Teeth
  • Calcified organs
  • Some tumors such as fibroids
  • Bone margins of amputated organs
  • Bone marrow specimens

26. List chemical agents used for decalcification.

  1. 10% Nitric acid
  2. Formal nitric acid
  3. Formic acid
  4. Potassium formate and formic acid
  5. Chelating agents such as EDTA

27. Differentiate between aspiration cytology and exfoliative cytology.

Aspiration cytology:

  • Involves study of cells obtained by invading body organs using an instrument
  • Examination of removed aspirates
  • Example: Fine needle aspiration

Exfoliative cytology:

  • Involves study of cells obtained from body surface and membranes such as skin
  • No need to invade body organs
  • Examples: Urine cells, bronchial washing, bronchial brushing

28. Give three examples of exfoliative cytology techniques.

  1. Pap smear of the cervix
  2. Urine cytology
  3. Bronchial washing/brushing

29. What is a Pap smear used for?

Detection of squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix.

30. Outline the steps in routine tissue processing (paraffin technique).

  1. Fixation - Using 10% formalin to maintain shape and volume
  2. Dehydration - Using increasing concentrations of alcohol to remove water from tissue
  3. Clearing - Using xylene to remove alcohol as it is immiscible with paraffin wax
  4. Infiltration - Using paraffin wax to maintain internal structure of tissue
  5. Embedding - Using paraffin wax to maintain external structure of tissue
  6. Cooling and fishing out - Using a slide containing albumin adhesives
  7. Sectioning/Microtomy - Using a microtome which cuts tissue into very thin slices
  8. Dewaxing - Using physical methods such as heat or chemical methods
  9. Rehydration - Using increasing concentrations of alcohol
  10. Staining - Using various histological stains such as Hematoxylin and Eosin to make cellular structures appear clearly and distinct
  11. Mounting - Placing the slide on a microscope
  12. Microscopy - Viewing prepared slide by adjusting magnification; for permanent slide, a cover slip is placed on top of tissue after mounting

Note: For calcified tissue such as bones, decalcification is done after fixation.

31. Why is decalcification necessary before tissue sectioning?

Decalcification is necessary to enable the microtome to cut through calcified tissues such as bone. Without removing the minerals, the hard calcified tissue cannot be sectioned into thin slices for examination.

Title: CHEMICAL PATHOLOGY PRACTICE EXAMINATION
Content:
MBPA 3600 - Year Three MBChB

Mount Kenya University - Department of Pathology

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES

  • Section A: Short Answer Questions (10 marks each) - Answer ANY TWO questions
  • Section B: Long Essay Questions (20 marks each) - Answer ANY ONE question
  • Time Allowed: 2 hours
  • Total Marks: 40 marks

SECTION A: SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (10 Marks Each)

Answer ANY TWO Questions

QUESTION 1

A 55-year-old diabetic patient presents to the emergency department with confusion, rapid breathing, and fruity breath odor. Random blood glucose is 28 mmol/L.

(a) Define diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). (2 marks)

(b) List FIVE biochemical investigations you would request to confirm and manage DKA. (5 marks)

(c) Explain the biochemical basis for the acid-base disturbance in DKA. (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 1

(a) Definition of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (2 marks)

  • DKA is a life-threatening acute metabolic complication of diabetes mellitus characterized by hyperglycemia (blood glucose >11 mmol/L), ketonemia/ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <15 mmol/L)
  • It results from absolute or relative insulin deficiency and excess counter-regulatory hormones

(b) Five biochemical investigations (5 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Blood glucose - to confirm hyperglycemia and monitor treatment
  2. Serum/urine ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate preferred) - to confirm ketonemia/ketonuria
  3. Arterial blood gas analysis - to assess acid-base status (pH, bicarbonate, pCO2)
  4. Serum electrolytes (Na+, K+, Cl-) - to calculate anion gap and monitor electrolyte imbalances
  5. Serum urea and creatinine - to assess renal function and hydration status

(c) Biochemical basis for acid-base disturbance (3 marks)

  • Insulin deficiency leads to increased lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation in the liver
  • This produces excessive ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone)
  • Ketone bodies are organic acids that accumulate in blood, causing metabolic acidosis with high anion gap
  • Compensatory respiratory alkalosis occurs through hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) to eliminate CO2

QUESTION 2

A 45-year-old man presents with severe chest pain radiating to the left arm. ECG shows ST-segment elevation.

(a) Name FOUR cardiac biomarkers used in the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. (4 marks)

(b) Describe the time course of troponin elevation and its clinical significance. (4 marks)

(c) State TWO conditions other than myocardial infarction that can cause troponin elevation. (2 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 2

(a) Four cardiac biomarkers (4 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Cardiac Troponin I (cTnI)
  2. Cardiac Troponin T (cTnT)
  3. Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB)
  4. Myoglobin

(b) Time course and clinical significance of troponin (4 marks)

  • Troponins begin to rise 3-4 hours after myocardial injury
  • Peak levels occur at 12-24 hours post-infarction
  • Remain elevated for 7-14 days (troponin I) or up to 21 days (troponin T)
  • Clinical significance: High sensitivity and specificity for myocardial injury; useful for early diagnosis, risk stratification, and detecting reinfarction
  • Serial measurements improve diagnostic accuracy

(c) Two other conditions causing troponin elevation (2 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Acute pulmonary embolism
  2. Chronic kidney disease/renal failure (Accept: myocarditis, heart failure, sepsis, severe hypertension, cardiac trauma)

QUESTION 3

A 35-year-old woman complains of fatigue, weight gain of 10 kg over 6 months, cold intolerance, and constipation.

(a) List FOUR thyroid function tests you would request. (4 marks)

(b) Describe the expected laboratory findings in primary hypothyroidism. (3 marks)

(c) Differentiate between primary and secondary hypothyroidism based on laboratory results. (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 3

(a) Four thyroid function tests (4 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
  2. Free Thyroxine (Free T4)
  3. Free Triiodothyronine (Free T3)
  4. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO antibodies)

(b) Expected laboratory findings in primary hypothyroidism (3 marks)

  • Elevated TSH (>4.5 mIU/L)
  • Low Free T4 (<12 pmol/L)
  • Low Free T3
  • May have positive thyroid antibodies (TPO, thyroglobulin antibodies) indicating autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease)

(c) Differentiation between primary and secondary hypothyroidism (3 marks)

Primary Hypothyroidism:

  • Elevated TSH, Low T4 and T3
  • Problem is in the thyroid gland itself

Secondary Hypothyroidism:

  • Low or normal TSH, Low T4 and T3
  • Problem is in the pituitary gland (reduced TSH secretion)

The key differentiator is TSH level: high in primary, low/normal in secondary

QUESTION 4

Explain the role of the kidney in maintaining acid-base balance.

(a) Describe THREE mechanisms by which the kidney regulates acid-base balance. (6 marks)

(b) Define metabolic acidosis and calculate the anion gap given the following values: Na+ 140 mmol/L, Cl- 100 mmol/L, HCO3- 15 mmol/L. (4 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 4

(a) Three mechanisms of renal acid-base regulation (6 marks - 2 marks each)

  1. Bicarbonate Reabsorption:
    • The proximal tubule reabsorbs approximately 80-90% of filtered bicarbonate
    • H+ is secreted into tubular fluid, combines with HCO3- to form H2CO3, which dissociates to CO2 and H2O
    • CO2 diffuses back into tubular cells and is reformed into HCO3- which enters blood
  2. Excretion of Titratable Acids (Phosphate Buffer System):
    • H+ ions are secreted and buffered by HPO4²- forming H2PO4-
    • This allows excretion of H+ without excessive lowering of urine pH
    • Accounts for about 30-40% of acid excretion
  3. Ammonia Buffer System:
    • Glutamine is metabolized in renal tubular cells to produce ammonia (NH3) and bicarbonate
    • NH3 diffuses into tubular lumen and combines with H+ to form NH4+ (ammonium)
    • NH4+ is trapped in tubular fluid and excreted in urine
    • Most important mechanism in chronic acidosis

(b) Definition and anion gap calculation (4 marks)

Definition (2 marks): Metabolic acidosis is a primary decrease in plasma bicarbonate (HCO3- <22 mmol/L) with or without compensatory decrease in pCO2, resulting in decreased blood pH (<7.35)

Anion Gap Calculation (2 marks):

  • Formula: Anion Gap = (Na+) - (Cl- + HCO3-)
  • Calculation: 140 - (100 + 15) = 25 mmol/L
  • Normal anion gap = 8-12 mmol/L
  • This represents HIGH anion gap metabolic acidosis

QUESTION 5

A 60-year-old man with chronic back pain is found to have hypercalcemia (serum calcium 3.2 mmol/L).

(a) List FOUR biochemical investigations you would perform to evaluate hypercalcemia. (4 marks)

(b) Describe the biochemical findings that would suggest primary hyperparathyroidism. (3 marks)

(c) State THREE clinical complications of prolonged hypercalcemia. (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 5

(a) Four biochemical investigations for hypercalcemia (4 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Serum parathyroid hormone (PTH)
  2. Serum phosphate
  3. Serum albumin (to calculate corrected calcium)
  4. 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels (Accept: alkaline phosphatase, serum protein electrophoresis, urea and creatinine)

(b) Biochemical findings in primary hyperparathyroidism (3 marks)

  • Elevated or inappropriately normal PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia
  • Low serum phosphate (due to increased renal phosphate excretion)
  • Elevated alkaline phosphatase (if bone involvement)
  • May have elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D
  • Increased urinary calcium excretion

(c) Three complications of prolonged hypercalcemia (3 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) and nephrocalcinosis
  2. Cardiac arrhythmias and shortened QT interval
  3. Neurological symptoms (confusion, lethargy, coma) (Accept: peptic ulcer disease, pancreatitis, bone disease, constipation)

QUESTION 6

A 28-year-old woman presents with jaundice. Laboratory results show: Total bilirubin 85 μmol/L (unconjugated 70 μmol/L), ALT 350 U/L, AST 320 U/L, ALP 150 U/L.

(a) Classify jaundice based on pathophysiology and give ONE example of each type. (6 marks)

(b) Based on the laboratory results above, what type of jaundice does this patient likely have? Justify your answer. (4 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 6

(a) Classification of jaundice (6 marks - 2 marks per type)

  1. Pre-hepatic (Hemolytic) Jaundice:
    • Excessive breakdown of red blood cells
    • Example: Sickle cell disease, hemolytic anemia, malaria
  2. Hepatic (Hepatocellular) Jaundice:
    • Dysfunction of hepatocytes affecting bilirubin metabolism
    • Example: Viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, Gilbert's syndrome
  3. Post-hepatic (Obstructive/Cholestatic) Jaundice:
    • Obstruction of bile flow in biliary tree
    • Example: Gallstones, pancreatic cancer, biliary stricture

(b) Type of jaundice and justification (4 marks)

Type: Hepatocellular (Hepatic) Jaundice (1 mark)

Justification (3 marks):

  • Markedly elevated transaminases (ALT 350, AST 320 U/L) indicate hepatocellular injury
  • Both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin are elevated with predominantly unconjugated (mixed pattern)
  • Alkaline phosphatase is only mildly elevated (not markedly raised as in cholestasis)
  • Pattern consistent with acute hepatitis (likely viral or drug-induced)

QUESTION 7

Discuss the clinical utility and interpretation of lipid profile tests.

(a) List FIVE components typically measured in a standard lipid profile. (5 marks)

(b) Explain the classification of lipoproteins based on density and their atherogenic potential. (5 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 7

(a) Five components of lipid profile (5 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Total cholesterol
  2. Triglycerides
  3. High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (HDL-C)
  4. Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (LDL-C)
  5. Very Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (VLDL-C) or calculated as non-HDL cholesterol

(b) Classification and atherogenic potential (5 marks)

Classification by density (2 marks):

  • Chylomicrons (lowest density)
  • VLDL (very low density)
  • LDL (low density)
  • HDL (high density)

Atherogenic potential (3 marks):

Atherogenic (Pro-atherogenic):

  • LDL cholesterol - primary atherogenic lipoprotein, deposits cholesterol in arterial walls
  • VLDL - carries triglycerides, remnants are atherogenic
  • Associated with increased cardiovascular risk

Anti-atherogenic (Protective):

  • HDL cholesterol - "good cholesterol"
  • Involved in reverse cholesterol transport (removes cholesterol from tissues to liver)
  • Higher levels associated with lower cardiovascular risk

QUESTION 8

A 50-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with abdominal pain and vomiting. Serum amylase is 1200 U/L.

(a) What is the most likely diagnosis? List THREE other biochemical tests useful in confirming this diagnosis. (4 marks)

(b) Explain the biochemical basis for elevated serum amylase in this condition. (3 marks)

(c) State THREE causes of elevated serum amylase other than your diagnosis in (a). (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 8

(a) Diagnosis and biochemical tests (4 marks)

Diagnosis (1 mark): Acute Pancreatitis

Three other biochemical tests (3 marks - 1 mark each):

  1. Serum lipase (more specific than amylase, remains elevated longer)
  2. Serum calcium (may be decreased due to fat saponification)
  3. Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP) - to assess for biliary obstruction (Accept: C-reactive protein, glucose, LDH, arterial blood gases)

(b) Biochemical basis for elevated amylase (3 marks)

  • Pancreatic inflammation and injury cause disruption of pancreatic acinar cells
  • Amylase leaks from damaged cells into surrounding tissue and bloodstream
  • Increased vascular permeability during inflammation allows enzyme entry into circulation
  • Serum amylase rises within 2-12 hours of onset, peaks at 12-72 hours, returns to normal in 3-5 days

(c) Three other causes of elevated serum amylase (3 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Parotitis (mumps, salivary gland disease)
  2. Perforated peptic ulcer or intestinal obstruction
  3. Renal failure (decreased clearance) (Accept: ectopic pregnancy, diabetic ketoacidosis, macroamylasemia)

QUESTION 9

A 40-year-old woman presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and bone pain. Serum calcium is elevated at 3.0 mmol/L.

(a) Explain the relationship between calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH). (4 marks)

(b) List THREE biochemical tests used to evaluate metabolic bone disorders. (3 marks)

(c) Differentiate between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism based on biochemical findings. (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 9

(a) Relationship between calcium and PTH (4 marks)

  • PTH is secreted by parathyroid glands in response to low serum calcium (inverse relationship)
  • PTH increases serum calcium through three mechanisms:
    1. Increases bone resorption (releases calcium from bone)
    2. Increases renal tubular calcium reabsorption (reduces urinary calcium loss)
    3. Increases renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (active vitamin D), which increases intestinal calcium absorption
  • High serum calcium normally suppresses PTH secretion (negative feedback)

(b) Three biochemical tests for metabolic bone disorders (3 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Serum calcium and phosphate
  2. Serum alkaline phosphatase (bone-specific ALP)
  3. 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (Accept: PTH, bone turnover markers like CTX, P1NP)

(c) Differentiation between primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism (3 marks)

Primary Hyperparathyroidism:

  • High PTH with HIGH serum calcium (hypercalcemia)
  • Low phosphate
  • Problem: parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism:

  • High PTH with LOW or NORMAL serum calcium
  • Often associated with chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency
  • Problem: appropriate PTH response to chronic hypocalcemia

QUESTION 10

Describe the principles of quality control in clinical biochemistry laboratories.

(a) Differentiate between accuracy and precision in laboratory testing. (4 marks)

(b) Explain the components of internal quality control (IQC). (4 marks)

(c) State TWO purposes of external quality assessment (EQA). (2 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 10

(a) Accuracy vs Precision (4 marks)

Accuracy (2 marks):

  • The closeness of a measured value to the true or accepted reference value
  • Measures systematic error or bias
  • Example: If true glucose is 5.0 mmol/L and test gives 5.1 mmol/L repeatedly, it's accurate

Precision (2 marks):

  • The reproducibility or repeatability of measurements
  • Measures random error
  • Example: If repeated measurements give 5.0, 5.1, 4.9, 5.0 mmol/L, this shows good precision
  • Can have precise results that are not accurate (consistent but wrong)

(b) Components of Internal Quality Control (4 marks)

  1. QC Materials (1 mark):
    • Use of control samples with known values run alongside patient samples
    • Include normal and abnormal level controls
  2. Levey-Jennings Charts (1 mark):
    • Plot QC results over time to monitor analytical performance
    • Establish mean and standard deviation limits
  3. Westgard Rules (1 mark):
    • Statistical rules to detect analytical errors
    • Examples: 1-2s (warning), 1-3s (rejection), 2-2s, R-4s rules
  4. Pre-analytical, Analytical, Post-analytical phases (1 mark):
    • Monitor all phases of testing process
    • Include specimen collection, handling, analysis, and result reporting

(c) Two purposes of External Quality Assessment (2 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Compare laboratory performance with other laboratories (inter-laboratory comparison)
  2. Identify systematic errors and ensure method standardization across laboratories

SECTION B: LONG ESSAY QUESTIONS (20 Marks Each)

Answer ANY ONE Question

QUESTION 11

Write comprehensive notes on Diabetes Mellitus covering:

(a) Classification of diabetes mellitus. (4 marks)

(b) Biochemical criteria for diagnosis of diabetes mellitus. (6 marks)

(c) Role of HbA1c in diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes. (5 marks)

(d) Complications of diabetes mellitus and relevant biochemical monitoring. (5 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 11

(a) Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (4 marks)

1. Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (1 mark):

  • Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
  • Absolute insulin deficiency
  • Usually presents in childhood/young adults
  • Requires insulin therapy

2. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (1 mark):

  • Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
  • Most common type (90-95% of cases)
  • Associated with obesity, sedentary lifestyle
  • Initially managed with lifestyle and oral agents

3. Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) (1 mark):

  • Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy
  • Usually resolves after delivery
  • Increases risk of future Type 2 DM

4. Other Specific Types (1 mark):

  • Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
  • Drug-induced (steroids, antipsychotics)
  • Pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis)
  • Endocrine disorders (Cushing's syndrome, acromegaly)

(b) Biochemical Criteria for Diagnosis (6 marks)

Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) (2 marks):

  • Diabetes: FPG ≥7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL)
  • Impaired Fasting Glucose: 6.1-6.9 mmol/L (110-125 mg/dL)
  • Normal: <6.1 mmol/L (<110 mg/dL)
  • Requires 8-hour fast

2-Hour Plasma Glucose during Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) (2 marks):

  • Diabetes: 2-hr PG ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL)
  • Impaired Glucose Tolerance: 7.8-11.0 mmol/L (140-199 mg/dL)
  • Normal: <7.8 mmol/L (<140 mg/dL)
  • 75g glucose load given

Random Plasma Glucose (1 mark):

  • Diabetes: Random PG ≥11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) with symptoms
  • Symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss

HbA1c (1 mark):

  • Diabetes: HbA1c ≥6.5% (48 mmol/mol)
  • Pre-diabetes: 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)
  • Normal: <5.7% (<39 mmol/mol)

(c) Role of HbA1c (5 marks)

What is HbA1c (1 mark):

  • Glycated hemoglobin - glucose attached non-enzymatically to hemoglobin
  • Reflects average blood glucose over preceding 2-3 months (lifespan of RBC)

Diagnostic Role (2 marks):

  • WHO approved HbA1c ≥6.5% as diagnostic criterion for diabetes
  • Advantages: no fasting required, less day-to-day variability, convenient
  • Limitations: not suitable in conditions affecting RBC lifespan (hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinopathies, recent blood transfusion, pregnancy)

Monitoring Role (2 marks):

  • Gold standard for assessing long-term glycemic control
  • Target: generally <7% (53 mmol/mol) for most diabetics, <6.5% for newly diagnosed
  • Should be measured every 3 months in poorly controlled patients, every 6 months in well-controlled patients
  • Predicts risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications
  • 1% reduction in HbA1c associated with 25% reduction in microvascular complications

(d) Complications and Biochemical Monitoring (5 marks)

Acute Complications (2 marks):

1. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA):

  • Monitor: blood glucose, ketones, arterial blood gases, electrolytes
  • Occurs mainly in Type 1 DM

2. Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS):

  • Monitor: blood glucose, serum osmolality, electrolytes
  • More common in Type 2 DM

3. Hypoglycemia:

  • Monitor blood glucose levels

Chronic Complications (3 marks):

1. Diabetic Nephropathy:

  • Monitor: urine albumin-creatinine ratio (microalbuminuria: 30-300 mg/g; macroalbuminuria: >300 mg/g)
  • Serum creatinine and eGFR

2. Cardiovascular Disease:

  • Monitor: lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides)
  • Cardiac biomarkers if symptomatic

3. Diabetic Neuropathy:

  • Clinical assessment primarily
  • May check vitamin B12 levels (metformin can cause deficiency)

4. Metabolic Monitoring:

  • Liver function tests (statins, fatty liver disease)
  • Electrolytes (diuretics, ACEI/ARBs)
  • Thyroid function (autoimmune association in Type 1)

QUESTION 12

Discuss Renal Function Tests in detail:

(a) Describe the biochemical assessment of glomerular function. (8 marks)

(b) Explain the biochemical assessment of tubular function. (6 marks)

(c) Discuss the role of urinalysis in evaluating renal disease. (6 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 12

(a) Biochemical Assessment of Glomerular Function (8 marks)

1. Serum Creatinine (2 marks):

  • Endogenous marker produced from muscle metabolism at constant rate
  • Filtered freely by glomerulus, not reabsorbed
  • Elevated in renal impairment (normal: 60-120 μmol/L)
  • Limitations: influenced by muscle mass, age, gender, diet
  • Not sensitive to early renal dysfunction (rises significantly only after 50% nephron loss)

2. Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) / Serum Urea (2 marks):

  • End product of protein metabolism
  • Filtered by glomerulus, partially reabsorbed in tubules
  • Normal: 2.5-7.5 mmol/L
  • Less specific than creatinine (affected by protein intake, hydration, GI bleeding, catabolic states)
  • BUN/Creatinine ratio useful: >20:1 suggests pre-renal azotemia

3. Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) (2 marks):

  • Most important measure of kidney function
  • Calculated using equations: CKD-EPI, MDRD
  • Uses serum creatinine, age, sex, race
  • Normal: >90 mL/min/1.73m²
  • CKD staging based on eGFR:
    • Stage 1: ≥90 (with kidney damage)
    • Stage 2: 60-89
    • Stage 3: 30-59
    • Stage 4: 15-29
    • Stage 5: <15 (kidney failure)

4. Creatinine Clearance (2 marks):

  • Direct measurement of GFR
  • Requires 24-hour urine collection and serum creatinine
  • Formula: (Urine creatinine × Urine volume) / (Serum creatinine × Time)
  • Normal: 90-130 mL/min for males, 80-120 mL/min for females
  • Gold standard uses inulin clearance, but creatinine is more practical

(b) Biochemical Assessment of Tubular Function (6 marks)

1. Urine Concentrating Ability (2 marks):

  • Water deprivation test
  • Measures ability to concentrate urine (specific gravity >1.020, osmolality >800 mOsm/kg)
  • Impaired in tubular dysfunction
  • Early marker of tubular disease

2. Urine Acidification Test (2 marks):

  • Assesses distal tubular function
  • Ammonium chloride loading test
  • Normal: urine pH should fall below 5.3
  • Impaired in renal tubular acidosis (RTA)
  • Types of RTA: Type 1 (distal), Type 2 (proximal), Type 4 (hyperkalemic)

3. Tubular Markers (2 marks):

Beta-2 Microglobulin:

  • Freely filtered, reabsorbed by proximal tubule
  • Elevated in urine indicates proximal tubular damage

N-Acetyl-Beta-D-Glucosaminidase (NAG):

  • Enzyme from tubular cells
  • Elevated in urine indicates tubular injury

Retinol Binding Protein:

  • Low molecular weight protein
  • Increased urinary excretion in tubular dysfunction

Amino acids and glucose in urine:

  • Abnormal presence indicates proximal tubular defects (Fanconi syndrome)

(c) Role of Urinalysis in Evaluating Renal Disease (6 marks)

1. Physical Examination (2 marks):

Color and Appearance:

  • Normal: pale to dark yellow, clear
  • Red/brown: hematuria, hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria
  • Cloudy: pyuria, infection, crystals

Specific Gravity:

  • Normal: 1.003-1.030
  • Fixed at 1.010: isosthenuria (tubular dysfunction)
  • Low: diabetes insipidus, overhydration
  • High: dehydration, SIADH

Volume:

  • Normal: 800-2000 mL/24hr
  • Oliguria (<400 mL/day): acute kidney injury
  • Polyuria (>3000 mL/day): diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus

2. Chemical Examination (Dipstick) (2 marks):

Protein:

  • Normal: <150 mg/24hr
  • Proteinuria indicates glomerular damage
  • Microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day): early diabetic nephropathy

Glucose:

  • Normally absent
  • Presence: diabetes mellitus, renal glycosuria, pregnancy

Blood:

  • Hematuria: glomerulonephritis, stones, tumors, UTI
  • Hemoglobinuria: hemolysis
  • Myoglobinuria: rhabdomyolysis

pH:

  • Normal: 5.0-7.0
  • Alkaline: UTI (urease-producing bacteria), RTA
  • Acidic: metabolic acidosis, high protein diet

Ketones:

  • DKA, starvation, alcoholic ketoacidosis

Bilirubin and Urobilinogen:

  • Hepatobiliary disease

3. Microscopic Examination (2 marks):

Cells:

  • RBCs: glomerulonephritis, stones, tumors
  • WBCs: infection, interstitial nephritis
  • Epithelial cells: tubular damage

Casts:

  • Hyaline casts: normal, concentrated urine
  • RBC casts: glomerulonephritis
  • WBC casts: pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis
  • Granular casts: tubular injury
  • Fatty casts: nephrotic syndrome

Crystals:

  • Calcium oxalate, uric acid: stone formation
  • Cystine: cystinuria

Bacteria:

  • UTI (>10⁵ CFU/mL significant)

QUESTION 13

Write detailed notes on Liver Function Tests:

(a) Describe the biochemical tests used to assess hepatocellular function. (8 marks)

(b) Explain the biochemical tests used to assess cholestasis and biliary obstruction. (6 marks)

(c) Discuss the pattern of liver function test abnormalities in different types of liver disease. (6 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 13

(a) Biochemical Tests for Hepatocellular Function (8 marks)

1. Aminotransferases (Transaminases) (2 marks):

Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT):

  • More specific for liver (found mainly in hepatocytes)
  • Normal: 7-56 U/L
  • Elevated in hepatocellular injury

Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST):

  • Found in liver, heart, muscle, kidney
  • Normal: 10-40 U/L
  • Less specific than ALT

Clinical Significance:

  • AST/ALT ratio <1: viral hepatitis, fatty liver
  • AST/ALT ratio >2: alcoholic liver disease
  • Very high levels (>1000 U/L): acute viral hepatitis, drug-induced hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis

2. Synthetic Function Tests (3 marks):

Serum Albumin:

  • Synthesized exclusively by liver
  • Normal: 35-50 g/L
  • Half-life: 20 days
  • Low in chronic liver disease, malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome
  • Indicates hepatic synthetic capacity

Prothrombin Time (PT) / INR:

  • Measures clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) synthesized by liver
  • Prolonged in liver disease (reduced synthesis) or vitamin K deficiency
  • INR >1.5 indicates significant hepatic dysfunction
  • Useful in acute liver failure assessment

Total Protein:

  • Normal: 60-80 g/L
  • Decreased in chronic liver disease
  • Includes albumin and globulins

3. Serum Bilirubin (2 marks):

Total Bilirubin:

  • Normal: 3-17 μmol/L
  • Elevated in hepatocellular disease, cholestasis, hemolysis

Direct (Conjugated) Bilirubin:

  • Normal: <5 μmol/L
  • Elevated in hepatobiliary disease

Indirect (Unconjugated) Bilirubin:

  • Calculated: Total - Direct
  • Elevated in hemolysis, Gilbert's syndrome

Pattern:

  • Predominantly unconjugated: hemolysis, Gilbert's
  • Predominantly conjugated: hepatocellular disease, cholestasis

4. Serum Ammonia (1 mark):

  • Normal: 10-47 μmol/L
  • Elevated in liver failure, portosystemic shunting
  • Useful in hepatic encephalopathy
  • Causes neurotoxicity

(b) Biochemical Tests for Cholestasis and Biliary Obstruction (6 marks)

1. Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) (2 marks):

  • Membrane enzyme found in bile canaliculi
  • Normal: 30-120 U/L
  • Markedly elevated in cholestasis (3-10 times normal)
  • Also elevated in bone disease, pregnancy, growing children
  • Isoenzyme studies differentiate liver from bone ALP
  • Modest elevation in hepatocellular disease

2. Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT) (2 marks):

  • Membrane enzyme in bile ducts
  • Normal: 8-61 U/L (males), 5-36 U/L (females)
  • Very sensitive for biliary disease
  • Elevated in cholestasis, alcohol use, enzyme-inducing drugs
  • Confirms hepatic origin when ALP is elevated
  • Most sensitive marker for alcohol abuse

3. 5'-Nucleotidase (1 mark):

  • Alternative to GGT
  • Normal: 2-15 U/L
  • Elevated specifically in liver disease
  • Confirms hepatic source of elevated ALP
  • Not affected by bone disease or pregnancy

4. Conjugated (Direct) Bilirubin (1 mark):

  • Elevated disproportionately in cholestasis
  • May appear in urine (bilirubinuria)
  • Causes dark urine
  • Associated with pale stools (reduced fecal urobilinogen)

(c) Pattern of LFT Abnormalities in Different Liver Diseases (6 marks)

1. Acute Viral Hepatitis (2 marks):

  • Marked elevation of ALT and AST (>500 U/L, often >1000 U/L)
  • ALT > AST
  • Mild to moderate elevation of bilirubin (conjugated > unconjugated)
  • Slight elevation of ALP (<3 times normal)
  • Normal or slightly prolonged PT
  • Albumin usually normal (acute process)
  • Pattern: Hepatocellular injury

2. Alcoholic Liver Disease (2 marks):

  • AST > ALT (AST/ALT ratio >2)
  • Moderate elevation of transaminases (<500 U/L)
  • Elevated GGT (very sensitive marker)
  • Elevated bilirubin in severe disease
  • Low albumin in chronic disease
  • Prolonged PT in advanced disease
  • May have macrocytic anemia (elevated MCV)
  • Pattern: Hepatocellular injury with synthetic dysfunction

3. Cholestatic/Obstructive Liver Disease (2 marks):

Extrahepatic Obstruction (gallstones, pancreatic cancer):

  • Marked elevation of ALP (>3-10 times normal)
  • Marked elevation of GGT
  • Elevated conjugated bilirubin
  • Mild elevation of transaminases (<5 times normal)
  • If complete obstruction: absent urobilinogen in urine

Intrahepatic Cholestasis (primary biliary cholangitis, drugs):

  • Similar pattern to extrahepatic
  • Elevated ALP and GGT
  • Elevated conjugated bilirubin
  • May have anti-mitochondrial antibodies (PBC)

Additional Patterns:

Cirrhosis:

  • Low albumin (<35 g/L)
  • Prolonged PT/elevated INR
  • Mild to moderate elevation of transaminases
  • Elevated bilirubin
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Pattern: Synthetic dysfunction predominates

Infiltrative Disease (metastases, amyloid):

  • Marked elevation of ALP
  • Normal or slightly elevated transaminases
  • Variable bilirubin

QUESTION 14

A 25-year-old woman presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, and tremors. Physical examination reveals exophthalmos and thyroid enlargement.

(a) List FOUR thyroid function tests you would request. (4 marks)

(b) Describe the expected laboratory findings in hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis). (3 marks)

(c) Differentiate between Graves' disease and toxic multinodular goiter based on clinical and laboratory features. (3 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 14

(a) Four thyroid function tests (4 marks - 1 mark each)

  1. Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
  2. Free Thyroxine (Free T4)
  3. Free Triiodothyronine (Free T3)
  4. TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb) or Thyroid stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) (Accept: Thyroid peroxidase antibodies, radioactive iodine uptake scan)

(b) Expected laboratory findings in hyperthyroidism (3 marks)

  • Suppressed/Low TSH (<0.5 mIU/L)
  • Elevated Free T4 (>25 pmol/L)
  • Elevated Free T3 (>6.5 pmol/L)
  • T3 may be disproportionately elevated (T3 toxicosis)
  • In subclinical hyperthyroidism: low TSH with normal T4 and T3

(c) Differentiation between Graves' disease and toxic multinodular goiter (3 marks)

Graves' Disease:

  • Positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb positive)
  • Diffusely enlarged thyroid gland
  • Associated with ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos) and dermopathy
  • More common in younger patients
  • Autoimmune etiology

Toxic Multinodular Goiter:

  • Negative TSH receptor antibodies
  • Nodular thyroid enlargement on palpation/scan
  • No ophthalmopathy
  • More common in older patients (>50 years)
  • Radioiodine uptake shows patchy/heterogeneous uptake

QUESTION 15

Discuss the principles of clinical toxicology and therapeutic drug monitoring.

(a) Explain THREE pre-analytical factors affecting specimen collection in toxicology. (6 marks)

(b) Describe the role of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) in patient management. (4 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 15

(a) Three pre-analytical factors in toxicology specimen collection (6 marks - 2 marks each)

1. Timing of Specimen Collection:

  • Critical for accurate interpretation of drug/toxin levels
  • Should be collected at specific times relative to drug administration (peak and trough levels)
  • For suspected poisoning, collect as soon as possible after exposure
  • Serial samples may be needed to assess elimination kinetics
  • Consider drug half-life when timing collections

2. Type of Specimen:

  • Blood (serum/plasma) most common for quantitative analysis
  • Whole blood required for some drugs (e.g., ciclosporin, tacrolimus)
  • Urine useful for screening and detecting drug metabolites
  • Gastric aspirate in acute poisoning
  • Hair and nails for chronic exposure assessment
  • Choice depends on drug properties and clinical question

3. Specimen Handling and Preservation:

  • Use appropriate anticoagulants (EDTA, heparin) as some drugs bind to certain tubes
  • Protect light-sensitive drugs (e.g., bilirubin, vitamin A)
  • Maintain proper temperature (some drugs unstable at room temperature)
  • Avoid hemolysis which can interfere with assays
  • Ensure proper labeling with patient details, time of collection, and drug administration time
  • Prompt transport to laboratory (some toxins degrade rapidly)

(b) Role of Therapeutic Drug Monitoring in patient management (4 marks)

Definition and Purpose (2 marks):

  • TDM is the measurement of drug concentrations in blood to optimize therapy
  • Ensures drug levels are within therapeutic range (between minimum effective concentration and toxic concentration)
  • Particularly important for drugs with narrow therapeutic index

Clinical Applications (2 marks):

Indications for TDM:

  1. Drugs with narrow therapeutic window (digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides, anticonvulsants)
  2. Suspected toxicity or treatment failure
  3. Patient compliance assessment
  4. Altered pharmacokinetics (renal/hepatic impairment, drug interactions)
  5. Dose optimization in special populations (pediatrics, elderly, pregnancy)

Benefits:

  • Prevents toxicity by maintaining levels below toxic threshold
  • Ensures therapeutic efficacy by maintaining adequate drug levels
  • Guides dose adjustments
  • Cost-effective by preventing adverse effects and treatment failures
