QUESTION 11 (LONG ESSAY)

Write comprehensive notes on Adrenal Cortex Disorders covering:

(a) Describe the hormones produced by the adrenal cortex and their functions. (6 marks)

(b) Discuss Cushing's syndrome including biochemical investigations and interpretation. (8 marks)

(c) Explain the biochemical findings in Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency). (6 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 11

(a) Hormones of the Adrenal Cortex and Their Functions (6 marks)

The adrenal cortex has three zones, each producing different hormones:

1. Zona Glomerulosa (2 marks):

  • Produces: Mineralocorticoids (mainly Aldosterone)
  • Functions of Aldosterone:
    • Regulates sodium and potassium balance
    • Increases sodium reabsorption in distal tubule and collecting duct
    • Increases potassium excretion in urine
    • Increases water retention (follows sodium)
    • Regulates blood pressure and blood volume
    • Controlled by renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and serum potassium

2. Zona Fasciculata (2 marks):

  • Produces: Glucocorticoids (mainly Cortisol)
  • Functions of Cortisol:
    • Regulates carbohydrate metabolism (increases blood glucose through gluconeogenesis)
    • Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects
    • Protein catabolism and lipolysis
    • Maintains vascular tone and blood pressure
    • Stress hormone response
    • Controlled by hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis via ACTH

3. Zona Reticularis (2 marks):

  • Produces: Androgens (mainly DHEA, DHEA-S, androstenedione)
  • Functions of Adrenal Androgens:
    • Precursors for sex hormones (testosterone and estrogen)
    • Contribute to secondary sexual characteristics
    • Particularly important in females for libido and pubic/axillary hair
    • In males, contribution is minor compared to testicular androgens
    • Controlled by ACTH

(b) Cushing's Syndrome - Biochemical Investigations (8 marks)

Definition and Causes (2 marks):

  • Cushing's syndrome: clinical state resulting from chronic exposure to excess cortisol
  • Causes:
    • ACTH-dependent (80%): Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma), ectopic ACTH (lung cancer)
    • ACTH-independent (20%): Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma
    • Exogenous: iatrogenic (chronic steroid therapy)

Biochemical Investigations (6 marks):

1. Screening Tests (2 marks):

24-hour Urinary Free Cortisol:

  • Normal: <250 nmol/24hr
  • Elevated (>3 times upper limit) confirms hypercortisolism
  • Reflects integrated cortisol production over 24 hours

Overnight Dexamethasone Suppression Test (1 mg):

  • Give 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 PM
  • Measure serum cortisol at 8 AM next morning
  • Normal: cortisol <50 nmol/L (suppressed)
  • Cushing's: cortisol >140 nmol/L (not suppressed)

Late-night Salivary Cortisol:

  • Normal circadian rhythm: cortisol lowest at midnight
  • Cushing's: loss of circadian rhythm, elevated midnight cortisol

2. Confirmatory Tests (2 marks):

Low-dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (2-day):

  • Give 0.5 mg dexamethasone every 6 hours for 2 days
  • Measure 24-hour urinary cortisol or serum cortisol
  • Normal: suppression of cortisol
  • Cushing's: no suppression

3. Tests to Determine Cause (2 marks):

Plasma ACTH Measurement:

  • ACTH suppressed (<5 pg/mL): ACTH-independent (adrenal tumor)
  • ACTH normal/elevated (>20 pg/mL): ACTH-dependent

High-dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (8 mg):

  • Give 8 mg dexamethasone overnight or 2 mg every 6 hours for 2 days
  • Cushing's disease (pituitary): >50% suppression of cortisol
  • Ectopic ACTH/adrenal tumor: no suppression

CRH Stimulation Test:

  • Give CRH intravenously
  • Cushing's disease: ACTH and cortisol rise
  • Ectopic ACTH/adrenal: no response

Bilateral Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (IPSS):

  • Gold standard to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH
  • Central:peripheral ACTH ratio >2 (baseline) or >3 (after CRH) indicates pituitary source

(c) Addison's Disease - Biochemical Findings (6 marks)

Definition (1 mark):

  • Primary adrenal insufficiency due to destruction of adrenal cortex (>90% loss)
  • Most common cause: autoimmune adrenalitis (70-90% of cases)
  • Other causes: tuberculosis, hemorrhage, metastases, adrenalectomy

Biochemical Findings (5 marks):

1. Baseline Biochemistry (2 marks):

  • Hyponatremia (<135 mmol/L): due to aldosterone deficiency and cortisol deficiency
  • Hyperkalemia (>5.5 mmol/L): due to aldosterone deficiency
  • Metabolic acidosis: impaired renal H+ excretion
  • Hypoglycemia: especially during stress, due to cortisol deficiency
  • Elevated urea: due to dehydration (pre-renal)
  • Hypercalcemia: may occur (mechanism unclear)

2. Hormonal Measurements (2 marks):

  • Low serum cortisol (<140 nmol/L at 8-9 AM)
  • Markedly elevated ACTH (>100 pg/mL): loss of negative feedback
  • Low aldosterone with elevated renin (high renin:aldosterone ratio)
  • Low DHEA-S: loss of adrenal androgen production

3. Diagnostic Test - ACTH Stimulation Test (Short Synacthen Test) (1 mark):

  • Give 250 μg synthetic ACTH (Synacthen) IV or IM
  • Measure serum cortisol at 0, 30, and 60 minutes
  • Normal response: cortisol rises to >550 nmol/L
  • Primary adrenal insufficiency: cortisol remains low (<550 nmol/L) with no rise
  • This is the definitive test for Addison's disease

QUESTION 12 (LONG ESSAY)

Discuss Water and Electrolyte Disorders:

(a) Explain the regulation of sodium and water balance in the body. (6 marks)

(b) Describe the causes, biochemical features, and clinical significance of hyponatremia. (8 marks)

(c) Discuss hyperkalemia including causes and biochemical management. (6 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 12

(a) Regulation of Sodium and Water Balance (6 marks)

Sodium Regulation (3 marks):

1. Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS):

  • Decreased renal perfusion or low sodium stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
  • Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
  • ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
  • Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone secretion from adrenal cortex
  • Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in distal tubule and collecting duct
  • Results in sodium retention and potassium excretion

2. Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP):

  • Released from atrial myocytes in response to atrial stretch (volume expansion)
  • Promotes sodium excretion (natriuresis) by kidneys
  • Inhibits renin and aldosterone secretion
  • Opposes RAAS action

3. Renal Regulation:

  • 65% sodium reabsorbed in proximal tubule
  • 25% in thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
  • 10% in distal tubule (aldosterone-sensitive)
  • Glomerulotubular balance maintains sodium homeostasis

Water Regulation (3 marks):

1. Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH/Vasopressin):

  • Produced in hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary
  • Released in response to:
    • Increased plasma osmolality (>295 mOsm/kg) detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors
    • Decreased blood volume/pressure detected by baroreceptors
  • Acts on V2 receptors in collecting duct
  • Inserts aquaporin-2 channels, increasing water reabsorption
  • Results in concentrated urine and diluted plasma

2. Thirst Mechanism:

  • Stimulated by increased osmolality and decreased blood volume
  • Complements ADH action in maintaining water balance

3. Osmoreceptor-ADH-Kidney Axis:

  • Normal plasma osmolality: 275-295 mOsm/kg
  • Hyperosmolality → ADH release → water retention → dilution
  • Hypo-osmolality → ADH suppression → water excretion → concentration

(b) Hyponatremia - Causes, Features, and Significance (8 marks)

Definition (1 mark):

  • Serum sodium <135 mmol/L
  • Most common electrolyte disorder
  • Reflects relative excess of water compared to sodium

Classification by Volume Status (3 marks):

1. Hypovolemic Hyponatremia (loss of both sodium and water, more sodium lost):

  • Renal losses: diuretics, salt-wasting nephropathy, adrenal insufficiency
  • Extra-renal losses: vomiting, diarrhea, burns, third-spacing
  • Urinary sodium: <20 mmol/L (extra-renal), >20 mmol/L (renal)

2. Euvolemic Hyponatremia (excess water retention, normal sodium):

  • SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion)
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Glucocorticoid deficiency
  • Psychogenic polydipsia
  • Drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide)
  • Urinary sodium: >20 mmol/L

3. Hypervolemic Hyponatremia (excess water > excess sodium):

  • Heart failure
  • Cirrhosis with ascites
  • Nephrotic syndrome
  • Advanced chronic kidney disease
  • Urinary sodium: <20 mmol/L (except renal failure)

Biochemical Features of SIADH (2 marks):

  • Hyponatremia with low plasma osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg)
  • Inappropriate urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg, often >300)
  • Elevated urinary sodium (>20 mmol/L) despite hyponatremia
  • Normal renal, thyroid, and adrenal function
  • No edema or dehydration (euvolemic)
  • Causes: malignancies (small cell lung cancer), CNS disorders, lung disease, drugs

Clinical Significance (2 marks):

Symptoms (severity depends on rate of decline):

  • Mild (130-135 mmol/L): often asymptomatic
  • Moderate (120-129 mmol/L): nausea, confusion, headache
  • Severe (<120 mmol/L): seizures, coma, respiratory arrest, death

Complications:

  • Cerebral edema (acute hyponatremia)
  • Osmotic demyelination syndrome (if corrected too rapidly)
  • Increased falls and fractures in elderly
  • Associated with increased mortality in hospitalized patients

Management Principles:

  • Treat underlying cause
  • Fluid restriction in euvolemic/hypervolemic
  • Hypertonic saline in severe symptomatic cases
  • Correct slowly: ≤10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination

(c) Hyperkalemia - Causes and Management (6 marks)

Definition and Significance (1 mark):

  • Serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L
  • Medical emergency when severe (>6.5 mmol/L)
  • Can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias

Causes (2 marks):

1. Increased Potassium Intake:

  • Excessive dietary intake (rare with normal renal function)
  • IV potassium administration
  • Potassium-containing medications

2. Decreased Potassium Excretion (most common):

  • Acute or chronic kidney disease (GFR <20 mL/min)
  • Hypoaldosteronism (Addison's disease, Type 4 RTA)
  • Drugs: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride), NSAIDs, heparin

3. Potassium Shift from Cells:

  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Insulin deficiency
  • Massive tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, hemolysis)
  • Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis
  • Beta-blocker overdose

4. Pseudohyperkalemia:

  • Hemolysis during blood collection
  • Prolonged tourniquet application
  • Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis (K+ released from cells)

Biochemical Management (3 marks):

Immediate Treatment (Severe: >6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes):

1. Cardiac Membrane Stabilization:

  • 10% Calcium gluconate 10-20 mL IV over 5-10 minutes
  • Stabilizes myocardium, no effect on K+ level
  • Monitor ECG

2. Shift Potassium into Cells:

  • Insulin + Dextrose: Regular insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL 50% dextrose
    • Lowers K+ by 0.5-1.5 mmol/L in 15-30 minutes
    • Monitor glucose
  • Salbutamol nebulizer: 10-20 mg
    • Beta-2 agonist drives K+ intracellularly
    • Additive effect with insulin
  • Sodium bicarbonate: 50-100 mEq IV (if metabolic acidosis present)
    • Corrects acidosis, shifts K+ into cells

3. Remove Potassium from Body:

  • Diuretics: Furosemide 40-80 mg IV (if renal function adequate)
  • Cation exchange resins: Calcium resonium 15 g PO/PR
    • Slower onset (hours)
    • Removes K+ via GI tract
  • Hemodialysis: Most effective for severe hyperkalemia with renal failure
    • Removes 25-50 mmol K+ per hour

Monitoring:

  • Serial potassium measurements every 2-4 hours
  • Continuous ECG monitoring if severe
  • Treat underlying cause
  • Stop offending medications

(a) Principles of Newborn Screening (6 marks)

Purpose and Rationale (2 marks):

  • Early detection of inherited metabolic disorders before clinical symptoms appear
  • Allows early intervention to prevent irreversible damage (intellectual disability, organ damage, death)
  • Target conditions: treatable, serious consequences if untreated, reliable screening test available
  • Cost-effective public health measure
  • Based on principle: early diagnosis + early treatment = better outcomes

Screening Methods (2 marks):

Specimen Collection:

  • Blood spot collected on filter paper (Guthrie card) from heel prick
  • Optimal timing: 48-72 hours after birth (after feeding established)
  • Too early: false negatives (metabolites not accumulated)
  • Collected before hospital discharge

Laboratory Testing:

  • Tandem Mass Spectrometry (MS/MS): most common method
    • Screens for multiple disorders simultaneously (30-50 conditions)
    • Measures amino acids, acylcarnitines, organic acids
    • High sensitivity and specificity
  • Immunoassays: for hormones (TSH for hypothyroidism, 17-OHP for CAH)
  • Enzyme assays: for specific enzyme deficiencies
  • DNA analysis: for specific genetic mutations

Conditions Screened (2 marks):

Amino Acid Disorders:

  • Phenylketonuria (PKU)
  • Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)
  • Homocystinuria
  • Tyrosinemia

Organic Acid Disorders:

  • Methylmalonic acidemia
  • Propionic acidemia
  • Glutaric acidemia

Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects:

  • Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD)
  • Long-chain and very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiencies

Others:

  • Galactosemia
  • Congenital hypothyroidism
  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Sickle cell disease
  • Biotinidase deficiency

Follow-up:

  • Positive screens require confirmatory testing
  • Genetic counseling for families
  • Initiate treatment promptly if confirmed

(b) Phenylketonuria (PKU) (8 marks)

Biochemical Basis (3 marks):

  • Autosomal recessive disorder
  • Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) enzyme
  • PAH converts phenylalanine to tyrosine in liver
  • Gene located on chromosome 12
  • Results in accumulation of phenylalanine in blood and tissues (>1200 μmol/L, normal 50-110)
  • Alternate pathways produce phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, phenylacetate)
  • Phenylketones excreted in urine (gives musty/mousy odor)
  • Toxic effects:
    • Phenylalanine competes with other amino acids for transport across blood-brain barrier
    • Interferes with neurotransmitter synthesis
    • Impairs myelination
    • Causes irreversible brain damage if untreated

Diagnosis (3 marks):

Newborn Screening:

  • Blood phenylalanine measured at 48-72 hours of life
  • Positive if phenylalanine >120 μmol/L
  • Classic PKU: >1200 μmol/L
  • Mild PKU: 600-1200 μmol/L
  • Mild hyperphenylalaninemia: 120-600 μmol/L (may not require treatment)

Confirmatory Tests:

  • Repeat quantitative plasma phenylalanine and tyrosine
  • Phenylalanine: tyrosine ratio >3:1 suggestive of PKU
  • Urine organic acids: presence of phenylketones
  • PAH enzyme activity assay (liver biopsy - rarely done)
  • Genetic testing: PAH gene mutation analysis
  • BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) loading test: to identify BH4-responsive PKU

Clinical Features if Untreated:

  • Intellectual disability (IQ <50)
  • Microcephaly
  • Seizures (25%)
  • Behavioral problems, autism
  • Hypopigmentation (fair skin, blonde hair, blue eyes) - tyrosine deficiency
  • Eczema
  • Musty body odor

Management (2 marks):

Dietary Management (cornerstone of treatment):

  • Phenylalanine-restricted diet started immediately after diagnosis
  • Limit natural protein intake (phenylalanine present in all proteins)
  • Use special phenylalanine-free medical formulas and low-protein foods
  • Target plasma phenylalanine: 120-360 μmol/L
  • Ensure adequate tyrosine supplementation (tyrosine becomes essential amino acid)
  • Diet must be lifelong (especially critical in first 10 years)
  • Monitor blood phenylalanine levels regularly (weekly in infancy, monthly later)

BH4 (Sapropterin) Therapy:

  • For BH4-responsive PKU variants (20-30% of cases)
  • BH4 is cofactor for PAH enzyme
  • Can lower phenylalanine levels, allow more dietary freedom

Maternal PKU:

  • Women with PKU must maintain strict dietary control before and during pregnancy
  • High maternal phenylalanine is teratogenic
  • Can cause microcephaly, congenital heart disease, intellectual disability in fetus (even if fetus doesn't have PKU)

Prognosis:

  • Early treatment (within first 2-3 weeks) prevents intellectual disability
  • Normal intelligence and development if well-managed
  • Excellent outcomes with dietary compliance

(c) Galactosemia - Biochemical Features (6 marks)

Definition and Types (2 marks):

  • Inherited disorder of galactose metabolism
  • Galactose cannot be converted to glucose
  • Three types based on enzyme deficiency:

Type I (Classic - most severe):

  • Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT)
  • Most common and severe form

Type II:

  • Deficiency of galactokinase
  • Milder, mainly causes cataracts

Type III:

  • Deficiency of UDP-galactose-4-epimerase
  • Variable severity

Biochemical Basis (2 marks):

Normal Galactose Metabolism:

  • Lactose (milk sugar) → Glucose + Galactose
  • Galactose pathway:
    1. Galactokinase: Galactose → Galactose-1-phosphate
    2. GALT: Galactose-1-phosphate + UDP-glucose → Glucose-1-phosphate + UDP-galactose
    3. UDP-galactose-4-epimerase: UDP-galactose → UDP-glucose

In Classic Galactosemia:

  • Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates (toxic metabolite)
  • Galactose accumulates in blood
  • Alternate pathways produce:
    • Galactitol (via aldose reductase) → accumulates in lens → cataracts
    • Galactonate → excreted in urine

Biochemical Findings and Clinical Features (2 marks):

Laboratory Findings:

  • Elevated blood galactose (>200 mg/dL)
  • Elevated galactose-1-phosphate in RBCs (toxic levels)
  • Galactosuria (reducing substance in urine positive, but glucose oxidase negative)
  • GALT enzyme activity absent or markedly reduced in RBCs (diagnostic)
  • Hypoglycemia (impaired gluconeogenesis)
  • Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis

Associated Biochemical Abnormalities:

  • Abnormal liver function tests: elevated AST, ALT, bilirubin
  • Prolonged prothrombin time (coagulopathy)
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Aminoaciduria (Fanconi-like syndrome)
  • Positive newborn screen (elevated galactose on blood spot)

Clinical Features if Untreated:

  • Presents in neonatal period (after milk feeding starts)
  • Vomiting, diarrhea, failure to thrive
  • Jaundice, hepatomegaly, liver failure
  • Cataracts (appear within weeks)
  • E. coli sepsis (increased susceptibility)
  • Intellectual disability
  • Ovarian failure in females (even with treatment)

Diagnosis:

  • Newborn screening: elevated galactose
  • Reducing substances in urine (positive Clinitest, negative glucose oxidase)
  • GALT enzyme assay in RBCs (definitive)
  • Genetic testing for GALT mutations
  • Elevated galactose-1-phosphate in blood

Management:

  • Lifelong galactose-free diet (lactose-free)
  • Eliminate milk and dairy products
  • Use soy or elemental formulas
  • Avoid foods with galactose
  • Monitor growth and development
  • Long-term complications may occur despite treatment (ovarian failure, learning disabilities, speech problems)

QUESTION 14 (LONG ESSAY)

Discuss Clinical Nutrition in detail:

(a) Describe the assessment and biochemical features of Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM). (8 marks)

(b) Explain the role and biochemical assessment of Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K). (8 marks)

(c) Discuss the clinical significance of trace elements (Iron, Zinc, Copper). (4 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 14

(a) Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) (8 marks)

Definition and Classification (2 marks):

  • Deficiency of protein and/or calories
  • Most common nutritional disorder worldwide, especially in children
  • Two main forms:

Marasmus:

  • Severe calorie deficiency with relatively preserved protein intake
  • Wasting, loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle mass
  • Body weight <60% of expected
  • Alert, no edema, no hepatomegaly

Kwashiorkor:

  • Adequate calories but severe protein deficiency
  • Edema (hypoalbuminemia)
  • Fatty liver, hepatomegaly
  • Skin and hair changes
  • Apathy, irritability

Marasmic-Kwashiorkor:

  • Combined features of both

Nutritional Assessment (3 marks):

Anthropometric Measurements:

  • Weight and height (BMI calculation)
  • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC)
  • Skin-fold thickness (subcutaneous fat assessment)
  • Z-scores (WHO growth standards)

Clinical Assessment:

  • Muscle wasting
  • Loss of subcutaneous fat
  • Edema
  • Skin and hair changes
  • Signs of vitamin/mineral deficiencies

Dietary History:

  • Caloric intake
  • Protein intake
  • Recent weight loss

Biochemical Assessment (3 marks):

Protein Status:

  • Serum Albumin: <35 g/L indicates malnutrition
    • Long half-life (20 days), not sensitive to acute changes
    • Affected by liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, inflammation
  • Serum Prealbumin (Transthyretin): <200 mg/L
    • Short half-life (2 days), sensitive to acute changes
    • Better for monitoring nutritional repletion
  • Transferrin: <200 mg/dL indicates protein depletion
    • Affected by iron status, inflammation
  • Retinol-Binding Protein: rapid turnover marker
  • Total Lymphocyte Count: <1500/μL (immune dysfunction)

Other Biochemical Markers:

  • Nitrogen Balance: Negative in PEM
    • Calculated: Nitrogen intake - Nitrogen output (24-hr urinary urea nitrogen + 4g)
  • Creatinine-Height Index: <60% indicates muscle protein depletion
    • 24-hr urinary creatinine reflects muscle mass
  • Serum Electrolytes:
    • Hyponatremia
    • Hypokalemia
    • Hypophosphatemia
    • Hypomagnesemia
  • Blood Glucose: Hypoglycemia common
  • Hemoglobin: Anemia (often multifactorial)
  • Lipid Profile: Low cholesterol, low triglycerides

Complications:

  • Impaired immune function, increased infections
  • Impaired wound healing
  • Edema (kwashiorkor)
  • Electrolyte imbalances
  • Hypothermia, bradycardia
  • Refeeding syndrome (if nutrition restarted too aggressively)

(b) Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K) (8 marks - 2 marks each vitamin)

Vitamin A (Retinol):

Functions:

  • Vision: component of rhodopsin (night vision)
  • Cell differentiation and growth
  • Immune function
  • Reproduction
  • Skin and mucous membrane integrity

Biochemical Assessment:

  • Serum retinol: Normal 30-70 μg/dL
  • Deficiency: <20 μg/dL
  • Retinol-binding protein (RBP)
  • Relative dose response test

Clinical Features:

  • Deficiency: Night blindness, xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia (blindness), impaired immunity
  • Toxicity: Hepatotoxicity, teratogenic, pseudotumor cerebri, bone pain

Sources: Liver, fish oils, dairy, eggs; provitamin A (beta-carotene) in carrots, dark leafy greens

Vitamin D (Calciferol):

Functions:

  • Calcium and phosphate homeostasis
  • Bone mineralization
  • Increases intestinal calcium absorption
  • Regulates PTH secretion
  • Immune modulation

Biochemical Assessment:

  • 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D]: best indicator of vitamin D status
    • Sufficiency: >75 nmol/L (>30 ng/mL)
    • Insufficiency: 50-75 nmol/L (20-30 ng/mL)
    • Deficiency: <50 nmol/L (<20 ng/mL)
  • 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (active form): not routinely measured
  • Elevated alkaline phosphatase in deficiency
  • Hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia in severe deficiency
  • Elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)

Clinical Features:

  • Deficiency: Rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults), muscle weakness, bone pain
  • Toxicity: Hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, renal stones, soft tissue calcification

Sources: Sunlight exposure (UVB), fatty fish, fortified milk, egg yolks

Vitamin E (Tocopherol):

Functions:

  • Major lipid-soluble antioxidant
  • Protects cell membranes from oxidative damage
  • Protects polyunsaturated fatty acids
  • Immune function
  • Prevents platelet aggregation

Biochemical Assessment:

  • Serum alpha-tocopherol: Normal 12-42 μmol/L
  • Deficiency: <12 μmol/L
  • Should be interpreted relative to serum lipids (vitamin E:lipid ratio)
  • Increased red cell hemolysis test (in vitro hydrogen peroxide hemolysis)
  • Elevated lipid peroxidation products

Clinical Features:

  • Deficiency: Rare (except in fat malabsorption, abetalipoproteinemia)
    • Hemolytic anemia in premature infants
    • Neuromuscular degeneration (spinocerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy)
    • Retinopathy
  • Toxicity: Rare, may interfere with vitamin K (bleeding)

Sources: Vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, wheat germ, green leafy vegetables

Vitamin K (Phylloquinone):

Functions:

  • Cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X
  • Synthesis of proteins C and S (anticoagulant)
  • Bone metabolism (osteocalcin carboxylation)

Biochemical Assessment:

  • Prothrombin Time (PT/INR): most practical test
    • Prolonged in deficiency
  • Serum vitamin K levels (not routinely done)
  • Undercarboxylated prothrombin (PIVKA-II)
  • Factors II, VII, IX, X levels decreased

Clinical Features:

  • Deficiency: Bleeding diathesis (easy bruising, GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage)
    • Hemorrhagic disease of newborn
    • Deficiency in fat malabsorption, prolonged antibiotic use, warfarin therapy
  • Toxicity: Rare with natural forms; interferes with warfarin if supplemented

Sources: Green leafy vegetables (K1), intestinal bacteria synthesis (K2), meat, dairy

(c) Clinical Significance of Trace Elements (4 marks)

Iron:

  • Function: Oxygen transport (hemoglobin, myoglobin), electron transport, DNA synthesis
  • Assessment:
    • Serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation
    • Serum ferritin (best indicator of iron stores): <30 μg/L indicates deficiency
    • Complete blood count: microcytic hypochromic anemia
  • Deficiency: Most common nutritional deficiency worldwide
    • Iron deficiency anemia, fatigue, impaired cognitive function, pica
  • Excess: Hemochromatosis, liver cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiac dysfunction
  • Sources: Red meat, liver, legumes, fortified cereals

Zinc:

  • Function: Cofactor for >300 enzymes, protein synthesis, immune function, wound healing, taste and smell, growth
  • Assessment:
    • Serum/plasma zinc: <70 μg/dL indicates deficiency
    • Not very sensitive (affected by inflammation, albumin)
    • Alkaline phosphatase (zinc-dependent enzyme)
  • Deficiency:
    • Growth retardation, delayed wound healing
    • Hypogonadism, impaired immunity, diarrhea
    • Dermatitis, alopecia, dysgeusia (altered taste)
    • Acrodermatitis enteropathica (genetic)
  • Toxicity: Rare, copper deficiency (competitive absorption)
  • Sources: Meat, shellfish, legumes, nuts, dairy

Copper:

  • Function: Cofactor for oxidase enzymes, iron metabolism (ceruloplasmin), collagen cross-linking, melanin formation, antioxidant (superoxide dismutase)
  • Assessment:
    • Serum copper: Normal 70-140 μg/dL
    • Serum ceruloplasmin: Normal 20-45 mg/dL
    • 24-hour urinary copper
  • Deficiency:
    • Anemia (impaired iron utilization)
    • Neutropenia, bone abnormalities
    • Menkes disease (genetic copper deficiency)
  • Excess: Wilson's disease (genetic copper overload)
    • Liver cirrhosis, neurological symptoms, Kayser-Fleischer rings
    • Low ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper
  • Sources: Organ meats, shellfish, nuts, seeds, whole grains

QUESTION 15 (LONG ESSAY)

Write comprehensive notes on Porphyrias:

(a) Explain the biosynthesis of heme and its regulation. (6 marks)

(b) Classify porphyrias and describe their biochemical features. (10 marks)

(c) Discuss the laboratory diagnosis of Acute Intermittent Porphyria. (4 marks)

ANSWER TO QUESTION 15

(a) Biosynthesis of Heme and Regulation (6 marks)

Heme Biosynthesis Pathway (4 marks):

Heme synthesis occurs in all cells but mainly in bone marrow (for hemoglobin) and liver (for cytochromes). The pathway involves 8 enzymes:

1. In Mitochondria:

  • ALA Synthase (rate-limiting enzyme):
    • Succinyl CoA + Glycine → δ-Aminolevulinic acid (ALA)
    • Requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as cofactor

2. In Cytoplasm:

  • ALA Dehydratase (Porphobilinogen Synthase):
    • 2 ALA molecules → Porphobilinogen (PBG)
    • Inhibited by lead
  • PBG Deaminase (Hydroxymethylbilane Synthase):
    • 4 PBG molecules → Hydroxymethylbilane (linear tetrapyrrole)
  • Uroporphyrinogen III Synthase:
    • Hydroxymethylbilane → Uroporphyrinogen III (cyclic tetrapyrrole)
  • Uroporphyrinogen Decarboxylase:
    • Uroporphyrinogen III → Coproporphyrinogen III

3. Back to Mitochondria:

  • Coproporphyrinogen Oxidase:
    • Coproporphyrinogen III → Protoporphyrinogen IX
  • Protoporphyrinogen Oxidase:
    • Protoporphyrinogen IX → Protoporphyrin IX
  • Ferrochelatase (Heme Synthase):
    • Protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺ → Heme

Regulation (2 marks):

  • ALA synthase is the rate-limiting and regulated enzyme
  • Negative feedback: Heme inhibits ALA synthase
  • Induction: Drugs, hormones, starvation induce ALA synthase (triggers acute porphyria attacks)
  • Erythropoietic pathway: Regulated by erythropoietin and iron availability
  • Hepatic pathway: Regulated by heme demand for cytochrome P450 enzymes

(b) Classification and Biochemical Features of Porphyrias (10 marks)

Porphyrias are classified based on:

  1. Site of enzyme deficiency: Hepatic vs Erythropoietic
  2. Clinical presentation: Acute vs Non-acute (cutaneous)

ACUTE HEPATIC PORPHYRIAS (4 marks):

1. Acute Intermittent Porphyria (AIP) - Most Common Acute Porphyria:

  • Enzyme Deficiency: PBG deaminase (Hydroxymethylbilane synthase) - 50% activity
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Markedly elevated urinary ALA and PBG during attacks
    • Urine darkens on standing (porphobilinogen polymerizes)
    • Normal porphyrin levels in remission
  • Clinical Features:
    • Neurovisceral crises: severe abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric symptoms
    • No skin photosensitivity
    • Triggered by: drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides), hormones, fasting, stress, infection
    • Life-threatening if untreated

2. Variegate Porphyria (VP):

  • Enzyme Deficiency: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Elevated fecal protoporphyrin and coproporphyrin
    • Elevated urinary ALA and PBG during attacks
  • Clinical Features: Acute attacks + skin photosensitivity

3. Hereditary Coproporphyria (HCP):

  • Enzyme Deficiency: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Elevated urinary and fecal coproporphyrin III
    • Elevated urinary ALA and PBG during attacks
  • Clinical Features: Acute attacks + skin photosensitivity (less common than VP)

4. ALA Dehydratase Deficiency Porphyria (ADP):

  • Enzyme Deficiency: ALA dehydratase
  • Biochemical Features: Elevated urinary ALA, normal PBG
  • Clinical Features: Very rare, acute neurovisceral symptoms
  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive

NON-ACUTE (CUTANEOUS) PORPHYRIAS (4 marks):

1. Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT) - Most Common Porphyria Overall:

  • Enzyme Deficiency: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (hepatic)
  • Inheritance: Can be acquired or inherited (autosomal dominant)
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Markedly elevated urinary uroporphyrin (urine may be pink/red)
    • Elevated plasma porphyrins
    • Normal ALA and PBG
  • Clinical Features:
    • Skin fragility, bullae on sun-exposed areas
    • Hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis
    • No acute attacks
  • Associations: Hepatitis C, HIV, alcohol, estrogens, iron overload, smoking
  • Treatment: Phlebotomy, hydroxychloroquine (low-dose)

2. Erythropoietic Protoporphyria (EPP):

  • Enzyme Deficiency: Ferrochelatase
  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Elevated erythrocyte and plasma protoporphyrin
    • Normal urinary porphyrins
  • Clinical Features:
    • Acute photosensitivity (burning, itching within minutes of sun exposure)
    • Begins in childhood
    • Chronic liver disease (10%) from protoporphyrin deposition

3. Congenital Erythropoietic Porphyria (CEP) - Günther's Disease:

  • Enzyme Deficiency: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase
  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive
  • Biochemical Features:
    • Elevated urinary uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I (isomer I, not normal isomer III)
    • Elevated erythrocyte porphyrins
    • Pink/red urine from birth
  • Clinical Features:
    • Severe photosensitivity from infancy
    • Hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly
    • Red/brown teeth (fluoresce under UV light)
    • Severe scarring, mutilation
    • Very rare

Summary Table (2 marks):

  • Acute attacks with neuro-visceral symptoms: AIP, VP, HCP, ADP (elevated urinary ALA and PBG)
  • Skin photosensitivity only: PCT, EPP, CEP
  • Both acute attacks and photosensitivity: VP, HCP (less common)

(c) Laboratory Diagnosis of Acute Intermittent Porphyria (4 marks)

During Acute Attack (2 marks):

Screening Tests:

  • Urinary Porphobilinogen (PBG): Qualitative test
    • Watson-Schwartz test or Hoesch test (rarely used now)
    • Modern: Quantitative PBG measurement
    • Markedly elevated (>5-10 times normal) during attacks
    • This is the most important diagnostic test
  • Urinary δ-Aminolevulinic Acid (ALA):
    • Also markedly elevated during attacks (but less specific than PBG)
    • ALA:PBG ratio <1 suggests AIP
  • Urine Appearance:
    • Fresh urine may be normal or pale
    • Darkens to port-wine/brown color on standing exposed to light
    • Due to spontaneous polymerization of porphobilinogen

Quantitative Tests:

  • 24-hour urine collection for ALA and PBG (quantitative)
  • Random urine ALA/PBG:creatinine ratio

Confirmatory Tests (1 mark):

  • Erythrocyte PBG Deaminase Activity:
    • Reduced to ~50% of normal
    • Confirms diagnosis
    • May be normal in some patients (splice variants)
  • Genetic Testing:
    • DNA analysis for HMBS gene mutations
    • Definitive diagnosis
    • Family screening

Between Attacks/In Remission (0.5 marks):

  • Urinary ALA and PBG may be normal or only mildly elevated
  • Enzyme assay or genetic testing needed for diagnosis

Differential Diagnosis (0.5 marks):

  • Rule out lead poisoning (elevated ALA, normal PBG)
  • Rule out other acute porphyrias (VP, HCP) by fecal porphyrin analysis
  • Plasma fluorescence scan at 626 nm (peaks in VP)

Additional Supportive Tests:

  • Hyponatremia (SIADH common during attacks)
  • Elevated liver enzymes
  • Tachycardia, hypertension
  • Urinary tract infection excluded

SECTION A: CASE-BASED SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (40 Marks Total)

QUESTION 1: SIADH / Hyponatremia (10 marks)

An elderly male smoker is admitted with acute confusion. Examination reveals digital clubbing and a right-sided pleural effusion. Laboratory results show:

  • Serum sodium: 118 mmol/L
  • Serum osmolality: 236 mOsm/kg
  • Urine osmolality: 350 mOsm/kg
  • Urine sodium: 50 mmol/L
  • Urea and creatinine: normal

Chest radiograph shows a right lower-zone mass suggestive of carcinoma.

a) What is the most likely cause of his hyponatremia? (2 marks)

b) State two biochemical features characteristic of SIADH. (2 marks)

c) Explain why the urine osmolality is high despite hyponatremia. (2 marks)

d) Name the lung tumour most commonly associated with SIADH. (2 marks)

e) State one major risk of rapid correction of hyponatremia. (2 marks)

ANSWER 1:

a) Most likely cause: (2 marks)

Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH) secondary to ectopic ADH production by lung carcinoma (paraneoplastic syndrome).

b) Two biochemical features of SIADH: (2 marks)

  1. Hyponatremia with low serum osmolality (<280 mOsm/kg) but inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, usually >300 mOsm/kg)
  2. Elevated urine sodium (>40 mmol/L) despite hyponatremia, indicating continued sodium excretion due to volume expansion

c) Explanation of high urine osmolality: (2 marks)

In SIADH, there is excessive and inappropriate secretion of ADH despite low serum osmolality. ADH acts on the collecting ducts of the kidney to increase water reabsorption, leading to concentrated urine. Normally, low serum osmolality should suppress ADH, resulting in dilute urine, but in SIADH this feedback mechanism is overridden.

d) Lung tumour most commonly associated with SIADH: (2 marks)

Small Cell Lung Carcinoma (SCLC) - accounts for approximately 75-80% of cases of ectopic ADH production. SCLC is of neuroendocrine origin and can synthesize and secrete ADH autonomously.

e) Major risk of rapid correction: (2 marks)

Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (ODS), formerly called Central Pontine Myelinolysis. Rapid correction (>10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours) causes acute osmotic stress on brain cells that have adapted to chronic hyponatremia, leading to irreversible brainstem damage with quadriplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, and altered consciousness.

QUESTION 2: Thiazide + Laxative Abuse (Hypokalemic Metabolic Alkalosis) (10 marks)

A 67-year-old woman presents with profound muscle weakness. She has a long history of laxative use and was recently started on a thiazide diuretic. Investigations show severe hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

a) What is the most likely biochemical abnormality? (2 marks)

b) Briefly explain how thiazide diuretics cause hypokalemia. (2 marks)

c) Explain how chronic laxative abuse produces metabolic alkalosis. (3 marks)

d) Mention one common ECG change seen in hypokalemia. (2 marks)

e) State the first-line management for severe hypokalemia. (1 mark)

ANSWER 2:

a) Most likely biochemical abnormality: (2 marks)

Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypochloremia - combined effect of thiazide diuretic and chronic laxative abuse leading to severe potassium and chloride depletion.

b) Mechanism of thiazide-induced hypokalemia: (2 marks)

Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, causing:

  • Increased sodium delivery to the collecting duct
  • Enhanced sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC)
  • Increased potassium secretion in exchange for sodium (via ROMK channels)
  • Net result: urinary potassium loss and hypokalemia

c) Mechanism of laxative-induced metabolic alkalosis: (3 marks)

Chronic laxative abuse causes:

  1. Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss initially - laxatives cause diarrhea with loss of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the colon
  2. Volume depletion - chronic diarrhea leads to extracellular fluid loss
  3. Contraction alkalosis - volume depletion stimulates aldosterone secretion, which:
    • Increases renal hydrogen ion excretion (via H+-ATPase in collecting duct)
    • Increases bicarbonate reabsorption in proximal tubule
    • Enhances potassium loss, worsening hypokalemia
  4. Hypokalemia perpetuates alkalosis - low potassium causes intracellular shift of hydrogen ions and increased renal acid excretion

d) Common ECG changes in hypokalemia: (2 marks)

U waves (prominent U waves after T waves, best seen in V2-V3)

Other changes include: ST depression, T wave flattening/inversion, prolonged QT interval, increased P wave amplitude

e) First-line management: (1 mark)

Intravenous potassium chloride replacement - KCl infusion (rate usually 10-20 mmol/hour via peripheral line, or faster via central line in severe cases), with continuous cardiac monitoring.

QUESTION 3: Shock + Acute Abdomen (Severe Metabolic Acidosis) (10 marks)

A 60-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain for 24 hours. He is shocked, has a rigid distended abdomen, and absent femoral pulses. Arterial blood gases show:

  • pH: 7.05
  • PaCO₂: 26.3 mmHg
  • PaO₂: 90 mmHg
  • HCO₃⁻: 7 mmol/L

a) Identify the acid–base disturbance present. (2 marks)

b) Explain the biochemical mechanism producing this metabolic acidosis. (3 marks)

c) Why is the PaCO₂ low in this patient? (2 marks)

d) What is the most likely underlying diagnosis? (2 marks)

e) State two causes of markedly elevated lactate in acute abdomen. (1 mark)

ANSWER 3:

a) Acid-base disturbance: (2 marks)

Severe metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation (partially compensated metabolic acidosis with high anion gap)

b) Biochemical mechanism: (3 marks)

The severe metabolic acidosis results from:

  1. Lactic acidosis - absent femoral pulses indicate vascular insufficiency (likely acute mesenteric ischemia or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm)
  2. Anaerobic metabolism - tissue hypoperfusion forces cells to undergo anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactate instead of CO₂ and water
  3. High anion gap - accumulation of lactate (unmeasured anion) increases the anion gap
  4. Shock state - inadequate tissue oxygen delivery leads to cellular hypoxia and multi-organ dysfunction with acid accumulation

c) Explanation of low PaCO₂: (2 marks)

Respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing) - the low pH stimulates peripheral and central chemoreceptors, triggering hyperventilation to blow off CO₂ and partially correct the pH. The expected compensatory PaCO₂ can be calculated using Winter's formula: Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2) = 1.5 × 7 + 8 = 18.5 mmHg (±2). The measured PaCO₂ of 26.3 mmHg indicates appropriate compensation.

d) Most likely underlying diagnosis: (2 marks)

Acute mesenteric ischemia (due to superior mesenteric artery occlusion/thrombosis)

Evidence supporting this:

  • Absent femoral pulses (peripheral vascular disease)
  • Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination
  • Rigid distended abdomen (bowel necrosis/perforation)
  • Severe lactic acidosis (bowel infarction)
  • Shock state

Alternative diagnosis: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with bowel ischemia

e) Two causes of elevated lactate in acute abdomen: (1 mark)

  1. Bowel ischemia/infarction - mesenteric vascular occlusion
  2. Septic shock - bowel perforation with peritonitis/sepsis

QUESTION 4: Head Injury (Respiratory Alkalosis) (10 marks)

A young woman is admitted unconscious following head trauma. CT scan reveals extensive cerebral contusions. She is hyperventilating at 38 breaths per minute. Arterial blood gas shows:

  • PaCO₂: 29 mmHg
  • HCO₃⁻: 19 mmol/L

a) What acid–base disorder is present? (2 marks)

b) Explain the mechanism of respiratory alkalosis in head injury. (3 marks)

c) Why is the bicarbonate level slightly reduced after 3 days? (2 marks)

d) State one effect of respiratory alkalosis on cerebral blood flow. (2 marks)

e) Which area of the brain regulates the respiratory drive? (1 mark)

ANSWER 4:

a) Acid-base disorder: (2 marks)

Acute respiratory alkalosis with partial metabolic compensation (or respiratory alkalosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis if >3 days)

b) Mechanism of respiratory alkalosis in head injury: (3 marks)

Head injury causes respiratory alkalosis through:

  1. Direct brainstem stimulation - cerebral contusions and increased intracranial pressure (ICP) directly stimulate the respiratory center in the medulla
  2. Central neurogenic hyperventilation - damage to inhibitory pathways or direct stimulation of respiratory centers causes uncontrolled hyperventilation
  3. Compensatory response to increased ICP - hyperventilation may be a physiological attempt to reduce ICP (low CO₂ causes cerebral vasoconstriction, reducing cerebral blood volume and ICP)
  4. Loss of normal respiratory control - disruption of cortical and subcortical modulation of breathing patterns

c) Why bicarbonate is reduced after 3 days: (2 marks)

Metabolic (renal) compensation for chronic respiratory alkalosis. The kidneys respond to sustained hypocapnia by:

  • Decreasing renal hydrogen ion excretion
  • Decreasing bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
  • Increasing bicarbonate excretion in urine

This process takes 2-3 days to become significant, lowering serum bicarbonate by approximately 4-5 mmol/L for every 10 mmHg decrease in PaCO₂.

d) Effect on cerebral blood flow: (2 marks)

Cerebral vasoconstriction with reduced cerebral blood flow (CBF)

Mechanism: Low PaCO₂ increases pH in the cerebrospinal fluid and brain extracellular fluid, causing arteriolar smooth muscle constriction. For every 1 mmHg decrease in PaCO₂, cerebral blood flow decreases by approximately 2-4%. This can be therapeutic in acute head injury (reduces ICP) but excessive hyperventilation can cause cerebral ischemia.

e) Brain area regulating respiratory drive: (1 mark)

Medulla oblongata (specifically the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups/centers in the medullary reticular formation)

SECTION B: STANDARD SHORT ANSWER QUESTIONS (50 Marks Total)

QUESTION 5: Quality Control in Clinical Chemistry (10 marks)

a) Define the following terms as used in quality control: (4 marks)

i) Accuracy
ii) Precision
iii) Sensitivity
iv) Specificity

b) Explain the difference between internal and external quality control. (3 marks)

c) List three pre-analytical factors that can affect biochemical test results. (3 marks)

ANSWER 5:

a) Definitions: (4 marks)

i) Accuracy – The closeness of a measured value to the true or accepted reference value. It indicates how correct a measurement is and reflects systematic error or bias.

ii) Precision – The reproducibility or consistency of repeated measurements of the same sample. It shows how close multiple measurements are to each other and reflects random error.

iii) Sensitivity – The ability of a test to correctly identify individuals with a disease (true positive rate).
Formula: Sensitivity = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives) × 100

iv) Specificity – The ability of a test to correctly identify individuals without a disease (true negative rate).
Formula: Specificity = True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Positives) × 100

b) Difference between Internal and External Quality Control: (3 marks)

Internal Quality Control (IQC):

  • Performed within the laboratory on a daily basis
  • Uses control materials (known concentrations) analyzed alongside patient samples
  • Monitors day-to-day precision and detects analytical errors
  • Ensures consistency and reliability of results over time
  • Uses Levy-Jennings charts and Westgard rules

External Quality Control (EQC/EQAS):

  • Involves inter-laboratory comparison programs (proficiency testing)
  • Identical samples distributed to multiple laboratories
  • Assesses accuracy and compares laboratory performance with peers
  • Identifies systematic errors, biases, and method-related problems
  • Conducted periodically (monthly/quarterly)

c) Three Pre-analytical Factors: (3 marks)

  1. Patient preparation – Fasting status, exercise, posture, stress, circadian rhythm, diet, medication, alcohol consumption
  2. Specimen collection – Incorrect tube type/order of draw, hemolysis, improper timing, prolonged tourniquet application, contamination from IV lines
  3. Specimen handling/storage – Improper temperature, delayed processing, exposure to light, inadequate mixing, evaporation, microbial contamination

QUESTION 6: Acid-Base Balance (10 marks)

a) Calculate the anion gap for a patient with the following results: (3 marks)

  • Sodium: 138 mmol/L
  • Chloride: 98 mmol/L
  • Bicarbonate: 12 mmol/L

b) Interpret the acid-base status of a patient with these blood gas results: (4 marks)

  • pH: 7.28
  • PaCO₂: 30 mmHg
  • HCO₃⁻: 14 mmol/L

c) List three causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis. (3 marks)

[hidden]

ANSWER 6:

a) Anion Gap Calculation: (3 marks)

Formula: Anion Gap = Na⁺ – (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)

Anion Gap = 138 – (98 + 12)
Anion Gap = 138 – 110
Anion Gap = 28 mmol/L

Normal range: 8-12 mmol/L (or 10-14 mmol/L depending on method)
Interpretation: Markedly elevated anion gap, consistent with high anion gap metabolic acidosis

b) Acid-Base Interpretation: (4 marks)

Primary disorder: Metabolic Acidosis

  • pH 7.28 (acidotic, normal: 7.35-7.45)
  • HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L (low, normal: 22-26 mmol/L)
  • PaCO₂ 30 mmHg (low, normal: 35-45 mmHg)

Compensation: Appropriate respiratory compensation

The low PaCO₂ indicates hyperventilation to eliminate CO₂.

Expected compensatory PaCO₂ using Winter's formula:
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2)
= 1.5 × 14 + 8
= 29 mmHg (±2) = 27-31 mmHg

Measured PaCO₂ (30 mmHg) falls within expected range, confirming appropriate respiratory compensation.

Conclusion: Partially compensated high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation

c) Three Causes of High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (MUDPILES): (3 marks)

  1. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) – accumulation of ketoacids (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) due to insulin deficiency
  2. Lactic Acidosis – from tissue hypoxia (Type A: sepsis, shock, severe hypoxemia) or metabolic causes (Type B: metformin, malignancy)
  3. Renal Failure (Uremia) – accumulation of sulfates, phosphates, and organic acids due to decreased GFR

Other causes: Methanol, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates (aspirin), Propylene glycol, Isoniazid

QUESTION 7: Lipid Profile Interpretation (10 marks)

A 50-year-old male patient presents with the following lipid profile results:

  • Total Cholesterol: 280 mg/dL
  • LDL-Cholesterol: 190 mg/dL
  • HDL-Cholesterol: 35 mg/dL
  • Triglycerides: 275 mg/dL

a) Interpret these results and state the lipid abnormalities present. (4 marks)

b) Calculate the VLDL cholesterol level. (2 marks)

c) What is the cardiovascular risk category for this patient? (2 marks)

d) Outline two lifestyle modifications you would recommend. (2 marks)

ANSWER 7:

a) Interpretation and Lipid Abnormalities: (4 marks)

  1. Hypercholesterolemia – Total cholesterol 280 mg/dL (Desirable: <200 mg/dL; High: ≥240 mg/dL)
  2. Elevated LDL-Cholesterol – LDL 190 mg/dL (Optimal: <100 mg/dL; Very high: ≥190 mg/dL) - major atherogenic lipoprotein
  3. Low HDL-Cholesterol – HDL 35 mg/dL (Normal for males: ≥40 mg/dL; Low: <40 mg/dL) - loss of cardioprotective effect
  4. Hypertriglyceridemia – Triglycerides 275 mg/dL (Normal: <150 mg/dL; High: 200-499 mg/dL)

Overall diagnosis: Mixed dyslipidemia/Combined hyperlipidemia (Type IIb hyperlipoproteinemia) - both cholesterol and triglycerides elevated

b) VLDL Cholesterol Calculation: (2 marks)

Formula: VLDL = Triglycerides / 5 (Friedewald equation, valid when TG <400 mg/dL)

VLDL = 275 / 5
VLDL = 55 mg/dL

(Normal VLDL: 5-40 mg/dL) - This is elevated

Verification: Total Cholesterol = LDL + HDL + VLDL
280 = 190 + 35 + 55 ✓

c) Cardiovascular Risk Category: (2 marks)

VERY HIGH RISK for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD)

Risk factors present:

  • LDL ≥190 mg/dL (automatic high-risk category requiring statin therapy)
  • Low HDL <40 mg/dL (independent risk factor)
  • Elevated triglycerides >200 mg/dL
  • Multiple lipid abnormalities (atherogenic dyslipidemia)
  • Male gender and age 50 years

10-year ASCVD risk likely >20%

d) Two Lifestyle Modifications: (2 marks)

  1. Dietary modifications:
    • Adopt Mediterranean or DASH diet
    • Reduce saturated fat to <7% of total calories
    • Eliminate trans fats
    • Increase soluble fiber (10-25 g/day from oats, beans, vegetables)
    • Increase omega-3 fatty acids (fatty fish 2× weekly)
    • Limit dietary cholesterol <200 mg/day
    • Reduce simple carbohydrates (helps lower triglycerides)
  2. Regular physical activity:
    • At least 150 minutes/week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (or 75 min vigorous)
    • Weight reduction if overweight (target BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m²)
    • Exercise reduces triglycerides, increases HDL, and improves insulin sensitivity

Additional recommendations: Smoking cessation (if applicable), alcohol moderation, stress management

QUESTION 8: Liver Function Tests (10 marks)

a) Differentiate between hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns of liver enzyme elevation. (4 marks)

b) A patient has the following results:

  • Total Bilirubin: 8.0 mg/dL
  • Direct Bilirubin: 6.5 mg/dL
  • ALT: 350 U/L
  • AST: 280 U/L
  • ALP: 140 U/L

Classify the type of jaundice and suggest two possible causes. (4 marks)

c) What is the significance of an AST/ALT ratio >2:1? (2 marks)

ANSWER 8:

a) Hepatocellular vs. Cholestatic Patterns: (4 marks)

HEPATOCELLULAR PATTERN (Hepatocyte injury):

  • Enzyme elevation: ALT and AST markedly elevated (>5-10× upper limit of normal)
  • Enzyme ratio: ALT typically > AST (except in alcoholic liver disease)
  • ALP elevation: Normal or mildly elevated (<2× ULN)
  • GGT: Normal or mildly elevated
  • Pathophysiology: Direct hepatocyte damage with intracellular enzyme leakage
  • Examples: Viral hepatitis (A, B, C), drug-induced hepatitis (acetaminophen, isoniazid), ischemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease

CHOLESTATIC PATTERN (Bile duct obstruction):

  • Enzyme elevation: ALP and GGT markedly elevated (>3-4× ULN)
  • ALT/AST: Normal or mildly elevated (<5× ULN)
  • Bilirubin: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin predominantly elevated
  • Pathophysiology: Impaired bile flow or bile duct obstruction
  • Examples: Extrahepatic: gallstones, pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma; Intrahepatic: primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, drug-induced cholestasis

b) Classification and Causes: (4 marks)

Type of Jaundice: HEPATOCELLULAR (HEPATIC) JAUNDICE

Evidence:

  • High total bilirubin: 8.0 mg/dL (Normal: 0.3-1.2 mg/dL)
  • Direct bilirubin predominance: 6.5/8.0 = 81% of total
    • 50% direct bilirubin indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Markedly elevated transaminases: ALT 350 U/L, AST 280 U/L (hepatocellular pattern)
  • ALT > AST ratio (350:280 = 1.25:1)
  • ALP relatively normal: 140 U/L (only mildly elevated, <2× normal)

This pattern indicates hepatocyte dysfunction with impaired bilirubin excretion into bile.

Two Possible Causes:

  1. Acute Viral Hepatitis (Hepatitis A, B, C, or E)
    • Causes direct hepatocyte necrosis and inflammation
    • Impairs bilirubin conjugation and excretion
    • ALT typically higher than AST
    • Associated with systemic symptoms (fever, malaise)
  2. Drug-Induced Liver Injury (DILI)
    • Hepatotoxic drugs: acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose, isoniazid, valproate, NSAIDs, statins
    • Can be predictable (dose-dependent) or idiosyncratic
    • May present as hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed pattern

Other causes: Autoimmune hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), alcoholic hepatitis, Wilson's disease

c) Significance of AST/ALT Ratio >2:1: (2 marks)

Highly suggestive of ALCOHOLIC LIVER DISEASE

Explanation:

  • AST/ALT ratio >2:1 has approximately 70% specificity for alcoholic liver disease
  • AST/ALT ratio >3:1 is nearly pathognomonic for alcoholic hepatitis
  • Mechanism:
    • Chronic alcohol consumption depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (vitamin B6), a cofactor required for ALT synthesis
    • This leads to disproportionate reduction in ALT activity
    • Alcohol also causes mitochondrial damage, releasing mitochondrial AST (mAST) into circulation
    • AST is also less specific to liver (found in heart, muscle, kidney, brain), so may be elevated from other alcohol-related organ damage
  • However, both AST and ALT are usually <300 U/L in alcoholic hepatitis (unlike viral hepatitis where levels can exceed 1000 U/L)

QUESTION 9: Cardiac Biomarkers (10 marks)

a) Explain the pattern of cardiac biomarker elevation following acute myocardial infarction for: (6 marks)

i) Troponin (cTnI or cTnT)
ii) CK-MB
iii) Myoglobin

b) What is the clinical significance of elevated BNP (B-type Natriuretic Peptide)? (4 marks)

ANSWER 9:

a) Pattern of Cardiac Biomarker Elevation in AMI: (6 marks)

i) Troponin (cTnI or cTnT):

  • Rise: Begins 3-4 hours after myocardial injury, detectable by high-sensitivity assays within 1-2 hours
  • Peak: 12-24 hours after onset of chest pain
  • Duration: Remains elevated for 7-14 days (cTnI) or 10-14 days (cTnT)
  • Specificity: Highly specific for myocardial injury (gold standard for AMI diagnosis)
  • Sensitivity: High-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn) can detect very small amounts of myocardial damage
  • Clinical use: Diagnostic for AMI, prognostic indicator, useful for detecting reinfarction (though long elevation period can complicate this)

ii) CK-MB (Creatine Kinase-MB):

  • Rise: Begins 4-6 hours after myocardial injury
  • Peak: 12-24 hours after onset
  • Duration: Returns to normal within 48-72 hours
  • Specificity: Less specific than troponin (also found in skeletal muscle, though in smaller amounts)
  • Clinical use: Useful for detecting early reinfarction due to shorter elevation period; can calculate relative index (CK-MB/total CK × 100; >5% suggests cardiac origin)
  • Advantage: Shorter duration makes it better for detecting reinfarction in first 72 hours

iii) Myoglobin:

  • Rise: Earliest biomarker, rises within 1-2 hours after myocardial injury
  • Peak: 6-12 hours after onset
  • Duration: Returns to normal within 24 hours
  • Specificity: Very low specificity (released from any muscle injury - cardiac or skeletal)
  • Sensitivity: High sensitivity for early detection but poor positive predictive value
  • Clinical use: Useful for early rule-out of AMI due to rapid kinetics; negative myoglobin 4-8 hours after symptom onset helps exclude MI

Summary table:

b) Clinical Significance of Elevated BNP: (4 marks)

BNP (B-type Natriuretic Peptide) is released from cardiac ventricular myocytes in response to ventricular wall stretch and pressure overload.

Clinical Significance:

  1. Diagnosis of Heart Failure:
    • Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP indicates heart failure (systolic or diastolic dysfunction)
    • BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL suggests heart failure
    • Helps differentiate cardiac dyspnea from pulmonary causes of dyspnea
    • High negative predictive value: normal BNP effectively rules out heart failure
  2. Severity assessment and prognosis:
    • BNP level correlates with NYHA functional class
    • Higher levels indicate worse ventricular function and prognosis
    • Useful for risk stratification in acute coronary syndromes
    • Elevated BNP in AMI indicates ventricular dysfunction and higher mortality risk
  3. Monitoring treatment response:
    • Declining BNP levels indicate response to heart failure therapy
    • Persistently elevated or rising BNP despite treatment suggests poor response
    • Guides therapy adjustment (diuretics, ACE inhibitors, etc.)
  4. Screening in at-risk populations:
    • Identifies asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction
    • Useful in hypertension, diabetes, post-MI patients
    • May detect subclinical heart failure

Note: BNP can be elevated in other conditions: renal failure, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, advanced age. Obesity decreases BNP levels.

SECTION C: CLINICAL BIOCHEMISTRY INVESTIGATIONS (10 Marks)

QUESTION 10: Diagnostic Test Panels (10 marks)

For each of the following clinical conditions, list the key biochemical investigations you would request:

a) Suspected glomerulonephritis (3 marks)

b) Suspected rhabdomyolysis (2 marks)

c) Suspected hemolytic anemia (2 marks)

d) Suspected multiple myeloma (3 marks)

ANSWER 10:

a) Glomerulonephritis Investigation Panel: (3 marks)

Immunological tests:

  • Complement levels: C3, C4 (low in post-infectious GN, lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinemia; normal in IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease)
  • Autoantibodies:
    • ANA (Antinuclear antibody) - for systemic lupus erythematosus
    • Anti-dsDNA (anti-double stranded DNA) - specific for lupus nephritis
    • ANCA (Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) - for vasculitis-associated GN (Wegener's, microscopic polyangiitis)
    • Anti-GBM antibodies - for Goodpasture syndrome/anti-GBM disease
  • Cryoglobulins - for cryoglobulinemic GN
  • Hepatitis serology: HBsAg, anti-HCV (hepatitis B and C can cause membranoproliferative GN)
  • ASO titer (Anti-Streptolysin O) - for post-streptococcal GN

Basic renal function tests:

  • Serum creatinine, urea, eGFR
  • Urinalysis: proteinuria, hematuria, RBC casts
  • 24-hour urine protein quantification

b) Rhabdomyolysis Investigation Panel: (2 marks)

Muscle injury markers:

  • Creatine Kinase (CK) - markedly elevated (often >5,000-10,000 U/L, can exceed 100,000 U/L)
  • Myoglobin: serum and urine myoglobin (causes tea-colored/dark urine)

Complications monitoring:

  • Renal function: Urea, creatinine, eGFR (monitor for acute kidney injury)
  • Electrolytes:
    • Potassium (hyperkalemia from muscle cell lysis)
    • Phosphate (hyperphosphatemia)
    • Calcium (hypocalcemia initially, then hypercalcemia during recovery)
  • Uric acid - elevated due to purine release from damaged muscle
  • Liver enzymes: AST, ALT (may be elevated)
  • Urinalysis: myoglobinuria (positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy)

c) Hemolytic Anemia Investigation Panel: (2 marks)

Markers of hemolysis:

  • LDH (Lactate Dehydrogenase) - markedly elevated (released from RBCs)
  • Haptoglobin - decreased or absent (binds free hemoglobin)
  • Indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin - elevated (from hemoglobin breakdown)
  • Serum free hemoglobin - elevated in intravascular hemolysis

Blood smear examination:

  • Peripheral blood smear - spherocytes, schistocytes, fragmented RBCs, polychromasia

Additional tests:

  • Reticulocyte count - elevated (compensatory bone marrow response)
  • Direct Coombs test (DAT) - positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Urinalysis: hemoglobinuria, urobilinogen

d) Multiple Myeloma Investigation Panel: (3 marks)

Protein studies:

  • Serum Protein Electrophoresis (SPEP) - detects M-spike (monoclonal protein band)
  • Urine Protein Electrophoresis (UPEP) - detects Bence Jones proteins (light chains)
  • Serum Free Light Chains (FLC) - κ (kappa) and λ (lambda) with κ/λ ratio
    • Abnormal ratio (<0.26 or >1.65) indicates clonal plasma cell disorder
  • Immunofixation electrophoresis - identifies the specific immunoglobulin type (IgG, IgA, IgD, IgM)
  • Quantitative immunoglobulins - IgG, IgA, IgM (one elevated, others suppressed)

Markers of disease burden and complications:

  • Calcium - hypercalcemia (from bone destruction)
  • Renal function: Creatinine, urea, eGFR (myeloma kidney/cast nephropathy)
  • Complete Blood Count - anemia (normocytic, normochromic)
  • β2-microglobulin - prognostic marker (elevated indicates higher tumor burden)
  • Albumin - often low (prognostic factor)
  • LDH - may be elevated (prognostic marker)

Bone involvement:

  • Skeletal survey/imaging (not biochemical, but essential)
  • Alkaline phosphatase - usually normal or low (distinguishes from metastatic bone disease)

END OF EXAMINATION

APPENDIX: QUICK REFERENCE FORMULAS

Anion Gap

Anion Gap = Na⁺ - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)

  • Normal: 8-12 mmol/L (or 10-14 mmol/L depending on method)

Osmolal Gap

Calculated Osmolality = 2(Na⁺) + Glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 Osmolal Gap = Measured Osmolality - Calculated Osmolality

  • Normal: <10 mOsm/kg

Corrected Calcium

Corrected Ca²⁺ = Measured Ca²⁺ + 0.8 × (4.0 - Albumin)

  • Use when albumin is abnormal

Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault)

CrCl = [(140 - age) × weight (kg)] / (72 × SCr)

  • Multiply by 0.85 for females

Winter's Formula (Expected PaCO₂ in Metabolic Acidosis)

Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2)

Friedewald Equation

LDL = Total Cholesterol - HDL - (Triglycerides/5)

  • Valid only when TG <400 mg/dL

Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)

FENa = [(UNa × PCr) / (PNa × UCr)] × 100

  • <1%: Pre-renal azotemia
  • 2%: Acute tubular necrosis

PASS MARK: 50/100

Time Allowed: 3 Hours

Title: QUALITY CONTROL IN CLINICAL CHEMISTRY
Content:
OVERVIEW

Quality Control (QC) in clinical chemistry ensures accuracy and reliability of laboratory test results through systematic monitoring of analytical methods and instruments.

Key Goal: Maintain high standards of laboratory testing to support accurate clinical decision-making and patient care.

INTERNAL QUALITY CONTROL (IQC)

Purpose

Monitor and maintain accuracy and precision within the laboratory on a day-to-day basis.

Key Components

1. Control Samples

  • Positive Controls
    • Contain known analyte concentration
    • Verify detection capability
  • Negative Controls
    • No analyte present
    • Ensure no false positives
  • Types:
    • Commercial controls (pre-prepared)
    • In-house controls (laboratory-prepared)

2. Control Charts

  • Levey-Jennings Charts
    • Plot control results over time
    • Detect trends and shifts in performance
  • Westgard Rules
    • Statistical rules to identify problems
    • Signal when corrective action needed

3. Frequency of Testing

  • Run with each batch of patient samples
  • At defined intervals based on:
    • Test volume
    • Test variability
    • Criticality of test

4. Calibration

  • Regular instrument calibration using standard reference materials
  • Create and maintain calibration curves
  • Relate instrument response to analyte concentration

5. Maintenance and Troubleshooting

  • Scheduled Maintenance
    • Prevent equipment failures
    • Ensure consistent performance
  • Troubleshooting
    • Investigate when QC falls outside acceptable limits
    • Resolve issues promptly

6. Documentation

  • Accurate records of:
    • QC procedures
    • Test results
    • Corrective actions taken
  • Maintain records of:
    • Calibration data
    • Control results
    • Maintenance activities

7. Statistical Analysis

  • Quality Metrics:
    • Mean (average value)
    • Standard Deviation (precision)
    • Coefficient of Variation (relative precision)
  • Trend Analysis
    • Identify patterns over time
    • Detect underlying problems early

EXTERNAL QUALITY ASSESSMENT (EQA)

Purpose

Compare laboratory performance with other laboratories and reference standards.

Components

Proficiency Testing

  • Analyze same samples as other laboratories
  • Compare results with peers or reference values
  • Identify discrepancies

Performance Evaluation

  • Identify issues with analytical procedures
  • Provides opportunities for improvement
  • Validates accuracy and reliability

QUALITY ASSURANCE (QA)

Overview

Broader than QC - encompasses ALL aspects of laboratory operations, not just testing.

11 Key Components

1. Quality Management System (QMS)

  • Development of policies and procedures
  • Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)
  • Comprehensive quality manual

2. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs)

  • Ensure consistency and standardization
  • Guide all laboratory processes
  • Regular review and updates

3. Training and Competency

  • Training programs on:
    • Techniques and equipment
    • Quality practices
    • Troubleshooting
  • Regular competency assessments

4. Equipment and Reagent Management

  • Regular calibration and maintenance
  • Monitor reagent quality and stability
  • Prevent errors from expired materials

5. Internal Audits

  • Regular audits to assess compliance
  • Identify areas for improvement
  • Implement corrective actions based on findings

6. External Quality Assessment

  • Participation in proficiency testing programs
  • Compare performance with other labs

7. Performance Monitoring and Improvement

  • Analyze data from QC, audits, and EQA
  • Identify trends and potential issues
  • Continuous improvement initiatives

8. Regulatory Compliance

  • Follow standards:
    • CLIA (Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments)
    • CAP (College of American Pathologists)
    • CLSI (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute)
    • ISO (International Standards)
  • Obtain and maintain accreditation

9. Risk Management

  • Assess potential risks to testing quality
  • Implement mitigation strategies
  • Develop contingency plans

10. Patient Safety and Confidentiality

  • Error reporting systems
  • Analyze errors and near-misses
  • Ensure confidentiality of patient information
  • Comply with privacy regulations

11. Customer Feedback

  • Gather feedback from healthcare providers and patients
  • Use feedback for service improvement
  • Address concerns promptly

THREE PHASES OF QUALITY CONTROL

PHASE 1: PRE-ANALYTICAL PHASE

Everything that occurs BEFORE sample analysis

Sample Collection

  • Patient preparation (e.g., fasting requirements)
  • Correct collection technique and equipment
  • Appropriate sample type and volume

Sample Handling and Transport

  • Proper storage at correct temperature
  • Timely transport to laboratory
  • Proper labeling for identification
  • Prevent sample degradation

Sample Processing

  • Centrifugation, separation, aliquoting
  • Integrity checks:
    • Not hemolyzed
    • Not clotted
    • Not compromised

Documentation

  • Accurate records of:
    • Sample collection
    • Handling procedures
    • Processing steps

Note: Pre-analytical phase accounts for majority of laboratory errors

PHASE 2: ANALYTICAL PHASE

The actual testing and measurement process

Instrument Calibration and Maintenance

  • Regular calibration with standards
  • Routine maintenance and servicing
  • Prevent malfunctions

Quality Control

  • Run control samples to verify methods
  • Ensure results within acceptable ranges
  • Troubleshoot issues immediately

Analytical Procedures

  • Use standardized procedures and reagents
  • Method validation for accuracy and precision
  • Follow protocols strictly

Data Accuracy and Precision

  • Monitor for errors and outliers
  • Accurate data recording
  • Verify calculations

PHASE 3: POST-ANALYTICAL PHASE

After results are generated until reported

Result Validation

  • Verify accuracy before reporting
  • Review for consistency
  • Assess clinical relevance

Result Reporting

  • Timely reporting to healthcare providers
  • Clear interpretation with:
    • Appropriate units
    • Reference ranges
  • Critical value alerts

Data Management

  • Detailed documentation of results
  • Secure storage and archiving
  • Maintain records for required period

Communication

  • Effective communication of results
  • Address queries and concerns
  • Coordinate follow-up actions

Error Reporting

  • Report and investigate all errors
  • Root cause analysis
  • Implement preventive measures

Continuous Improvement

  • Evaluate entire testing process
  • Identify areas for optimization
  • Implement improvements based on findings

QUALITY CONTROL MATERIALS

1. Control Samples

  • Commercial Controls: Pre-prepared with known concentrations
  • In-House Controls: Laboratory-prepared materials

2. Calibration Standards

  • Primary Standards: Highly pure substances with definitive concentrations
  • Secondary Standards: Prepared from primary standards or certified materials

3. Proficiency Testing Materials

  • External proficiency testing samples
  • Blind samples for unbiased evaluation

4. Reference Materials

  • Certified Reference Materials (CRMs): Well-documented, certified values
  • Reference Intervals: Established from characterized populations

5. Control Charts

  • Levey-Jennings Charts: Plot results over time
  • Westgard Rules: Statistical criteria for identifying problems

6. Internal QC Materials

  • Daily or batch controls
  • Multi-level controls (different concentrations across analyte range)

7. External QC Materials

  • External proficiency testing materials
  • Compare performance with other laboratories

8. Stability Testing Materials

  • Determine shelf-life of reagents and controls
  • Test stability under various conditions

9. Reagent and Instrument Checks

  • Monitor reagent quality continuously
  • Regular instrument performance checks
  • Verify proper operation

10. Documentation

  • QC Logs: Control results, calibration data, maintenance activities
  • Reports: Proficiency testing results, corrective actions, performance evaluations

BEST PRACTICES

✓ Follow manufacturer instructions for all QC materials and equipment

✓ Establish regular monitoring schedule for controls and calibration

✓ Review and analyze QC data regularly - don't just record

✓ Train staff thoroughly on proper use and interpretation

✓ Maintain consistency and standardization across all processes

✓ Document everything - procedures, results, and actions

✓ Take prompt corrective action when issues arise

✓ Participate in proficiency testing programs

✓ Ensure regulatory compliance at all times

✓ Implement continuous improvement based on data

KEY REGULATORY BODIES

WHY QUALITY CONTROL MATTERS

Patient Care

✓ Ensures accurate patient results
✓ Supports correct clinical decision-making
✓ Improves patient outcomes

Laboratory Standards

✓ Prevents medical errors
✓ Maintains laboratory credibility
✓ Demonstrates professional competence

Regulatory Compliance

✓ Meets regulatory requirements
✓ Maintains accreditation
✓ Ensures legal compliance

KEY TAKEAWAYS

  1. QC is ongoing - not a one-time activity but continuous monitoring
  2. All three phases matter - pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical
  3. Documentation is essential - for traceability and compliance
  4. Errors must be addressed immediately - with root cause analysis
  5. QA encompasses QC - broader scope covering all operations
  6. Staff competency is critical - regular training and assessment needed
  7. External validation important - through proficiency testing
  8. Patient safety is paramount - ultimate goal of all QC activities

End of Notes

Prepared for: Clinical Chemistry Students
Source: Dr. Lilian Bosire, MKU Lecturer, Pathologist

Title: Analytical Techniques & Laboratory Principles
Content:
ANALYTICAL TECHNIQUES IN CLINICAL CHEMISTRY

Analytical techniques are essential tools for detecting, quantifying, and characterizing substances in biochemical analyses. These methods allow laboratories to identify what's in a sample and how much is present.

1. SPECTROPHOTOMETRY

Measures how much light a sample absorbs at specific wavelengths.

Main Types:

  • UV-Visible Spectrophotometry - Works in the 200-800 nm range
  • Fluorescence Spectrophotometry - Measures light emitted after the sample is excited

Common Uses: Measuring nucleic acids, proteins, and metabolites

2. CHROMATOGRAPHY

Separates different compounds in a mixture based on how they move between two phases.

Main Types:

  • Gas Chromatography (GC) - For gases and volatile compounds
  • Liquid Chromatography (LC/HPLC/UHPLC) - For non-volatile compounds
  • Thin-Layer Chromatography (TLC) - Uses a coated plate for separation

Common Uses: Purifying substances, identifying what's in a mixture, measuring amounts

3. ELECTROPHORESIS

Separates charged particles using an electric field. Particles move based on their size and charge.

Main Types:

  • Agarose Gel - Best for DNA and RNA
  • PAGE - Best for proteins and nucleic acids
  • Capillary Electrophoresis - High-resolution separation in a tiny tube

Common Uses: DNA sequencing, analyzing proteins, identifying different forms of proteins

4. MASS SPECTROMETRY (MS)

Identifies molecules by measuring their mass-to-charge ratio.

Main Types:

  • Quadrupole MS - Uses electric fields to sort ions
  • Time-of-Flight (TOF) - Measures how long ions take to travel
  • Tandem MS (MS/MS) - Multiple rounds of analysis for detailed information

Common Uses: Identifying unknown compounds, measuring biomolecules, studying protein structure

5. IMMUNOASSAYS

Uses the specific binding between antibodies and antigens to detect substances.

Main Types:

  • ELISA - Uses enzymes attached to antibodies
  • Immunofluorescence - Uses fluorescent tags
  • Western Blotting - Combines separation and antibody detection

Common Uses: Detecting hormones, antibodies, and other proteins

6. OTHER IMPORTANT TECHNIQUES

Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS)

  • Measures how free atoms absorb light
  • Used to measure trace metals in blood or water

Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR)

  • Uses magnetic fields to study atomic structure
  • Determines molecular structure, especially in drug development

Electrochemical Methods

  • Measures electrical properties like voltage and current
  • Used in glucose meters and ion detection

Gravimetry

  • Simply weighs substances to determine concentration
  • Used for metals and inorganic compounds

Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR)

  • Detects when molecules bind to a surface
  • Studies how proteins interact with each other or with DNA

LABORATORY AUTOMATION

Automation means using machines and technology to do repetitive lab work with minimal human involvement. This makes labs faster, more accurate, and more efficient.

WHY AUTOMATE?

Key Benefits:

  • Reduces human errors
  • Processes many samples at once
  • Saves time for staff to focus on complex work
  • Produces consistent, reliable results
  • Keeps digital records automatically
  • Safer for lab workers

CORE PRINCIPLES OF AUTOMATION

Standardization

  • Every test is done the exact same way every time
  • Follows set protocols automatically
  • Results are consistent and reliable

Precision and Accuracy

  • Machines measure more precisely than humans
  • Less chance of errors in pipetting or mixing
  • Same results when repeated

Efficiency

  • Can handle multiple samples simultaneously
  • Much faster than manual methods
  • Increases how many tests can be done per day

Integration

  • Different machines connect and share data
  • Sample goes from preparation through testing to results automatically
  • No need to manually transfer information

Data Management

  • Creates digital records of everything
  • Easy to track and review
  • Flags errors automatically

Quality Control

  • Built-in checks ensure equipment is working correctly
  • Monitors reagents and calibration automatically
  • Maintains consistent conditions

Safety

  • Reduces exposure to dangerous chemicals
  • Prevents repetitive strain injuries
  • Maintains controlled environments

Flexibility

  • Can be programmed for different types of tests
  • Adjusts to handle more or fewer samples as needed

Cost Efficiency

  • Reduces need for manual labor over time
  • Uses reagents more efficiently
  • Less waste

ADVANCED AUTOMATION TECHNOLOGIES

Robotics

  • Handles samples automatically
  • Dispenses precise liquid amounts
  • Sorts and organizes plates

Artificial Intelligence (AI)

  • Analyzes data and finds patterns
  • Helps make decisions
  • Improves accuracy

Internet of Things (IoT)

  • Allows remote monitoring of equipment
  • Collects data automatically
  • Manages multiple systems from one location

BASIC STATISTICS FOR LABORATORY WORK

Statistics help us understand if our test results are reliable and meaningful.

PRECISION VS ACCURACY

Precision (Repeatability)

  • How close multiple measurements of the same sample are to each other
  • A precise test gives very similar results each time
  • Measured by Standard Deviation (SD) and Coefficient of Variation (CV)
  • Lower numbers mean better precision

Example: Testing the same blood sample 5 times and getting: 95, 96, 95, 96, 95 mg/dL is precise

Accuracy (Correctness)

  • How close a measurement is to the true value
  • An accurate test gives results close to what the real value is
  • Measured by bias and error rate

Example: If blood glucose is actually 100 mg/dL and the test reads 99 mg/dL, it's accurate

Key Point: A test can be precise but not accurate (consistently wrong), or accurate but not precise (right on average but scattered results). Best tests are both precise AND accurate.

PREDICTIVE VALUES

These tell us how reliable a test result is.

Positive Predictive Value (PPV)

  • If the test says "positive," what's the chance the person actually has the disease?
  • Higher PPV means fewer false alarms

Negative Predictive Value (NPV)

  • If the test says "negative," what's the chance the person is truly disease-free?
  • Higher NPV means we're not missing cases

What Affects These Values:
